Unattached, yet moving among men as though attached; free of clinging, his bonds undone; the same toward foe and friend—he, O lord of the earth, is truly the liberated one.
Shaven-headed and clad in ochre robes, they wander forth for the sake of alms, bound by snares of many kinds, gathering up the empty bait of the world.
Those witless men who, forsaking the threefold Veda and their livelihood, abandon even their sons, yet still accept the three-staved support and a garment—
know that the ochre robe upon one not purged of passion is but a means to getting; the shaven heads of these flaunters of piety, I hold, serve only to win them a living.
Sustaining holy men—the naked, the shaven, and the matted-haired—with ochre robes, deerskins, and bark garments, O great king, master your senses and win the worlds.
He who day after day, as of old, establishes the sacred fires, serves the needs of his elders, and offers sacrifices with their gifts of cattle—who, then, is more righteous than he?
King Janaka is sung of in this world as one who knows the truth of things; yet even he was once overcome by delusion—do not you fall under the sway of delusion.
Thus is the duty followed by men ever devoted to giving, endowed with the virtue of compassion, and free of desire and wrath—
"protecting our subjects and holding fast to the highest giving, devoted to the brāhmaṇas and speakers of truth, we shall attain the worlds we long for."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I know the scriptures, my dear brother, both the lower and the higher; I know too the twofold word of the Veda—"perform action" and "renounce action."
The scriptures are tangled and embroidered over with conflicting reasons; and the sure conclusion, of whatever measure it be, I know in due form.
But you are versed in weapons alone, faithful to the vow of a warrior; you are in no way able to penetrate the meaning of the scriptures to its very truth.
Even by one who discerns the subtle meaning of scripture and is skilled in the settled truths of dharma, I should not be addressed thus—if indeed you truly perceive dharma.
Yet the words you have spoken, resting on a brother's affection, are reasonable and fitting, O son of Kuntī; for that I am pleased with you, Arjuna.
In all the duties of war and in every skill of action, no one your equal is to be found in the three worlds.
But where the subtle teaching of dharma is concerned, that ground is hard for you to cross over, Dhanaṃjaya; you ought not to call my understanding into doubt.
You know only the science of war; you have not waited upon the elders, and you do not grasp the considered conclusions of those who know matters both in brief and at length.

Austerity, renunciation, and right observance—such is the settled view of the wise, dear one; each of these is higher and more excellent than the last, and this is the path that leads to the supreme good.
But you do not hold to this, Pārtha; you say there is nothing higher than wealth. On this I shall set you right, showing how wealth is not the foremost thing.
For righteous folk are seen given to austerity and to the study of sacred lore, sages joined to austerity, whose worlds are everlasting.
Steadfast men whose beards had not yet grown, and others dwelling in the forest, countless and wholly without wealth, have gone to heaven by the study of the sacred word.
By the northern path the noble ones, through the restraint of the senses, casting off the darkness born of unwisdom, have reached the worlds of those who renounce.
But that shining path you behold to the south—these are the worlds of men of ritual action, who have resorted to the cremation grounds.
But indescribable is that goal which the seekers of liberation behold; therefore renunciation is held the foremost good, though it is hard to make known.
Following the scriptures, the wise have taken their stand, asking 'might it be thus here, might it be thus,' in their longing to discern the essence from the dross.
Going beyond the doctrines of the Vedas and the forest treatises, they split open the plantain trunk—and found in it no pith at all.
Then, by sheer process of exclusion, within the body made of the five elements they declared, by inference from its signs, a Self joined with desire and aversion.
He cannot be grasped by the eye, and That cannot be pointed out by speech; impelled by the force of past deeds, He revolves through living beings.
Having made the mind range over what is good and curbed all craving, casting off the unbroken stream of action, one may become free of every support and happy.
When such is the path, attainable only by subtle insight and trodden by the good, how, Arjuna, can you praise wealth, which is so full of harm?
For thus do men learned in the ancient scriptures see it, O Bhārata—men ever devoted to ritual acts, to giving, to sacrifice, and to works.
There are men hard to turn aside, learned and full of arguments, yet fixed in the lore they first heard, deluded, declaring 'this does not exist.'
Scorners of the immortal truth, holding forth in the assemblies of men, they wander the whole earth, voluble and widely read.
Whom even we do not fully understand—who here is fit to understand them, men so wise, so true, so great, the foremost in knowledge of scripture?
By austerity one attains greatness; by wisdom one finds what is great; by renunciation the knower of dharma ever wins happiness, O son of Kuntī.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: At this break in the discourse, the eloquent Devasthāna of mighty austerities spoke these well-fashioned words to Yudhiṣṭhira.
The words spoken by Phalguna—that there is nothing higher than wealth—on these I shall set you right; hear it with single-minded attention.
O Ajātaśatru, by righteousness the whole earth has been won by you; having won it, you ought not, O king, to cast it away in vain.
A four-runged ladder it is, established upon action; mount it rung by rung, mighty-armed king, in due order.
Therefore, Pārtha, sacrifice with great sacrifices rich in priestly gifts; some sages sacrifice by sacred study, and others by the sacrifice of knowledge.
Know that some are steadfast in works and some steadfast in austerity, O Bhārata; for so, O king of kings, runs the teaching of the Vaikhānasa hermits.
For one who strives for the sake of wealth, not striving would be the weightier good; greater fault would grow in the man who leaned upon that wealth.
With great toil men amass goods for the sake of wealth; and one athirst for wealth, in his folly, does not even perceive the slaying of an unborn child.
He gives to the unworthy, and gives not to the worthy; for want of discerning the unworthy from the worthy, even the duty of giving is hard to fulfill.
Riches were created by the Ordainer for sacrifice, and man was ordained the sacrificer and the guardian; therefore all wealth is to be employed in sacrifice alone, and only thereafter desire.

By manifold sacrifices laden with offerings of food, Indra of mighty power surpassed all the gods; having thereby gained the rank of Indra he shines forth—therefore all is to be employed in sacrifice.

The great-souled Mahādeva, god of gods, in the all-sacrifice offered up his very Self and so became glorious; pervading and upholding all the worlds with his fame, the radiant one clad in a hide shines resplendent.
Marutta, the son of Avikṣit, a king and a mortal, by his abundance overcame the lord of the gods; in his sacrifice Royal Splendor herself took up her seat, and where every vessel was of gold.

Hariścandra, lord among kings, of whom you have heard—by sacrifices he worshipped, a doer of merit, freed from sorrow; though a man, by his prosperity he surpassed Śakra—therefore all is to be employed in sacrifice.
Devasthāna said: On this very matter they recount this ancient tale—what Bṛhaspati, when questioned in due season by Indra, answered.
Contentment is the very height of heaven; contentment is the supreme happiness; nothing stands more firmly and rightly established than satisfaction.
When a man draws in his desires from every side, as a tortoise draws in its limbs, then the Self, self-luminous, grows serene through its own self alone.
When he fears nothing and nothing fears him, and he conquers desire and aversion, then he beholds the Self.
When toward all beings he neither rages nor bears ill will, then in deed, in thought, and in word he attains to Brahman.
Thus, O son of Kuntī, beings perceive this dharma and that, each in its own way and in its own time; understand this therefore, O Bhārata.
Some praise tranquillity, others again exertion; some praise neither the one nor the other, and others still praise both together.
Some men praise sacrifice, others renunciation; some praise giving, while certain ones praise receiving; and some, abandoning all, sit silent in meditation.
Some praise kingship and the protection of all, slaying, smiting, and cutting down; while certain ones live in utter solitude.
Surveying all this, the considered judgment of the wise is this: the dharma that lies in doing no harm to living beings is the one esteemed by the good.
Harmlessness, truthful speech, fair sharing, steadfastness, forbearance, the begetting of children upon one's own wife, gentleness, modesty, and freedom from fickleness—
wealth whose chief aim is dharma—so Manu, son of the Self-existent, declared; therefore, O son of Kuntī, govern thus with every effort.
For the kṣatriya who stands firm in kingship, ever self-controlled, the same toward what is dear and not dear, eating the remnants of sacrifice, knowing the true meaning of the science of statecraft—
intent on curbing the wicked, intent on the advancement of the good—such a knower of dharma should rule, having set his subjects firmly on the path of righteousness.
Then, having passed his royal fortune on to his son, dwelling in the forest and living on its wild produce, by the rule of the ascetics, unwearied, let him await his appointed hour.

The king who lives thus, resolved in the dharma of kings—for him both this world and the next shall be fruitful, O lord of men; but liberation, in my view, is very hard to reach and beset with many obstacles.
Thus pursuing dharma, devoted to truth, giving, and austerity, endowed with the virtues of compassion, free of desire and wrath—
intent on the protection of their subjects, established in the highest self-restraint—through battle waged for the sake of cattle and brāhmaṇas they have attained the supreme goal.

Thus the Rudras together with the Vasus, and the Ādityas too, O scorcher of foes, the Sādhyas, and the bands of royal sages, taking refuge in this dharma, vigilant, attained heaven thereafter by their own meritorious deeds.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: At this break in the discourse Arjuna spoke again these words to his eldest brother, the lord whose mind was sunk in despondency.
Having gained an unrivalled kingdom by the dharma of a kṣatriya, O knower of dharma, and having conquered your foes, O best of men, why do you grieve so bitterly?
For kṣatriyas, O great king, death in battle is held to surpass many sacrifices; call to mind the dharma of the kṣatriya.
For brāhmaṇas, austerity and renunciation are declared the ordained means to the world beyond; but for kṣatriyas, O lord, death in battle is appointed.
The dharma of the kṣatriya is most fierce, ever bound to the sword, it is declared—and slaying too, O best of the Bharatas, with the weapon in battle at its proper hour.
Even for a brāhmaṇa, O king, who abides by the dharma of the kṣatriya, life is praised in this world; for the kṣatriya order is grounded in the brahman.
Neither renunciation, nor begging, nor austerity, O lord of men, are ordained for the kṣatriya, nor living upon the goods of another.
And you are the knower of all dharmas, devoted with your whole being, O bull of the Bharatas, a king, wise and skilled, who in this world has seen both the higher and the lower.
Cast off the grief born of anguish and gird yourself for action; the heart of a kṣatriya above all is hard as the thunderbolt.
Having conquered your foes by the dharma of the kṣatriya and gained a kingdom free of thorns, master of yourself, O lord of men, be devoted to sacrifice and to giving.
Indra was indeed the son of Brahmā, yet by his deeds he became a kṣatriya; of his kinsmen of wicked ways he slew nine times ninety.
And that deed of his is honored and praised, O lord of peoples; by it he attained the lordship of Indra over the gods—so have we heard.
So do you, O great king, sacrifice with sacrifices rich in priestly gifts, even as Indra did, O lord of men, your fever of grief long since departed.
Grieve not at all over what has come to pass, O bull among kṣatriyas; those who fell have gone, by the dharma of the kṣatriya and purified by the sword, to the supreme goal.
What has come to pass had to be so, O bull of the Bharatas; for what is ordained, O tiger among kings, cannot be overstepped.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by Guḍākeśa, the son of Kuntī, O Bhārata, the Kaurava said nothing at all; whereupon Dvaipāyana spoke.
The words of Bībhatsu are right, and this is true, Yudhiṣṭhira; the householder's stage of life is declared by scripture to be the supreme dharma.
Follow your own dharma, O knower of dharma, according to scripture and according to rule; for it is not ordained that you abandon the householder's life for the forest.
For upon the householder the gods, the ancestors, the sages, and his dependents ever live; cherish them, O lord of the earth.
Birds, beasts, and all creatures, O lord of the earth, are sustained by householders alone; therefore the householder's is the foremost stage of life.
This stage, of these four orders of life, is the hardest to follow; tread it, Pārtha, with a steady mind—hard to tread as it is for those whose senses are weak.
Your knowledge of the Vedas is complete, and great austerity has been practiced by you; you ought now to bear the yoke of the kingdom of your fathers and forefathers.
Austerity, sacrifice, and sacred learning, the life of alms, the curbing of the senses, meditation, the practice of solitude, contentment, and giving according to one's power—
Such, O great king, are the pursuits that bring the brāhmaṇas to perfection; and now I shall declare those of the kṣatriyas as well, though they are already known to you.
Sacrifice, learning, exertion, a refusal to rest content in the pursuit of fortune, the wielding of stern punishment, and the protection of the subjects—
the full knowledge of the Veda, austerity well practised, the amassing of abundant wealth, and the bestowing of it upon worthy recipients—
these are the deeds of kings, O lord of peoples, and when well performed, so we have heard, they secure for them both this world and the next.
Among these, O son of Kuntī, the wielding of punishment is called the highest; for strength abides ever in the kṣatriya, and in strength the rod of chastisement is grounded.
These, O king, are the pursuits that bring the kṣatriyas to perfection; and upon this very theme Bṛhaspati also spoke this verse:
"The earth swallows up these two, as a serpent swallows the creatures that dwell in its hole: the king who will not give battle, and the brāhmaṇa who will not go forth to wander."
And the royal sage Sudyumna too, we have heard, attained the supreme perfection through the wielding of punishment, even as Dakṣa, son of Pracetas, attained it.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Holy one, by what deed did Sudyumna, that lord of the earth, attain the supreme perfection? I wish to hear of that king.
Vyāsa said: On this point too they recount an ancient tale. There were two brothers, Śaṅkha and Likhita, both steadfast in their vows.
The two of them had their dwellings, lovely and set apart from each other, furnished with trees ever in flower and fruit, along the river Bāhudā.
Now once it happened that Likhita came to the hermitage of Śaṅkha; and Śaṅkha, as chance would have it, had gone forth from his hermitage.
Then Likhita, having come to the hermitage of his brother Śaṅkha, plucked down some fruits that were fully ripe.
Taking them up, the twice-born one ate them without misgiving; and even as he was eating, Śaṅkha returned to the hermitage.
Seeing his brother eating, Śaṅkha said to him: "Whence did you obtain these fruits? By what right do you eat them?"
Touching water and saluting his elder brother, he replied, as though with a smile: "They were taken by me from this very place."
Then Śaṅkha, filled with sharp wrath, said to him: "This is theft you have done, taking the fruits of your own accord. Go, present yourself before the king, and make your deed known."

"Say: 'O best of kings, this that I have done is the taking of what was not given. Knowing me to be a thief, observe your own duty: swiftly inflict, O lord of men, the punishment due to me, a thief.'"
Thus addressed, and in obedience to his word, O mighty-armed one, Likhita, firm in his vow, went up to Sudyumna, the lord of the earth.
And Sudyumna, hearing from his frontier-guards that Likhita had come, went out to meet him on foot, together with his ministers, that lord of men.
Coming up to that best of those who know the brahman, the king said to him: "Tell me the reason for your coming, holy one; whatever it be, consider it already done."
Thus addressed, the sage among brāhmaṇas said this to Sudyumna: "You have promised that you will do it; having heard my request, you must perform it."
"Fruits not granted by my elder, O bull among men, were eaten by me; for that, O king, chastise me, and do not delay."
Sudyumna said: If the king is held by you to be the authority in the matter of inflicting punishment, then, O bull among brāhmaṇas, he must equally be the authority in the matter of pardon.
You, whose deeds are pure and whose vows are great, are hereby pardoned. Name some other desire, and I shall do as you bid.
Vyāsa said: But the brahman-sage, though urged by the great-souled king, would choose no other boon save that punishment alone.
Thereupon the guardian of the earth had the two hands of the great-souled Likhita cut off; and he, having received his punishment, departed.
Going to his brother Śaṅkha, he said this in his distress: "I have received my punishment; pardon now, holy one, your foolish brother."
Śaṅkha said: I am not angry with you, O knower of duty, nor have you wronged me; but your duty had been transgressed, and now your expiation has been made.
Go swiftly to the Bāhudā and offer there, as the rite prescribes, the water-libations to the gods, the fathers, and the seers; and set not your mind upon unrighteousness.
Vyāsa said: Hearing those words of Śaṅkha, Likhita then plunged into the holy river and set about the offering of water.
Thereupon his two hands appeared again, as fair as lotuses risen from the water; and in wonder he showed those hands to his brother.
Then Śaṅkha said to him: "This was wrought by me through my austerity. Let there be no doubt in you on this account—it is the divine will alone that is here ordained."
Likhita said: Why then, O greatly resplendent one, did you not purify me at the very first, you whose austerity has such power, O best of the twice-born?
Śaṅkha said: Thus it was for me to do; I am not the wielder of punishment over you. And now that lord of men is purified, and so too are you, together with the fathers.
Vyāsa said: That king, O best of the Pāṇḍavas, made foremost by that deed, attained the supreme perfection, even as Dakṣa, son of Pracetas, attained it.
This is the duty of kṣatriyas—the protection of the subjects who stray from the path, O great king. Do not, therefore, set your mind upon grief.
Hear the wholesome counsel of your brother here, O best of those who know duty: it is punishment indeed, O lord of kings, that is the kṣatriya's law, not the shaving of one's head as an ascetic.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Once more the great seer Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana spoke this weighty word to Ajātaśatru, the son of Kuntī:
Dear son, those longings that your austere brothers cherished, O great king Yudhiṣṭhira, while they dwelt in the forest—
let these mighty warriors, O best of the Bharatas, now attain them. Rule the earth, O Pārtha, as Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, ruled it.
A sorrowful sojourn in the forest has been endured by these austere men; now, at the end of their sorrow, let these tigers among men taste happiness.
Having enjoyed righteousness, profit, and pleasure together with your brothers, O Bhārata, then afterwards you may set forth, O lord of peoples.
Discharge your debt to guests, to the fathers, and to the gods, O Bhārata, son of Kuntī; then will you go to heaven.
Offer sacrifice with the Sarvamedha and the Aśvamedha, O joy of the Kurus; then afterwards, O great king, you will attain the supreme goal.
And having joined all your brothers in sacrifices with abundant priestly gifts, you will win unequalled fame, O scion of Pāṇḍu.
We know your mind, O tiger among men, O joy of the Kurus; but hear me now, how a king, acting thus, falls not away from righteousness.
For one who seizes wealth and one who restrains the wicked, those skilled in righteousness reckon the merit equal, O lord of men, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
The king who, awaiting the right place and time, shows toward the robber the wisdom born of the scriptures—he is not stained by any sin.
The king who takes the sixth part of the harvest as his due yet does not protect the realm—that prince takes upon himself a fourth part of all the people's sin.

Learn, too, how a king, standing thus, falls not away from righteousness: by restraining the wicked in conformity with the books of law, free from fear, heedless of desire and anger, even-eyed toward all like a father.
When, O greatly resplendent one, fate strikes the king at the moment of action and causes that act to fail, in that case they declare no transgression on his part.
By force or by stratagem the enemies must surely be subdued. He should make no pact with the wicked, nor put the kingdom up for sale.
The brave, the noble, and the learned are to be honoured, O Yudhiṣṭhira; and those rich in cattle and in wealth are to be protected with especial care.
In the conduct of lawful affairs the deeply learned are to be appointed; yet the discerning man should not place his whole trust in any single person, however endowed with virtues.
A king who fails to protect, who is ill-disciplined, vain, unbending, and envious, is bound to sin and is called untamed.
When the king is struck down by fate, those who, going unprotected, perish and are slain by thieves—all that is the king's guilt.
When the counsel has been good, the policy sound, and the manly deed accomplished duly as prescribed, there is no unrighteousness, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Undertakings come to ruin, and they also succeed, by fate; but when human effort has been made, no sin touches the prince.
On this matter, O tiger among kings, I shall relate to you this tale—what befell the ancient royal sage Hayagrīva, O prince.
He slew his foes and was himself slain in the fray—that hero of untiring deeds, steadfast and without an ally, at last overcome, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having done the deed of subduing his foes and exercised the highest skill in protecting his people—having done his work and won renown in noble battle—Vājigrīva rejoices now in the world of the gods.
Heedless of his own life, drawing his bow in the battles, cut down by weapons and beset by marauders—Aśvagrīva, devoted to his duty, that great soul made perfect, rejoices in the world of the gods.

The bow was his sacrificial post, the string his cord, the arrow his ladle, the sword his oblation-spoon, the blood his clarified butter; the chariot, swift as thought, his altar, the battle his fire, and the four chief steeds his four officiating priests.

Having offered his foes into that sacrificial fire, the swift lion among kings was freed from sin; and having offered up his own life-breaths in the final ablution of the battle, Vājigrīva rejoices in the world of the gods.

Guarding the realm with deliberate, wise policy, heedless of his own life, ever devoted to sacrifice, that great soul, pervading all the worlds with his fame—the thoughtful Vājigrīva rejoices in the world of the gods.

Cherishing the divine accomplishment and the human science of statecraft, and guarding the earth by the rules of right policy—therefore the king Hayagrīva, that great soul devoted to righteousness, rejoices in the world of heaven.

Learned, liberal, full of faith, and grateful—having forsaken the world of men once his deeds were done, the king has won the realm of the wise, the discerning, the honoured, those who lay down their bodies in battle.

Having duly received the Vedas and studied the scriptures, having rightly protected his realm, that great soul—having established the four orders each in its own duty—Vājigrīva rejoices in the world of the gods.

Having won his battles and protected his subjects, having drunk the soma and gratified the foremost of the twice-born, having justly wielded the rod of punishment over his people—spent in battle, he rejoices in the world of the gods.

He whose conduct men praise, whom the good and the learned, themselves worthy of honour, hold in honour—having won heaven and gone to the realms of heroes, that great soul of holy fame has attained perfection.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard the words of Dvaipāyana, and Dhanaṃjaya being still wroth, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, addressed Vyāsa and replied to him.
Neither this earthly kingdom nor enjoyments of every kind give any joy to my mind today; this grief roars within me and rends me.
And hearing the women who, bereft of their heroes and their sons, wail in their lamentation, I can find no peace, O sage.
Thus addressed, Vyāsa, the best of those skilled in yoga, knower of duty and master of the Vedas, made this reply to the deeply wise Yudhiṣṭhira:
Not by action is it gained, nor by anxious thought; nor is there any giver of it to a man. By the working of succession it has been ordained by the Ordainer: in due time a man obtains all things.

Not by intellect, nor by study of the scriptures, nor by their special gifts can men attain anything out of its season; yet even a fool at times obtains his ends, for time draws no distinction in respect of what is to be accomplished.
Out of the time of fruition, craft yields no result, nor do spells, nor medicines; yet those very same, gathered together by time, succeed and prosper when the season of fruition comes.

In due time the swift winds blow forth; in due time the rain comes to the clouds; in due time the water bears its lotuses and lilies; and in due time the trees put forth their blossoms in the forests.

In due time the nights grow dark and bright again; in due time the moon comes to its full orb. Not out of season do the trees bear flower and fruit; not out of season do the rivers run with swollen flood.

Not out of season do birds and serpents go to rut, nor deer and elephants, nor the great beasts of the mountains; not out of season do women conceive in the womb, nor do the cold, the heat, and the rains come at the wrong time.
None dies nor is born out of due time; nor does the child begin to speak before its season; not before its time does one attain to youth; nor does the seed once sown sprout out of season.

Not before its time does the sun draw to its conjunction, nor out of season does it sink to the western mountain; not unseasonably do they wax and wane—the moon, and the sea with its garland of mighty waves.
On this point, too, men recite an ancient tale, Yudhiṣṭhira—the song that was sung by King Senajit when he was stricken with grief.
This unconquerable cycle touches all mortals alike; for ripened by time, all human beings come at last to die.
Some men slay others, O king, and those in turn are slain by yet others; yet this, O king, is but a worldly manner of speaking—none truly kills, and none is truly slain.
One man thinks, 'He slays,' while another thinks, 'He does not slay'; but by their very nature are fixed the arising and the passing-away of beings.
When wealth is lost, or a wife, or when a son or a father has died, the man who broods, 'Ah, what misery!' only heaps fresh fuel upon his grief.
Why then do you grieve, when you yourself, in your delusion, are the one to be grieved over? Why do you mourn? Look how within sorrows lie further sorrows, and within fears further fears.
Not even this self is mine, yet the whole earth is mine; as it is mine, so is it others'—seeing thus, a man is not bewildered.
A thousand occasions for grief and a hundred for joy assail the fool day after day, but never the wise man.
Thus, in their portions and in their season, the dear and the hateful—sorrows and joys alike—revolve among living creatures.
There is only sorrow and no happiness—therefore it is sorrow alone that is truly felt; sorrow springs from the torment of craving, and what we call pleasure springs from the torment of sorrow.
Hard upon pleasure follows pain, and hard upon pain follows pleasure; no one meets with sorrow forever, nor does anyone meet with happiness forever.
For at the end of sorrows there is joy, and at the end of joy there is sorrow; therefore let him who desires lasting happiness abandon them both.
Whatever be the occasion of grief or anguish or of sinking swoons of sorrow, whatever be the root of one's distress—let a man cast it off, though it be a very limb of his own.
Be it pleasure or pain, the dear or the unwelcome, whatever comes, as it comes let him meet it with an unconquered heart.
Only behave, dear friend, but a little unkindly toward your wives or your sons, and you will learn at once who belongs to whom, and by what bond, and how.
Those who are most dull in the world, and those who have passed beyond the reach of intellect—these alone flourish in happiness; it is the man between who is yoked to suffering.
Thus spoke that greatly wise Senajit, O Yudhiṣṭhira—he who knew the higher and the lower, who knew the world, who knew the dharma, who knew both joy and sorrow.
He who is happy amid another's misery can never himself be truly happy; for sorrows have no ending—from one is born the next.
Pleasure and pain, being and non-being, gain and loss, death and life—all these touch a man here in their turns; therefore let the steadfast man neither exult nor rage.

The consecration for a sacrifice, the protection won by warfare, right governance of the realm through the science of just rule, the giving away of wealth as sacrificial fees, and true knowledge—let him know these to be the purifying things.

The great-souled king who guards his realm wisely and with sound policy, who is selfless and devoted to sacrifice, who moves through all the worlds as the very embodiment of dharma—he, when he has cast off his body, rejoices on high in the world of the gods.

Having won his battles and protected his realm, having drunk the Soma and increased his subjects, having wielded the rod of justice over the people with discernment, the king who is spent in war rejoices in the world of the gods.

Having rightly mastered the Vedas and studied the sacred treatises, having rightly protected his realm, and having established the four orders each in its own dharma, the king, his self made pure, rejoices indeed in the world of the gods.
He whose conduct men still revere even when he has gone to heaven—townsfolk, country-folk, and ministers alike—that king is the best of kings.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: With young Abhimanyu slain, and the sons of Draupadī, and Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and Virāṭa, and King Drupada, lord of the earth—
and Vasuṣeṇa who knew the dharma, and the prince Dhṛṣṭaketu, and so many other lords of men from diverse lands, all fallen in the battle—
grief will not release me, the slayer of my kinsmen, sick at heart, the cruelly fierce craver after a kingdom, the destroyer of my own line.
He on whose lap I once rolled and played as a child—that son of Gaṅgā was by me, greedy for a kingdom, struck down.
When I beheld him reeling beneath the arrows of Pārtha, shuddering as though smitten by thunderbolts, his gaze fixed upon Śikhaṇḍin—
that towering grandsire, a lion among men like an aged lion still tall, when I saw him strewn over with keen arrows, my mind was rent with anguish.
As he sank facing the east, dislodged from his chariot by the arrows, swaying like a mountain about to fall—then did a darkness of despair come over me.
He, bow and arrows in hand, that scion of Kuru who for many days did battle with the Bhārgava upon Kurukṣetra in that mighty fray—
he, the son of the river, the hero, challenged in battle from a single chariot the whole assembled warrior-host of kings at Vārāṇasī, to win brides—
he by whose blazing weapon King Ugrāyudha, that unassailable emperor, was burnt up—he it is whom I have slain in battle.
Guarding the moment of his own death, he who would not bring down with arrows the Pāñcāla prince Śikhaṇḍin—he was laid low by Arjuna.

When I saw him fallen to the earth and drenched in blood, in that very hour a most fierce fever entered into me, O best of sages—he by whom we were reared as children, he by whom we were guarded and kept.
He was slain by me—greedy for a kingdom, sinful, a slayer of my elder, a fool—for the sake of a kingship that lasts but a little while.
And the preceptor, that great archer, honoured by all the lords of earth—I came up to him in battle and, sinful as I was, spoke a lie to him concerning his son.

That burns my very limbs—the words my teacher spoke to me: 'You are a man of truthful speech, O king; if my son still lives, do not deceive me with falsehood'—so the brahmin, trusting in the truth, questioned me upon it.
Taking an elephant as my screen, I played him false—I, exceedingly greedy for a kingdom, sinful, a slayer of my teacher.

Wrapping myself in the cloak of truth, I told my teacher on the field, 'Aśvatthāman is slain'—when it was the elephant that had been struck down. To what worlds shall I go, having done so dreadful a deed?
And in that I caused the slaying of Karṇa, who never fled in battle, my own most fierce elder brother—who is a greater doer of evil than I?
And young Abhimanyu, born like a lion among the mountains—it was I, in my greed, who sent him into the army that Droṇa guarded.
From that day on I cannot bear to look upon Bībhatsu, nor upon lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa—a sinner I, like one who has slain an unborn child.
And Draupadī too, who deserved no sorrow, now bereft of her five sons—I grieve for her, as for the earth stripped of its five mountains.
So I, the wrongdoer, the sinner, the cause of the earth's ruin, shall sit here even thus and waste away this body of mine.
Know me from this day to have sat down to fast unto death, I who slew my teacher—so that in other births as well I may never again become the destroyer of my house.
I will not eat, nor will I in any wise take water; I will wither away the dear breath of my life, staying here, O you whose wealth is austerity.
Go now wherever you please; I freely give you leave, having made my peace with you. Grant me, all of you, your leave in turn—I shall cast off this body.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: To Pārtha as he spoke thus, overwhelmed with grief for his kinsmen, Vyāsa, the best of sages, restraining him, said, 'Not so!'
Beyond all measure, great king, you ought not to grieve. Once more I shall declare it to you, O lord: this was ordained by fate.
Unions and separations are the certain lot of all born creatures; like bubbles upon the waters, they come into being and pass away.
All that is heaped up ends in wasting away; all that rises up ends in falling; all unions end in separation, and life itself ends in death.
Pleasure ends in pain, and so does sloth; diligence is painful, yet it gives rise to happiness; prosperity, fortune, modesty, steadfastness, and success do not dwell with the slothful.
Friends cannot suffice to make one happy, nor enemies to make one wretched; wisdom does not suffice to win wealth, nor does wealth suffice to win happiness.
As you were created by the Ordainer for your works, son of Kuntī, so perform them; for from that alone comes your success—you are not your own master, O king.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As the eldest son of Pāṇḍu, scorched by grief for his kinsmen, was minded to give up his life, Vyāsa drove away his sorrow.
Vyāsa said: On this point, too, men recite an ancient tale, the song of Aśman, O tiger among men; hear it, Yudhiṣṭhira.
King Janaka of Videha, plunged in pain and grief, questioned upon his doubt the wise brahmin Aśman.
Janaka said: In the coming or the going of kinsmen and of wealth, how should a man who desires his own welfare bear himself?
Aśman said: From the very moment a man's self comes into being, straightway thereafter these manifold sorrows and joys come upon him.
And when one or another of these befalls him, whatever he then resorts to carries off his understanding, as the wind sweeps away a cloud.
'I am nobly born, I am accomplished, I am no mere common man'—by these three grounds is a man's mind flooded with conceit.
His mind thus overflowing, he squanders the enjoyments his fathers amassed, and once impoverished he comes to think it well to seize the goods of others.
Him, transgressing all bounds and grasping at what is not his due, kings hold back—as hunters hold back a deer with their arrows.
Those men who are twenty years of age, or thirty, will not endure beyond a hundred years, O king.
For these most grievous sorrows let a man prescribe a remedy by his understanding, regarding all the while, here and there, the lot of every living creature that bears breath.
The source of mental sorrows is the bewilderment of the mind, or the onset of what is unwished-for; a third cause there is not.
Thus do these sorrows, of every kind, come upon a man here, and so too do those that arise from bodily contact.
Old age and death devour all beings, like two wolves—the strong and the weak alike, the lowly and the great alike.
No man can ever escape old age and death, not though he has conquered this whole earth to the very shores of the sea.
Whether it be pleasure or pain that has drawn near to creatures, all of it must be undergone, helpless as they are; there is no turning it aside.
In the first age of life, or in the middle, or in the last, O lord of men, these conditions are not to be shunned, yet the things one longs for turn out otherwise.
Parting from the well-beloved, and union with the unloved, gain and loss, pleasure and pain—all follow the appointed ordinance.
The coming-forth of beings, and likewise the laying-down of the body, and the toil of effort by which men obtain things—all this is fixed and ordained.
Smell, colour, taste, and touch arise and cease by their own nature; even so do pleasures and pains follow the appointed ordinance.
Sitting, lying down, going, rising up, drinking, and eating—all are fixed for every living creature, and come to pass by time alone.
Even physicians fall ill; the strong become utterly weak; men rich in women turn impotent—strange is the turning of time.
Birth in a noble house, valor, health, and steadfastness, good fortune and enjoyment—all are won only through what is destined to be.
The poor, who wish for none, have sons in abundance; while the wealthy, striving and longing for many, have none at all.
Disease, fire, water, the sword, starvation, beasts of prey, poison, death by the noose, and a fall from a height—such are a creature's ends.
Whatever departure is appointed for a man, by that cause he goes; none is seen to overpass it, nor, once it is past, to be subject to it again.
For here, O lord of men, a wealthy man is seen to perish while still young, and a poor man, sorely afflicted, lives a hundred years.
Men who possess nothing are seen to live long, while those born in a prosperous house perish like moths in a flame.
In this world the prosperous, for the most part, have no power to enjoy; yet the poor, O ruler of men, can digest even wood.
"It is I who do this," thinks the man driven by time—the evil-souled one, committing every kind of sin out of his discontent and craving.
Women, dice, the hunt, and drink—these attachments the wise condemn; yet many men, even the deeply learned, are seen ensnared by them.
Thus, through time, all things—desired and undesired alike—come to touch every being, and no cause for it can be found.
The wind, the ether, and fire, the moon and the sun, day and night, the stars, the rivers, and the mountains—who makes or sustains them?
Cold and heat, and the rains as well, revolve in their turn by time; even so, O bull among men, do the joys and sorrows of mortals.
Neither herbs nor scriptures, neither oblations nor recitations can save a man once he is overtaken by death or by old age.
As two logs of driftwood come together upon the great ocean, and having met, drift apart again—such is the meeting of beings.
Those attended by retinues of men and women, by song and music, and those who are forlorn, living on others' food—toward all of these time acts alike.
Thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives, have been experienced through our wanderings in existence—whose are they, and whose are we?
No one truly belongs to him, nor does he belong to anyone; this gathering with wife, kin, and the host of friends is but a meeting upon the road.

"Where was I? Where am I? Where shall I go? Who indeed am I, and to what end do I abide here? Wherefore, and for whom, should I grieve?"—thus should one steady the mind, when union with what is dear is impermanent and the round of existence turns like a wheel.
The wise know that the world beyond is never seen beforehand by direct perception; yet one who wishes to prosper must place his faith without transgressing the sacred traditions.

One should perform the rites due to the ancestors and the gods, and practice the duties of dharma; the learned man should offer sacrifice according to the ordinance, and pursue the threefold aim of dharma, artha, and kāma.
This whole world is sinking down into the deep ocean of time, where old age and death are the great sea-monsters—and not one being is aware of it.
Many physicians, who have studied the whole science of medicine together with its appurtenances, are seen overwhelmed by diseases.
Though they drink astringent decoctions and clarified butters of many kinds, they cannot pass beyond death, any more than the great ocean passes beyond its shore.
Even those skilled in elixirs, who have administered their tonics well, are seen broken by old age, as trees are broken by mighty elephants.
Likewise, those rich in austerity, devoted to the study of scripture, the givers of gifts and the performers of sacrifice—none of these cross beyond old age and death.
For the days never return, nor the months, nor again the years; for all beings that are born, neither the fortnights return nor the nights.
Helplessly, in the course of time, this perishable man sets out upon that vast and certain road which is traveled by all beings.
Either the body departs from the living soul, or the soul departs from the body; this companionship with wife and other kinsmen is but a meeting upon the road.
No everlasting union is ever obtained by anyone, not even with one's own body—how much less, then, with any other?
Where now, O king, is your father today? Where now is your grandfather? You do not see them now, nor do they see you.
For no man is a witness of heaven or of hell; but the sacred tradition is the eye of the good—O king, follow it here.
Having fulfilled the vow of chastity, one should beget offspring and offer sacrifice, free of envy, that he may discharge his debt to the ancestors, the gods, and the great seers.

Devoted to sacrifice and settled in the begetting of offspring, having first lived as a chaste student and apportioned his obligations, he wins both heaven and this world, having cast away the falsehood that lay within his heart.
For a king who duly practices dharma and gathers wealth as is fitting, whose wheel of sovereignty rolls onward, his fame grows ever greater throughout all worlds, moving and unmoving.
Vyāsa said: Having thus understood this discourse in its fullness, complete in its reasoning, the king of Videha, his understanding purified, took leave of Aśman and went home, his grief stilled.

So too do you, O unfaltering one, let go of grief; arise, you who are the equal of Śakra, and come to gladness. By the dharma of the warrior the earth has been won by you; enjoy it, O son of Kuntī, and do not despair.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and son of Dharma, kept silent, Guḍākeśa the Pāṇḍava addressed Hṛṣīkeśa.
"Tormented by grief for his kinsmen, the Dharma King, scorcher of foes, is here sunk in an ocean of sorrow—console him, O Mādhava.
We are all once more cast into doubt, O Janārdana; you, O mighty-armed one, are able to dispel his sorrow."
Thus addressed by the great-souled Vijaya, Govinda the lotus-eyed, the unfaltering one, turned toward the king.
For Keśava was one whom the Dharma King could not refuse; from boyhood onward Govinda had been dearer to him even than Arjuna.
Taking hold of the king's arm, anointed with sandal and like a pillar of stone, the mighty-armed scion of Śūra spoke, seeking to comfort him.
Resplendent was Kṛṣṇa's face, with its fair teeth and lovely eyes, like a full-blown, unfolded lotus awakened by the sun.
"Do not grieve, O tiger among men, with the grief that wastes the body; for those who fell on this field of battle are not to be easily regained.
As gains obtained in a dream prove false upon waking, even so, O king, are those warriors who have passed away in the great battle.
For all those heroes, the ornaments of war, departed facing the foe; not one of them was struck down from behind, nor while fleeing.
All those heroes, having yielded up their own lives fighting in the great combat, purified by the sword, have attained heaven; you ought not to grieve for them.
On this very matter they recite an ancient tale—how Nārada spoke to Sṛñjaya, who was stricken with grief for his son.
"I and you, O Sṛñjaya, and all creatures alike, shall move on, never released from joys and sorrows—what, then, is there to lament?
Hear of the supreme good fortune of kings, as I recount it; give heed, O monarch, and thereafter you will cast off your sorrow.
Hearing of those mighty kings who have died, drive away your anguish; listen to me in full detail.
Hear from me, O Sṛñjaya, that Marutta, son of Avikṣit, has died—he to whose sacrifice the gods came, the all-creating ones, with Indra and Varuṇa, led by Bṛhaspati, to that great-souled king.

He who drew Śakra, the king of the gods, lord of a hundred sacrifices, into rivalry; whom the learned Bṛhaspati, wishing to please Śakra, refused to officiate for—and for whom Saṃvarta then conducted the rites, to vex Bṛhaspati.
While that king, best of monarchs, ruled the good, the earth shone forth, ripening her crops untilled, and garlanded with sacred shrines.
At the great sacrifice of Avikṣit's son, the All-Gods were the assembly-members, the Maruts were the servers, and the Sādhyas too attended that great-souled king.
When the hosts of the Maruts drank Marutta's soma, the sacrificial gifts he gave surpassed those given to gods, to men, and to Gandharvas alike.
If even he died, O Sṛñjaya—he who was richer than you in the four blessings and more meritorious than your son—then do not grieve for your son.
We have heard, O Sṛñjaya, that Suhotra, son of Vitithi, has died—he for whom Maghavān rained down gold for a whole year.
He upon whose accession the earth, called "the wealth-bearing," became true to her name, O lord of men; while that ruler of the realm reigned, the rivers carried gold.
Maghavān, honored by the world, O king, let fall into the rivers tortoises and crabs, crocodiles and sea-monsters and dolphins—all of gold.
Seeing the golden fish, sea-monsters, and turtles fallen by the thousands and hundreds, the son of Vitithi then smiled.
That boundless gold, gathered together in the Kurujāṅgala, he distributed with a collected mind to the brāhmaṇas as he sacrificed at the outspread rite.

If even he died, O Sṛñjaya—he who was richer than you in the four blessings and more meritorious than your son—then do not grieve for your son, who gave no sacrificial gifts and offered no sacrifice; be calm, O son of Śvitya, and do not mourn.
We have heard, O Sṛñjaya, that Aṅga, of the great chariot, has died—he who set free a thousand thousand white horses.
And a thousand thousand maidens, adorned with gold, he drove forth as sacrificial fee while sacrificing at the outspread rite.
A hundred hundred-thousands of bulls, garlanded with gold, each followed by a thousand cows, he drove forth as the sacrificial fee.
While Aṅga sacrificed upon the mountain at Viṣṇu's stride, Indra grew exhilarated with the soma, and the twice-born with the sacrificial gifts.
At his sacrifices, O lord of kings, numbering a hundred over and over, the gifts he gave surpassed those given to gods, to men, and to Gandharvas.
No man has been born, nor will another be born, who shall bestow such gifts as the wealth Aṅga gave away at the seven forms of the soma sacrifice.
If even he died, O Sṛñjaya—he who was richer than you in the four blessings and more meritorious than your son—then do not grieve for your son.
We have heard, O Sṛñjaya, that Śibi, son of Uśīnara, has died—he who could roll up this whole earth like a hide.
Making the earth resound with the great roar of his chariot, he brought the world under a single parasol with his one victorious car.
As many cattle and horses as there are today, together with the beasts of the wild—so many cows did Śibi, son of Uśīnara, bestow at his sacrifice.
Prajāpati deemed that none could bear his burden—none past nor yet to come among all kings, O Bhārata—save Śaibya, son of Uśīnara, the royal seer of Indra's prowess.

If even he died, O Sṛñjaya—he who was richer than you in the four blessings and more meritorious than your son—then do not grieve for your son, who gave no sacrificial gifts and offered no sacrifice; be calm and do not mourn.
We have heard, O Sṛñjaya, that Bharata, son of Duḥṣanta, has died—the son of Śakuntalā, the great archer of abundant wealth and splendor.
He who bound thirty horses for the gods along the Yamunā, twenty along the Sarasvatī, and fourteen along the Gaṅgā.
With a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred rājasūyas did Bharata, son of Duḥṣanta, of great splendor, perform his rites of old.
The mighty deeds of Bharata, among all kings, the other princes could not attain, even as mortals cannot reach the sky with their arms.
He who, having bound more than a thousand horses and laid out the sacrificial altar, gave to Kaṇva a thousand lotuses of gold — that was Bharata.
If even he died, O Sṛñjaya — he who was endowed with the four excellences more fully than you, and more meritorious by far than your son — then do not grieve for your son.
We have heard that Rāma, son of Daśaratha, also died, O Sṛñjaya — he who ever showed compassion for his subjects as for sons born of his own body.
In whose realm no widows were left without protection — to all alike Rāma was as a father, when he ruled the kingdom.
The rain-clouds poured in their season, the crops were full of savor, and there was ever abundance of food while Rāma governed the kingdom.
No living being drowned in the waters, fire burned no one without cause, and there was no fear born of beasts of prey while Rāma governed the kingdom.
The subjects lived for thousands of years, blessed with thousands of sons, free of disease and with all their aims fulfilled, while Rāma governed.
There was no quarrel even among women with one another — how much less among men — and the people were ever steadfast in dharma while Rāma governed the kingdom.
The trees bore flowers and fruit perpetually and were free of blight, and every cow yielded a droṇa-measure of milk while Rāma governed the kingdom.
That great ascetic, having dwelt fourteen years in the forest, performed ten unrestricted horse-sacrifices, rich in jārūtha offerings.
Dark-hued, youthful, red-eyed, with the stride of a rutting elephant, Rāma ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years.
If even he died, O Sṛñjaya — he who was endowed with the four excellences more fully than you, and more meritorious by far than your son — then do not grieve for your son.
We have heard that King Bhagīratha too died, O Sṛñjaya — at whose far-extended sacrifice Indra, drinking the soma, grew flushed with intoxication.
The lord Pākaśāsana, foremost of the gods, by the might of his arms conquered many thousands of the asuras.
He who, sacrificing at his far-extended rite, gave away as priestly fee a thousand thousand maidens adorned with gold.
Every maiden was seated in a chariot, and every chariot was yoked with four horses; to each chariot a hundred elephants, lotus-marked and garlanded with gold.
A thousand horses followed behind each single elephant, a thousand cows behind each horse, and a thousand goats and sheep behind each cow.
As he dwelt in seclusion, Gaṅgā Bhāgīrathī once sat upon his lap; and from her, of old, Urvaśī came to be.
To Bhagīratha, scion of Ikṣvāku, the sacrificer who gave abundant fees, Gaṅgā who courses through the path of the three worlds came as a daughter.
If even he died, O Sṛñjaya — he who was endowed with the four excellences more fully than you, and more meritorious by far than your son — then do not grieve for your son.
We have heard that Dilīpa too, son of Ilavila, died, O Sṛñjaya — whose many deeds the twice-born recount.
That lord of the earth, with collected mind, gave away at his great sacrifice this very earth, abounding in wealth, to the brāhmaṇas.
As he sacrificed, at each rite his household priest gave away a thousand golden elephants as priestly fee.
At whose sacrifice there stood a great and splendid sacrificial post of gold, which the gods, with Śakra at their head, drew near as they performed the rite.
Upon that golden post whose top-ring was of gold, six thousand gods and gandharvas danced in seven companies.
There in their midst Viśvāvasu himself played upon the vīṇā, and every being believed, "It is for me that he plays."
This of King Dilīpa other kings could not match: that women laden with gold lay sleeping at ease upon the roads.
Even those men who but looked upon King Dilīpa — fierce-bowed, truth-speaking, exceedingly great of soul — won heaven by it.
Three sounds never ceased in Dilīpa's dwelling: the chant of the Vedic recitation, the twang of the bowstring, and the cry "Let it be given!"
If even he died, O Sṛñjaya — he who was endowed with the four excellences more fully than you, and more meritorious by far than your son — then do not grieve for your son.
We have heard that Māndhātṛ, son of Yuvanāśva, died, O Sṛñjaya — whom the Marut gods drew forth as an embryo from his father's side.
He who grew within the belly of the great-souled Yuvanāśva, born of the consecrated ghee — that splendid king, conqueror of the three worlds.
Seeing him, godlike in form, lying upon his father's lap, the gods asked one another, "Whom shall this child suckle?"
"He shall suckle from me!" — thus Indra came forward; and so Śatakratu gave him the name Māndhātṛ.
Then, for the nourishment of the great-souled one, the hand of Indra let a stream of milk flow into the mouth of Yuvanāśva's son.
Suckling at Indra's hand, in a single day he grew by a year; in twelve days, O king, he became as one of twelve years.
In a single day this whole earth submitted to him — the righteous-souled, great-souled hero, equal to Indra in battle.
For Māndhātṛ conquered in battle the kings Āṅgāra, Marutta, Asita, Gaya, Aṅga, and Bṛhadratha.
When the son of Yuvanāśva did battle with Āṅgāra, the gods, at the twangings of his bow, thought, "The heavens are splitting apart!"
From where the sun rises to where it sets — all that is called the domain of Yuvanāśva's son, Māndhātṛ.
Having sacrificed with a hundred horse-sacrifices and a hundred royal consecrations, that lord of the earth gave to the brāhmaṇas red-gold fish.
Of gold they were, a yojana in height and ten yojanas in length; what remained over from the twice-born, the other people shared among themselves.
If even he died, O Sṛñjaya — he who was endowed with the four excellences more fully than you, and more meritorious by far than your son — then do not grieve for your son.
We have heard that Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, also died, O Sṛñjaya — he who conquered this whole earth together with its oceans.
That king ranged across it stage by stage at each cast of the yoke-pin, adorning it with altars; sacrificing with holy rites, he traversed the whole earth.
Having sacrificed with a thousand rites and a hundred horse-sacrifices, he gratified the lord of the gods with three mountains of gold.
In the great array of the war between gods and asuras, having slain the daiteyas and dānavas, Yayāti, son of Nahuṣa, apportioned the whole earth.
Having settled his sons — Yadu, Druhyu, and the rest — in the border-lands, and consecrated Pūru in his own kingdom, he set out for the forest together with his wife.
If even he died, O Sṛñjaya — he who was endowed with the four excellences more fully than you, and more meritorious by far than your son — then do not grieve for your son.
We have heard that Ambarīṣa, son of Nābhāga, died, O Sṛñjaya — the holy one whom the subjects chose as their protector, O best of kings.
He who, at his far-extended sacrifice and with collected mind, gave to the brāhmaṇas a thousand thousand kings, each of whom had performed ten thousand sacrifices.
"This men of old never did, nor shall any others do it hereafter" — thus the recipients of the priestly fees acclaimed Ambarīṣa, son of Nābhāga.
A hundred thousand kings and a hundred hundred kings, all having performed horse-sacrifices, attained through him the southern course of the dead.
If even he died, O Sṛñjaya — he who was endowed with the four excellences more fully than you, and more meritorious by far than your son — then do not grieve for your son.
We have heard that Śaśabindu of the Caitraratha line died, O Sṛñjaya — that great-souled one who had a hundred thousand wives.
He who had a thousand thousand sons of the line of Śaśabindu, all clad in golden armor and all supreme archers.
A hundred maidens followed behind each one of those princes, a hundred elephants behind each maiden, a hundred chariots behind each elephant.
A hundred horses of fine breed and garlanded with gold behind each chariot, a hundred cows behind each horse, and so too a hundred goats and sheep behind each cow.
This boundless wealth, O great king, Śaśabindu bestowed upon the brāhmaṇas at his great horse-sacrifice.
If even he died, O Sṛñjaya — he who was endowed with the four excellences more fully than you, and more meritorious by far than your son — then do not grieve for your son.
We have heard that Gaya, son of Amūrtarayas, died, O Sṛñjaya — that king who for a hundred years ate only what remained from the oblations.
To whom Agni granted boons; and Gaya then asked these boons: "May my giving be inexhaustible, and may my faith in dharma ever increase."
"May my mind delight in truth — through your grace, O eater of oblations." And he obtained all those desires from the fire-god: so have we heard.
With the new-moon and full-moon rites and the four-monthly sacrifices, again and again, that one of great splendor sacrificed for a thousand years.
A hundred thousand cows and a hundred hundred horses he gave, rising up to give again and again, for a thousand years.
He gratified the gods with soma, the twice-born with wealth, the ancestors with the svadhā offerings, and his own wives with the things they desired, O bull among men.
Having fashioned an earth of gold, ten fathoms broad and twice as long, the king gave it as priestly fee at his great horse-sacrifice.
As many as are the grains of sand of the Gaṅgā, O king, O bull among men — just so many cows did Gaya, son of Amūrtarayas, bestow.
If even he died, O Sṛñjaya — he who was endowed with the four excellences more fully than you, and more meritorious by far than your son — then do not grieve for your son.
We have heard that Rantideva, son of Saṃkṛti, died, O Sṛñjaya — that one of great renown who, having duly propitiated Śakra, obtained a boon.
"May our food be abundant, may we be granted guests, may our faith never desert us, and may we never have to beg of anyone."
The beasts, both of the village and of the wild, came of their own accord to wait upon him — the great-souled and glorious Rantideva, firm in his vows.
From the moisture seeping out of the heap of hides a great river streamed forth; and from this that great river became renowned as the Carmaṇvatī.

In the wide-spread assembly the king gave golden niṣkas to the brāhmaṇas; and where the twice-born cried out, "A niṣka for you, for you!" he would say, "A thousand for you," and so approach the brāhmaṇas.

Whatever served for the monthly offering or as utensils for the rite — the pots, the cooking-vessels, the cauldrons, the dishes, and the pans — not one thing of the wise Rantideva's was other than gold.
On whatever night one lodged in the house of Rantideva, son of Saṃkṛti, a hundred cows and twenty thousand more were slaughtered.
There the cooks, wearing well-polished jeweled earrings, would cry out: "Eat your fill of the broth — today there is not so much meat as before!"
If even he died, O Sṛñjaya — he who was endowed with the four excellences more fully than you, and more meritorious by far than your son — then do not grieve for your son.
We have heard that the great-souled Sagara also died, O Sṛñjaya — that tiger among men of the line of Ikṣvāku, of more than human valor.
Sixty thousand sons followed behind him as he went, like the hosts of stars trailing the moon, lord of the constellations, in a cloudless sky at the season's end.
He to whom the whole earth bowed in submission of old, beneath a single royal canopy, and who gratified the gods with a thousand horse-sacrifices —
who bestowed a palace of golden pillars, all of gold, thronged with couches and filled with women whose eyes were like the petals of the lotus —
who granted to the worthy twice-born their desires both great and small, so that at his command the brāhmaṇas divided that wealth among themselves —
who in his wrath caused the earth to be dug out, marking it with the sea, and from whose name the great water itself came to be called the ocean —
if even he died, O Sṛñjaya — he far richer than you in the four blessings and far more meritorious than your son — then grieve not for your son.
We have heard, O Sṛñjaya, that King Pṛthu, son of Vena, has died — he whom the great seers assembled together to consecrate in the vast forest.
"He shall make the worlds prosper" — thus was he proclaimed Pṛthu; and "he saves us from harm" — therefore is he remembered as kṣatriya.
When the people beheld Pṛthu, son of Vena, they cried, "We are won to him in love"; and so, out of that devotion, the name rājan arose for him.
While the son of Vena ruled, the earth yielded grain unploughed, honey filled cup upon cup, and the cows gave milk by the droṇa-measure.
Free of disease, all their aims fulfilled, and afraid of nothing, men dwelt as they desired, in the fields and in their homes.
When he wished to cross the sea, its waters stood still; the rivers did not heave up against him, and his banner met no hindrance.
In the great rite of the horse-sacrifice that king gave to the brāhmaṇas one and twenty mountains of gold, each three reeds in height.
If even he died, O Sṛñjaya — he far richer than you in the four blessings and far more meritorious than your son — then grieve not for your son.

Why do you brood in silence, O Sṛñjaya? Do you not, O king, hear these words of mine? If you do, then my speech has not been uttered in vain — wholesome counsel rightly spoken, as if to one about to die.

Sṛñjaya said: I do hear this speech of yours, O Nārada — rich in wondrous meaning, fragrant with holiness like a garland — a recital, bright with their fame, of those great-souled royal sages and doers of holy deeds, told to dispel my grief.

Not in vain have you spoken, O great seer; at the mere sight of you, Nārada, my sorrow is gone. I long to hear your words, O speaker of the sacred truth; I cannot have my fill of them, as of a draught of the nectar of immortality.

O you whose sight is never barren, if you would show favour to me, O lord, scorched by sorrow for my son, then by your grace let my dead son live again this day, and let me be joined with him once more.

Nārada said: That dear son of yours who has passed away — the Gold-Spitter whom Parvata granted you — that very son I now give back to you again, Hiraṇyanābha, endowed once more with a span of a thousand years.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How did the son of Sṛñjaya come to be the Gold-Spitter? For what reason was he granted by Parvata, and by what cause did he die?
If a man's allotted span was a thousand years, how then did Sṛñjaya's son die before he had even reached his boyhood?
Was "Gold-Spitter" but a name only, or was it truly so that he spat gold? This I wish to learn.
Vāsudeva said: I shall tell you how it came to pass, O lord of men. Long ago there were two seers, Nārada and Parvata, honoured throughout the worlds.
Uncle and sister's son, those two mighty ones came down here of old from the world of the gods, wishing in their fondness to roam awhile among mortals.
On purifying oblation-food fit for sacrifice, and on the very fare of the gods, Nārada the uncle, and Parvata the sister's son, sustained themselves —
both endowed with ascetic power, wandering over the surface of the earth, and tasting human pleasures, they ranged about as was fitting.

Loving and joyful, they made there a compact: "Whatever resolve should arise in the heart, whether good or ill, it must be disclosed to the other; to do otherwise shall bring a curse upon the false one."
"So be it," the two world-honoured great seers vowed; and coming to King Sṛñjaya, son of Śvitya, they said this to him:
"We two shall dwell with you, sir, for a time, for your good; be duly attentive to us, O guardian of the earth." "So be it," said the king, and honouring them, he waited upon them well.
Then one day, to those two great-souled ones who had so come to him, the king, exceedingly pleased, said: "This is my daughter, of fair complexion.

This is my one and only daughter, and she shall attend upon you both — lovely to look upon, flawless of limb, endowed with good character and conduct, tender and maidenly, and like the filament of a lotus."
"Excellent, gentle one," said the two; and so addressed, the king commanded her: "Daughter, wait upon these brāhmaṇas as upon gods and as upon a father."
And that maiden, walking in righteousness, said "So be it" to her father, and according to the king's command she honoured the two and waited upon them.
By her ministering thus, and by her matchless beauty, love swiftly and all at once took hold of Nārada's heart.
And then desire grew in the heart of that great-souled one, as the lord of the stars, the moon, waxes slowly at the onset of the bright fortnight.
Yet that knower of the law, out of shame, did not disclose his fierce passion to his sister's son, the great-souled Parvata.
But by his ascetic power and by Nārada's bearing, Parvata came to know it; and in anger at Nārada, stricken with desire, he then cursed him bitterly.
"You made a compact with me without reservation: that whatever resolve should arise in the heart, whether good or ill,
it should be disclosed to one another. That word of yours, O brāhmaṇa, you have made false; and therefore I say this to you.
You did not tell me earlier of the desire stirring within you for the maiden Sukumārī; for that reason I now lay this curse upon you.
Since you, a teacher and an expounder of the sacred word, an ascetic and a brāhmaṇa, have broken the compact made between us two —
therefore, in deep wrath, I shall curse you; hear me. Sukumārī shall indeed become your wife — of that there is no doubt;
but from the moment of the wedding onward, O lord, the maiden — and other men besides — shall behold you as a monkey, stripped of your own form."
And when Nārada had heard that speech from Parvata, then the uncle in his turn cursed his sister's son in anger:
"Though endowed with austerity, with chastity, with truth, and with self-restraint, and ever devoted to righteousness, you shall not attain a dwelling in heaven."
Having cursed each other thus, in deep wrath and intolerant of one another, the two parted ways, like a pair of mighty elephants enraged.
Parvata, the great sage, wandered over the whole earth, honoured everywhere as was his due by his own splendour, O descendant of Bharata.
Then Nārada, foremost in righteousness, lawfully won that maiden, the blameless Sukumārī, the daughter of Sṛñjaya.
But that maiden, in accordance with the curse, beheld Nārada — from the very moment the marriage-mantras were pronounced — as a monkey.
Yet Sukumārī did not scorn the divine seer, monkey-faced though he was; on the contrary, she remained full of affection for him.
Devoted to her husband, she waited upon him and did not, even in thought, turn to another — neither god, nor sage, nor yakṣa — to take as her lord.
Then once the venerable Parvata went into a certain solitary forest, and there he caught sight of Nārada.
Then, having saluted him, Parvata said to Nārada: "Be gracious to me, O lord, and grant me leave to enter heaven."
Then Nārada, beholding Parvata seated before him with hands folded in supplication and downcast — himself yet more downcast — said to him:
"You first cursed me, saying, 'You shall become a monkey'; and afterward, stung by resentment, I cursed you too, saying, 'From this day forth you shall not attain a dwelling in heaven.'
This is not worthy of you, for you stand to me in the place of a son." And so the two sages then withdrew, each from the other, the curses they had laid.
Then, seeing Nārada radiant with glory and of godlike form, Sukumārī fled, fearing he must be some other woman's husband.
Then Parvata, seeing the blameless one fleeing, said to her: "This is your own husband; there is no need to doubt it here.
The seer Nārada, the venerable lord, a soul supremely righteous, is yours alone, his heart cleaving to none but you. Let there be no doubt of this in your mind."

Reassured in many ways by the great-souled Parvata, and having heard of that taint of the curse upon her husband, she returned to her own nature; then Parvata went to heaven, and Nārada went to his home.
This great seer Nārada, before whose eyes all things are made manifest, will himself, if asked, tell you how it came to pass, O best of men.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the king, the son of Pāṇḍu, replied to Nārada: "Venerable one, I wish to hear of the origin of the Gold-Spitter."
So addressed by the King of Righteousness, the sage Nārada recounted how it had come to pass concerning the Gold-Spitter.
"It is even so, O great king, as Keśava has told it. But what remains of this matter, that I shall relate to you, since you ask.
I and Parvata — my sister's son, the great sage — wishing for lodging, came to Sṛñjaya, the best of the victorious.
There, honoured by him with rites prescribed by ordinance, and well provided with every comfort, we dwelt in his house.
When the rains had passed and the time for departure was at hand, Parvata spoke to me these words, weighty and timely:
"We two have dwelt, most highly honoured, in the house of this lord of men for the appointed time. Now, O brāhmaṇa, let us take thought what should be done in return."
Then I said, O king, to the fair-seeming Parvata: "All this rests with you, my lord, my sister's son.
Let the king be offered a boon and obtain whatever he desires; by the power of our austerities let him gain his wish, if you think it fitting."
Then Parvata, the bull among sages, summoned the fair-seeming King Sṛñjaya and spoke these agreed-upon words:
"We two are pleased, O king, with the honours you have rendered us, born of your sincerity. With our leave, O best of men, think now upon a boon.
Whatever, without offence to the gods, lies within the measure of what is possible for a mortal, that take, O great king; for you are deemed by us worthy of honour."
Sṛñjaya said: If you two are pleased with me, then by that alone my purpose is achieved; this very thing is for me the highest gain, attained and rich in fruit.
Nārada said: To him, who spoke thus, Parvata replied once more: "Choose, O king, the desire that has long abided in your heart."
Sṛñjaya said: I long for a son — a hero, valiant and firm in his vows, long-lived and greatly blessed, splendid as the king of the gods.
Parvata said: This desire of yours shall be fulfilled, but he shall not be long-lived; for this resolve in your heart is meant to surpass the king of the gods.
And from his spitting of gold he shall become the Gold-Spitter; and he, splendid as the king of the gods, must be guarded against the king of the gods.
Nārada said: Having heard this speech of the great-souled Parvata, Sṛñjaya then sought to win him over, saying, "Let it not be thus."
"Let my son be long-lived, O sage, by the power of your austerity." But Parvata said nothing at all to him in reply, out of regard for Indra.
To that grieving king I then spoke once again: "Remember me, O great king; when remembered, I shall show myself to you."
"Your beloved son, gone into the power of the Lord of the Dead, I shall give back to you in that very form. Do not grieve, O lord of the earth."
Having spoken thus to the king, we two departed as we had wished; and Sṛñjaya, his desire fulfilled, entered his own palace.
Then to Sṛñjaya, the royal sage, in the course of time, was born a son of mighty valor, blazing as it were with splendor.
He grew in due season like a great lotus in a lake, and he became Golden-Spittle: rightly did that name belong to him.
That most wondrous thing spread through the world, O best of the Kurus; and the lord of the gods came to know of the boon granted by the two great-souled ones.
Then the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra, fearing to be overthrown, took his stand upon the counsel of Bṛhaspati and lay in wait for an opening against the boy.
He charged the thunderbolt, that divine weapon embodied in form: "Become a tiger and slay this prince!" — so he commanded, O lord.
"Grown great in might, this one will surely overthrow me, O thunderbolt — this son of Sṛñjaya, even as Parvata bestowed him."
Thus addressed by Śakra, the thunderbolt, conqueror of hostile cities, continually followed the boy, watching for an opening.
And Sṛñjaya, having gained a son radiant as the king of the gods, the king rejoiced; and then, with his harem, he took to dwelling in the forest.
Then once, on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī, by a forest stream, the child ran about at play, his nurse beside him.
The boy, about five years of age, with the prowess of a lordly elephant, in his great strength came upon a tiger that had sprung up all at once.
Crushed by it, the king's son, trembling, fell lifeless to the earth; and at that the nurse cried out in anguish.
And having slain the prince, that tiger vanished on the very spot, made to disappear then by the magic of the king of the gods.
Hearing the cry of the nurse as she wept in utmost distress, the lord of the earth himself ran to that place.
He beheld the boy lying lifeless, his blood drained, robbed of all joy, like the moon fallen from the sky.
Lifting onto his lap that son with the crushed chest, drenched in blood, he lamented over him in his anguish.
Then the mothers of the boy, weeping, wasted with grief, ran to that place where King Sṛñjaya was.
Then the king, his mind turned inward, called me to mind; and I, knowing that he had thus thought of me, came into his sight.
Lost in grief, he was made to hear from me these very words which the hero of the Yadus has told to you, O lord of the earth.
And the boy was restored to life by me then, with Vāsava's consent; for what is destined must be so, and it cannot be otherwise than that.
Thereafter the prince Golden-Spittle, of great renown and valor, gladdened the hearts of his father and his mother.
When his father had gone to heaven, that mighty one of terrible prowess ruled the kingdom for a thousand and a hundred years.
Then, having performed many great sacrifices with abundant priestly gifts, that one of great splendor satisfied both the gods and the ancestors.
And having begotten many sons to continue the line, in the fullness of long time, O king, he came to the law of Time.
So you, O lord of kings, turn back this grief that has arisen within you, even as Keśava and Vyāsa of mighty austerity have counseled you.
Take up the kingdom of your fathers and forefathers, and bear hard the burden of rule; and by performing holy great sacrifices you shall attain the worlds you desire.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: To the king Yudhiṣṭhira, fallen silent and grieving, the ascetic Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, knower of the truth of dharma, then spoke.
"The protection of subjects is the dharma of kings, O lotus-eyed one. Dharma is the standard of the world, and constant conformity to dharma is the rule."
"Hold fast, O king, to the station of your fathers and forefathers; and the dharma that lies among the brāhmaṇas is eternal, established by the Veda."
"That is the standard of standards, everlasting, O bull of the Bharatas; and of that dharma in its entirety the kṣatriya is the protector."
"And whatever man within his realm strikes against his command, that wrecker of the world's course is to be restrained by force of arms."

"Whoever, fallen under the sway of delusion, makes the standard no standard — be he a servant, or a son, or even some ascetic — those wicked ones the king should restrain by every means, or put to death."
"A king who acts otherwise than this incurs guilt; for he who does not guard dharma when it is perishing is himself a slayer of dharma."

"Those slayers of dharma were struck down by you, together with their followers. Acting in your own dharma, why then do you grieve, O Pāṇḍava? For a king must slay, must give, and must protect his subjects according to dharma."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "I do not doubt the word you speak, O treasury of austerity; for dharma is no hidden thing to you, O best of all upholders of dharma."
"Yet many who ought not to have been slain were slain by me for the sake of the kingdom; those things I ought not to have done, O brahmin, sear me and burn me."
Vyāsa said: "Either God may be the doer, O Bhārata, or the individual man, or chance prevails in the world, or the fruit is held to be born of action."
"If men, appointed by God, perform their deeds both good and ill, O lord of earth, then that fruit goes to God."
"For just as a man may fell a tree with an axe in the forest, the guilt would belong to the feller, and in no way to the axe."
"Or if men were to gain the fruit of the deed because they took up the means, still the guilt wrought by rod and sword would not be found in the man."
"And this is not held to be right, O son of Kuntī — that one should reap the fruit of what another has wrought. Therefore lay it upon God."
"Or if the man is the doer of his deeds, both fair and foul, and no other agent is found, then in that case do some other good."
"For no one anywhere, O king, can turn back from what is destined; and the guilt wrought by rod and sword is not found in the man."
"Or if you think, O king, that the world rests upon chance, then in that case too the evil deed has neither been nor shall be."
"But if responsibility for good and evil must be assigned to the world, then the most fitting thing in the world is the lifted rod of kings."
