"And again, if deeds come round full circle in the world, O Bhārata, then these men reap the fruit, fair and foul, of their own doing — such is my view."
"Thus, true and yielding good counsel, is the certain fruit of action. Cast it off, O tiger among kings; do not set your mind on grief in this way."
"For one acting in his own dharma, even when there is reproach, O Bhārata, this abandonment of self, O king, is unbecoming of you."
"Atonements are ordained here for the doers of deeds, O son of Kuntī; one possessed of a body may perform them, but the bodiless would meet ruin."
"Therefore, O king, while you yet live, you shall perform the atonement; but if you do not make atonement, you shall burn for it hereafter, O Bhārata."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Slain are sons and grandsons, brothers and fathers too, fathers-in-law, teachers, maternal uncles, together with grandfathers."
"And great-souled kṣatriyas, kinsmen and friends alike, companions and relatives and brothers, O grandfather —"
"and many lords of men, gathered from diverse lands — all were brought to death by me alone, greedy for the kingdom, O grandfather."
"Having slain such men as those — guardians of the earth, ever steadfast in dharma, heroes who again and again drank the soma — what shall I attain, O treasury of austerity?"
"Day and night now I burn, brooding again and again upon this earth, bereft of those lordly lions among kings in all their splendor."
"Beholding the terrible slaughter of kinsmen, enemies slain by the hundred and other men by the millions, I am consumed with anguish, O grandfather."
"What now shall be the lot of those noble women, bereft of their own sons, their husbands, and their brothers?"
"Reviling us — the dreadful Pāṇḍavas, bringers of the end, leagued with the Vṛṣṇis — gaunt and wretched, falling down upon the ground,"
"those women, seeing no more their fathers, brothers, husbands, and sons, will all give up their dear lives and go to the abode of Yama."
"Of this I have no doubt, O best of the twice-born: through their tender love, and clearly through the subtlety of dharma, we shall incur the slaughter of women as well."
"We, having slain our friends and wrought sin without end, shall fall headlong into hell, head downward indeed."
"We shall cast off our bodies by fierce austerity, O most virtuous one. Declare to me, O grandfather, the several modes of holy life."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard that speech of Yudhiṣṭhira, the seer Dvaipāyana then, pondering it keenly with his intellect, spoke to the Pāṇḍava.
"Do not give way to despair, O king; recall the dharma of the warrior. By their own dharma these kṣatriyas were slain, O bull among kṣatriyas."
"Coveting sovereignty entire and great glory upon the earth, bound by the ordinance of fate, they went to their destruction through Time."
"Not you are the slayer, nor Bhīma, nor Arjuna, nor the twins; it is Time that, by the law of succession, takes the life-breaths of embodied beings."
"By that Time were they gathered in — Time, which has neither mother nor father, which has no one to favor, which is the witness of creatures' deeds."
"This is but the instrument of that Time, O bull among men: that it slays beings by means of beings — that is its sovereign form."
"Know Time to be the very embodiment of action, the witness of good and evil, whose outcome is the qualities of pleasure and pain, the bestower of the fruit of Time."
"Consider too, O mighty-armed one, the deeds of those men, by reason of which, as causes of their own destruction, they fell into the power of Time."
"And recognize your own disposition toward restraint and vow and virtuous conduct, even when you were made to do such a deed, constrained by ordinance."
"As a contrivance fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ lies in the power of him who set it, so by action joined with Time is this world set whirling."
"For seeing this coming-to-be of a man without apparent cause, and his perishing by mere chance, grief and joy are alike of no avail."
"Yet whatever falsehood here ensnares your mind, for the sake of that, O king, atonement is enjoined: perform it."
"And this is heard, O Pārtha, of the war of gods and asuras of old: the asuras were the elder brothers, and the gods the younger."
"Among them too, for the sake of sovereignty, there arose a great upheaval; the war lasted, it is said, two and thirty thousand years."
"Making the earth one ocean, awash with blood, the gods then slew the daityas and won for themselves the triple heaven."
"Even so, having gained the earth, brāhmaṇas versed to the end in the Vedas, deluded by pride, attached themselves to the aid of the dānavas."
"Renowned as the Śālāvṛkas throughout the three worlds, O Bhārata, those eighty-eight thousand too were slain by the gods."
Those evil-souled men who, seeking the destruction of dharma, become the promoters of adharma, must be slain—even as the fierce Daityas were slain by the gods.
If by killing one man the welfare of the rest of a family is secured, or by destroying a family or even a kingdom, then such an act does no injury to right conduct.
For there is, O lord of men, a dharma that wears the form of adharma, and an adharma that wears the form of dharma; this the wise man must learn to discern.
Therefore steady your heart, O Pāṇḍava, for you are learned; you have followed the path trodden of old by the gods themselves, O Bhārata.
Men such as you do not go to hell, O bull of the Pāṇḍavas; comfort these your brothers and your friends, O scorcher of foes.
For he who, set upon a sinful undertaking, is wholly possessed by that intent—who acts in that same spirit while doing it, and remains shameless once it is done—
in him, it is said, all that taint reaches its fullness: for such a one there is no expiation, nor any lessening of the evil deed.
But you are of pure birth, made to act by another's fault; unwillingly you wrought this deed, and now you grieve for having done it.
The horse-sacrifice, the great offering, is declared to be the expiation; perform it, O great king, and thus you shall be cleansed of evil.
Maghavat, the chastiser of Pāka, having vanquished his foes together with the Maruts, by performing one sacrifice after another a hundredfold, became the Lord of a Hundred Sacrifices.
Cleansed of sin, having won heaven and attained the worlds where bliss arises, Śakra, surrounded by the host of the Maruts, shone resplendent, lighting up the quarters.
As the lord of Śacī is honored in the world of heaven amid the Apsarases, the sages wait upon him, and the gods too attend that ruler of the wise.
Even such are you, who here by your valor have passed over the whole earth, and by your valor have conquered its guardian-kings, O sinless one.
Go to their cities and kingdoms, O king, surrounded by your friends, and consecrate their brothers, sons, and grandsons each in his own realm.
Even the children, even those still in the womb—speaking words of comfort, gladdening all your subjects, do you protect the earth.
And where there is no son, there consecrate the daughters; for womankind is set upon desire, and thus they will lay aside their grief.
When you have thus brought solace to all the kingdoms, O Bhārata, offer the horse-sacrifice, as Indra the victorious did of old.
Those great-souled warriors are not to be mourned, O bull among Kṣatriyas; by their own deeds they met their ruin, bewildered by the power of fate.
The duty of a Kṣatriya you have fulfilled, and your kingdom is won unstained; walk now in that dharma, O son of Kuntī, which yields the higher good in the life beyond.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: By doing what deeds in this world does a man come to need expiation, and by doing what is he set free? Tell me that, O grandsire.
Vyāsa said: By leaving undone the ordained acts, by performing the forbidden ones, and by living falsely—thus does a man come to need expiation.
The student of the Veda upon whom the sun rises while he still sleeps, or upon whom it sets, the man with diseased nails, the man with discolored teeth—

the man married before his elder brother and the man whose younger brother weds before him, the forsaker of the Veda and the reviler of it, the husband of a remarried woman, and the man who weds before his elder brother—
he who has broken his vow of chastity, the slayer of a twice-born man, he who abandons sacred learning to an unworthy recipient and he who withholds it from a worthy one—
the village-priest, O son of Kuntī, the seller of a king's secrets, and the slayer of a Śūdra woman—of these, each earlier-named is the more to be condemned.
He who slaughters an animal in vain, he who sets fire to a forest, he who serves another with falsehood, and he who opposes his teacher—
and he who casts away his sacred fires, and likewise the seller of the Veda, and he who has broken his sworn agreement—all these are counted among the sins.
I shall also tell of the things that ought not to be done; learn them from me—deeds opposed to the world and the Veda; hear them with single-minded attention.
The abandonment of one's own duty and the practice of another's; the officiating at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice; and the eating of what ought not to be eaten;
the forsaking of one who has come for refuge, the failure to support a dependent, the selling of flavored liquids, and the slaying of beasts of the brute-born kind;
the failure of a capable man to perform the kindling of the fires and the like, and the withholding of all those things, O Bhārata, that ought ever to be given—
the failure to bestow sacrificial fees, and the laying of hands upon a Brāhmaṇa's property—all these the knowers of dharma declare to be deeds not to be done.
The son who divides the inheritance against his father's will, he who defiles his teacher's bed, and he who fails to beget offspring—through such unrighteousness a man becomes a doer of adharma.
These deeds have now been told, both at length and in brief—the deeds by doing or by failing to do which a man comes to need expiation.
But hear now under what particular circumstances these very same deeds, when performed, do not stain men with guilt.
If a man slays in battle even one versed in the end of the Veda who comes against him with weapon raised, intent on killing, he does not by that become a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.
And moreover, O son of Kuntī, a sacred verse upon this is recited in the Vedas; I declare to you that dharma as ordained by the authority of the Veda.
He who slays a Brāhmaṇa fallen from his rightful conduct, an aggressor with weapon poised, does not thereby become a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa; it is one wrath answering another.
In peril of life, or through ignorance, even one devoted to dharma who drinks strong liquor—if unprompted to it—deserves once more to be purified by the sacraments.
All this concerning the eating of what should not be eaten has been told to you, O son of Kuntī; through the ordinance of expiation all of it is purified.
For the approaching of the teacher's bed, when done at the teacher's bidding, does not defile a man: Uddālaka begot Śvetaketu through a pupil in just this way.
He who commits theft for his teacher's sake in times of distress is not bound by it, provided he does not turn to it again and again out of wilful desire.
He who takes such property, save that of a Brāhmaṇa, incurs no fault; and he who does not himself partake of it is not tainted by sin.
A falsehood may be spoken to save life, one's own or another's; and so too for the teacher's sake, in matters concerning women, and in the making of marriages.
A vow is not broken by an emission of seed in a dream by any means; an oblation of clarified butter upon the kindled fire is ordained as the expiation.

There is no offense of marrying before an elder brother who has become an outcaste, or who has gone forth as an ascetic or a mendicant; and the taking of his wife in such a case is no violation of dharma.
One should neither slaughter an animal in vain nor cause it to be done; for the sacramental slaying of beasts, when ordained by the rule, is in truth a grace bestowed upon them.
What is given to an unworthy Brāhmaṇa through ignorance is no offense; and so too the imparting of learning, for due cause, whether to a worthy or an unworthy recipient.
For women who have transgressed there is an atonement free of blame; by it even she is purified, and the husband is not thereby defiled.

Knowing its true nature, the sale of Soma may be made without fault; the dismissal of a dependent who is incapable is without offense; and the burning of a forest, when done for the sake of cattle, is no transgression.
These deeds have been told, by doing which a man incurs no fault; now I shall declare the expiations at length, O Bhārata.
Vyāsa said: By austerity, by rites, and by gifts, O Bhārata, a man cleanses away his sin—if, once purified, he does not return to it again.
Eating but once a day, wandering for alms, performing his own observance, a skull in his hand and a club at his side, chaste, ever alert,
free of malice, sleeping upon the ground, proclaiming his deed before the world—after twelve full years the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa is set free.
In six years a man who lives on penitential fare is cleansed of the slaying of a Brāhmaṇa; eating but once each month, he is freed in three years.
He who eats but once a month is purified within a single year, of this there is no doubt; and likewise, O king, one who abstains from food is freed even by a lesser term.
By the rite of the horse-sacrifice he is purified, of this there is no doubt; and whatever men bathe at its concluding ablution—
all of them become cleansed of sin, so runs the highest sacred tradition; and he who is slain in battle for a Brāhmaṇa's sake is freed from the guilt of Brāhmaṇa-slaying.
By bestowing a hundred thousand cows upon worthy recipients, the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa is set free from that and from all sins as well.
He who gives twenty-five thousand tawny milch-cows is freed from all his sins.
In peril of life, by giving a thousand milch-cows with their calves to the virtuous who are poor, a man is freed from his guilt.
He who gives a hundred Kāmboja horses to Brāhmaṇas of disciplined life, O guardian of the earth, he too is released from his sin.
He who fulfills the heart's desire of even a single man, O Bhārata, and who, having given, does not proclaim it abroad—he too is released from his sin.
A twice-born man who, having once drunk strong liquor, then drinks it fire-hot, thereby purifies himself both in this world and the next.
By casting himself from the heights of Meru, or by entering the fire, or by setting forth upon the Great Journey, he is freed from all his sins.
A Brāhmaṇa who has drunk liquor, having sacrificed with the Bṛhaspati-sava rite, may once more join the assembly of Brāhmaṇas—so runs the sacred tradition of the Brāhmaṇas.
He who, having drunk liquor, makes a gift of land without grudging and drinks no more, O king—that man, once sanctified by the sacraments, is purified.
He who has defiled his teacher's bed should lie down upon a heated slab of iron, or, taking his own member in his hand, should go forth gazing upward.
By the surrender of the body he is freed from the evil deed; and women who keep restraint for a year are released from such deeds.
He who performs the Great Vow, or gives away all that he possesses, or is slain in battle for his teacher's sake, is released from the evil deed.
He who has served another with falsehood, and he who has opposed his teacher, by rendering to him what is dear, are released from that sin.
For the breaking of the vow of chastity, one should observe the penance prescribed for the slaying of a Brāhmaṇa, clad in an ass's hide for six months; thus is he freed from his guilt.
He who has carried off another's wife, and he who has seized another's wealth, by holding a vow for a full year, are thus freed from their guilt.
From whomever one has stolen, to him one should give back wealth of equal worth; by such manifold means is one freed from that guilt.
By a penance of twelve nights well observed, or of no fewer than ten, both he who married before his elder brother and the elder brother so passed over are made pure, O Bhārata.
He should then take a wife, ever delivering his forefathers thereby; and upon the woman no fault falls, nor is she tainted by it.
For in conjugal union, purified by the season, a four-month observance is ordained; by it women are made pure, so the knowers of dharma understand.
But women suspected of sins are not to be approached by a man who knows; by their monthly courses they are made pure, as a vessel is cleansed by ashes.
For Brāhmaṇas the whole of dharma is ordained, complete on all four feet; for the Kṣatriya the dharma is ordained drawn short by one foot.
So too for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra, foot by foot it is diminished; by this measure one should determine the greater and lesser weight of their duties.
Having slain a creature of the animal kingdom, or having felled many other sorts of trees, a man should subsist on air alone for three nights and openly proclaim what he has done.
For approaching a woman one may not lawfully approach, O king, this penance is ordained: for six months he must go about clad in wet garments and sleep upon ashes.
This same rule applies to all forbidden deeds, by the procedure declared by the Brāhmaṇas, grounded in precedent, scripture, and reasoning.
Even by reciting the Sāvitrī in a clean place, eating sparingly, doing no harm, neither dull nor given to idle chatter, a man is freed from all his sins.
By day he should remain ever standing under the open sky, by night he should sleep beneath it, and three times by day and three times by night he should enter the water with his garments on.
While bound by this vow he should not speak with women, Śūdras, or the fallen; having committed sins through ignorance, the twice-born man so vowed is set free.
After death a man obtains the fruit of good and evil, with the elements as his witnesses; and whichever of the two preponderates, that is the fruit the doer reaps.
Therefore, when he has done an evil deed, let him by gift, by austerity, and by good works so increase the fruit of merit that it comes to outweigh the rest.
As an antidote to evil deeds he should perform good works, and give away his wealth without ceasing; thus he is released from sin.
For a penance proportioned to the sin has been laid down; yet, save for the great sins, an expiation is indeed prescribed.
In all matters of what may and may not be eaten, and likewise of what may and may not be spoken, in cases of ignorance and of knowledge alike, O king, the ordinances grant their dispensations.
A sin done knowingly becomes in every case a grave one; but where the fault arises from a lapse made in ignorance, expiation is ordained.
Sin can be wiped away by the procedure as it has been declared; but this procedure is ordained only for the believer who has faith.
For unbelieving men, devoid of faith and given over to the vice of hypocrisy, this procedure is never to be seen at all.
The conduct of the cultivated and the dharma the cultivated uphold, O best of the upholders of dharma, must be honored, O tiger among men, by one who seeks happiness both here and hereafter.
Thus, O king, you shall be freed of sin by that cause already stated, whether by reason of the slaying of these men for the protection of others, or by reason of a king's proper duty.
Or, if some compassion still remains in you, you may perform a penance; but do not go to your ruin through conduct fit only for the ignoble.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by the venerable one, Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of dharma, reflected for a moment and then replied to the sage whose wealth was austerity.
What is to be eaten and what is not to be eaten, and what gift is held praiseworthy, and who is a worthy recipient and who is not — tell me this, O grandsire.
Vyāsa said: On this point too they relate an ancient tale, the dialogue between the Siddhas and Manu, the Lord of Creatures.
In the days of old the Siddhas, devoted to austerity and vows, having come together, questioned about dharma the mighty Lord of Creatures as he sat there at the beginning of time.
How is one to eat, how to give, how to study, how to practice austerity? Declare to us all, O Lord of Creatures, what ought and what ought not to be done.
Thus addressed by them, the venerable Manu, son of the Self-Existent, replied: Listen, as it truly is, to dharma told both in full and in brief.
Not taking what is not given, giving, study, austerity, non-injury, truthfulness, freedom from anger, forbearance, and sacrifice — these are the marks of dharma.

That very thing which is dharma becomes unrighteousness when set in the wrong place or the wrong time; even taking, falsehood, and injury may be dharma — for dharma, it is taught, is conditioned by circumstance.
For those who understand, both dharma and its opposite are twofold; abstention from action and engagement in action — such is the twofold division both in worldly life and in the Veda.
From abstention comes immortality, while mortality is the fruit of action; one should know that the fruit of evil is evil, and that of good is good alone.
Of these two there exist, according to their good and evil nature, both the divine and what is joined to the divine, both the breath of life and dissolution.

When evil deeds are done without forethought, a good fruit may yet arise hereafter, in doubtful measure, or even for a purpose seen in this world; and for what is done without forethought an expiation is ordained.

As for deeds done in anger and delusion — by precedent, scripture, and reason it is shown that the affliction of the body and of the mind, in things pleasant and unpleasant, is quieted by medicines, by sacred formulas, and by penances.
The customs of castes, of guilds, and of settlements, and the laws of families in every respect, one should not forsake; for there is no dharma among those in whom dharma is not found.
What ten men learned in the Vedas and the law-books, or three who are reciters of dharma, declare when a matter arises — that is dharma in a case of doubt concerning dharma.
Red earth, and likewise ants, and the śleṣmātaka fruit, and poison too — these are not to be eaten by the Brāhmaṇas.
Not to be eaten by Brāhmaṇas are those fishes that are without scales, four-footed creatures other than the tortoise, frogs, and whatever else is born of the water.
Bhāsa birds, swans, eagles, cakravāka geese, cranes, waterfowl, the heron, the diver-bird, vultures, and crows and owls as well —
all flesh-eating birds, and four-footed beasts furnished with fangs, those that have teeth on both jaws, and all that have the four canine teeth —
the milk of ewes, mares, she-asses, and she-camels, of cows newly calved, and of women and of doe-deer as well — of these the Brāhmaṇa should not drink.
Food connected with a death, food connected with childbirth, and whatever has not yet passed its tenth day, is not to be eaten nor drunk; so too the milk of a cow within ten days of calving.
The food of a carpenter, of a tanner of hides, of an unchaste woman, of a washerman, of a physician, and likewise of a watchman, is not to be eaten.

So too the food of those denounced by guilds or villages, of those who live off women of the stage, of a younger brother married before the elder and of eunuchs, and of bards and those skilled in dicing —
and food brought though it was being refused, food that has soured or gone stale, food tainted with liquor, defiled leavings, and whatever has been left as a remnant — all this is not to be eaten.
Preparations of flour, of meat, of sugarcane, of greens, and likewise of milk, and barley-meal, parched grain, and gruel of curds and meal, are not to be eaten when they have stood long.
Milk-rice, a dish of rice and sesame, meat, and cakes prepared to no sacred purpose, are not to be eaten nor partaken of by Brāhmaṇa householders.
Only after he has honored the gods, the ancestors, men, the sages, and the household deities is the householder entitled to eat.
As a mendicant who has gone forth, so should the householder dwell within his own home; living thus, abiding with his beloved wife, he attains to dharma.
The righteous man should not give a gift for the sake of fame, nor out of fear, nor to one who has done him a service, nor to those given to dancing and singing, nor to jesters.
Not to a drunkard, nor to a madman, nor to a thief, nor to a physician, nor to one bereft of speech or pallid, nor to one maimed in limb, nor to a dwarf —
nor to a wicked man, nor to one of base family, nor to one not consecrated by the vows; a gift to a Brāhmaṇa unlearned in scripture, who does not expound the sacred word, is a gift that is dead.
What is given improperly, and what is improperly received, turns to the ruin of them both — of the giver and of the taker alike.
As a man who would cross the sea clinging to a log of khadira wood or to a stone sinks down, so do both the giver and the receiver sink alike.
As a fire heaped over with damp wood does not blaze up, so is the recipient of gifts who is devoid of austerity, of study of the scriptures, and of good conduct.
As water held in a skull, or as milk in a dog-skin bag, is spoiled by the fault of its vessel, so is sacred learning in one bereft of good conduct.
To one who is without sacred formulas, without vows, ignorant of the scriptures, yet free of malice — out of compassion a gift may be given, even to such poor men as these.
Yet a gift should not be given even out of compassion to a wretch who works harm — neither on the plea that the worthy have practiced it, nor again on the plea that it is dharma.
A gift made without good cause to a Brāhmaṇa devoid of dharma incurs the fault of an unworthy recipient — on this I have no doubt.
As an elephant made of wood, as a deer made of leather, so too a Brāhmaṇa who does not study — these three bear but the name.
As a eunuch is barren among women, as a cow with a cow yields no fruit, as a bird without wings — so is a Brāhmaṇa without the sacred formulas.
As grain stored in an empty village, as a well without water, as an oblation poured where there is no fire — even so is an offering made to one untrained in sacred rites.
A fool who destroys the offerings due to the gods and the ancestors, an enemy who carries off their substance, does not deserve to attain the higher worlds.
All this has been told to you as it truly came to pass, O Yudhiṣṭhira; in brief it has been declared, yet it is a great matter to be heard, O bull of the Bharatas.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I wish to hear at length, O venerable one, O great sage, O best of the twice-born, the whole of the duties of kings and of all the four castes.
And how, in times of calamity, statecraft is to be ordered by a ruler of the earth, and how, keeping to the path of righteousness, I might win the whole earth.
For this discourse on expiation, enlarged with the matter of foods lawful and forbidden, has stirred my curiosity and seems to awaken delight in me.
The practice of dharma and the rule of a kingdom seem forever at war with one another, and by this my mind is confounded as I ponder it without cease.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: To him the mighty Vyāsa, best of those who know the Vedas, who knew all that was of old, glancing toward Nārada, spoke.
If you wish to hear the whole of dharma, O Yudhiṣṭhira, go forth, O mighty-armed one, to Bhīṣma, the aged grandsire of the Kurus.
In all the mysteries he will cut away the doubts that abide in your mind — the son of Bhāgīrathī, the all-knowing, the knower of all dharma.
He whom the divine goddess, the celestial river that flows by three paths, brought to birth; he who beheld face to face all the gods with Śakra at their head.
Having again and again gratified with due homage the divine seers, with Bṛhaspati at their head, the lord learned the science of statecraft.
That whole science which the Brāhmaṇa Uśanas, preceptor of gods and demons, knows, this best of the Kurus obtained together with all its commentary.
From Cyavana of the Bhārgava line the great-minded one received the Vedas with their supplementary limbs, and also from Vasiṣṭha, firm in his vows.
He who of old learned from the eldest son of the grandsire, the youth of blazing splendor, who knew the true nature of the path of the inmost Self.
From the mouth of Mārkaṇḍeya he gained the whole law of the ascetics, and from Rāma weapons, and from Śakra he obtained them too, O bull of the Bharatas.
He whose death, though born among men, comes only by his own will; and though he is without offspring, the holy worlds in heaven are said to be his.
He in whose assembly the holy Brāhmaṇa-seers ever sat as members; for whom nothing whatever among the things to be known by knowledge remains unknown.
He, the knower of dharma, versed in the subtle truth of dharma and of its purport, will declare it to you; go to him before that knower of dharma releases his life-breaths.
Thus addressed, the son of Kuntī, far-sighted in wisdom and of great splendor, spoke to Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, best of those who speak.
Having wrought a most terrible carnage of my kinsmen, one that makes the hair stand on end, having become a sinner against the whole world and the cause of the earth's ruin —
having caused him to be slain in battle by guile, though he fought without crookedness — by what right am I fit to approach him with my questions?
Then, desiring the welfare of the four castes, the mighty-armed one of great splendor, best of the Yadus, spoke again to that best of kings.
It is not fitting now, O best of kings, to persist so stubbornly in grief: whatever the venerable Vyāsa has told you, do that.
The brāhmaṇas, O mighty-armed one, and your brothers of vast vigor, wait upon you full of expectation, as men scorched by heat await the rain-cloud.
The kings who survived the slaughter, and the whole of the four orders gathered together, and your realm of Kurujāṅgala, O great king—all look to you.
If only to please these high-souled brāhmaṇas, and at the command of this teacher Vyāsa of measureless splendor,
and of your friends, beginning with me, and of Draupadī, O scorcher of foes—do what they wish, O slayer of enemies, and work the welfare of the world.
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, the lotus-eyed king of great austerity rose up for the good of all the world.
That tiger among men was entreated in person by Viṣṭaraśravas, and by Dvaipāyana, and likewise by Devasthāna and by Jiṣṇu,
and entreated by these and many others, the high-minded Yudhiṣṭhira cast off the sorrow of his heart and his anguish.
A hearer of counsel, a treasury of sacred learning, skilled in what is heard and worthy to be heard, the son of Pāṇḍu resolved himself and attained peace of mind.
Encircled by them like the moon by the constellations, the king, placing Dhṛtarāṣṭra before him, entered his own city.
Wishing to enter, that knower of dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira son of Kuntī, paid worship to the gods and to the brāhmaṇas by the thousand.
Then a new, gleaming chariot, draped with woolen blankets and antelope hides, yoked to sixteen white oxen marked with auspicious signs—
honored with holy hymns and praised by the great sages, he mounted it as the god Soma mounts his chariot made of nectar.
Bhīma of terrible prowess, son of Kuntī, took up the reins, while Arjuna held aloft the white, sun-bright parasol.
And that white parasol held above his head shone forth, pale as the lord of stars, like a cloud in the sky.
And the two heroes, the sons of Mādrī, splendidly adorned, then took up his two yak-tail fans, gleaming white with the radiance of moonbeams.
Those five brothers, fully adorned, mounted upon the chariot, then appeared, O king, like the five elements all together.
Mounting a gleaming chariot yoked to swift horses, Yuyutsu, O king, followed behind the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas.
Mounting a bright golden chariot yoked to Saiṇya and Sugrīva, Kṛṣṇa, together with Sātyaki, followed the Kurus.
And the eldest, the father of Pārtha, O Bhārata, went on in a palanquin borne by men, in front of the Dharma-king, in the company of Gāndhārī.
And all the women of the Kurus, Kuntī and Kṛṣṇā Draupadī, went in conveyances high and low, with Vidura at their head.
Then chariots in multitude and adorned elephants, foot-soldiers and horses too, followed along behind.
Then, praised with eloquent words by panegyrists, bards, and minstrels, the king went on toward the city named after the elephant.
That procession of the mighty-armed one was without compare on earth, thronging and tumultuous and unrestrained, thronged with people glad and well-fed.
For Pārtha's coming, the city and the royal road were duly decked out by the men who dwelt in the city.
The royal road was hung with white garlands, with banners and altar-platforms, and richly perfumed with incense.
And the royal palace was wreathed about with powders of fragrant scents, with manifold flowers and priyaṅgu blossoms, and with hanging strings of garlands.
And at the city gate, firm new jars filled with water, maidens, flowers, and goats were set in place here and there.
So into the city, its gates finely adorned, the son of Pāṇḍu, praised with auspicious words and surrounded by his friends, made his entry.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As the sons of Pṛthā made their entry, many thousands of the city's people, eager for the sight, came thronging together.
That royal road, its squares richly adorned, shone forth, O king, like the great ocean swelling at the rising of the moon.
The houses along the royal road, jeweled and lofty, seemed to tremble, O Bhārata, with the weight of the women crowding them full.
Softly, as though abashed, those women praised Yudhiṣṭhira, and Bhīmasena and Arjuna, and the two sons of Mādrī, the Pāṇḍavas.
"Blessed are you, Pāñcālī, who attend, O fair one, upon these best of men, as Gautamī attended upon the great sages.
Your deeds are not in vain, nor your keeping of vows, O lovely lady." Thus, O great king, the women then praised Kṛṣṇā.
With their words of praise, O Bhārata, and the murmur of voices among them, and the sounds born of their joy, the city was filled with stir.
Passing in due order along that royal road, adorned and resplendent, Yudhiṣṭhira drew near to the royal palace.
Then all the subjects, both townsfolk and country-folk, drawing near from this side and that, spoke words pleasing to the ear:
"By good fortune you conquer your foes, O lord of kings, O slayer of enemies; by good fortune the kingdom is regained, through righteousness and through might.
Be you our king here, O great king, for a hundred autumns; guard your subjects in righteousness, O sovereign, as Indra guards the third heaven."
Thus honored with auspicious rites at the gate of the royal house, and receiving on every side the blessings uttered by the twice-born,
the king entered the palace, the likeness of the abode of the king of the gods, and having heard words joined with victory, stepped down from the chariot.
Entering within, the glorious one approached the household deities and worshipped them with jewels, with perfumes, and with garlands in every way.
Then the glorious and far-famed one came forth once more and beheld the comely brāhmaṇas standing in attendance.
Surrounded then by the twice-born eager to pronounce their blessings, he shone like the spotless moon ringed about by the host of stars.
The son of Kuntī honored those twice-born ones according to rule, placing first his preceptor Dhaumya and his elder father as well.
With flowers and sweetmeats, with jewels and abundant gold, with cattle and garments, O lord of kings, and with sundry things to each one's desire.
Then arose the proclamation of the holy day, as though propping up the heavens, O Bhārata, sacred, gladdening to friends, and sweet to the ear.
There, O king, the speech of the twice-born who knew the Vedas, sounding like the cry of swans, was heard, rich in meaning, in words, and in syllables.
Then the thunder of kettledrums and the delightful sound of conches, the clamor of those who proclaimed victory, broke forth there, O sovereign.
And when the assembly of the twice-born had fallen silent there once more, the rākṣasa Cārvāka, disguised as a brāhmaṇa, addressed the king.
There the friend of Duryodhana, cloaked in the guise of a mendicant—a Sāṃkhya ascetic, tuft-haired and bearing the triple staff, brazen and devoid of fear—
surrounded then by all the twice-born, more than a thousand, eager to pronounce their blessings, steadfast in austerity and restraint, O lord of kings—
that wicked one, wishing evil upon the high-souled Pāṇḍavas, without so much as consulting those twice-born ones, spoke thus to the king:
"All these twice-born ones declare, laying their words upon me: Shame be upon you, a base king, a slayer of your own kin!
What good is the kingdom to you, son of Kuntī, having wrought this ruin of your kindred and slain your elders? Death were better than to live."
Hearing this from that dreadful rākṣasa, the twice-born ones were sorely shaken and cried out, stung by his words.
Then all those brāhmaṇas, and King Yudhiṣṭhira too, abashed and deeply troubled, fell silent, O lord of the people.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Be gracious to me, my lords, as I bow and beseech you. I am stricken with calamity and have but now returned; you ought not to reproach me.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, O king, O lord of the people, all those brāhmaṇas said: "This is not our word. May good fortune be yours, O sovereign!"
And those high-souled brāhmaṇas, knowers of the Vedas, made pure by austerities, then knew him for what he was with the eye of insight.
The brāhmaṇas said: This is the friend of Duryodhana, a rākṣasa named Cārvāka, who in the guise of a wandering ascetic seeks to do that one's bidding.
We do not speak thus, O righteous one; let such fear of yours depart. May welfare attend upon you together with your brothers.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then all those brāhmaṇas, swollen with wrath, the pure-souled ones, with cries of "huṃ" and with rebukes struck down the wicked rākṣasa.
Burnt up by the fiery power of those expounders of the Veda, he fell, like a budding tree scorched by the thunderbolt of great Indra.
Honored, the twice-born departed, having saluted the king; and the king, the Pāṇḍava, with his company of friends, was filled with joy.
Vāsudeva said: The brāhmaṇas, dear one, are ever to be honored by me in this world. These are gods who walk the earth, whose poison is in their speech, yet easily made gracious.
Long ago, dear one, in the Kṛta age, a rākṣasa named Cārvāka, O mighty-armed one, performed austerities at Badarī for many years.
Offered a boon by Brahmā again and again, he chose, O Bhārata, safety from all living beings.
The Lord of the world then granted him that matchless boon—safety from all beings—save only in the case of contempt for the twice-born.
But that wicked rākṣasa, having gained the boon, of boundless prowess, fierce in his deeds and mighty in strength, set himself to torment the gods.
Then the gods, assembling, sore harried by his might, spoke this to Brahmā, seeking the destruction of that rākṣasa:
The imperishable god said to them: A means has been ordained by me whereby his death shall come about before long, O Bhārata.
A king named Duryodhana shall be his friend, O sovereign; bound by affection for him, this one will hold the brāhmaṇas in contempt.
Then the twice-born, enraged and provoked by his outrage, mighty in speech, shall burn up the wicked one, and so he shall come to destruction.
Here lies that rākṣasa Cārvāka, slain by the rod of Brahman, O best of kings; grieve not, O bull of the Bharatas.
Your kinsmen, O sovereign, were slain by the law of the warrior, and the high-souled heroes, those bulls among kṣatriyas, have gone to heaven.
Therefore stand firm in welfare; let no weariness be yours, O steadfast one. Smite your foes, protect your subjects, and sustain the twice-born.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the king, son of Kuntī, his anger gone and his fever gone, glad of heart, sat down facing east upon a supreme golden seat.
Facing him, upon a couch spread with a sumptuous covering, sat the two tamers of foes, Sātyaki and Vāsudeva.
Placing the king between them, the two great-souled ones, Bhīmasena and Arjuna, seated themselves upon two smooth jewelled stools.
Upon a bright ivory couch-seat adorned with Jāmbūnada gold, Pṛthā too sat together with Sahadeva and Nakula.
Sudharman, Vidura, Dhaumya, and Dhṛtarāṣṭra of the Kuru line seated themselves, each upon a separate seat blazing like fire.
Yuyutsu, Saṃjaya, and the renowned Gāndhārī—all of them took their places there where King Dhṛtarāṣṭra sat.
Seated there, the righteous one touched white flowers, svastika emblems, unbroken grains, the earth, gold, silver, and gems.
Then all the subjects, placing the household priest at their head, came bearing many auspicious offerings to behold the king of righteousness.
They brought earth and gold and jewels of many kinds, and the consecration-vessel filled with every requisite for the rite.
There were full jars of gold, of udumbara wood, of silver, and of earthenware, with flowers, parched grain, kuśa grass, and milk-curds.
There were kindling-sticks of śamī, palāśa, and puṃnāga wood, honey and clarified butter, a ladle of udumbara wood, and conches adorned with gold.
Authorized by the Dāśārha, the household priest Dhaumya there smeared and consecrated by the prescribed marks an altar sloping toward the northeast.
Upon a smooth seat covered over with a tiger's skin, auspicious on every side, firm-footed and steady, shining bright as the oblation-eating fire,
having seated the great-souled one and Kṛṣṇā, the daughter of Drupada, the wise priest offered into the purifying fire with rite and mantra duly observed.
He consecrated Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, as lord of the earth; and so did the royal sage Dhṛtarāṣṭra and all the subjects.
Then they caused cymbals, drums, and kettledrums to resound; and the king of righteousness accepted all of it according to the law.

And, generous with abundant gifts, he honored them all according to the ordinance; then with a thousand gold pieces he had the brāhmaṇas pronounce blessings—those accomplished in Vedic study and endowed with good character and conduct.
Well pleased, O king, the brāhmaṇas pronounced blessing and victory, and, crying out like swans, they extolled Yudhiṣṭhira:
"Mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Pāṇḍu, by good fortune you are victorious! By good fortune, O greatly radiant one, you have attained your own dharma by your valor.
By good fortune the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva and Bhīmasena son of Pāṇḍu, and you too, O king, are well, and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī as well.
Delivered from this slaughter of heroes, your foes slain in battle, swiftly now, O son of Pāṇḍu, perform the duties that the time to come requires."
Then, honored in return by the virtuous, Yudhiṣṭhira the king of righteousness took possession of the great kingdom together with his friends, O Bhārata.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard that speech of the subjects, fitting to the place and the time, King Yudhiṣṭhira then spoke this reply in answer.
"Blessed in the world are the sons of Pāṇḍu, whose virtues—whether truly theirs or not—the foremost of brāhmaṇas, gathered here, proclaim.
Surely we are worthy of your favor—such is my conviction—since, free of envy, you call us thus endowed with merit.
The great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra is our father and our highest deity; those who wish my pleasure must abide by his command and his good will.
For this very purpose I go on living, after having wrought the great slaughter of my kinsmen: that I, ever unwearied, must render him service.
And if I am worthy of the favor of you, my friends, then toward Dhṛtarāṣṭra you ought to conduct yourselves just as before.
For he is the lord of the world, of you, and of myself; to him alone belongs the whole earth, and the Pāṇḍavas one and all. This word of mine you must take to heart.

"Having attended upon the king, go now as you please." So dismissing all the townsfolk and country-folk, the joy of the Kurus, scion of the Kauravas, appointed Bhīmasena to the office of heir-apparent.
For counsel and decision and the deliberation of the sixfold policy of state, he gladly appointed Vidura, who was perfect in wisdom.
To the oversight of what was done and left undone, and to the reckoning of income and expenditure, he assigned Saṃjaya, prosperous and endowed with abundant virtues.
To the mustering of the army, the rations and the wages, and the supervision of the workmen, the king assigned Nakula.
To the repelling of hostile armies and the crushing of the insolent, the great king Yudhiṣṭhira appointed Phalguna.
To the Vedic rites of the twice-born and to other sacred duties, the scorcher of foes appointed Dhaumya, the best of household priests.
Sahadeva he appointed to remain ever at his side; for by him the king was to be guarded in every circumstance, O lord of peoples.
Whomever he judged fit for whatever tasks, to those very tasks the lord of earth, well pleased, appointed them.
To Vidura, Saṃjaya, and the great-minded Yuyutsu, the slayer of enemy heroes, righteous-souled and devoted to dharma, spoke thus:
"Whatever needs to be done from one occasion to the next for this king, my father, all of it you must accomplish, vigilant and exactly as is fitting.
And whatever affairs of the townsfolk and country-folk arise from day to day, those you must, with the king's leave, attend to according to the law."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, noble of mind, had the śrāddha rites performed, each separately, for those of his kinsmen who had fallen in the battle.
King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, of great renown, gave for his sons the funeral offerings, complete with every desirable thing—food, cattle, wealth, and jewels of varied kinds and great worth.
And Yudhiṣṭhira, for Karṇa and for the great-souled Droṇa, for Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Abhimanyu, and for the rākṣasa son of Hiḍimbā,
and for Virāṭa and the rest of his helpful friends, and for Drupada and the sons of Draupadī—together with Draupadī he made the offerings.
Designating thousands of brāhmaṇas, each one singly in turn, he gratified them with wealth and garments, with jewels and with cattle.
And for those other rulers of earth who had no kinsfolk left to them, the king, naming each one, performed the rites for the dead.
Assembly-halls and many watering-stations and tanks the son of Pāṇḍu caused to be made as funerary memorials for all his friends.
Thus freed of his debt to them, and having attained beyond reproach among the worlds, the king became one who had fulfilled his duty, governing his subjects with righteousness.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra as before, and Gāndhārī and Vidura likewise, and all the Kaurava ministers and retainers, he honored fittingly.
And whatever women there were whose heroes were slain, whose sons were slain, all of them the compassionate Kaurava king honored and protected.
And to the wretched, the blind, and the helpless, with houses, clothing, and food, the king, devoted to kindness, the sovereign, showed his grace.
Having conquered the whole earth and discharged his debt against his foes, King Yudhiṣṭhira, without a rival and at ease, dwelt in contentment.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Consecrated and having gained the kingdom, the greatly wise Yudhiṣṭhira, purified and with palms joined, spoke to the lotus-eyed Dāśārha:
"By your grace, O Kṛṣṇa, by your statecraft and your strength, by your wisdom, O tiger of the Yadus, and by your valor,
this kingdom of my fathers and forefathers has been regained by me. Homage to you, O lotus-eyed one, again and again, O subduer of foes!
You alone they call the Puruṣa; you they call the lord of the Sātvatas; with names of many kinds the supreme sages praise you.
Maker of all, homage be to you; Soul of all, source of all—Viṣṇu, Jiṣṇu, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Vaikuṇṭha, supreme among beings!
In the ancient age you entered the womb of Aditi for seven nights; you alone are the child of Pṛśni, and they call you also Triyuga, he of the three ages.
You are called Śuciśravas, Hṛṣīkeśa, Ghṛtārci, and Haṃsa; three-eyed, you are the one Śambhu, the all-pervading, and Dāmodara as well.
You are the Boar, Agni, Bṛhadbhānu of mighty radiance, the bull Vṛṣaṇa, marked by the emblem of Tārkṣya; the vanquisher of armies, the Puruṣa, Śipiviṣṭa, the wide-striding one.
Lord of speech, the terrible, the army-leader, the true one, giver of food and strength, the hidden one; the unfallen, the overthrower of foes, the maker and unmaker, the bull.
You are Kṛtavartman, you are the Mountain, Vṛṣagarbha, Vṛṣākapi; dweller in the sea, the Wave, the three-peaked, threefold-abode, threefold, the unfallen.

Sovereign, the vast, the self-ruling, and king of the gods; giver of dharma, the becoming; the all-pervading, the Earth, the all-surpassing, Kṛṣṇa, and the one whose path is dark-tracked—that too are you.
The doer of right sacrifice, the healer, the Whirlpool, Kapila, and the Dwarf are you; the Sacrifice, the steadfast, the Bird, and Jayatsena—so you are called.
Śikhaṇḍin, Nahuṣa, Babhru, you are the toucher of heaven, Punarvasu; Subabhru, the Ox, Rukma are you, Suṣeṇa, and likewise the Drum.
Rim of the sunbeams, the radiant Lotus, the Lotus-flower, the bearer of flowers; the Ṛbhu, the all-pervading, subtlest of all are you, and as the Sāvitra hymn you are recited.
You are the ocean of waters, you are Brahmā, the purifying, the abode, and the bow; they call you Hiraṇyagarbha, the Svadhā and the Svāhā, O Keśava.

You are the womb of this all and its dissolution, O Kṛṣṇa; you alone bring forth this universe in the beginning, and this universe lies under your sway, O womb of all. Homage be to you, who bear in your hands the Śārṅga bow, the discus, and the sword!

Praised thus by the king of righteousness in the midst of the assembly, the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa, well pleased, the foremost of the Yādavas, greeted that Bhārata, the eldest son of Pāṇḍu, with words full and gracious.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the king dismissed all his subjects, and, given leave, they returned each to his own dwelling.
Then the wise King Yudhiṣṭhira, comforting Bhīma of terrible prowess, and Arjuna, and the twins, spoke to them:
"Your bodies hacked by the enemy with weapons of every kind in the great battle, you have grown utterly weary, sorely tormented by grief and wrath.
On my account, O best of men, you endured wretched dwellings in the forest, as though you were base-born men.
Now enjoy this victory at your ease and to your heart's content; rested and recollected, tomorrow I shall meet with you again."
Then the palace of Duryodhana, graced with lofty mansions, strewn with many jewels and thronged with serving-women and serving-men,
sanctioned by Dhṛtarāṣṭra and bestowed by his brother, the mighty-armed Vṛkodara took into his possession, as Maghavat took Mount Mandara.
And as with Duryodhana's palace, so with Duḥśāsana's, ringed with rows of mansions and adorned with golden archways,
filled with serving-women and serving-men and abounding in wealth and grain—the mighty-armed Arjuna took into his possession by the king's command.
The dwelling of Durmarṣaṇa, finer than the house of Duḥśāsana, resembling the palace of Kubera and adorned with gems and gold,
the king of righteousness, Yudhiṣṭhira, well pleased, O great king, gave to Nakula, worthy of the best, who had been worn thin in the great forest.
And the splendid foremost mansion of Durmukha, gold-adorned, full of women with eyes like lotus-petals and crowded with couches,
he bestowed upon Sahadeva, ever the doer of his pleasure; and receiving it, he rejoiced as the giver of wealth rejoiced in gaining Kailāsa.
Yuyutsu and Vidura, and Saṃjaya of great splendor, and Sudharmā and Dhaumya too—each departed to his own dwelling.
Together with Sātyaki, Śauri, that tiger among men, entered Arjuna's dwelling, as a tiger enters a mountain cave.
There, well provided with food, dishes, and drink, they rested at ease; and waking refreshed, they attended upon King Yudhiṣṭhira.
Janamejaya said: When the mighty-spirited Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira had won the kingdom, whatever else he did, O brāhmaṇa, that you ought now to tell me.
And whatever the blessed Hṛṣīkeśa, the supreme teacher of the three worlds, that hero, did—that too, O sage, you ought to expound.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hear, O lord of kings, faultless one, as I truly recount what the Pāṇḍavas did, with Vāsudeva set before them.
Having won the kingdom, the mighty-spirited Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira established the four varṇas, fittingly, each in its own dharma.
And to a thousand great-souled brāhmaṇas who had completed their studentship, the Pāṇḍava had a thousand niṣkas of gold proclaimed for each one.
Likewise he satisfied with their desires his dependents, his servants, those who had taken refuge with him, and his guests, even the destitute and the petty disputants.
To Dhaumya, his household priest, he gave cattle by the ten thousand, and wealth, gold, silver, and garments of many kinds.
And toward Kṛpa, O great king, he conducted himself as toward a teacher; and that righteous one of steadfast vows did honor to Vidura.
With food, dishes, and drink of many kinds, with garments, beds, and seats, that best of givers gladdened all who had taken refuge with him.
Having restored what had been won to peace, that king of great renown, O best of kings, did honor to Yuyutsu, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Having entrusted that kingdom to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, to Gāndhārī, and to Vidura, King Yudhiṣṭhira, O king, dwelt as though at ease.
And having thus brought the whole city to contentment, O Janamejaya, he approached the great-souled Vāsudeva with palms joined in reverence.
Then upon a great couch, adorned with jewels and gold, he beheld Kṛṣṇa seated, dark as a rain-cloud upon Meru.
Blazing with his beauty, adorned with divine ornaments, wrapped in yellow silk—like a jewel set within gold.
Resplendent with the Kaustubha jewel resting upon his breast, like the eastern mountain crowned by the rising sun—he for whom no likeness exists anywhere in the three worlds.
Approaching that great-souled one, Viṣṇu in human form, he then, sweet of speech, spoke this with a smile.
Has your night passed in comfort, O best of the wise? Are all your faculties of knowledge serene, O Acyuta?
For relying upon that divine intelligence of yours, O best of the wise, we have attained the kingdom, and the earth abides under our sway.
By your grace, O blessed one whose stride ranges through the three worlds, victory has been won and foremost glory; nor have we fallen from dharma.
But to Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira, speaking thus, the blessed one said nothing at all; he passed instead into meditation.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What is this great marvel? You are meditating, O you of immeasurable valor. Is all well with these three worlds, O refuge of the worlds?
Having taken up the fourth path of meditation, O supreme Person, you have withdrawn, O god; therefore my mind is filled with wonder.
For the breath of fivefold function that moves within your body has been restrained by you, and all your senses have been set within the mind.
Your senses and your mind have been gathered into the intellect, and that whole host, O god, has been merged by you into the Knower of the Field.
The hairs of your body do not stir; your intellect is steady, and so your mind. You have become as a post, a wall, a stone, motionless and free of all striving, O Mādhava.
As a lamp set in a windless place burns unflickering, O Acyuta, so are you, O blessed god, unwavering and firm in resolve.
If I am worthy here to hear it, and if it is no secret of yours, cut away my doubt, O god, for I have taken refuge in you and beseech you.
For you are the maker and the unmaker; you are the perishable and the imperishable; you are without beginning or end, and the primordial one—you alone, O supreme Person.
To me who have taken refuge in you, a devotee bowing with my head, tell the true nature of this meditation, O best of the upholders of dharma.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, having set his mind, intellect, and senses back upon their own objects, the blessed one, the younger brother of Vāsava, said this with a smile.
Lying upon his bed of arrows, Bhīṣma, that tiger among men, like a fire sinking into stillness, meditates upon me; therefore my mind has gone toward him.
He whose twang of bowstring and slap of palm-guard, like the crashing of a thunderbolt, even the king of the gods could not endure—toward him have I gone in mind.
He who, charging swiftly upon the whole circle of kings, long ago carried off three maidens—toward him have I gone in mind.
He who fought against the Bhārgava for three-and-twenty days and nights, and was not overcome by Rāma—toward him have I gone in mind.
That prince whom Gaṅgā bore in her womb by ordained law, the disciple of Vasiṣṭha—toward him, my dear, toward him, O king, have I gone in mind.
That mighty-spirited, wise one who holds the divine weapons and the four Vedas with their ancillary sciences—toward him have I gone in mind.
The beloved disciple of Rāma the son of Jamadagni, O Pāṇḍava, the repository of all branches of knowledge—toward him have I gone in mind.
Having made the whole company of his senses one, restraining his mind by his understanding, he has come to me for refuge; therefore my mind has gone toward him.
For he, O bull among men, knows the past, the future, and the present—that best of the upholders of dharma; therefore my mind has gone toward him.
For when that tiger among men has gone to heaven by his own deeds, the earth, O Pārtha, will be like a night whose moon has set.
Therefore, Yudhiṣṭhira, go to Bhīṣma, the son of Gaṅgā, of terrible prowess, clasp his feet, and ask whatever is in your mind.
Ask him of the fourfold Vedic lore, of the fourfold sacrificial priesthood, of the four stages of life, and of the dharma of the four varṇas, O lord of the earth.
When Bhīṣma, that bearer of the Kauravas' burden, has set like the sun, these branches of knowledge will grow scant; therefore I urge you on.
Hearing that true and excellent speech of Vāsudeva, the knower of dharma, his throat choked with tears, said this to Janārdana.
What you have said concerning the power of Bhīṣma, O Mādhava, is even so; of this there is no doubt in me, O giver of honor.
For the great fortune of Bhīṣma and the power of that great soul have been heard by me from the lips of great-souled brāhmaṇas as they recounted them.
And what you, the maker of the worlds, declare, O slayer of foes, that word is beyond all questioning, O joy of the Yādavas.
Yet since your mind is set upon doing me grace, O Mādhava, placing you before us, we shall go to behold Bhīṣma.
When the blessed sun has turned, he will depart to the other worlds; therefore, O mighty-armed one, the Kaurava deserves the sight of you.
For the sight of you, the primordial god, the perishable and the imperishable alike, would be his gain; for you are the treasure-house made of Brahman.
Hearing this speech of Dharmarāja, the slayer of Madhu said to Sātyaki, who stood at his side, "Let my chariot be yoked."
Then Sātyaki, going forth from the presence of Keśava, said to Dāruka, "Let Kṛṣṇa's chariot be yoked."
Hearing at once the word of Sātyaki, he made ready the finest chariot, its body adorned with gold, embellished with facets of cat's-eye and crystal, its wheels bound with gold;
radiant as the rays of the sun, swift-going, adorned with diverse and varied gems and jewels, blazing like the newly risen sun, bearing its wondrous Garuḍa-banner and its pennons;
yoked well with the finest horses led by Sugrīva and Sainya, swift as thought, their bodies adorned with gold—Dāruka, with palms joined, announced it ready to Acyuta, O lion among kings.
Janamejaya said: But lying upon his bed of arrows, the grandsire of the Bharatas, how did he relinquish his body, and what yoga did he hold to?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Listen attentively, O king, having become pure and composed, to the relinquishing of his body by the great-souled Bhīṣma, O tiger of the Kurus.
As soon as the sun had turned upon its northern course, he, fully composed, gathered his self into the Self alone.
Like the sun with its rays spread wide, Bhīṣma, pierced by hundreds of arrows, lay invested with surpassing splendor, surrounded by the foremost of brāhmaṇas.
By Vyāsa renowned for Vedic lore, by Nārada the divine sage, by Devasthāna, by Vātsya, and by Aśmaka and Sumantu;
by these and by other hosts of sages, greatly blessed and great of soul, who held faith and self-restraint foremost, he was encircled as the moon by the planets.
And Bhīṣma, that tiger among men, lying upon his bed of arrows, with deed, with mind, and with speech, meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, abiding with palms joined.
With a full-resounding voice he praised the slayer of Madhu, the lord of yoga, the lotus-naveled, Viṣṇu, the ever-victorious, the lord of the world.
With palms joined, having become pure, that foremost of those skilled in speech, Bhīṣma, supremely righteous of soul, then hymned the Lord Vāsudeva.
"The speech I would set forth, seeking to propitiate Kṛṣṇa—by that speech, both expansive and concise, may the supreme Person be pleased.
Pure, intent upon him, having yoked my whole self with all my being, I take refuge in that Lord of creatures, the Swan who dwells in purity, the supreme one set on high.
In whom all beings abide and into whom they enter, become his qualities, within the Lord of beings, as beads of gems upon a thread.
On whom, the eternal, outstretched, firm thread, the universe rests like a garland—the All, woven of being and non-being, upon him whose limbs are all things, the maker of all.
Whom they call Hari, thousand-headed, with a thousand feet and eyes, the god Nārāyaṇa, the supreme refuge of the universe.
The subtlest of the subtle, the most massive of the massive, the weightiest of the weighty, and the best even of the good.
Whom in the hymns and the recitations, in the sittings and the secret teachings, they extol as the doer of true deeds, the Truth among the true Sāman chants.
The fourfold one in his four forms, abiding in goodness, the lord of the Sātvatas, whom they worship as god with divine and secret supreme names.
The god whom the goddess Devakī brought forth from Vasudeva, for the safeguarding of the earthly Veda, as the firestick brings forth blazing fire.
Whom the undistracted one, free of all craving, having worshipped Govinda for the sake of the infinite, beholds as the self, stainless, dwelling within his own self.
In ancient lore he is proclaimed the Person; at the beginnings of the ages he is proclaimed Brahmā; at the dissolution he is proclaimed Saṃkarṣaṇa—him, worthy of worship, we worship.
Whose action surpasses Vāyu's and Indra's, whose splendor surpasses the sun's and fire's, whose self surpasses intellect and the senses—in him, the Lord of creatures, I take refuge.
Whom indeed they call the maker of all, the lord of the world both moving and unmoving, the overseer of the universe, the imperishable, the supreme abode.
To him whom Aditi bore as a golden-hued embryo, destroyer of the Daityas, the one brought forth in twelvefold form—to him whose Self is the Sun, homage.
To him who in the bright fortnight gladdens the gods and in the dark fortnight the ancestors with the nectar, and who is king over the twice-born—to him whose Self is the Moon, homage.
To the Person beyond the great darkness, shining with flame, whom having known a man transcends death—to him whose Self is the Knowable, homage.
To him, the Vast, whom they hymn in the bṛhatī verse and in the recitation, in the fire and in the great sacrifice, whom assemblies of brahmins chant—to him whose Self is the Veda, homage.
To him whose abode is Ṛk, Yajus, and Sāman, whose form is the fivefold oblation, whom they extend as the seven-threaded rite—to him whose Self is the Sacrifice, homage.

To him who is the fair-winged bird named the Yajus, whose body is the chant, whose head is the trivṛt hymn, whose eyes are the Rathaṃtara and Bṛhat sāmans—to him whose Self is the Praise-song, homage.
To him who was born in the thousand-pressing session as the seer of the world's creators, a golden-hued bird—to him whose Self is the Swan, homage.
To him whose limbs are the words, whose joints are the junctures, marked by vowels and consonants, whom they call the eternal Imperishable Syllable—to him whose Self is Speech, homage.
To him who builds up the dike of the good with cosmic order, the womb of immortality, and with the limbs of dharma, purpose, and right conduct—to him whose Self is Truth, homage.
To him whom those who follow diverse duties, seeking the diverse fruits of duty, worship through their diverse observances—to him whose Self is Dharma, homage.
To him, the Unmanifest abiding in the manifest, whom the great seers seek out, the Knower of the field seated within the field—to him whose Self is the Field, homage.
To him whom the Sāṃkhyas declare to be the seeing Self, abiding in the self, encompassed by the sixteen constituents and reckoned the seventeenth—to him whose Self is Sāṃkhya, homage.
To him whom the sleepless, who have mastered the breath, who are established in purity, with senses restrained, behold as a light while in meditation—to him whose Self is Yoga, homage.
To him whom, when both demerit and merit have ceased, the tranquil renouncers, freed from fear of rebirth, attain—to him whose Self is Liberation, homage.
To him who, at the close of a thousand ages, with blazing flame as the radiant fire, devours all beings—to him whose Self is the Terrible, homage.
To him who, having devoured all beings and made the world a single ocean, sleeps alone as a child—to him whose Self is Illusion, homage.
To that thousand-headed Person of measureless Self, whose Self is the yoga-slumber that circles round the four oceans, homage.
To him, the lotus-eyed one, in whose single lotus rising from the navel of the Unborn the whole universe is established—to him whose Self is the Lotus, homage.
To him in whose hair are the rain-clouds, in the joints of whose every limb are the rivers, and in whose belly are the four oceans—to him whose Self is the Waters, homage.
To him who revolves through the ages by his portions—days, seasons, fortnights, and years—the maker of creation and dissolution—to him whose Self is Time, homage.
To him whose mouth is the brahmins, whose arms are the warriors, whose whole thighs and belly are the commoners, and on whose feet the śūdras rest—to him whose Self is the social orders, homage.
To him whose mouth is Agni, whose head is the sky, whose navel is space, whose feet are the earth, whose eye is the Sun, and whose ears are the quarters—to him whose Self is the worlds, homage.
To him whom they declare, by the Vaiśeṣika categories, to be the guardian of the objects for those engaged amid sense-objects—to him whose Self is the Protector, homage.
To him who, composed of food, drink, and fuel, increasing the sap and the vital breath, sustains all beings—to him whose Self is the Breath of Life, homage.
To him who is beyond Time, beyond the sacrifice, beyond both being and non-being, beginningless yet the beginning of the universe—to him whose Self is the All, homage.
To him who deludes living beings with the bonds of affection and passion, for the sake of preserving creation—to him whose Self is Delusion, homage.
To him whom the knowers reach, having known this self-knowledge, the knowledge abiding within the five—to him whose Self is Knowledge, homage.
To him of immeasurable body, with infinite eyes on every side, boundless and beyond all measure—to him whose Self is the Object of Contemplation, homage.
To him with matted locks, bearing the staff, ever pot-bellied in form, girded with the water-pot—to him whose Self is Brahmā, homage.
To him who bears the trident, lord of the gods, the three-eyed great one, smeared with ashes, his liṅga upraised—to him whose Self is Rudra, homage.
To him who has become the Self of the five elements, the Self of the origin and end of beings, free from anger, malice, and delusion—to him whose Self is Peace, homage.
To him in whom is all, from whom is all, who is all, who is on every side, and who is eternally made of all—to him whose Self is the Whole, homage.
O Maker of all, homage be to you, Self of all, source of all; you are the deliverance of beings, standing beyond the five elements.
Homage to you in the three worlds, homage to you in the three beyond, homage to you in all the quarters—for you are the supreme refuge of all.
Homage to you, Lord Viṣṇu, origin and dissolution of the worlds; for you, Hṛṣīkeśa, are the maker and the unconquered destroyer.
By that grace I behold your divine manifestations upon the three paths, and I behold in its very truth that eternal form of yours.
By your head the heaven is pervaded, by your feet the goddess Earth, and by your stride the three worlds—you are the eternal Person.
For those who pay homage to Govinda, the imperishable one robed in yellow and resembling the flax-flower, no fear exists.
As truth is pervaded by Viṣṇu, as the oblation is pervaded by Viṣṇu, as all is pervaded by Viṣṇu—so let my sin be destroyed.
For the devotee who has taken refuge in you and longs to win the goal he desires—meditate upon that which is his highest good, O lotus-eyed one, best of gods.
Thus is Viṣṇu praised, the womb of knowledge and austerity yet himself unborn; worshipped with the sacrifice of speech, may the god Janārdana be gracious to me.
Having spoken this much, his mind wholly fixed upon him, Bhīṣma then made obeisance to Kṛṣṇa with the single word "Homage."
And Mādhava, having through his yogic power perceived Bhīṣma's devotion, departed—Hari going to bestow the divine knowledge that beholds the three times.
When that utterance had ceased, those expounders of the sacred word, their throats choked with tears, then honored the great-minded Bhīṣma with their words.
And those foremost of brahmins, praising Keśava, the supreme Person, all softly extolled Bhīṣma as well, again and again.
And the supreme Person, having recognized Bhīṣma's devout discipline, rose at once with delight and mounted his chariot.
Keśava and Sātyaki went in one chariot; in another rode the two great-souled ones, Yudhiṣṭhira and Dhanaṃjaya.
Bhīmasena and the twins together mounted one chariot, while Kṛpa, Yuyutsu, and the charioteer Saṃjaya took another.
Those bulls among men set forth in chariots vast as cities, making the earth tremble with the mighty thunder of their wheel-rims.

Then that best of men, glad of heart, heard along the way the words uttered by the brahmins in your favor; and the slayer of Keśin, with gladdened mind, greeted in return the other folk who bowed before him with joined palms.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Hṛṣīkeśa, and King Yudhiṣṭhira, and Kṛpa and all the rest, and the four Pāṇḍavas as well—
in their chariots vast as cities, splendid with pennants and banners, swiftly went to Kurukṣetra, drawn by fleet-footed horses.
They came down upon Kurukṣetra, thick with hair, marrow, and bones, where those great-souled warriors had laid down their bodies—
heaped as if with mountains formed of the bodies and bones of elephants and horses, and strewn with men's skulls like conch-shells.
Covered with thousands of funeral pyres, cluttered with armor and weapons, it was like a banqueting-ground of Death, just then feasted upon and cast aside.
Beholding Kurukṣetra, roamed by hosts of spirits and frequented by troops of rākṣasas, those great chariot-warriors swiftly went on.
As he went, the mighty-armed delight of all the Yādavas spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira of the valor of the son of Jamadagni.
"Yonder, O Pārtha, seen from afar, are those five lakes of Rāma, in which he satisfied the ancestors with the blood of the warriors.
Having thrice-seven times made the earth free of warriors, the lord Rāma then desisted here from that deed."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "In that you tell me the earth was then made thrice-seven times free of warriors by Rāma—herein lies a great doubt of mine.
When the seed of the warrior race had been burned away by Rāma, O bull of the Yadus, how came the warrior race once more into being, O you of boundless valor?
How was the warrior race rooted out by the great-souled, venerable Rāma, O bull of the Yadus, and how did it again attain increase?"
"For in the great Bhārata war warriors were slain by the millions, and the earth thus came to be strewn with warriors, O best of speakers.
Sever this doubt of mine thus, O scion of Vṛṣṇi, you whose banner bears Garuḍa; for from you, Kṛṣṇa, younger brother of Vāsava, comes our highest authority."

Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, even as he journeyed on, the lord, elder brother of Gada, recounted to him in full and truly—to Yudhiṣṭhira of matchless might—how it was that the earth came to be thronged with warriors.
Vāsudeva said: Hear, O son of Kuntī, so much of Rāma as I have heard from the great seers as they told the cause of it and of his birth.
and how warriors were slain by the millions by the son of Jamadagni—those who, having sprung up again in the royal lines, were slain once more in the Bhārata war.
Jahnu's son was Ajahnu, and his son was Ballava; his son was the law-knowing king named Kuśika.
On earth, the peer of the thousand-eyed god, he undertook fierce austerity, with the wish: "May I obtain a son unconquered, a lord of the three worlds."
Seeing him fierce in austerity, the thousand-eyed Purandara, able himself to be begotten as a son, came in person, O Bhārata.
That lord over the lords of the worlds attained sonship to him, O king; the son who was born, named Gādhi, descended of Kuśika, was the chastiser of Pāka.
To him was born a daughter named Satyavatī, O sovereign king; and the lord Gādhi gave her to Ṛcīka, son of the sage Aurva.
Then well pleased, O son of Kuntī, delight of the Kurus, the descendant of Bhṛgu cooked a sacrificial porridge for the sake of a son, and one likewise for Gādhi.
And summoning his wife, Ṛcīka of the line of Bhṛgu then said: "This porridge is to be consumed by you, and this one by your mother.
To her will be born a radiant son, a bull among warriors, unconquerable by warriors in the world, a slayer of the bulls among warriors.
And for you too, fair lady, this porridge will ordain a son, steadfast, endowed with austerity, of tranquil nature, the foremost of the twice-born."
Having spoken thus to his wife, Ṛcīka, the delight of the Bhṛgus, wise and devoted to austerity, went away into the forest.
At this very time King Gādhi, bent on a pilgrimage to the holy fords, arrived together with his wife at the hermitage of Ṛcīka.
Taking up the two portions of porridge, O king, Satyavatī then, calm and following her husband's word, gladly presented them to her mother.
But her mother, O son of Kuntī, gave her own portion to her daughter, and unknowingly took her daughter's portion for herself.
Then Satyavatī bore in her womb the embryo destined to be the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas, of blazing form and terrible to behold.
Seeing her thus, Ṛcīka, perceiving the matter by the power of meditation, then spoke to his fair-complexioned wife, O tiger among kings.
"You have been deceived by your mother, gentle lady, through the exchange of the sacrificial offerings; for now a son of cruel deeds and mighty strength shall be born to you.
And a brother shall be born to you who is the very embodiment of Brahman, rich in austerity; for through my penance I infused into that offering the whole power of the sacred word."
Thus addressed by her husband, the blessed Satyavatī then fell at his feet with her head bowed and, trembling, spoke these words:
"You ought not, O blessed one, to utter today such words as these—'You shall obtain a son who is a degenerate among Brahmins,' O great sage."
Ṛcīka said: "This was not the wish I intended in your case, gentle lady; that your son should be of fierce deeds—the cause of this is the offering and your mother."

Satyavatī said: "Were you to wish it, O sage, you could create whole worlds; how much more easily then could I, through you, obtain a son who is peaceable in spirit and upright, O best of those who recite the sacred prayers."
Ṛcīka said: "Never before, gentle lady, have I spoken a false word even in jest—how much less when I have kindled the fire and prepared the offering with sacred mantras.

Satyavatī said: "Let it be, then, that such a one shall be my grandson—and yours as well; but may I obtain a son who is peaceable in spirit and upright, O best of those who recite the sacred prayers."
Ṛcīka said: "To me there is no difference between son and grandson, O fair-complexioned one; even as you have spoken, gentle lady, so shall it come to pass."
Vāsudeva said: Then Satyavatī gave birth to a son of the line of Bhṛgu—Jamadagni, devoted to austerity, tranquil, and peaceable in spirit.
And Gādhi, son of Kuśika, obtained as his heir Viśvāmitra, equal to the Brahmin sages and endowed with the whole power of the sacred word.
Jamadagni, son of Ṛcīka, begot the most terrible Rāma—master of every branch of learning, supreme, accomplished in the science of archery, the slayer of the Kṣatriyas, blazing like fire.
Now at that very time there lived the mighty son of Kṛtavīrya, Arjuna by name, a lustrous Kṣatriya of the lineage of the Haihayas.
He ruled the whole earth with its seven continents and its cities by the strength of his own arms and weapons in battle, and by the highest righteousness.
O Kaurava, when he was begged by the hungry Citrabhānu—the Fire—that valiant one of a thousand arms granted alms to Agni.
With his arrows the valiant king set ablaze villages, towns, cowherds' settlements, and cities, for Citrabhānu was eager to consume them in flame.
Through the power of that lord among men, Kārtavīrya, the great-glowing Fire burned the mountains and forests as well.
Fanned by the wind, Citrabhānu, together with the Haihaya, burned the deserted forest hermitage of the son of Varuṇa.
Then, O unfallen one, when his hermitage had been burned by Kārtavīrya, the valiant sage Āpava in his wrath cursed Arjuna, O great king:
"Because in your folly you did not spare this forest of mine but let it be burned, therefore in battle, O Arjuna, Rāma shall sever your arms."
Yet Arjuna, O great king, was mighty, ever peaceable in spirit, devoted to the Brahmins, a refuge to those who sought it, generous, and heroic, O descendant of Bharata.
His sons were exceedingly strong, but through the curse they became the instruments of their father's slaying—arrogant they were, and cruel at all times.
They carried off the calf of Jamadagni's cow, O bull of the Bharatas, without the knowledge of the wise Kārtavīrya, lord of the Haihayas.
Then the son of Jamadagni, endowed with manly valor, severed the arms of Arjuna and brought back to his own hermitage the lowing calf from their inner apartments, O lord of kings, that mighty lord.
But those witless sons of Arjuna then banded together and went, unannounced, to the hermitage of the great-souled Jamadagni.
With their broad-headed arrows they struck off his head from his body, O ruler of men, while the great-souled Rāma had gone out to gather firewood and kuśa grass.
Then, in his fury at his father's murder, Rāma, filled with utmost wrath, vowed to rid the earth of Kṣatriyas and took up his weapon.
Then that tiger of the Bhṛgus, the valiant one, advancing in his might, swiftly slew the sons and grandsons of Kārtavīrya, every one of them.
Having slain thousands of Haihayas, the descendant of Bhṛgu, filled with utmost wrath, made the earth into a mire of blood, O king.
Having thus rid the earth of Kṣatriyas, that one of vast splendor, overcome by deep compassion, withdrew into the forest.
