Then, after some thousands of years had passed, that lord, irascible by nature, was driven to fierce agitation.
For the grandson of Viśvāmitra, son of Raibhya, the great ascetic Parāvasu, O great king, taunted him and said in the assembly of men:
"Those worthy men who gathered at the sacrifice held at the fall of Yayāti—Pratardana and the rest—were they not Kṣatriyas, O Rāma?
False to your vow are you, O Rāma; you boast in the assembly of men, yet out of fear of the Kṣatriya heroes you have taken refuge in the mountain."
Hearing then these words of Parāvasu, the descendant of Bhṛgu, seeing the earth once more thickly peopled with hundreds of Kṣatriyas, took up his weapon again.
Then those Kṣatriyas, O king, who in their hundreds had been spared by him, had grown up and become mighty lords of the earth.
He swiftly slew them again, O ruler of men, even the very children; yet once more the earth was filled with those still in the womb.
And each embryo, as soon as it was born, he slew again; yet the Kṣatriya women managed to save some of their sons.
Thrice seven times that lord rid the earth of Kṣatriyas, and then, at the close of a horse-sacrifice, he gave it as the priestly fee to Kaśyapa.
Then, for the sake of the surviving Kṣatriyas, the illustrious Kaśyapa, pointing with the hand that held the sacrificial ladle, spoke these words, O king:
"Go to the farther shore of the southern ocean, O great sage; never henceforth, O Rāma, may you dwell here within my domain."
Then, out of dread of the son of Jamadagni, the ocean fashioned for him the land of Śūrpāraka, that western tract of the earth.
But Kaśyapa, O great king, having received this earth and placed it under the governance of the Brahmins, entered the great forest.
Then the Śūdras and the Vaiśyas, acting wantonly each as he pleased, behaved disgracefully toward the wives of the foremost of the twice-born, O bull of the Bharatas.
In a kingless world the weak are oppressed by the stronger, and no man here holds secure ownership over his wealth.
Then in course of time the earth, no longer duly protected by Kṣatriyas who guard the law, began to sink into the nether regions.
Then Kaśyapa upheld upon his thigh the earth as she was sinking, O king; and from this, men say, the earth is called Urvī.
Then the goddess Earth, having propitiated Kaśyapa, besought him, naming as her protectors the strong-armed Kṣatriyas:
"There are, O Brahmin, certain bulls among Kṣatriyas, hidden by me among men, born in the lineage of the Haihayas; let these protect me, O sage.
There is an heir of the Pauravas, the son of Viḍūratha, O lord, who was reared by bears upon the mountain Ṛkṣavat, O Brahmin.
So too the heir of Saudāsa was protected out of compassion by Parāśara, the sacrificer of immeasurable might.
He performs all menial tasks for that sage like a Śūdra, and so is known as Sarvakarman, 'doer of every work'; let that prince protect me.
The son of Śibi, of great splendor, Gopati by name, was protected in the forest by cattle; let him protect me, O sage.
The son of Pratardana, of great renown, Vatsa by name, was reared among the calves in the cow-pen; let that prince protect me.
And Aṅga, the grandson of Dadhivāhana and son of Diviratha, was likewise protected by Gautama upon the bank of the Gaṅgā.
The mighty-armed Bṛhadratha, honored with prosperity upon the earth, that blessed one, was protected by black-tailed monkeys upon Gṛdhrakūṭa.
And in the line of Marutta, three Kṣatriyas of Turvasu's race, equal in valor to the lord of the Maruts, were protected by the ocean.
These heirs of the Kṣatriyas, renowned here and there, let them duly protect me; then shall I stand firm and unshaken.
The fathers of these men, and likewise their grandfathers, were slain in battle for my sake by Rāma of untiring deeds.
To them too I must surely make requital; for I do not desire to be protected forever by one who is without valor.
Then Kaśyapa gathered together those whom the Earth had named and consecrated them as guardians of the earth—Kṣatriyas esteemed for their valor.
From their sons and grandsons the dynasties were established. Thus it was that this came to pass of old, concerning which you ask me, O Pāṇḍava.

Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Even as he spoke thus, that foremost hero of the Yadus, addressing Yudhiṣṭhira, the best of the upholders of righteousness, swiftly drove on in that chariot, like the blessed Sun pervading the three worlds with his rays.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, having heard of that deed of Rāma, King Yudhiṣṭhira, filled with the utmost wonder, replied to Janārdana:
"Ah, O scion of Vṛṣṇi, what valor was that of the great-souled Rāma, like to Śakra's, whereby in his wrath he rid the earth of Kṣatriyas!
By cattle, by the ocean, and by black-tailed monkeys, bears, and apes were the bearers of the Kṣatriya lineages protected, trembling in fear of Rāma.
Ah, blessed indeed is this world, and fortunate are the men upon the earth, wherein such a righteous deed was wrought by a Brahmin, O unfallen one."
As they journeyed on thus, O dear one, those two—the unfallen Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira—came to where the lordly son of Gaṅgā lay upon his bed of arrows.
Then they beheld Bhīṣma lying upon his couch of arrows, wrapped about in the net of his own radiance, like the evening sun, like blazing fire.
He was attended by sages as Indra of the hundred sacrifices is attended by the gods, in that most holy region beside the river Oghavatī.
Beholding him from afar, Kṛṣṇa and the King of righteousness, and the four Pāṇḍavas, and those headed by the son of Śaradvat—
—alighting then from their mounts, restraining their restless minds and gathering together the host of their senses, they approached the great sages.
And having paid homage to those sages headed by Vyāsa, Govinda, Sātyaki, and the Kauravas thereafter drew near to the son of Gaṅgā.
Then, having inquired after the increase of his austerities, the Yadus and the Kauravas, those bulls among men, all surrounded the son of Gaṅgā and sat down.
Then, observing the son of Gaṅgā—like a fire slowly dying down—Keśava, his heart somewhat grieved, spoke thus to Bhīṣma:
"Are your faculties of knowledge, O king, clear as they were of old? And is your understanding undisturbed, O best of speakers?
Does your body not burn with the pain of the arrows' wounds? For pain of the body is harder to bear even than pain of the mind.
By the boon granted by your father, you may die at your own will, O lord—for so the righteous-natured Śaṃtanu wished; yet this is no ground for tranquility of spirit."
Even a very fine splinter lodged in the body breeds pain; how much more for you, O Bhārata, pierced through and through by a mass of arrows.
Truly there is no need to instruct you on the origin and dissolution of living beings, for you, O Bhārata, could teach the highest good even to the gods.
For whatever has been, will be, and now is, O bull among men, all of it lies as if placed in your palm, ripe with wisdom as you are.
The cycle of transmigration of beings and the ripening of the fruit of dharma are known to you, O man of great wisdom; you are a treasury made of brahman.
For though set in a flourishing kingdom, whole of limb and free of sickness, surrounded by a thousand women, I see you here as one whose seed flows ever upward, chaste.
In the three worlds, O king, save for Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu—true to his word, of mighty valor, heroic, devoted to dharma alone—
of no one have we ever heard, dear sire, who, lying on a bed of arrows, has by sheer power held off death that arises by nature's own course.
In truth, in austerity, in giving, in the conduct of sacrifice, in the science of archery and in the Veda, and ever in vigilant discernment—
of no great chariot-warrior like you have we ever heard: free of cruelty, pure, self-controlled, devoted to the welfare of all beings.
For you are able, with but a single chariot, to conquer the gods together with the gandharvas, the suras, asuras, and rākṣasas—of this there is no doubt.
For you, O mighty-armed Bhīṣma, are the peer of Vāsava among the Vasus; ever do the brāhmaṇas declare you the ninth, yet second to none in your virtues.
For I know you well, O best of men—you who by your own power are renowned even among the thirty gods, you of surpassing might.
Among men, O lord of men, never have I seen nor heard of any man anywhere on earth who is your equal in virtues.
For in all virtues, O king, you surpass even the gods; indeed, by your austerity you are able to create the worlds with all that moves and is still.
Therefore, O Bhīṣma, drive away the grief of this eldest son of Pāṇḍu, who burns with sorrow over the destruction of his kinsmen.
For all the dharmas declared for the four varṇas, O Bhārata, intertwined with those of the four stages of life, are known to you.
Those duties proclaimed in the fourfold Vedic lore and in the fourfold priestly office, O Bhārata, and those eternal dharmas fixed in Sāṃkhya and Yoga—
and that one foremost dharma which, when practiced, stands unopposed by any of the four varṇas—that too, O son of Gaṅgā, is known to you.
The lore of legend and ancient tale is known to you in its entirety, and the whole science of dharma stands ever fixed within your mind.
And whatever matters in this world breed doubt, there is no one in the world but you to cut them away, O bull among men.

Therefore, O lord of men, draw out by your wisdom the grief that has risen in the mind of this son of Pāṇḍu; for one such as you, with the vast reach of supreme understanding, exists for the peace of bewildered folk.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard the words of the wise Vāsudeva, Bhīṣma raised his face a little and, with palms joined, spoke these words.
Homage to you, O blessed Viṣṇu, source of the worlds' arising and ending; for you are their maker, O Hṛṣīkeśa, and their unconquered destroyer.
O maker of all, homage be to you, O Self of all, source of all; you are the final release of beings, abiding beyond the five elements.
Homage to you in the three worlds, homage to you beyond the three; O Lord of Yoga, homage be to you, for you are the supreme refuge of all.
By the words you have spoken concerning me, O best of men, I now behold your divine manifestations along the three paths.
And I see in truth that eternal form of yours: the seven courses of the wind of boundless splendor are held fast within you.
By your head the heaven is filled, by your feet the goddess Earth; the quarters are your arms, the sun your eye, and in your might stands Śakra established.
We perceive your body, O Acyuta, dark as the flax-flower and robed in yellow, like a cloud charged with lightning.
For the devotee who has taken refuge in you and longs to win the desired goal, ponder, O lotus-eyed one, that which is his highest good, O best of the gods.
Vāsudeva said: Because your devotion to me is supreme, O bull among men, therefore, O king, my divine form has been shown to you.
For never, O lord of kings, do I reveal myself to one who is without devotion, nor to a devotee who is crooked, nor to one without self-restraint, O Bhārata.
But you are my devotee, ever steadfast in uprightness, given to self-control, austerity, truth, and giving, and pure.
You are worthy, O Bhīṣma, to behold me by your own austerity, O king; for there have drawn near to you those worlds from which one does not return again.
Fifty-six days, O foremost hero of the Kurus, remain of your life; thereafter, O Bhīṣma, when you have let go the body, you shall attain to the auspicious risings of the fruits of your deeds.
For these gods, the Vasus, all mounted in their celestial cars and blazing like fire, wait unseen upon you, until the sun, attaining its course, moves northward.

The moment the blessed sun, by force of time, has turned and reached the northern quarter, you shall go, O foremost of heroes, to those worlds which the wise man, once he has gained, returns from no more.
And once you, O Bhīṣma, have departed this world, all knowledge will pass away entire, O hero; therefore have we all gathered close about you, for the discernment of dharma.
To Yudhiṣṭhira, true to his word, whose learning is stricken by grief for his kinsmen, speak the meaningful word joined to dharma, wealth, and concentration, and so dispel his sorrow.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, having heard those salutary words of Kṛṣṇa, joined with dharma and wealth, Bhīṣma the son of Śaṃtanu replied with palms joined.
O Lord of the worlds, mighty-armed, auspicious one, Nārāyaṇa, Acyuta—having heard your words, I am overwhelmed with joy.
And what shall I declare in your presence, O Lord of Speech, when all that can be uttered is already gathered within your own speech?
For whatever has been done in the world, whatever is to be done and is being done, all of it has issued forth from you, O god; the worlds are made of your understanding.
He who would describe the world of the gods in the very presence of the king of the gods—such a one would be expounding the matters of the sciences of dharma, pleasure, and wealth before you.
My mind is troubled by the striking of the arrows, O slayer of Madhu; my limbs sink, and my understanding does not grow clear.
Nor have I any flash of insight to speak even a little, O Govinda, tormented as I am by arrows like poison and fire.
My strength wanes, my wit decays, and my life-breaths hasten away; my vital points burn, and my mind is likewise bewildered.
From weakness my speech falters; how then shall I dare to speak? Be gracious to me, I pray, O delight of the house of the Dāśārhas.
Forgive me therefore, O mighty-armed Acyuta, that I should say nothing at all; even Vācaspati, speaking in your presence, would falter.
I no longer rightly know the quarters, nor the sky, nor the earth; it is solely by your power that I endure, O slayer of Madhu.
Therefore, O lord, do you yourself speak swiftly that which is for the good of the King of Dharma; for you are the source of all sources of sacred lore.
How, when you abide—you the eternal, the maker of the worlds—could anyone such as I hold forth, as a pupil might in the presence of his teacher?
Vāsudeva said: Fitting is this speech in you, O bearer of the Kauravas' burden, of mighty valor, of great inner strength, who perceive all things.
And as for what you have told me, O son of Gaṅgā, concerning the pain of the arrows' striking—accept herein a boon, O Bhīṣma, granted by my grace, O lord.
No faintness, no swoon, no burning, no pain shall overcome you, O son of Gaṅgā, nor yet hunger and thirst.
All forms of knowledge shall shine forth within you, O sinless one, nor shall any clinging of the intellect arise in you anywhere.
And your mind, O Bhīṣma, shall ever abide in the quality of sattva, freed from passion and darkness, like the lord of stars released from the clouds.
And whatever you ponder that is joined to dharma, or to wealth as well, in that your understanding shall be foremost.
And this fourfold host of beings, O tiger among kings, you shall behold, O man of boundless prowess, by recourse to the divine eye.
Endowed with the eye of knowledge, O Bhīṣma, you shall behold the fourfold web of creatures in their very truth, as a fish is seen in clear water.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then all those great seers, together with Vyāsa, worshipped Kṛṣṇa with words joined to the Ṛc, Yajus, and Sāman.
Then a divine rain of flowers of every season fell from the vault of heaven upon the place where the Vārṣṇeya was, together with the son of Gaṅgā and the Pāṇḍavas.
And celestial instruments sounded, and the troops of apsarases sang; nor was anything harmful or unwelcome seen there at all.
An auspicious, gentle, pure breeze blew, bearing every fragrance; and toward the quarter grown calm the beasts and birds cried out, themselves at peace.
Then, after a moment, the blessed thousand-rayed day-maker appeared in the west, as though burning a forest at the world's far edge.
Then all the great seers rose up and took leave of Janārdana, of Bhīṣma, and of King Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then Keśava made obeisance, and so did the Pāṇḍava, and Sātyaki and Saṃjaya, and Kṛpa the son of Śaradvat.
Then those devoted to dharma, duly honored by the seers, said "Tomorrow we shall meet again," and went their ways in haste, each as he pleased.
In the same way, having taken leave of the son of Gaṅgā, Keśava and the Pāṇḍavas, turning round him to the right, mounted their splendid chariots.
Then with chariots whose poles were of gold and ivory, with rutting elephants like mountains, with swift-going horses like Suparṇa, and with foot soldiers bearing bows and the rest—
that army moved on, vast in its march, both before the chariots and behind them likewise, as the great river Narmadā flows before and behind on reaching the mountain that abounds in bears.
Then the blessed maker of night rose up before them, gladdening that host, and joining once more with their own virtue the herbs whose sap the day-maker had drunk up.

Then those bulls of the Yadus and the Pāṇḍavas, entering the city whose radiance rivaled the city of the gods, withdrew each to his own fitting and stately mansion, weary, as lions withdraw to their dens.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, having entered his dwelling, the slayer of Madhu fell asleep, and awoke when but a single watch of the night remained.
Mādhava, taking to the path of meditation, surveyed all forms of knowledge, and thereafter meditated upon the eternal brahman.
Then those versed in scripture and ancient lore, well trained and sweet of throat, sang the praises of Vāsudeva, the maker of all, the Lord of creatures.
Those who keep time by clapping recited, and the singers sang, and conches, drums, and tabors were sounded by the thousand.
And the most enchanting sound of lutes, small drums, and flutes, spread wide like a peal of laughter, was heard from his mansion.
And likewise from King Yudhiṣṭhira's dwelling there rose up sweet voices charged with benediction, blended with song and instrument.
Then the Dāśārha, the mighty-armed Acyuta, having risen and bathed, with palms joined, having murmured the secret prayer, stood by attending upon the sacred fires.
Then Mādhava caused a thousand brāhmaṇas, each versed in the four Vedas, to pronounce their benedictions, presenting to each one a thousand cows.
Having performed the rites of auspicious touch and beheld himself in a spotless mirror, Kṛṣṇa then spoke to Sātyaki.
"Go, scion of Śini, go to the king's dwelling and learn whether the mighty-splendored Yudhiṣṭhira is ready to go and behold Bhīṣma."
Then at Kṛṣṇa's word Sātyaki went swiftly, and approaching King Yudhiṣṭhira he spoke.
"The fine chariot of wise Vāsudeva is yoked, O king; Janārdana will set out for the presence of the son of the river-goddess."
"That Kṛṣṇa awaits you, O Dharmarāja of great splendor; whatever should next be done in this matter, that you ought to do."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Let my fine chariot be yoked, O Phalguna of incomparable splendor; we must not go with soldiers — we ourselves alone shall go."
"And Bhīṣma, the foremost of the upholders of dharma, must not be troubled by me; therefore let even the forerunners turn back, O Dhanaṃjaya."
"From this day onward the son of Gaṅgā will declare the highest mystery; therefore, O son of Kuntī, I do not wish for any gathering of common folk."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard that speech, Dhanaṃjaya the son of Kuntī announced to him, O bull among men, that the fine chariot was yoked.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, with the twins and with Bhīma and Arjuna, set out for Kṛṣṇa's dwelling — like all created beings come together.
As those great-souled Pāṇḍavas were approaching, the wise Kṛṣṇa too, together with the scion of Śini, mounted his chariot.
Standing in their chariots, having greeted one another and inquired after a comfortable night, those great chariot-warriors set out in fine chariots that rumbled like thunderclouds.
Dāruka urged on Vāsudeva's horses — Meghapuṣpa and Balāhaka, Sainya and Sugrīva.
Those horses of Vāsudeva, driven on by Dāruka, then sped forward, O king, scoring the earth with the tips of their hooves.
Swift and mighty, as though devouring the sky, they descended upon Kurukṣetra, the field of dharma entire.
Then they went to where the lord Bhīṣma lay upon his bed of arrows, surrounded by brahmin-seers as Brahmā is by the hosts of gods.
Then Govinda alighted from the chariot, and so did Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva, the twins, and Sātyaki; raising their right hands, they paid honor to the seers.
Encircled by them like the moon by the constellations, the king approached the son of Gaṅgā as Vāsava approaches Brahmā.
That mighty-armed one, gripped by dread out of fear, gazed upon him lying on his bed of arrows like the fallen sun.
Janamejaya said: "When the righteous one of great spirit, true to his word, master of himself, vowed to the gods, the blessed and unfaltering Bhīṣma lay upon his bed of arrows —
"when Bhīṣma, the delight of Śaṃtanu, the son of Gaṅgā, that tiger among men, lay upon the hero's couch, attended on every side by the Pāṇḍavas —
"what discourses arose at that gathering of heroes, when all the armies had been slain? Relate that to me, O great sage."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Bhīṣma, the burden-bearer of the Kurus, lay upon his bed of arrows, the perfected seers, with Nārada at their head, came near, O king.
And the kings who had survived the slaughter, with Yudhiṣṭhira at their head, and Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Kṛṣṇa, and Bhīma, Arjuna, and the twins as well.
Those great-souled ones, drawing near to the grandsire of the Bharatas, the son of Gaṅgā, grieved over him as over the fallen sun.
And having reflected for a moment, Nārada, whose vision is godlike, spoke to all the Pāṇḍavas and to the surviving princes.
He declared that the time had come: "Let this Bhīṣma be questioned, for the son of Gaṅgā is setting like the radiant sun, O descendant of Bharata."
"He is about to surrender his life-breaths; draw near to him, all of you, and ask, for he knows the whole and manifold duties of the four orders."
"This aged one will soon attain the worlds of those who cast off the body; question him quickly upon the doubts that abide in your minds."
Thus addressed by Nārada, the rulers of men went up to Bhīṣma; but, unable to question him, they looked upon one another.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu, said to Hṛṣīkeśa: "None other than you, O son of Devakī, is able to question the grandsire."
"Do you, O invincible slayer of Madhu, draw him first into speech; for you, dear one, are the supreme knower of all dharma among us all."
Thus addressed by the Pāṇḍava, the blessed and unfaltering Keśava then approached the unassailable one and drew him into speech.
Vāsudeva said: "Has the night passed in comfort for you, O best of kings? Has your understanding, with its faculties unclouded, returned to you?"
"Do all branches of knowledge shine clear within you, O sinless one? Is your heart not faint, and is your mind not distressed?"
Bhīṣma said: "Burning and bewilderment, weariness and exhaustion, faintness and pain — all at once, by your grace, O sinless Govinda, have departed."
"What has been and what shall be and what now is, O one of supreme splendor — all that I behold, like a fruit set in the palm of my hand."
"The duties declared in the Vedas, and those laid down in the Vedānta — all of them I clearly perceive through the boon you have granted, O unfaltering one."
"The dharma declared by the virtuous, that too abides in my heart; and I am a knower of the duties of countries, castes, and families, O Janārdana."
"The meaning that lies in the duties of the four stations of life, that too is fixed in my heart; and I comprehend the duties of kings in their entirety, O Keśava."
"And wherever something must be said, that I shall say, O Janārdana; for by your grace an auspicious understanding has entered my mind."
"I have become as it were a youth again, fortified by meditation upon you; I am able to speak of what is best, by your grace, O Janārdana."
"But why do you yourself not declare what is best to the Pāṇḍava? What is it you wish to say in this matter? Tell it quickly, O Mādhava."
Vāsudeva said: "Know me to be the root of glory and of the good, O Kaurava; from me have all states of being arisen, whose nature is the existent and the non-existent."
"When the cool-rayed one is called the moon, who in the world would marvel? Just so, when I am full of glory, who would marvel?"
"But further glory is to be conferred upon you by me, O one of great splendor; therefore, Bhīṣma, my abundant resolve has been set upon you."
"For as long as the earth shall stand firm, O protector of the earth, so long shall your undying fame range throughout the worlds."
"And whatever you shall declare, Bhīṣma, to the Pāṇḍava who questions you, shall endure upon the face of the earth like the pronouncements of the Vedas."
"And whoever shall yoke himself to himself by this authoritative measure shall, after death, enjoy the fruit of all meritorious deeds."
"For this reason, Bhīṣma, a divine understanding has been bestowed upon you by me — that your glory might spread the more abroad."
"For as long as a man's fame spreads in the world upon the earth, so long, it is determined, does his imperishable station endure."
"The kings who survived the slaughter sit about you, O king, wishing to inquire into the duties of dharma; expound them to these, O descendant of Bharata."
"For you are advanced in years, endowed with learning and good conduct, and skilled in the duties of kings, both those of old and those that came after."
"From your birth onward no one has ever seen a crookedness in you; all the princes know you as one who understands the subtleties of dharma."
"To them, O king, as a father to his sons, declare the highest polity; for the seers and the gods have ever been honored by you."
"Therefore it must indeed be spoken by you here, as I see it without remainder — the duties of dharma, to those who wish to learn, and again to one who, being good, is asked."
"And it should be spoken by the learned — so the wise declare to be dharma; for a grievous fault befalls one who does not answer, O lord."
"Therefore, being questioned about the eternal duties of dharma by sons and grandsons who seek to know, do you, learned one, expound them, O bull of the Bharatas."

Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the mighty-splendored delight of the Kurus spoke these words: "So be it — I shall declare the duties of dharma; firm now are my speech and my mind by your grace, O Govinda, for you are the eternal self of all beings."
"But let King Yudhiṣṭhira question me about the duties of dharma; thus shall I be pleased, and I shall declare those duties, O sinless one."
"At whose birth — that bull among kings, righteous and great-souled — all the seers rejoiced: let that Pāṇḍava question me."
"He to whom there is no equal among all the Kurus of blazing fame who walk in dharma: let that Pāṇḍava question me."
"He in whom dwell ever firmness, self-restraint, chastity, forbearance, and dharma, and vigor and splendor: let that Pāṇḍava question me."
"He in whom are all these — truth, charity, austerity, purity, tranquility, skill, and composure: let that Pāṇḍava question me."
"He, righteous of soul, who would not, from desire nor anger, nor fear nor for the sake of gain, commit unrighteousness: let that Pāṇḍava question me."
"He who honors with hospitality his kinsmen, guests, and servants, and those who seek shelter and dependence with him: let that Pāṇḍava question me."
"He who is ever true, ever forbearing, ever devoted to knowledge, fond of guests, and who gives always to the virtuous: let that Pāṇḍava question me."
"He who is ever devoted to sacrifice and study, and always intent upon dharma, tranquil, and versed in the secret of sacred lore: let that Pāṇḍava question me."
Vāsudeva said: "Possessed of utmost modesty, that righteous Yudhiṣṭhira, terrified by the fear of your curse, does not approach you."
"Having wrought the destruction of the world, this lord of the world, O ruler of peoples, terrified by the fear of your curse, does not approach you."
"Having slain with his arrows those worthy of worship and honor — the devoted, the elders, kinsmen, and friends, all deserving the guest-offering — he does not approach you."
Bhīṣma said: "As the dharma of brāhmaṇas is charity, study, and austerity, so for kṣatriyas, O Kṛṣṇa, it is the casting down of the body in battle."
"He who slays in battle fathers, grandfathers, sons, elders, kinsmen, and friends who have set out in a wrongful cause — that is dharma indeed."
"The kṣatriya who slays in battle those wicked men who have broken their compact and are greedy — even elders, O Keśava — he is a knower of dharma."
"When challenged in battle, the kinsman of the warrior-caste must always fight; for war is in accord with dharma, conducive to heaven and to the worlds — so Manu declared."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by Bhīṣma, the Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira drew near humbly and stood before him in his sight.
Then he clasped his feet, and Bhīṣma welcomed him, and kissing him upon the head, said to him then: "Be seated."
Then the son of Gaṅgā, the bull among all bowmen, said to him: "Question me freely, dear son; have no fear, O best of the Kurus."
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having bowed down to Hṛṣīkeśa and saluted the grandsire, and having sought the leave of all his elders, Yudhiṣṭhira began to question him.
The knowers of dharma declare that kingship is the highest dharma; yet I deem it a mighty burden. Speak to me of it, O king.
Tell me in particular of the duties of kings, O grandsire; for the whole world of the living, the duties of kings are the final refuge.
In the duties of kings, O Kaurava, the three aims of life are bound together, and the dharma of liberation too is plainly and wholly comprised therein.
As the reins are to the horse and the goad to the elephant, so is the dharma of a king remembered to be the rein that guides the world.
If this dharma, honored by royal sages, fell into confusion, the world would lose its stability and all would be thrown into disorder.
As the rising sun destroys the demonic darkness, so do the duties of kings cast off the inauspicious course that leads from the bright worlds.
Therefore, first of all, declare the very essence of the duties of kings, O grandsire, best of the Bharatas; for you are the foremost among the wise.
From you comes the highest tradition for us all, O scorcher of foes; for Vāsudeva himself accounts you supreme in wisdom.
Bhīṣma said: Homage to the great Dharma, homage to Kṛṣṇa the creator; having bowed to the brāhmaṇas, I shall declare the eternal duties.
Hear from me in their entirety, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the duties of kings as I expound them, attentive and composed, and whatever else you desire to know.
At the very outset, O best of the Kurus, a king who desires to give joy to his people must conduct himself toward the gods and the twice-born according to ordinance.
By worshipping the deities and the brāhmaṇas, O upholder of the Kurus, a king becomes free of his debt to dharma and is honored by the world.
And in exertion, my son, always strive, O Yudhiṣṭhira; for without exertion, fate alone does not bring about the success of kings' aims.
These two together work in common—fate and exertion alike; yet I hold human effort to be supreme, while fate is said to be already determined.
And when an undertaking has failed, do not give way to grief; discipline labors on, my son—this is the highest policy of kings.
For apart from truth there is no cause of success for kings; a king devoted to truth rejoices both here and hereafter.
Even for the seers, O king of kings, truth is the highest wealth; and likewise for a king there is no greater ground of trust than truth.
Endowed with virtues, of good character, self-restrained, gentle, righteous, master of his senses, fair to look upon and large of aim—such a one never falls from prosperity.
In all your dealings hold to uprightness, O delight of the Kurus, tempered yet by the discernment of policy and by the safeguard of the three Vedas.
A king who is always gentle becomes despised by all on every side; yet from one who is harsh the people recoil. Therefore practice both.
The brāhmaṇas must ever be exempt from punishment, O best of givers; for they are the highest order of beings in the world, those called brāhmaṇas, O Bhārata.
Two verses were sung of old by the great-souled Manu, O king of kings; you ought to keep them in your heart amid your own duties, O Kauravya.
Fire arose from the waters, the kṣatriya from the brāhmaṇa, iron from stone; their all-pervading energy is quenched within their own sources of birth.
When iron strikes the stone, when fire meets the waters, and when the kṣatriya turns in hatred against the brāhmaṇa—then those three come to ruin.
Knowing this, O great king, the twice-born are ever worthy of your homage; the best of the twice-born, possessed of tranquillity, uphold the earthly Brahman.
And even so, O tiger among men, those who would wreck the order of the world—such men must ever be held in check by force of arms.
Two verses were sung long ago by Uśanas, the great seer, my son; mark them well, O most wise king, with single-minded attention.
Even one who has reached the end of the Vedas, if he comes weapon-raised against him in battle, a king mindful of dharma should strike down in keeping with his own duty.
For he who guards dharma when it is being destroyed is a knower of dharma; by that deed he does not become a slayer of the unborn—the wrath of the offender falls upon himself.
And even so, O best of men, the twice-born must be protected; though they have offended, the king should but banish them to the edge of his realm.
Even toward one of them accused of crime he should show compassion, O lord of peoples—whether in the slaying of a brāhmaṇa, the defiling of a teacher's bed, or the killing of the unborn.
And for a brāhmaṇa hated by the king, banishment to the edge of the realm is ordained; never at any time should bodily punishment be visited upon them.
And these men should ever be held dear, O best of men; for kings have no greater treasury than a gathering of able men.
Among the six kinds of fortresses determined by the treatises, O great king, in all of them the fortress of men is held the hardest to overcome.
Therefore the wise king must ever show compassion toward the four orders; a king righteous of soul and truthful in speech gives joy to his subjects.
Yet you must not be forever forbearing, O best of men; for an over-gentle, ever-forgiving king is unrighteous, like an elephant that suffers all.
In the treatise of Bṛhaspati certain verses were laid down of old upon this very matter, O great king; hear them as I recite them to you.
A king who is always forbearing the low-born will hold in contempt; like the driver of an elephant, the people will seek to mount upon his very head.
Therefore let a king be neither always gentle nor always harsh, but glorious like the sun in spring—neither cold nor scorching with heat.
By direct observation, by inference, by analogy, and by instruction, O great king, your own people and your foes alike must always be examined.
And forsake all vices, O giver of bounteous gifts; not that he should wholly abstain from pleasures, but he should shun attachment to them.
For a man given to vice is ever despised in the world; and a ruler too full of hatred fills the world with dread.
A king must always conduct himself after the manner of a pregnant woman, O great king; and hear the reason why this is enjoined.
For just as a pregnant woman forsakes what her own heart finds pleasant and seeks instead the good of the child within her, so too must a king act, beyond all doubt.
A king who follows dharma, O best of the Kurus, must ever conduct himself thus, surrendering his own pleasure for whatever serves the good of the world.
And your firmness you must never abandon at any time, O Pāṇḍava; for the command of one who is resolute and unwavering in justice is never thwarted.
And jesting with your servants must not be constant, O best of speakers; do not indulge in it, O tiger among kings—hear from me the fault therein.
Dependents grown over-familiar come to despise their master; they keep not to their proper place and transgress his word.
When sent on errands they make objection; they pry into secrets, beg for what should not be begged, and have served to them food that ought not to be eaten.
They grow angry and blaze forth, they usurp his land, and by bribery and deceit they thwart the conduct of affairs.
They wear down his realm with counterfeits, they cling to women with wanton eyes, and they array themselves in dress equal to his own.
Shameless, they break wind and spit in his very presence, O tiger among men, and openly mock his words.
They mount, without leave, the horse, the elephant, or the chariot reserved for the king's own use, when the ruler is given to mirth and is soft of temper.
"This deed of yours, O king, was ill-done; this conduct of yours was unseemly"—thus, in the assembly, do men who pass for friends speak.
When he is angered they but laugh; honored, they take no pleasure; and they are ever quarrelsome, contending against one another for cause.
They let his counsel leak away and lay bare his misdeeds; scornfully and in mere sport they carry out his command—even as to his ornaments and his food, his bath and his anointing.
Heedless and at their ease, O tiger among men, they listen to him with contempt; they decry their own offices and forsake them, O Bhārata.
They are not content with their wages and seize what is the king's due; they wish to toy with him as with a bird held on a string, and they say abroad in the world, "This king is led by us."
These faults and many others besides arise, O Yudhiṣṭhira, when a king is given over to softness and to merriment.
Bhīṣma said: A king must be ever exerting himself, O Yudhiṣṭhira; for a king bereft of effort fades away, like a woman left without a husband's care.
The blessed Uśanas spoke a verse upon this matter, O lord of peoples; with single mind, O king, mark it as I recite it to you here.
These two the earth devours, as a serpent swallows the creatures that lodge in its holes: a king who offers no resistance, and a brāhmaṇa who never goes abroad.
This, O tiger among men, you ought to lay to heart: make peace with those fit for peace, and set yourself against those to be opposed.
Whoever within your kingdom of seven limbs should act perversely against it—be he your teacher or your friend—he is to be struck down all the same.
For this ancient verse was sung by King Marutta of old, upon the governance of a kingdom, O king of kings, after the teaching of Bṛhaspati.
Even a teacher, if he is arrogant and knows not what should and should not be done, who has strayed onto the wrong path—the forsaking of him is ordained.
By the wise King Sagara, son of Bāhu, his eldest son Asamañja was cast off, for the sake of the welfare of the citizens.
Asamañja, of old, used to drown the children of the citizens in the Sarayū, O king; therefore his father rebuked him and sent him into exile.
By the seer Uddālaka too was Śvetaketu, of great austerity, his beloved son, cast off, for he had dealt falsely with the brāhmaṇas.
Herein the eternal dharma of kings is just this: to give joy to the people, to safeguard truth, and to deal uprightly in all affairs.
He should not lay hands on others' wealth, and should cause what is due to be given in its season; valiant, truthful, and forbearing, such a king does not swerve from his path.
Keeping his counsel secret, having conquered wrath, settled in his grasp of the meaning of the treatises, ever devoted to dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa alike.
A king ought to have his weak points covered over by the three Vedas; for kings there is no better defense against wrongdoing than this concealment.
The duties of the four orders must be guarded by the ruler of the earth; for to prevent the confusion of dharma is the eternal dharma of kings.
A king should neither be over-trusting nor wholly without trust, and should ever weigh in his mind the merits and faults of the sixfold policy.
A king who marks the weak points of his foes is ever praised, who knows the import of the three aims and rightly employs spies and secret agents.
Devoted to the gathering of his treasury, the equal of Yama and Vaiśravaṇa, and a knower of the tenfold group concerning stability, growth, and decline.
He should be a supporter of the unprovided and a watchful guardian of those already in his service; and a king should be of pleasant countenance, addressing men with a smile.
A waiter upon the aged, one who has conquered sloth and is free of greed, his mind fixed in the conduct of the good; for the good are the very mirror of right conduct.
And he should never at any time take wealth from the hands of the good; but from the wicked he may take it, and to the good he should bestow it.
He should strike in his own person and seize, his self under control and his instruments under control; a giver in season and an enjoyer in season, and a man of pure conduct as well.
Let him take as allies men who are valiant, loyal, not to be bought away, well-born, free of disease, refined and allied with the refined, self-respecting and not contemptuous of others.
Men learned in knowledge, knowing the ways of the world, mindful of the world beyond, devoted to the duties of dharma, good, and as unshakable as mountains.
Such men the king should ever make his companions, keeping their welfare foremost. He should be their equal in enjoyments, exalted above them only by the royal parasol and the power of command.
His conduct, both seen and unseen, should at all times be the same. Acting thus, the lord of men finds no grief in this world.
But a king who suspects everyone and seizes everything—crooked and greedy—is soon brought to ruin by his own people.
The pure guardian of the earth, devoted to winning the hearts of his people, does not fall though seized by foes; and if he falls, he rises again.
Free of anger, free of vice, gentle in punishment, his senses mastered—such a king becomes as trustworthy to his creatures as the Himālaya.
Wise, endowed with the virtues of justice, intent upon the weak points of his enemies, fair to look upon for all the classes, and knowing both policy and the failure of policy.
Swift in action, his anger conquered, readily gracious, magnanimous, of healthy constitution, disciplined, energetic in his undertakings, and not given to boasting.
The king whose enterprises are seen to be begun but never yet finished off—that king is the best of kings.
He in whose realm men move about without fear, like sons in their father's house—that king is the best of kings.
He whose townsfolk and country-dwellers do not have to hide their wealth, and who discern between sound and unsound policy—that king is the best of kings.
He whose people, dwelling in his realm, are devoted each to his own work, taking no pleasure in conspiracy, self-restrained, and protected according to the ordinances—
obedient, biddable, well-disciplined, not given to strife, and delighting in giving within his realm—he is a true king.
In whose realm there is no trickery or deceit, no fraud, no envy—that guardian of the earth holds dharma eternal.
He who honors the sciences, is amenable to counsel, devoted to the welfare of his townsfolk, follows the dharma of the good, and is liberal—that king deserves his kingdom.
He whose spies, whose counsel, and whose deeds done and undone are never known to his foes—that king deserves his kingdom.
And this verse was once sung by the great-souled descendant of Bhṛgu, in the telling of the deeds of Rāma, concerning the king, O Bhārata:
"First let a man find a king, then a wife, then wealth. When there is no king, whence comes a wife for the world, and whence comes wealth?"
Therefore, O king, for the lions among kings there is no other eternal dharma than plain and manifest protection; protection is the sustaining of the world.
And these two verses were uttered by Manu, son of Pracetas, concerning the duties of kings, O lord of kings; hear them now with single-minded attention.
"These six a man should abandon, as one abandons a leaking boat upon the sea: a teacher who does not teach, an officiating priest who has not studied,
a king who does not protect, a wife of unkind speech, a cowherd who longs for the village, and a barber who longs for the forest."
Bhīṣma said: This is the very cream of the duties of kings that I have given you, Yudhiṣṭhira; for the venerable Bṛhaspati commends no other dharma.
The venerable Viśālākṣa, and Kāvya of great austerities, and the thousand-eyed great Indra, and Manu son of Pracetas,
and the venerable Bharadvāja, and the sage Gauraśiras—these authors of the science of kingcraft, devoted to brahman and expounders of brahman,
commend protection alone as the dharma of kings, O best of upholders of dharma, you whose eyes are coppery as the lotus. And now hear of the means to achieve it.
Spies and secret agents, giving in season without envy, taking by right means but not seizing by wrong ones, O Yudhiṣṭhira—
the gathering of good men, valor, skill, truth, the welfare of the subjects, and the breaking up of the enemy's faction by crooked means and by straight—
not forsaking the good, sustaining the well-born, laying up what should be laid up, and the service of the wise as well—
the constant heartening of his troops, the watching over of his subjects, tirelessness in his undertakings, and the increasing of the treasury—
the guarding of the city, wariness, the breaking up of conspiracies among the townsfolk, and attention to dilapidated dwellings and to those who are sinking into ruin—
the application, urged by the occasion, of the two kinds of punishment, and the proper watching over enemies, neutrals, and friends—
the suborning of the enemy's servants, and—from observing how others fare—being himself distrustful, while reassuring the other side—
following the dharma of statecraft, constant exertion, never despising one's foes, and ever shunning the ignoble:
For Bṛhaspati declared that exertion is the very root of the kings' dharma; learn from me the verses upon this.
By exertion the nectar of immortality was won; by exertion the Asuras were slain; by exertion the great Indra attained supremacy in heaven and on earth.
The man steadfast in action stands above those steadfast only in speech; the men steadfast in speech wait upon and please the one steadfast in action.
For a king devoid of exertion, however wise he be, is forever there for his foes to trample, like a serpent stripped of its venom.
And an enemy is not to be despised by the stronger, even though he be weak; for even a small fire burns, and a little poison kills.
An enemy possessed of but a single horse, taking refuge in a stronghold, can scorch this region and that even of a prosperous king.
The secret counsel of a king for the sake of victory, his gathering of allies, whatever crookedness may be in his heart and whatever serves his purpose—
whatever crooked deed of his is to be carried out, he should sustain it under a show of straightforwardness, and to deceive the world he should perform the most righteous-seeming acts.
For kingship is a vast machine, hard to be borne by the undisciplined; it cannot be carried by a gentle man—it is a supreme place of slaughter.
Kingship, that bait coveted by all, can never be held in this world by straightforwardness alone; therefore one must ever act by a blend of both, Yudhiṣṭhira.
And even should disaster befall him while he protects his subjects, that too is great dharma for him; for such is the conduct of the guardians of the earth.
This much of the duties of kings I have set forth to you in brief; whatever further doubt you have, speak it, O best of speakers.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then the venerable Vyāsa, and Devasthāna together with Aśman, and Vāsudeva, and Kṛpa, and Sātyaki, and Saṃjaya likewise—
crying "Well said, well said!" and thrilled with joy, their faces as it were abloom, they praised that tiger among men, Bhīṣma, the best of the upholders of dharma.
Then with downcast heart that best of the Kurus spoke to Bhīṣma, gently touching his feet, his eyes brimming with tears:
"Tomorrow now I shall ask you of my doubts, grandsire; the sun too is going to its setting, having drunk up the earth's moisture."
Then Keśava and Kṛpa, and Yudhiṣṭhira and the others, having saluted the twice-born and circumambulated the son of the great river, mounted their chariots filled with gladness.

And those firm in their vows, those scorchers of foes, having bathed in the Dṛṣadvatī, performed the water-rites, and made their auspicious recitations, and having worshipped the twilight according to the ordinance, then entered the city named for the elephant.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, rising at daybreak and performing the morning rites, the Pāṇḍavas and the Yādavas went forth in chariots vast as cities.
And reaching Kurukṣetra and coming to the sinless Bhīṣma, son of Gaṅgā, best of charioteers, they asked whether his night had passed in ease.
Having saluted the seers, Vyāsa and the rest, and being greeted by them all, they sat down all around Bhīṣma, surrounding him on every side.
Then the king of great splendor, Yudhiṣṭhira the Dharmarāja, having honored and saluted Bhīṣma, spoke to him with joined palms:
"This word that goes about, 'king, king,' O Bhārata—how did it first arise? Tell me that, grandsire.
Equal in hands, head, and neck, equal in intellect, senses, and self, equal in his capacity for pain and pleasure, equal in back, arms, and belly—
equal in seed, bone, and marrow, equal too in flesh and blood, equal in his breathing out and in, possessed of a body and life-breath like the rest—
the same in birth and death, the same in all the qualities of men—how does one man stand above those of surpassing intellect and the brave?
How does one man protect the whole earth, thronged with heroes, champions, and noble men—and the world besides yearns for his favor?
By the contentment of one man the whole world grows content; when he is troubled, all the world is troubled too—such is the settled truth.
All this I wish to hear truly, O bull of the Bharatas; expound it to me as it really is, O best of speakers.
No small cause can this be, O lord of peoples, that before one man the whole world bows down as before a god."
Bhīṣma said: With self under control, O best of men, hear it all in full—how kingship first arose in the beginning, in the Kṛta age.
There was no kingdom, no king, no punishment, and no one to inflict it; by dharma alone all the people protected one another.
But as men guarded one another thus by dharma, O Bhārata, they came at last to utter weariness, and thereupon delusion entered into them.
Fallen under the sway of delusion, O bull among men, those men, through the bewildering of their judgment, let their dharma perish.
And when their judgment was lost, the men, mastered by delusion, then fell one and all under the sway of greed, O best of the Bharatas.
Then, as men reached out to grasp at what was not theirs, another thing called desire arose there among them, O lord.
And as they fell under the sway of desire, a thing called passion laid hold of them; impassioned, they no longer knew what should and should not be done, Yudhiṣṭhira.
Going to those who were forbidden, speaking what was not to be spoken, eating what was not to be eaten, O lord of kings—they shunned neither fault nor virtue.
When this world of men was thus thrown into ruin, then the Veda perished; and from the perishing of the Veda, O king, dharma too came to its destruction.
When the Veda and dharma were lost, the gods then fell into terror; and in their terror, O tiger among men, they went to Brahmā for refuge.
Coming to the venerable Brahmā, the grandsire of the world, those gods, all afflicted with grief, sorrow, and fear, spoke with joined palms:
"Venerable one, the eternal Veda that dwelt in the world of men is lost through such states as greed and delusion, and thereupon fear has entered into us.
And by the perishing of the Veda, dharma too has perished, O Lord; thereby we have been brought level with mortals, O lord of the three worlds.
For our rain falls downward, but the mortals rain upward by their offerings; and since their rites have ceased, we have thereby fallen into peril."
Ponder for us, O Grandsire, what here is our highest good; that power of ours which sprang from your power is now perishing.
Then the blessed Self-Born spoke to all those gods: I shall devise what is best; let your fear depart, O bulls among the gods.
Then, born of his own mind, he composed a hundred thousand chapters, wherein dharma, and likewise artha, and kāma too were set forth.
This group, proclaimed by the Self-Born as the trivarga, the threefold aim; and the fourth, namely mokṣa, a distinct aim and a distinct group of its own.
And for mokṣa too another triad was declared: sattva, rajas, and tamas; while stability, increase, and decline are the triad that springs from the rod of rule.
The self, the place, and the time, the means, the deed to be done, the allies, and the cause as well: this is remembered as the sixfold set born of statecraft.
The triple Veda, and philosophic inquiry, and economy, O bull of the Bharatas, and the broad science of statecraft: these branches of knowledge are there shown forth.
The safeguarding and surveillance of ministers, the guarding of the king's son, espionage by manifold means, and surveillance of various kinds.
Conciliation, and the giving of gifts, division, and punishment, O Pāṇḍava, and a fifth, indifference: these too are here set forth in full.
Counsel too is described entire, and likewise the matter of sowing dissension, and the failure of counsel, and the fruit that lies in its success or failure.
And treaty of manifold name, the inferior, the middling, and the superior, that called of fear, of honor, and of wealth, is described in full.
And the four seasons for a campaign, and the elaboration of the threefold aim; conquest joined with righteousness, and likewise conquest for gain.
And the demonic conquest too is thus described in full; and the threefold character of the fivefold set is here set forth.
The open and the hidden form of force is then declared: the open is there of eight kinds, while the covert is of vast extent.
Chariots, elephants, horses, and foot soldiers too, O Pāṇḍava, levied labor, boats, spies, and guides upon the road: these are the eight.
These, O Kaurava, are the open limbs of an army; and the mobile and immobile applications of powders, poisons, and the like are also told.
In what is touched and in what is eaten, secret poisoning of many kinds is recorded; the foe, the friend, and the neutral, these too are described.
The full merits of routes, and likewise the merits of terrain, self-protection, the heartening of troops, and the oversight of spies.
The manifold marshalings of men, elephants, chariots, and horses, battle arrays of various name, and the wondrous skill of warfare.
Portents and downfalls, the well-fought fight and the well-managed retreat, and the lore of tempering weapons, O bull of the Bharatas.
The disasters of an army are set forth, and likewise the rousing of an army to joy; the time for harrying and assault, and the time of peril, O Pāṇḍava.
And the contrivance of trenches, and the deployment of stratagems, and the harassing of a hostile realm by fierce bands of robbers and forest folk.
By arsonists and poisoners, by spies in disguise, by suborning the heads of guilds, and by the cutting down of crops.
By the corrupting of elephants, by the breeding of mistrust, by cutting off provisions, and by seizing the roads.
The fitting decline and growth of the kingdom with its seven limbs, the right employment of an envoy's powers, and the increase of the realm.
The handling of foe, neutral, and friend is rightly told; and the crushing and the repulse of those who are stronger.
Most subtle litigation, and likewise the clearing away of thorns; peace, the exertion of effort, and the gathering and amassing of goods.
The maintenance of the unsupported, the care of dependents, giving at the proper time of need, and abstention from the vices.
Likewise the virtues of a king, and those virtues that belong to a commander, and the merits and faults of the instrument and of the agent as well.
The manifold tokens of malice, and the conduct of dependents, wariness toward all, and the shunning of negligence.
The desire to gain the ungained, and likewise the increase of what is gained, and the giving of what has grown to worthy recipients according to rule.
The disbursing of wealth for the sake of dharma, for the sake of gain, and for the sake of pleasure, and a fourth in the warding off of calamity: these too are here described.
The fierce vices born of wrath, and likewise those born of desire, ten in all, O best of the Kurus, are here declared.
Hunting, dicing, drink, and women, O bull of the Bharatas, the teachers call those born of desire, and they were here proclaimed by the Self-Born.
Harshness of speech, and ferocity, and harshness in punishment, oppression of oneself, prodigality, and the squandering of wealth.
Engines of many kinds, and their workings, are described; the crushing assault, the repulse, and the shattering of standards.
The destruction of sacred trees, the breaking of sieges and the ruin of workshops, the removal of obstacles, the march, and the means of attendance are described.
Of small drums, kettledrums, conches, and war drums, O best of warriors, the gathering of materials and the chief vital points: these are the six.
The settling of what is won, the honoring of the good, union of purpose with the learned, and knowledge of the rite of the morning oblation.
The touching of auspicious things, the care of the body, the ordering of food, and constant piety as well.
How a man should rise unaided, truthfulness, sweet words, the holding of festivals and assemblies, and the rites that arise on the raising of standards.
Conduct both open and concealed in all the offices of state, O tiger of the Bharatas, and constant vigilance.
The immunity of brāhmaṇas from punishment, the just infliction of punishment, and the safeguarding of merit on behalf of dependents and one's own kindred.
The protection of the townsfolk and the increase of one's own realm, and that deliberation upon the circle of states, O king, the doctrine of the twelve kings.
And the doctrine of the seventy-two, which was declared by the Self-Born, and the laws of regions, of castes, and of families are fully described.
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are here described, and the means and the pursuit of wealth, manifold and with abundant sacrificial fees.
The working of sorcery by roots, and illusion and magic, are here described, and the fouling of flowing streams and of still waters is set forth.
By whatsoever means the world might be kept from straying from the path of the noble, all that, O tiger among kings, is described in the science of statecraft.
Having wrought this auspicious treatise, the blessed Lord, well pleased, then spoke to all the gods led by Śakra.
For the benefit of the world and for the establishing of the threefold aim, this wisdom, the very cream of eloquence, has been brought forth.
For this, joined with the rod of chastisement, works the protection of the world, and, intent on restraint and on favor, it shall move among the worlds.
And this is guided by the rod, and it guides the rod in turn; therefore it is called daṇḍanīti, the rule of the rod, and it pervades the three worlds.
Holding the essence of the six measures of policy, it shall stand foremost among the great-souled; and by the greatness of that rod, the rule has its clear mark.
And the broad course of policy, by which all this is spread abroad, and the lore of the ancient tales, and the origin of the great sages.
The succession of holy fords, and the lineage of the constellations, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the whole order of the four life stages, and likewise the rite of the four priests.

The system of the four classes, and likewise the fourfold knowledge of the Vedas, is here described; the epic histories and the subsidiary Vedas, and the whole science of right reasoning, are set forth.
Austerity, knowledge, and non-injury, truth and falsehood, the highest polity, attendance upon elders, giving, purity, and exertion as well.
And compassion for all beings, all this is here described; whatever upon the earth has passed into speech, all of it has been brought together.
In that treatise of the Grandsire, O Pāṇḍava, this is beyond doubt: dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are here all proclaimed entire.
Then the blessed Śaṃkara first received that science of polity, he of many forms, the wide-eyed, Śiva, Sthāṇu, the lord of Umā.
Perceiving the dwindling of the ages and of the lifespan of men, the blessed Śiva then abridged the treatise of great import that Brahmā had made.
It was called the Vaiśālākṣa, after the wide-eyed one; that Indra received, the well-versed in sacred lore, of great austerity, in ten thousand chapters.
The blessed Puraṃdara too abridged that treatise into five thousand chapters, my son, and it is called the Bāhudantaka.
But into three thousand chapters Bṛhaspati, the lord, abridged it by his wisdom, and it is called the Bārhaspatya.
Into a thousand chapters Kāvya declared the abridgment of that treatise, he of boundless wisdom, the master of yoga, of great austerity.
Thus, out of regard for the world, this treatise was abridged by the great sages, perceiving the waning lifespan of mortals, O Pāṇḍava.
Then the gods, assembling, said to Viṣṇu, the lord of creatures: Appoint that one who alone among mortals is worthy of supremacy.
Then, having reflected, the blessed god Nārāyaṇa, the lord, brought forth a mind-born son, full of splendor and free of passion.
But Virajas, O greatly fortunate one, desired no sovereignty upon the earth; his mind was bent solely upon renunciation, O Pāṇḍava.
Kīrtimat was his son; he too passed beyond the five senses; and Kardama was his son, and he too performed great austerity.
Of Kardama the lord of creatures there was indeed a son named Anaṅga, a protector of the people, a good man, skilled in the science of statecraft.
Anaṅga's son Atibala, versed in polity, having attained it, came to the kingship of the earth; but then he fell under the sway of his senses.
Now the daughter of Death, O king, mind-born, named Sunīthā, renowned throughout the three worlds, gave birth to Vena.
Him, lawless toward his subjects and a slave to passion and hatred, the sages who expound the sacred word struck down with blades of kuśa grass made potent by mantras.
The sages, by force of mantra, churned his right thigh; thereupon there was born of him upon the earth a misshapen man of stunted limbs.
Like a charred stump to look upon, red-eyed and black-haired, to him the sages who expound the sacred word said, 'Sit down' (niṣīda).
From him sprang the Niṣādas, cruel, dwelling in mountains and forests, and the others by hundreds of thousands, the barbarians abiding in the Vindhyas.
Again those great sages churned his right hand; thereupon a man arose, like a second Indra in his form.
Clad in armor, his sword girded on, bearing arrows and bow, knowing the Vedas and their auxiliaries, and a master of the science of archery.
In him, that best of men, the whole science of statecraft took its abode, O king; then the son of Vena, with hands joined in reverence, spoke to those great sages.
"A most subtle understanding has arisen in me, one that perceives both dharma and worldly gain. By it, what is it that I must do? Tell me that truly."
"Whatever task, sound in purpose, you shall enjoin upon me, that I will surely perform—herein there is no need for hesitation."
Then those gods and those supreme seers spoke to him: "Wherever dharma stands fixed, that practice without misgiving."
"Casting aside both the pleasing and the unpleasing, even-minded toward all creatures, banishing far from you desire and anger, greed and pride."
"Whatever man in the world should swerve from dharma, he is to be restrained by you with your two arms, you who ever keep your gaze upon dharma."
"And take this vow in thought, in deed, and in word, again and again: 'I shall protect the sacred order of Brahman upon the earth.'"
"'And whatever has here been declared the polity of dharma, founded upon the science of just punishment, that I shall carry out without misgiving, never acting at my own caprice.'"
"And vow, O lord, 'The twice-born are exempt from punishment by me,' and 'I shall guard the world from all confusion of order,' O scorcher of foes."
Then the son of Vena said to those gods, led by the seers: "If the brāhmaṇas be my helpers, then so let it be, O bulls among the celestials."
"So be it," the expounders of the Veda said to the son of Vena; and Śukra, that treasure-house full of sacred wisdom, became his household priest.
The Vālakhilyas were his counselors, and the Sārasvata host became his retinue; the great seer, the venerable Garga, became his astronomer.
"With himself as the eighth"—such is the high tradition recounted among men; and the first of his bards arose then, the Sūta and the Māgadha.
And he brought about, rightly, the levelling of the earth; for great had been the unevenness of the ground before, so we have heard.
He was consecrated to the protection of the people by the god Viṣṇu, by Śakra together with the gods, by the seers, and by Brahmā.
The Earth herself, O Pāṇḍava, came to serve him, bearing her jewels, as did the Ocean, lord of rivers, and Himavān, best of mountains.
And Śakra bestowed upon him inexhaustible wealth, O Yudhiṣṭhira, and the great Meru, the golden mountain itself, gave him its gold.
And the venerable lord of the yakṣas and rākṣasas, he whose mount is a man, gave him wealth sufficient for dharma, for gain, and for pleasure.

Horses and chariots and elephants, and men by the tens of millions, sprang forth at the mere thought of the son of Vena, O Pāṇḍava; and there was neither old age nor famine, neither anguish of mind nor disease.
No fear ever arose there—from creeping things, from thieves, nor from one another—because of the protection of that king.
By him this Earth was milked of the seventeen kinds of grain, and by the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and nāgas of whatever each of them desired.
By that great-souled one was this world made to abound in dharma, and all his subjects were gladdened by him—therefore is he called rājan.
From his shielding the brāhmaṇas from harm he is called kṣatriya; and this Earth, made famous through his wealth, is held by the good to be Pṛthivī.
And Viṣṇu, the eternal, himself made this ordinance: "No one shall ever transgress against you, O king," O lord of the earth.
And by his ascetic power the venerable Viṣṇu entered into that lord of the earth; therefore the world bows before kings as before a god, O king.
Guarded ever by the science of just rule, O lord of men, no one could assail him—and because of his constant watch through spies and his vigilance, none dared.
When the king is the equal of any other in his own person and in his instruments of rule, what cause is there that the world should remain in his power, save divine ordinance and his innate worth?
From the brow of Viṣṇu there arose then a golden lotus, whence was born the goddess Śrī, the wife of wise Dharma.
And from Śrī, Artha was born through Dharma, O Pāṇḍava; thus Dharma, and likewise Artha, and Śrī, are established in kingship.
And through the spending of his merit, having descended from heaven to the earth, a man is born a king, my son, subject to the rule of just punishment.
Endowed upon the earth with that greatness which is of Viṣṇu, such a man becomes endowed with wisdom and attains to majesty of soul.
This ordinance of the gods none transgresses; and the world abides in the power of one alone, if it is governed accordingly.
For an auspicious deed, O lord of kings, conduces to weal—that of the one man, though the equal of others, in whose word this world abides.
For whoever has looked upon his face, gentle one, becomes obedient to his will, beholding it as gracious, full of meaning, and fair of form.
Therefore in the world, O lord of kings, it has ever been proclaimed by the wise: "The gods and the gods among men are equal," O lord of peoples.
All this concerning the greatness that resides in kings has now been related to you in full, O best of the Bharatas. What else shall be set forth here?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then once more, having saluted the grandsire, the son of Gaṅgā, and having become composed with palms joined, Yudhiṣṭhira put his question.
"What are the duties common to all the orders, and what severally are those of the four castes? What are held to be the duties of the four stages of life, and what the duties of a king?"
"By what does a realm prosper, by what does a king grow great, and by what do the citizens and the retainers flourish, O bull of the Bharatas?"
"As for treasury, army, and fortress, and allies and counselors, as well as officiating priests, household priests, and teachers—what manner of men should a king shun?"
"In whom should kings place their trust in any calamity, and against what should one's own self be firmly guarded? Tell me that, O grandsire."
Bhīṣma said: Homage to mighty Dharma, homage to Kṛṣṇa the ordainer! Having made obeisance to the brāhmaṇas, I shall declare the eternal duties.
Freedom from anger, truthful speech, fair sharing, and forbearance; the begetting of offspring upon one's own wife, purity, and freedom from malice.
Uprightness, and the maintenance of those who depend upon one—these nine belong to all the castes alike. But the duty that is the brāhmaṇa's alone, that I shall now declare to you.
Self-restraint, O great king, the ancients declared to be the foremost duty; in the study of the Veda and the teaching of it, the brāhmaṇa's work is fulfilled.
Should wealth come to such a one, while he abides in his own proper work, doing no forbidden deeds, tranquil, and contented in the satisfaction of wisdom—
let him beget a line of offspring, and then give gifts and offer sacrifice; for it is held by the good that wealth should be enjoyed only when it has been shared out.
But the brāhmaṇa who has accomplished his task through the study of the Veda alone may do other works or may not; he, being friendly to all, is called a true brāhmaṇa.
The duty that belongs to the kṣatriya also I shall declare to you, O Bhārata: a king should give but not beg, should sacrifice but not officiate as priest for others.
He should not teach, but should study; he should protect his subjects; ever ready for the slaying of marauders, he should show his valor in battle.
Of those rulers who have offered sacrifices and are learned in the Veda, those very ones who are conquerors in battle are the foremost winners of worlds.
The kṣatriya who returns from battle with his body unwounded—those versed in the ancient lore do not praise that deed of his.
For the slaying of the foes of the kṣatra-order is declared to be his foremost duty; there is no act more fitting for him than the crushing of marauders.
Giving, study, sacrifice, the practice of yoga, and the securing of welfare are enjoined upon him; therefore a king who seeks dharma must above all be ready to fight.
Having established all his subjects each in their own duties, the lord of the earth should cause all their undertakings to be brought to fulfillment in accordance with dharma.
A king may be deemed to have accomplished his task through the protecting of his people; he may do other works or may not, and is then called a prince of Indra's stamp.
The duty that here belongs to the vaiśya also I shall declare to you, O Bhārata: giving, study, sacrifice, and the gathering of wealth by honest means.

Diligent, the vaiśya should tend all his cattle here as a father tends his children; any other work that he should undertake would be a forbidden deed for him; for by guarding them he shall indeed attain great happiness.
For Prajāpati, having created the cattle, made them over to the vaiśya, while to the brāhmaṇa and to the king he made over all the people.
I shall declare his means of living and that whereby he sustains himself: of six cows he may take the milk of one, and from a hundred he may take a pair.
On the produce a seventh part, and likewise a small share on horn and hoof; and of grain and of all seeds—this is his yearly maintenance.
And it must never be the vaiśya's wish to say, "I will not guard the cattle"; and if the vaiśya is willing, they are by no means to be guarded by any other.
The duty that belongs to the śūdra also I shall declare to you, O Bhārata: Prajāpati appointed the śūdra to be the servant of the castes.
Therefore service to the castes is enjoined upon the śūdra; and by his ministering to them he shall attain great happiness.
Let the śūdra serve these three castes without spite; and let the śūdra never in any way make hoardings of wealth.
For a baser man, having gained wealth, would bring his betters under his sway; but if permitted by the king, a righteous one may do so at his pleasure.
I shall declare his means of living and that whereby he sustains himself; for the śūdra is said to be one whom the castes are bound to maintain.
An umbrella, a turban, a mat of fragrant grass, sandals, and fans—worn or used articles such as these are to be given to the śūdra who serves.
Garments that have become unfit to wear and are worn out by the twice-born are to be assigned to the śūdra alone; for that is his rightful portion.

And whatever śūdra should come willing to serve among the twice-born, by that one his fitting maintenance is to be provided, so say those who know dharma; a portion of food is to be given to the one who does not forsake his master, and the aged and the feeble among such are to be supported.

And the master must not be abandoned by the śūdra in any calamity; rather, when the master's substance is exhausted, he must be supported all the more, for the śūdra has no property of his own, since his wealth is such as the master may rightfully take.

For the three castes the sacrifice has been declared to be by means of the threefold Veda, O Bhārata; but for the śūdra the sacred utterance is enjoined to be the cry of svāhā and the reverential salutation.

With these two the śūdra, keeping his vows, may himself sacrifice by means of the simple cooked-food offerings; the sacrificial fee for such an offering, they say, consists of a vessel filled with food.
A śūdra named Paijavana gave a hundred thousand as the sacrificial fee, according to the rite of Indra and Agni—so have we heard.
Hence for all the castes the sacrifice of faith is enjoined; for faith is a great divinity, and it is that which sanctifies those who sacrifice.
The supreme divinity the brāhmaṇas worshipped here, each by his own rite and among one another, with their long sacrificial sessions and with those several eternal desires.

By the brāhmaṇas alone were the creations of the three castes brought forth; and they who are gods even of the gods—whatsoever they should pronounce, that indeed is supreme; therefore all sacrifices are brought about through the castes, not by self-interested desire.
A twice-born one who knows the Ṛk, the Yajus, and the Sāman should ever be honored like a god; but he who lacks the Ṛk, the Yajus, and the Sāman is a blight upon the realm of Prajāpati.

Sacrifice springs from devout intent, my son, among all the castes, O Bhārata; the gods do not strive after the sacrifice of one who destroys it, nor do other men; therefore among all the castes the sacrifice of faith is enjoined.

The brāhmaṇas ever worshipped their own divinity by their own rite, and so they caused the other castes to sacrifice; thus it was. That mighty law has been made known to us, ordained by Brahmā and beheld among the three castes.

Hence the castes are upright in their inborn duties; they are brought forth in due order, and this is the ripening of that ordinance: one is the Sāman, one the Yajus, and one the Ṛk, and one is the brāhmaṇa—yet among these an uncertainty has been observed.
On this matter, O lord of kings, those versed in ancient lore recite the verses sung of sacrifice, concerning the Vaikhānasa sages who longed to perform the rite.
Whether the sun has risen or not yet risen, the man of faith, his senses subdued, pours the oblation into the fire according to dharma; for faith, indeed, is the great cause.
Whatever of his oblation has spilled is reckoned the lesser, and whatever has not spilled the higher; manifold are the forms of sacrifice and varied the fruits of its diverse acts.
He who comprehends these rites fully, firm in the certainty of knowledge, a twice-born endowed with faith—that man is fit to perform the sacrifice.
Be he a thief, or wicked, or even the worst of evildoers—if he desires to perform the sacrifice, they call him a good man even so.

The seers praise him, and this is good beyond all doubt; for it is settled that by every means and by men of all varṇas the sacrifice must be performed—since nothing equal to sacrifice is found in the three worlds.
Therefore they declare that a man free of envy must sacrifice, taking refuge in the purity of faith and giving according to his means.
Bhīṣma said: Hear now, O mighty-armed one of true valour, of the four stages of life and of the duties of the four varṇas, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
The forest-dweller's life, the mendicant's begging, and householdership—that great stage—and the stage of studentship: this fourth they call the order embraced by brāhmaṇas.
Having undergone the rite of the matted lock and attained the state of the twice-born, having taken up the rites beginning with the kindling of the sacred fire, and having studied the Veda—
whether with a wife or without one, self-possessed and with senses restrained, having discharged his obligations he may pass from the householder's stage into the forest-dweller's order.
There, having mastered the forest treatises, that knower of dharma, with seed drawn upward, having begotten offspring, attains oneness with the Imperishable.
These very observances of the sages of upward-drawn seed are what the learned brāhmaṇa must first perform here, O king.
For the brāhmaṇa who has fulfilled his studentship, O lord of peoples, fitness for the mendicant's life is commended here, for one bound on liberation.
There he should sleep wherever the sun sets him, without sacred fire, without a home, living on whatever he chances to find—a sage, controlled, his senses conquered.
Free of craving, the same toward all, without enjoyments, unaltered—the brāhmaṇa, having reached this stage of peace, attains oneness with the Imperishable.

Having studied the Vedas and discharged every duty, having begotten offspring and tasted his pleasures, let him, composed, pursue that hard-to-tread dharma of householdership, beheld in the law of the sages.

Content with his own wife, approaching her in her season, observing his appointed duties, neither false nor crooked, sparing in food, devoted to the gods, grateful, truthful, gentle, free of cruelty, and forbearing—

controlled, obedient, heedful in offerings to gods and ancestors, ever a giver of food to the twice-born, free of envy, giving to all who wear the marks of an order, and constant in the three sacred fires—such should the householder be.
And on this, my son, the great seers of mighty soul recite the Song of Nārāyaṇa, weighty in meaning and fraught with the highest austerity; mark it well as I declare it.
