Truth and uprightness, the honouring of guests, dharma and wealth, and delight in one's wife—these are the joys to be cultivated, in this world and the next alike: such is my view.
The maintenance of sons and wife, and likewise the full recitation of the Vedas—that stage of the virtuous the supreme seers declare the most excellent.
The brāhmaṇa who, devoted to sacrifice, thus dwells duly in householdership, having purified well the householder's way of life, attains in heaven a stainless fruit.
At his laying down of the body, his cherished, undecaying desires are deemed to wait upon him, leading to the infinite—beings with eyes, heads, and faces on every side.
Eating alone, reciting alone, moving alone, O Yudhiṣṭhira, serving but one teacher, covered with the grime of penance—
the student, ever vowed, ever bent on consecration, self-mastered, should dwell always doing his appointed task and reciting the Veda without questioning.
Rendering constant service, let him bow low before his teacher, neither wholly withdrawn from the six prescribed acts nor wholly given over to them.
He does not act beyond his sanctioned office, nor serve one who is hostile: this, my son, is held to be the proper station of the student.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Tell me of those duties—auspicious, pleasant, of great consequence, free of harm, approved by the world, easy of means, and bringing happiness to such as I am.
Bhīṣma said: For the brāhmaṇa, O lord, four stages of life are ordained here; the three other varṇas follow after them, O best of the Bharatas.

Many heaven-winning duties have been declared, O king, that have the kṣatriya for their mainstay; these are not recorded among matters of illustration, for in the warrior's code everything is ordained in due order.
A man who, being a brāhmaṇa, takes to the works of the kṣatriya, the vaiśya, and the śūdra is censured in this world as dull of mind, and in the next world he goes to hell.
The name appointed in the world for a slave, a dog, a wolf, or a beast—that very name apply, O Pāṇḍava, to a brāhmaṇa settled in forbidden work.
For one engaged in the six prescribed acts in all four stages of life, endowed with every duty, fully formed, his self perfected—
for such a purified brāhmaṇa, delighting in austerity, free of craving and bountiful, the worlds are those named Imperishable.
Whatever deed a man does, of whatever kind, by whatever means and wherever—of just that kind, and by just such means, does he reap its quality.
Through usury, through farming and trade, and through the sustaining of life, you ought to understand, O lord of kings, the great reckoning measured by sacred study.
Time, impelled by time and fixed in the cycle of time, performs of necessity its deeds—the highest, the lowest, and the middling.
Finite are the gifts and the meritorious acts of old; but the world devoted to its own proper duty is imperishable, facing every way.

Bhīṣma said: The drawing of the bowstring, the slaughter of foes, farming, trade, the herding of cattle, and likewise menial service for the sake of gain—all this is the gravest forbidden conduct for a brāhmaṇa.
But the six sacred acts of the brāhmaṇa are to be practised by the wise householder; and for the brāhmaṇa who has discharged his duties, dwelling in the forest is commended.
Service of a king, wealth from farming, livelihood by trade, crookedness, the offspring of an unchaste woman, and usury—all these he should shun.

A brāhmaṇa in name only, O king, becomes a śūdra—he who is ill-conducted and fallen from dharma, the husband of a low-born woman, the slanderer, the dancer, the village drudge, and the doer of forbidden work.

Whether reciting the Vedas or not, O king, he is equal to śūdras, and like a slave he is one whose food may be taken; all these become the equals of śūdras, and them, O king, one should exclude from the rites of the gods.

In one of unbridled appetite, of cruel ways, of violent nature, who has cast off dharma and his own proper conduct, O king, the offerings to gods and ancestors and all else that should be given become things not to be given to him.
Therefore the dharma ordained for the brāhmaṇa is self-restraint, purity, and uprightness, O king; and likewise all the orders of the brāhmaṇa were in days of old sent forth by Brahmā himself.

He who is controlled, a drinker of the soma, noble in character, compassionate, all-enduring, free of craving, upright, gentle, without cruelty, and forbearing—he indeed is the brāhmaṇa, and not the other, the doer of evil deeds.

The śūdra, the vaiśya, and the king's son, O king—all the worlds, desiring dharma, lean upon them; yet, deeming the varṇas bound fast in the duties of mere birth, Viṣṇu does not desire them, O son of Pāṇḍu.

And were this fourfold order of varṇas not to exist in the world for all the world, the doctrines of the Veda too would not be; nor would all the sacrifices and all the works of the world, and at once none would be established in the orders of life.
And he among the three varṇas who would wish to follow the orders of life and to perform the duties prescribed for those orders—hear of them, O Pāṇḍava.
For the śūdra who has discharged his duty of service and accomplished the begetting of offspring, having gained leave of the king, O lord of the earth—
even for one who has gone but a little way, or who has gone the way of the ten duties, all the orders of life are ordained, save only that of the cravingless ascetic.
But they do not prescribe the mendicant's begging for that practiser of dharma, nor likewise for the vaiśya, O lord of kings, nor indeed for the king's son.
Having discharged his duties, advanced in years, and having laboured fully for the king, the vaiśya, with the king's leave, may pass into the round of the orders of life.
Having studied the Vedas according to dharma and the treatises on kingship, O sinless one, having performed the rites beginning with the begetting of offspring and partaken of the soma—
having guarded all his subjects according to dharma, O best of speakers, having performed the Rājasūya, the Aśvamedha, and other sacrifices likewise—
having gathered all as prescribed and given his sacrificial fees to the brāhmaṇas, having won victory in battle, whether little or much—
having set upon the throne, as guardian of the people, a son, O Pāṇḍava, or some other approved kṣatriya of another lineage, O bull among kṣatriyas—
having duly honoured the ancestors with rites for the fathers according to rule, and having worshipped the gods with sacrifices and the seers with the Vedas, all with diligence—
and when the end of life has come, he who would seek another order of life may, O king, passing through the orders in their due succession, attain perfection.
In the manner of a royal seer, O lord of kings, by following the path of the mendicant's begging, even one who has left behind the householder's dharma may roam abroad out of his desire to live.
Yet this is not the final, perfected work of the three—nor of the four orders of those who dwell in the stages of life, O tiger among kings, so they declare, O bull of the Bharatas.

Much depends on the kṣatriyas, who practise the dharma highest among men in the world; all the duties of the three varṇas, together with their subsidiary duties, derive from the dharma of the king—so I hear from the Veda.
As, O king, within the footprint of an elephant the tracks of all creatures born are merged, so know that all the duties, in every state, are wholly merged within the duties of the king.

Men learned in dharma call the other duties of small support and small fruit; but the noble declare that the kṣatriya's dharma, of great support and abounding in blessings, is foremost, and not another.

All duties have the king's dharma for their chief; by it are all duties protected; in the king's dharma lies the renouncing of all things, O king, and in renunciation, they say, lies the foremost and most ancient dharma.

Were the science of governance destroyed, the threefold Veda would sink, all duties would fall into confusion and cease to be, and all the duties of the orders of life would be undone, were the kṣatriya's ancient royal dharma forsaken.

All renunciations are seen within the king's dharma; all consecrations are declared within the king's dharma; all disciplines are declared within the king's dharma; all the worlds have entered into the king's dharma.
As living beings, struck down in the realm of nature, serve to oppress those who hold to dharma, so the duties, sundered from the king's dharma, in no condition uphold their own proper law.

Bhīṣma said: The duties of the four orders of life and the duties of birth, O Pāṇḍava, and those that have the guardians of the worlds for their height, are all established within the kṣatriya's dharma.
All these duties rest in the kṣatriya's code, O best of the Bharatas; in the world of the living, the cravingless too are established within the kṣatriya's dharma.
The dharma of those who dwell in the orders of life is unseen and of many gates; its nature they expound as eternal, by scriptural tradition alone.
Others, disputants, with holy words declare a settled doctrine of the world; not knowing the certainties of the duties, they take their delight in what has no demonstrable end.
But the dharma that abounds in manifest happiness, that has the self for its witness, that is free of deceit and is the good of all the world—that is firmly established among the kṣatriyas.

As for the brāhmaṇas who abide in the dharma of the orders of life, O Yudhiṣṭhira, and likewise for the three other varṇas, the teaching reckoned of old, peerless in the duties of kingship, has been won here through good conduct, and leads to the worlds.

It has been told to you, O lord of kings, how in days of old very many valiant kings resorted to Viṣṇu of mighty splendour, the god lord of all beings, the sovereign Nārāyaṇa, for the sake of the science of governance.
Each weighing one by one his own deeds in his station, the kings of old waited reverently upon him, abiding by his word of illustration.

The Sādhyas, the gods, the Vasus and the two Aśvins, the Rudras, the All-gods, and the hosts of the Maruts—gods created of old by the First God—these perfected ones too conduct themselves within the kṣatriya's dharma.

On this I shall set forth for you a dharma that is the settling of right purpose. When all bounds had been broken and the cause of the Dānavas alone prevailed, there was a king, O lord of kings, named Māndhātā, mighty in valour.
Long ago that guardian of the earth, out of a longing to behold him, performed a sacrifice directed toward the god Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, middle, or end.
That king, O tiger among kings, that Māndhātā, bowed his head and clasped the feet of the Supreme One, of the great-souled Viṣṇu, at the sacrifice.
Viṣṇu revealed himself to him, assuming the form of Vāsava; and the king, surrounded by virtuous princes, worshipped that Lord.
Between that assembly of kings and that great-souled one there took place this great dialogue concerning Viṣṇu, O you of mighty splendour.

Indra said: What do you desire, O best of the upholders of dharma, that you wish to behold the immeasurable one — Nārāyaṇa, the primeval first god, of boundless illusion and unmeasured being and might?
That god of universal form cannot be seen face to face even by me, nor even by Brahmā. Whatever other desires lie within your heart, O king, those I shall grant — for you are a king among mortals.
Steadfast in truth, devoted to dharma, master of your senses, a hero firmly delighting in the gods — for your wisdom, your devotion, and your supreme faith, I therefore grant you a boon as you wish.

Māndhātā said: Without doubt, O Lord, I shall behold the primeval god, having won his favour with my head bowed. Renouncing pleasures, longing for dharma, I wish to go to the forest, to the righteous path that the worthy frequent.

By the kṣatriya dharma, vast and immeasurable, I have won the worlds and established my own fame. But that dharma which proceeded from the primeval god, the foremost in the world — that I do not know how to fulfil.

Indra said: Should you walk without an army and turned away from dharma, you would still attain the highest goal only by remaining vigilant. For the kṣatriya dharma proceeded from the primeval god, and the other duties came afterward, as its remainders.

Those remainders, though created with limits, become endless and lead well onward, being grounded in the kṣatriya dharma. Into this dharma all the other duties have entered; therefore men call this dharma the highest.
For in olden days the gods and the seers of measureless might were all delivered by deeds, when Viṣṇu, through the kṣatriya dharma, crushed their foes.
For had that Lord, the wealth-bearing and immeasurable one, not slain all the enemies, there would be no brāhmaṇas, no maker of the worlds and the rest, no true dharma, and no primal dharma at all.

Had that immeasurable best of the gods not in olden times conquered this earth by his valour, the four varṇas and the duties of the four āśramas would all be no more, through the destruction of brahman itself.

The eternal duties, seen in their hundredfold forms, are set in motion again and again by the kṣatriya dharma; in age after age the primal duties are set forth. Therefore men call the kṣatriya dharma the foremost in the world.

Self-sacrifice, compassion for all beings, knowledge of the world, the granting of release, protection, and the deliverance of the despairing and the afflicted — all these are found, for kings, in the kṣatriya dharma.
The lawless, driven by desire and wrath, do not fall into sin out of fear of the king; while the disciplined others, endowed with every virtue and of righteous conduct, righteously practise dharma.
All beings, who must be cherished like sons by kings through the dharma proper to their station, move about in the world unharmed — of this there is no doubt.
The kṣatriya order, devoted to all duties, foremost in the world and eternal, has the imperishable as its everlasting bound — itself imperishable and facing every direction.

Indra said: Of such valour, endowed with all virtues, the kṣatriya dharma is the highest among all duties. It must be upheld by you, O noble lions among men; for in its reversal would come the ruin of the people.

Let the king know as his foremost dharma the cultivation of the land, the rites of consecration befitting a king, the renunciation of begging, the protection of the people, compassion for all beings, and the surrender of his body in battle.

The sages declare renunciation the highest; best of all is he who would lay down his body. In the duties of kingship all is forever given up — these protectors of the earth are ever a witness before your eyes.

By wide learning, by service to the teacher, or by the slaying of an enemy, men declare it dharma. Let the kṣatriya, a celibate ever devoted to duty, longing for dharma, walk alone through the stages of life.

When affairs touching the common good are afoot, carefully shunning both favour and disfavour, by establishing and protecting the four varṇas, and by those several disciplines, observances, and inborn means—

—by all such exertions they declare the dharma of the stages of life to be the kṣatriya dharma, the foremost, endowed with every virtue. Those varṇas who do not practise each their own duty, those very duties are pronounced ill-performed.

Men who are forever lost in lawless gain they call mere beasts in human form. Inasmuch as it leads to right conduct, away from greed for gain, the order of the kṣatriya dharma is therefore the better.

That course belonging to the brāhmaṇas versed in the three Vedas, and that mode of life enjoined upon brāhmaṇas — this they call the brāhmaṇa's foremost work; doing otherwise, he is like a śūdra, fit to be slain by the sword.
The duties of the four āśramas and the duties of the Veda, O king, are to be followed by the brāhmaṇa; no other should know them in any way.
For one who conducts himself otherwise, that mode of livelihood is not allowed; dharma is made manifest by deeds — as is a dog, so is he.
A brāhmaṇa established in forbidden acts does not deserve honour; useless in his proper works, men know him to be unworthy of trust.

These duties and all the varṇas are to be upheld by heroes, by kṣatriyas — this is their dharma. Therefore the duties of kingship are foremost, and no others; the duties of heroes, with valour foremost, are in my judgement supreme.
Māndhātā said: The Yavanas, Kirātas, Gāndhāras, Cīnas, Śabaras, Barbaras, Śakas, Tuṣāras, Kahvas, Pahlavas, Āndhras, and Madrakas;
the Oḍras, Pulindas, Ramaṭhas, Kācas, and barbarians of every kind; and the men sprung from brāhmaṇa and kṣatriya stock, the vaiśyas, and the śūdras—
how should all these who dwell within a realm practise dharma, and how are all those who live as outlaws to be set in order by men such as I?
This I wish to hear, O Lord; tell it to me; for you have become a kinsman to us kṣatriyas, O lord of the gods.
Indra said: Service to mother and father must be rendered by all outlaws, and likewise service to the teacher and the elders, and to those who dwell in the āśramas.
Service to the protectors of the earth, too, must be rendered by all outlaws; and the rites enjoined by Vedic dharma are likewise ordained as their dharma.
Offerings to the ancestors, the digging of wells, watering-sheds, and resting-places, and gifts in due season to the twice-born — these too they should bestow.
Non-injury, truth, freedom from anger, the giving and safeguarding of livelihood, the support of one's children and wife, purity, and the absence of malice;
the sacrificial fees of all sacrifices are to be given by one who desires prosperity; and the costly cooked-food offerings are to be performed by all outlaws.
These works of such kinds, ordained of old, O sinless one, are the duties of all people, to be performed here, O king.
Māndhātā said: There are seen in the world, among all the varṇas, men who are outlaws — moving under another guise, present even within the four āśramas.
Indra said: When the rod of justice is ruined and the duty of kingship cast aside, beings fall into utter confusion through the wickedness of the king, O lord of men.
Countless mendicants and bearers of false marks will arise, and a confusion of the āśramas, once this Kṛta age has passed away.
Heedless of the supreme courses of the ancient duties, men will take to the wrong path, driven by desire and wrath.
When the evildoer is restrained by the rod of justice in the hands of the great-souled, then dharma — true, eternal, and supreme — does not waver.
Whoever slights the king, who is a guide even to the world beyond, for him neither gift, nor oblation, nor funeral rite ever bears any fruit.
The lord of men, sovereign over mortals, become divine and everlasting, devoted to dharma — even the gods hold such a king in high honour.
For the Lord Prajāpati, who created this whole world, desires the kṣatriya order for the sake of setting the duties in motion and bringing them to rest.
He who, with understanding, keeps in mind the course of dharma once set in motion — he is worthy of my honour and my worship; in him the kṣatriya order stands established.
Bhīṣma said: Having spoken thus, that Lord Viṣṇu, surrounded by the host of the Maruts, departed to his abode, the imperishable, the supreme station.
With dharma thus rightly set in motion of old, O sinless one, what man of sense and wide learning would slight the kṣatriya order?
Things begun unjustly, and likewise things so abandoned, pass to ruin midway, as a man without sight perishes upon the road.
With the wheel set turning at the beginning, and devoted to that first foundation, conduct yourself accordingly, O tiger among men; this I declare to you, O sinless one.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I have heard the four āśramas of men as the ancients told them; expound their meaning to me who ask, O grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: All these duties are known to you, Yudhiṣṭhira, even as they are known to me, O mighty-armed one — duties approved by the virtuous.
But as for the dharma that passes under another guise, about which you ask me, Yudhiṣṭhira, O best of the upholders of dharma, hear that now, O lord of men.
All these, O son of Kuntī, O bull among men, are found in those who, devoted to righteous conduct, perform the works of the four āśramas.
For the king free from desire and hatred, who rules by the rod of justice and looks with even regard upon all beings, there comes the standing of the mendicant's āśrama, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
For the hero who knows when to take and when to give, and likewise restraint and favour, and who lives by the rule laid down, there comes the standing of the āśrama of security.
For him who rescues his kinsmen, relations, and friends fallen into distress, O Yudhiṣṭhira, there comes the standing of the āśrama of consecration.
For him who performs his daily observances, and the sacrifices to beings, to the ancestors, and to men, in ample measure, O Pārtha, there comes the standing of the forest-dweller's āśrama.
By the protection of all beings and the safeguarding of his own realm, the king undertakes consecrations of many kinds; thus there comes to him the standing of the forest-dweller's āśrama.
Constancy in the study of the Veda, patience, the honouring of the teacher, and likewise service to the preceptor — these bring the standing of the brāhmaṇa's āśrama.
For him who ever treads a straight and guileless path toward all beings, O Bhārata, there comes the standing of the brāhmaṇa's āśrama.
For him who bestows ample wealth upon forest-hermits, upon brāhmaṇas, and upon those versed in the three Vedas, O Bhārata, there comes the standing of the forest-dweller's āśrama.
For him who shows compassion toward all beings, O Bhārata, and is devoted to gentleness, there comes a standing that embraces every state.
For him who shows compassion toward the young and the old in every condition, O Kaurava, O Yudhiṣṭhira, there comes a standing that embraces every state.
By rendering deliverance to beings overpowered by force, O foremost of the Kurus, and to those who come seeking refuge, O Kaurava, a man may dwell in the householder's life.
By giving protection in every way to beings moving and unmoving, and by ever offering honour as is due, a man may dwell in the householder's life.
Restraint and favour toward elder and younger wives, toward brothers, sons, and grandsons, O Pārtha — that is the householder's life, and that is its austerity.
The protection of the worthy, deserving of honour, who are known among the people as masters of themselves, O tiger among men, brings the standing of the householder's āśrama.
He who in his own house, O Bhārata, takes up the duties belonging to all the āśramas by the giving of food — that is the householder's life, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
The man who stands firm in the dharma created by the Ordainer, fittingly and truly, attains the unsurpassed fruit of all the āśramas.
In whatever man his virtues never perish, O son of Kuntī, him too they call one established in an āśrama, that best of men, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Granting honour according to station, according to age, and likewise according to lineage, a man dwells in truth within all the āśramas, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
By upholding the customs of the land, O son of Kuntī, and likewise the customs of the lineage, O tiger among men, a king becomes a dweller in all the āśramas.
By honouring in due season the prosperity of beings and likewise their offerings, O tiger among men, one may dwell in the āśrama of the virtuous.
And he who, holding to the tenfold dharma, watches over the dharma of all the world, O son of Kuntī — that king becomes a dweller in an āśrama.
Of the good and skilled in dharma who practise dharma in the world, protected within a king's domain, a fourth part of their merit becomes the share of that lord of the earth.
But those kings who fail to protect men who delight in dharma and are devoted to dharma, O tiger among men — they take upon themselves the sin of such men.
And those who serve as helpers in the protection rendered by kings, O Yudhiṣṭhira—all of them, O sinless one, are sharers in the merit, though the righteous act be performed by another.

For the householder's life, O tiger among men, they declare to be the station that embraces all the orders of life, of luminous determination and purifying—the very one we ourselves reverently uphold.
But the man who looks upon all creatures as upon his own self, who has laid down the rod and conquered his anger—he, departing this world, attains happiness.
Raised up by dharma, with goodness for its strength, bearing the banner of the bridge of dharma, swift and driven by the wind of renunciation upon its course—this boat shall carry you across.
When the desire that abides in his heart has turned away from everything, then a man becomes established in goodness, and thereafter he attains to Brahman.
Serene in disposition and through yoga, O lord of men, O tiger among men, you shall attain dharma by delighting in the protection of your subjects.
Make your effort in the protection of the brāhmaṇas devoted to the study of the Vedas and of pure deeds, and of all the world besides, O sinless one.
Whatever dharma a man practices in the forest and in the hermitages, O Bhārata, a hundredfold of that dharma the king attains through his protection.
Thus has the manifold dharma been declared to you, O best of the Pāṇḍavas. Practice it, this eternal dharma beheld by the men of old.
Single-minded toward the four orders of life and the four classes, O Pāṇḍava, O tiger among men, you shall attain dharma by delighting in their protection.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The four orders of life have been told here, and likewise the four classes. Tell me, grandfather, what is the most essential duty toward the realm.
Bhīṣma said: This is the most essential duty toward the realm—the consecration of a king. A realm without an Indra is feeble, and bandits overwhelm it.
In kingless realms dharma cannot stand firm, and men devour one another. In every way, fie upon the kingless state!
"This king is chosen as an Indra"—so runs the sacred utterance. As Indra is honored, so should the king be honored by one who desires prosperity.
"In kingless realms one should not dwell"—so the Vedic teaching declares. In kingless realms not even Agni bears the oblation to the gods.
Yet should a mightier one come forward seeking the kingdom—upon realms that are kingless, or whose king has been slain—
he should be met and welcomed with honor: this is the wise counsel here. For there is nothing more evil than the evil of being without a king.
If he looks upon the realm with favor, all will be well; for a mighty one, once enraged, could leave nothing whole.
The cow that is hard to milk earns the greater suffering; but the cow that yields her milk easily—her they do not torment at all.
What bends without being heated, that they do not heat at all; and the wood that is already bent of itself, that they do not trouble to bend.
By this likeness the steadfast man should bow to the stronger. He who bows to the stronger bows verily to Indra himself.
Therefore a king must always be installed by one who desires prosperity. Neither wealth nor wife is secure for those who live in a kingless state.
The wicked man delights to seize another's wealth where there is no king; but when others in turn snatch his own away, then he longs for a king.
Then even the wicked find no security at all; for from one, two carry off the spoil, and from those two, many others again.
The free man is made a slave, and women are carried off by force. For this reason the gods appointed protectors of the people.
Were there no king in the world, no wielder of the rod upon the earth, the stronger would roast the weaker as men roast fish upon a spit.
In olden times the kingless people perished, so we have heard, devouring one another as the big fish in the water devour the small.

Then they gathered together and made covenants, so we have heard: "The man cruel of speech, the one who deals in violence, the adulterer, and he who would seize what is not his own—such men shall be cast out by us."
For the assurance of all the classes alike, without distinction, they made this covenant—yet they did not abide by the covenant they had made.
Then, united and stricken with distress, they went to the Grandfather: "Without a sovereign we are perishing, O Lord; appoint for us a sovereign."
"One whom we may all together honor, and who shall guard us round about." To them he appointed Manu; but Manu did not assent to them.
Manu said: I am afraid of so cruel a task, for kingship is exceedingly hard to bear, above all among men who are forever false in their conduct.

Bhīṣma said: The people answered him: "Do not fear—the guilt of this task shall pass to those who do the wrong. One head in fifty of our cattle and of our gold, and a tenth part of our grain, we shall give you to enrich your treasury."
"The foremost of men, skilled in the use of weapons, shall follow you as the gods follow great Indra."
"You, O king, grown mighty, unassailable, full of majesty, shall establish us all in happiness, as Kubera does the Nairṛtas."
"And whatever dharma the people, well-guarded by the king, shall practice—a fourth part of that dharma shall come to rest in you."
"Sustained by that great dharma, won through our happiness, protect us on every side, O king, as Indra of a hundred sacrifices protects the gods."
"Go forth swiftly to victory, blazing like the sun with its rays. Scatter the pride of our enemies; may dharma forever conquer for us."
Forth he went, that one of mighty splendor, surrounded by a great host, endowed with high birth, blazing as it were with majesty.
Beholding his greatness, as the gods behold that of great Indra, all the people trembled, and set their minds upon their own duties.
Then he traversed the earth, like the rain-bearing cloud, quelling the wicked on every side and yoking each man to his own task.
Thus whatever men anywhere on earth should desire prosperity, let them first of all install a king, for the favoring of the people.
And let them bow before him with devotion, as pupils ever bow before their teacher, as the gods before the thousand-eyed one—so should the people stand near their king.
The man honored by his own people, even a stranger holds in high regard; but one despised by his own kin, strangers too will hold in contempt.
The contempt of strangers for a king brings unhappiness to all. Therefore the parasol, the conveyance, garments and ornaments,
and foods and drinks, and dwellings too, they should give to the king—seats and couches and every appointment of comfort besides.
Let the king be guarded in himself, hard to assail, one who speaks first with a smile; and when addressed, let him answer men sweetly.
Let him be grateful, firm in devotion, generous in sharing, master of his senses; when looked upon, let him look back gently, frankly, and graciously.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Why do the brāhmaṇas call the king a divinity, O bull of the Bharatas—him who is sovereign over men? Tell me that, grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recite an ancient tale—how Vasumanas questioned Bṛhaspati, O Bhārata.
A king named Vasumanas, of Kosala, the best of the wise, accomplished in understanding, questioned the great seer Bṛhaspati.
Versed in courtesy, he performed for Bṛhaspati every act of homage, and taking his place at the seer's right hand, he bowed in due form,
and asked the way of kingship, devoted to the welfare of all beings, seeking the good of his subjects, the root of which is dharma, O lord of the people.
By what do creatures prosper, and by what do they come to ruin? Honoring whom, O greatly wise one, might they attain the highest happiness?
Thus questioned by the great king of Kosala, of measureless might, Bṛhaspati, unperturbed, declared to him the honoring due to a king.
The dharma of the world, O great king, is seen to have its root in the king. It is from fear of the king alone that the people do not devour one another.
For the king alone, by his dharma, brings to peace the whole world when it is in turmoil and unrest; and having brought it to peace, he shines forth in splendor.
For as, O king, were the moon and the sun not to rise, all creatures would sink into blind darkness, unable to see one another,
as fish in waterless shallows, or birds where none can cry out, would range about at their pleasure, falling upon one another again and again,
crushing and trampling and overpowering one another, they would swiftly pass into annihilation—of this there is no doubt—
even so, without a king, these subjects would perish; they would sink into blind darkness, like cattle without a herdsman.
The strong would seize the possessions of the weak, and slay those who resisted, were the king not to protect them.
Conveyances, garments, ornaments, and jewels of every kind the wicked would seize by violence, were the king not to protect.
In this world there would be no holding of property as "this is mine"; universal ruin would set in, were the king not to protect.
Mother, father, the aged, the teacher, the guest, the elder—men would torment or even kill them, were the king not to protect.
Manifold weapons would fall in many ways upon those who walk in dharma, and unrighteousness would take firm hold, were the king not to protect.
Slaughter, bondage, and torment would forever be the lot of the wealthy, and men would find no sense of ownership, were the king not to protect.
All within would become a void, this world would fall to the bandits, and men would sink into dreadful hell, were the king not to protect.
The rearing of stock would not go on, nor tillage, nor the trader's road; dharma would sink, and the threefold Veda would be no more, were the king not to protect.
Sacrifices would not be performed in due form with their proper gifts, nor weddings, nor assemblies, were the king not to protect.
Bulls would not be set to their work, nor would the churns be turned, and the cattle-stations would go to ruin, were the king not to protect.
Terrified, sick at heart, sunk in lamentation and bereft of sense, everything would perish in a moment, were the king not to protect.
The year-long sacrificial sessions would not be held free from all fear, endowed with their due gifts, were the king not to protect.
The brāhmaṇas, the ascetics, bathed in learning and bathed in austerity, would not study the four Vedas, were the king not to protect.
Hand would rob hand, and all the dikes of order would be broken; everything, stricken with fear, would scatter in flight, were the king not to protect.
The people, with their brāhmaṇas slain and themselves struck down, would find no union with dharma; the doer would go his way ruled by his own senses' whim, were the king not to protect.
Misrule would prevail, and there would arise a confusion of the classes; famine would invade the realm, were the king not to protect.
For men, guarded by the king, sleep with their house-doors thrown open at their pleasure, free on every side from all fear.
No one will endure even a harsh word—how much less the laying-on of a hand—if among men the king is a righteous protector.
And women, unaccompanied by men, adorned with all their ornaments, go their way without fear, when the lord of the earth protects.
They take refuge in dharma alone, they do no violence to one another, and they show each other kindness—when the lord of the earth protects them.
The three orders perform their great sacrifices, each in its own manner, and devoted men study the scriptures—when the lord of the earth protects them.
This world is rooted in livelihood and is forever upheld by the threefold Veda; all of this proceeds rightly when the lord of the earth protects it.
When the king takes up the noblest yoke and bears his subjects forward with a great application of strength, then the world is at peace.
In whose absence there would be the utter ruin of all beings, and in whose presence their continuance is ensured—who would not honor him?
He who bears the burden of the king—a burden that brings happiness to all the world—and abides ever in his welfare and his pleasure, wins both worlds.
The man who plots evil against him even in thought will, beyond doubt, suffer affliction here, and after death fall into hell as well.
The lord of the earth must never be despised on the grounds that he is but a man, for this is a mighty deity standing here in human form.
For he assumes, ever according to the occasion, five forms: he becomes Agni, and the Sun, and Death, and Vaiśravaṇa, and Yama.
For when the king, falsely served, burns up the wicked with fierce splendor, then he becomes Fire.
When the lord of the earth, through his spies, watches over all beings, and goes about securing their welfare, then he becomes the Sun.
And when in anger he destroys impure men by the hundred, together with their sons and grandsons and ministers, then he becomes the Ender.
But when he restrains all the unrighteous with sharp punishments and favors the righteous, then he becomes Yama.
And when he gratifies his benefactors with streams of wealth, and strips away the various treasures of those who do him harm—
when he bestows fortune upon one and withdraws it from another, then, O king, the lord of the earth becomes Vaiśravaṇa in the world.
One who is capable, untiring in his deeds, who seeks lawful gain and bears no grudge against his lord, must never stand in censure of him.
For no man who acts against the king can obtain happiness—be he son, or brother, or friend, even were he the king's own equal.
Fire whose course is black, blazing with the wind for its charioteer, may leave some remnant behind; but for the man whom the king has fallen upon, no remnant is found anywhere.
All things that belong to the king and are under his protection a man should shun from afar; he should recoil from seizing the king's property as he would from death.
He who lays hands upon it perishes at once, like a deer that touches a snare; the wise man should guard the king's property here as if it were his own.
Into a great and terrible hell, bottomless, the senseless men who steal the king's wealth fall, there to remain for many a long night.
King, lord, sovereign, emperor, kṣatriya, master of the earth, ruler of men—he who is extolled by such titles, who would not wish to honor him?
Therefore one who would prosper—disciplined, self-conquered, his senses restrained, intelligent, mindful, and capable—should take service with the lord of the earth.
The king should honor a counselor who is grateful, wise, generous of spirit, steadfast in devotion, master of his senses, ever firm in dharma, and constant in his proper conduct.
He should rely upon a man of firm devotion, of seasoned wisdom, knowing dharma, his senses controlled, valiant, of no mean deeds, and free of any forbidden following.
The king makes a man bold; the king makes the feeble man thrive; whence can there be happiness for one upon whom the king has fallen? The king makes happy the man he favors.

The king is the very heart of his people, weighty above all; their recourse, their foundation, and their highest happiness. Men who take refuge in the lord of men rightly conquer both this world and the next.
And the ruler of men too, having governed the earth with self-restraint, with truth, and with goodwill, and having worshipped with great sacrifices, attains in glory an honored place in heaven.
Thus addressed by his teacher, that best of kings, the heroic Kausalya, with diligent effort carried out the protection of his subjects.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What further duty in particular remains for a king to perform? How is the realm to be protected, and how are enemies to be guarded against?
How should he employ his spies, and how win the confidence of the orders? How should he deal with his servants, how with his wives, and how with his sons, O Bhārata?
Bhīṣma said: Hear in full, O great king, with close attention, the conduct of a king—what must first be done by the ruler himself, or by one of a kingly nature.
The king must always conquer himself first, and only then his enemies; for how can a ruler of men who has not conquered himself vanquish his foes?
Self-conquest amounts to just this: the mastery of the five-fold group of the senses. A ruler of men whose senses are subdued is able to crush his foes.
He should post guard-companies in the fortresses and at the junctions, O delight of the Kurus, and in the groves about the city and in its parks as well.
And in all the assembly-places and the market-towns, and in the heart of the city, O tiger among men, and likewise within the royal residence.
Then he should appoint secret agents disguised as idiots, blind men, and deaf men—well-tested, shrewd persons able to endure hunger, thirst, and the heat of the sun.
And with a steady mind, O great king, he should set such agents upon all his ministers, upon allies of the three kinds, and upon his own sons.
In the city and in the countryside, and among the neighboring kings, the agents to be deployed should be so placed that they do not know one another.
And he should detect the spies sent in by the enemy, O bull of the Bharatas—in the marketplaces, in the pleasure-houses, in the gatherings, and among the mendicants;
in the gardens and the parks, in the assemblies of the learned, in the brothels and at the crossroads, in the council-halls and the rest-houses.
In this way the discerning king should foil the enemy's espionage with espionage of his own; for when the enemy's spies are foiled, all his designs are foiled, O Pāṇḍava.
But when a king perceives by his own judgment that he is the weaker, he should take counsel with his ministers and conclude a peace with the stronger power.
While his weakness is still unknown, the discerning king should make peace with his adversary—whether because he is in haste, or because he seeks to gain some particular object.
With those who are virtuous, of great energy, knowing dharma, and upright, the king should ally himself, governing his kingdom by dharma.
When the great-minded king perceives that he is being undone, he should strike down those who first did him injury and all who are hated by the people.
A ruler who can neither do good nor do harm, and who is in his nature impossible to overthrow—such a one is to be left to himself.
The discerning king should march upon an enemy who is unaware, who has no ally to call upon, who is without near support, who is preoccupied, negligent, and weak.
The hero, when his army is sound and well-nourished and he himself at ease, should order the campaign—but only after first making due provision both for the march and for the city.
And though some king be valiant, if he will not submit to him, then one inferior in strength and prowess should wear him down and so subdue him.

He should harass that king's realm with sword, fire, and stupefying poison, and should foment quarrels among his ministers and favorites; for open war must always be avoided by the wise man who covets dominion.

Bṛhaspati declares that the gaining of one's object is by three means: by conciliation, by gifts, and by sowing dissension, O ruler of men; and the wise man should rest content with whatever object he can secure thereby.
And the king of boundless wisdom should take a tax from his subjects, a sixth part, O delight of the Kurus—and that for their very protection.
Whatever wealth, great or small, belongs to those who follow the tenfold path of dharma, he should not seize precipitately—and this for the protection of his townsfolk.
As one's sons, so are the townsfolk to be regarded—of this there is no doubt; and affection toward them is to be shown in the conduct of public affairs.
And the king should appoint a wise son, who discerns all matters, to oversee judicial affairs continually; for therein the kingdom rests secure.
Over the mines, the salt-works, the customs-tolls, the ferries, and the elephant-forests, the king should set trusted ministers, or faithful men devoted to his welfare.
A king who ever wields the rod of punishment rightly attains dharma; the constant and rightful exercise of punishment is, for a king, commended as dharma itself.
A king should be learned in the Vedas and their auxiliaries, wise, given to austerity, ever liberal in giving, and devoted to sacrifice, O Bhārata.
All these virtues should abide ever firm in a king; but if a king neglects his duties, whence comes heaven for him, and whence renown?
But when a king is hard pressed by a stronger king, he should call upon his allies of the three kinds and make his arrangements accordingly.
He should post cowherd-stations along the roads, and even break up the outlying villages, and bring all their people within the suburbs and lesser towns.
He should bring the wealthy folk and the leaders of his forces into those regions that are well-guarded and easily defended, soothing them again and again.
The ruler of men should himself gather in the standing crops; and where they cannot be brought in, he should have them thoroughly burned with fire.
As for crops still standing in the enemy's fields, he should suborn men to corrupt them, or else destroy the whole of his foe's substance with his own forces.
On the rivers and along the roads he should always break down the bridges; he should drain off all the water, and what cannot be drained off he should foul.
Whether disputing over the immediate moment or over the future, he must repel his neighboring foe in battle—even when the hour for an ally's aid has come.
And all about the fortresses the king should have all the lesser trees cut down to their roots—but he should spare the sacred trees of the shrines.
Of the full-grown trees he should have the branches lopped off likewise; but of the sacred trees of the shrines, even the felling of a leaf is by all means to be avoided.
He should have proper parapets constructed, and likewise openings that admit the sky; and he should fill the moats so that they teem with stakes, crocodiles, and great fish.
There should be small barred gateways for the city to breathe through; and these too must be guarded with all care, just like the main gates.
At the gates he should ever set up massive engines, and should mount the śataghnīs, and keep them all under his own command.
He should bring in stores of timber, and have wells dug; and he should also cleanse the wells made earlier by those in want of water.
Houses thatched with grass he should plaster over even with mud; and in the month of Caitra he should clear the grass out of the city for fear of fire.
The ruler of men should have meals cooked only by night; by day no fire should burn in any house, save in that of the keeper of the sacred fire.
In the smithies and the lying-in houses fire may burn, but kept under control; and when fire is brought into the dwellings, the flame must be held in check.
And a heavy penalty should fall upon any man in whose house a fire is found by day; and this the king should proclaim aloud, for the safeguarding of the city.
Beggars, wandering cart-folk, the drunk and the deranged, and strolling players he should keep outside, O best of men; for otherwise they prove a source of mischief.
At the crossroads, the bathing-places, the council-halls, and the rest-houses, the king should everywhere station an informant of a station suited to each place.
The ruler of men should have the royal highways made broad, and should ordain the watering-booths and the market-rows each according to its proper place.
The storehouses, the armories, and the granaries of every kind, the stables for horses and the stalls for elephants, and the headquarters of the army—
the moats too, O Kaurava, the broad roads and the narrow passes—let no one ever look upon these, for they are secret matters, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then a king hard pressed by an enemy's forces should lay up stores—oil, honey, clarified butter, grain, and medicines of every kind.
Of charcoal, of kuśa and muñja grass, of the leaves of palāśa and reed, and of fodder, fuel, and resin, let him have stocks gathered up.
And of weapons of every sort—lances, swords, javelins, and armor—and of such things, let the lord of men have stores laid by.
All medicines too, with their roots and fruits, and physicians of the four kinds, he should especially keep at hand.
Actors and dancers, wrestlers and conjurers as well, should adorn the fair city and gladden the people in every way.
And wherever suspicion may arise—whether of a servant or of a counselor, of the townsfolk or even of the king himself—he should keep those persons under his own control.
When a task is accomplished, O lord of kings, he should honor men with gifts of wealth, with fitting marks of esteem, and with kind words of many kinds.
Having driven off the enemy or slain him, O joy of the Kurus, the king becomes free of his debt, as is shown in the scriptures.
Seven things are to be guarded by a king; learn them from me: his own self, his ministers, his treasury, his armed force, and his allies,
and likewise his realm and his capital, O joy of the Kurus. This sevenfold kingdom must be protected with diligence.
The sixfold policy, the triad of aims, and the other triad besides—he who knows these, O tiger among men, enjoys this earth.
What is called the sixfold policy, learn that now, O Yudhiṣṭhira: making peace and then staying still; marching forth after concluding an alliance;
waging war and then staying still; setting out on a campaign; the policy of division among others; and taking refuge with a stronger power.
And the triad that has been spoken of—hear it now with single mind: decline, stability, and growth; that is the one triad.
Dharma, profit, and pleasure—these are to be pursued, each in its proper season; for it is through dharma that the protector of the earth governs the earth for long.
On this matter there are two verses sung by Aṅgiras himself; O son of the Yādava woman, blessings upon you—it is fitting that you hear these too.
Having performed all his duties, having well protected the earth, and having guarded his people, he flourishes in happiness in the world beyond.
What use is austerity to that king, and what use his sacrifices, whose subjects, left unprotected, are all bereft of dharma?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The science of punishment and the king—the two taken together, both of them—through whose doing of what does success come about? Tell me that, O grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: Hear from me, O king, as I declare it duly here, O Bhārata, the great majesty of the science of punishment, in well-established words backed by reasons.
The science of punishment, rightly applied by the lord, keeps the four orders to their own duties, and holds them back from acts contrary to dharma.
When the four orders abide each in its own duty, when the bounds of conduct are unconfused, when the science of punishment has wrought security and the people have nothing to fear from any quarter—
then the three orders make their effort in the Soma rites as enjoined; know therefore that the happiness of gods and men alike rests secure upon this.
Whether the age is the cause of the king, or the king is the cause of the age—let no such doubt remain in you: it is the king who is the cause of the age.
When a king conducts himself by the science of punishment rightly and in its entirety, then sets in that best of ages named the Kṛta Yuga.
In the Kṛta age dharma prevails; nowhere is unrighteousness to be found; and among all the orders the mind takes no pleasure in unrighteousness.
The acquisition and keeping of goods proceed for the people—of this there is no doubt—and the rites enjoined by the Vedas come to pass without defect.
All the seasons too are pleasant and free of sickness, and the voices, complexions, and minds of men grow serene.
No diseases arise then, nor is any man seen short-lived; no widows are there, and no cruel man is born.
The earth yields its harvest without tillage, and so too do the plants spring up; bark, leaf, fruit, and root all become full of potency.
No unrighteousness is found there, but dharma alone, entire. Know these to be the qualities of the Kṛta age, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
When a king follows the science of punishment in three parts, letting the fourth part go, then the Tretā age sets in.
A fourth part of evil then attends upon the three parts of good; and the earth yields its harvest only when tilled, and so too the plants.
When a king, abandoning half, follows but half of right policy, then sets in that age named the Dvāpara.
Then half of evil attends upon the two parts of good; and the earth yields its harvest only when tilled, and that too with scant fruit.
When the lord of the earth forsakes the science of punishment entirely and afflicts his people by misrule, then enters the Kali age.
In the Kali age unrighteousness is most abundant, and dharma scarcely anywhere; and among all the orders the mind falls away from its own duty.
Śūdras live by begging and Brāhmaṇas by menial service; the acquisition and keeping of goods is undone, and the confusion of orders prevails.
The rites enjoined by the Vedas are performed with defects, and all the seasons turn unpleasant and breed disease.
The voices, complexions, and minds of men diminish; diseases arise then, and men die before their span is full.
Widows are found then, and the people are born cruel; in one place the rain-cloud pours, in another the grain springs up.
All the savors waste away to nothing—when the lord of the earth, intent upon the science of punishment, no longer wills to guard his people aright.
The king is the maker of the Kṛta age, and of the Tretā and the Dvāpara; the king is the cause of the fourth age as well.
By bringing about the Kṛta age the king attains heaven unending; by bringing about the Tretā the king attains a heaven not unending.
By ushering in the Dvāpara he partakes of heaven in due measure; by ushering in the Kali the king reaps endless sin.
Then the evildoer dwells in hell for everlasting years; sunk in the defilement of his people, he gains only infamy and sin.
Setting the science of punishment foremost, the discerning Kṣatriya should ever strive to gain what is not yet won, and to preserve what is won.
Drawing the boundary lines of the world, fostering the world, the science of punishment well administered is as a mother and as a father.
In her all beings have their being—know this, O bull of the Bharatas. This is the supreme dharma: that the king be wielder of the science of punishment.
Therefore, O Kaurava, guard your people by dharma, skilled in policy; conducting yourself thus and protecting the people, you shall win that heaven hard to win.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: By what conduct, O knower of conduct, should the lord of the earth bear himself, that with ease he may attain ends fruitful in happiness, both here and after death?
Bhīṣma said: Here is the set of six-and-thirty virtues, joined with six-and-thirty merits; practicing these virtues, the man endowed with virtue gains the good thereof.
Let him follow the duties without harshness; let him let go of attachment, yet not become a denier; let him pursue profit without cruelty, and pursue pleasure without arrogance.
Let him speak kindly without meanness; let him be brave without boasting; let him be a giver, yet not pour gifts on the unworthy; let him be bold, yet not unfeeling.
Let him not make peace with the base, nor wage war with kinsmen; let him not employ the untrusted as his agents; let him accomplish his ends without oppression.
Let him not speak of his designs among the wicked, nor proclaim his own merits; let him not take from the good, nor lean upon a worthless man.
Let him not inflict punishment without examination, nor make his counsel known; let him not bestow upon the greedy, nor trust in those who have wronged him.
Let the king be free of envy, his wives well guarded; let him be pure, yet not squeamish; let him resort to women not overmuch, and eat what is wholesome, not what is harmful.
Without stiffness let him honor the honorable; let him serve his elders without guile; let him worship the gods without hypocrisy, and desire only blameless prosperity.
Let him serve, setting aside undue familiarity; let him be diligent, yet not a man heedless of the right time; let him conciliate, but not for the sake of enjoyment; let him favor, yet not slight.
Let him not strike without due knowledge; having slain his foes, let him leave no remnant; let him not show anger without cause, nor be soft toward those who do harm.
Thus conduct yourself, established in your kingdom, if you desire what is good here; for acting otherwise, a lord of men comes upon peril beyond all measure.
He who follows all these virtues as they have been told, having enjoyed blessings here, is exalted in heaven after death.

Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard this discourse of the son of Śāntanu, Yudhiṣṭhira, surrounded by the foremost of the Pāṇḍavas, then bowed to his grandfather, and that wise king did even as had been told.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How, while protecting his people, may a king not be bound by sin and not offend against dharma? Tell me that, O grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: In brief, my son, I shall declare to you the settled duties; for of the duties told at length one could never reach the end.
The twice-born who are steadfast in dharma, learned, devoted to the Vedic vows, and virtuous—honor them and lodge them in your house.
Rising up to meet them, clasping their feet, and saluting them, you should then perform all your affairs together with your household priest.
Having accomplished the rites of dharma and performed the auspicious ceremonies, you should cause the Brāhmaṇas to pronounce blessings for the gaining of your ends and for victory.
Endowed with uprightness, with firmness, and with understanding, O Bhārata, one should take up wealth for wealth's purpose, and shun desire and anger.
The fool who, setting desire and anger foremost, pursues wealth as a king, grasps neither dharma nor wealth.
Do not employ the greedy and the foolish in matters of pleasure or of wealth; in all your tasks employ those free of greed and possessed of understanding.
For a fool set over affairs, unskilled in matters of business and filled with passion and spite, afflicts the people by his misconduct.
Through the sixth-part tribute, through tolls, and through the fines of offenders, and through wages, as guided by the law-books, you should seek the increase of wealth.
Having levied the lawful tax upon the realm ever according to rule, the king, unwearied, should provide for the acquiring and keeping of goods, leaving nothing undone.
The protector, the giver, ever devoted to dharma and unwearied, free from passion and spite—him men come to love.
Do not seek the increase of wealth through gain won by unrighteousness; for him who follows wrong precepts, both dharma and wealth are unstable.
A king who follows wrong precepts attains no store of wealth; and that wealth of his, ill-placed, all perishes utterly.
Driven by greed for wealth, he works his own undoing, for in his folly he oppresses the people with levies that the scriptures nowhere sanction.
For he who, craving milk, should cut away the cow's udder would get no milk at all; just so a realm afflicted by misrule does not thrive.
But he who tends the milch cow with care wins milk continually; even so, the king who draws upon his realm with prudent means reaps its fruit.
A realm well guarded and enjoyed by skilful means, Yudhiṣṭhira, ever brings forth an unmatched increase of the treasury.
The people, well protected by the king, yield him grain and gold, as a contented mother yields her milk freely to her own and to others alike.
Be like the gardener, O king, not like the charcoal-burner; so disposed, you will be able, by protecting your realm, to enjoy it long.
If, through a campaign against a hostile power, your wealth should be exhausted, then by conciliation alone should you seek to gather what wealth lies among men who are not brāhmaṇas.
Let not your mind waver at the sight of a brāhmaṇa possessed of wealth, not even in the direst extremity, O Bhārata, and how much less when you are prosperous?
Rather should you give wealth to them according to your power and their desert; consoling and protecting them, you will attain heaven, hard though it be to win.
Thus, by conduct grounded in dharma, protecting the people, you will attain an end that is good, meritorious, and crowned with renown, O joy of the Kurus.
Protect the people through righteous administration, O Pāṇḍava; so engaged, Yudhiṣṭhira, you will not be bound by the fetters of sorrow.
This indeed is the supreme dharma, that the king protect his people; for the protection of beings in accordance with dharma is the highest compassion.
Therefore those skilled in dharma hold this to be the supreme dharma: that the king, devoted to protection, shows compassion toward all beings.
The sin a king commits in a single day by failing to guard the people from fear—only after a thousand years does he reach the end of its consequence.
The merit a king earns in a single day by protecting the people righteously—its fruit he enjoys in heaven for ten thousand years.
Whatever worlds are won by him who has sacrificed well, studied well, and practised austerity—those a king attains in a moment by protecting the people righteously.
Thus diligently upholding dharma, O son of Kuntī, having gained the fruit of merit here, you will not be bound by the fetters of sorrow.

And in the world of heaven you will attain great splendour, O Pāṇḍava. Duties such as these are impossible for those who are not kings; therefore it is the king alone, and no other, who can win so vast a reward.
Having won a flourishing kingdom and ruling it righteously, gratify Indra with the soma offering, and your friends and people with the fulfilment of their desires.
Bhīṣma said: He who would protect the good and root out the wicked—he alone, O king, is the man the king should appoint as his royal chaplain.
On this point too they recite an ancient tale: the dialogue between Purūravas, son of Ilā, and Mātariśvan, the Wind.
The son of Ilā said: Whence was the brāhmaṇa born, and whence the other three classes? And by what cause is one superior to the rest? Explain this to me, O Wind.
The Wind said: From the mouth of Brahmā was the brāhmaṇa created, O best of kings; from his arms the kṣatriya was brought forth, and from his thighs, they say, the vaiśya.
To serve these three classes, O bull among men, the fourth class was fashioned thereafter: the śūdra, made from his feet.
The brāhmaṇa, the very moment he was born, came into being upon the earth as lord over all creatures, for the safekeeping of the treasury of dharma.
Then he made the kṣatriya, the second class, as the protector of the earth and the wielder of the rod, for the guarding of the people.
The vaiśya should sustain these three classes with wealth and grain, and the śūdra should serve them—such is the ordinance of Brahmā.
The son of Ilā said: To whom does this earth, together with its wealth, rightfully belong—to the twice-born or to the kṣatriya? Tell me this truly, O Wind.
The Wind said: All this, whatever exists upon the earth, belongs to the brāhmaṇa; by reason of his birth as the eldest, those skilled in dharma know it to be his.
The brāhmaṇa enjoys only what is his own, wears what is his own, and gives away what is his own; for the twice-born is the guru of all the classes, eldest and most excellent.
As a woman, in the absence of her husband, takes the husband's brother as her lord, so the earth, by reason of succession, takes the kṣatriya as her lord.
This is the first rule for you; another is meant for times of distress—if, by way of dharma, you seek the highest place in heaven.
Whoever should conquer territory should make it over to a brāhmaṇa—one endowed with sacred learning and good conduct, knowing dharma and given to austerity—
to one content in his own duty, who is not greedy for wealth, who could guide the king by an understanding complete in every respect.
For a brāhmaṇa born in a good family, of ripened wisdom and disciplined speech, leads the king toward what is good, his eloquence flowing in wondrous strains.
Whatever dharma the king practises as shown to him by the brāhmaṇa—being attentive, free of arrogant speech, and steadfast in the vow of kṣatriya duty—
by that very measure he, grown wise, abides long in renown; and of all that dharma the royal chaplain is a sharer.
In just this way, all the people who take refuge in the king, conducting themselves well and abiding in their own duties, are beset by no fear from any quarter.
Whatever dharma they practise within the realm, well protected by the king—of that dharma the king obtains a fourth share.
Gods, men, ancestors, gandharvas, serpents, and rākṣasas all live upon sacrifice—and there is no sacrifice where there is no king.
By what is offered from here the gods and likewise the ancestors live; and upon the king alone rests the securing and preserving of this dharma.
In the heat one finds comfort in shade, in water, and in the breeze; in the cold one finds comfort in fire, in clothing, and in the sun.
The mind delights in sound, touch, taste, form, and smell; yet in all these enjoyments it is the man free of fear who finds true happiness.
He who is the giver of freedom from fear, his is the very greatest reward; for in the three worlds there is no gift equal to the gift of life.
The king is Indra, the king is Yama, the king is Dharma himself; the king bears all these forms, and by the king is all this upheld.

Bhīṣma said: The king should appoint as his chaplain one who is learned and deeply versed in scripture, who has weighed well both dharma and artha—both immeasurable—each in close relation to the other.
Those kings whose chaplain is righteous of soul and knowing of dharma, and who are themselves endowed with such virtues—with them, O king, all is well in every way.
Both together cause the people, the gods, and the ancestors near and far to flourish—the two who, joined together and steadfast in dharma, are worthy of trust and rich in austerity.
Friends to each other, in mutual accord and of one mind—through the honour paid to brahman and kṣatra the people would attain happiness.
But by the dishonouring of these two the people would surely perish; for brahman and kṣatra together are called the root of all duties.
On this point too they recite an ancient tale: the dialogue between the son of Ilā and Kaśyapa—mark it well, Yudhiṣṭhira.
The son of Ilā said: When brahman forsakes kṣatra, or when kṣatra in turn forsakes brahman, which of the two then enjoys the stronger power, and through which of them does the weakness set in?
Kaśyapa said: Ruined becomes the realm of the kṣatriya wherein brahman and kṣatra fall into discord; there the brigands come to enjoy the power, and there the good men waste away into weakness.
Their bulls do not thrive, nor their cows; no churning-stick stirs the curds, nor do they sacrifice; nor do their sons study the Veda—when the kṣatriyas abandon brahman.
No bull thrives in their household ever; they do not study with their offspring, nor do they sacrifice; degraded, they become as brigands—those brāhmaṇas who abandon the kṣatriyas.
For these two are ever bound together in upholding each other: kṣatra is the womb of brahman, and the twice-born are the womb of kṣatra.
When these two are ever devoted to each other, they attain a great and firmly seated splendour; but if their ancient union is broken, then all falls into utter confusion.
Then he who would cross over finds no raft, like a boat cast adrift upon fathomless depths; the four-fold order falls into confusion, and thereupon the people are set on the path to ruin.
The tree of brahman, when guarded, rains down honey and gold; but left unguarded, it rains down only tears and evil without end.

When one who is no celibate, fallen away from right discipline, yet a brāhmaṇa, seeks protection within the brahman order, there the god rains only by rare chance, and there calamities hard to bear assail again and again.
Where a sinner who has slain a woman or a brāhmaṇa finds approval in the assembly, and feels no fear even in the king's presence—from that does danger arise for the kṣatriya.
When sin is wrought by sinners beyond all measure, then is this god Rudra born; the wicked by their wickedness bring forth Rudra, and then he destroys all alike, the good and the wicked.
The son of Ilā said: Whence is Rudra, and of what nature is this Rudra? By living beings the living are seen to be destroyed. Explain this to me, learned Kaśyapa—whence is this god Rudra born?

Kaśyapa said: Rudra is the self within the hearts of men; he slays both one's own body and the body of another. They call Rudra like the onslaughts of the wind; his form is like forest fires and like thunderclouds.

The son of Ilā said: No one can wrap up the wind, nor does the thundercloud rain, nor the forest fire blaze, in the same fashion as is seen among men; for it is through desire and hatred that a man is bound and is set free.
Kaśyapa said: As a fire blazing in a single house may swiftly burn down the whole village, so this god works delusion, and thereupon all are touched by merit and demerit together.

The son of Ilā said: If the rod of punishment touches the man of merit without distinction, when sin is wrought by sinners, then for what reason should one do good, and for what reason should one refrain from evil?

Kaśyapa said: Because the evildoers are not cast off, the same punishment touches the innocent through their commingling; the green is burned together with the dry by reason of their mingling. Let one therefore never mingle in any way with those who do evil.

The son of Ilā said: Here the earth bears up the good and the wicked alike; here the sun warms the good and the wicked alike; here the wind blows upon the good and the wicked alike, and the waters likewise carry the good and the wicked alike.
Kaśyapa said: Thus indeed it is in this world, but not so in the world beyond, O prince; after death there is a wide difference between the two—him who does good and him who does evil.

The world of merit flows with honey, its flame is clarified butter, its light is gold, and it is the very navel of immortality; there, after death, the man of holy conduct rejoices—there is no death, no old age, and no sorrow.
The world of evil is hell, devoid of light, ever full of pain and abounding in grief; there the evildoer laments over himself, falling through many years without any foothold.

Through mutual discord between brāhmaṇas and kṣatriyas the people enter into pain hard to bear; knowing this, the king should indeed here appoint as chaplain a learned man, not one of meagre knowledge.
And he should consecrate such a one along with himself; so is the dharma ordained, for the brāhmaṇa is declared foremost of all here, by the law of dharma.
For first of all were the brāhmaṇas created, so those who know dharma understand; and by reason of his birth as the eldest, all that is highest has come to him.
Therefore the brāhmaṇa is to be honoured and worshipped, the first to partake of the offered food; whatever is best and most excellent should, by dharma, be presented to him.
This must without fail be done by the king, however mighty he may be; for brahman makes kṣatra to flourish, and from kṣatra brahman flourishes in turn.
Bhīṣma said: The securing and preserving of the realm is said to rest upon the king; and the securing and preserving of the king himself rests upon the chaplain.
Where brahman quells the unseen dangers of the people, and the king with his two arms quells the seen, that realm thrives in happiness.
On this point too they recite an ancient tale: the dialogue between King Mucukunda and Vaiśravaṇa.
Mucukunda, lord of the earth, having conquered this whole earth, and wishing to test his own might, marched against the lord of Alakā.
Then King Vaiśravaṇa loosed his Rākṣasas upon him, and those night-roving demons advanced, crushing his armies.
As his host was being slaughtered, Mucukunda, that subduer of foes and ruler of men, reproached his learned house-priest.
Then Vasiṣṭha, the foremost knower of Brahman, having performed fierce austerity, struck down the Rākṣasas there and so found a way through.
Then King Vaiśravaṇa showed himself to Mucukunda, and, as the armies were being slain, spoke these words.
"Mightier than you were the kings of old, together with their house-priests; yet they did not conduct themselves as you do here.
Those lords of the earth too, skilled in arms and mighty as they were, came and waited humbly upon me, the dispenser of joy and sorrow.
If there is strength in your arms, it is that you should display. Why do you presume so far by the power of a Brāhmaṇa?"
Then Mucukunda, though angered, answered the lord of wealth with these words, grounded in reason, unflustered and unperturbed.
"This Brahman and Kṣatra were created of a single origin by the Self-existent One, yet with their distinct allotments of power; together they guard the world.
The power of austerity and sacred formula is ever established in the Brāhmaṇas; the power of weapons and arms is ever established in the Kṣatriyas.
By the union of these two the protection of the people must be carried out; and yet, O lord of Alakā, you reproach me for acting in just this way."
Then Vaiśravaṇa said to the king and his house-priest: "I do not bestow a kingdom upon anyone unless it has been ordained for him.
Nor do I wrest away what has been ordained — know this, O lord of the earth. Rule, O hero, this whole earth, given by me to you."
Mucukunda said: "I do not wish to enjoy a kingdom given by you, O lord of the earth. It is my desire to possess a kingdom won by the might of my own arms."
Bhīṣma said: Then King Vaiśravaṇa was struck with the utmost wonder, beholding Mucukunda standing firm and unshaken in the Kṣatriya's duty.
Then King Mucukunda governed the earth, rightly won by the might of his arms, holding faithfully to the Kṣatriya's duty.
Thus the king who knows Brahman and acts with Brahman foremost conquers the earth as yet unconquered, and attains great glory.
The Brāhmaṇa should ever keep his sacred libations, and the Kṣatriya his weapons ever ready; for upon these two depends everything that exists in the world.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: By what manner of life does a guardian of the earth make his people prosper, and conquer the holy worlds? Tell me this, O grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: The king should be given to charity and to sacrifice, O Bhārata, devoted to fasting and austerity, and intent upon the protection of his people.
And the king should ever guard all his subjects by dharma, with diligence and vigilance, and should honor the righteous.
For when dharma is honored by the king, it is thereupon honored everywhere; whatever the king practices, that is pleasing to the people.
And he should ever hold the rod of punishment raised, like Death itself toward his enemies; he should slay robbers on every side, and should not from mere caprice spare anyone.
For whatever dharma the people, well guarded by the king, here practice — of that dharma, O Bhārata, the king obtains a fourth part.
In what they study, what they sacrifice, what they give, what they worship — of all this the king, guarding the people with dharma, is partaker of a fourth.
But whatever evil is done in the realm when the king fails to protect his people — of that sin too, O Bhārata, the king obtains a fourth part.

Some say he bears the whole of it; the settled view is that he bears the greater half of the deed, O guardian of the earth — for he is then deemed cruel and a speaker of untruth. Hear by what means the king is freed from such a defilement.
If wealth carried off by thieves cannot be recovered, it should be made good from his own treasury — even by one who is poor and lives in want.
The property of Brahman and the Brāhmaṇas alike must ever be guarded by all the classes; whoever does injury to the twice-born should not be suffered to remain in the realm.
For when the property of Brahman is guarded, all is guarded; and when their favor has been gained, the king has accomplished his task.
As living creatures depend upon the rain-cloud, and as birds upon a great tree, so men depend for their living upon that king who is the accomplisher of all their aims.
For a king who is slave to his desires, ever crooked of mind, cruel and overgreedy, can never protect his people.

Yudhiṣṭhira said: I am no seeker after the pleasures of kingship; I do not desire the kingdom even for a moment. It is for the sake of dharma that I welcome sovereignty — yet here no dharma is to be found.
Enough, then, for me of a kingdom in which dharma is not found. I shall go away to the forest, out of my longing to practice dharma.
There, in the holy forests, laying down the rod, my senses subdued, I shall worship dharma as a sage, feeding on roots and fruits.
Bhīṣma said: I know that mind of yours — it is born wholly of the virtue of mercy; yet by pure mercilessness toward self alone one cannot attain to greatness.
Rather, finding you gentle, self-controlled, exceedingly noble and exceedingly righteous, the world will think you weak, a man unmanned by squeamish piety, and will hold you in little esteem.
Look to the duties of kings, befitting your fathers and forefathers. This conduct in which you wish to stand is not the way of kings.
For not by resorting to a mercy tainted with faint-heartedness — but by the protection of your people — have you indeed attained the fruit of dharma.
For neither Pāṇḍu nor Kuntī ever prayed for such a blessing as this for you, my child — nor for the kind of cleverness by which you now act with such subtlety.
Valor, strength, and resolve your father ever invoked for you; greatness of soul, strength, and magnanimity Kuntī prayed for on your behalf.
Ever do the gods through Svāhā and the fathers through Svadhā — both, the human offerings and the divine — ever do fathers and deities desire such blessings in their sons.
Charity, study, sacrifice, and the protection of the people — for this dharma, and against its opposite, you were born into the very station of your birth.
O son of Kuntī, of those who are yoked in due season to the burden, who bear the load laid upon them — even though they sink beneath it, their fame does not sink.
He who, fully self-restrained on every side, bears the burden without faltering — from his blameless deed and word comes that perfection which belongs to action itself.
No one here has ever passed his life by an utter and undivided abstention from action — be he a righteous man, a householder, a king, or again a student of sacred lore.
That deed which is mostly good, though small, is itself noble; what is done is better than what is left undone, and there is nothing more sinful than inaction.
When a man of good lineage, knowing dharma, attains the highest lordship, then, O king, the welfare and security of all conduce to their good.
One man by gifts, another by force, another by gracious and truthful speech — thus, having gained a kingdom, the righteous king should win men over on every side.
That king through whom learned men, born in good families and afflicted by the fear of want, find satisfaction and stability — what dharma is higher than this?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What is more conducive to heaven than this? What joy is higher than this? What is the supreme lordship beyond this? Tell me, if you think fit.
