Yudhiṣṭhira said: Great is this path of dharma, O Bhārata, and many-branched; which among all the duties is held to be the most worthy of being practiced here?
What deed, in your judgment, is weightier than all duties, whereby a man may attain to dharma both here and in the world beyond?
Bhīṣma said: The worship of mother and father and of teachers I hold in highest esteem; the man devoted to this wins the worlds and great renown.
Whatever deed these, well-honored, may command, my son—whether it accord with dharma or seem against it—that must be done, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Without their leave one should ordain no other duty for oneself; that which these sanction is, by firm conviction, dharma itself.
These very three are the three worlds; these very ones the three āśramas; these very ones the three Vedas; these very ones the three sacred fires.
The father is the Gārhapatya fire, the mother is remembered as the Dakṣiṇa fire, and the teacher is the Āhavanīya; this triad of fires is the most venerable.

Being heedful toward these three, you shall conquer the three worlds: by serving the father this world, by serving the mother the next, and by serving the teacher you shall ever walk in the world of Brahmā.
Conduct yourself rightly toward these three, O Bhārata; in the three worlds you shall win renown—blessings upon you—and dharma of most abundant fruit.

One should never surpass them, never eat before them, never wrong them, but ever attend upon them; that indeed is the highest good deed, and thereby, O lord of men, you shall gain fame, merit, glory, and the heavenly worlds.
For him by whom these three are honored, all worlds are honored; but for him by whom these are unhonored, all rites bear no fruit.
Neither this world nor the world beyond belongs to him, O scorcher of foes, by whom these three venerable ones are ever left unhonored.
Neither in this world nor in the next does his fame shine forth, nor is any other blessing declared to await him hereafter.
To these very ones I render up all my labor in deed; thereby it became for me a hundredfold and a thousandfold, and so, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the three worlds shine open before me.
A teacher of good conduct surpasses ten learned reciters of the Veda; a preceptor surpasses ten such teachers; and a father ten preceptors.

But one mother surpasses ten fathers, or even the whole earth, in the weight of her venerableness; there is no elder equal to the mother. Yet the teacher is weightier than both father and mother—such is my conviction.
Both mother and father join together in one's birth; father and mother fashion the body, O Bhārata; but the second birth shaped by the teacher's instruction is divine, free from age and death.
Mother and father are ever inviolable, even when they do one wrong; he who acts thus is not defiled, nor do they defile him. The gods, together with the seers, know those who strive for dharma.
He who fills one's ears with what is true, speaking the right and bestowing the deathless—him I deem both father and mother; against him one should never bear malice, knowing what he has done.
They who, having heard knowledge, do not revere the teacher close at hand, in thought or in deed—just as they ought to be regarded by their teachers, so too must their teachers be honored by them.
Therefore the teachers must be worshiped, and shared with diligently, and honored, by one who desires the ancient dharma.
By whatever pleases the fathers, the grandfather too is pleased; by whatever delights the mother, the earth herself is honored.

By whatever pleases the preceptor, Brahman itself is worshiped; therefore the teacher is more worthy of worship than mother and father alike; and the seers and the gods, together with the ancestors, are gladdened thereby.
By no manner of conduct should the teacher ever be despised; nor is the mother, nor the father, such as the teacher is.
They deserve no contempt, nor do they defile him; the gods, together with the seers, acknowledge the honoring of teachers as supreme.
They who do violence to preceptor, father, or mother, in thought or in deed—their sin is greater than the slaying of an unborn child; than they there is no worse doer of evil in the world.
For the betrayer of a friend, the ingrate, the slayer of a woman, and the slanderer—for these four we have never heard of any expiation.
All this has been set forth by way of injunction, as what a man ought to do here in the world; this is the highest good, and nothing surpasses it; surveying every duty, this has been declared.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How should a man conduct himself who wishes to abide in dharma, O Bhārata? Learned one, declare it to me who would know, O bull of the Bharatas.
Both truth and falsehood stand pervading the worlds; of the two, O king, which should a man resolved upon dharma practice?
What is truth, what is falsehood, and what is the eternal accord with dharma? At what time should one speak the truth, and at what time should one utter what is false?
Bhīṣma said: The speaking of truth is good; nothing is higher than truth. Yet that which in this earthly world is most hard to discern, that I shall tell you, O Bhārata.
There are times when truth should not be spoken and falsehood ought to be uttered, where falsehood becomes truth and truth becomes falsehood.
In such a case the fool is bewildered, where truth is not fixed; only after discerning truth and falsehood does one become a knower of dharma.
Even a man ignoble, of unripe wisdom, and most cruel may attain great merit—as Balāka did by the slaying of a blind creature.
And what wonder is it that a deluded man, though desiring dharma yet ignorant of it, may incur great sin—as Kauśika did at the Gaṅgā?
Such is this further question, wherein dharma is most hard to declare and hard to reckon; here one must determine it by reasoning.
The teaching of dharma was made for the welfare of beings; that which is joined with non-injury is dharma—such is the firm conclusion.
From its upholding they call it dharma; by dharma are creatures upheld; that which is joined with upholding is dharma—such is the firm conclusion.
Some say dharma is that which the scripture enjoins; others deny it. Yet we do not cavil at this, for not everything is laid down by rule.
To those who, seeking to seize wealth unjustly, ever covet it, that should not be disclosed; that is dharma—such is the firm conclusion.
If by silence there be escape, here one should by no means speak; or if one must needs speak, or if his silence would arouse suspicion, then let him speak.
There it is judged better to speak falsehood than truth, whereby one is freed from dealings with the wicked, even by a false oath.
And to such men no wealth should be given, by any means, so long as it can be helped; for wealth given to the wicked torments even the giver.

When one is willing to seize a boon even at the cost of his own life, those witnesses who, to establish the truth, would speak there—if they leave that unsaid which ought to be said, all of them are speakers of falsehood.

In peril of life and in marriage, falsehood ought to be spoken, for the safeguarding of wealth and for the sake of another's dharma; yet he who, craving others' dharma, would beg it as alms becomes base.
Having promised, one must give; but he who is coerced may put it off to the morrow. Whoever has fallen from the compact of dharma and taken his stand in unrighteousness—
that knave who, casting off his own dharma, would seek to live by deceit—such a sinner, living by treachery, must be destroyed by every means.
'Wealth, and wealth alone'—such is the resolve of all the wicked here, who are insufferable, unfit to dine with, and through their treachery sunk into ruin.
Fallen away from gods and men, they are even as the departed dead; yet harder to bear for them than the seizing of their wealth is to be parted from life.
'Let this dharma find favor with you'—so should one earnestly speak to them; for there is no dharma among the wicked—such is the firm conclusion.

He who slays one brought to such a pass is not smeared with sin; he slays one already slain by his own deeds; that man, already as good as dead, is but slain. Whoever would make any pact with those of ruined understanding—
As crows and as vultures, so too those who live by fraud—at the last release of the body they are reborn into such wombs as these.
As a man behaves toward another, so toward him one ought to behave—that is dharma: against the man of guile one must act with guile, and the man of good conduct must be met with goodness.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When beings are afflicted by this and that condition on every side, tell me, grandfather, by what means one may cross over these hard straits.
Bhīṣma said: Those twice-born who conduct themselves as prescribed within the prescribed stages of life, with selves restrained—they cross over the hard straits.
They who do not mutter prayers out of hypocrisy, whose livelihood is well-ordered, and who curb the objects of sense—they cross over the hard straits.
They who ever lodge their guests, who are ever free from envy, and ever devoted to the study of the Veda—they cross over the hard straits.
They, skilled in dharma, who attend upon mother and father, and who shun sleeping by day—they cross over the hard straits.
They who go to their own wives, righteous in conduct, each in her due season, and who are devoted to the fire-oblation—they cross over the hard straits.
Those kings who do not exact wealth through greed, though wrapped in passion, but guard their realms—they cross over the hard straits.
Those heroes in battle who, casting aside the fear born of death, seek victory by righteous means—they cross over the hard straits.
They who do no evil in deed, in thought, or in word, who have laid down the rod against living beings—they cross over the hard straits.
They who speak the truth here even when the loss of life is at hand, who stand as a measure of conduct for all beings—they cross over the hard straits.
Those brāhmaṇas who do not pursue Vedic recitation on the days when study is forbidden, who are ever given to austerity and of noble penance—they cross over the hard straits.
They whose deeds are without trickery of purpose, whose words are kind and true, and whose aims are aims of the good—they cross over the hard straits.
They who practice austerity, chaste from boyhood, who have completed their bath of learning, Veda, and vows—they cross over the hard straits.
They in whom the passion of rajas is wholly stilled and the darkness of tamas wholly quenched, great souls established in truth—they cross over the hard straits.
They of whom none is afraid and who fear none, to whom the world is even as their own self—they cross over the hard straits.
Those good men, those bulls among men, who are not tormented by another's fortune, and who have turned away from coarse village food—they cross over the hard straits.
They who bow to all the gods and give ear to all the duties of righteousness, who are full of faith and self-controlled — these cross beyond every peril.
They who seek no honour for themselves yet pay honour to others, and who, though honoured, take no pride in it — these cross beyond every peril.
They who, desiring offspring, perform the śrāddha rites on each appointed lunar day with a wholly purified mind — these cross beyond every peril.
They who never give way to wrath, who calm those who are wrathful, and who are not angered by their dependants — these cross beyond every peril.
Those men who in this life ever abstain from honey and from flesh, and from intoxicating drink from their very birth — these cross beyond every peril.
They whose eating is but to sustain life, whose union is only for the sake of offspring, and whose speech is solely for the utterance of truth — these cross beyond every peril.
And they who are devoted to Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of all beings, the origin and the dissolution of the world — these cross beyond every peril.
This Acyuta, eyed like the red lotus, clad in yellow, mighty of arm, who is to you well-wisher, brother, friend, and kinsman —
who, were he to will it, could wrap up all these worlds together like a hide — the Lord of inconceivable nature, Govinda, the Supreme Person —
He, O bull among men, stands firm in the welfare and the pleasure of the victorious Arjuna; this is your own unassailable Vaikuṇṭha, the Supreme Person, O king.
They who in this world take refuge with devotion in this Nārāyaṇa, in Hari, do cross beyond every peril — of this I have no doubt.
And they who recite this passage on the crossing of perils, who cause it to be heard, and who have the brāhmaṇas recite it — these too cross beyond every peril.
Thus, O sinless one, have I declared to you this summary of the duties to be performed, whereby a man may cross beyond perils both in this world and the next.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: There are men ill-natured yet fair of seeming, and men of good nature who appear ill-favoured; such men, dear father, how are we to know them?
Bhīṣma said: On this point too they recount an ancient story, the dialogue of the tiger and the jackal; mark it well, Yudhiṣṭhira.
Long ago, in the prosperous city of Purikā, there reigned a king named Paurika, cruel and basest of men, who took delight in harming others.
When his lifespan was spent he passed to an undesirable destiny, and, defiled by his former deeds, attained the state of a jackal.
Recollecting his former birth, he came to a supreme detachment, and would not eat flesh, even when others brought it to him.
Doing harm to no living being, truthful in speech, firm in his vow, he made his meal at will of fallen fruits.
A cremation ground became the dwelling that this jackal approved, and out of attachment to his place of birth he cared for no other abode.
All his fellow jackals, unable to endure his purity, sought to unsettle that resolve of his with words full of feigned courtesy.
"Dwelling in this dread forest of the dead, you wish to win purity? This is sheer contradiction in you, seeing that you are a flesh-eater.
Be then as we are: we will give you food to eat. Cast off your scruple about purity and eat — for only what is eaten is truly yours."
Hearing these words of theirs, composed in mind he answered them with speech sweet, gentle, reasoned, and free of harshness:
"My birth is no warrant for me; it is by conduct that good lineage is made. I will strive after that course of action by which renown is spread abroad.
If my dwelling is in the cremation ground, look rather to my inner composure. It is the self that bears the fruit of deeds; it is not one's station that is the mark of righteousness.
If a man should slay a brāhmaṇa within a holy hermitage, or give a cow in gift outside one — would that not be a sin all the same, or that gift be rendered void?
You, in your utter greed, take delight in nothing but eating; but the faults that follow as the consequence — those, being deluded, you do not see.
A way of living that breeds distrust, that is blameworthy, tainted by the stripping away of true gain, and unwelcome both here and hereafter — such a course I do not approve."
Holding him to be pure and wise, a tiger of famed prowess paid him honour as to an equal of himself, and of his own accord raised him to the office of counsellor.
"Gentle one, your character is known to me; go now your way along with me. Choose whatever enjoyments you desire, and abundant things to be avoided are yours to set aside.
We are reputed to be fierce; this we make known to you. We strike, but with mildness first — and so your welfare shall be attained."
Then, having honoured these words of the great-souled lord of beasts, the jackal, bowing a little, spoke this courteous reply:
"Worthy of you, O king of beasts, is this speech of yours concerning me, in that you seek out helpers who are pure and skilled in righteousness and statecraft.
Greatness cannot be governed without a minister, O hero, nor with a wicked minister who is an enemy to one's very body.
One should strive after helpers who are devoted, free of secret leagues, not wrangling with one another, eager for conquest, and untouched by greed.
Such men — proven beyond all tests of temptation, wise, intent upon your good, high-minded and greatly blessed — you should honour as teachers, as fathers.
Yet, lord of beasts, by reason of my contentment nothing else appeals to me; I crave no pleasures, no enjoyments, no lordship in dependence upon you.
For my character will not consort with your old retainers; ill-natured, they will set you against me, sowing division on my account.
As a refuge you are praiseworthy even for other illustrious ones — disciplined of self, greatly fortunate, and not harsh even toward the wicked.
Far-seeing, of great energy, large-aimed, mighty in strength, accomplished, and one whose acts are never in vain — you are adorned with the qualities that are to be.
Yet I am content with my own lot; a service so undertaken is a painful way of life, and I am no adept in attendance, being a free rover of the woods.
All the reproaches and faults that fall upon the king belong to those who live as his dependants; but the life of the forest is unattached, fearless, and unconstrained.
The fear that lodges in the heart of one summoned by a king does not abide in the hearts of the contented who feed on roots and fruits in the forest.
Be it water won without toil, or be it sweet food got at the cost of fear — weighing the matter, I see that happiness lies where there is tranquillity.
Not so many servants have been punished by kings for their own offences as servants have been wrongly defamed by slander and brought to ruin.
But if this office must indeed be undertaken by me, if the lord of beasts so wills it, then I desire a compact to be made as to how I am to be dealt with.
My recommendations are to be respected by you, and my salutary counsel heeded; and the mode of life you have appointed for me must remain firmly fixed.
I shall never take counsel together with your other ministers; the politic, seeking their own ends, would speak idle slanders against me.
Meeting with you alone, in private, I would speak for your good; nor in the affairs of your kinsmen am I to be consulted as to what is good or ill.
After taking counsel with me, you must not afterward destroy those ministers; and, angered at men of my party, do not let your rod of punishment fall upon them.
"So be it," said the lord of beasts, and thus honoured by him, the jackal — though of the tiger's own race in spirit — attained the office of chief counsellor.
Seeing him so honoured and set to his charge, the former retainers, banding together, came to hate him again and again.
Soothing the jackal with a show of friendship and drawing him into their circle, those evil-minded ones sought to make him equally party to their misdeeds.
For they who before were accustomed to ways otherwise, plundering the goods of others, were now, held in check by the jackal, unable to take any property at all.
And those who longed for his downfall sought to seduce him with fair speeches, and with great wealth they tried to corrupt his mind.
But that man of great wisdom never swerved from his steadfastness; whereupon his foes, making a contrivance, set themselves to destroy him.
The flesh that the lord of beasts desired, dressed and made ready there, they themselves carried off and laid within the jackal's own dwelling.
For what purpose it was stolen, by whom, and what had been plotted — all this was known to him; yet for good reason he bore it in silence.
This compact had been made by him on taking up the ministership: "No slander, O king, is to be admitted by you, if you desire friendship here."
When the meal was to be served, that flesh was nowhere to be seen, and the king of beasts gave command: "Let the thief be sought out."
And by their false contrivance it was reported to the lord of beasts that the flesh had been carried off to him by your learned minister, who thinks himself so wise.
Then the tiger, hearing of the jackal's supposed knavery, grew full of wrath; the king became unforgiving and resolved upon his death.
Seeing this flaw exposed in him, those former ministers spoke out: "He is bent on the ruin of all our livelihoods.
And this deed of his, of such a kind, is shielded only by the master's favour. He whom our lord heard him to be before, this one is not."

"Righteous in words alone, but by nature cruel — this wicked one cloaks himself in righteousness and takes up a hollow show of conduct; it is for self-interest and for the sake of his food that he has expended his labour upon vows."
Holding the carrying-off of the flesh to be proven, the tiger, on these words of theirs, then gave the command: "Let the jackal be put to death."
Hearing the tiger's word, the tiger's mother thereupon came to admonish the king of beasts with words meant for his good:
"My son, this charge, contrived out of fraud, should not be accepted by you; through the impure faults born of the rivalry of office, the pure man is made to seem foul.
No one can endure another's rise; advancement breeds enmity, and even upon the pure man who does his duty it is fault alone that is made to fall.
To the greedy the pure are hateful, to cowards the bold, to fools the wise, to the poor the rich, to the unrighteous the most righteous, and to the ill-favoured the fair of form.
Many learned men are greedy, and all who live by deceit would fasten a fault upon the faultless, were he wise as Bṛhaspati himself.
And this flesh of yours that today was carried off from an empty house — he who will not even accept it when offered — let the matter first be well weighed.
There are the false who wear the look of truth, and the true who appear false; manifold are the natures one sees, and concerning them inquiry is fitting.
The sky appears to have a floor, the firefly seems like fire; yet there is no floor in the sky, nor fire in the firefly.
Therefore, though a matter be seen with one's own eyes, it is right to examine it; for he who acts on matters after testing them does not afterward repent.
It is no hard thing, my son, that a lord should put another to death; but in this world the forbearance of the powerful is praiseworthy and most to be chosen.
This one, my son, was set up by you and made famed among the neighbouring chiefs; with difficulty is a worthy vessel found — keep him as your friend.
For whoever takes a pure man, defamed by the faults of others, to be otherwise than he is, has himself a corrupted ministry, and quickly comes to ruin.
Then from that very league of the jackal's enemies someone came forth, a righteous soul, and by him it was told how this fraud had been wrought.
Then, his character recognized, he was honoured, set free, and embraced again and again with affection by the lord of beasts.
But the jackal, learned in the science of polity, having taken leave of the lord of beasts and burning still with that resentment, wished to fast unto death.
There the tiger, his eyes brimming with tears of affection, held the jackal back, that most righteous one, honouring him in return with marks of honour.
Beholding him thus moved by affection into agitation, the jackal, bowing low, spoke these words in a voice choked with tears.
"First I was honoured by you, and afterwards dishonoured; I was made the resort of others' designs. I am not fit to dwell with you any longer."
"Servants who were content, then fallen from their station, cast down from their honour, those withdrawn of their own accord, and those drawn away by enemies—
the impoverished, the greedy, the cruel, those tormented by imprisonment, the proud whose wealth has been seized, and those grasping ones who, once cast off, have been taken back—
and whoever have been afflicted, those lying in wait for a flood of calamities, those who lie concealed with hostile intent—all these become instruments of the foe."
"Toward me, who was treated with contempt and then reinstated, how will you ever come to trust again, and how shall I again come to trust you?"
"Having taken me in as capable, having installed and tested me, you broke the agreement that was made and dishonoured me."
"Of one who has first been proclaimed a man of good character in the assembly, his fault should not be spoken of by one who would keep his pledge."
"How then will you place trust in one so slighted, and so long as I distrust you, my own disquiet will remain?"
"You are suspicious, I am afraid; the others are forever watching for an opening, unaffectionate and hard to satisfy—and this business is full of treachery."
"What is broken is rejoined only with difficulty, and what is joined is sundered only with difficulty; but a friendship that is severed and then patched together does not abide in true affection."
"It is but rarely that one is seen unafraid in dealings between oneself and another; the feelings men show are governed by self-interest, while genuine affection is hard to find."
"The knowledge of men is most hard to attain, for their minds are unsteady and wavering; whether able or unable, scarcely one in a hundred is rightly understood."
"Men's advancement comes without cause, and their casting down comes without cause; and out of fickleness of mind they are prone to make much of both good and ill."
Having spoken conciliation of many kinds, grounded in dharma and statecraft, and having appeased the king, the jackal went away into the forest.
Not accepting the entreaty of that lord of beasts, the wise jackal, having fasted unto death and abandoned his body, went to heaven.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What ought a king to do, and by doing what does he become happy? Declare all this to me truly, O best of the upholders of dharma.
Bhīṣma said: Come, I shall declare it to you; listen to the one sure rule of action—how a king ought to act here, and by doing what he becomes happy.
One must not conduct oneself in the manner of which we have heard tell. There is a notable story of a camel; mark it, Yudhiṣṭhira.
A great camel, who remembered his former births and was born in the age of Prajāpati, undertook a most severe austerity in the forest, firm in his vow.
At the close of that austerity the Lord became gratified, and the Grandfather then offered him the choice of a boon.
The camel said: O blessed one, by your grace may this neck of mine grow long, so that it may reach a full hundred yojanas to forage, O mighty lord.
Bhīṣma said: "So be it," said the great-souled bestower of boons; and the camel, having obtained that excellent boon, went off to his own forest.
On account of that gift of a boon, the dull-witted creature gave himself over to sloth; deluded by fate and ill-natured, he no longer cared to walk about to forage.
Once, stretching out in this way his neck of a hundred yojanas, he grazed with an untiring heart; and thereupon a great wind arose.
That beast, having laid his own head and neck within a cave, settled down; then a very great rain came on, flooding the world.
Then a jackal, his limbs gripped by cold and worn with hunger, together with his mate, tormented by the water, quickly entered that cave.
And that flesh-eater, beholding it and sorely wasted with hunger, thereupon devoured the neck of the camel, O bull of the Bharatas.
But when that beast became aware that he himself was being eaten, then, grievously pained, he made an effort to draw his neck back in.
As the beast contracted his neck this way and that, up and down, even so was he devoured by that jackal and its mate.
And the jackal, having slain the camel and eaten of it, then, when the wind and rain had passed, came forth from the mouth of the cave.
Thus was destruction met with by that ill-witted camel; behold the great calamity that came upon him through the course of his sloth.
You too, abandoning this manner of conduct, with senses restrained through discipline, should act; for Manu declared that victory is rooted in intelligence.
Deeds of intellect are the best, O Bhārata; those of the arms are middling; those of the legs are lowest, and mere bearing of burdens is lowest of all.
The kingdom abides with one who is capable, who has mastered his senses, who keeps his counsel secret, who is learned, and who has good helpers, O sinless one.
And the affairs of one who acts after due examination prosper here, Yudhiṣṭhira; with good helpers the whole earth can be governed.

This was told of old by the good who know the law, O you whose majesty equals great Indra's; and I too have spoken it to you according to the vision of the scriptures—so apply yourself diligently to it and go forth, O king.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When a weak king, O bull of the Bharatas, has obtained a kingdom, how should he hold his ground, without resources, against an enemy of overwhelming strength?
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recount an ancient tale, a dialogue of the rivers and the ocean, O Bhārata.
The ocean, the everlasting abode of the foes of the gods, lord of the rivers, asked all the rivers about a doubt that had arisen within him.
"I see shade-giving trees struck down root and branch, carried here by you in your fullness—yet among them never the reed."
"The reed is slight of body and of little substance, and grows upon your very banks; is it that, despising it, you cannot uproot it, or has it rendered you some service?"
"This I wish to hear—the opinion of you all—why it is that the reed is not brought under sway, while you break down these banks of yours."
Then the river Gaṅgā spoke an answering word, meaningful, reasoned, and convincing, to the ocean, the lord of rivers.
"These trees stand fixed each in its place, each rooted in a single spot; then, out of senseless contrariness, they forfeit that place."
"The reed, seeing the rushing current come on, bows down, but the other does not; and when the current has passed by, it regains its place and stands."
"Knowing the time and knowing the occasion, ever yielding and not rising stubbornly, compliant and unstiffened—and for that reason the reed comes to no harm."
"Those herbs, trees, and shrubs that bend down and rise again with the force of wind and water—they do not meet with overthrow."
"For he who, when a mighty foe has grown strong and bent on slaughter and destruction, does not at the first bear with his onset, swiftly perishes."
"But the wise man who moves about knowing the strength and weakness, the power and the valour, both of himself and of his foe—he does not come to overthrow."
"Just so, when the wise man deems his enemy too strong, let him resort to the way of the reed; this is the mark of true discernment."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When a learned man, gentle, is reviled in the assembly by a fool grown insolent and harsh, what should he do, O Bhārata, O subduer of foes?
Bhīṣma said: Hear, O guardian of the earth, how this matter is sung. The man of good understanding ever bears with the abuse of the man of feeble understanding.
By not growing angry when reviled, the forbearing man gains the other's merit and is freed of his own ill deeds; while the one who answers anger with anger wipes away that gain.
One should disregard such a man as one would a lapwing crying out as if in distress; for having incurred the world's hatred, he gains nothing for his pains.
Thus he forever boasts of that base deed, saying, "Such a one, esteemed in the assembly of men, was told off by me!"—while the other stands there abashed, withered, and as good as dead.
One who boasts shamelessly of a deed not worth boasting of—such a basest of men is to be disregarded by him who is self-controlled.
Whatever the dull-minded man may say, one should ever bear with it; for what can a base fellow do, whether he praise or blame, croaking witlessly to no purpose like a crow in the forest?
If the contest of the evildoer were waged only with words, then words alone would be his object; but no such limited object belongs to one who seeks to destroy.
By his conduct and gestures he proclaims the baseness of his own begetting, like a peacock dancing and as it were displaying its nakedness.
With one for whom there is nothing in the world unspeakable and nothing whatever undoable, the pure man should hold no converse, for his deeds are foul.
The man who praises one's virtues to the face but slanders behind the back—such a man is like a dog in the world, bound for the loss of all blessed worlds.
Whatever such a man gives in charity or offers in sacrifice, even for a hundred men, he destroys it in an instant by his slander behind the back.
Therefore the wise man should at once shun such a one of evil mind, as the good shun the flesh that a dog has touched.
For the wicked man, uttering reproach against the noble, lays bare his own faults, as a serpent raises high its lifted hood.
He who, witless, wishes to retaliate against such a one as he carries on his own doings, sinks into the dust, like an ass plunging into a heap of ashes.
That hyena in human shape, never at peace, forever bent on slandering men, bellowing like a maddened elephant—him one should forsake as one would a most savage dog.
Walking the path frequented by the irresolute, fallen away from self-control and from good breeding, evil, ever bent on hostility and on others' ruin—shame upon that man of wicked mind!
Even when answered back by these men again and again, hearken and do not grow distressed; for the steadfast of mind condemn any contest between the high and the low.
In his rage he might strike with the flat of his hand, or pelt one with dust or with chaff, or bare his teeth to terrify—for all this is to be expected of a fool grown angry and cruel.
The man who in the assembly bears with the reproach heaped on by the basest of wretches, and who ever recites this instruction concerning the wicked, suffers nothing unpleasant that words can bring.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O Grandfather, greatly wise, this is a great doubt of mine; it must be resolved by you, O king, for you are the founder of our line.
O father, the traffic of words of men of evil conduct and evil mind has been told; and so I ask of you further.
What is beneficial for the machinery of the kingdom and brings happiness to the family, and what conduces to security and increase both in the future and in the present—
and what delights sons and grandsons and furthers the increase of the realm, and what is wholesome in food and drink and for the body—tell that to me.
A king who has been consecrated, established in his kingdom and surrounded by friends—or else beset by those who are no friends—how should he win the love of his subjects?
For one who delights in favouring the wicked, overborne by affection and passion, who through want of mastery over his senses craves the company of base men—
His servants, all of good lineage, fall away into worthlessness, and that king is never blessed with the fruits that loyal servants bring.
To me, who stand in doubt, you—the equal of Bṛhaspati in wisdom—ought to expound these duties of a king, hard indeed to grasp.
You are our expounder, O tiger among men, devoted to the welfare of our line; and so too is the keen-witted Kṣattṛ (Vidura), who counsels us always.
Having heard from you the word that serves our house and brings forth the welfare of the realm, I shall sleep content and at ease, as though sated with imperishable nectar.
What manner of servants, endowed with virtues, should stand close at hand? With men of what character and what lineage should one's course of governance be conducted?
For no king, bereft of servants, can be a protector all alone; and as for this realm, all people of good birth proclaim it so.
For a kingdom cannot be governed by one alone, O Bhārata; without helpers, dear son, no aims whatsoever can be won—nor, once won, ever kept secure, O bull of the Bharatas.
Bhīṣma said: He whose every servant is skilled in knowledge and discernment, well-wishing, of good birth, and affectionate—he enjoys the fruit of kingship.
He whose counsellors are well-born, incorruptible, long resident at his side, givers of sound counsel to the king, and versed in the knowledge of connections—
who make provision for what has not yet come, are expert in the knowledge of timing, and grieve not for what is past—he enjoys the fruit of kingship.
He whose helpers share alike in his sorrow and his joy, who act in truth and are bent on the care of his interests—he enjoys the fruit of kingship.
He whose countryfolk, ever near at hand, are free from distress, not mean of spirit, and steadfast upon the path of the good—he comes to partake of the fruit of kingship.
That king is best whose treasury and revenue-records are kept always by men who swell the treasury—men trusted and content.
His granary, when guarded by the incorruptible and the trusted, men intent on storing up, worthy of their trust and free from greed, becomes a source of strength.
He in whose city the conduct of affairs is seen to bear the fruit of action, recorded clean as if by Śaṅkha and Likhita—he comes to partake of the fruit of righteousness.
And the king who has won his men to himself, who knows the duties of a king and lays hold upon the sixfold body of policy—he gains the fruit that springs from dharma.
Bhīṣma said: On this matter too they recount an ancient tale, ever instructive in the world and walked by the path of the good.
It is fitting to this very theme—what I heard in a penance-grove, told to Rāma the son of Jamadagni by the best of the sages.
In a certain great forest, untrodden by men, there dwelt a sage who lived on roots and fruits, self-restrained and master of his senses.
Devoted to consecration and self-discipline, serene, supreme in private study of the Veda, pure, his soul cleansed by fasting, he stood always upon the path of the good.
Beholding the goodness of that wise one as he sat there, all the creatures who roamed the forest would gather close about him.
Lions and tigers, śarabhas, and great rutting elephants, leopards, rhinoceroses, and bears, and others dreadful to look upon—
all these blood-eating beasts would come, asking after his welfare, lowly as disciples before that sage and eager to do him pleasure.
Having paid their respects, they would all depart as they had come; but one tame beast, a dog, would never leave the great sage.
Devoted, ever attached to him, gaunt and feeble from fasting, feeding on heaps of fruit and root, serene, and gentle as a cultured being in form.
Seated at the feet of that great sage, the dog's nature had grown well-nigh human, and it was bound to him by a deep and tender love.
Then there came on a leopard of mighty strength, a blood-eater, bent upon the dog—utterly savage, cruel, like Death the ender of all.
Licking its lips, athirst, busily lashing its tail, its jaws agape, broken with hunger, it craved that flesh for its prey.
Seeing that fierce beast advancing, O lord of men, the dog, desiring life, spoke to the sage there—hear now what it said, O sagacious one.
"Blessed one, here is the leopard, the foe of dogs, and it means to slay me; by your grace let there be no fear of it for me, O great sage."
The sage said: "No fear of the leopard need you have, nor of death in any wise. Cast off the form of a dog—you become a leopard, my child."
Bhīṣma said: Then the dog, turned into a leopard, his form bright as gold of Jambū, his limbs dappled, glistening and glad, dwelt in the forest without fear.
Then there came on a most fearsome tiger, its jaws agape, gripped by hunger, licking its mouth at the leopard, greedy for its blood.
Seeing the tiger, fanged and forest-ranging, broken with hunger, the leopard, to save its life, took refuge with the sage.

Then, by the sage who ever bore for him the love bred of long dwelling together, that leopard was turned into a tiger, mightier than his foes; and seeing this, the tiger that had come did not strike him down, O lord of peoples.
But the dog, having attained tigerhood, now strong and a flesh-eater, no longer felt any longing then for fare of roots and fruits.
As the lord of beasts forever craves the dwellers of the wood, even so, great king, did that tiger then become.
The tiger, sated on the deer he had slain, lay sleeping at the foot of the hermit's hut; then to that spot came an elephant in rut, risen like a thundercloud.
His temples streaming with rut, tall, marked with the lotus-sign, his head broad and high, finely tusked, vast of body, his cry deep as a thundercloud's.
Seeing that rutting elephant approach, proud in its frenzy, the tiger, terrified by fear of the elephant, went to the sage for refuge.
Then that best of sages led the tiger into elephanthood; and seeing him like a great cloud, the other elephant was filled with dread.
Then with joy he roamed among the lotus-beds and the dense śallakī thickets, adorned with the pollen of the lotuses.
And so, as the elephant disported himself in contentment, the days and nights of that sage who dwelt in his hut of leaves passed pleasantly by.
Then there came to that place a lion, ruddy-maned, born of a mountain cavern, terrible, the destroyer of the elephant kind.
Seeing that lion advance, the elephant, distraught with fear of the lion, took refuge with the sage, trembling and stricken with dread.
Then that lordly elephant, turned into a lion by the sage, reckoned the wild lion as nothing, being now of like kind with it.
And seeing him, the wild lion fled away, its voice and strength failing for fear; while the new-made lion dwelt happily at the hermitage in that same forest.
But the other lesser beasts who dwelt in the penance-grove were no longer to be seen—forever cowering in fear and clinging to their lives.
At length, by the working of fate, there came one that did harm to all living things, mighty, a blood-eater, a terror to creatures of every kind—
a śarabha, eight-footed, walking with limbs upraised, a forest-ranger, came to the abode of that sage to slay the lion.
That śarabha the sage made surpassing in strength, O subduer of foes; and then the wild śarabha, beholding before the sage a śarabha mighty and most fierce, fled swiftly away in fear.
Thus set by the sage into the estate of a śarabha, he kept ever at the sage's side and enjoyed the happy condition of a śarabha.
Then all the herds of deer, terrified by the śarabha, fled from the forest to every quarter, O king, in fear and clinging to their lives.
And the śarabha, grown utterly savage, ever bent on the slaughter of living things, that flesh-eater no longer desired the peaceful fare of fruit and root.
Then the śarabha, seized by a mighty thirst for blood, sought to slay that very sage—ungrateful, born of the womb of a dog.
Then, perceiving him by the power of his penance through the eye of knowledge, the sage of great wisdom, knowing all, spoke thus to that dog:
"A dog, you attained leopardhood; a leopard, you came to tigerhood; the tiger became an elephant fierce in rut, and the elephant attained lionhood;
the lion, endowed with surpassing strength, passed further into a śarabha. Overcome by affection, I gave no thought to the lineage of your stock."
"Since thus, O wicked one, you wish to do harm to me who am sinless, therefore, returning to your own birth, a dog you shall once more become."
Then, through hatred of the sage's person, the wicked-souled and foolish śarabha, cursed by the sage, took on once more his form of a dog.
Bhīṣma said: That dog, restored to his own nature, fell into the depths of misery; rebuked with a "Begone!" by the sage, the wretch was cast out of the penance-grove.
Thus a wise king, having tested a man's good conduct and purity, his uprightness, disposition, and worth, his lineage, his behaviour, his learning and self-control,
his compassion, strength, valour, temper, calmness, and forbearance—should appoint such well-trained servants each to the office for which he is fit.
A guardian of the earth ought not to appoint a servant without testing him; the king who is thronged with men of low birth does not prosper in ease.
A man of good birth, appointed by the king, by reason of that good birth never sets his mind on wickedness, even when reproached though he be guiltless.
But a man of low birth, appointed through the ruin of worthier folk, having gained a lordship hard for him to win, if reproached will turn to enmity.
One well-born, trained, and wise, skilled in knowledge and discernment, knowing the true sense of all the treatises, enduring, and native to the land;
grateful and strong, patient, self-disciplined, master of his senses, free from greed, content with what he has, and eager for the good of his master's friends;
a minister who knows place and time, devoted to the gathering of all things needful, honoured, steady of mind, well-wishing, and never slothful;
of fitting conduct within his own domain, skilled in alliance and in war, knowing the threefold ends of the king, and beloved of townsfolk and countryfolk alike;
versed in the truth of entrenchments and battle-arrays, skilled in heartening the troops, knowing the meaning of gesture and demeanour, and expert in the march and the campaign;
learned in the training of elephants, free of arrogance, bold, deft, self-controlled, strong, and acting fittingly;
pure, surrounded by pure folk, well-attired and pleasing to behold, a leader skilled in statecraft, endowed with the sixty virtues—
unstubborn, humble, capable, soft of speech, steadfast, gentle, of great means, and able to provide for place and occasion—
the king who appoints such a minister and never slights him—his realm spreads wide as the moonlight of the lord of planets.
A king endowed with these very virtues, skilled in the treatises, supreme in dharma and intent on guarding his subjects, is one to be desired.
Steadfast, forbearing, pure, swift, knowing in due season the worth of manly effort; willing to learn, learned, a good listener, and skilled in weighing for and against;
of keen intellect, sure of memory, doing all things as justice requires, self-controlled, ever speaking kindly, and forbearing in adversity;
deciding for himself in giving and withholding, easy of approach, pleasant to behold, ever stretching out a hand to the distressed, trusting and trusted, and devoted to right policy;
not given to boasting of himself, not indifferent, not one to act at random, a doer of deeds that never fail once undertaken, and beloved of his servants.
He who keeps his people loyal, unhaughty, ever serene of face, generous, watchful over his servants, free from anger, exceedingly great of soul—
measured in punishment yet not lax in punishment, an enforcer of the duties of dharma, with spies for his eyes, watching his foes, ever skilled in dharma and artha—
such a king, endowed with a hundred virtues, is the one to be desired. And his warriors too, O lord of men, should be furnished with every excellence of quality.
Good men should be sought out as allies who can uphold the realm, and they must not be slighted by a king who longs for prosperity.
Warriors valiant in battle, grateful, expert in weapons, versed in the codes of dharma, attended by their bands of foot-soldiers,
enriched with wealth and honor, skilled in the maneuvering of chariots, adept with arrows and weapons—the king who has such men, his is this earth.
The king who is ever intent upon winning over all men, disposed to exertion, and rich in friends—that king is the best of kings.
With a thousand horses mounted by heroes, O Bhārata, and with men won over to his side, the whole earth may be conquered.
Bhīṣma said: The ruler of men who, after the fashion of the dog, appoints servants each to his own proper station in their fitting tasks—he enjoys the fruit of his kingdom.
A dog should not be raised beyond his proper station and honored above his measure; should the dog be promoted, he overleaps his own place and grasps for another.
Wise servants, endowed with good birth and lineage and settled in their own tasks, should be promoted; promotion to a station unfit for them is not proper.
The king who assigns to his servants tasks suited to them enjoys the fruit that springs from servants endowed with merit.
The śarabha should be placed in the śarabha's station, the lion in the post fit for a lion in his might, the tiger as a tiger, and the leopard as a leopard.
Servants are to be set, according to rule, in tasks befitting them; they should never be placed against the grain by one who seeks the fruit of their labor.
The witless ruler of men who, overstepping due measure, places his servants against the grain—he does not win the affection of his subjects.
Neither the foolish, nor the mean, nor those of unbridled senses, nor men of low birth should be kept at his side by a king who seeks his own welfare.
Men who are good, capable, brave, learned, free from envy, not mean, pure, and skilled—these should be his attendants.
Humble, devoted, patient, pure, well-born by nature, and of good repute—men who are above reproach each in his own station—such should be the king's outer officers.
At a lion's side the man should ever be a lion; even one who is no lion, when joined with a lion, gains a lion's reward.
But the lion who is surrounded by dogs, though bent on the fruit of a lion's deeds, cannot enjoy a lion's reward when waited upon by dogs.
Thus, O lord of men, with such men—brave, wise, deeply learned, and well-born—one may conquer the whole earth.

Neither one ignorant of medicine, nor a crooked man, nor an unlearned one, nor one without great wealth should be taken to his side as a servant by guardians of the earth, O best of those who employ servants.
Like arrows loosed, men intent upon their master's business speed forth; toward those servants who seek the king's good he should employ gentle, conciliating words.
The treasury must always be guarded by kings with diligent effort, for kings are rooted in the treasury; be one who makes the treasury his root.
Let your granary too be ever full, well stocked with grain, and always entrusted to honest men; be one devoted to wealth and grain.
Let your servants be ever ready and skilled in battle; and skill in the handling of horses is desired here as well.
Watchful over your kinsmen and relations, surrounded by friends and connections, and seeking the welfare of the townsfolk's affairs—so be, O delight of the Kauravas.
This conclusive wisdom and insight I have declared to you; the dog is your illustration, my son. What more do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Many a course of royal conduct you have set forth, O Bhārata—observances ordained of old by the ancients, who knew the dharma and the purposes of kingship.
That very teaching, declared at length, seen by the ancients and held to be the opinion of the good—the essence of the duties of kings—expound to me, O bull of the Bharatas.
Bhīṣma said: The protection of all beings—this is held to be the highest duty of the warrior caste. Hear, O lord of earth, how he may render such protection.
As the peacock, devourer of serpents, wears its many-colored plumes, so should the king who knows dharma assume a form of many kinds.
Sharpness, crookedness, sternness, truth, and uprightness—holding the mean and abiding in firmness of character, he attains happiness.
In whatever matter a certain hue would serve his interest, that color and form he should assume; for a king of many forms, even the subtlest aim does not fail.
He should ever keep his counsel guarded, mute as the autumn peacock; soft of speech and slender of frame, prosperous, he should be deeply versed in the sciences.
At the gateways of calamity let him be watchful, as at the outpourings of water; and as the rain-waters of the mountain seek the heights, so let him resort to the twice-born and the perfected sages.

Desiring his ends, the king should raise his crest like a banner of dharma; ever should he hold the rod of punishment uplifted, and act without negligence—observing income and outlay in the world, as a bird flits from tree to tree.
He should be cleanly among his own flock, and scatter the matters at hand with his feet; once fledged he should stir himself to motion, and guard himself against any weakness.
He should lay bare the faults of his foe and shake off the enemy's party; like a peacock among the blossoms in the forest, so should he go about gathering his aims.
He should take refuge with kings who are exalted, flourishing, and steadfast as mountains; he should seek a shade unperceived and resort to a hidden shelter.

With neck darkened as in the rains, let him plunge into the night in lonely places; like the peacock by its very nature, let him move unobserved among women. He should never cast off his armor, but guard himself by himself.
In the haunts of spies he should shun open approaches and snares; he should harass that ground, then vanish again into the thicket.
He should slay the wrathful, the deeply venomous, the foes who move by crooked ways; he should not resort to immature plumes, but make his dwelling in secure abodes.

Ever like the peacock, he should at will pursue what binds him to his purpose, and gather wisdom from every side, as the peacock gathers insects in the thickets. Thus, peacock-like, should the king protect his own realm.

The discerning one should ordain a policy that fosters his own growth: the restraint of self through intellect, the overthrow of others' designs by intellect, and the attainment of self-mastery through intellect—this is the teaching of the scriptures.

He should reassure his foe with conciliation while marking well his own strength; through self-examination he should weigh his judgment by judgment. The wise man, mind set on conciliatory means, discerns what should and should not be done.

He should be steadfast, his thought concealed, and speak only when speech is fitting; for the wise man, even were he Bṛhaspati in intellect, who lets out talk too closely held will revert to his true nature, like heated black iron plunged in water.
The lord of earth should inquire into all undertakings, both his own and his rival's, as they are taught in the authoritative scriptures.
The mean man, the cruel, the wise, the brave, and the one skilled in affairs—each he should appoint to his own proper task, along with whatever others excel in counsel.
Even without himself overseeing those set in their fitting tasks, he should keep them all in tune, as a stretched lute-string holds its notes.
Without conflict with any of the duties, he should do what pleases all; the king of whom each man says, 'He is mine,' stands unshaken like a mountain.
Holding firm resolve, as the sun holds forth its far-reaching ray, he should guard dharma alone, making the pleasing and the unpleasing equal in his eyes.
Men of good family, nature, and country, knowers of dharma, gentle of speech, in the prime of life, faultless, devoted to his welfare, masters of their senses,
free from greed, well-trained, self-restrained, and firmly grounded in the duties—such men the king, the guardian of dharma and artha, should establish in all affairs.
In this very manner, attentive and content, aided by his spies, he should watch over the coming and the going of all undertakings.
For the king whose wrath and favor are never spent in vain, who himself oversees his affairs, and whose treasury is founded on his own resolve—the very earth, the bearer of wealth, is his.
He whose favor is manifest and whose punishment is justly proportioned, who is guarded in himself and whose realm is guarded—that king is one who knows the dharma of kings.
He should ever survey his realm, as the rising sun surveys with its rays; he should know his spies through other spies, and so, by his wit, never be brought to fever.
He should take what comes in its due season, and the king should not betray his aim; day after day the wise one should milk the earth as one milks a cow.
As the bee gathers honey from the flowers little by little, so the king should take his substance and lay up his store.
Whatever remains after the protection of the realm, that serves dharma and pleasure alike; the king, learned in the scriptures and self-possessed, should both accumulate and disburse in turn.
He should not despise a small gain, nor scorn his enemies; he should understand himself through intellect, and should not place trust in the witless.

Steadfastness, skill, self-restraint, foremost intellect, fortitude, valor, regard for place and time, and vigilance—these eight are the kindling-fuels for the increase of wealth, be it small or great.
A spark of fire, when sprinkled with ghee, grows great, and a single seed becomes many thousands; marking well these vast workings of decline and increase, let the wise man never scorn the small.
A foe, whether child or grown or aged, will always strike down the heedless man; in due time another would tear away his very root—so the knower of the right moment is the best of kings.

An enemy would carry off one's fame, obstruct one's dharma, and lastingly cripple one's power in the matter of wealth—whether that foe and hater be weak or strong. Therefore the self-controlled man should never make light of a foe.

The ruin of the foe, the gathering of wealth and its protection, and the twin ends of dharma and pleasure conjoined—the intelligent man should bring these and yet more to fruition; therefore the king should rely upon the man of intellect.

Kindled intellect destroys even the strong; strength, when guarded by intellect, increases; an enemy, though waxing, sinks before intellect—and the deed that follows upon intellect is the deed that is praised.

The steadfast man who desires all the objects of desire, though his body be slight and clothed in but little vigor, yet as he strives for himself with wealth and honor, fills no small measure as a vessel of his own good.

Therefore the king, even when held in the grip of his foes, should gather the root of fortune from every side; though long oppressed, let him, by the force of his self-regard, be like the sudden flash of the lightning.
Knowledge, or austerity, or abundant wealth—all this can be won by resolute effort; the brahman dwells, intent, within embodied beings; therefore let one know that effort is the source of plenty.
Where the wise and the high-minded abide, where Śakra, Viṣṇu, and Sarasvatī dwell, and where all beings ever reside—therefore let the learned man not despise the body.

The greedy man one should ever overcome by gifts, for the greedy never reach contentment with another's wealth; every greedy man is grasping in the enjoyment of the fruits of action, and he who is bereft of wealth forsakes both dharma and pleasure.
Wealth, food, sons and wife, and prosperity—the greedy man covets all these from others; in the greedy all faults arise here below; therefore the king should not take greedy men into his service.
In a meeting he should urge on even the lowliest good man; the wise one should crush all the enterprises and aims of those who hate him.
A counselor renowned among the righteous, discreet, trustworthy, and well-born, O Pāṇḍava—such a one, O king, is fully fit for the governance of the realm.
The duties of the god among men, ordained by rule and here told in brief—mark them with your understanding; the king who, following these, ordains them is able to protect the earth.
If happiness born of misrule, of disorder, and won by violence of many kinds is seen, yet for that lord of earth there is no abiding course, and no supreme happiness arising from his realm.

Distinguished by wealth, honored for their wisdom and conduct, endowed with merit, their valor proven in battle, and tried in their virtues—such good men the self-possessed king here soon allies to himself, and so destroys his foes.

He should look to expedients by the various paths of action, and never fix his mind upon what is no true expedient; for the man who sees only flaws attains neither surpassing fortune, nor abundant fame, nor wealth.

Having discerned, among friends, both the rising of affection and its waning, and having weighed the two—he who would bear a heavy burden, that one alone the wise man should declare to be a true and steadfast friend.

These duties of a king that I have declared to you, set your mind upon them, and upon the protection of men; thus shall you easily win the fruit of merit, for the whole world is rooted in the highest dharma.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: This eternal dharma of kings has been declared by you, grandfather, and the great Rod is sovereign; upon the Rod everything rests.
Of the gods, of the seers, and of the great-souled ancestors, of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas, and of mortals especially—
of all living beings in the world, and of those that dwell among the beasts as well, the Rod, all-pervading and of mighty splendour, is the supreme good, O lord.
Thus has it been declared by you that all things, moving and unmoving, are subject to the Rod; and the world is seen to cling to it—gods, asuras, and men alike.
This I wish to know in its true essence, O bull of the Bharatas: What is the Rod? Of what kind is the Rod? What is its form? What is its final ground?
What is its nature? How does it come to be? How many forms does it bear? How does it hold sway? How does that Rod keep watch, attentive of spirit, over the people?

And who is it that keeps watch, guarding this realm of before and after? Which is known to be the prior, and which the other that is named the Rod? In what does the Rod abide, and what is held to be its course?
Bhīṣma said: Hear, O Kaurava, what the Rod is and how it is administered; for that on which all things depend, that alone is the Rod here.

The name of dharma, great king, is held to be 'administration of justice' (vyavahāra); for that which is heedful in the worlds, how should its abolition come to pass? It is for this purpose that the administration of justice holds its character as such.

Moreover this was declared of old by Manu at the very beginning, O king: he who rightly protects his subjects with a well-administered Rod, even-minded toward friend and foe alike—he alone is dharma itself.
Now this saying was uttered first of all by Manu in olden times, and its origin too was declared by Vasiṣṭha—the great word of Brahmā.
Because this saying was uttered first, men know it as the 'prior word'; and from the telling of the administration of justice, it is here called vyavahāra.
From the Rod, well-administered, the threefold aim of life ever proceeds; for the Rod is the supreme divine power, in form like fire with upward-leaping flame.
Dark as the petal of the blue lotus, four-fanged and four-armed, eight-footed, many-eyed, with pointed ears and bristling hair,
matted-locked, double-tongued, copper-faced, clad in the hide of the lion, king of beasts—this terrible form the Rod ever bears, hard to withstand.
Sword and mace, bow and spear, trident, hammer and arrow, pestle, axe and discus, the javelin, the staff, the lance, and the iron pike—
whatever weapons of war there are at all here, the Rod, being the soul of them all, moves embodied through the world.
Splitting, cleaving, crushing, slicing, rending, and tearing asunder, slaying and charging onward—the Rod alone moves abroad.
It is the Sword, the Slayer, Dharma, the Keen-pathed, the Unassailable, Womb-of-fortune, Victory, the Chastiser, Administration-of-justice, the Watcher-over-subjects;
the Scripture, the Brāhmaṇa's spell, the Chastiser who has become the prior word, Guardian-of-dharma, the Imperishable, the God, the Truth-faring, the Ever-faring, the Seizer;
the Unattached, son of Rudra, eldest of men, bringer of weal—these names of the Rod have been recounted, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
For the Rod is the Lord Viṣṇu, the Sacrifice, Nārāyaṇa the master; bearing forever its great form, it is called the Supreme Being.
As she is called the daughter of Brahmā—Lakṣmī, Polity, Sarasvatī—the science of governance by the Rod is the sustainer of the world; for the Rod is of many bodies.
Gain and loss, pleasure and pain, dharma and its opposite, strength and weakness, ill fortune and good fortune, merit and demerit, virtue and its absence,
desire and aversion, season and month, night and day and moment, displeasure and grace, joy, anger, calm and restraint,
fate and human effort, release and bondage, fear and fearlessness, harm and harmlessness, austerity, sacrifice, self-control, and poison and its absence,
the end, the beginning, and the middle, and the unfolding of all deeds; intoxication, negligence, and arrogance, hypocrisy, steadfastness, right conduct and wrong;
incapacity and capacity, pride and rigidity, expense and saving, discipline and emission, the timely and the untimely, O Bhārata;
falsehood, knowledge and ignorance, truth, and faith and faithlessness likewise, cowardice and resolve, gain and loss, victory and defeat;
harshness and gentleness, death, arrival and non-arrival, failure and success, what should and should not be done, strength and weakness;
envy and freedom from envy, dharma and its opposite likewise, shamelessness and shame, modesty, prosperity and adversity—
splendour in action, learning, power of speech, insight into truth: such, O Kaurava, is the manifold form of the Rod in this world.
Were there no Rod here, men would crush one another; it is for fear of the Rod that they do not slay one another, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Guarded day by day by the Rod, O king, the subjects make the king prosper here; therefore the Rod is the final refuge.
Swiftly it sets this world in order, O lord of men. Dharma, established upon truth, abides among the brāhmaṇas.
The foremost twice-born, joined to dharma, become joined to the Veda; from the Vedas arose sacrifice, and sacrifice gladdens the gods.
And the gods, ever well pleased, deliver their gifts to Indra; and Śakra in turn gives food, showing favour to these subjects.
And the life-breaths of all beings ever rest upon food; therefore the people stand firm, and the Rod keeps watch over them.
And serving such a purpose, the Rod has passed into kṣatriyahood; protecting the subjects it keeps ever watch, well-ordained and imperishable.
Lord, Person, Breath, Being, Wealth, Lord-of-creatures, Soul-of-beings, and Living-self—by these eight names it is proclaimed.
The Rod alone bestowed upon him both abiding sovereignty and lordship; joined with power and statecraft, it is ever fivefold in nature.
Lineage, arms, wealth, ministers, and wisdom are declared to be the forces; and another force, O Yudhiṣṭhira, is to be acquired by the eight kinds of resources.
Elephants, horses, chariots, foot-soldiers, ships, and corvée labour likewise, guides and spies—that is remembered as the eightfold army.
Of this well-equipped eightfold force there are the elephants and their riders, the horsemen and the foot-soldiers, the ministers, and those who supply provisions,
the mendicant agents and the judges, the astrologers and the readers of omens, the treasury, the allies, the grain, and all the implements.
What they here know to be the seven-membered, eight-limbed body of the kingdom—of that the Rod is the very limb, and the Rod is its very source.
By the Lord, through effort, for the kṣatriya to uphold, the Rod was given, even-souled; for this Rod is eternal. Among kings none other is more worthy of worship than he who reveals dharma as it is.

By Brahmā, for the protection of the world and for the establishing of each one's own dharma, there arose, resting on the sovereign's authority, yet another administration of justice; hence that which is seen conjoined with it bears the mark of the sovereign's authority.
But administration of justice whose essence is the Veda is called that which rests on the Veda's authority; it is original, O tiger among men, and yet another kind is that taught by the law-books.
And that Rod which has been spoken of, bearing the mark of the sovereign's authority, is to be known as resting in the lord of men, and as resting on the Rod's own authority.

Though seen as resting on the Rod's authority, it is remembered as being of the nature of administration of justice; and that which is remembered as administration of justice has its essence in the domain of the Veda.
And that whose essence is born of the Veda is dharma, the revealer of virtues; arising upon the authority of dharma, it is dharma as it truly is, made manifest by the perfected of soul.
Administration of justice, the protector of the subjects, ordained by Brahmā, O Yudhiṣṭhira, upholds the three worlds; its essence is truth, and it is the increaser of well-being.

That which is the Rod has been seen by us as the eternal administration of justice; and that which has been seen as administration of justice, that we have heard to be dharma; and that which is the Veda is verily dharma, and that which is dharma is the path of the good.

Brahmā, the Lord of creatures, was the first to be, the grandfather; for he is the maker of all the worlds—with their gods, asuras, and rākṣasas, with men and serpents—and he is the creator of beings.
Hence this administration of justice of ours bears the mark of the sovereign's authority; and therefore we have spoken this exposition of administration of justice.
Mother and father, brother, wife, and household priest—for kings there exists none exempt from the Rod who does not abide in his own dharma.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recite this ancient story. Among the Aṅgas there was a radiant king known as Vasuhoma.
That king, ever devoted to dharma and of great austerity, went together with his queen to Muñjapṛṣṭha, honoured by the hosts of divine seers.
There, on a peak of Himavat, on Meru the golden mountain, at the Muñja banyan where Rāma ordained the cutting away of his matted locks—
from that time onward, O lord of kings, by the seers of strict vows that region, frequented by Rudra, was called Muñjapṛṣṭha.
There, endowed with many virtues ever born of sacred lore, approved by the brāhmaṇas, he became the equal of a divine seer.
Once there came to visit him the undaunted lord of earth, the friend of Śakra and the honoured one, Māndhātā, scourge of his foes.
Approaching the king Vasuhoma, and seeing him eminent in austerity, Māndhātā stood before him with humility.
Vasuhoma in turn offered the king the cow and the welcome-water, and then inquired after the welfare of his eight-membered kingdom.
Following duly the usage practised of old by the good, Vasuhoma asked him, O king: 'What may I do for you?'
Greatly pleased, Māndhātā spoke to that best of kings, the deeply wise Vasuhoma, as he sat, O delight of the Kurus:
'The doctrine of Bṛhaspati, O king, you have studied entire, and likewise the treatise of Uśanas is fully known to you, O lord of men.
This I wish to hear: how does the Rod come into being? What is it that keeps watch from the first, and what is said to be supreme?
And how, abiding in the kṣatriya, does the Rod now stand established? Tell me, O greatly wise one; I shall give you the teacher's fee.'
Vasuhoma said: Hear, O king, how the Rod came to be—the sustainer of the world, for the disciplining and protection of the subjects, the eternal soul of dharma.
The Lord Brahmā, grandfather of all the worlds, wishing to sacrifice, found no officiating priest equal to himself—so we have heard.
That god bore an embryo within his head for a multitude of years; and when a full thousand years were complete, the embryo fell forth as he sneezed.
He came to be a Lord of creatures named Kṣupa, O subduer of foes; and he then served as the officiating priest at the sacrifice of that great-souled one, O king.
But while that sacrificial session of Brahmā was in progress, O bull among kings, because of the glad and untroubled course of things, that Rod became hidden from view.
And when it had vanished, confusion arose among the subjects: there was no longer what ought to be done nor what ought not, nor what was fit or unfit to eat.

What was fit or unfit to drink—whence then any right ordering? They fell to harming one another; there was no distinction then of the lawful and the forbidden, and another's property and one's own were held to be the same.
They plundered one another like dogs snatching at meat; the strong slew the weak, and all proceeded without bound or restraint.
Then the Grandsire, having worshipped the boon-granting Lord Viṣṇu, the eternal, and the great god Mahādeva, spoke thus.
Here you ought, of your sole grace, to show compassion: so ordain it that this confusion of all order may not come to pass.
Then that Lord, bearer of the trident and the matted locks, having meditated long, the best of gods, brought forth from himself, by himself, the Rod of Chastisement.
And from that he brought forth Policy, the goddess Sarasvatī, who treads the way of dharma; that science of governance by the Rod is renowned throughout the three worlds.
Again that Lord, whose chief weapon is the trident, having meditated long, appointed for each several order of beings its own particular ruler.
He made the thousand-eyed god the lord of the deities, and Yama, son of Vivasvat, he made the lord of the ancestral fathers.
Kubera he made lord of riches and of the rākṣasas; Meru he made lord of the mountains, and the great ocean lord of the rivers.
Over the realm of the waters and of the gods he set Varuṇa as sovereign; Death he made lord of living breaths, and the Oblation-eater (Agni) lord of the fiery energies.
As lord and guardian of the Rudras the Lord appointed the great-souled Mahādeva, the wide-eyed, the eternal one.
Vasiṣṭha he made lord of the brāhmaṇas, Jātavedas (Agni) of the Vasus; the Sun he made lord of the radiances, and the Moon of the constellations.
The rayed one (Soma) he made lord of the herbs; and the youthful, twelve-armed Skanda he ordained as the chief lord and king of the spirit-hosts.
He made Time the lord of all, whose nature is destruction and restraint, master of fourfold Death, of sorrow, and of joy.
The Lord whose body is all things, the king of kings, the master of wealth, the trident-bearer, is the ruler of all the Rudras: so runs the sacred tradition.
To that one Kṣupa, the son born after Brahmā, he gave dominion, making him the foremost overlord of creatures and of all who uphold dharma.
Then Mahādeva, when that sacrifice was concluded according to rule, gave the Rod, the guardian of dharma, with due honour, to Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu gave it to Aṅgiras; Aṅgiras, best of sages, gave it to Indra and Marīci; and Marīci gave it to Bhṛgu.
Bhṛgu gave that Rod, conjoined with dharma, to the seers; the seers gave it to the guardians of the worlds, and the world-guardians to Kṣupa.

Kṣupa gave it to Manu, the son of the Sun; and the Lord of the Śrāddha (Manu), to fulfil the subtle ends of dharma, gave it to his sons — that Manu, the Sun's son, bestowed it as the very principle of protection.
Chastisement must be apportioned and meted out by dharma, not at whim: harsh rebuke, restraint, imprisonment, fines of gold, and outward correction —
and maiming of the body, or death — but not for a trifling cause — these several bodily torments, the surrender of life, and banishment.
In due succession that Rod keeps watch, guarding the people: Lord Indra keeps watch, and from Indra, Agni the radiant.
After Agni, Varuṇa keeps watch, and after Varuṇa, Prajāpati; and after Prajāpati, Dharma keeps watch, whose essence is discipline.
After Dharma keeps watch Resolve, the eternal son of Brahmā; and after Resolve, fiery energy keeps watch, protecting all.
After that energy the herbs keep watch, and after the herbs the mountains; and after the mountains, Sap keeps watch, by virtue of the quality of savour.
The goddess Nirṛti keeps watch, and after Nirṛti the heavenly lights; the Vedas are the foundation after the lights, and then the Horse-headed Lord (Hayaśiras).
After him Brahmā the Grandsire keeps watch, the imperishable Lord; and after the Grandsire, the great god, Lord Śiva, keeps watch.
After Śiva, the All-Gods, and after the All-Gods, the seers; after the seers, Lord Soma, and after Soma, the eternal deities.

After the deities, the brāhmaṇas keep watch in the world — know this well — and after the brāhmaṇas, the kṣatriyas guard the worlds by dharma; the unmoving and the moving alike eternally rest upon the kṣatriyas.
The people keep watch in this world, and over them keeps watch the Rod; that Rod, which gathers all things into itself, is a lord equal to the Grandsire.
Time keeps watch at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end, O Bhārata — the Lord of all the worlds, the great god, Prajāpati.
The God of gods, Śiva, Śarva, keeps watch forever, the Lord — the matted-haired one, Śaṃkara, Rudra, Bhava, Sthāṇu, the consort of Umā.
Thus is this Rod proclaimed, at the beginning, the middle, and the last; by it let the guardian of the earth, the knower of dharma, conduct himself according to justice.
Bhīṣma said: Whatever man should hear this teaching of Vasuhoma, and having heard it should conduct himself rightly — that king shall attain all his desires.
Thus have I declared to you, O bull among men, all concerning that Rod, the restrainer of every world that has gone astray from dharma, O Bhārata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Father, I wish to hear the settled truth concerning dharma, wealth, and desire; for the whole conduct of life in this world rests entirely upon these three.
In what are dharma, wealth, and desire rooted, and what is the source of these three? How do they cleave to one another, and yet operate each apart?
Bhīṣma said: When men are well-minded toward the discernment of the world's right ordering, then the three cleave together in their arisings, abidings, and ceasings within Time.
The body is rooted in dharma; wealth is its means, and desire is called the fruit of wealth. All these are rooted in resolve, and resolve has the sense-objects for its essence.
And the sense-objects, one and all, serve wholly for the sustaining of life; this is the root of the triad — while their cessation is called liberation (mokṣa).
Dharma is the safeguarding of the body; wealth is sought for the sake of dharma; and desire here has delight for its fruit — yet all these are charged with the quality of passion (rajas).
He should pursue these as they lie near to hand, yet not abandon them in his mind; freed from darkness (tamas), he should hold to them all — dharma and the rest — making desire their goal.
He of best understanding, regarding the triad, should grasp at once by the higher intellect what is to be known in any matter, and not by the meaner intellect, plodding day by day.
The taint of dharma is evil intent; the taint of wealth is hoarding; the taint of desire is reckless revelry — each, moreover, turning back upon its own quality.
On this point too they recount an ancient tale, the dialogue of both Kāmanda and Aṅgāriṣṭha.
Having saluted the seer Kāmanda as he sat, and observing the proper occasion, the king Aṅgāriṣṭha then put his question.
When a king commits a sin, driven by the force of desire and delusion, O seer, what may serve to destroy the sin of such a man when he comes to repent?
And when, out of ignorance, a king practises unrighteousness here thinking it righteousness, and it has become notorious in the world, how should he turn back from it?
Kāmanda said: He who, casting off dharma and wealth, pursues desire alone, comes by that abandonment of dharma and wealth to the ruin of his wisdom in this world.
Delusion is the destroyer of wisdom, and likewise the destroyer of dharma and wealth; from it, in turn, are born unbelief and wicked conduct.
When a king does not restrain the depraved men of evil conduct, the people shrink from him as from a serpent that has entered the house.
The people no longer follow him, nor the brāhmaṇas, nor the virtuous; thereupon he meets with utter ruin, and comes besides to be slain.
