Cast down and despised, he lives a life of misery; and the very life that such a fallen man lives is but death made plain.
On this matter the teachers declare the means of expiating sin: the threefold sacred knowledge (the Vedas) is to be cultivated, and honour shown to the brāhmaṇas.
He should be high-minded in dharma, and marry into a noble house; he should also wait upon brāhmaṇas endowed with forbearance and wisdom.
He should murmur prayers, be given to ablutions, gracious of countenance, set upon naught else; he should consort with the righteous, having shut the evildoers out.
He should conciliate others with sweet speech and likewise with deeds, saying ever 'Thus am I,' while proclaiming the virtues of others.
For one of such sinless conduct soon becomes held in high esteem, and quells even grievous sins — of this there is no doubt.
Whatever supreme dharma the elders may declare, that do accordingly; for through the grace of the elders you shall attain the highest good.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: These men, O best of men, ever praise upon the earth, before all else, good character as the foundation of dharma; thence arises in me a great doubt.
If it can be understood by us, O foremost of the upholders of dharma, I wish to hear all of it — how this good character is to be acquired.
How then is good character attained? I wish to hear, O Bhārata; and by what marks is it described? Tell me, O best of speakers.
Bhīṣma said: Long ago, O bestower of honour, Duryodhana here told this to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, tormented as he was at the sight of such prosperity come to others.
At Indraprastha, O great king, in the hall of you and your brothers, there was that mockery he suffered — hear all of it, O Bhārata.
Having seen that hall of yours and its unsurpassed splendour, Duryodhana, seated then, reported it all to his father.
And Dhṛtarāṣṭra too, having heard Duryodhana's words then, spoke this speech to Duryodhana, who was attended by Karṇa.
Why do you torment yourself, my son? I wish to hear the truth of it; and having heard, I shall console you, if you will but conduct yourself rightly.
You have attained great lordship, O conqueror of hostile cities; all your brothers are at your service, and so are your friends and kinsmen.
You clothe yourself in fine mantles, you eat rice with meat, thoroughbred steeds bear you along — why then do you grieve, my little son?
Duryodhana said: Ten thousand high-souled graduate sages dine from vessels of gold in Yudhiṣṭhira's dwelling.
And having seen that celestial hall, furnished with celestial flowers and fruits, the horses dappled like the partridge, and jewels of every kind —
having seen that splendid prosperity of the sons of Pāṇḍu, rivalling Indra's, the vast prosperity of my foes, I grieve, O bestower of honour.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: If you desire prosperity such as that which is in Yudhiṣṭhira, my son, or even greater, O tiger among men, then be a man of good character, my little son.
For by good character the three worlds can be conquered — of this there is no doubt; nothing in the world is unattainable for those of good character.
In a single night Māndhātā, in three days Janamejaya, in seven nights Nābhāga, won possession of the whole earth.
For all these kings were men of good character, endowed with self-restraint; therefore the earth, won over by their virtues, came to them of her own accord.
On this point too they recount this ancient tale, told of old by Nārada concerning good character, O Bhārata.
By Prahlāda the kingdom of the great-souled Mahendra was wrested away; relying upon good character, that daitya brought the three worlds under his sway.
Then Śakra, with joined palms, presented himself before Bṛhaspati and, that man of great wisdom, said: 'I wish to know what is the highest good.'
Then the Lord Bṛhaspati related to him the supreme knowledge that leads to the highest weal, to the lord of the gods, O scion of Kuru.
'Thus much is the highest good' — so Bṛhaspati declared; but Indra asked again, 'Wherein might there be something yet greater?'
Bṛhaspati said: There is a great excellence in the high-souled Bhārgava, my son; go and acquire learning there once more, Purandara—blessings upon you.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Then that one of vast renown and surpassing splendor, seeking his own greater good, joyfully acquired knowledge anew from the Bhārgava.
Granted leave even by him, the high-souled Bhārgava, the Lord of a Hundred Sacrifices said once again to Śukra, 'Is there yet a greater good?'
But the Bhārgava, knower of dharma, replied, 'The high-souled Prahrāda possesses knowledge of special excellence'; and thereupon Indra was delighted.
Then the Chastiser of Pāka, having become a brāhmaṇa, that wise one approached Prahrāda and said, 'I wish to learn what is the highest good.'
But Prahrāda said to the brāhmaṇa, 'I have no leisure, O bull among the twice-born, occupied as I am with the sovereignty of the three worlds; therefore I cannot instruct you.'
The brāhmaṇa then spoke these words: 'At what time will you have leisure? Whatever interval falls between your duties, then I wish to be instructed.'
Then King Prahrāda was pleased with the expounder of the Veda, and saying 'So be it,' he imparted to him the truth of knowledge at an auspicious time.
And the brāhmaṇa too, according to custom, rendered to his teacher unsurpassed service with his whole being, just as that one desired in his heart.
And he was asked by the brāhmaṇa many times: 'How, O subduer of foes, did you obtain the sovereignty of the three worlds, O knower of dharma? Tell me the cause of it.'
Prahrāda said: I never bear ill will, O best of the twice-born, thinking 'I am king'; when the wise speak their wisdom, my son, I restrain myself and bear it patiently.
Trusting in me, they speak freely and ever guide me; and when I am devoted to the path of wisdom, eager to listen and free of envy,
those teachers heap their instruction upon me—a man of righteous soul, conqueror of anger, self-controlled, with senses subdued—as bees gather honey from flowers.
Thus, savoring the essences ground fine upon the tongue's tip of the learned, I stand above those of my own kind as the moon stands above the stars.
This is the nectar upon the earth, this the unsurpassed eye: the wisdom on a brāhmaṇa's lips—having heard it, one goes forward in life.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: 'This is the highest good,' said Prahrāda to the expounder of the Veda; and then, having been served by him, the lord of the Daityas spoke these words.
I am pleased with your fitting service to your teacher, O most excellent of the twice-born. Choose a boon—blessings upon you—and I shall grant it, of that there is no doubt.
'It is already done,' said that brāhmaṇa to the lord of the Daityas; but Prahrāda, well pleased, said, 'Let the boon be taken nonetheless.'
The brāhmaṇa said: If you are gracious to me, O king, and if you wish my welfare, then I desire to obtain your conduct—this is my boon.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Then the lord of the Daityas was both pleased and seized by great fear, for at the boon named by the brāhmaṇa he thought, 'This one is of no small power.'
'So be it,' Prahrāda said to him then, astonished; but having bestowed the boon upon the brāhmaṇa, he was filled with sorrow.
When the boon had been given and the brāhmaṇa had departed, great anxiety came upon Prahrāda, O great king, and he could reach no certainty.
As he brooded thus, my son—O lord of great splendor—a radiance in bodily form, like a shadow given shape, then forsook his body.
Prahrāda asked that mighty-bodied being, 'Who are you?' It replied, 'Surely I am Conduct. Cast off by you, I now depart.'

'In that excellent brāhmaṇa, O king, I shall dwell, O blameless one—he who, having become your pupil, was ever steadfastly devoted to you.' Having spoken thus, it vanished and entered into Śakra, my lord.
When that radiance had gone, another of like form then issued forth from his body, and Prahrāda said, 'Who are you?'
'Know me, Prahrāda, to be Dharma. Where that most excellent of the twice-born has gone, there too I shall go, O lord of the Daityas; for where Conduct is, there am I.'
Then another, O great king, blazing as it were with splendor, issued forth from the body of the high-souled Prahrāda.
Asked 'Who are you?', that one of great splendor replied to him, 'I am Truth, O foremost lord of the Asuras; I shall follow Dharma hence.'

When that being had followed after Dharma, yet another being came forth from him; and questioned by the high-souled one, it said, 'Know me, Prahrāda, to be Right Practice; for where Truth is, there am I.'

When that one had gone, a great white being came forth from his body, and being questioned it said, 'Know me to be Strength; where Right Practice is, there am I.' So saying, it went there where Right Practice had gone, O lord of men.
Then a radiant goddess came forth from his body. The lord of the Daityas asked her who she was, and she answered, 'I am Śrī, Fortune herself.'
'Happily have I dwelt in you, O hero of truthful valor; but forsaken by you, I shall depart—for I go where Strength has gone.'
Then fear arose in the high-souled Prahrāda, and he asked her once more, 'Where do you go, O dweller in the lotus?'
'For you, O goddess true to your vow, are the supreme mistress of the world. And who is that most excellent of brāhmaṇas? I wish to learn the truth of it.'
Śrī said: That celibate student whom you instructed was Śakra himself; whatever sovereignty over the three worlds was yours, that has been carried off by him, my lord.
For by good conduct, O knower of dharma, you had conquered all the worlds; and knowing this, mighty Indra has taken your conduct from you, my lord.
Dharma, Truth, Right Practice, Strength, and I myself, O greatly wise one, are ever rooted in Conduct; of this there is no doubt.
Bhīṣma said: Having spoken thus, Śrī departed, and all those others with her, O Yudhiṣṭhira. But Duryodhana said again to his father these words.
I wish to know the true nature of conduct, O delight of the Kurus, and by what means good conduct is attained; tell me that way.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: The means was set forth earlier by the high-souled Prahrāda; yet hear in brief, O ruler of men, how good conduct is attained.
Freedom from malice toward all beings in deed, thought, and word, together with kindness and giving—this is what is praised as good conduct.
Whatever deed, however manly, would not be for the good of others, or would make one ashamed—that one should by no means do.
But one should so act that one may be praised in the assembly. This, in brief, is good conduct as it has been declared, O best of the Kurus.
Even though the ill-conducted may somewhere attain fortune, O king, they do not enjoy it long, my son, but fall, uprooted to the very root.
Knowing this truly, be a man of good conduct, my boy, if you desire a fortune far surpassing that of Yudhiṣṭhira, my son.
Bhīṣma said: This Dhṛtarāṣṭra told to his son, O ruler of men. Do you do likewise, O son of Kuntī, and then you shall obtain its fruit.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: You have told me that conduct is foremost in a man, O grandsire. How did hope arise, and what is it? Tell me that.
A great doubt has arisen in me, O grandsire, and there is none other than you to resolve it, O conqueror of hostile cities.
O grandsire, a great hope rested in me regarding Suyodhana—that, when war came, he would do what was fitting, my lord.
A very great hope arises in every man, and when that hope is shattered, the grief is, beyond doubt, as bitter as death.
And so I, my hopes destroyed, was made a fool by that evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O lord of kings; behold the dullness of my spirit.
I deem hope greater than a mountain with its trees, greater even than the sky, O king, or rather wholly immeasurable.
And this hope, O best of the Kurus, is hard to fathom and most hard to fulfill; and because of its very unattainability, I see nothing else harder to attain than it.
Bhīṣma said: On this I shall recount to you, Yudhiṣṭhira—mark it well—the ancient tale of what befell Sumitra and the sage Ṛṣabha.
A royal sage named Sumitra, of the Haihayas, had gone hunting, and having pierced a deer with a smooth-jointed arrow, he gave chase to it.
That deer, of boundless vigor, bore off the arrow and fled, and the mighty king pursued it swiftly from close behind.
Then that swift deer ran over low ground and high alike, O lord of kings, and in but a moment it came onto level ground.
Then the king, in his youthful vigor and inborn strength, bow and sword in hand, gave chase, gliding like a swan.
Crossing streams and rivers, pools and woods, passing them over and beyond, he pursued on, ranging through the forest.
But that deer, O king, of its own will, drawing near the king again and again, would then dart away once more with very great speed.
Though struck by his many arrows, that forest-ranging creature, as if in sport, O lord of kings, would again draw near him.
And again, summoning its swiftness, that fleet leader of the deer-herd, outstripping him again and again, O lord of kings, would once more draw near.
Sumitra, scourge of his foes, taking up a dreadful, vital-piercing, most excellent shaft, loosed it from his bow at the deer.
Then, by but the distance of a league, that lord of the deer-herds, slipping from the path of the arrow, stood still as if laughing.
When that arrow had fallen blazing to the ground, the deer entered the great forest, and the king ran on after it.
Having entered the great forest, the king then came upon a hermitage of ascetics, and, weary, he sat himself down.
Seeing him bearing his bow, worn out with toil and hungered, the sages gathered round and paid him honor as the rites prescribe.
The sages asked that tiger among kings his purpose: 'For what gracious errand, O fair-faced one, have you come to this grove of penance?'
'On foot, your sword girded on, bearing bow and arrows, O lord of men—this we wish to learn: whence have you come, O bestower of honor? In what lineage were you born, and what is your name? Tell us.'
Then that king, O bull among men, in due order related all to those twice-born ones, and rendered them service, O Bhārata.

'Born in the line of the Haihayas, Sumitra, the delight of my friends, I roam slaying the herds of deer with arrows by the thousand, guarded by a mighty host, with my ministers and my women's quarters.'
'A deer pierced by my arrow runs on with the barb in it; following it as it fled, I have come by chance to this forest, into your presence—my fortune lost, my hopes destroyed, wasted with toil.'
'What grief indeed is there other than this—that I, worn down with toil, have reached your hermitage, my hopes destroyed, the marks of royalty undone?'
'Neither the loss of my royal insignia nor of my city, O you whose wealth is penance, brings me grief so keen as my hope that has been shattered.'

'As the mighty mountain Himavān or the great ocean could not, for their vastness, be matched against the space between heaven and earth, so, O foremost in penance, have I never reached the end of hope.'
'All is known to you, for you who are rich in penance are all-knowing; you, sirs, are most highly blessed—therefore I shall ask you my doubt.'
'A man filled with hope, or else the firmament—which of these, by reason of its greatness, appears to you the greater in the world? This I wish to hear in truth: what here is hard to attain?'
'If it be a secret, O you ever-devoted to penance, then do not tell it here; but if it be no secret, I wish to hear it, O bulls among the twice-born.'
'Or if this question I have raised would be a hindrance to your penance, then I shall desist from it; but if there is occasion for such discourse, then speak.'
I wish to hear, in its truth and in the fullness of its causes, this whole matter; for you, ever steadfast in austerity, may set it forth with a composed mind.
Bhīṣma said: Then, of all those assembled sages, the foremost of seers, the brahmin-sage named Ṛṣabha, smiling as it were, spoke thus.
Long ago, O tiger among kings, O mighty lord, as I wandered among the sacred fords, I came upon the divine hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
There stood that lovely jujube tree and the lake Vaihāyasa, and there, O king, Aśvaśiras recites the eternal Vedas.
Having duly made my offerings of water to the ancestors and the gods at that lake, I then proceeded to the hermitage.
There, where the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa ever take their delight, I went, not far off, to a certain hermitage to take up my lodging.
Then I beheld a sage approaching, clad in bark and deerskin, exceedingly lean and tall — a treasury of austerity named Tanu.
O mighty-armed one, in stature he was eightfold beyond other men, yet, O royal sage, such gauntness as his I had never anywhere seen.
His body, O lord of kings, was as slender as a little finger; his neck, his arms, his feet, and his hair were a wonder to behold.
His head was in keeping with his frame, and so too his ears and eyes; yet his speech and his bearing, O best of kings, were as those of ordinary men.
Seeing that emaciated brahmin, I grew afraid and deeply troubled in heart; and having saluted his feet, I stood before him with hands folded in reverence.
Having announced my name, my lineage, and my father, O bull among men, I slowly took my seat upon the place he indicated.
Then, O great king, in the midst of the sages, that best of the upholders of dharma recounted discourses bound up with righteousness and worldly profit.
And even as he was speaking, a lotus-eyed king drew near on swift horses, together with his army and his retinue of the inner apartments.
Brooding over his son lost in the forest and stricken with the deepest grief — the wise and greatly renowned father of Bhūridyumna, foremost of the Raghus.
"Here I shall behold that son of mine, here I shall see him" — thus, O king, fashioned by hope, that monarch had once ranged through this forest.
"Hard indeed is it for me to behold him, that most righteous one; my only son, lost in the great forest" — thus again and again he lamented.
"Hard is he for me to behold, yet great is my hope; encompassed in every limb by it, I am surely about to die — of this there is no doubt."
Hearing this, the venerable Tanu, the very best of sages, with head bowed and absorbed in meditation, remained for a moment as if motionless.
Marking him sunk in thought, the king, most sorrowful and wretched of spirit, spoke these words, again and again, softly and ever more softly.
"What, O brahmin-sage, is hard to attain, and what may there be of hope? Let the venerable one declare this, if it be no secret kept from me."
Now this venerable great sage had once been slighted by that very king, who, in his ill fortune, had taken to a childish frame of mind.
For when, O king, the sage had asked of him a golden pitcher and garments of bark, that brahmin-sage, rebuffed, became disheartened and free of all hope.
Having spoken thus and saluted that sage honoured by the world, the righteous king, wearied, sat down — even as you do now, O best of men.
Then the great sage, bringing the welcome-offering and water for the feet, presented all to the king according to the rite of the forest-dwellers.
Thereupon all those sages, encircling that bull among men and setting him before them, took their seats, as the Seven Sages encircle the Pole-star.
And there they questioned that unvanquished king as to his every purpose and the reason for his entering the hermitage.
The king said: I am the king called Vīradyumna, renowned in all quarters; I have come to the forest to seek my lost son, Bhūridyumna.
He is my only son, O foremost of brahmins, and but a child, O sinless one; nowhere in this forest is he to be seen, and I roam about in search of him.
Ṛṣabha said: When the king had spoken these words, the sage, his face downcast, fell silent there and made the monarch no reply.
For that brahmin had once been little honoured by this king, and so, O lord of kings, he had undertaken a long austerity, lean and wasted with hope.
"Never in any wise shall I accept a gift from kings, nor yet from men of the other castes" — having so resolved in his mind.
"For hope, abiding within, makes a man babble like a child; that hope I will utterly drive away" — thus resolved, he stood firm.
The king said: What is the leanness of hope, and what is hard to attain here upon earth? Let the venerable one declare this, for you are a seer of dharma and of worldly good.
Ṛṣabha said: Then, calling all of it to mind, the venerable, lean-bodied brahmin Tanu, as if to remind the king, spoke to him thus.
In leanness, O king, there is nothing to equal hope, O lord of men; and it was because she is so hard to fulfil that I made my entreaties of princes.
The king said: Lean and not-lean I have grasped, O brahmin, from your words; and its hard-to-attain nature too, O twice-born, is to me like a saying of the Veda.
Yet a doubt, O greatly wise one, has arisen in my heart; this, O best of men, you ought to declare to me truly, for I ask it of you.
What, then, is leaner even than you? Let the venerable one declare this, if it be no secret of yours, O brahmin — what in this world is hard to attain?

Lean-bodied Tanu said: Hard to find, or rather not to be found, is the petitioner who keeps his composure as if undisturbed; yet harder still to find, my son, is he who does not scorn the one who comes to ask.
The hope that, having heard a promise, is not requited as is fitting and to the utmost of one's power — that hope, clinging to all beings, I deem the leaner one.
A father of an only son, when that son is lost or gone abroad, who can learn nothing of his fate — his hope I deem the leaner one.
The hope of women at their delivery, the longing of the aged for a son, and likewise, O lord of men, the hope of the wealthy — these I deem the leaner.
Ṛṣabha said: Hearing this, O king, that monarch, together with his retinue of the inner apartments, touched the sage's feet and fell with his head before that bull among the twice-born.
The king said: I implore your grace, O venerable one; I long to be reunited with my son. Choose a boon, O brahmin, whatever you desire, in due form.
Ṛṣabha said: And the lotus-eyed king spoke this word to him: "Even as you have declared, O brahmin, so it is true; there is nothing false herein."
Then the venerable Tanu, foremost of the upholders of dharma, laughing aloud, swiftly brought back his son by the power of austerity and of sacred lore.
Having brought back the son and then admonished the king, that best of the upholders of dharma revealed himself to be Dharma in his own form.
And having shown his own divine form, wondrous to behold, free of sin and free of wrath, he departed and ranged through the nearby forest.
This I myself beheld, O king, and this word I heard; therefore drive swiftly from you this hope, the leaner of the two.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, O great king, by the high-souled Ṛṣabha, Sumitra straightway drove from him then that hope, the leaner one.
Even so do you also, O son of Kuntī, having heard this speech of mine, grow steadfast, O king, like Himavān, the noblest of mountains.
For you are one who has both seen and heard in the hard straits where great deeds were done; having heard me, O great king, you ought not to grieve here any longer.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: As of nectar, so of your speaking I can never have my fill; therefore tell me yet more of dharma, O grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: On this point too they recount this ancient tale, the dialogue between Gautama and the high-souled Yama.
Upon Mount Pāriyātra stood the great hermitage of Gautama, where Gautama dwelt for a time; hear of that too from me.
For sixty thousand years did that Gautama perform his austerity; and to that sage of fierce penance, steadfast and matured by his austerity—
—then came, O tiger among men, Yama, the guardian of the worlds; and he beheld that sage Gautama, the muni rich in austerity.
Knowing him for Yama who had come in his might, that brahmin-sage, that treasury of austerity, with hands folded and self-controlled, drew near to him.
And the King of Dharma, the moment he beheld that bull among men, made his salutation and addressed him courteously, saying, "What shall be done?"
Gautama said: By doing what may a man discharge his debt to mother and father? And how does a man attain to those auspicious worlds so hard to win?
Yama said: By one ever endowed with austerity and purity, and devoted to truth and to dharma, honour must be rendered straightway, day after day, to mother and father.
And sacrifice must be offered with many horse-sacrifices well furnished with their proper gifts; thereby a man attains to worlds wondrous to behold.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: For a king forsaken by his friends and beset by many foes, his treasury exhausted and his forces broken, O descendant of Bharata—what recourse remains?
—whose ministers and helpers are corrupt, whose counsels have leaked out on every side, who is slipping from his kingdom and sees no other way?
—assailed by a hostile army, weak before a stronger foe, his realm left unordered, and himself heedless of place and time?
When conciliation cannot be had, nor the sowing of division for want of pressure to apply—and life itself is at stake, or wealth—what then is the righteous course?
Bhīṣma said: A secret matter of dharma you have asked of me, O bull of the Bharatas; unasked, I should not venture to declare this dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira.
For dharma, O bull of the Bharatas, is subtler than speech and than thought; only when one has heard it and waited upon it through good conduct does a man somewhere become virtuous.
By action governed by intelligence a man becomes wealthy, or else he does not; such is the question you have pressed, and it must be resolved by you with your own discernment.

Hear, O descendant of Bharata, of an expedient abounding in dharma, meant for the sustaining of one's course. I would not, for dharma's own sake, wish for such a dharma; yet what brings pain in the taking from the wealthy here is held, in the end, to be allowable.
Following out the settled conclusion of all the courses of conduct—the more constantly a man regards the sacred teaching, the more he understands, and the more his understanding gives him delight.
From want of understanding arises a man's misapplication of means; for from want of understanding comes misapplication, whereas right application, in turn, is the maker of prosperity.
Without misgiving and without cavil, hear this my word: it is from the wasting of a king's treasury that the wasting of his forces is born.
Let the king bring a treasury into being, as water is drawn from waterless places; and when the time comes, let him show favour. This is the fitting dharma here and now.
Resorting to this dharma of expedients, practised by men of old—one dharma belongs to the powerful, and another, O descendant of Bharata, in times of distress.
A treasury comes first, it is said, then dharma; yet wisdom is weightier than dharma. He who is too weak, even on attaining dharma, does not come by a just course of conduct.
Since wealth is not won by any single, unbending way, therefore in time of distress even what is unrighteous is taught to bear the mark of dharma.
"In what does unrighteousness arise?" — this the wise have known; and as to what is nearest to the kṣatriya, on this very point you are in doubt.
That whereby his dharma may not languish, and whereby he may not fall under the power of the foe — that, they say, is to be done here; let him not bring himself to ruin.
The man whose self is composed should, by every means, strive to raise himself up—neither for the sake of dharma, nor for another, nor merely for his own self; this is the settled conclusion.

Herein, my son, lies the conviction of those skilled in dharma, in the subtleties of righteousness: that exertion is the livelihood of the warrior, and that he lives by the might of his arms—so runs the sacred teaching.
When his means of livelihood are blocked, from whom may a kṣatriya not take what he needs—save only from the property of an ascetic and the property of a brāhmaṇa, O Bhārata?
Just as a brāhmaṇa, sinking into distress, may officiate at sacrifices even for those unworthy of his ministry and may eat forbidden food, so too is it in this case—of this there is no doubt.
For one hard-pressed, what door is barred, what path forbidden to one held down? When a man is sorely pressed, he breaks out even where there is no proper door.
With the loss of his treasury and his army comes defeat before all the world; yet for him the life of a beggar is not ordained, nor the livelihood of a vaiśya or a śūdra.
For one who does not depend upon others, the livelihood nearest to his own dharma is right; pursuing first the primary rule, he may live by the secondary rule in its stead.

For one fallen into calamity, even a livelihood gained by irregular means among the rules of dharma is allowed; indeed this has been seen even among brāhmaṇas when their means of living are exhausted.
What doubt, then, could there be in the case of a kṣatriya? This is ever certain: let him take from those who have more, and let him in no way sink into ruin.
The kṣatriya is known as both the slayer and the protector of the people; therefore, while guarding them, the kinsman of the warrior-order must take what is needful.
Apart from doing harm, O king, there is no livelihood here for anyone—not even for the lone sage who roams and subsists upon what springs up in the forest.
One cannot live by adopting the way of life laid down by Śaṅkha and Likhita—least of all, O best of the Kurus, by one who desires to protect the people.
In time of calamity, mutual protection must always be practiced here between the king and the kingdom: this is the eternal dharma.
As the king in times of distress guards the kingdom with his abundant wealth, so too, when calamity strikes, must the king be protected by the kingdom.
When his kingdom is overtaken by famine, the king should not hold back his treasury, his army of punishment, his forces, his allies, or whatever else he has stored up.
Those who know dharma understand that the seed-grain must be procured through devoted service; and here they cite the teaching of Śambara, the master of great illusions.
Shame upon the life of that king in whose realm even the lowest of men perishes for lack of livelihood—he who has truly heeded the words of Śibi.

The king's foundation is the strength of his treasury; and the treasury, in turn, is the root of his army; that army is the root of all observances of dharma; and the people, in turn, are the root of dharma itself.
Without pressing upon others here, no treasury can be amassed—and whence then an army? Yet one who presses upon them for this purpose ought to incur no fault.
Even what ought not to be done is done for the sake of sacrifice in the rites of sacrifice; for this same reason the king ought to incur no fault.

One thing serves a worthy end; another, contrary to it, serves no worthy end; yet another serves a positively harmful end—all of these, indeed, bear the mark of purpose. Thus with his intellect should the wise man clearly discern what action to resolve upon.
One thing serves the purpose of sacrifice; in another there is no purpose for the sacrifice; yet another serves the very means of the sacrifice—all of these are instruments of sacrifice.
Here I shall set forth a comparison that illumines the truth of dharma: men fell a tree to make the sacrificial post; and those trees that stand in the way—
—certain trees standing close beside it they surely cut down as well; and these, in falling, strike down still other forest trees.
Just so, O scorcher of foes, those men who stand in the way of a great treasury—without striking them down I see no success to be had in this matter.
By wealth one wins both worlds, the world beyond and this one here; and it is a true word of dharma that the man without wealth is as though he were not at all.
By every means let him take wealth for the purpose of sacrifice; the fault is not the same, O Bhārata, in things to be done and things not to be done.
These two, O king, can in no way coexist, O Bhārata; for nowhere in the forests do I ever see men grown rich.
Whatever wealth is seen here upon the earth, this man hankers after it, thinking, 'This should be mine, this should be mine.'
There is no dharma equal to kingship, O scorcher of foes; the wise commend kingship as the dharma of kings—save where calamity dictates otherwise than this.
Some amass their hoards of wealth by giving and by ritual works, the ascetics by austerity, and yet others by intellect and skill.

They call the man without wealth weak; through wealth a man grows strong. All things are attainable by the wealthy; the man with a treasury crosses every difficulty. From the treasury flow dharma and desire, the world beyond and this world too.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: For a king grown weak, slow to act, tender-hearted toward his kinsmen, whose townsfolk and countryfolk have turned against him, and whose stores of wealth are gone—
—whose chief ministers are suspect, O Bhārata, whose counsel has leaked out, who can win no allies, and whose counselors are wholly divided—
—assailed by an enemy host, weak before a stronger foe, his mind sunk in calamity: tell me, what course of action yet remains?
Bhīṣma said: If the would-be conqueror be an outside foe, skilled in dharma and statecraft and pure of conduct, let the king swiftly make peace with him, releasing his prisoners one after another.
But if the would-be conqueror be a man of unrighteous aims, strong and set upon wickedness, then by restraining himself the king should bind that one to a treaty.
Or else, abandoning his capital, he may cross over the calamity by some other means; for whether it endures or passes, he, while yet alive, may earn his wealth anew.
As for those calamities that can be crossed by mere renunciation of possessions—what man who knows wealth and dharma would there cast away his own self, which is worth more?
Let him shrink from being made captive; what pity is there for a rival's wealth? Yet so long as it can be avoided, the self must in no way be surrendered.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When the inner realm is in revolt and the outer is hard-pressed, when the treasury is drained and the counsel has leaked away—what course of action yet remains?
Bhīṣma said: Let him swiftly seek peace, or else be swiftly fierce in valor; or let him swiftly withdraw his footing—this much is the wisdom for the hour of crisis.
With an army that is devoted, well-nourished, and high in spirit, O lord of the earth, a king conquers the world even with but a small force.
Slain, he ascends to heaven; victorious, he dwells upon the earth; but he who lays down his life in battle attains to the same world as Indra.
Having gauged the temper of all the people and chosen the path of gentleness, the king should, to win their trust, conduct himself with humility, or else resolve to put on his marching sandals.
Or, should he wish to withdraw, let him conciliate as he pleases; and having gone in disguise with an ally, let him then himself set out to act.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When the highest dharma has decayed and lawlessness oversteps all the world, when every means of livelihood upon the earth has fallen prey to robbers—
—by what means, O grandfather, is a brāhmaṇa to live in such a time, when the basest of ages has come, without abandoning, out of tenderness, his sons and grandsons?
Bhīṣma said: When such a time has come, one must live by relying upon the power of discernment. All of this is for a good end; nothing of it is for an ill end.
He who takes from the wicked and bestows upon the good, making of himself a bridge between them—he indeed is one who knows dharma entire.
With righteous indignation, O king, not disturbing the stability of his own rule, he may take even what was not given, holding the giver's wealth to be his own.
Of one who, purified by the power of discernment, moves even among censured deeds—steadfast, accomplished in conduct and discernment—who is fit to say anything against him?
Those whose livelihood is wrought by strength take pleasure in no other; they grow ever greater through their splendor, the mighty ones, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Whatever ordinary teaching is grasped without discrimination, that the middling sort follow; but the wise man pursues, beyond it, the higher truth.
His officiating priests, his household priest, his teachers—the honored brāhmaṇas worshiped with due rites—the king should not harass; harassing them, he incurs grievous faults.
These are the standard for the world, these the eternal eye; taking them for his measure, let the king plumb the matter, and by them judge it good or ill.
Many are the things that village-dwellers say against one another in anger; on the strength of their words the king should neither honor a man nor punish him.
Slander should never be spoken, nor in any way listened to; rather, one should stop one's ears, or go away to some other place.
This is not the conduct of the good—neither slander nor talebearing; the good, O Yudhiṣṭhira, speak only of the virtues that are in the good.

As two trained oxen, evenly yoked, well-broken and drawing true, take up the yoke and bear it, so should the king conduct himself; and as his helpers bear their share, so let the others bear theirs likewise.

Some hold right conduct to be the weightier mark of dharma; others, who delight in the way of Śaṅkha and Likhita, do not think so. Whether out of softness or out of greed, those latter would speak words of this kind.
In this they see even sage-given authority for sustaining the man who strays into forbidden deeds; and nowhere is any standard found equal to that of the sages.
Even the gods chastise the basest of men who persists in forbidden deeds; for one who gains wealth by deceit falls away from dharma.
That dharma which is honored on every side by the good, who are the source and cause of prosperity, and which is sanctioned by one's own heart—upon that let a man resolve.
He who knows dharma endowed with its fourfold quality is the true knower of dharma; for the track of dharma, like that of a snake, is hard to trace out.
As the hunter follows the trail of a wounded deer through the thicket by the falling of its blood, so should one follow out the track of dharma.
Thus, O unfaltering one, must one walk by the path made smooth by the good; understand this to be the conduct of royal sages, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Bhīṣma said: From his own realm and from the realm of his foe the king should raise his treasury; for from the treasury, O son of Kuntī, dharma, whose root is kingship, proceeds.
Therefore let him raise a treasury, and having gathered it, let him guard it; and having guarded it, let him be gracious with it: this is the eternal dharma.
A treasury arises neither through utter purity nor through cruelty; taking his stand upon the middle ground, the king should pursue the gathering of his treasury.
Whence a treasury for the weak? And whence strength for him who has no treasury? Whence a kingdom for the weak? And whence prosperity for one who is no king?
For one of high station the loss of fortune is as death itself; therefore let the king ever increase his treasury, his forces, and his allies.
Men despise a king whose treasury is depleted; they are not content with little from him, yet they grow bold to press their demands.
It is by reason of his fortune that a king receives the highest honor; and that fortune conceals his faults, as a garment conceals the secret parts of a woman.

The very people he once wronged now court his prosperity, yet he finds them ever like jackals, as though bent on his destruction. Whence, O best of the Bharatas, can there be happiness for such a king?
Let him strive on and never grow weary, for exertion itself is manliness; he would sooner break, even where there is no joint to break, than bend before anyone here.

He may even take refuge in the forest and roam with bands of brigands, yet he should not consort with brigands who have cast off all restraint; for an army of brigands, O Bhārata, is easily had for deeds of terror.
From one who is utterly without restraint all people recoil; even brigands grow wary of those who act without any mercy.
Let him therefore establish a restraint that gladdens the hearts of the people; for even a little restraint is honored here in the world.
The man who has concluded, 'There is neither this world nor the next,' is not one in whom trust can ever be placed; for in a nihilist, fearful and suspicious, no confidence can rest.
As the seizure of others' goods is forsworn by the good, so is harm forsworn by robbers who keep within bounds; and living beings come to love even bandits who observe their proper limits.

The slaying of one who does not fight, the violation of women, ingratitude, the seizing of a Brahmin's wealth, leaving nothing behind, the carrying off of a woman, and ambush by lying in wait—these are reckoned shameful even among robbers.

Even one who shuns these deeds remains a robber still; yet those who do not aim at another's utter ruin, O Bhārata, who, even when they have a victim wholly in their power, resolve not to strip him bare—such are of firm purpose.
Therefore even robbers, when a man lies wholly in their power, should leave him something; one should not, thinking 'I stand in strength,' commit acts of cruelty.
Those who leave a remnant, my son, see a remnant left for themselves on every side; but for those who leave nothing, there is ever fear arising from that very leaving of nothing.

Bhīṣma said: On this matter those versed in old lore recite a saying about the outcome of works: for the discerning Kṣatriya, dharma and artha are alike things directly perceived; therein no obstruction should be raised, for the deferring of dharma to an unseen world is a thing remote.
Calling unrighteousness righteousness is like a wolf's footprint; for no one here has ever clearly seen the fruit of righteousness and unrighteousness laid plain.
Let a man wish only to be strong, for all things lie within the strong man's sway; it is the strong who in this world wins prosperity, power, and ministers.
He who is without wealth is as one fallen; the little that is his is but leavings. Much that would be unwholesome in another is no harm in the strong man, and nothing can save the weak from his fear.
Both have their rightful claim in truth, and both deliver from great fear; yet I hold strength to be above dharma, for from strength does dharma proceed.
Dharma rests upon strength as all that moves rests upon the earth; as smoke follows the wind into its sway, so dharma follows strength.

In one who lacks the strength to rule, dharma clings to strength as a creeper to a tree; dharma is subject to the mighty as pleasure to those who possess the means of enjoyment. Nothing is unattainable to the mighty; to the mighty all things are pure.
A man of evil conduct whose strength is spent must keep within bounds; and even then the whole world shrinks from him as from a wolf.
Cast down and despised, he lives his life in misery; and a life that is degraded is no better than death itself.
When men say of him that he is ruined by his wicked conduct, he is sorely tormented, pierced through by that arrow of their words.
Here the teachers declare this concerning deliverance from sin: let him devote himself to the threefold Veda and wait upon the twice-born.
Let him win their favor by gentle speech and by deeds as well; let him be high-minded, and let him marry into a great house.
Let him say, 'Thus and thus am I,' while proclaiming the virtues of others; let him recite his prayers, be devoted to ablutions, gracious in bearing, and sparing of speech.
Having performed much that is hard to do, let him enter into the company of Brahmin and Kṣatriya, untroubled though men speak much of this thing and that against him.

Sinless in such conduct, he soon comes to be held in high esteem; he may enjoy ease and wealth, and by this manner of life he safeguards himself; in this world he gains honor, and in the next a great reward.
Bhīṣma said: On this point too they tell an ancient tale, of how a robber who kept within proper bounds was not lost in the world beyond death.
He was a fierce striker, wise, valiant, learned, free from cruelty, a guardian of the imperishable dharma, devoted to the Brahmins and a worshipper of his elders.
Born of a Niṣāda woman by a Kṣatriya, upholding the duty of the warrior, a Naiṣādi named Kāpavya attained perfection even through the calling of a robber.
At dusk and in the early forenoon he roamed the forest, rousing the herds of deer, skilled in the ways of every kind of game and learned in the watering-pools.
Knowing all the forest tracts, ever ranging the Pāriyātra range, versed in the dharma of all beings, his arrows never failing, firm of weapon.
Single-handed he overcame armies many hundreds strong; and his aged, blind parents he honored there in the great forest.
With honey and flesh, with roots and fruits and food both fine and coarse, he honored and fed them, and waited upon them well.
Protecting the forest-dwelling Brahmins who had renounced the world, he slew deer for them and brought the game to them in the great wood.
Those who would not accept it, fearing to take a robber's food, he would leave it within their dwellings and depart at the break of day.
Him many thousands of robbers, lawless and pitiless in their deeds, chose to be their chieftain.
The robbers said: O knower of the hour, the place, and the time, wise one, steadfast in conduct and firm of weapon, be our headman, our chief, approved by all of us.
Whatever you bid us, that shall we do; protect us according to what is right, as a mother, as a father would.
Kāpavya said: Slay not a timid woman, nor a child, nor an ascetic; one who does not fight must not be killed, and women must not be seized by force.
By a man who fights with any creature whatsoever, a woman must never be slain; ever should welfare be wished to cow and Brahmin, and for their sake should one do battle.
The standing grain must not be destroyed, nor the work of the plough hindered, for by it the gods, the ancestors, and guests are honored.
Among all beings the Brahmin deserves to go unharmed; and to them such reverence must be shown as may cost even all one possesses.
He against whose downfall these, enraged, take counsel—for him there is no protector in any of the three worlds.
Whoever would scorn the Brahmins or wish their destruction—his own ruin is as sure and as certain as the rising of the sun.
Abiding here, let our band look for its due to the full of its power, and march against all who will not yield us our portion.
Punishment is ordained for correction, not for slaughter—so it is determined; yet for those who oppress the well-behaved, their killing is held to be a duty.
Those who make their living by the harassing of the realm are destroyed by that very thing, as worms perish along with the carcass they consume.
But those robbers who live here according to the law of dharma—even they, though robbers, may swiftly attain perfection.
Bhīṣma said: All this they performed, the teaching of Kāpavya; they all gained their livelihood and turned away from their evil deeds.
By that work Kāpavya attained a great perfection, securing the welfare of the good and turning the robbers from their sins.
Whoever shall ever recite this deed of Kāpavya, from the creatures of the wild he shall meet no fear at any time.
No fear has he from mortals, nor in any way from immortals, neither from the good nor from the wicked, O king; for he is a lord and guardian in the forests.
Bhīṣma said: On this matter those versed in old lore recite the verses sung by Brahmā, telling by what path kings should raise up their treasury.
The wealth of those given to sacrifice may not be taken, for it is the gods' own; it is only from robbers and from men who perform no sacred rites that the Kṣatriya may rightly take.
These subjects, O Bhārata, are for the Kṣatriyas both to be protected and to be drawn upon; for there is no other source of wealth for the Kṣatriya here.
Let his wealth be either for the sake of his strength or for the sake of sacrifice; for men cut down plants that cannot be eaten and cook from them only what is fit to be enjoyed.
He who honors neither the gods, nor the ancestors, nor mortals with oblation—such a man's wealth those who know the Veda call a wealth that serves no end.
That wealth a righteous lord of the earth may take, O king; for such treasure gives no joy to the worlds, and a king should not keep a hoard of that kind.
He who takes from the wicked and bestows upon the good, making of himself a bridge between them—him I deem one who truly knows dharma.
As certain creatures that spring from the ground, whether endowed with speech or not, come into being unsought, so does the man who offers no sacrifice spread his line.
Just as is the manner of being of gadflies and gnats, of egg-laying ants and the like, such is the lot of those who do not sacrifice; and accordingly is dharma ordained for them.
For just as dust, grass, and chaff arise of themselves upon the ground, so here may dharma be subtle, and subtler yet.
Bhīṣma said: And on this very matter hear, with untroubled mind, this most excellent tale that bears upon the procrastinator and the determining of what should and should not be done.
In a pool of water neither too deep nor too shallow, abounding in fish, O son of Kuntī, three friendly śakula-fish were companions together.
Of these three water-dwellers, one was Knower-of-the-Right-Moment, another Far-Sighted, and the third was Procrastinator.
Once the fishermen began on every side to drain that pool away through various channels into the lower hollows.
Perceiving the pool dwindling and the danger drawing near, Far-Sighted then spoke to his two friends:
This calamity has fallen upon all that dwell in the water; let us go swiftly elsewhere, while yet the way is not ruined.
He who by sound counsel wards off a misfortune not yet come falls into no peril; let it please you both—let us go.
But Procrastinator, who was there, said: It is well spoken; yet no haste need be made just yet—such is my settled mind.
Then Knower-of-the-Right-Moment said to Far-Sighted: When the time comes, nothing fitting shall be neglected by me.
Thus addressed, Far-Sighted of great wisdom set forth, and by one of the channels he made his way to a deep reservoir of water.
Then, seeing that the basin's water had drained away, those who lived by fishing snared the fish by various devices.
As that basin, its water run out, was churned and stirred, Procrastinator with the rest was caught.
But Knower-of-the-Right-Moment, seeing the fish being strung up on cords, slipped in among the others and swallowed the line.
Holding the swallowed line within him, he remained just so; and there the fishermen took them all to be strung together upon it.
Then, as the fish were being rinsed in clear water, Knower-of-the-Right-Moment let go the cord and swiftly won his freedom.
But Procrastinator, dull of spirit, of feeble wit and senseless, met his death, a fool whose faculties were already as good as struck dead.
So he who through folly fails to recognize the moment fully come perishes swiftly, like the fish Procrastinator.
The man who at the outset does not do what is best, thinking 'I am skilled enough,' falls into peril—as did Knower-of-the-Right-Moment.
But the man who makes fit provision for what has not yet come attains exceeding good fortune—as did that Far-Sighted one.
Moments and instants and watches, days and hours, kṣaṇas and lavas, fortnights and months and seasons, and like measures the years—
The earth is called 'place'; but Time is not to be seen with the eye—it is rather that which, by right means, serves for the achievement of the end desired.
These two, place and time, in the treatises on dharma and artha and in the treatises on liberation, the seers have pointed out as foremost, dear to men who are masters of their desires.
The disciplined man who acts after due examination should rightly bring together the place and the time he intends, and by these two he shall win the fruit he seeks.

Yudhiṣṭhira said: In every case you have declared intelligence the best, O bull of the Bhāratas—the foresight that reaches what is yet to come, and that which meets what has arisen; while the procrastinating mind is the bringer of ruin.
This I wish to hear, O best of the Bharatas: that supreme wisdom by which a king, though surrounded by enemies, would not lose his way.
O you who are skilled in dharma and statecraft, wise one, master of all the śāstras, I ask you, best of the Kurus; you ought to expound this to me.
How a king beset by many foes should conduct himself—this I wish to hear, all of it, in proper order.
For when a king stands in difficult straits, his hostile enemies—many against one—strive to root him out, inflamed by earlier injuries.
Pressed on every side, weak against the mighty, alone and without help—how could such a one possibly hold his ground?
How, O bull of the Bharatas, should he tell friend from foe, and how should he act in the space between an enemy and a friend?
When, O king, an enemy of well-known character turns to friendship, what should a man do, and by doing what would he be at ease?
With whom should he make war, and with whom should he forge a treaty, and how should one without strength conduct himself when set in the midst of enemies?
This, O scorcher of foes, is the highest of all matters of action; yet there is none who can speak of it, and one who can grasp it is hard indeed to find.
None save Bhīṣma, son of Śaṃtanu, true to his word and master of his senses—so search it out, O mighty-armed one, and tell me all of this.
Bhīṣma said: This follow-up question befits you, Yudhiṣṭhira, and is rich in merit. Hear from me in full, my son, the secret to be observed in times of distress, O descendant of Bharata.
An enemy turns into a friend, and a friend too turns hostile, according as interests align; for the course of things forever follows that course.
Therefore one should both place trust and wage war, having weighed place and time in deciding what is to be done and what is not.

The wise who seek their own good should always be ready both to make peace and to take resolute action; even with enemies one may make a treaty, and one's life must be guarded, O descendant of Bharata.
For the foolish man who would never make terms with his enemies gains no advantage whatsoever, nor any fruit, O descendant of Bharata.
But he who makes a pact with an enemy and breaks with a friend, looking to where his interest lies, wins a very great reward.
On this they relate an ancient tale, the dialogue of a cat and a mouse upon a banyan tree.
In a certain great forest there stood a mighty banyan, screened by a network of creepers and thronged with flocks of many kinds of birds.
Broad of trunk, like a cloud in mass, cool of shade and lovely, the tree had grown up near a wilderness and was haunted by beasts of prey.
Sheltering at its root, having made himself a burrow with a hundred mouths, there dwelt a very wise mouse named Palita.
And taking to its branches there dwelt at ease above a cat named Lomaśa, a destroyer of birds and other creatures.
Now there came a hunter who had made his dwelling in that wilderness, and every day, when the sun had set, he would set his snare.
Having laid out his nooses of sinew duly there, he would go home and sleep at ease while the night wore on toward dawn.
There every night beasts of many kinds were caught; and once the cat, careful though he was, was nonetheless ensnared.
When that enemy, his perpetual would-be slayer, was thus bound, the very wise Palita, recognizing the moment, roamed about quite free of fear.
As he ranged through that forest, moving in confidence and questing for food, before long he caught sight of a piece of meat.
Climbing up onto the very snare, he began to eat that meat, laughing in his heart at his rival caught above him.
But while he was intent upon the meat, glancing about at one point he saw another, fearsome enemy of his drawing near.
It was a mongoose named Harika—the color of an arrow's reed-blossom, a dweller in burrows of the earth, quick-moving and copper-eyed.
Drawn in haste by the scent of the mouse, it had come up eager to feed, licking its mouth and standing on the ground with face upturned.
And on a branch he saw yet another foe, lodged in a hollow—an owl named Candraka, sharp of beak and a prowler of the night.
Having come within reach of both the mongoose and the owl, and seized then by very great fear, this thought arose in him:
"In this most grievous calamity, with death close at hand and terror sprung up on every side—how is one who seeks his own welfare to act?"
Thus blocked on all sides, seeing danger alike in every quarter, he was tormented by fear, and he resolved upon this supreme course.
"This calamity is all but ruin, and life hangs on the slimmest chance; perilous on every side, this distress has come upon me."
"If I dart down to the ground, the mongoose will have me; the owl, if I stay here; and the cat, once free of the snare."
"Yet a wise one such as I ought not give way to confusion. I will strive for my life so long as I can hold my breath."
"For the wise, endowed with understanding and versed in the science of policy, do not lose their heads on meeting calamity, or even on gaining great fortunes."
"Yet at this moment I see no refuge here other than the cat; for this creature too stands in difficulty, and he has great need of me."
"How, desiring to live, am I today hunted by three enemies? Therefore I shall take refuge with this very foe, the cat."
"Resorting to the lore of statecraft, I shall point out what is for his good, by which means I may, through deliberate cunning, baffle this assembly of enemies."
"This utter enemy of mine has fallen into the gravest of straits; he is bewildered—if by circumstance he can be made to grasp his own interest..."
"...then, having met with disaster, he may make a treaty with me. The teachers say that even the embrace of a powerful enemy who has come close should be made by one in difficulty who longs to live."
"For a wise enemy is better than a foolish friend; indeed, my very life now rests upon my enemy, the cat."
"Come, I shall lay before him a reason touching his own preservation; perhaps now, through these circumstances, this enemy may turn prudent."
Then the mouse, who knew the true course of interests and the seasons for peace and for war, addressed the cat with these conciliatory words:
"In friendship I speak to you, O cat. Are you still alive? I do desire your life, for our welfare lies in common."
"You need not despair, good friend; you shall live as before. I will deliver you—indeed I would lay down my own life for your sake."
"There is, it seems to me, a sound and ample means by which you may win your release, just as I may win my safety."
"I have hit upon this device, having reasoned it through in my own mind, for my sake and for yours alike; for our good is shared."
"This mongoose and this owl, malicious of mind, stand near me on either side. So long, O cat, as one does not assail me, I am for the moment safe."
"Hooting, with restless eyes, this owl is watching me from where it perches on a branch of the tree; of it I am sorely afraid."
"Among the good, friendship is sealed by seven steps together; you are my fellow-dweller and a wise one. I will make a true companionship of it—you have no cause to fear death."
"For you, O cat, cannot cut the noose without me. I will cut your noose, if you do not harm me."
"You dwell in the tree's crown, and I at its root. The two of us have long lived here in this very tree, as you well know."
"One who trusts no one at all, and one in whom no one ever trusts—the wise praise neither, for both are forever uneasy of heart."
"Therefore let our friendship grow, and let there be a true union between us; for the wise do not commend an act that is purposeless and let slip its proper time."
"Mark, then, this reasoning of interest just as it stands: I desire your life, and you desire mine."
"A man crosses a deep, great river by means of a log; he carries the log across, and he in turn is carried across by the log."
"Such will be our compact, and it shall carry us safely through: I will bring you across, and you will bring me across."
Having spoken thus to that end, for the good of both, Palita—his argument cogent and fit to be accepted—bided his time and watched.
Then, hearing his well-spoken words, the cat, his discerning enemy, made this reply—reasoned and worthy of acceptance:
Intelligent and gifted in speech, dwelling on those words and looking to his own desperate plight, he received them graciously, with conciliation alone.
Then the cat Lomaśa, his teeth keen at the tips and his eyes like beryl gems, gazed gently down at the mouse and said:
"I rejoice, good friend—blessings on you—that you wish me to live. And if you know the way to our good, let it be done; do not hesitate."
"For I am sorely fallen into distress, and you are in even worse straits than I. Let a treaty be made between the two of us in distress; do not hesitate."
"Do what the moment demands, and let our undertaking succeed for us both. Once I am freed from this peril, your good deed shall not be lost."
"My pride is laid aside; I am devoted to you, your disciple, a doer of your bidding, obedient to your command; I have come to you for refuge."
Thus addressed, Palito spoke this salutary word to the cat, now brought under his sway—a word fitly framed and full of meaning:
"Noble is what you have said—no wonder in one like you. But hear from me the course I have in mind for our good."
"I will creep up close beneath you. From the mongoose comes my great fear. Protect me and do not slay me—I am able to win you your release."
"From the owl as well guard me, for the vile thing covets me. I will cut your nooses, friend—I swear it to you in truth."
Hearing that speech, coherent and fitting and full of sense, Lomaśa looked up at Palita in joy and welcomed him warmly.
Having honored Palita, the cat, now set upon friendship, the steady one, after careful thought, spoke—glad, and indeed in haste:
"Come quickly—blessings on you—you are a friend dear to me as life itself. For by your favor, wise one, I shall swiftly regain my life."
"Whatever I, in this plight, am able to do for you today, command it, and I will do it. Let there be a treaty between us, my friend."
"Once freed by you from this peril, together with my friends and kin, I will do all your bidding, whatever pleases you and serves your good."
"And once delivered from this disaster, good friend, may I too kindle your affection, and may I be able to repay you."
Having made the cat grasp where his own interest lay, the mouse then crept up in full confidence and conducted the business aright.
Thus reassured by the cat, that learned mouse slept trustingly upon the cat's breast, as upon a father's or a mother's.
But seeing the mouse clinging to the cat's body, the mongoose and the owl, their hopes dashed, went off to their lairs.
Clinging to the cat's body, the grey-furred one, knowing place and time and awaiting the right moment, began to gnaw through the snares, O king, slowly, ever so slowly.
Then the cat, tormented by his bonds, watching the mouse cutting away at the snares without haste, grew anxious and impatient.
And so the cat began to urge on the grey one, the mouse, who was taking his time in cutting through the snares.
"Why, good friend, do you not hasten? Now that your end is gained, do you make light of me? Cut the snares, O slayer of foes, before the dog-cooking outcast comes!"
Thus pressed to hurry by that one, the wise grey mouse spoke to the cat, whose understanding had not ripened—words measured and serving his own good:
"Be still, good friend; you need not rush, you need not be flustered. It is I here who know the moment, and the right moment shall not be let slip.
A deed begun out of season serves no purpose when done; that very deed begun in season serves a great purpose.
Were I to free you out of season, from you alone would danger come to me. Therefore wait for the moment—why do you hurry so, my friend?
When I see the outcast approaching, weapon in hand, then—the danger now being common to us both—I will cut your snare.
Freed at that instant, you will climb straight up the tree; for then you will have no concern at all save saving your life.
Then, once you have fled away, terrified and frightened, O shaggy one, I shall slip into my burrow while you make for a branch.
Thus addressed by the mouse with words serving his own good, the cat—shrewd, well-versed in the meaning of speech, and clinging to life—replied:
Pressed by his own need, the shaggy one, behaving now with all due deference, spoke to the slow-acting mouse:
"This is not how the good do a friend's work out of affection—not the way I, in my haste, delivered you from peril.
In that same haste you should do me good in turn. Make the effort, O most wise one, that all may be well with us both.
Or is it that, remembering our old enmity, you are dragging out the time? Consider how wrongful such conduct would be: plainly, my life would be cut short.
Whatever offense I once did you in my ignorance, that you should not hold in your heart. I beg your pardon—be gracious to me."
To the cat speaking thus, the mouse—wise, learned in the treatises, and esteemed for his intelligence—then spoke these excellent words:
"I have heard you, O cat, looking to your own interest; now understand me too, looking to mine.
A friend to be won over as though one were afraid, a friend bound up with danger—from such a one the hand must be well guarded, as from a serpent's mouth.
He who, having made a pact with a stronger power, does not guard himself—that pact, like unwholesome food eaten, turns to his ruin.
No one is anyone's friend, no one anyone's well-wisher; interests are bound to interests as wild elephants are bound by tame elephants.
For once a task is done, no one regards the doer of it; therefore one should have all one's tasks carried out with something still left undone.
And even at that moment you, gripped by terror of the outcast, will be intent on flight and unable to seize me.
The mass of strands is cut through; one strand alone remains. That too I shall cut at once—be at ease, O shaggy one.
As the two of them conversed thus, each still caught in his plight, the night wore to its close, and fear came over the shaggy one.
Then, as dawn came on, there appeared a misshapen man, dark-tawny, broad of haunch, wild-haired and harsh, ringed about by a pack of dogs—
spike-eared, huge-mouthed, grizzled, fearful to look upon, an outcast named Parigha, weapon in hand, came into view.
Seeing him, like a messenger of Yama, the cat, his wits unstrung with terror, said in fear to the grey one: "What will you do now?"
And the mongoose and the owl too, sorely frightened at the sight of that terrible figure, in an instant gave up all hope.
Strong and clever, and now allied together, the two—because of the mouse's good policy—could not be overpowered by force.
Seeing the cat and mouse, who had made their pact for a purpose, the owl and the mongoose hastened off, each to his own dwelling.
Then the mouse cut through that last strand of the cat's, and the cat, set free, sprang up that very tree.
And the grey one, released from that danger and from his dreaded foe, entered his burrow, while the shaggy cat took to a branch.
The outcast, taking up his trap and looking all about, his hopes ruined, in a moment withdrew from that place and went home, O bull of the Bharatas.
Then, released from that danger and his hard-won life regained, the shaggy one, perched at the treetop, spoke to the grey one in his burrow:
"Without making any agreement, I came to you suddenly in my distress. Grateful as I am, and after the good I have done you—surely you do not now distrust me?
Having won my trust and granted me my life, why is it that, now the time has come to enjoy a friend, you do not come near me?
He who first makes friends but afterward does not keep faith with them—that fool wins no friends in times of hardship and calamity.
Now I have been made your friend by your own power, comrade; having gained me as a friend, you ought to enjoy my fellowship.
All the friends I have and all my kinsmen will honor you, as pupils honor a beloved teacher.
And I myself will honor you, together with all your band of friends and kin. What grateful soul would not honor the giver of his life?
Be the lord over me, over my body and my house and all my goods; be my guide and director.
Be my counselor, O wise one, and rule me as a father does; you have no cause to fear me—by my own life I swear it."
"In intellect you are Uśanas himself; in strength, it is we who hold command. Endowed with your counsel and our might, one would surely win victory."
Thus soothed with the utmost conciliation by the cat, the mouse, who knew where his true good lay, spoke smooth words serving his own welfare:
"All that you have said I have heard, O shaggy one; now hear me too as I speak, and what seems true to me.
Friends must be discerned, and enemies likewise understood. This is seen to be a most subtle matter in this world, one the wise hold in regard.
There are well-wishers in the guise of foes, and foes in the guise of friends; men beguiled by their soothing do not see through them, fallen under the sway of passion and greed.
There is no such thing as an enemy by birth, nor any friend by birth; it is through the workings of interest that friends are made, and foes as well.
As long as a man sees his own advantage in another's living, so long does that other thrive; and so long is he that man's friend—until the reverse becomes true.
There is no such thing as a stable friendship, nor any fixed enmity; for it is by the working of interest that friends arise, and foes likewise.
A friend turns to an enemy in some turn of time, and an enemy turns to a friend; for self-interest is the stronger force.
He who trusts in friends and does not trust in foes, not understanding how interest works—his life is unsteady.
He who, not understanding how interest works, sets his mind on what seems fair—whether in a friend or in a foe—his judgment too is unsteady.
One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor even the trustworthy trust too far; danger born of misplaced trust cuts away one's very roots.
For it is through the working of interest that one finds a father, a mother, sons, maternal uncles, nephews, and kindred and relations alike.
Mother and father will forsake even a beloved son who has fallen, and the world looks after its own self—behold the sovereignty of self-interest.
I hold him to be of a treacherous mind who, the very instant after his release, seeks to do a deed by easy means—of this there is no doubt.
Brought down to this very dwelling-place from the banyan, you, in your rashness, did not notice the trap set out before you.
A reckless one is no good even to himself—how then could he be to others? Therefore the reckless man ruins all his undertakings, beyond doubt.
You say something sweet—"You are dear to me here." That is all a making of falsehood; hear me out upon it in full.
From a cause one becomes dear; from a cause one becomes hateful. This world of the living seeks its own gain; no one is dear to anyone.
The fellowship of brothers born of one womb, or of husband and wife with each other—nowhere here do I recognize any affection without a cause.
Even if brothers grow angry, or a wife, in some other matter, they hold affection by their very nature; no other person holds it so.
One man becomes dear by gifts, another by pleasant speech, another by spells, oblations, and muttered prayers; man holds affection for the sake of his own ends.
Affection between us arose when a cause arose; in some other matter there is none, and when the ground of that cause is destroyed, that affection turns away.
What cause, then, can I suppose makes me dear to you—other than as something to be eaten? And of that too I am well aware.
Time fashions the occasion, and self-interest follows after it; the wise man discerns his own interest, and the world follows the wise.
But you should not speak in this fashion to one who knows, one learned in his own interest. Out of season and standing in no peril, this talk of yours is only for your own ends.
Therefore I shall not stray from my own interest, standing firm in the matter of peace and war; for like the shapes of clouds, alliances alter from moment to moment.
This very day an enemy, then this very day a friend, and again this very day an enemy—behold the fickleness of expedients.
There was friendship between us only so long as the cause existed before; it has departed together with that very cause, which was bound to the moment.
For you are utterly my enemy, who by force of circumstance became my friend. That business is now accomplished, and your nature has returned to enmity.
Knowing as I do, in their truth, the treatises laid down in this wise—how should I enter a snare of your making? Tell me that.
By your strength I was set free, and by my strength were you; the mutual favor being now rendered, there is no further coming together.
For you, good friend, have today gained your end, and we too have accomplished ours; you have no further use for me—save to make a meal of me.
I am the food and you the eater; I am weak and you are strong. No pact can hold between us two, since our strengths are so unequal.
I take the measure of your wisdom: that the very instant after your release you are surely seeking your prey by easy means—of this there is no doubt."
It was for the sake of food that you were bound, and once freed you came forth driven by hunger; surely, having outwitted one who knows the treatises, you mean to devour me this very day.
I know that you are hungry, and that this is your hour to feed; and so, having deceived me, you are hunting once more for your prey.
And as for your offering up your own children and wife to me, professing to render me service—friend, that is not a thing I can permit.
Seeing me in your company, why would your beloved wife and your sons, devoted and fond of you, not eat me up with delight?
I will not join with you; the reason for our union has passed. Wish me well from where you stand, if the good deed I did is remembered.
What wise creature, being fit to be the food of a foe who is afflicted and famished and on the prowl for prey, would walk into his reach?
May it be well with you—I shall go; even from afar I shrink from you. I will not come together with you; be at peace, O hairy one.
Nearness to the strong is never to be commended; even from one who seems calmed, O wise one, the mighty must always be feared.
But if you have need of any object, tell me—what shall I do for you? I will gladly grant you anything, but never my own self.
For one's own sake one must be ready to give up offspring, kingdom, jewels, and wealth; surrendering even all one has, a man should guard his self by his own self.
Of sovereignty, wealth, and jewels, though they pass into a rival's hands, we have seen and heard that for the living there is a getting back again.
But the surrender of the self is not, like wealth and jewels, a thing to be desired; the self must be guarded by every means—by wife and by riches alike.
For men who keep the practice of self-protection and who act only after careful scrutiny, no calamities arise that are born of their own faults.
Those weak ones who rightly understand their stronger foes—their resolve, fixed for their own sake, is never shaken.
Thus openly upbraided by Palita, the cat, grown ashamed, spoke these words to the mouse:
I honour your wisdom, for you who are devoted to my good have spoken in keeping with the truth of things, though I differ from you in view.
But you ought not, O good one, to judge me otherwise than as I am: my friendship for you arose from your having granted me my very life.
I know what is right, I know merit, and above all I am grateful; and I am tender toward friends, and toward such as you especially so.
Therefore, O good one, things being as they are, you ought not to drive me away; if driven off by you, I would give up my life, kinsmen and all.
The wise hold that a word of reproach is, for high-minded ones like me, as good as death; you who know the truth of dharma ought not to suspect me.
Being thus flattered by the cat, the mouse, weighing in his mind the cat's deep designs, spoke these words:
You are a worthy one, and I have heard your case; I am pleased, yet I do not trust. Not by praises, nor by floods of wealth, can I be won over by you again.
For the wise do not fall under a foe's power without cause, my friend; and on this matter mark the two verses composed by Uśanas:
In a task common to oneself and an enemy, having made a pact with the stronger, one should act warily and with skill; and once the end is gained, one should not trust.
Therefore in every condition one should guard one's own life; for goods and offspring and all besides belong only to the living.
The sum of the treatises on policy is held to be supreme distrust toward men; hence distrust is an abundant blessing to oneself.
The distrustful, even though weak, are not slain by their foes; but the trustful, even though strong, are swiftly slain by the weak.
From such as you, O cat, my self must always be guarded; and you too should guard your self from that low-born outcast of polluted birth.
While the mouse was speaking thus, the cat, seized with sudden dread, fled at once in haste to his own den.
Then Palita, the wise one who knew the true purport of the treatises, having proved the power of his own intelligence, betook himself to another hole.
Thus by his wise understanding the weak one outwitted the mighty; many foes were outmatched by Palita alone.
Even with a capable enemy the prudent man should make a pact; the mouse and the cat were both delivered by their mutual reliance.
Thus have I shown you at length the path of the kṣatriya's duty, O lord of earth; now hear it once more in brief.
Though they had made enmity with each other, the two formed a perfect friendship; yet the mind of each was set on outwitting the other.
In such a case the wise one prevails by relying rightly on the strength of his wit; but a wise man may be outdone, through heedlessness, even by fools.
Therefore, though fearful, let him bear himself as fearless; though distrustful, as one who trusts. For the vigilant man is not unseated, nor, once unseated, does he perish.
In season, peace even with a foe; in season, strife even with a friend—this, those who know the truth ever declare must be done, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Reflecting thus, O great king, and grasping the meaning of the treatises, let him remain intent and vigilant, and act as one afraid before danger comes.
His arrangements and his counter-arrangements alike should be made as by one in fear; for from fear arises the discernment that is born of unremitting effort.
For one who fears before danger comes, O king, no danger arises; but for the fearless, through his confidence, a very great danger is born.
Yet counsel must never be wholly withheld from a man on the grounds that he is timid; for through such a misjudgement, knowledge passes from the ignorant to those who watch for an opening.
Therefore, though afraid, bearing himself as fearless, and though distrustful, as one who trusts, let him weigh the gravity of his affairs and never practise any falsehood.
