Thus has this old tale been told by me, O Yudhiṣṭhira; having heard it, conduct yourself fittingly in the midst of your friends.
Having attained the highest wisdom, and the difference between foe and friend, and the seasons for peace and for war, and the means of deliverance in calamity—
in a task shared with an enemy, having made a pact with the stronger, let him conduct the alliance with skill, and, once his end is gained, not trust.
This policy, not at odds with the three aims of life, O Yudhiṣṭhira—rise up to it after what you have heard, and ever more bring joy to your subjects.
Let your course be taken together with the brāhmaṇas, O Pāṇḍava; for the brāhmaṇas are the highest good, in heaven and here, O Bhārata.
These are the knowers of dharma, ever grateful, O lord; honoured and pure in their deeds, they win victory beforehand, O ruler of men.
You shall gain a kingdom and the highest good, O king, and glory and renown, and the continuance of your line, each in due right and due order.

This well-spoken lesson of peace and war between two parties, O Bhārata, wrought by surpassing intelligence—having thus regarded it, a ruler of earth, O king, must ever practise it amid the circle of his foes.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The counsel has been given, O mighty-armed one—that there is no trusting in foes. But how is a king to conduct himself if he can nowhere place his confidence?
From trust, indeed, a king's greatest peril arises, O king; yet how can a king who places no trust conquer his foes, O lord of the earth?
Resolve this doubt of mine; my mind is utterly bewildered, O grandsire, having listened to this discourse on distrust.
Bhīṣma said: Hear, son of Kuntī, what passed in the dwelling of Brahmadatta—the colloquy that Brahmadatta held with Pūjanī, O son of Pṛthā.
In Kāmpilya there dwelt within the inner apartments of Brahmadatta a bird named Pūjanī, who had lived with him a long while.
She understood the cries of all creatures, like the jīvajīvaka bird; all-knowing and versed in every duty was she, though born in the brute kind.
There she gave birth to a single son of radiant lustre, and at that very same time a son was also born to the king's queen.
Going to the shore of the sea, she brought back two fruits, for the nourishment of her own son and of the king's son alike.

One fruit she gave to her own son and the other to the prince—a fruit like the taste of the nectar of immortality, increasing strength and splendour; and from eating it the prince attained the utmost growth.

Held in the nurse's hands, he would play with that bird; but one day, in a lonely place, taking up the bird that was born at the same time as himself, he killed it, O lord of kings, and then returned to the nurse's hands.
Then the bird returned, O king, bringing fruit, and beheld her son slain by that child and lying upon the ground.
Her face full of tears, wretched at seeing her son slain, Pūjanī, scorched with grief and weeping, spoke these words:
In a kṣatriya there is no fellowship, no affection, and no friendship; for a purpose they cleave to you here, and once their end is gained they cast you off.
No trust should be placed in kṣatriyas, who would destroy all alike; even after doing harm they keep soothing you forever, to no purpose.
This very day I shall take upon him a fitting vengeance in kind—upon this ingrate, this cruel one, this gross betrayer of trust.
To slay one born and reared together with you, one who ate beside you, and one who came to you for refuge—threefold is the guilt of this deed.
So saying, with both her claws she tore out the eyes of the king's son, and then, composed once more, Pūjanī spoke these words:
A sin done deliberately recoils upon its doer that very moment; for those whose deeds bring their requital, good and evil do not pass away unanswered.
If any evil deed has been done, should its fruit not be found in the doer himself, it falls upon his sons, or, failing that, upon his grandsons and their descendants.
Brahmadatta said: A wrong was indeed done by us, and requital has been done by you; the two are now made even. Dwell here, Pūjanī; do not go.
Pūjanī said: Where a wrong has once been committed, to linger on in that same place the wise do not commend; better there to slip away.
Though soothing words be employed, O king, one in whom enmity has arisen should not be trusted; the fool is swiftly destroyed, for enmity is not stilled.
Among those who have made enmity with each other, it descends upon sons and grandsons; and when sons and grandsons are destroyed, it follows them into the next world.
For all who have made enmity, distrust brings ease; in no way at all should trust be placed in a destroyer of trust.
One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor even the trusted should one trust. Let one freely inspire trust in others, but in others place no trust.

Mother and father are the best of kinsmen; a wife is but a comrade in old age; a son is no more than one's own seed; a brother is a foe; a friend has a hand that is wet only while you feast—the self alone is the knower of its own joy and sorrow.
Among those who have made enmity with each other no true peace can come about; and that reason for which I dwelt here has now passed away.
Even when a creature who has done harm before is honoured with wealth and respect, his mind remains distrustful, for the earlier wrong terrifies him by its own force.
Where there is honour at first and dishonour afterward, the man of spirit, honoured and then slighted, should abandon that dwelling.
I have dwelt in your house a long while, unharmed; now this enmity has arisen. Fare well—I take my leave.
Brahmadatta said: When one requites a deed by repaying it in kind, in that he commits no offense; thereby he is freed of his debt. Dwell here, Pūjanī; do not depart.
Pūjanī said: Between the wrong that was done and the one who did it, friendship is never knit together again; the heart there knows the truth, both of the doer and of the deed.
Brahmadatta said: Between the deed and the one who did it friendship can be knit together again; a quieting of enmity is seen, and one need not again suffer evil.
Pūjanī said: Enmity once begun is not undone. Let no one trust, thinking 'I have been appeased'; the fool is destroyed through his trust. Therefore it is better not to meet at all.
Those who cannot be subdued by force, nor even by sharp-honed weapons, are mastered by soft words, as bull-elephants are by cow-elephants.
Brahmadatta said: From living together affection arises, even among those who would end one's life, and mutual trust as well, as between the dog and the outcaste dog-cooker.
Among those who have wronged one another, the enmity, softened by their living together, does not abide, like water resting on a lotus leaf.
Pūjanī said: Enmity arises from five sources, and the wise understand this: that caused by a woman, that born of property, that born of speech, and that born of a rival's offense.
In such a case the one who inflicts the injury must be slain, especially by a kṣatriya, whether openly or in secret, after weighing place, strength, and the rest.
When enmity has been incurred, no trust should be placed even in one who seems a friend; the enmity persists concealed, like fire hidden within wood.
Not by wealth, not by harsh measures, not by soothing words, nor by learning is the fire of enmity quenched, O king, any more than the Aurva-fire is quenched in the ocean.
For the kindled fire of enmity, or a deed born of offense, does not subside, O lord of men, without burning out one side or the other; only by the destruction of one party does it cease.
Even toward one honored with gifts and respect, if he was the first to do harm, there is no real peace and no trust; the remembered deed itself drives one to fear by its force.
In no injury have I been at fault toward you, nor you toward me; through trust I dwelt here before, but now I trust no longer.
Brahmadatta said: It is by Time that every act is wrought, and likewise the manifold deeds; by Time alone do they come to pass. Who here truly offends against whom?
Both alike come to pass, death and birth as well; both are brought about by Time, and on that ground each creature lives.
Some are slain all at once, while others, one by one, are not; Time consumes living beings as fire consumes the fuel it reaches.
Neither I nor you are the true cause in the doings, good or ill, that pass between us; it is Time that forever apportions to embodied beings their joy and their sorrow.
So dwell here in affection, unharmed as long as Time allows; what was done I have forgiven; do you too forgive, Pūjanī.
Pūjanī said: If Time is your sole authority, then no one would harbor enmity at all; why then do kinsmen seek to avenge a kinsman when he is slain?
Why did the gods and the demons of old strike down one another, if it is by Time that release comes, and joy and sorrow, existence and non-existence?
Why do physicians wish to prepare medicine for the sick, if men are ripened by Time alone? What use, then, are remedies?
Why is loud lamentation made by those stunned with grief, if Time is your sole authority? And why is there any merit attaching to those who act?
Your son slew my offspring, and he was killed by me in turn; thereafter I should rightly have been seized and bound by you, O lord of the earth.
For I, in grief for my young, committed an evil deed against your son; therefore you ought to strike at me. Hear now the truth I tell.
Men desire birds either for food or for sport; no third relation is possible save killing or caging. Be patient and consider this.
Some, from fear of being killed or caged, have taken up the discipline of release; those who know dharma call the suffering born of death and calamity a grievous thing.
Dear to every being is its own life; dear to every being are its young. Everyone shrinks from sorrow; happiness is what everyone craves.
Old age is sorrow, Brahmadatta; the loss of one's wealth is sorrow; sorrow is dwelling with what one dislikes, and sorrow is the parting from what one loves.
Sorrow arises from enmity and bondage, from violence, and likewise from a woman; sorrow alternates ceaselessly with joy, turning about from person to person.
Some unwise men declare that another's sorrow is no real sorrow; but it is he who has not himself known sorrow who prattles so before a crowd.
But one who grieves, afflicted by sorrow, how could he dare to speak so? He who has tasted all sorrow feels it in another as he feels it in himself.
What I have done to you, O king, and what you have done to me, that cannot be wiped away even in a hundred years, O subduer of foes.
In what we two have done to each other no reconciliation is possible; for as you remember your son again and again, the enmity will arise anew.
He who, with enmity close at hand, wishes to make peace, can no more reunite it than the pieces of a shattered earthen pot.
Distrust, declared by those versed in the science of statecraft, yields happiness; and long ago Uśanas spoke two verses to Prahrāda.
Those who, being enemies, place their faith in a foe, whether he is truthful or untruthful, are destroyed by their trusting, as one might be by honey set among dry grass.
For enmities are not quenched in families even to the tenth generation; and there will always be those to recount them, so long as a single man of the line survives.
Kings, concealing their enmities, speak soothingly; then they crush their foe, as one dashes a brimming pot upon a stone.
Never should one trust, O king, after having wrought evil against anyone here; for having injured others, one reaps sorrow through misplaced trust.
Brahmadatta said: Through distrust men gather no wealth, nor do they strive for anything; ever in fear of one side or another, they become as good as dead.
Pūjanī said: He whose two feet here are wounded, yet who goes about upon them, sees those very feet worn raw, even though he treads with utmost care.
He who, with eyes already aching, looks straight into the wind, surely suffers a yet sharper pain from the wind within his eyes.
He who in his delusion takes to a perilous road, not knowing his own strength, finds in that the end of his life.
The man who plows his field without regard to the rains, falling short in human effort, never wins his harvest.
And he who takes wholesome food, though it be bitter or astringent and unpleasant to the taste, makes himself fit for long life and well-being.
But the man who, having eaten what is wholesome, then out of greed eats other food, heedless of the consequence, finds in that the end of his life.
Destiny and human effort both stand by mutual support; for the high-minded, action is the rule; only the feeble rely upon destiny alone.
One should perform the act conducive to one's good, whether harsh or gentle; but the man of idle habit, possessing nothing, is forever devoured by misfortunes.
Therefore, even where the outcome is in doubt, one must still exert oneself; men should accomplish what serves their own good, even at the cost of all they have.
Learning, valor, skill, strength, and steadfastness as the fifth: these the wise call one's innate friends, by which they make their way in the world.
A dwelling, household goods, a field, a wife, and friendly folk: these they call one's acquired possessions, which a man may gain anywhere.
The wise man finds delight everywhere and shines everywhere; he frightens no one, and when threatened himself, he does not fear.
For the intelligent man, wealth, however small, ever increases; through skill he accomplishes his work, and through self-restraint he stands secure.
Of men of little understanding, bound fast by attachment to home, an evil wife devours the very flesh, as a she-tiger devours cattle.
"My home, my fields, my friends, my own land": so cling some, and thus, in their perversity of mind, men sink to ruin.
From a land sick with calamity, oppressed by disease and famine, one should fly away to dwell elsewhere, or settle where one is ever held in honor.
Therefore I shall go elsewhere to dwell; I cannot bring myself to stay here. What your son has done is past all undoing, O king.
A bad wife, a bad son, a bad king, a bad friendship, a bad alliance, and a bad country: all these one should shun from afar.
In a bad friend there is no trust; in a bad wife, where is delight? In a bad realm there is no peace; in a bad country one cannot make a living.
With a bad friend, whose goodwill is ever unsteady, there is no true fellowship; in a bad alliance there comes only dishonor, and the ruin of one's interests.
She is a wife who speaks what is dear; he is a son in whom there is contentment; that is a friend in whom there is trust; that is a country where one can live.
He is a king of firm rule under whom there is no oppression; nor is that a true kinship which wishes to keep a man in poverty.
Wife, country, friends, sons, kinsmen, and relations: all of this thrives under a virtuous king whose guide is dharma.
Under one ignorant of dharma, the subjects go to their dissolution for want of restraint; the king is the root of the threefold aim, when he guards it with unflagging care.
Having levied a sixth part as tribute, he should employ that tribute well; the king who does not rightly protect his subjects is but a royal thief.
The king who, having himself granted safety, does not duly hold to that pledge, takes upon himself the sin of all the world, and, his mind set on unrighteousness, goes down to hell.
But the king who, having granted safety, ever holds firm to his pledge is to be known as the maker of all happiness, guarding his subjects by dharma.
Father, mother, teacher, protector, Fire, Vaiśravaṇa, and Yama: these seven qualities of a king did Manu, the lord of creatures, proclaim.
The king is a father to the kingdom, one who has compassion for his subjects; but when he is led astray, a man goes astray as well.
Like a mother he cherishes them, and succors the helpless; like fire he burns the wicked, and in restraining men he becomes a very Yama.
Upon the deserving he lavishes wealth, a granter of wishes like Kubera; he is a teacher through his instruction in dharma, and a protector through his guarding care.
The king who gladdens by his virtues the people of the city and the countryside does not lose his realm, for he upholds both virtue and dharma.
For the lord of earth who himself looks well into the affairs of city and countryside rejoices in happiness, in this world and the next.
That king whose subjects, ever anxious, are crushed by the burden of taxes and are stripped bare by calamities, goes to his downfall.
But that king under whom the subjects flourish, like the great lotus in a lake, shares in the fruit of every sacrifice and is honored in the world.
War with one stronger than oneself, O king, is in no way to be commended; for one at strife with a stronger foe, where is the kingdom, and where the happiness?
Bhīṣma said: Having thus spoken, the bird, taking leave of King Brahmadatta, the ruler of men, departed to the quarter she desired.
This converse of Brahmadatta with Pūjanī I have now recounted to you, O best of the Bharatas. What else do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When, through the waning of the age, dharma has dwindled away and the world too, O Bhārata, is oppressed by bandits, how should one conduct oneself, O grandsire?
Bhīṣma said: Listen, O descendant of Bharata, and I shall expound to you the polity for times of calamity—how, when the hour demands it, a king should conduct himself, even setting compassion aside.
On this they recite an ancient tale: the colloquy between Bharadvāja and the king Śatruṃtapa.
A king named Śatruṃtapa, a great chariot-warrior of the Sauvīras, approached Kaṇiṅka and asked him for a clear ruling on policy.
How is one to win what has not yet been won? By what means is the won made to grow? How should one guard what has grown, and how dispense what has been guarded?
Thus questioned for a settled ruling, the brāhmaṇa, whose own conclusions were firm, made this reasoned reply to him.
Let him keep the rod ever uplifted and his prowess ever displayed; let him be without any flaw himself yet sharp to detect flaws, and quick to seize upon the openings of his foes.
Before one whose rod is always raised the people tremble greatly; therefore by the rod alone should he hold all creatures in check.
Just so do the wise who perceive the truth give their praise; therefore, of those four expedients, the rod is declared the chief.
When the foundation is cut at the root, all who lived upon it are undone; for how should the branches stand when the great tree is severed at its root?
The wise man should first of all cut down the very root of the rival party, and thereafter pursue its allies and its whole faction without exception.
Well-counselled, well-charged, well-fought, well-fled—at the very moments when calamities arise let him so act, and not hesitate.
In speech alone let him seem all modesty, while at heart he is keen as a razor; let his words be smooth and gentle from the outset, and let him put away both lust and wrath.
In any affair that involves a rival, the discerning man, though he has made a treaty, should not trust it; rather, his purpose once accomplished, let him withdraw at once.
Wearing the guise of a friend, he should appease his enemy with conciliating words, yet shrink from him perpetually, as from a serpent that has crept into the house.
Him whose mind he would outwit, the dull-witted let him pacify with what is past or with what is yet to come; the shrewd, with what is present at hand.
Folded hands, an oath, soft words, the bowing of the head in speech, and even the shedding of tears—all this must he who desires prosperity be ready to perform.
Let him carry his foe upon his very shoulder so long as the time runs adverse; but when the hour has come, let him dash him to pieces as one shatters a pot upon a stone.
Better, O lord of kings, that a man blaze for even a single moment like a brand of tinduka wood, than that he smoulder long, flameless, like a fire of chaff.

With a useless or an ungrateful man one should not pursue a profitable end; yet so long as the gain may still be enjoyed, the ingrate may be used—for once his purpose is fulfilled, he scorns his helper. Therefore let him conduct all his affairs in such a way that something still remains undone.
Whatever is best in the cuckoo, the boar, Mount Meru, an empty house, the serpent, and the dappled deer—that let him take to himself and practise.
Rising again and again, ever attentive, let him go to the houses of his foe and inquire after his welfare, even when he wishes him ill.
The slothful do not gain their ends, nor do the weaklings, nor the overproud, nor those who dread the gossip of the world, nor those who are forever biding their time.
Let no enemy discern a flaw in him, while he discerns the flaw in the enemy; let him draw in his limbs like a tortoise and guard his own vulnerable point.
Let him plot his ends like a heron, charge like a lion, snatch like a wolf, and break away like a hare.
Drink, dice, women, the hunt, song and music—these let him enjoy with measure, for excessive attachment to them is fraught with ruin.
He may make himself a bow of straw and lie down in a deer's posture; in a time for blindness let him be blind, and may even take refuge in deafness.
Having met with the right place and the right time, let the discerning man exert his valour; for valour that has overshot place and time bears no fruit.
Weighing the seasonable and the unseasonable, his own strength and weakness, and knowing too the relative strength of the two sides, let him then direct himself accordingly.
The king who, having brought his enemy low by the rod, does not then subdue him, embraces his own death—as a she-mule conceiving a foal embraces hers.
Let him be full of blossom yet bear no fruit; or fruitful, yet hard to climb; let him be unripe though seeming ripe, and never let himself crumble away to anyone.
Let him hold out a hope tied to a future time, and then couple that hope with an obstacle; let him ascribe the obstacle to some pretext, and the pretext, in turn, to some cause.
So long as the danger has not yet come, let him make his arrangements like one who is afraid; but seeing the danger actually arrived, let him strike like one who fears nothing.
Without venturing into risk a man beholds no good fortune; but having ventured into risk, if he survives, he beholds it.
Let him foresee what has not yet come, and ward off the danger that is at hand; and from the rise and fall of things let him discern whatever may already have come to pass.
To forsake the happiness whose hour is present, and to hanker after a happiness yet to come—this is no policy of the wise.
He who, having made a pact with his enemy, sleeps in trustful ease, awakens only when he has fallen—like one who has dozed off at the top of a tree.
By whatever deed serves—be it gentle or be it harsh—let him lift up his own afflicted self; and once he is strong again, let him practise dharma.
Whoever are the rivals of his rivals, all of these let him win over to himself; and let him also be alert to the spies set upon him by his foes.
Espionage must be well organized, both for his own realm and against the other's; and let him send heretics, ascetics, and the like into the enemy's kingdom.
In gardens and pleasure-grounds, at watering-sheds and lodging-houses, in taverns and brothels, at sacred fords and in assembly-halls—
—there sinful men who transgress dharma, the spies and thorns of society, congregate; discovering them, let him restrain them, and even put them down.
Let him not trust the untrustworthy, nor yet trust even the trustworthy; for danger pursues the trusting man, and let him never trust without first putting to the test.
Having won his adversary's confidence by some genuine-seeming pretext, then, when the moment comes and his footing is even a little unsteady, let him strike him down.
Let him be suspicious even of what seems beyond suspicion, and ever wary of one already suspected; for danger born of one suspected can cut a man down, root and all.
By a show of devotion, by silence, by the ochre robe, by matted locks and the deerskin, let him win the trust of one who hates him, and then seize upon him as a wolf upon its prey.
Be it a son, or a brother, or a father, or a bosom friend—if they stand in the way of his purpose, they are to be struck down by him who would increase his fortune.
Even a teacher, if he is arrogant, ignorant of what should and should not be done, and gone astray upon a wrong path—for him the rod becomes the fitting discipline.
By rising to greet, by salutation, by gifts bestowed on this man or that, let him be a striker who deals abundant blows in return, like a sharp-beaked bird.
Without cutting into the vital points of others, without doing some terrible deed, without striking—as a fisherman slays his fish—a man wins no surpassing glory.
None is by birth an enemy, and none, indeed, is by birth a friend; it is from the interplay of power that friends and foes alike arise.
Let him by no means release a foe, though he plead piteously; let him feel no pity in that, but slay the man who first did the wrong.
Effort, free of all spite, must ever be made in winning men over and showing them favour; and with equal effort must restraint and punishment be applied by him who desires prosperity.
When about to strike, let him speak kindly, and even after striking let his words be kind; nay, having struck off his victim's head, let him weep and mourn for him.
Let him conciliate with soft words, with honour shown, with forbearance—this giving of grounds for hope is what he who desires prosperity must do.

Let him not engage in a fruitless feud, nor try to cross a river by the strength of his own arms alone; it is profitless and life-shortening—like gnawing on a cow's horn, wherein the teeth are merely worn away and no juice is got at all.
In the threefold aim of life there are three kinds of affliction and three kinds of consequence; knowing the consequences and their undoing, let him shun the affliction.
A remnant of debt, a remnant of fire, and likewise a remnant of an enemy—each, however small, if left unchecked, will grow again and again.
A debt left to mount, enemies left despised, and ailments left neglected—these bring on grievous ruin.
Let him not be one who does his work by halves; let him be ever vigilant—for even a thorn ill-extracted festers and causes trouble for a long time.
By the slaying of its men, by the spoiling of its roads, and by the wrecking of its mines, let him bring the enemy's kingdom to ruin.
With the eye of a vulture, the stillness of a heron, the wariness of a dog, the valour of a lion, untroubled yet suspicious as a crow, let him move with the gait of a serpent.
When guild-chiefs are being suborned and favourites courted away, let him keep close watch over his ministers, both as to their dividing and their banding together.
Men scorn him as soft, and shrink from him as harsh; therefore in a time for harshness let him be harsh, and in a time for gentleness let him be gentle.
By gentleness one overcomes the very gentle, and by gentleness one overcomes the fierce; there is nothing gentleness cannot accomplish—therefore gentleness is the keener weapon.
He who is gentle when the time is for gentleness and fierce when the time is for fierceness, he accomplishes his ends and prevails over his foes.
Being at odds with a wise man, let him not trust in the thought, "I am far away"; for long are the arms of the intelligent, with which, once injured, he injures in return.

Let him not embark on what he cannot cross to the farther shore; let him not seize what the enemy can seize back again; let him not dig at what he cannot uproot; let him not strike at one whose head he cannot strike off.

Thus has this counsel, bound up with crookedness, been spoken; yet a man should not himself act in this way. But how else is he to recognize such devices when an enemy employs them? It is for this that I, desiring your good, have told it to you.
Having heard this salutary counsel duly delivered by the brāhmaṇa, the lord of the Suvīra realm, undaunted in mind, acted upon it, and together with his kinsmen enjoyed a blazing prosperity.

Yudhiṣṭhira said: When the supreme dharma, which surpasses all the worlds, has decayed—when unrighteousness has been raised to the rank of righteousness, and righteousness has lapsed into unrighteousness—
—when all bounds are broken asunder and the very settled order of dharma is convulsed, when the world is oppressed by kings or by thieves, O lord of peoples—
—when all the orders of life are bewildered and their proper rites overthrown, and men, from desire, delusion, and greed, behold only fear, O descendant of Bharata—
—when all are distrustful and ever afraid, O king, when men are slain by treachery and deceive one another—
—when the lands are ablaze and the order of brāhmaṇas is sorely afflicted, when the rain-cloud withholds its rain and mutual dissension has arisen—
—when every means of livelihood upon the earth has fallen into the hands of brigands: by what means, then, is a brāhmaṇa to live, once so vile a time has come?
How, O ruler of men, should one who is unwilling to abandon his sons and grandsons out of compassion conduct himself in such calamities? This tell me, grandfather.
And how should a king conduct himself when the world has fallen into turmoil? How, O scorcher of foes, is he to fall away neither from gain nor from dharma?
Bhīṣma said: Rooted in the king, O great monarch, are security, prosperity, and good rains—and so too, among the people, are diseases, death, and the terrors that beset them.
The Kṛta age, the Tretā, the Dvāpara, and the Kali, O bull of the Bharatas—all of these are rooted in the king; of this I have no doubt.
But when that time has come which works the undoing of the people, then one must live by taking one's stand upon the strength of discernment.
On this very matter they recite an ancient tale: the dialogue between Viśvāmitra and a Caṇḍāla in his hamlet.
At the juncture of the Tretā and the Dvāpara ages, long ago, by the ordained course of fate, there fell a fearful drought, O king, lasting twelve years.
When the creatures had multiplied and the close of the age drew near, at the time of the Tretā's passing and the ushering in of the Dvāpara,
the thousand-eyed Indra rained not; the planet Bṛhaspati turned contrary; and the Moon, his marks reversed, went the southern path.
At the end of night there was not even dew, let alone ranks of clouds; the rivers, their flooding waters shrunk away, in places sank wholly underground.
Lakes and streams, wells and springs alike were seen stripped of their luster, drained of their nature by the working of fate.
The land's water-resting places were dried up; its halls and watering-booths abandoned; its sacrifices and Vedic recitation ceased; its auspicious cries of vaṣaṭ fallen silent.
Tillage and the keeping of cattle had collapsed; buying and selling in the markets had stopped; the gatherings of the guilds had ended; the great festivals were utterly lost.
The earth was strewn with bones and skeletons, thronged with people crying alas; her cities mostly emptied, her village-dwellings burned to ash.
Here by thieves, there by the sword, elsewhere by desperate kings, and through mutual terror besides, she was left for the most part empty and unpeopled.
Her resolve in the gods departed, bereft of her old folk and her children, stripped of cattle, goats, and buffalo, men plundering one another in turn,
her brahmins slain, her safeguards slain, her stores of herbs all perished, peopled mostly by men turned ashen-gray—such did the earth become in that hour.
In that dreadful season, when dharma had waned, O Yudhiṣṭhira, famished mortals wandered, devouring one another.
The sages, casting off their vows, forsaking their sacred fires and their gods, abandoned their hermitages and ran about hither and thither.
Then the venerable Viśvāmitra, the great seer, himself without a home, beset by hunger though wise, ran roaming on every side.
Once, as he strayed about, he came upon the settlement of dog-cookers—savage men, slayers of living creatures—somewhere in the forest.
It was littered with broken pots, draped about with dog-skins, crowded with the cracked bones of boars and asses, with skulls and crocks.
It was spread over with the garments of the dead, its ornaments made of cast-off funeral flowers, its huts and shrines marked out with garlands of shed snake-skins.
It was hemmed about with godlings' shrines, their banners owl-feathered, decked out with iron bells and ringed about with packs of dogs.
Entering it, overpowered by hunger, the great seer, son of Gādhi, intent on his search for food, set himself to the utmost effort.
Yet nowhere, for all his begging, did Kauśika find any flesh, any grain, any root or fruit, or aught else whatever there.
"Alas, into what straits I have come!"—so resolving, Kauśika sank to the earth from weakness there in that Caṇḍāla hamlet.
The sage fell to pondering: "What now would be the right thing for me to do? How might my death not be in vain?"—so, O best of kings.
And the sage caught sight of a haunch of dog's flesh stretched out, in the Caṇḍāla's hut, O king—flesh of a creature freshly killed by the blade.
Then he reflected: "Theft must I commit from this place, for now no other means whatever exists to keep my life.
In dire need theft is sanctioned—from a superior, an equal, or a lower man; yet it grows ever graver in that order, and this is the rule: first do no theft at all.
What is taken should first be taken from a lower man, then from an equal; and only when no other course remains may one take even from a superior and righteous person.
I, then, in taking from the possession of these lowest of the low, see no guilt of theft; this meat I shall take."
Fixed in this resolve, the great sage Viśvāmitra slept where he had fallen, in that very spot, O Bhārata.
Seeing the night well advanced, while the Caṇḍāla hamlet slept, the venerable one rose softly and stole into the hut and its shrine.
But the Caṇḍāla, though still asleep, his eyes gummed shut with rheum, harsh, his voice cracking, a man grim to look upon, spoke out:
"Who tampers with the haunch while the Caṇḍāla hamlet sleeps? I am awake, I am not sound asleep—you are a dead man!"—so cried the fierce fellow.
"I am Viśvāmitra"—so on the instant he answered him, fear coming upon him all at once, agitated by that deed.
When the Caṇḍāla heard that speech of the great seer of disciplined soul, startled, he sought to spring up at once from his bed.
Shedding tears from his eyes, with reverence and folded hands, he said to Kauśika in the night: "Brahmin, what is it you mean to do?"
And Viśvāmitra, soothing the outcaste, said: "I am starving, my life ebbing away; I mean to take this haunch of dog.
My life-breaths fail; my memory perishes from hunger; and though I know full well my own dharma, I shall take this haunch of dog.
When, roaming for alms, I find nothing here in your dwelling, then is my mind set upon this sin: I shall take the haunch of dog.
A man parched will drink foul water; for one seeking food there is no shame; here hunger corrupts dharma—I shall take the haunch of dog."
"Agni is the mouth and the household priest of the gods, the pure-footed lord; even as he, the all-devourer, is Brahman, so know me to be by the law."
To him the Caṇḍāla replied: "Great seer, hear my words, and when you have heard, so order yourself that you fall not away from dharma.
The wise declare the dog the basest of beasts; and basest even of its body is this part, the haunch of its thigh.
This is no rightly resolved purpose, O great seer—a deed perverse: the stealing of a Caṇḍāla's property, and that of food unfit to eat besides.
Look rather, I pray, for some other means to sustain your life; let there be no ruin of your austerity through greed for meat, O great sage.
For one who knows, the unsanctioned path is not to be taken; the confounding of dharma must not be wrought. Forsake not dharma—you, the foremost of those who know it."
Then, O king, bull of the Bharatas, thus addressed, Viśvāmitra the great sage, tormented by hunger, answered him once again:
"A very long time has passed for me without food as I have run about, and no means whatever is to be found for sustaining my life.
By this means or that, by whatever deed soever, the man who is sinking should keep himself alive; once able, he may then practice dharma.
Indra's is the dharma of the Kṣatriyas, the fire-god's that of the brahmins; the fire of Brahman is my strength—in this strait I shall eat, driven by hunger.
By whatever means one may live, that very thing must be done, without affliction; life is better than death—living, a man may yet attain dharma.
I, therefore, longing to live, resolve, with full deliberation, to eat even this food unfit to be eaten; let your honor consent to it."
"Living, I shall practice dharma and shall drive off my evils by austerities and by knowledge, as lights drive off the great darkness."

The dog-cooker said: "By eating this you will gain no other life, no long span of days, nor any fullness as of the nectar of immortality. Beg some other alms; let not your mind be set on eating dog—for the dog is no food for the twice-born."

Viśvāmitra said: "In this famine no other flesh is easy to come by, O dog-cooker, nor grain, nor have I any wealth. Tormented by hunger, helpless, without hope, I deem this dog's flesh to hold the six savors well enough."

The dog-cooker said: "Five among the five-clawed beasts are fit to eat for the brahmin and the kṣatriya, O twice-born; if the scripture is your authority, set not your mind upon what may not be eaten."
Viśvāmitra said: "The demon Vātāpi was once devoured by Agastya in his hunger; I, fallen into calamity and shaken, shall eat the haunch of dog."
The dog-cooker said: "'Fetch some other alms'—so I say; you ought not to do this thing. Surely this is not to be done; yet take the haunch of dog, if you will."
Viśvāmitra said: "The cultured are the warrant in matters of dharma; their conduct I would follow. Better than eating pure food I deem this haunch of dog to be, here, a thing fit to be eaten."
The dog-cooker said: "What is practiced by the base is no eternal dharma; what is not the established usage is not to be imitated. Do not by sophistry make a lie of the truth."
Viśvāmitra said: "Being a seer, you ought to do nothing fallen, nothing despised; yet I hold the dog and the deer to be alike, and therefore the haunch of dog fit to be eaten."

The dog-cooker said: "What is done for a brahmin's sake by a seer in his need—that too carries the sanction to be eaten. But that alone is dharma in which there is no sin, and it is to be guarded by every means."

Viśvāmitra said: "This brahmin is my friend, my very self, dear to me and most worthy of honor in the world; wishing to sustain him, I shall take this haunch—of cruel men such as these I have no fear."

The dog-cooker said: "Gladly do men give up their very lives, and do not redress their straits with forbidden food; and so, O learned one, they win here all their desires. Endure your hunger, then, if you must, holding fast."

Viśvāmitra said: "There is, to be sure, doubt about the state after death; but the loss of one's deeds is beyond doubt. With my heart set on this—'I may yet come back'—and guarding the root of life, I shall eat the forbidden food."

"He is content who knows the manifold to be set out within the realm of intellect, while through delusion oneness appears, as the skin and the eye are taken as one. And even if from doubt I commit a sin, I shall not become such as you yourself are."
The dog-cooker said: "This is a grief that brings about my fall—so runs my thought—that I, an evildoer, should reprove you who are a true brahmin."
Viśvāmitra said: "The cattle drink the water even while the frogs croak on. You have no warrant in matters of dharma; do not be a praiser of yourself."
The dog-cooker said: "It is as a well-wisher that I counsel you, for I feel compassion toward you, O twice-born. Lay hold, then, of what is for your good; take not the dog from greed."
Viśvāmitra said: "If you are my well-wisher, desiring my welfare, then rescue me from calamity. I know myself by the law; let go your hold upon the dog's haunch."

The dog-cooker said: "I have no heart to give you this, nor yet to look on idly while my own food is carried off; both of us would be smeared with our own defilement—I as the giver, and you, O brahmin, as the one who takes it."

Viśvāmitra said: "Today, having done this crooked deed, I shall live and practice the great purification; and with my soul made wholly pure, I shall lay hold of dharma itself. Tell me, then, which of these two is the weightier."

The dog-cooker said: "The self alone, they say, is witness in the works of the world; you yourself know what is wrong herein. As for him who would honor dog's flesh as food fit to eat—for him, I think, there is nothing left to shun."

Viśvāmitra said: "Whether in the taking of this or in the eating of it lie a fault, the exception to the rule must ever be reasoned out by the canons of right. Where there is no harm done and no shred of falsehood in speech, there the act of eating is no grave thing."

The dog-cooker said: "If this is your reasoning for eating it, then neither the Veda nor any other dharma is your warrant; and so, O chief of the twice-born, in eating what may not be eaten I see no fault, just as you have said."

Viśvāmitra said: "The eating of this is not seen to be a deadly sin; the dictum here runs, 'By drinking spirits one falls.' Each several deed has its own measure, just so; and a mere trifle does not undo the rightful act."

The dog-cooker said: "From an improper place, from a lower man, or from a thing reviled—such a taking afflicts even the learned man of good conduct. And he who recovers his standing through attachment must yet endure the penalty even so."
Bhīṣma said: Having spoken thus, the outcaste then desisted from Kauśika; and Viśvāmitra, his mind made up, took the haunch of dog after all.
Then the great sage, bent on living, seized the five-membered haunch; and having prepared it, he went off with his wife into the forest, that great sage.
But at that very time Vāsava sent down his rain, bringing all creatures back to life, and made the healing herbs to grow again.
And the venerable Viśvāmitra too, his guilt burned away by austerity, in the course of long time attained a perfection most wondrous.
Thus the wise man, undaunted in spirit, fallen into calamity yet eager to live, knowing the means, should by every means lift his stricken self out of distress.
Holding fast to this resolve, one should ever strive to stay alive; for the man who lives wins merit and beholds good fortune.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, the wise man, self-controlled, taking his stand upon discernment in distinguishing right from wrong, should conduct himself in this world.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: This dreadful teaching that has been set forth seems hardly credible, well-nigh false. Is there indeed any limit of robber-conduct that I might avoid?
I am bewildered, I despair; my hold on dharma has been loosened. Ponder as I may, I can find no resolve to act.
Bhīṣma said: This instruction in dharma that I give you does not come from scripture alone; it is a descent of insight, the honey gathered by the wise.
Many kinds of wisdom must a king bring to bear from this side and that; this course of life cannot be carried on by a dharma of a single branch.
Wisdom is begotten in kings who ever practice dharma, and then, O Kaurava, victory is theirs: know this as my word.
For kings supreme in wisdom, longing for conquest, are the ones who triumph; dharma must be applied by the king with judgment, this way and that.
The dharma of kings is not ordained by a dharma of a single branch; whence should the weak have wisdom, as was set forth before?
He who knows no doubleness, when the path forks into two, is bound to fall into doubt; the doubleness of judgment must be understood beforehand, O Bhārata.
Wisdom runs to one side and the other, branching like a river; and people understand the dharma that is uttered each in his own differing way.
Some have right understanding, others a false one; but the good, having grasped a thing just as it truly is, take up that knowledge.
The enemies of dharma plunder the scriptures, and out of their emptiness proclaim a discord in the sciences of meaning.
Seeking to make a living by learning, hungry for fame on every side—all such are the vilest of men, the enemies of dharma.
Of unripe mind and dull, they do not know things as they truly are; ever unskilled in the scriptures, they are nowhere firmly grounded.
Those who look only for faults in the scriptures plunder them; and so the understanding of the sciences proceeds astray, not aright.

Those who by belittling the learning of others advertise their own—armed with speech, drunk on the daggers of their words, as though they had milked dry the fruit of learning—know them, O Bhārata, for hucksters of knowledge, like very rākṣasas.
If the whole of dharma is known to you through pretext, it will desert you; for we have heard that the declaring of dharma is not by mere speech, nor by mere cleverness.
So Maghavat himself declared the teaching of Bṛhaspati; and yet no word here is uttered without a ground.
By the discipline they have learned for themselves some others resolve their course; but the wise here call the conduct of worldly life itself dharma.
The dharma laid down by the good a learned man should not reason away on his own out of impatience, from confusion over the scriptures, or from ignorance, O Bhārata.
When a wise man speaks in an assembly, scripture passes out of sight; he is approved for his speech, by a judgment grounded in tradition received.
Out of ignorance, because his word is a source of knowledge, men deem it sound; this is not to be cast aside, this scripture is not without purpose.
Uśanas of old said to the Daityas, when resolving their doubts: just as there is no knowledge that cannot be made plain, so indeed it is.
Whom can you satisfy with that whose root is cut? And who would heed this speech laid down upon what is untrue?
For you were created for fierce action, yet you will not look to it. Come, consider this statecraft, if you wish to thrive—the polity by which one man is set free and for whose sake another rejoices.
The goat, the horse, the warrior—these were made alike by Brahmā; hence for those whose nature is not fierce no course of life can succeed.
The fault that lies in slaying one who ought not to be slain is held to lie equally in not slaying one who ought to be slain; this very thing is the limit a king must not transgress.
Therefore let the king, stern, establish his subjects each in their own duty; for otherwise they would range about devouring one another like wolves.
That king in whose realm bands of robbers make away with others' goods—as crows snatch fish from the water—is verily a disgrace to the warrior caste.
Making well-born men your counsellors, men endowed with knowledge of the Veda, rule the earth, O king, protecting your subjects by dharma.
The lord of earth who takes up a man of low birth and no fit deeds, knowing no difference between the two, makes of his warrior-rule a thing unmanned.
Neither the wholly fierce nor the wholly gentle is here commended by dharma; transgress neither extreme—having been fierce, become mild.
Hard is this duty of the warrior, in whom such tenderness abides; you were created for fierce action—therefore rule the kingdom.
The constant restraint of the unruly, the guarding of the well-disciplined—thus spoke the wise Śakra concerning times of distress, O bull of the Bharatas.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Is there indeed a limit even of robbers that another should not overstep? I ask you, O best of the good—tell me this, grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: One should serve the brāhmaṇas, men grown great in learning, ascetics, rich in sacred lore, good character, and conduct; for this is the highest purification.
The conduct you keep toward the gods—let that be yours toward the brāhmaṇas always; for by brāhmaṇas in their wrath deeds of many kinds have been wrought, O king.
From their favor comes foremost glory, from their displeasure the reverse; for when pleased the brāhmaṇas are like nectar, and when enraged like poison.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Grandfather, great in wisdom, versed in all the scriptures, tell me the dharma of one who protects a suppliant who has sought his shelter.
Bhīṣma said: Great is the dharma, O great king, in the protection of one who has come for refuge; and you indeed are worthy to ask this question, best of the Bharatas.
Kings beginning with Nṛga, O king, having protected those who came to them for refuge, attained, O great monarch, the highest perfection.
For it is told how, by a dove, an enemy who had come for refuge was honored as was right and entertained with the bird's own flesh.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How was it that long ago an enemy came for refuge to a dove and was fed with the bird's own flesh, and what destiny did that dove attain, O Bhārata?
Bhīṣma said: Hear, O king, a divine tale, destroyer of all sins, told to King Mucukunda by Bhārgava of old.
This very matter, O Pārtha, the king Mucukunda asked of Bhārgava in days gone by, bowing low, O bull of the Bharatas.
To him as he sat attentive, Bhārgava told the tale of how perfection was won by the dove, O lord of men.
A tale joined with the settled truths of dharma and bound up with desire and gain—hear it attentively, O king, mighty-armed, as I tell it.
A certain man of base conduct, reckoned as cruel as Death itself, ranged over the earth, sinful and dreadful, a fowler of birds.
Black-limbed as a raven, harsh, bent wholly upon evil, narrow at the waist, thin-necked, short-legged, and great of jaw.
He had no friend at all, no kinsman, no relation; for by all of these he had been cast off because of that dreadful trade of his.
Taking up his cage, he would forever kill the birds in the forest and make a trade of those winged creatures, O lord of men.
While that evil-souled man lived thus by his livelihood, a very long time passed, and yet he did not perceive his own unrighteousness.
To him, with his wife for sole companion, taking his constant pleasure, bewildered by the working of fate, no other way of life seemed good.
Then once, as he stood in the forest, there arose a great tumult of wind, as though casting down the very trees.
The sky grew thick with clouds, adorned with circling lightnings, and in a moment was wholly covered, like a harbor crowded with the ships of the sea.
And the god of a hundred sacrifices, rejoicing, with masses of streaming rain filled the earth with water in an instant.
Then, while the world was awhirl with the downpour, he wandered, his wits gone, tormented by the cold, all through that forest, his inmost soul in turmoil.
That slayer of birds could find neither low ground nor high; for the path through that forest was filled with the flood of waters.
The birds, struck down by the force of the wind, lay then huddled close; the deer, the lions, and the boars stood crowded upon the high ground.
Terrified by the mighty wind and rain, those dwellers of the forest, distressed by fear and tormented by hunger, wandered together through the wood.
But he, his limbs smitten by the cold, kept moving and did not halt; and amid the thickets of the wood he spied a great tree dark as a raincloud.
Seeing the heaven grown rich with stars, fair as the white lily, clear and freed of clouds, the fowler, undone by the cold,

that evil-souled man looked about him at the quarters of the sky and at the hour; and since the nearest village lay far from that spot, O lord, he made up his mind to dwell that night there in the forest.
Reverently folding his hands, he spoke to the tree: I go for refuge to whatever divinities dwell here in this place, O Bhārata.
Laying his head upon a stone and strewing leaves over the ground, that slayer of birds, overcome with great misery, then fell asleep.
Bhīṣma said: Now upon a branch of that tree, O king, a bird with his dear mate had long dwelt there, his plumage bright and varied.
His mate had gone forth at dawn to forage and had not returned; and seeing that night had come on, the bird grew sore distressed.
Great was the wind and rain, and my beloved does not come. What can be the cause that even now she has not returned?
May it be well with my beloved out there in the forest! For without her this home of mine is empty today.
If she of the red-cornered eyes, of dappled body and sweet voice, my darling, does not come to me today, then I have no use for life.
Devoted to the duty of a wife, virtuous, dearer to me than my own breath—that gentle creature knows when I am weary and tormented by hunger.
Loving and devoted to his good, tender and faithful to her lord—the man on earth who has such a wife is blessed indeed.
A wife is declared to be a man's highest protector here, the companion in life's journey for one who in this world is otherwise without help.
So too for a man overwhelmed by sickness and ever sunk in hardship, there is no medicine for one in distress like a wife.
There is no kinsman like a wife, no refuge like a wife; in all the world there is no helper like a wife for the accomplishing of dharma.
As the bird thus lamented there in his grief, his mate, who had been seized by the slayer of birds, heard his speech.
She whose husband is not content with her should not be called a woman at all; for, with the fire itself as witness, the husband is the refuge of a wife.
Reflecting thus, stricken with grief, the hen-dove then, held captive by the fowler, addressed her sorrowing husband with these well-weighed words.
Listen, I will tell you what is best for you; hear it, and act accordingly. Above all, my beloved, be a protector of one who has come to you for refuge.
This fowler lies here, having taken shelter in your dwelling, tormented by cold and afflicted by hunger; offer him due hospitality.
For whoever should slay a brāhmaṇa, or a cow—mother of the world—or one who has come for refuge: the sin of these is one and the same.
That mode of life ordained for us pigeons by the law of our kind is one to be ever followed in righteousness by a self-possessed creature such as you.
A householder who follows dharma to the best of his power attains, after death, the imperishable worlds—so we have heard.

You, O twice-born, are now blessed with offspring and have sons besides; therefore, casting off all tenderness for your own body and embracing dharma and its purpose, offer this man hospitality, so that his heart may be pleased.
Having spoken these words while caught in the snare-cage, the wretched hen-bird, overwhelmed with grief, gazed upon her husband.
Hearing his wife's words, charged with the reasoning of dharma, he was filled with great joy, his eyes brimming with tears.
Looking upon that fowler, the bird honored him diligently with the rites prescribed by ordinance—the bird honoring the one who lived by killing birds.
And he said: "Welcome to you. Tell me, what may I do for you? You must feel no distress; you are now within your own home."
"Speak quickly, sir—what shall I do, what do you desire? I say this to you out of affection, for you have come to us for refuge."
"Hospitality must be shown with care to one who has come for refuge, and most especially by a householder devoted to the five sacrifices."
"The householder who, through delusion, does not perform the five sacrifices wins, by the law, neither this world nor the next."
"So speak with full confidence; whatever you ask in words, all of it I shall do. Do not let your mind dwell in sorrow."
Hearing these words of the bird, the fowler replied: "The cold indeed torments me; let some protection against the frost be arranged."
Thus addressed, the bird, having carefully spread out such dry leaves as he could upon the ground for kindling a fire, swiftly went off.
Going to a charcoal-burner's place, he fetched fire and returned; then upon the dry leaves he kindled the flame into a blaze.
Having made a great, well-blazing fire, he said to the refuge-seeker: "Warm your limbs in full confidence and without any fear."
So addressed, the fowler said "So be it" and warmed his limbs; his life-breath restored by the fire, he then said to the bird:
"I wish for food to be given by you, for hunger torments me." Hearing his words, the bird answered:
"I have no store of wealth by which I might dispel your hunger, for we forest-dwellers live always upon whatever comes to hand."
"We keep no hoard, like the sages in the wood." Having spoken thus, the bird's face turned pale.
"How then is this to be done?"—sunk in this anxious thought, O best of the Bharatas, he kept reproaching his own way of life.
But after a moment, regaining his composure, the bird said to the slayer of birds: "I shall satisfy you; wait but a moment."
Having said this, the pigeon, kindling the fire to a blaze with dry leaves, filled with great joy, spoke again:
"From the gods, from the sages, and from the great-souled ancestors I have heard before of the supreme dharma that lies in honoring a guest."
"Grant me this favor today—truly I tell you this: my resolve is fixed upon honoring my guest."
Then the bird, true to his vow, as if smiling, circumambulated that fire three times and entered into it, O lord of the earth.
Seeing the bird enter into the midst of the fire, the fowler reflected in his mind: "What is this I have brought about?"
"Alas, for me, a cruel man, contemptible by reason of my own deeds, a most great and terrible sin will surely come—there is no doubt."
In many ways and at great length the fowler lamented thus, reproaching his own deeds, as he beheld the twice-born bird come to such an end.
Bhīṣma said: Then the fowler, watching the pigeon fallen into the fire and overwhelmed with pity, spoke again these words:
"What a thing have I, a cruel and witless man, done! For as long as I live this sin will dwell forever in my heart."
Reviling himself, he said again and again: "Shame upon me, the dull-witted, ever bent upon treachery, who, abandoning every good deed, became a hunter of birds!"
"This is, beyond doubt, a rebuke to me, a cruel man—delivered by the great-souled pigeon who gave his own flesh."
"I shall give up my own dear life and forsake my children and wife, for dharma has been taught to me by that supremely righteous pigeon."
"From this day forth I shall dry up my own body, stripped of all enjoyments, as the scant water of summer is dried away."
"Enduring hunger, thirst, and heat, grown gaunt with veins drawn taut, I shall pursue, through fasts of many kinds, the way to the world beyond."

"Lo, by the offering of his body, the honoring of a guest has been shown! Therefore I shall practice dharma, for dharma is the supreme goal—I have seen what dharma is, such as the righteous practice it, in that best of birds."
Having spoken thus and made his resolve, the fowler of cruel deeds, taking up the Great Departure, set forth with a vow firmly fixed.
Then his staff, his sticks, his snare, and his cage—and the pigeons he had bound—he loosed and set free.
Bhīṣma said: When the fowler had gone, the grieving hen-pigeon, remembering her husband and weeping, fainting with sorrow, spoke:

"I cannot recall, beloved, that I ever once did anything to displease you. Every widowed woman, O sky-ranger, even one with many sons, becomes an object of pity to her kin—a noble-hearted woman bereft of her husband."
"Ever was I cherished by you and soothed with great regard, again and again, with words sweet, tender, and most delightful."
"In the caverns of the mountains, by the cascades of the rivers, and on the lovely crowns of the trees, I was made happy by you, my beloved."
"In our flights through the sky I knew happiness with you, my love; I sported with you—but now none of that is left to me at all."
"A father gives but a measured portion, a mother a measured portion, a son a measured portion; but a husband, who gives without measure—what woman would not honor him?"
"There is no protector like a husband, and no happiness like a husband; renouncing all her wealth and possessions, a woman's refuge is her husband alone."
"I have no use, my lord, for life in this world without you. What virtuous woman bereft of her husband could bring herself to live?"
Having lamented thus in many a piteous way, the deeply grieving, devoted wife entered the blazing fire.
Then she beheld her husband, clad in shining garments, seated in a celestial chariot, honored by the great-souled doers of good deeds.
He wore bright garlands and garments and was adorned with every ornament, surrounded by a hundred million celestial cars belonging to those of holy renown.
Then the bird, gone to heaven, was reunited with his wife; honored for that deed of his, he rejoiced there together with her.
Bhīṣma said: The fowler, O king, saw the pair seated in the celestial chariot; and seeing the husband and wife, he reflected, out of his grief, upon the good path.
"By what manner of austerity might I attain the supreme goal?" Having resolved this in his mind, he set out upon his journey.
Taking up the Great Departure, the fowler who had lived by killing birds became still, living on air alone, free of all sense of "mine," in longing for heaven.

Then he saw a broad and lovely lake, adorned with lotuses, thronged with flocks of many birds, its cool waters fair—a sight at which even one tormented by thirst would be satisfied, of this there is no doubt.
But the fowler, O king, grown exceedingly gaunt with fasting, gladly approached a forest inhabited by beasts of prey.
Having made his great resolve, the fowler entered in; and even as he entered the forest, he was caught fast by thorns.
His limbs torn by the thorns, his skin made wet with blood, he wandered through that desolate place teeming with all manner of wild beasts.
Then in that forest, from the friction of great trees driven by the wind, there arose a mighty fire, bearer of oblations.
That forest, dense with trees and tangled with creepers and boughs, the fire consumed in fury, blazing like the flame at the end of an age.
Attended by flaming sparks fanned up by the wind, it burned that dreadful forest thronged with beasts and birds.
Then, with a heart full of gladness, seeking the release of his body, the fowler ran toward that swelling fire.
Then, consumed by that fire, the fowler, his sins destroyed, attained the supreme perfection, O best of the Bharatas.
Then, his anguish gone, he beheld himself established in heaven, shining like Indra amid the yakṣas, gandharvas, and siddhas.
Thus indeed the pigeon and the devoted hen-pigeon, together with the fowler, went to heaven through their meritorious deeds.
And whatever woman of such a kind follows after her husband, she too shines forth at once, dwelling in heaven like that hen-pigeon.
Thus did this come to pass of old: the righteous destiny, won through meritorious deeds, of the great-souled fowler and of the pigeon.
Whoever should ever hear this, and whoever should recite it, no misfortune befalls him, even should his mind grow heedless.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, great is this dharma, O best of the upholders of dharma. Even for slayers of cattle there may be expiation of their sinful deed; but there is no expiation for him who would slay one who has come to him for refuge.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: One who commits a sin unknowingly, O best of the Bharatas—how is he freed from that wrong? Tell me this.
Bhīṣma said: On this matter I shall relate to you an ancient tale—what Indrota the brāhmaṇa, son of Śunaka, said to Janamejaya.
There was a king of great valor, Janamejaya, son of Parikṣit; unwittingly, the slaying of a brāhmaṇa came upon that lord of the earth.
All the brāhmaṇas, together with his household priests, forsook him; and the king, burning day and night, went off to the forest.
Abandoned by his subjects, he did great works of merit; he practiced austerity beyond all measure, burning the while with remorse.
On this I shall tell a tale that confirms and amplifies this dharma: burning with his evil deed, Janamejaya set forth.
Wishing to choose him as priest, he came to Indrota, son of Śunaka, of firm-fixed vows, and clasped him, pressing hard upon his feet.
Then the great sage, afraid, rebuked him most severely: "You who have wrought a great sin, slayer of an unborn child—why have you come here?"
"What is there for you to do with us? Touch me not, by any means whatever! Go, go—your presence here surely gives us no pleasure."
Your odor is as of blood, and the sight of you is as of a corpse; though resembling one who is wholesome, you are inauspicious, and you wander about, dead, as though alive.
Inwardly dead, your soul unpurified, brooding upon evil alone, you wake, you sleep, you live, you move about at ease.
Vain is your life, O king, and in torment you live; it is for evil that you were created, for the basest of deeds.
Desiring much good, fathers strive for sons through austerity, through sacrifices to the gods, through worship and through forbearance.
Behold this line of your fathers, gone to hell on your account; fruitless are all the bonds of hope they had set upon you.
Toward those Brāhmaṇas, by honoring whom men obtain heaven, long life, fame, and happiness, your hatred is ceaseless and without purpose.
Quitting this world, you will fall headlong, through your sinful deeds, for years uncounted and years without end.
Devoured there by creatures and vultures, white-necked and iron-beaked; and even thence, returning once more, you will pass into a sinful womb.
As for your thought, O king, that there is no world beyond this—whence then?—the messengers of Yama, in Yama's abode, shall make you remember it well.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, Janamejaya answered that sage: 'What is blameworthy, you blame; what is censurable, you censure—do not so reproach me.'
You reproach me as one deserving reproach; therefore I seek your favor, for all this is my own doing, and I burn as though cast into the fire.
Looking back upon my own deeds, my mind takes no delight; surely a terror dreadful even beyond the son of Vivasvat has come upon me.
Without drawing out that barb, how shall I be able to live? Laying aside all your wrath, speak to me, O Śaunaka.
I shall again become the cook-house of the Brāhmaṇas, rich in offerings; let there be a remnant of this house, let not this line be undone.
For of us, cursed by the Brāhmaṇas, no remnant ought to remain—of us who cannot grasp the sacred texts, nor the knowledge that comes from sure certainty of the Veda.
Sorely afflicted, I shall speak yet again of what is fitting now; for again and again they perish, as men without dharma and without prayer.
And they sink down low, like the Pulindas and Śabaras; for those who offer no sacrifice can in no way attain that world beyond.
Without yet knowing my understanding, which is as a child's before the learned, O Brāhmaṇa, look kindly upon me, O Śaunaka, as a father upon his sons.
Śaunaka said: What wonder is it that a wise man should do much of what is fitting? Having become learned, he is not tormented on account of living beings.
Mounting the palace of wisdom, himself beyond sorrow, he grieves for the multitude, and with his wisdom looks down upon them as one upon a mountain looks upon those who stand upon the earth.
Yet he does not grasp it there, nor does he see the things that ought to be done—being weary of soul, or remote, or held in reproach among all the good.
Having known the power that lies on both sides, he knows the greatness that is in the scripture: attain here the great peace, and let Brahman be your refuge.
Fair indeed is that other-worldly reward for those who do not anger the Brāhmaṇas—if you grieve for your sins, and if you look toward dharma.
Janamejaya said: I grieve for my sin, and I practice no unrighteousness; and I in turn desire one who wishes me well and who serves me, O Śaunaka.
Śaunaka said: Cutting away both stubbornness and pride, I desire your gladness, O king; abide in the welfare of all beings, and keep dharma in remembrance.
Not from fear, nor from meanness, nor from greed do I call upon you; let the gods, together with the Brāhmaṇas, hear that my word is true.
I, who seek nothing from anyone, call upon you and upon dharma, while all beings cry out, 'Alas! Shame!'
Those who know not dharma will speak against me, and men who are no friends will speak against me; and my friends, hearing those words, will burn with great distress for me.
Only some, of great wisdom, will understand what must be done; know what I have done, dear one, toward the Brāhmaṇas, O descendant of Bharata.
So act that on my account they may obtain security; and promise that you will do no harm to the Brāhmaṇas, O lord of men.
Janamejaya said: Neither by word, nor by thought, nor ever again by deed shall I do harm to the Brāhmaṇas, O sage; I touch your very feet.

Śaunaka said: Therefore I shall declare to you, whose mind is turned back to it, the dharma—you who, prosperous, mighty, and content, now look toward dharma; and that, having first been harsh, is the more wondrous still.

Living beings show favor through their own conduct, O king; surely the whole world resolves what is good and what is bad accordingly—wherein you, having become such as you were, today look toward dharma.
That, forsaking most delicious food and enjoyments, one should take his stand in austerity—this too is a marvel among beings, O Janamejaya.
That a weak man should be a giver, or a wretched one rich in austerity—this they call no wonder, for it stands not far off.
For this very thing, when done wholly without reflection, is mere wretchedness; therefore let it be done with discernment, and thereby virtue will arise in it.
Sacrifice, giving, compassion, the Vedas, and truth, O lord of the earth—these five are purifiers, and well-performed austerity is the sixth.
That very thing is the supreme purifier of kings, O Janamejaya; by rightly laying hold of it, you shall attain the more excellent dharma.
Going to holy places is remembered as the supreme purifier; and indeed they recite these verses that were sung by Yayāti.
The mortal who would set out, or would live out his span of life once more—let him, having performed sacrifice with single devotion, then renounce it and practice austerity.
They call Kurukṣetra holy, and Pṛthūdaka upon the Sarasvatī, where, having bathed or drunk, one need not grieve over death on the morrow.
To Mahāsaras, to the Puṣkaras, to Prabhāsa and Uttaramānasa, and to Kālodaka indeed you shall go, having gained your span, to live again.
Resorting to the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī, you should wander along them; devoted to the recitation of scripture, you should perform your ablutions at all the sacred sites.
He declared renunciation, the dharma of giving up, to be the highest of purifiers; and here too they recite these verses made by Satyavat.
Even as a child, in truth, is neither doer of merit nor doer of sin—for in all beings there is no abiding sorrow, whence then could there be happiness?
So it is for those who are by nature thus, who go through every kind of contact, and who for the most part give up life, when merit and sin alike lie open before them.
But that which is the greater among the duties of a king, that I declare to you: by strength and by sharing out gifts, conquer heaven and purify yourself.
The man who has such strength and vigor is the lord of dharma; for the welfare of the Brāhmaṇas, do you traverse this earth.
Even as you once cast them down, so now win their favor, though you be reproached, though you be forsaken in many ways.
Knowing the vision of the self, O learned one, be not angered with the thought 'I am not'; striving in your own duties, achieve the highest good.
One king there is who becomes dreadful as frost or fire; and another becomes like the plough or the thunderbolt, O scorcher of foes.
One must not think a man wholly lost, nor again as past all cure; nor should one ever cling, among the wicked, to the thought 'I am undone.'

Grieving over a wrong deed, one is freed from a quarter of the sin; resolving 'I shall not do this again,' he is freed from a second; resolving 'I shall practice dharma alone,' he is freed from a third.
The good is to be approved by a man who wishes to prosper: those who frequent fragrant things become fragrant accordingly, and those who frequent foul-smelling things become foul accordingly.

One devoted to the practice of austerity is at once freed from sin; tending the fire for a year, the accused man is released; tending the fire for three years, even the slayer of an embryo is wholly freed.
By delivering from death as many living beings of that same kind, by their own nature perishing, as he had slain, the slayer of an embryo is wholly freed.
Or he should plunge into the waters, reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa thrice; that is even as the final bath of the horse-sacrifice—so Manu declared.
Swiftly he drives away his sin, and likewise obtains honor; and toward him living beings grow gracious, even those dull and dumb.

The gods and demons all together, O king, came to Bṛhaspati, the teacher of the gods, and questioned him: 'You know the fruit in dharma, when done, O great sage, and likewise in the other, in hell, the world of sin.'
'But for one in whom both good deeds should be present, which of the two would there prevail in victory? Tell us, O great sage, the fruit of works: how does one of virtuous conduct drive away sin?'

Bṛhaspati said: Having first committed sin unwittingly, he who then performs meritorious deeds with deliberate purpose—such a one of virtuous conduct drives away that sin, as a soiled garment is cleansed by the use of lye.
Having done a sin, a man should not think 'I am undone'; rather, faithful and free of malice, he should ever wish to do good.
As one repairs the holes of a garment with good thread, so does the man who, having done a sin, takes up the doing of good.
As the sun, rising again, drives away all darkness, so one who practices good drives away all his sin.
Bhīṣma said: Having thus addressed king Janamejaya, Śaunaka of Indrota's line had him perform, according to rule, the horse-sacrifice.
Then that king, his stain removed, endowed with majesty in the likeness of blazing fire, entered his own kingdom, that wearer-down of foes, as the full-bodied moon enters the sky.
Bhīṣma said: Hear, O Pārtha, as it befell, an ancient tale—the dialogue of the vulture and the jackal that took place long ago at Vidiśā.
Certain grief-stricken people, taking up a child who had not yet reached his youth—the very all-in-all of their family—wept, overwhelmed with sorrow.
Having taken up the dead child, they stood facing the cremation-ground, and passing him from lap to lap, they wept then upon the ground.
At the sound of their weeping a vulture drew near and spoke these words: 'Leave this one whose single self has passed, and depart from the world of the living without delay.'
'Here thousands of men, and thousands of women too, have been brought together by Time; how then could these ever be without kinsmen?'
'Look upon the whole world, beset with pleasures and pains; union and separation are met with by turns.'
'Those creatures who take up the dead and carry them, and those who follow after them, they too depart, each according to the measure of his own life-span.'
'Enough of lingering in this cremation-ground, thronged with vultures and jackals, heaped with skeletons, dreadful, terrifying to all living beings.'
'No one who has met the law of Time lives again, whether dear or hated; such is the course of living beings.'
'Everyone who is born into the world of mortals must surely die; upon the path ordained by the Ender, who shall bring the dead to life?'
'In a world where labor draws to its close, and as the sun is going down, let each go to his own abode, casting off his love for the son.'
Then, having heard the vulture's words, those kinsmen, crying aloud, O king, set forth, abandoning the son upon the ground.
And then, having made their resolve, forsaking their own offspring, despairing of his life, they set out upon the road and went their way.
But a jackal, colored like a crow or a storm-cloud, coming forth from his hole, called out to them as they departed: 'Pitiless indeed are these mortals!'
"The sun yet stands in the sky, you fools — show your love and do not be afraid. The hour takes many forms; perhaps even now the child may yet revive."
"Having laid him upon the ground, stripped of all love for your son, why do you abandon the boy at the cremation ground and go away so pitilessly?"
"Have you no tenderness for this son, this sweet-spoken child, by the mere sound of whose speech you would melt into delight?"
"Do you not see how strong is the love for offspring even among beasts and birds, though from rearing them no profit ever comes to them?"
"For four-footed creatures, for birds and insects, for all beings bound by affection, this love is, in its bearing on the world beyond, like the sacrificial rites of sages."
"For these creatures that delight in their young, no advantage is seen either in this world or the next — and yet they go on sustaining their offspring."
"When they no longer behold their beloved young, no grief abides in them; nor, once grown, do those offspring ever nourish their mother and father in return."
"Whence then this love among men, in whom grief is destined to dwell? How will you forsake this son, the very perpetuator of your line, and go your way?"
"Long shed your tears, long gaze upon him with love; for things dear as these are, above all, hard to give up."
"Of one fallen low, hard-pressed, and facing the cremation ground, where the kinsmen take their stand, no stranger will stand beside him."
"To every creature its own life is dear, and every creature comes to know love; behold how strong is the love of the good even among the beasts of the wild."
"How can you abandon and go from this boy, with his long, lotus-restless eyes, adorned as for a fresh wedding, bathed and decked with garlands?"
Bhīṣma said: Having heard the jackal's words of piteous lamentation, all those people then turned back for the corpse's sake.
The vulture said: Ah, shame! Addressed by this cruel, dull-witted, base little jackal, O men of feeble resolve, why do you turn back?
"Forsaken by the five elements, empty, reduced to the state of a mere log and devoid of motion — why do you grieve for him? Why do you not rather grieve for your own selves?"
"Practice fierce austerity, by which you may be freed from sin. By austerity all things are won; what will lamentation accomplish?"
"Know that fortunes, with their embodied forms, are unwelcome too, whereby this world passes on, bequeathing grief that has no end."
"Wealth and cattle and gold, gems and jewels too, and offspring — all are rooted in austerity, and through the practice of austerity are won."
"As it has been wrought, so among beings is their measure of joy and sorrow attained; a creature is born already having taken up its sorrows and its joys."
"Not by the father's deeds does the son fare, nor the father by the son's; by separate paths they go, each leaving behind his own good and evil works."
"Practice righteousness with diligence, and likewise turn back from unrighteousness; and conduct yourselves, each in due season, toward the gods and toward the twice-born."
