Bhṛgu said: O brāhmaṇa, O sinless one, I shall recount to you the movement of the wind, and how the mighty air sets the bodies of living creatures in motion.
Fire, resting in the head, guards over the body; and the prāṇa breath, moving in the head and in that fire, sets all in motion.
That living being is the Self of all beings; he is the eternal Person; he is mind, intellect, and ego-sense, the elements, and their objects.
Thus here he is everywhere sustained by the prāṇa, and by the samāna from behind, each air abiding in its own proper course.
Resting upon the base of the bladder, the rectum, and the digestive fire, the apāna circulates, bearing away urine and excrement.
That single one which operates in the three — in effort, in action, and in strength — they who know the inner Self call the udāna.
And the air that is set within all the joints in the bodies of men is taught to be the vyāna.
The fire diffused throughout the bodily constituents, driven on by the samāna, abides there, setting the chyles, the constituents, and the humors in their course.
Between the apāna and the prāṇa, joined together with prāṇa and apāna, well established in its own seat, the digestive fire thoroughly cooks the food.
The mouth is joined with the anal passage, which at its end is called the rectum, the channel; from this arise all the channels of embodied beings.
And from the meeting together of the vital airs their concourse arises; what is to be known as heat and fire is that which cooks the food of embodied beings.
The prāṇa, borne on the rush of fire, is checked at the end of the rectum; then, coming back upward, it again casts up the digestive fire.
The seat of the digested food lies below the navel, the seat of the undigested above it; in the midmost navel of the body all the vital airs are gathered.
Spread out from the heart, sideways, upward, and downward, the ten vessels, impelled by the vital breath, carry the chyle of food.
This is the path of the yogins, by which they reach that supreme station; steadfast, with weariness conquered and posture mastered, they have placed the Self within the head.
Thus the fire is set within all the prāṇas and apānas of embodied beings, abiding there forever, as one gathered within a cooking-pot.
Bharadvāja said: If it is the wind that breathes, the wind alone that moves, that breathes and that speaks, then the soul is of no purpose at all.
If the state of heat is of fire, if it is by fire that the food is cooked, and if it is fire that digests, then the soul is of no purpose at all.
When a creature is dying, no soul is found to be present; the wind alone forsakes it, and its state of warmth perishes.
If the soul were like the wind, if it were but conjunction with the wind, it would be visible like a whirl of air and would go off together with the troops of winds.
And if it is a conjunction with the wind, and if for that reason it perishes — then it is like another vessel of water poured out from the great ocean.
Or as water poured into a well, or a lamp cast into the fire, is swiftly lost when thrown in, even so does that soul perish.
In this body, which is the common ground of the five, whence comes life — when, by the loss of any one of them, there is no holding together of the remaining four?
Water perishes from want of food, the wind from the stopping of breath; space perishes from the breaking of the body's cavity, and fire perishes from lack of nourishment.
And the earthy element wastes away through disease, wounds, and afflictions; when any one of these is injured, the aggregate breaks apart fivefold.
When that body has dissolved into its five elements, what does the soul run after? What does the soul feel, or what does it hear or speak?
"This cow will carry me across when I am in the world beyond" — but when the creature who gives her dies, whom shall that cow carry across?
When the cow, the receiver, and the giver alike go to their dissolution here in this very world, whence shall there be any meeting of them again?
For one consumed by birds, or fallen from a mountain peak, or devoured by fire, whence shall there be any coming back to life again?
If, when a tree is felled, the root does not sprout again, yet its seeds carry on — but the dead man, where shall he come again?
Only the seed, created in the beginning, is what carries on; the dead, once dead, utterly perish — from seed alone does seed proceed.
Bhṛgu said: There is no perishing for living beings, nor for what is given and what is done. The living creature passes into another body, while only the body wastes away.
The living soul, though housed in the body, does not perish when the body is destroyed—just as fire does not perish when the firewood is burnt up.
Bharadvāja said: If the soul knows no destruction, just as fire does not, then why, when the fuel has been wholly consumed, is that fire no longer to be found?
I take it that a fire grown quiet for want of fuel has perished, for neither its course, nor its measure, nor its abiding form can any longer be seen.
Bhṛgu said: When the fuel is spent, the fire, though still existing, is not seen; for, having passed into the ether and being without support, it is hard to grasp.
So too, when the body is forsaken, the soul abides like the ether and cannot be grasped, by reason of its extreme subtlety—exactly as the fire is not grasped. Of this there is no doubt.
It is fire that upholds the vital breaths; know that fire to be the living soul. Sustained by the breath, that fire is extinguished when respiration is checked.
When that bodily fire is extinguished, the body, now bereft of consciousness, falls and returns to the state of earth; for earth is its final resting place.

In all things that move and likewise in all that are fixed, the wind merges into the ether and the fire follows after it. Therein lies the oneness of these three, while the remaining two are established in the earth.
Where there is space, there is wind; where there is wind, there is fire. These are to be understood as formless, whereas water and earth possess form.
Bharadvāja said: If fire and wind, earth, ether, and water are present in embodied beings, then what are the marks of the soul within them? Declare this to me, O sinless one.
The body of living beings is made of the five elements, delights in the five objects, and is joined with the five forms of perception. Of what nature is the soul within it? This I wish to know.
When the body—a compound of flesh and blood, a heap of fat, sinew, and bone—is cleft open, the soul is nowhere to be found within it.
If the body, though endowed with the five elements, is itself without a soul, then who is it that feels the pang, whether the pain be bodily or of the mind?
It is the soul that hears what is spoken; the ears do not hear it of themselves—for when the mind is distracted, nothing is heard. Hence, O great seer, the soul would seem to serve no purpose.
With the eye joined to the mind one sees all that is to be seen; but when the mind is troubled, one looks yet does not truly see.
Again, one overcome by sleep neither sees nor speaks, neither hears nor smells, nor knows touch and taste.
Who is it that rejoices and grows angry, that grieves and is dismayed? Who is it that desires, reflects, and hates, and who is it that utters speech?

Bhṛgu said: Here nothing belongs in common to the five elements; the inner Self alone, being one, bears the body. It it is that knows smells and tastes and sound, and touch and form, and whatever other qualities there are.

Within the fivefold frame, perceiving the five qualities and pervading every limb, dwells the inner Self. It it is that knows the pains and pleasures here; but once parted from it, the body knows nothing.
When the fire has neither form nor touch nor the quality of warmth, then, the bodily fire being quenched, the Self forsakes the body and passes from sight.
All this is made of water; water is the very substance of embodied beings. Therein dwells the Self—Brahmā born of mind, the world-maker present in all creatures.
Know that Self to be the very ground of the welfare of all the worlds—the one who dwells within this body as a drop of water rests upon a lotus leaf.
Know him to be the Knower of the Field, ever devoted to the good of the world; and know these—darkness (tamas), passion (rajas), and goodness (sattva)—to be the qualities of the living soul.
The wise call consciousness a quality of the soul; it acts and sets all things in motion. Beyond it they speak of the Knower of the Field—he who set in motion the seven worlds.

There is no destruction of the soul when the body is sundered; falsely do the unknowing call a man dead. The soul, passing into another body, journeys on; the breaking of the body is but the dispersal of its five elements.
Thus, hidden and enveloped, the soul moves within all beings; yet by the foremost, subtle intellect it is beheld by those who perceive the truth.
The wise man who, in the first and last watches of the night, ever yokes himself in concentration, eating but little and pure in soul, beholds the Self within the self.
For through the serenity of his mind, having abandoned action both good and evil, the man of tranquil soul, abiding in the Self, attains imperishable bliss.
The fire born of mind within bodies is what is called the living soul. Such is the creation of Prajāpati, set forth in this inquiry into the elements and the Self.
Bhṛgu said: First of all, Brahmā the Lord of creatures brought forth the brāhmaṇas alone, fashioned from his own radiance and shining like the sun and fire.
Then the Lord ordained, for the sake of heaven, truth and dharma, austerity and the eternal sacred lore, right conduct, and purity.
The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, daityas, asuras, and great serpents; the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and nāgas; the piśācas, and likewise human beings;
the brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras, O best of the twice-born, and whatever other hosts among the multitudes of beings there are—all these too he fashioned.
White was the color of the brāhmaṇas, red that of the kṣatriyas, yellow the color of the vaiśyas, and black that of the śūdras.
Bharadvāja said: If the four orders are to be distinguished by color, then surely among all the orders a mingling of colors is to be seen.
Desire, anger, fear, greed, grief, anxiety, hunger, and weariness arise in all of us alike; by what mark, then, is the order distinguished?
Sweat, urine, and dung, phlegm, bile, and blood—the body of every man oozes with these; by what, then, is the order distinguished?
Countless are the kinds of moving creatures and of fixed; among these, of so many varied colors, whence comes any fixed determination of order?
Bhṛgu said: There is in truth no distinction among the orders; this whole world is Brahman. Created of old by Brahmā, it came through deeds to its division into orders.
Those twice-born who, loving desire and pleasure, fierce, prone to wrath, and delighting in bold deeds, forsook their own dharma and turned ruddy of limb—these passed into the state of kṣatriyas.
Those who, taking up a livelihood among cattle and living by the plow, turned yellow and did not keep to their own dharma—these twice-born passed into the state of vaiśyas.
Those who, loving violence and falsehood, greedy, living by every kind of work, turned black and fell from purity—these twice-born passed into the state of śūdras.
Thus, sundered by these several deeds, the twice-born passed into other orders; yet dharma and the performance of sacrifice are never forbidden them.
These four orders, for whom the sacred speech of Brahman was ordained by Brahmā of old, through greed fell into a state of ignorance.
The brāhmaṇas who abide in the discipline of dharma—their austerity does not perish, for they ever uphold the sacred lore, the vows, and the restraints.
This sacred lore was brought forth of old, yet those who do not know it, being unlearned in it—from them arise, here and there, manifold other kinds of beings.
Piśācas, rākṣasas, and pretas, and the barbarian races in their many forms—their knowledge and discernment lost, given over to conduct and pursuits of their own willful choosing.

Those creatures who bear the consecrations of the brāhmaṇas and are resolved upon their own dharma are brought forth by the seers through their own austerity, while others again are created by other beings.
Sprung from the First God, rooted in Brahman, imperishable and undecaying—that creation is called the mind-born, wholly devoted to the discipline of dharma.
Bharadvāja said: By what does one become a brāhmaṇa, or a kṣatriya, O best of the twice-born, or a vaiśya, or a śūdra, O brāhmaṇa-sage? Declare this, O best of speakers.
Bhṛgu said: He who is consecrated and purified by the rites that begin with the birth-ceremony, accomplished in the study of the Veda, and established in the six duties;
who stands firm in purity and right conduct, eats only what remains after offering, holds his teacher dear, is constant in his vows, and devoted to truth—he indeed is called a brāhmaṇa.
In whom are seen truth, charity, self-restraint, freedom from malice, kindliness, forbearance, compassion, and austerity—he is remembered as a brāhmaṇa.
He who follows the work befitting a kṣatriya, is devoted to the study of the Veda, and takes delight in giving and receiving—he indeed is called a kṣatriya.
He who, pure, devotes himself unceasingly to farming, the tending of cattle, and trade, and is accomplished in the study of the Veda—he is named a vaiśya.
He who takes pleasure in eating all things, does every kind of work, is impure, has forsaken the Veda, and is without right conduct—he indeed is remembered as a śūdra.
If this mark be found in a śūdra and be lacking in one twice-born, then in truth the śūdra is no śūdra, nor is the brāhmaṇa a brāhmaṇa.
The curbing of greed and of anger by every means—this is to be known as the true purifier, and likewise the mastery of oneself.
One should ever guard one's austerity from anger, one's prosperity from envy, one's learning from honor and dishonor alike, and one's very self from heedlessness.
He whose every undertaking here is free from the bond of craving, and who has offered up everything in renunciation—he is the true renouncer, and he alone is wise.
Doing harm to no living being, let him walk in the way of friendliness toward all. Where there is no trust one should not go; where there is trust, let him fix his mind.
Casting off all possessions, let him through wisdom subdue his senses; thus he shall attain that sorrowless state, free from fear both here and hereafter.
The sage who is constant in austerity, self-controlled and self-restrained, desiring to conquer what is yet unconquered, must remain unattached amid all attachments.

Whatever is grasped by the senses—that is the manifest; such is the settled truth. But that which lies beyond the senses, to be apprehended only by inference through its marks, is to be known as the unmanifest.

Let him restrain the mind within the breath and hold the breath fixed in Brahman; passing from extinction into extinction itself, let him think upon nothing whatsoever. Brahman is bliss for the brāhmaṇa, and thereby indeed he attains it.
Ever joined to purity, endowed with right conduct, and full of compassion toward all beings—such is the mark of the twice-born.
Bhṛgu said: Truth is Brahman, truth is austerity; truth it is that brings forth all creatures. By truth the world is upheld, and by truth one goes to heaven.
Falsehood is the very form of darkness, and by darkness a man is led downward. Those seized by darkness do not behold the light, for it is veiled by darkness.
Heaven, they say, is light, and hell is darkness; both of these are reached by the wayfarers of the world according to their truth and falsehood.
In this world, then, the manner of life is of this twofold kind, mingled of truth and falsehood—dharma and its opposite, light and darkness, sorrow and likewise joy.
Therein, what is truth is dharma; what is dharma is light; what is light is joy. And therein, what is falsehood is unrighteousness; what is unrighteousness is darkness; what is darkness is sorrow.
Of the pains, bodily and mental, and of the pleasures whose end is yet pain, it is here spoken; and the discerning, beholding the creation of the world, are not deluded.
Therefore let the discerning man strive for release from sorrow; for the happiness of beings is fleeting, both in this world and in the next.
As the moonlight of the moon seized by Rāhu no longer shines, so for beings overwhelmed by darkness all happiness slips away.

That happiness, then, is said to be of two kinds—bodily and mental. Here and in the world beyond, all undertakings and exertions are declared to have happiness for their aim; for there is no fruit of the threefold ends of life more excellent than this. This is the desirable, the supreme good; the undertaking of dharma and of wealth is its cause, and its arising has happiness for its purpose.

Bharadvāja said: As for what you have declared—that women are the highest of pleasures—this we do not accept. For to these seers, established in greatness, this supreme good is not beyond reach, and yet they do not crave it. It is heard, moreover, that the Lord Brahmā, maker of the three worlds, abides alone, chaste, and does not give himself over to the pleasures of desire. And the Lord Umā's consort, the Sovereign of the universe, when Desire assailed him, brought him to quietude by rendering him bodiless. Therefore we say that this is not embraced by the great-souled, and that it is not, after all, so excellent a good. I cannot accept this from your honored self, though your honor has indeed said that women are the highest of pleasures.

Bhṛgu said: From falsehood, indeed, darkness arose; those seized by darkness follow after unrighteousness alone, and not dharma. Enveloped by anger, greed, delusion, pride, falsehood, and the like, they win no happiness, neither in this world nor in the next. They are strewn over by the torments of manifold diseases, and afflicted by killing, bondage, sickness, distress, and the like; they are tormented by the pains born of hunger, thirst, and weariness, and by the terrors born of fierce winds, excessive heat, and bitter cold. By bodily pains they are tormented, and by mental griefs born of the destruction and loss of kin and wealth, and by yet others born of old age and death, they are overcome.
But he who is untouched by these pains, bodily and mental, knows true happiness. These ills do not arise in heaven; there, indeed, it comes to pass that—
in heaven the breeze blows full of ease and the fragrance is sweet; there is no hunger, thirst, or weariness, no old age, and nothing evil.
In heaven there is unbroken happiness; here below both happiness and sorrow; in hell, they say, there is sorrow alone—but the supreme state is poised beyond them all, in perfect equanimity.
The earth is the mother of all beings, and women are of her nature; the male is Prajāpati, the lord of creatures, and in him they know the seed to be a thing made of radiant fire.
Such is the fashioning of the worlds, ordained of old by Brahmā; and creatures revolve through their births, each one enveloped by its own deeds.
Bharadvāja said: What fruit do they declare for giving, for the practice of dharma duly performed, for austerity well undergone, for recitation of the Veda, and for oblation offered into fire?
Bhṛgu said: By oblation sin is allayed; in recitation of the Veda is the highest peace; by giving, they say, comes enjoyment; and by austerity a man may attain all things.
Giving, they declare, is of two kinds: for the next world and for this. Whatever is given to the good awaits its giver in the world beyond.
But the gift that is given to the unworthy yields its enjoyment here below; for as a gift is given, so is the fruit obtained.
Bharadvāja said: What is the practice of dharma, and for whom? What is the mark of dharma? And of how many kinds is dharma? This you ought to tell me.
Bhṛgu said: Those wise ones who are devoted to the practice of their own dharma obtain the fruit of dharma; but he who does otherwise falls into bewilderment.
Bharadvāja said: As for this system of the four stages of life, ordained of old by the brahmin sages—the observances proper to each of them you ought now to tell me.

Bhṛgu said: Of old, by the Blessed One who acts for the welfare of the worlds, the four stages of life were appointed for the protection of dharma. Among these they name first the stage of dwelling in the teacher's house: there, rightly disciplined in purity, rite, modesty, and restraint, his self subdued, the student should at both twilights wait upon the sun, the fire, and the gods; casting off sloth and torpor, with his inmost being purified by salutation to the teacher, by study and the hearing of the Veda, he should touch water at the three sacred junctures of the day, ever devoted to the vow of chastity, to the tending of the sacred fire, and to service of his teacher; offering up to his teacher all that he gathers by begging and the rest, never adverse to carrying out the teacher's word and command, and intent upon that recitation which he wins by his teacher's grace.
The twice-born who, propitiating his teacher, attains the Veda—of him there is this verse: he wins the fruit of heaven, and his heart's desire is fulfilled.

The householder's life, indeed, they call the second stage; all the marks of its proper conduct we shall expound. For those who have completed their studentship and taken wives, who seek the fruit of practising dharma together, the household stage is ordained. Here is the attainment of dharma, wealth, and desire—the means to the threefold aim. With regard to that, taking wealth by blameless action—wealth won through eminence in Vedic recitation, or made by brahmin sages, or drawn from the heart of the mountains, or gained by the grace of the gods through the practice of oblation and restraint—the householder should carry on his household life. For this, they declare, is the root of all the stages of life; for from it alone do the shares of alms and offering proceed even to those who dwell in the teacher's house, to wandering mendicants, and to all others who keep their vows, restraints, and resolved observances of dharma.

And there is the furnishing of goods to the forest-dwellers. For the most part these are holy men, beholders of the good and wholesome path, devoted to recitation of the Veda, who roam the earth to visit the sacred fords and to behold its regions; toward them are owed the rising up to greet them, salutation, freedom from envy, gracious speech, a kindly face, and the honour, according to one's means, of a seat, a bed, and food.
From whose house a guest turns away, his hope broken—of this there is a verse: that guest, leaving his own ill deed behind for the host, departs taking the host's merit with him.

Moreover, in this stage the gods are gladdened by the rites of sacrifice, the ancestors by funerary offerings, the seers by the study, hearing, and retention of the Veda, and Prajāpati by the begetting of offspring.
Tender toward all beings, one should speak words pleasant to the ear; and here there are two verses on this: slander and injury, and harshness too, are here condemned.
Contempt, egotism, and hypocrisy are blamed; but non-violence, truth, and freedom from anger are the austerity that belongs to every stage of life.

And in this stage too there is the having of garlands, ornaments, garments, unguents, and perfumes; the delights of dancing, song, and music; sights that ravish the ear and please the eye; the enjoyment of foods of every kind—to be chewed, eaten, drunk, licked, and sucked; the contentment of dalliance with one's own wife; and the attainment of the pleasures of desire.
He in whose household life the qualities of the threefold aim are ever fulfilled—he, having known its joys here, attains the destiny of the virtuous.
The householder who lives by gleaning, delighting in the practice of his own dharma, who has renounced the pursuit of sensual pleasure—for him heaven is not hard to win.

Bhṛgu said: The forest-dwellers, following the dharma of the seers, roam practising austerity by the holy fords, the rivers and their springs, in well-secluded forests thronged with deer, buffalo, boar, wild antelope, and elephant. Having renounced the garments, food, and enjoyments of the village, they keep a measured, varied, and regulated diet of wild herbs, roots, fruit, and leaves. They stand or sit at their stations, sleeping on bare earth, on stones, gravel, sand, grit, or ashes, their bodies clad in kāśa and kuśa grass, in skins and bark, wearing their hair, beard, nails, and body-hair uncut. They touch water at the appointed times and perform without lapse the rites of oblation and offering at their due hours; their rest is won amid the gathering of fuel, kuśa grass, and flowers, the offering of oblations, and the cleansing for it. Their skin everywhere scorched and cracked by cold, heat, and wind, their flesh and blood worn away by the performance of dharma ordained in manifold restraints, disciplines of yoga, and observances, reduced to skin and bone yet supreme in steadfastness, they bear up their bodies by the power of their inner being.
And he who, self-restrained, follows this course of conduct ordained by the brahmin sages would burn away his faults as fire consumes, and would conquer the worlds that are hard to conquer.

Again, such is the conduct of the wandering mendicants: loosing themselves from attachment to fire, wealth, wife, and retinue, and shaking off the bonds of their own affection, they go forth as wanderers. To them a clod, a stone, and gold are all alike; their minds unattached to undertakings aimed at the threefold worldly aim, they bear themselves equally toward foe, friend, and the indifferent. By word, thought, and deed they do no harm to any beings—those born from the womb, from eggs, from sweat, those that sprout from the ground, or those that stand unmoving. Homeless, frequenting the mountains, the river-sands, the roots of trees, and the shrines of the gods, they go for lodging to a town or a village—five nights in a town, a single night in a village—and entering it, only to sustain their breath of life, they wait at the dwellings of the twice-born whose works are unmixed, taking such alms as fall unasked into their bowl, having turned away from desire, anger, pride, delusion, greed, meanness, hypocrisy, slander, conceit, and violence.
The sage who goes his way having granted freedom from fear to all beings—of him there is this verse: from no beings whatsoever does fear ever arise for him.

Having made the fire-offering reside within his own body, he who pours oblations into the fire of the body through his own mouth, with the offerings gathered in his round of begging, surpasses the worlds of those who tend the fire of the altar.

The twice-born who keeps the stage of liberation as it has been declared—pure, endowed with a well-resolved understanding—comes to rest in the world of Brahman, serene like a flame with no fuel to feed it.
Bharadvāja said: A world beyond this world is heard of, yet is not seen. That world I wish to know; this you ought to tell me.
Bhṛgu said: On the northern slope of the Himavat, a holy region endowed with every excellence, there lies a land that is holy, secure, and lovely—it is called the most blessed of worlds.
For there the people are free of sinful deeds, pure, utterly spotless, abandoned by greed and delusion, and untouched by any affliction.
That land is like heaven, for there, it is said, are auspicious qualities: death prevails only in its due time, and diseases do not touch them.

There is no coveting of others' wives; each man delights in his own wife. There is no slaying of one another, and no greed for goods; no dharma performed merely for show exists there, nor does doubt ever arise.

There the fruit of what is done is obtained before one's very eyes: some, furnished with couches, vehicles, and seats, dwelling in palaces and mansions, are surrounded by all that they desire, adorned with ornaments of gold.
To some there falls but enough to sustain the breath of life; and some, with great toil, manage barely to keep themselves alive.
Here below some men are devoted to dharma, others are deceitful; some are happy, some are wretched; some are without wealth, while others are rich.
Here arise toil, fear, delusion, and sharp hunger, and the greed of men bred of wealth, by which even the wise are led astray.
Here is anxiety of many kinds over deeds of dharma and of unrighteousness; the wise man who understands them both is not stained by sin.
Fraud with concealed design, deceit, theft, slander, fault-finding, the injuring of others, violence, calumny, and falsehood—
he who indulges in these, his austerity wastes away; but the learned man who does not commit them, his austerity grows ever greater.
This world is the field of action; having done here what is good or evil, by good deeds one attains good, and by doing evil, the opposite.
Here of old Prajāpati, and the gods together with the hosts of seers, having sacrificed and offered up their austerity, were purified and took their refuge in the world of Brahman.
The northern region of the earth is the holiest and most blessed of all; there are born those people of this world who are doers of meritorious deeds.
But others, doing evil deeds, are born in the wombs of beasts; and yet others, their span of life run out, perish upon the face of the earth.
Bent on devouring one another, possessed by greed and delusion, they revolve here below alone; they do not go to that northern quarter.
Those wise ones who, self-restrained and chaste, wait upon their teachers—they come to know the path to all the worlds.
Thus has this dharma, fashioned by Brahmā, been told by me in brief; for he who truly knows the dharma and the unrighteousness of the world, he is the wise one.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed by Bhṛgu, O king, the valiant Bharadvāja, that soul of highest dharma, in wonder paid homage to Bhṛgu in return.
This, O king, is the origin of the world, declared to you in full, O greatly wise one. What more do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The rule of right conduct, dear father, as you would set it forth, I wish to hear, O sinless one who knows the dharma; for in my judgment you are the knower of all things.
Bhīṣma said: Men of evil conduct, of evil deeds, of corrupt understanding, fond of reckless ventures—these are known abroad as the wicked; the good are marked by their right conduct.
Those men who pass neither dung nor urine on the king's highway, among cattle, or amid the grain—they are the virtuous.
Having performed the required cleansing and the satisfying of the gods with libations—this they call the dharma of men—one should touch water and so cross the river.

One should ever wait upon the sun, and should not sleep at the rising of the day-maker; murmuring the twilight prayer at evening and at dawn, one should keep both the first and the latter junctures of the day.
Moistened in the five places, facing east and keeping silence, one should take one's meal; one should not disparage food and victuals, but should eat both the savoury and the unsavoury.
One should not rise up with wet hands, nor sleep at night with wet feet—this mark of right conduct was declared by the divine seer Nārada.
A draught-ox that loves cleanliness, a temple-stall of the gods, a crossing of four roads, and a righteous brahmin—about these one should ever make the rightward circuit of reverence.
To share food in common with all guests, with servants, with one's own kin, and with dependants—this is praised in a man.
At evening and at dawn is the eating ordained by the gods for men; no meal between these is sanctioned, and so one becomes as a faster.
Offering oblation at the time of oblation, and approaching his wife at her fertile season, the wise man who has no traffic with any other woman becomes thereby as a celibate.
The leavings of a brahmin's meal are as nectar, made as it were the very heart of one's mother. Let a man wait upon truth; truth it is that the good revere.
Flesh consecrated with the sacrificial formula one who has turned away from the eating of flesh may take; but he should not eat flesh slain in vain, and should shun the flesh of the back.
Whether in one's own land or in another's, one should not let a guest go fasting; having won the fruit of voluntary rites, one should render it up to one's elders.
To one's elders a seat should be given, and salutation should be made; those who honour their elders are blessed with long life, with fame, and with fortune.
One should not gaze upon the rising sun, nor upon another's wife unclothed; and the lawful union one should practise in its proper season and in secret.
The holy ford of fords is the heart; the pure thing among pure things is the heart. All purification is that wrought by the noble, even down to the touching of a hair.
At every meeting one should ever utter a kindly inquiry after another's welfare; and to the brahmins, at evening and at dawn, salutation is prescribed.
In the temple-stall of the gods, among cattle, in the course of the brahmins' rites, in Vedic recitation, and in eating, one should keep the right hand uplifted.
Of wares one should praise the goodly ware; of tillage, that the ploughing prospers; of crops, that they yield abundantly; and of cattle, that the draught-beast draws well.
At a meal one should always say it is well-furnished; of the drink, that it satisfies; of the milk-rice, gruel, and pottage of sesame and rice, that they are well-cooked.
When the trimming of the beard is undertaken, when one sneezes, at bathing, and at eating, and for all the sick, a blessing of long life is the fitting greeting.
One should not make water facing the sun, nor look upon one's own ordure; and one should shun lying upon the same couch with a son's wife, and eating together with her.
The familiar "thou" and the calling by name one should avoid toward elders; toward inferiors and equals, with both alike, there is no fault in it.
The heart of those of sinful conduct betrays their sin by its disturbance; knowingly concealing it before the assembled people, they come to ruin.
The little-learned conceal the sin they have knowingly committed; men do not see them, but the dwellers in heaven see them.
For the sin done by the sinner follows after him as sin alone; and the dharma wrought by the righteous man follows after its doer.
The fool here remembers not the sin he has done; yet as the doer passes through his rebirths, it overtakes him—just as Rāhu comes upon the moon, so does the sinful deed come upon the witless man.
Wealth heaped up in hope, that is not enjoyed here in its season—the wise do not commend it; for death does not wait.
The wise declare that the dharma toward all beings is of the mind; therefore toward all beings one should bear oneself benevolently in mind.
Alone, each by himself, should one practise dharma; in dharma there is no fellowship. Once one has met one's appointed lot, what can a companion do?
The gods are the source of men, and the nectar of the gods is in heaven; in the state after death, the happiness that springs from dharma is enjoyed by them everlastingly.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: That which is here pondered concerning a man and bears the name of adhyātma, the inner self — what that adhyātma is, and from what it arises, tell me, grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: Since you ask me, O Pārtha, about this thing called adhyātma, I shall expound it to you, my child — that happiness which is the surest path to good.
Knowing which, a man finds joy and well-being in the world; its fruit is attained at once, and it works the welfare of all beings.
Earth, wind, ether, water, and fire as the fifth — these are the great elements, the source and the dissolution of all created things.
Sprung from them, into them again and again all things return — the great elements within beings, as the waves return into the sea.
As a tortoise stretches forth its limbs and draws them in again, so the Self of all beings, having sent forth the elements, withdraws them once more.
The maker of beings set the five great elements within all creatures, and made their unequal proportion among them; this the living soul beholds within itself.
Sound, the ear, and the bodily orifices — these three are born of ether; from wind come skin, touch, motion, and speech, these four.
Form, the eye, and digestion — this threefold is called the property of fire; taste, moisture, and the tongue are remembered as the three qualities of water.
Smell, the organ of smell, and the body — these three are the qualities of earth. The great elements are five, but the mind is called the sixth.
The senses together with the mind are its faculties of knowing, O Bhārata; the intellect they call the seventh, and the knower of the field is the eighth.
The eye serves only for seeing, the mind creates doubt, the intellect serves for determination, and the knower of the field stands by as a witness.
What lies above the soles of the feet, and what one sees below and above — know that by this all this inner expanse is pervaded.
In a man the senses are to be wholly understood; and know tamas, rajas, and sattva to be the states that rest upon them.
Having grasped this by the intellect, and considering little by little the coming and going of beings, a man attains the highest peace.
The intellect guides the qualities, and the intellect too guides the senses with the mind as their sixth; in the absence of intellect, whence the qualities?
Thus all this, the moving and the unmoving, is made of that; it dissolves and arises again, and therefore is so declared.
That by which one sees is called the eye, that by which one hears the ear; that by which one smells they call the nose, and by the tongue one knows taste.
By the skin one touches objects of touch; the intellect is again and again transformed; that by which one resolves upon some object — that is the mind.
The seats of the intellect, with their several objects, are fivefold; the five senses which they name — over these the Unseen presides.
The intellect, presided over by the soul, moves among three states: at times it gains delight, at times it grieves,
and at times it abides neither in pleasure nor in pain. Thus, established in three states, it dwells in the minds of men.
This intellect, whose very nature is these states, does not pass beyond the three of them — as the wave-bearing ocean, lord of the rivers, does not pass beyond its great shore.
When the intellect passes beyond a state, it comes to rest in another within the mind; for rajas, once stirred into motion, follows after that state.
For it ever sets all the senses to work. Delight is sattva, grief is rajas, and delusion is tamas — these are the three.
Whatever states there are in this world, they all lie within these three. Thus has the whole course of the intellect been expounded to you, O Bhārata.
All the senses are to be conquered by the wise; sattva, rajas, and tamas ever cleave to living creatures.
And a threefold sensation is seen in all beings — the sāttvika, the rājasa, and the tāmasa, O Bhārata.
The touch of pleasure is the quality of sattva, the touch of pain the quality of rajas; when joined with the quality of tamas, both become beyond the reach of ordinary dealing.
Whatever is joined with delight, arising in body or in mind, there the sāttvika state prevails — so let one then regard it.
And whatever is joined with pain and breeds discontent of the self — let one calmly reflect that rajas has been set in motion.
And whatever is joined with delusion, that which is as if unmanifest, beyond reasoning and not to be known — let one mark that as tamas.
Exultation, delight, joy, happiness, tranquillity of mind — these, however they may arise, are the sāttvika qualities.
Discontent, torment, grief, greed, and impatience — these are the marks of rajas, seen with cause and without cause.
Conceit, delusion, heedlessness, sleep and drowsiness — these, however they may arise, are the manifold tāmasa qualities.
The mind ranges far, runs many ways, and is the very seat of craving and doubt; he whose mind is well restrained is happy, both in the hereafter and here.
Behold this distinction between the subtle pair, the mind-stuff and the knower of the field: the one sends forth the qualities, the other sends forth no qualities.
As the gnat and the fig are forever conjoined, yet are each other's other, so is the conjunction of those two.
Distinct by nature, yet ever conjoined — as fish and water are conjoined, even so are those two.
The qualities know not the Self, but he knows the qualities in every way; he is the beholder of the qualities, yet he ever thinks himself their author.
With the senses, of which the intellect is the seventh — motionless and unknowing — the Supreme Self performs the office of a lamp, like a lamp itself.
For the mind-stuff sends forth the qualities, and the knower of the field looks on; this is the abiding conjunction of those two, the mind-stuff and the knower of the field.
There is no resting-place for the mind-stuff, nor any for the knower of the field; the mind-stuff sends forth the mind, but never the qualities.
When by the mind he rightly reins in their rays, then his Self shines forth, like a lamp burning within a jar.
The sage who, abandoning the works of nature, takes constant delight in the Self, and becomes the very self of all beings — he attains the highest goal.
As a water-ranging bird, though it dips, is not stained, even so the man of perfected wisdom moves among beings.
Knowing such to be its very nature, let a man move through life with his own understanding, neither grieving nor exulting, and act free of envy.
By the working of its own nature it constantly sends forth the qualities, fully formed, as a spider sends forth its thread; the qualities are to be understood as like that thread.
Once destroyed, they do not return, yet their cessation is not directly perceived; what is beyond the senses is established by inference from what is seen.
Thus some conclude, while others hold that there is cessation; weighing both these views, let one decide according to one's own understanding.
Loosing thus the hard knot of the heart, woven of the divisions of the intellect, let one dwell in ease; with doubt cut away, let one grieve no more.
As stained men, plunging into a brimming river, attain purity, so, O wise one, know this knowledge to be.
As one who knows the farther shore is not distressed in crossing a great river, even so are they who know the adhyātma, that highest knowledge which is absolute oneness.
Having grasped all this, and considering little by little, with the intellect, the coming and going of all beings, a man thereby attains the supreme peace.
He to whom the threefold aim is known, who is a light foregoing all, is set free; seeking with the mind, disciplined, a seer of truth, free of longing.
And the Self cannot be seen divided among the senses, scattered here and there, hard to conquer for those whose selves are unperfected.
Having understood this, one becomes awakened; what other mark of the awakened is there? Knowing it, the wise reckon themselves to have done all that is to be done.
For the wise there is none of that fear which would be the great fear of the ignorant; for no one has any goal beyond it, though, where a quality is present, men speak of inequality.
What a man does without forethought of aim wipes out what was done before; that twofold deed is neither hateful — whence then pleasing? — for him who acts thus, it bears its fruit here.
Behold in the world the afflicted folk, crying out and grieving much over this and that; and behold there the skilled who grieve not, who ever know that twofold state.
Bhīṣma said: Come, I shall declare to you, O Pārtha, the fourfold yoga of meditation, knowing which the supreme sages attain everlasting perfection.
Even as meditation is rightly to be practised, so do the yogins practise it — the great sages, content in knowledge, their minds gone to nirvāṇa.
They return no more, O Pārtha, freed from the flaw of rebirth; the taint of birth worn away in them, they are established in their own true being.
Beyond the pairs of opposites, abiding ever in purity, liberated, ever taking refuge in things unattached, undisputed, and bringing peace to the mind.
There let the sage hold his mind one-pointed, cleaving to sacred study; gathering the host of the senses into one, let him sit motionless as a log.
Let him not catch sound with the ear, nor feel touch with the skin, nor perceive form with the eye, nor tastes with the tongue.
All objects of smell too let the knower of yoga abandon through meditation; the strong man should not desire these things that torment the fivefold band of senses.
Then, the discerning one, having dissolved the fivefold band into the mind, should compose the wandering mind together with the five senses.
The mind, ranging abroad, without support, five-gated, ever shifting — in the first path of meditation let the steadfast one bring it inward and compose it.
When this man gathers the senses and the mind into one, this is the first path of meditation, which I have described.
That mind of his, restrained at the first, with the senses as its sixth, will soon quiver and start up bewildered, as lightning flashes in a thunder-cloud.
As a drop of water, restless upon a leaf, trembles on every side, even so does his thought become upon the path of meditation.
Composed for a brief moment, it rests upon the path of meditation; then again the wandering mind takes the road of the wind, restless as the wind.
Undespairing, his distress gone, his drowsiness gone, free of envy, let the knower of the yoga of meditation again compose his thought through meditation.
Reflection, reasoning, and discernment arise in the sage who composes himself — this is the first meditation, from the beginning.
Though tormented by the mind, let him still bring about composure; let the sage not fall into despair, but work the welfare of his own self.
As heaped-up piles of dust, ashes, and dung, suddenly drenched with water, do not yield to thorough soaking,
and as dry, unmoistened powder may grow but a little damp, yet step by step, slowly, all of it comes to be thoroughly soaked,
even so let him slowly steep the host of the senses, and draw it in step by step; thus will it be rightly stilled.
The mind itself, O Bhārata, and the fivefold band, having reached the first path of meditation, are stilled by constant practice of yoga.
Neither by human effort nor by any working of fate does such happiness come to a man—that happiness belongs only to him whose self is thus restrained.
United with that happiness, he delights in the labor of meditation; for thus the yogins go to that nirvāṇa which is free from all affliction.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: You have expounded the four stages of life and likewise the duties of kings, and many ancient narratives of diverse kinds, resting on various themes.
From you, O great-minded one, I have heard discourses joined with dharma; yet one doubt remains in me, and you should resolve it.
I wish to hear, O descendant of Bharata, the reward attained by those who practice recitation. What fruit is declared for those who murmur the sacred words, and in what abode do such reciters dwell?
And you should tell me, O blameless one, the whole rule of recitation. What is this matter of the reciters—is it the practice of Sāṃkhya, or of Yoga, or of ritual action?
Is this merely a rite of sacrifice, or what is it that is called the muttered prayer? Declare all this to me, for in my judgment you are the knower of all things.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they relate an ancient tale—what once befell of old between Yama, and Kāla, and a certain brāhmaṇa.

In the Vedānta, renunciation alone governs the practice of recitation; the peace that arises from the teaching of the Vedas rests in Brahman. Both these paths abide there—and yet are not so wholly abiding.
As it is heard among men, O king, so the reason shall be set forth here; and herein concentration of the mind, as also the conquest of the senses, is taught.
Truthfulness, the tending of the sacred fire, the frequenting of solitary places, meditation, austerity, self-restraint, patience, freedom from envy, and moderate eating—
the withdrawal from objects of sense, sparing speech, and tranquility—this is the dharma of active engagement; now hear of the dharma of withdrawal.

As action ceases for the celibate who practices recitation, so should he abandon all this without remainder, just as it has been taught, having reached the threefold path—the manifest, the unmanifest, and that which has no support.
Seated upon a heap of kuśa grass, kuśa in hand, his crown of hair bound with kuśa, wrapped in bark garments, and there in the midst veiled about with kuśa—
he should make obeisance to the objects of sense yet dwell upon them no longer; having brought the mind to evenness, he should set the mind upon the mind alone.
With the intellect he meditates upon Brahman, murmuring the salutary sacred text; or else, established in deep absorption, he lays even that text aside.
Here he generates meditation through the support and power of the sacred text—pure of self, subdued by austerity, freed from hatred and desire,
without passion or delusion, beyond the pairs of opposites, he neither grieves nor clings; he is no doer of deeds that ought not to be done, nor of deeds that ought—such is his abiding.
He should never set the mind in motion through the working of egoism, nor be intent upon grasping at the self; he is neither contemptuous nor wholly inactive.
Devoted to the practice of meditation, disciplined, full of meditation, resolute in meditation, having generated deep absorption within meditation, he by degrees relinquishes even that.
In that very state, having renounced all things, happy and without striving, he gives up his vital breaths and takes refuge in the body of Brahman.
Or else, if he desires not the dwelling in the body of Brahman, he ascends, abiding on the path, and is born no more anywhere at all.
Established in the knowledge of the Self, become tranquil and free from affliction, he attains the Self—immortal, stainless, and pure.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The highest of attainments among destinies has been told for the reciters here. Is this their one and only goal, or do they go to another as well?
Bhīṣma said: Listen attentively, O king and lord, to the destiny of the reciters, how they go to many a hell, O bull among men.
The reciter who does not perform this as it was taught before, but practices it only in part, descends here into hell.
He who performs it with contempt, who feels neither contentment nor remorse—such a reciter goes to hell; of this there is no doubt.
And all who are made of egoism are bound for hell; the man who despises others shall become one who descends into hell.
He who, deluded, performs his recitation with covetous longing—wherever he directs that longing, to that very hell he comes.
And the reciter who turns toward lordly power takes delight therein; that very thing becomes his hell, and from it he is not released.
The reciter who, deluded, performs his recitation out of passion—wherever his passion falls, there and there again he is born.
The man of evil mind, his wisdom unformed, who abides in a wavering mind, goes to a wavering destiny, or else attains hell.
The reciter who is a fool, his wisdom unformed, falls into delusion; through that delusion he goes to hell, and having gone there, he grieves.
The reciter who, clinging stubbornly with the thought "I am the doer," murmurs his prayer—neither perfected nor disciplined—attains hell.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: That supreme, causeless, unmanifest reality abides in Brahman; the reciter who has become real—why then should he enter a body again?
Bhīṣma said: Through false understanding many hells have been declared; the office of the reciter is praiseworthy, yet these faults belong to its very nature when misused.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What manner of reciter goes to hell? Describe this to me, for curiosity has arisen in me, and you should tell it.
Bhīṣma said: You are born as a portion of Dharma, and by your very nature you are most righteous; listen attentively, O blameless one, to a discourse whose root and refuge is dharma.
Those abodes yonder of the gods, the supreme-souled ones, of manifold forms and colors and of manifold shapes and fruits—
the celestial palaces that move at will, and the assembly halls, and the varied pleasure-gardens, O king, and the lotus-ponds of unsullied waters—
the abodes of the four guardians of the worlds, of Śukra and of Bṛhaspati, of the Maruts, the Viśvadevas, the Sādhyas, and the Aśvins as well,
and of the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the other dwellers in heaven—all these, my son, are but hells compared with the abode of the Supreme Self.
That state is free from fear and without cause, not enveloped in the dread of affliction—freed from the two, freed from the three, from the eight and again from the three.
It is devoid of the four marks and free from the four causes, without elation, without rejoicing, without sorrow, its weariness wholly gone.
There Time itself is ripened; there Time holds no dominion. That Self, O king, is the lord of Time and likewise the ruler even of heaven.
Having reached the absolute aloneness of the Self and gone there, one grieves no more. Such is that supreme abode, and such are those hells beside it.
All these hells have been declared to you exactly as they are; compared with that highest abode here, all are reckoned as hells.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: The dispute among Kāla, Mṛtyu, and Yama, and the brāhmaṇa, O most excellent one, was mentioned before; you should now relate it.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they relate an ancient tale—what befell Ikṣvāku, the son of the Sun, and a brāhmaṇa.
And of Kāla and Mṛtyu likewise—learn from me what befell them: how that converse of theirs came about, and in what place it took place.
There was a certain brāhmaṇa, a reciter, of righteous conduct and great renown, knower of the six Vedāṅgas, exceedingly wise—a Kauśika of the Paippalāda line.
His knowledge of the six Vedāṅgas was direct and immediate, and he was deeply versed in the Vedas as well; he dwelt at the foot of the Himālaya.
He performed the supreme austerity proper to Brahman, restrained, murmuring the sacred text; and so a thousand years passed for him under that vow.
To him the Goddess showed herself in person, saying, "I am pleased"; yet he, still murmuring his recitation, kept silent and said nothing to her at all.
Out of compassion for him the Goddess became gladdened then; and so the Mother of the Vedas honored that recitation of his.
Then, his recitation completed, the righteous-souled one rose and bowed his head at the feet of the Goddess, and spoke these words:
"By good fortune, O Goddess, you are gracious to me and have come into my sight; and if indeed you are pleased, let my mind delight in recitation."
Sāvitrī said: What do you seek, O sage among brāhmaṇas? What desired thing shall I do for you? Speak, O best of those who recite, and all that shall be yours.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed by the Goddess, the brāhmaṇa, knower of dharma, then said: "Let my desire toward recitation grow stronger again and again.
And may the concentration of my mind increase day by day, O auspicious one." "So be it," the Goddess then answered him sweetly.
And the Goddess, wishing to do him a further kindness, spoke this besides: "You shall never go to that hell to which other bulls among the twice-born have gone.
You shall go to the abode of Brahman—the causeless, the blameless. I shall accomplish this, since you have entreated me here."

"Recite, restrained and single-minded, and Dharma will come to you. Kāla, Mṛtyu, and Yama too shall come into your presence, and there shall be a dispute, in accordance with dharma, between you and them."
Having spoken thus, the blessed Goddess went to her own abode; and the brāhmaṇa too remained reciting then for a celestial hundred years.
When that vow of the wise brāhmaṇa was completed, Dharma, well pleased, then showed himself in person to that twice-born one.
Dharma said: O twice-born one, behold me—I am Dharma, come to look upon you. Hear from me too what fruit of recitation you have attained.
All the worlds have been won by you, both the celestial and the human; transcending all the hells of the gods, O virtuous one, you shall go beyond.
Give up your vital breaths, O sage, and go to the worlds you desire; abandoning your own body, you shall then attain those worlds.
The brāhmaṇa said: Enough of the worlds for me, O Dharma; go you wherever you please. I will not cast off this body, lord, with all its many sorrows and joys.
Dharma said: Inevitably, sir, your body must be relinquished, O bull among sages. Let heaven be ascended, O brāhmaṇa—or what else, O blameless one, is your pleasure?
The brāhmaṇa said: I take no pleasure in dwelling in heaven apart from this body, lord. Go, Dharma; I have no wish to go to heaven without my own self.
Dharma said: Cease to set your mind upon the body; cast off the body and be happy. Go to the stainless worlds, where, once gone, you grieve no more.
The brāhmaṇa said: I delight in reciting, O illustrious one; enough of the eternal worlds. Either I shall go to heaven with my body, lord, or not at all.
Dharma said: If you do not wish to give up your body, then behold, O twice-born one—here are Kāla, and Mṛtyu, and Yama, come to you.
Bhīṣma said: Then the son of Vivasvat, and Kāla, and Mṛtyu—these three, O lord—approaching that illustrious brāhmaṇa, spoke thus:
"Of this austerity, well performed and well conducted, the attainment of fruit is supreme for you. I am Yama, and I speak to you.
Duly have you attained the highest fruit of this recitation; the time has come for you to ascend to heaven. I am Kāla, and I have come to you.
Know me to be Mṛtyu, O knower of dharma, come in person in embodied form, urged on by Kāla, O brāhmaṇa, to lead you hence this very day."
The brāhmaṇa said: Welcome to the son of the Sun, and to the great-souled Kāla, and to Mṛtyu, and to Dharma. What service shall I render you?
Bhīṣma said: Having offered them the welcome-water and water for the feet at that meeting, he, exceedingly pleased, said: "By my own power, what may I do for you?"
At that very time, O lord, having undertaken a pilgrimage to the sacred fords, Ikṣvāku came there, to the place where those sages were assembled.
That royal sage, the best of kings, honored them all and bowed before them, and inquired after the welfare of every one of them.
Then the brāhmaṇa, having offered him a seat, water for his feet, and the guest-offering, and having exchanged greetings of welfare, spoke these words.
"Welcome to you, great king. Tell me whatever you desire here. What may I do for you according to my power? Let your honor declare it to me."
The king said: "I am a king, and you are a brāhmaṇa, established in the six prescribed duties. I shall give you some wealth; tell me what you would ask of me."
The brāhmaṇa said: "Brāhmaṇas, O king, are of two kinds, and dharma too is held to be twofold—the path of engagement and the path of withdrawal. I have withdrawn from the acceptance of gifts."

"Give your gifts, O ruler of men, to those who follow the path of engagement; I do not accept them. What is your wish? What may I give you? Tell me, O best of kings—what shall I accomplish for you by my austerity?"
The king said: "I am a kṣatriya; I know not anywhere the word 'give to me.' 'Grant me battle'—such is the speech we are wont to utter, O best of the twice-born."
The brāhmaṇa said: "You are content with your own dharma, and so, O king, are we content with ours. Neither has the upper hand over the other; do then as you wish."
The king said: "You said before, 'I shall give according to my power.' I beg of you: let the fruit of this japa of yours be given to me, O twice-born one."
The brāhmaṇa said: "You boasted that your speech ever asks only for battle. Yet there is no battle between you and me—why, then, do you now ask of me at all?"
The king said: "Brāhmaṇas are said to be armed with the thunderbolt of speech, while kṣatriyas live by the strength of their arms. This, O sage, is a fierce war of words between you and me."

The brāhmaṇa said: "That same pledge of mine still stands even now. What shall I give you according to my power? Tell me, O lord of kings, and I shall give it without delay, so far as my means allow."
The king said: "That fruit which you have won by reciting your prayer through a full hundred years—give that to me, if your honor is minded to give."
The brāhmaṇa said: "Then let the highest fruit of what I have recited be taken. Receive, without hesitation, half the fruit thereof."
"Or rather, O king, take the whole fruit of my recitation as you wish, if it is everything that you desire here."
The king said: "I have no need of the whole—blessings upon you. I asked only for the prayer's fruit. May it be well with you; I shall go. But tell me, what is that fruit?"
The brāhmaṇa said: "I know not what fruit I have won; I have given what I recited. Let Dharma here, and Time, and Yama, and Death be witnesses to this."
The king said: "What use to me is the fruit of this merit, when its measure is unknown? Let the sage keep that fruit; I do not wish for what is uncertain."

The brāhmaṇa said: "I shall not take back what I have given; the fruit has been given by my word, and a word once given may not be gainsaid. The spoken word is binding, O royal sage—upon me and upon you alike."
"Never in any way did I make a calculation of gain in my recitation. O tiger among kings, how then should I know its fruit?"
"'Give to me,' was said by you, and 'I give,' was said by me in answer. I shall not falsify my word; guard the truth, and stand firm."
"If now you will not honor my word, spoken thus, a great unrighteousness will fall upon you, O king, wrought by your own falsehood."
"It is not fitting for you to utter a false word, O subduer of foes; and still less can I bring myself to speak falsely."
"I promised before, without reservation, 'I shall give.' Take it, then, without hesitation, if your honor stands in truth."
"For having come here, O king, you begged of me the fruit of my recitation. Take, then, what I have surrendered, and stand firm in truth."
"For the man addicted to falsehood there is neither this world nor the next; he cannot deliver his forefathers—how much less, O king, his descendants?"
"Neither sacrifice, nor Vedic study, nor giving, nor the vows can deliver a man in the world beyond, O bull among men, as truth can."
"The austerities you have already performed, and the austerity you shall yet perform through hundreds and thousands of years—none of it surpasses truth."
"Truth is the single-syllabled brahman; truth is the single-syllabled austerity; truth is the single-syllabled sacrifice; truth is the single-syllabled sacred lore."
"Truth keeps watch within the Vedas; the highest fruit is held to lie in truth. From truth come dharma and self-restraint; all things rest upon truth."
"Truth is the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; truth is the sacrifice and its ordinance; truth too is the practice of vows; and truth is the very syllable Oṃ."
"Truth is the birth of living beings, and truth is their continuance. By truth the wind blows on its course; by truth the sun gives forth its heat."
"By truth the fire burns; heaven is established upon truth. Truth is the sacrifice, the austerity, the Vedas, the chants, the sacred verses, and the goddess Sarasvatī."
"Dharma and truth, so we have heard, were once set upon a balance; and while the two held the scale even, truth proved the weightier."
"Where there is dharma, there is truth; all things grow by truth. Why, then, O king, do you wish to do an act of untruth?"
"Set your heart firmly upon truth; commit no falsehood, O king. Why do you make of your inauspicious word, 'give to me,' a thing of untruth?"
"If you will not receive the fruit of the recitation given by me, O king, then, fallen from your own duties, you will wander through the worlds in misery."
"He who, having promised, will not give, and he who, having begged, will not receive—both these are men of untruth. You ought not to make yourself false."
The king said: "To fight and to protect—such, indeed, is the dharma of the kṣatriya, O twice-born one. Kṣatriyas are called givers; how, then, should I take from you?"
The brāhmaṇa said: "I did not solicit you, O king, nor did I come to your house. You it was who came here and begged of me; how, then, will you now refuse to receive?"
Dharma said: "Let there be no dispute between you two. Know me to be Dharma, come hither in person. The brāhmaṇa is endowed with the fruit of giving, and the king with the fruit of truth."
Heaven said: "Know me, O lord of kings, to be Heaven, come here in embodied form. Let there be no dispute between you two; you both are equal in the fruit you have earned."
The king said: "I have no business with heaven; go, O Heaven, as you please. If the sage wishes to give, then let him in turn accept my wealth."
The brāhmaṇa said: "If in my childhood, through ignorance, I once stretched out my hand to receive, yet now I follow the dharma marked by withdrawal, reciting the sacred text."

"Me, a brāhmaṇa long withdrawn from the world, why, O king, do you seek to tempt? I shall accomplish my purpose by my own means; I desire no fruit from you, O king. Devoted to austerity and to sacred study, I have ceased from the acceptance of gifts."
The king said: "If, O sage, the highest fruit of your recitation has been surrendered by you, then whatever fruit belongs to us two, let it here be held by us together."
"The twice-born are appointed to receive, and those born of royal lineage to give. If dharma has been truly heard by us, O sage, then let the fruit be shared by us both."
"Or else, let there be no sharing between us: take then the fruit that is mine. Accept the merit I have wrought, if you would show me your grace."
Bhīṣma said: Then two men of strange demeanor appeared, ill-clad, clutching and clinging to each other, and spoke these words.
"You owe me nothing," said the one; "I do owe you," said the other. "This is the dispute between us; let this king be our judge."
"I speak the truth in this: you owe me nothing." "It is you who speak falsely here; I do owe a debt to you."
The two of them, both sorely troubled, said this to the king: "Let the matter be examined, so that we two may not stand here in disgrace."
Virūpa said: "O tiger among men, I owe to Vikṛta here the fruit of a cow; yet though I would pay it, Vikṛta will not accept it from me, O lord of earth."
Vikṛta said: "This Virūpa owes me nothing at all, O ruler of men. He speaks falsely, and it is to you, O king, that he makes this false appearance."
The king said: "Virūpa, what is it that you owe to him? Tell me, and having heard it I shall act accordingly—such is the resolve of my mind."
Virūpa said: "Listen attentively, O king, how it is that I owe this to Vikṛta here, in its entirety, O royal sage, O bull among men."
"Long ago, O sinless one, this man, for the sake of gaining merit, gave a fine milk-cow, O royal sage, to a brāhmaṇa devoted to austerity and sacred study."
"And I, O king, came to Vikṛta and begged of him the fruit of that gift; and Vikṛta gave it to me with a wholly purified inner heart."
"Thereafter I did a meritorious deed for my own purification: I bought two tawny cows, fond of their calves and abundant in milk."
"And those two, O king, I bestowed, as was prescribed and with full faith, upon one who lived by gleaning. That same merit, O lord, I would now once more render back to him."
"Having received that, I would now repay it here twofold for the one cow. O tiger among men, who in this matter is in the right, and who at fault?"
"Thus disputing, we two have come before you here, O king. Do what is right or what is wrong, but settle us in due conduct and resolve our quarrel."
"If he will not accept my gift, even as this man once gave to me, then let your honor, standing firm in this, set us upon the right path, O lord."
The king said: "Why do you not accept the debt now offered to you? Even as it has been granted to you, so receive it without delay."
Vikṛta said: "'Let it be given,' was said by him, and 'I give,' was said by me. He owes me nothing in this matter; let him go wherever he wishes."
The king said: "You do not accept it though he offers—this seems to me unjust. You, I judge, deserve punishment; of that there is surely no doubt."
Vikṛta said: "I gave it to him, O royal sage; how then should I take it back again? If herein lies my offense, decree my punishment, O lord."
Virūpa said: "If you will in no wise accept what is offered by me, then this king, the upholder of dharma, will restrain and chastise you."
Vikṛta said: "What was my own I gave here when begged of me; how should I take it back again today? Go, your honor—I grant you leave to depart."
The brāhmaṇa said: "You have heard, O king, what these two have related. Take, then, without hesitation, what I promised to you."
The king said: "A weighty matter is here laid before us two, deep as a thicket. How shall this firm resolve of the reciter be carried through?"
"If, then, I do not accept what the brāhmaṇa has surrendered, how shall I not today be tainted with a grievous fault?"
Bhīṣma said: And that royal sage said to the two: "Your purpose accomplished, you may now depart. Let it not be, now that you have come to me, that the dharma of kings should prove false."
"One's own dharma must be upheld—such is the firm conclusion for kings. Yet the dharma of the brāhmaṇa weighs heavy; it has entered me, who am no longer master of myself."
The brāhmaṇa said: "Take it; I owe it to you. I have heard your request. If you will not receive it, O king, I shall surely curse you—of that there is no doubt."
The king said: "Shame upon the dharma of kings, which decides such a matter thus! For this reason I must accept it—how else might the scales be made even?"
"Behold, O sir, this hand of mine is stretched out as never before, to receive the deposit. What you owe me, O sage, let it now be given."
The brāhmaṇa said: "Whatever merit I have gained by reciting the sacred text—receive it all, if indeed any merit of mine exists."
The king said: "This water has fallen upon my palm, O best of the twice-born. Let it be shared, let it be held in common—and let your honor too accept it."
Virūpa said: Know us two to be Desire and Wrath; it was by us that you were made to act. And as for the equality of which you spoke, your worlds and his are indeed equal.
This brāhmaṇa holds nothing back from you; this testing was done for your sake. Time, Dharma, and Death, Desire and Wrath — such are you two.
All has been rubbed together upon the touchstone of mutual proof, as you have seen. Go now to the worlds you have won by your own deeds, wherever you wish.
Bhīṣma said: I have fully proclaimed to you the attainment of fruit by the reciters — the course, the abode, and the worlds, and how they are won by the reciter.
He who studies the saṃhitā goes forth to Brahmā the Supreme; or else he draws near to Agni, or enters into the Sun.
If, through his fiery nature, he takes delight there, then, deluded by attachment, he assumes the qualities of those realms.
So too in Soma and in Vāyu; clothed in the body of earth and ether, still bound by attachment, he dwells there, partaking of their qualities.
But if there he becomes free of attachment, he passes beyond all uncertainty; longing for the supreme and imperishable, he enters into That alone once more.
Having passed from the immortal to the immortal, grown cool, freed of self-clinging, become Brahman, beyond all pairs of opposites — he is happy, at peace, and untouched by ill.
He attains that abode of Brahman from which there is no returning, the One named the Imperishable — that station free from sorrow, free from age, and serene.
Transcending the Puruṣa that is marked off by four signs, by six, and by sixteen, he attains the ether-like Absolute.
But if, his nature still passionate, he desires, he presides over all that; and whatever he prays for, that he attains by the mind alone.
Or else, free of craving and released from all things, he looks upon all the worlds set forth before him as in a hall, and rejoices there in happiness.
Such, great king, is the course of the reciter. All this I have declared to you. What further do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When that had been spoken, what answer did the two then make — the brāhmaṇa, or else the king? Tell me that, grandfather.
Or did the two then depart to that place of which you have spoken? What dialogue passed between them, and what did they do there?
Bhīṣma said: Having assented, saying "So be it," and having honored Dharma, O lord, and reverenced the worthy ones — Yama, Time, Death, and Heaven —
and having bowed his head to all the bulls among brāhmaṇas, those of old and the others assembled there, the brāhmaṇa spoke these words to the king:
"Endowed with this fruit, O royal sage, go to your holy reward; and with your leave I would recite once more."
"For long ago, O mighty one, the goddess granted me a boon, O lord of peoples: 'Faith shall be ever yours as you recite.'"
The king said: "If thus your perfection bears no fruit, yet you have faith to recite, then come, brāhmaṇa, along with me, and obtain the reciter's reward."
The brāhmaṇa said: "A very great effort has been made here in the presence of all. Equal in fruit, let us two go together to wherever our course leads."
Bhīṣma said: Knowing the resolve of the two, the lord of the thirty gods drew near, together with the gods and likewise with the guardians of the worlds.
The Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the Maruts, and the mighty luminaries, the rivers, mountains, and oceans, and the many places of pilgrimage —
the austerities, the rule of ritual conjunction, the Vedas, the chanted syllables, Sarasvatī, Nārada, and Parvata, Viśvāvasu, Hāhā and Hūhū —
the gandharva Citrasena with his retinue of attendants, the nāgas, the siddhas, and the sages; the God of gods, Prajāpati; and Viṣṇu the thousand-headed, the inconceivable deity — all came together.
In the midspace, O lord, kettledrums and trumpets sounded; divine showers of blossoms fell upon those great souls, and troops of apsarases danced everywhere on every side.
Then Heaven himself, in visible form, spoke these words to the brāhmaṇa: "You are perfected, O blessed one; and you too are perfected, O king."
Then, O king, the two together, each in due order, both performed the withdrawal of the senses from their objects.
Prāṇa and apāna, udāna, samāna, and vyāna — having fixed these breaths in the mind, they then placed the mind upon the vital breaths.
Steady in their posture there, the two slowly held the mind, with eyes upon the tip of the nose, below the brows, fixed upon the seat within.
With bodies wholly motionless, gaze unwavering, deep in concentration, masters of their seat, they fixed the very self within the crown of the head.
Then, bursting through the region of the palate of the great-souled brāhmaṇa, a vast flame of light went up to the third heaven.
Then a great cry of wonder arose in all the quarters; and that light, hymned with praise, entered then into Brahmā.
Then the Grandfather, rising to meet that radiance — the Puruṣa no larger than a span — said "Welcome," O lord of peoples.
And further he spoke another word, a sweet one: "The yogins have a fruit equal to that of the reciters — herein is no doubt."
"For yoga the fruit, in comparison with these, is direct vision; but for the reciters the rising-up to meet them is a greater distinction still."
Saying "Let him dwell in me," he then restored him to awareness once more; and the brāhmaṇa, his fever of passion gone, entered into His mouth.
The king too, by this same method, entered then into the blessed Grandfather, just as the tiger among brāhmaṇas had done.
Then the gods, having saluted the Self-Existent, spoke: "This effort was for the reciter's sake, and for that we have come."

"These two have been honored alike by you, and alike in their fruit. The fruit of the yogin and of the reciter has this day been seen to be very great. Let these two pass beyond all the worlds and go wherever they wish."
Brahmā said: "Whoever recites the Mahāsmṛti, and likewise the auspicious Anusmṛti — those two also, by this method, would attain to a shared world with me."

"And whoever is devoted to yoga — he too, of this there is no doubt, would by this method attain my worlds at the body's end. Let it be so; I shall bring it about, that each may reach his proper station for perfection."
Bhīṣma said: Having spoken thus, the god then vanished on the spot; and the gods, taking their leave of him, departed each to his own dwelling.
And all those great souls, having honored Dharma there, followed after, O king, all of them with hearts well pleased.
This is the fruit of the reciters, and their course has been proclaimed, just as I have heard it, great king. What further do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What is the fruit of the yoga of knowledge, of the Vedas, and of self-restraint? And how is the Self of beings to be known? Tell me that, grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recite an ancient story — the discourse between Manu the Lord of creatures and the great sage Bṛhaspati.
Bṛhaspati, the great sage, foremost of the host of divine seers, bowing as a disciple to his teacher, asked this ancient question of Prajāpati, the most excellent upon the earth:

"For what cause is the rite of sacred formulas set in motion? What fruit do the brāhmaṇas declare to lie in knowledge? And that which is not made manifest by the words of the formulas — let it be told to me truly, O blessed one."

"That great fruit which is sought by those versed in the treatises, the scriptures, and the formulas, through many sacrifices and gifts of choice cattle — what is it, and how, and where shall it come to be?"

"The earth and earth-born things, the wind and the midspace, the water-dwellers and the water, the heaven and the heaven-dwellers — that ancient source from which they sprang, let it be told to me, O blessed one."
"Since a man longs for knowledge, his striving is directed to that end. Yet I do not know the supreme and ancient One — and how then should I undertake a striving that is false?"

"Though I have studied the Ṛc and the bodies of Sāman and the Yajus chants, the meters, the course of the constellations, etymology, grammar with the ritual codes, and phonetics — still I do not know the primordial nature of beings."
"Let your honor declare to me all this: what fruit there is in knowledge or in action; and how the embodied one falls away from the body, and how it comes again to a body."

Manu said: Whatever is dear to a man they call his pleasure; that very same thing, when unwished-for, they call his pain. "May the wished-for be mine, and may the other not be" — for this the rule of action is set in motion. "May neither the wished-for nor the unwished-for come upon me" — for this the rule of knowledge is set in motion.

The works of ritual action in the Vedas are rooted in desire; freed from these, a man may attain the Supreme.
