As men behold the season, the year, the lunar days, cold and heat, the pleasant and the unpleasant, all as things gone by—of such a kind is the dissolution of a living being.
For when one is beset by old age or by perishing death, what is weakest perishes first, just as the weakest part of a house gives way before the rest.
The senses, the mind, the breath, the blood, the flesh, and the bone perish each in its order and return into their own elements.
The ordering of the world's affairs, the coming of the fruits of giving and of duty, the very purpose for which the words of the Veda exist, and the customs of common life—
thus, when rightly weighed in the mind, these many grounds for doubt are present; and saying 'this exists, that exists,' one arrives at no certainty at all.
For those who ponder thus, running after this conclusion and that, the understanding settles somewhere at last, and there it grows old like a rooted tree.
Thus all creatures, made wretched by gains and by losses, are dragged about by the scriptures as elephants are dragged about by their drivers.
Coveting riches and the things that bring boundless pleasure, these many men squander all and, falling into a still greater misery, let go the bait and pass into the power of death.
For one who perishes, whose life is unstable, what use are kinsmen and the keeping of friends?—for he who departs leaves all behind, and once gone in an instant, returns no more.
For earth, ether, water, fire, and wind forever sustain the body; perceiving this, whence should delight arise?—for one who is perishable, no lasting refuge is to be found.
Beholding this speech, free of guile, without deceit, supremely sound, attested by the self, the king was amazed, and set himself once more to inquire thus.
Bhīṣma said: But Janaka, lord of his people, having been instructed by the supreme sage, inquired yet again concerning being and non-being in the world beyond.
Reverend one, if it be that after death some consciousness arises for someone, then in that case what will ignorance avail, or what will knowledge accomplish?
All would end in annihilation—consider this too, O best of the twice-born: what difference will it make whether a man be heedful or heedless?
For if there is no contact among the elements, or contact only among perishable things, for whose sake should one strive after a rule? What here is certain in truth?
To him, veiled in darkness, bewildered as it were, and distressed, the sage Pañcaśikha, calming him once more with his words, spoke.

There is here no ending in annihilation, nor is there any abiding in fixed existence; for this aggregate too—of body, senses, and mind—operates, each part resting upon the other in their several works.
The elements are this fivefold branching—ether, wind, fire, water, earth; by their own nature they hold together, and by their own nature they fall apart.
Ether, wind, heat, moisture, and whatever is earthen—this fivefold gathering is called the body, manifold in nature; knowledge, heat, and wind make up the threefold sum of action.
The senses and their objects, the inherent nature, consciousness, the mind, the outbreath and inbreath, the modifications, and the elements—all these issue forth here.
Hearing, touch, the tongue, sight, and the nose as well—these five are called the senses, qualities led on by the mind.
Therein, joined with discernment, is the abiding threefold feeling, which they call pleasure, pain, and that which is neither pain nor pleasure.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, and then bodily shape—these five, six-qualitied, persist until death for the accomplishing of knowledge.
In them lies the issuing of action and the determining of the meaning of all truths; that they call the supreme radiance, the understanding, imperishable and great.
For one who beholds this aggregate of qualities as though it were the self, the endless misery born of false views does not subside.
And when it is seen as 'not the self,' then neither 'I' nor 'mine' holds sway: upon what foundation can the clinging stream of misery then rest?
Here there is right-mindedness, the supreme teaching of renunciation: hear it, as it is spoken, for it shall be for your liberation.
For renunciation alone is the way; of all the works that are enjoined, when wrongly practiced, the constant toil is held to be but a bringer of pain.
In the renouncing of wealth lie ritual acts; in the renouncing of enjoyment, the vows; in the renouncing of pleasure, the discipline of austerity; but in the renouncing of all, fulfillment.
This path of all-renunciation, free of duality, has been shown for the casting off of misery; otherwise an evil course would be the lot of man.
Having named the five organs of knowledge, with the mind as the sixth in consciousness, I shall now declare the five organs of action, the mind again being the sixth.
The two hands are to be known as the organ of action, the two feet as the organ of motion, the generative member for begetting and for pleasure, and the anus as the organ of excretion.
And speech, for the sake of particular sounds, they know as the fifth, attended by the others; thus the mind, with the understanding, should set free these eleven.
The two ears, sound, and the mind—these three make up the grasping of what is heard; so too in touch, in form, and likewise in taste and smell.
Thus these qualities are five triads for the apprehending of their objects, whereby each threefold state arises in its turn.
The sāttvika, the rājasa, and the tāmasa—these are the three, in which the threefold feeling, with all its means, is brought forth.
Elation, fondness, joy, happiness, a wholly tranquil mind—arising from no cause or from some cause within the mind—this is the sāttvika quality.
Discontent, anguish, grief, greed, and impatience—these are the marks of rajas; they are seen to arise with cause or without.
Want of discrimination, delusion, heedlessness, sleep, and torpor—however they come to be, these are the manifold tāmasa qualities.
Therein, whatever arises in body or in mind joined with delight, one should regard as the working of the sāttvika state.
But whatever is joined with affliction and unpleasing to the self, one should reflect that rajas has there come into play.
And whatever arises in body or mind joined with delusion, beyond reasoning and beyond knowing, that one should understand to be tamas.
For that being which rests upon the ear—sound abides in the ear; yet neither of the two suffices, by itself, for the cognition of sound, nor for any other cognition.
So too the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth—in touch, form, taste, and smell—these, together with awareness and the mind.
The simultaneous functioning of their own activities resides in these ten; know awareness to be the eleventh, and understanding shall be the twelfth.
When these do not function together, there is no tāmasic annihilation; but when they rest in simultaneous action, that is the ordinary commerce of the world.
Even having released the senses, having earlier seen what was heard from tradition, one who reflects does not roam astray, being attended by these three qualities alone.
When the mind, stricken by darkness, swiftly makes an unsteady wandering and comes to rest in time, that they call the tāmasa pleasure.
Whatever, joined to scriptural lore, does not wholly come to rest—there too it takes on darkness, manifest like untruth.
Thus has this quality been enumerated, conditioned by its own activity; in some it functions rightly, in some it functions not at all.
Thus the ponderers of the inner self call this aggregate the field; and the conscious state that abides in the mind is called the knower of the field.
This being so, what annihilation is there, or how should there be anything eternal, when all beings act from their own nature, each by its proper cause?
As rivers that have entered the ocean abandon their distinct forms and their names, yet do not surrender their own substance—of such a kind is the dissolution of a being.
This being so, whence should consciousness arise again in the state after death, when the living self is wholly commingled and is grasped only midway?
But he who knows this insight of release, and unwearying seeks the self, is not stained by the unwished-for fruits of action, as a lotus-leaf is not by the water poured upon it.

Freed from the many firm bonds—those of offspring and of the gods—when he abandons both pleasure and pain, then, liberated and without mark, he attains the highest course; and beyond the proofs of scripture, the lore of tradition, and its rites of blessing, he reposes, passed beyond the fear of old age and death.
When merit is spent and sin has departed, and the fruit that springs from these has perished, the unattached, taking their stand upon the stainless, markless ether, behold the great.
As the spider, turning round and round, abides though let fall when its thread is spent, so the liberated one casts off misery, which is shattered as a clod that strikes against a mountain.
As the ruru deer leaves behind its old horn, or as the serpent in due course casts its skin, and goes without a backward glance, so the liberated one abandons misery.
As a bird, forsaking a tree that is falling into the water, flies off unattached, so this one, abandoning pleasure and pain, liberated and without mark, attains the most exalted course.
And there is too this verse sung by the king of Mithilā, who, beholding his city set ablaze with fire, said himself, so it is told—'Truly, not even a husk of mine is burning here.'

This station of immortality the king of Videha, having himself been here instructed by Pañcaśikha, surveyed in its entirety and with its meaning made certain; and supremely happy, freed of grief, he went his way.

For he who recites this teaching, sure of liberation, never falls away and ever beholds it thus; he does not suffer calamities, free of grief, and is released, as the king of Mithilā was upon coming to Kapila.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Doing what does a man attain happiness, doing what does he meet with misery, and doing what does he move through the world fearless and perfected, O descendant of Bharata?
Bhīṣma said: The elders, grounded in the sacred lore, praise self-restraint above all—self-restraint for every one of the social orders, and for the Brāhmaṇa most especially.
For one who is not self-controlled, the due accomplishment of rites is not obtained; rite, austerity, and the Vedas—all rest upon self-restraint.
Self-restraint increases one's spiritual power; self-restraint is called the purifier; the self-restrained man, free of sin and fearless, attains the great.
The self-restrained man sleeps in ease and awakens in ease; he moves through the world in ease, and his mind grows serene.
Spiritual power is upheld by self-restraint; the harsh man does not attain it, and forever he sees within himself a host of separate enemies.
As from beasts of prey, so from the unrestrained there is ever fear for living beings; for their restraint the king was created by the Self-Existent.
In all the stages of life self-restraint is held supreme; and whatever fruit there is in the duty of those stages, a greater is declared to lie in self-restraint.
I shall tell the marks of those whose sum is self-restraint: absence of meanness, freedom from agitation, contentment, and a trusting heart;
freedom from anger, constant uprightness, no overbearing speech, no conceit, honoring of elders, freedom from envy, compassion toward beings, and absence of slander;
the shunning of gossip, of falsehood, of praise and of blame; desiring the good and coveting nothing, such a man wins the trust of men.

Stirring no enmity, of gracious conduct, equable in blame and praise, of good ways, endowed with character, serene in spirit, master of himself, and wise—he gains honor in the world and, after death, goes to heaven.
Devoted to the welfare of all beings, he hates no man out of pride; unshakable as a great deep lake, sated with wisdom, he abides serene.
Since from him there is no fear to any being, and security to all, the self-restrained and wise man becomes one worthy of the homage of all creatures.
He neither exults in great gain nor grieves in calamity; he, of measured wisdom, is called the self-restrained, O twice-born one.
Endowed with sacred learning and with good and auspicious deeds practiced by the virtuous, ever joined with self-restraint, such a man enjoys a great reward.
Freedom from envy, patience, tranquillity, contentment, gentle speech, truthfulness, charity, and freedom from restlessness — this is not the path of the wicked of soul.

Having mastered desire and anger, chaste and conquering his senses, the brāhmaṇa of stern vows, striving valiantly in dread austerity and awaiting his hour, should walk the worlds self-possessed, as one beyond all harm.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: When the twice-born, devoted to their vows, eat this oblation, this food intended for the brāhmaṇas — how is that, grandfather?
Bhīṣma said: Those who, observing vows not enjoined by the Veda, eat thus are merely doers of deeds; and those who eat while bound by vows the Veda enjoins are breakers of their vows, Yudhiṣṭhira.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: That which the common folk call austerity — namely fasting — is this austerity, O great king, or what truly may austerity be?

Bhīṣma said: That which people deem austerity — fasting for a month or a fortnight — is but the ruin of one's own self-discipline; it is not austerity, so the good hold. Renunciation and humility — these are taught to be the highest austerity.
One should ever be a faster and ever a celibate; the wise man should ever be a sage and should ever worship the deity.
A householder devoted to dharma, ever wakeful, O Bhārata, should ever abstain from flesh and should ever recite the sacred texts.
He should ever eat what is like nectar and never feed on what is like poison; he should ever be one who eats the leavings of the offering, and ever cherish his guests.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How is one ever a faster, how a celibate, how an eater of the offering's leavings, and how ever a cherisher of guests?
Bhīṣma said: He who never eats anything at all between the morning meal and the evening meal — he is the perpetual faster.
The brāhmaṇa who approaches his wife only in her season is a celibate; and that man is so who is ever truthful in speech and ever devoted to knowledge.
He who does not eat flesh taken in vain becomes an abstainer from flesh; ever charitable and pure, and wakeful even though he sleep by day.
He who eats only after his dependants and guests have eaten — know, Yudhiṣṭhira, that such a one wholly partakes of nectar.
That twice-born one who never eats until others have eaten — by such abstention is heaven won by him.
He who eats only what remains after the gods, the ancestors, the dependants, and the guests have been served — him they call an eater of the leavings of the offering.
For such men there are worlds without end in the abode of Brahmā; attended by apsarases, they move about as dwellers of heaven.
Those who partake of food together with the gods and the ancestors, and who delight in their sons and grandsons — theirs is the most surpassing destiny.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Whatever deed is done in this world, whether good or evil, surely binds a man to the yoking of its fruit, O Bhārata.
Is man indeed the doer of that deed, or is he not? — such is my doubt. This I wish to hear from you in its truth, grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: On this point too they recount an ancient tale, the dialogue between Prahrāda and Indra, Yudhiṣṭhira.
Unattached, his sins shaken off, nobly born and deeply learned, free of rigidity, free of self-conceit, established in goodness, devoted to right conduct —
holding blame and praise alike, self-controlled, dwelling in an empty house, knowing the rising and the passing-away of beings both moving and unmoving —
never angered, never elated amid things unwelcome or welcome, looking with an even eye on both gold and a clod of earth —
steadfast in the knowledge of the soul's highest good, firm in resolve, knowing the higher and lower of beings, all-knowing, looking on all alike —
Śakra, desiring to understand that wisdom of his, approached Prahrāda — seated apart, his senses restrained — and spoke thus.
Whatever qualities make a man esteemed among men in this world — all those qualities, never departed from you, do we observe in you.
And yet your mind seems here level with that of the simple folk. Regarding yourself as you do, what do you hold to be the good in this world?
Bound in fetters, fallen from your station, brought under the power of your foes, bereft of fortune — Prahrāda, in a plight to be mourned, you do not mourn.
Is it through the attainment of wisdom, O Daitya, or through firmness of resolve, that you remain serene in form, Prahrāda, even as you behold your own calamity?
Thus urged by him, the steadfast one, firm in his resolve, spoke in gentle words, setting forth his own wisdom.
He who does not understand the arising and the ceasing of beings — in him there is rigidity born of folly; but for one who perceives truly there is no rigidity.
From their own nature all states of being arise and likewise cease, both the existent and the non-existent; human effort has no place therein.
And in the absence of human effort there is no agent of one's own; but for him who fancies he acts of himself, conceit may sometimes arise here.
He who deems himself the doer of good and of ill — his wisdom is flawed, ignorant of its own true form: such is my judgement.
If man were truly the doer for his own welfare, O Śakra, then surely his undertakings would all succeed, and he would never meet defeat.
For even among those who strive, the coming-to-pass of the undesired and the not-coming-to-pass of the dear is seen; whence, then, is human effort efficacious?
We see, for some men, the coming-about of the undesired and the gaining of the desired without any effort at all — that comes of their nature.
Some comely of form and most excellent in intellect are seen craving the gain of wealth from men ill-formed and of little intellect.
When all the qualities, fair and foul, settle upon a man, driven by his own nature — then what cause is there for his pride therein?
All this proceeds from nature alone — such is my settled conviction. My wisdom rests within the self; for me there is nothing otherwise.
Yet here I hold the yoking of fruit, fair or foul, to be born of deeds; the whole domain of deeds I shall declare — hear it.
As a crow by its cawing makes known its boiled rice, even so are all deeds but the mark of one's own nature.
He who knows only the modifications and knows not the supreme primal nature — in him there is rigidity born of folly; but for one who perceives truly there is no rigidity.
For one who, in firm conviction, understands that all states of being arise here from nature — what can arrogance or conceit do to him?
I know the whole ordinance of dharma and the impermanence of beings; therefore, O Śakra, I do not grieve, for all this is bound to come to an end.
Free of mine-ness, free of self-conceit, free of craving, released from bondage, serene and undeparted from myself, I behold the rising and the passing-away of beings.
For one whose wisdom is perfected, who is self-controlled, free of thirst and free of craving, who sees through the knowledge of the world — no toil of mind remains, O Śakra.
In primal nature and in its modifications I have neither attachment nor aversion; nor do I see any foe who today claims me as his own.
Not above, not below, not athwart, nor anywhere, O Śakra, do I desire aught; neither in knowing, nor in the knowable, nor in not-knowing is any refuge found.
Śakra said: By what is this wisdom won, by what is peace attained? Declare to me that means, Prahrāda, rightly, as I ask.
Prahrāda said: By uprightness, by vigilance, by serenity, by self-possession, and by service to the elders, O Śakra, a man attains the great.
From nature he gains wisdom, by nature he comes to peace; from nature alone is all that whatsoever you behold.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed by the lord of the Daityas, Śakra fell to wonder; and well-pleased then, O king, he honoured those words.
Then the sovereign lord of the three worlds, having honoured the Daitya chief, took leave of the lord of the Asuras and departed to his own abode.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: With what understanding should a king, fallen from his fortune, crushed by the rod of Time, wander over the earth? Tell me that, grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: On this point too they recount an ancient tale, the dialogue between Vāsava and Bali, the son of Virocana.
Having conquered all the Asuras, Vāsava approached the Grandsire, bowed down with hands joined in reverence, and asked about Bali.
He whose wealth, however much he gave, was never once diminished — that Bali I cannot find. O Brahmā, tell me where Bali is.
It was he who set as the sun, he who illumined the quarters, he who, unwearying, poured down the rains in their season. That Bali I cannot find. O Brahmā, tell me where Bali is.
He was the Wind and Varuṇa, he the Sun and the Moon; he was Agni who warms all beings, and he the very Earth. That Bali I cannot find. O Brahmā, tell me where Bali is.
Brahmā said: This is not seemly in you, O Maghavan, that you ask this; yet one questioned should not utter falsehood — therefore I shall tell you of Bali.
Among camels, or among cattle, among asses, or again among horses, that creature shall come to dwell, the best of his kind, in an empty house, O lord of Śacī.
Śakra said: If, O Brahmā, I should meet with Bali in that empty house, should I slay him or not slay him? Instruct me in this, O Brahmā.
Brahmā said: Do not, O Śakra, harm Bali; Bali does not deserve to be killed. Yet you may, Vāsava, question him on points of right, as you please.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed by the Blessed One, great Indra then ranged over the earth, mounted upon the shoulder of Airāvata and girt with majesty.
Then he beheld Bali, cloaked in the form of an ass, having made his dwelling in an empty house, just as the Blessed One had foretold.
Śakra said: Fallen into the womb of an ass, you feed now on chaff, O Dānava. This birth of yours is the lowest — do you grieve, or do you not grieve?
What never was seen, that, alas, I now behold: you come under the power of your foes, bereft of fortune and of friends, your might and valour fallen away.
Once, surrounded by your kinsmen with a thousand chariots, you would go scorching all the worlds, holding us as nothing.

With you at their head, the Daityas stood obedient to your command, and under your sovereignty the earth yielded harvests untilled. And now this calamity is yours — do you grieve, or do you not grieve?
When you stood upon the eastern shore of the ocean, licking your lips as you distributed wealth to your kinsmen — how then was your mind?
When women of the gods, gathered in their thousands, danced for you through many a span of years in your pleasure-garden, you blazing with splendour —
all of them garlanded with lotuses, all of them gleaming like gold — how is your mind now and how was it then, O lord of the Dānavas?
Yours was a great parasol of gold, adorned with gems, beneath which the gandharvas danced, six thousand of them in seven bands.
Yours, as you sacrificed, was a vast sacrificial post all of gold, where you gave away ten myriads of thousands of cattle.
And when, as sacrificer, you ranged over the whole earth by the rite of casting the yoke-pin — what then was in your heart?
I do not see your golden vessel, nor your parasol, nor your fan; nor do I see the garland given you by Brahmā, O sovereign of the Asuras.
Bali said: You do not see my golden vessel, nor my parasol, nor my fan; nor shall you see the garland given me by Brahmā, O Vāsava.
You ask after my jewels, but they are laid away in a hidden cavern; when my time shall come again, then you shall behold them.
Yet this does not befit either your renown or your lineage—that you, whose ends are fulfilled, should wish to taunt me, whose ends are unfulfilled.
For in sorrows they do not grieve, nor in prosperities do they exult—those wise and good men whose insight is perfected, who are satisfied in knowledge and patient of heart.
But you, Puraṃdara, boast with a common mind; when you shall come to be as I now am, then you will speak no longer in this fashion.
Bhīṣma said: Then once more, O Bhārata, Śakra, laughing, spoke thus to him—who was hissing forth speech like a serpent—provoking him to answer.
Once, encircled by your kinsmen with a thousand chariots, you would ride forth scorching all the worlds, holding us as nothing—
and now, O Bali, beholding this most pitiable condition of your own, forsaken by kinsmen and friends—do you grieve, or do you not grieve?
Having of old won matchless delight and held the worlds within your sway, do you now grieve at this downfall, or do you not grieve?
Bali said: Perceiving this turning of Time upon myself to be impermanent, therefore, Śakra, I do not grieve; for all this surely has its end.
These bodies of living beings have an end, O lord of the immortals; for that reason, Śakra, I do not grieve, nor is this state of mine the fruit of any wrongdoing.
Life and the body, departing hence, are born together; together the two grow, and together the two perish.
Having come, helpless, merely to such a state of being as this—if I understand it thus, what anguish can there be for me who knows?
Destruction is the appointed end of beings, as the ocean is the end of rivers; men who rightly understand this are not bewildered, O wielder of the thunderbolt.
But those who do not so understand, given over to passion and delusion, sink down on meeting hardship, they whose discernment is destroyed.
For on attaining wisdom a man casts off all his taint; freed from evil he gains purity of being, and abiding in that purity he grows wholly serene.
But those who fall back from it, or are born again and again, the wretched ones, are tormented, driven on by misfortunes.
Success and failure, life and likewise death, and whatever yields the fruit of pleasure or of pain—I neither hate nor desire.
The man who slays anyone slays one already slain, and himself is already slain; neither of those two understands—neither he who slays nor he who is slain.
Whoever, O Maghavan, plays the man by slaying and conquering, is in truth no doer at all; rather it is the Doer alone who does that deed.
For who brings about, for the world, both its destruction and its arising? What is done is done by that very doing, and even of that doer there is another beyond.
Earth, wind, ether, water, and fire as the fifth—from these elements all creatures spring; over that, what room is there for lamentation?
The man of great learning and the man of little, the strong and the weak, the fair to look upon and the misshapen, the fortunate and the luckless—
Time, profound, gathers all to itself by its own power; when one has come under Time's dominion, what anguish can there be for me who knows?
It burns only what is already burned, and slays only what is already slain; only what is already lost is lost, and a man obtains only what was beforehand his to obtain.
It has no island—how then a farther shore?—nor is any nearer bank to be seen; pondering it, I behold no end to this divine ordinance.
If, while I looked on, Time did not destroy created beings, then there might be in me joy and pride and wrath, O lord of Śacī.
But knowing me a husk-eater in a house emptied of people, wearing the form of an ass, you point me out and revile me.
Yet were I to wish it, I could fashion my own self into many shapes—shapes so terrifying that, at the mere sight of them, it is you who would flee from me.
Time takes all to itself, Time bestows all; by Time is everything ordained—do not make a show of manly prowess, Śakra.
Of old, when I was wrathful, O Puraṃdara, all things trembled; yet I know, Śakra, the eternal law that governs this world.
Do you too consider this, and do not yield to self-conceit; neither origin nor might ever rests within oneself.
Your mind is still that of a boy, as much today as it was before; reflect, O Maghavan, and attain the wisdom that is final and resolved.
Gods, men, the fathers, gandharvas, serpents, and rākṣasas—all were once within my sway; all that you know well, O Vāsava.
"Homage be even to that quarter wherein dwells Bali Vairocana"—thus they would approach me, bewildered by their grudging minds.
I do not lament for that, nor for my own downfall, O lord of Śacī; so settled is my conviction—I abide in the power of the Ruler.
For one is seen, born of high family, comely and full of valor, living in misery together with his ministers—because it was destined so to be.
And one of mean family, a fool, ill-born, is seen, O Śakra, living in happiness together with his ministers—because it was destined so to be.
A woman fair and graced with beauty is seen unfortunate, O Śakra; while one without auspicious marks and ill-formed is seen fortunate, O Śakra.
This was not wrought by me, Śakra, nor was this wrought by you, O Śakra—that you have come to such a state, O wielder of the thunderbolt, or that we have come to such a state as this.
It is no deed of yours, nor of others—how then of mine, O Śatakratu? Prosperity, or want of prosperity, is wrought merely by the turning of Time.
I see you shining in splendor, the king of the gods established in your place, glorious and radiant, and thundering over me.
And were it not that Time stands thus, having overpowered me, I would this day strike you down with my fist—thunderbolt and all.
But this is no time for valor; this is the time of forbearance that has come. Time establishes all; Time, even so, ripens all to its consummation.
If Time has come upon me, the mighty lord of the dānavas, thundering and scorching—upon whom else will it not come?
For the splendors of all twelve of you great-souled Ādityas were once carried off by me single-handed, O king of the gods.
It was I who drew up the waters and I who poured them down, O Vāsava; I who scorched the three worlds, and I alone who gave them light.
I guarded and I plundered, I gave and I took away, I bound and I restrained—lord and master over all the worlds.
All that dominion of mine has now departed, O lord of the immortals; overwhelmed by the armies of Time, nothing of it shines forth for me any more.
I am not the doer, nor are you, nor is any other the doer, O lord of Śacī; for the worlds are enjoyed in their turn, Śakra, just as it chances.
Those who know the Veda call it the dwelling of months and fortnights, enclosed by day and night, having the seasons for its doors and the year for its mouth.
Some men, by their reflection, declare all this to be a matter for meditation; and of this fivefold meditation I shall make my inquiry in five ways.
Brahman is profound and unfathomable, vast as the ocean of waters; and they declare it to be without beginning or end, the imperishable, the supreme.
Having entered into creatures as their distinguishing mark, it is yet in itself without mark; the men who perceive the truth hold it to be ever-abiding and eternal.
One thinks, "it has departed," mistaking the transformation of beings for that; but it could not be a thing to be reached merely thus, since it is beyond Nature itself.

For it is the goal of all beings; not having reached it, where will you go? It cannot be outrun by one who runs, nor left behind by one who stands still; and the five senses, in any of their five ways, do not perceive it.
Some call it Agni, some call it Prajāpati, and others the seasons, the months, the fortnights, the days, and likewise the moments.
Others call it the forenoon, the afternoon, the midday; yet others call it the muhūrta—calling that which is one by many names. Know that to be Time, in whose power all this lies.
Many thousands of Indras have passed away, O Vāsava, endowed with strength and valor even as you are, O lord of Śacī.
And you too, O Śakra, exceedingly strong, king of the gods, towering in might—when the hour comes, mighty Time will lay to rest.
It is that which seizes all this to itself; therefore, Śakra, be steadfast. By me, by you, and by those before us, it could never be overpassed.
This unsurpassed royal Fortune that you have won and think, "she abides in me"—that is false; for she stays nowhere in one place.
She has dwelt with thousands of Indras far more distinguished than you; and the fickle one, abandoning me, has gone over to you, O lord of the wise.
Do not act thus again, Śakra; it behooves you to be at peace. Forsaking you too when you have come to such a state, she will swiftly pass on to another.
Bhīṣma said: Then Śatakratu beheld the radiant Fortune of the great-souled Bali, in her own embodied form, even then departing from his body.
Seeing her shining with such brilliance, the blessed Pākaśāsana, the lord Vāsava, his eyes wide with wonder, questioned Bali.
"O Bali, who is this crested one, gleaming and beautiful, who has stepped forth from you and stands there, adorned with armlets, blazing with her own splendor?"
Bali said: I know her neither as an asura-woman, nor divine, nor human; question her yourself, or do not—do as you please, O Vāsava.
Śakra said: Who are you, O crested and gleaming one, who have stepped forth from Bali? Tell me, who do not know it, your name, O you of bright smile.
Who are you that stand there like an apparition, blazing with your own splendor, having forsaken the lord of the daityas, O fair-browed one? Tell me that in truth.
Śrī said: Neither Virocana knew me, nor Bali Vairocana; they call me Duḥsahā, the Unendurable, and they know me too as Vidhitsā, the Will-to-ordain.
They call me Bhūti and Lakṣmī, and Śrī as well, O Vāsava; you, Śakra, do not know me, and all the gods know me not.
Śakra said: Why is this, O Duḥsahā—is it for my sake, or is it for Bali's sake that you forsake him, you who have dwelt with him so long?
Śrī said: Neither the Ordainer nor the Disposer disposes of me in any way; it is Time, Śakra, working through its turnings. Do not, O Śakra, despise him for this.
Śakra said: How was Bali forsaken by you, and for what cause, O crested one? And how would you not forsake me too? Tell me that, O you of bright smile.
Śrī said: I rest in truth, in giving, in the keeping of vows, in austerity, in valor, and in dharma; but Bali has turned away from these—therefore I have left him.
Having ever been devoted to the brahmans, truthful of speech, his senses subdued, he came to spite the brahmans, and, defiled by leavings, he touched the clarified butter.
Having of old been devoted to sacrifice, this man, his soul deluded and oppressed by Time, declared to the worlds, "Worship me alone."
Cast off from him, then, O Śakra, I shall dwell in you, O Vāsava; but I must be upheld by one ever-heedful, through austerity and through valor.
Śakra said: Is there among gods and men, or among all beings, any single man able to bear you alone, O dweller in the lotus?
Śrī said: Neither god, nor gandharva, nor asura, nor rākṣasa—there is none, O Puraṃdara, who is able to bear me alone.
Śakra said: Tell me, O blessed one, in what manner you might abide in me forever; that word of yours I shall fulfill—and it behooves you to speak the truth.
Śrī said: I shall abide with you forever, O lord of the gods, in the manner you desire. Mark this well: by the ordinance ordained in the Veda, divide me fourfold.
Śakra said: I shall indeed set you in place to the best of my power and strength; yet let there never be any overstepping by me, O Lakṣmī, while I remain near you.
Among men it is the Earth herself, the all-bearing, the mother of beings, who can endure your foot, for she is able—so I hold.
Śrī said: Here is one foot of mine set down, this one that rests upon the Earth. Now, O Śakra, set my second foot firmly in its place.
Śakra said: It is the Waters among men, flowing and ministering to all, that shall endure your foot; the Waters are equal to enduring it.
Śrī said: Here is one foot of mine set down, this one that rests upon the Waters. Now, O Śakra, set my third foot firmly in its place.
Śakra said: He in whom the gods and the sacrifices, in whom the Vedas are established—Agni—shall bear your third foot, held firm and secure.
Śrī said: Here is one foot of mine set down, this one that rests upon the Fire. Now, O Śakra, set my fourth foot firmly in its place.
Śakra said: Those who among men are the good, devoted to brahman and speakers of truth—let them endure your foot; the good are equal to enduring it.
Śrī said: Here is one foot of mine set down, this one that rests upon the good. Thus deposited, O Śakra, dispose me among living beings.
Śakra said: Whoever among living beings here should assail you, who have been duly set in place by me, that one shall be my enemy—so let them hear my word.
Bhīṣma said: Then Bali, the king of the Daityas, forsaken by Śrī, spoke thus: As far as the sun blazes in the east, so far also over the southern quarter,

and so far too the maker of day shall blaze over the west and over the north; when at midday the Sun shall reach his setting—then once more shall come the war of gods and Asuras, and then I shall be your conqueror.
When the Sun, standing in a single place, shall scorch all the worlds, then in the war of gods and Asuras I shall be your conqueror, O Śatakratu.
Śakra said: By Brahmā I have been instructed that you are not to be slain; therefore, O Bali, I do not loose my thunderbolt upon your head.
Go where you will, O lord of the Daityas; may it be well with you, O great Asura. The Sun shall never scorch from a station fixed at the zenith.
For his appointed course was ordained from of old by the Self-existent: ceaselessly he wheels about, warming the creatures with truth.
His course is of six months, the northern and likewise the southern, by which the Sun travels through the worlds, dispensing cold and heat.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed by Indra, O Bhārata, Bali the lord of the Daityas went to the southern region, while Purandara went to the north.
Having heard this utterance sung by Bali, known as 'the discourse free of egotism,' the Thousand-eyed One then ascended into the sky.
Bhīṣma said: On this very theme they recount an ancient tale, the colloquy of Śatakratu and Namuci, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
To Namuci, bereft of fortune yet seated unshaken like the ocean, knowing the rising and the passing of all beings, Purandara spoke thus:
Bound in fetters, fallen from your station, brought into the power of your foes, and stripped of fortune—O Namuci, do you grieve, or do you not grieve?
Namuci said: Nothing is gained by grief, and the body is wasted by it, while one's enemies rejoice; there is no help in grieving.
Therefore, O Śakra, I do not grieve, for all this is bounded by an end; through anguish both beauty and dharma fall away, O lord of the gods.
Having truly subdued that sorrow born of dejection when it comes, the discerning one should turn his mind upon what is pleasing to the heart and wholesome.
For in the very measure that a man sets his mind upon the good, in that measure do all his aims grow favorable—of this there is no doubt.
One alone is the Ruler; there is no second ruler. The Ruler governs the man lying yet in the womb. Directed by him, like water down a slope, even as I am appointed, so do I move along.
Discerning well both being and non-being, I know the better course, yet I do not pursue it; fulfilling well the fond hopes of friends—even as I am appointed, so do I move along.
In whatever measure a thing is to be attained by him, in just that measure he attains it; and as whatever is to come to pass, so exactly does it come to pass.
Wherever the Ordainer joins the embryo, again and again, there alone does it dwell, and not where it itself would wish.
He whose conviction is ever this—'This state that has befallen me was destined to be mine'—such a one is never bewildered.
For those struck down by the turns of fate there is found no real assailant; this alone is the suffering—that the hater thinks, 'I am the doer.'

Upon whom in this world do calamities not press—the seers and the gods and the great Asuras, the elders learned in the threefold lore, and the sages in the forest? Yet those who know the higher and the lower are not thrown into confusion.
The wise man neither rages nor clings, neither sinks into despair nor exults, nor grieves amid the straits and ruin of his fortunes; by his very nature he stands unmoved, like the Himālaya.

He whom the highest success of his aims does not elate, and whom, when its hour comes, calamity does not bewilder, who meets pleasure and pain and the state between them all alike—that man is a true bearer of the yoke.
Whatever condition a man may come into, in that let him find contentment, untormented; thus would he drive from his body the swelling anguish born of the mind, the bringer of toil.

That man of understanding who, having come into the assembly, the council, the company of its members, feels no dread of the assembly, who has plunged into the truth of dharma and stands by it—he is a bearer of the yoke.

The deeds of the wise are hard to trace; surely the wise man is not bewildered in the hour of bewilderment. Even when fallen from his station, the aged Gautama was not bewildered, though he had met with such grievous calamity.
Not by the power and might of counsel, nor by wisdom, nor by manly effort, does a mortal gain what is not to be gained—so what cause for lament is there in that?
Whatever the Ordainers appointed of old for one born thus—that very thing shall I undergo; what can death do to me?
What is to be obtained, that alone he obtains; where he is to go, there alone he goes; what is to be reached, that alone he reaches—both the sorrows and the joys.
That man who, knowing this in its fullness, is not bewildered, skilled amid pleasures and pains—he indeed is lord of all riches.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: For a man sunk in grievous calamity, in the loss of his kin, O guardian of the earth, or again in the loss of his kingdom—what is the better course?
For you are our highest expounder in this world, O bull of the Bharatas; this I ask of you, and you should declare it to me here.
Bhīṣma said: For one parted from sons and wife, from comforts and from wealth, sunk in grievous calamity, steadfastness is the better course, O king.
For one who is endowed with firmness the body does not waste away, and through the body's soundness he wins back his fortune once more.
That king, dear son, whose men hold to a sattvic way of conduct—his are stability and firmness and resolve in his undertakings.
On this very theme they recount once more an ancient tale, the colloquy of Bali and Vāsava, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
When the war of gods and Asuras was over, and the Daityas and Dānavas destroyed, when the worlds had been measured out by Viṣṇu's stride, and Śatakratu was king of the gods,
when the gods were being worshipped with sacrifice and the four orders were established, when the triple world was flourishing and the Self-existent was content,
the lord, attended by the Rudras, the Vasus, the Ādityas, and by the two Aśvins and the seers, by the Gandharvas and the lords of serpents and the Siddhas and others,
mounting Airāvata, the four-tusked and well-tamed lord of elephants, decked with splendor, Śakra ranged throughout the triple world.
Once, by the shore of the ocean, in a certain mountain cavern, the wielder of the thunderbolt beheld Bali the son of Virocana, and drew near to him.
Beholding him, Indra the lord of the gods, seated on Airāvata's brow and surrounded by the hosts of heaven, the lord of the Daityas neither grieved nor trembled.
Seeing Bali standing unmoved and unafraid, Śatakratu, mounted upon the best of elephants, spoke thus:
O Daitya, you do not tremble—whether from valor, or from service to your elders, or from being purified by austerity; in any case this is most hard to do.
Brought into the power of your foes, fallen from a station unsurpassed—O son of Virocana, upon what do you rely that, when there is cause for grief, you do not grieve?
Having gained supremacy over your own kind and enjoyed pleasures unsurpassed, now robbed of your own host and kingdom—tell me, why do you not grieve?
For having once been lord in the seat of your fathers and forefathers, why do you not grieve to see it today carried off by your rivals?
Bound by Varuṇa's fetters and smitten by the thunderbolt, your wife taken, your wealth taken—tell me, why do you not grieve?
That you do not grieve, fallen from fortune and stripped of majesty, is hard indeed; for at the loss of the kingdom of the three worlds, who else would have the heart to live?
Having heard him speak these words and other harsh ones besides, Bali the son of Virocana, contemning him, calmly and unflustered replied:
When I am thus utterly subdued, O Śakra, what use is this boasting of yours? I see you standing with the thunderbolt upraised, O Purandara.
Formerly you were powerless; somehow you have come into power. Who other than you would deign to utter these most cruel words?
But he who, though able, shows mercy to a foe in his power, to a hero fallen into his very hands—him they account a true man.
For in battles between two contending parties there is no certainty: one attains victory, and one attains defeat.
And let this not be your settled persuasion, O bull among the gods—that the lord of all beings was conquered by your valor through main strength.
This was not done by us, O Śakra, nor was this done by you, O Śakra—that you have come to such a state, O wielder of the thunderbolt, or that we have come to such a state.
What you are today, that I once was; and what we now are, that you shall become. Do not despise me, thinking, 'It is by some evil deed of his own doing.'
For a man comes upon pleasure and pain by turns; by the turning of fate you have attained the lordship of Śakra, O Śakra, and not by your own deed.
Time leads me on in its time, and this same Time leads you on as well; therefore I am not now as you are, nor are you as we are.
Neither dutiful service to mother and father, nor worship of the gods, nor any other practice of virtue, brings happiness to a man on its own.
Not learning, not austerity, not giving, not friends, not kinsmen are able to rescue a man oppressed by Time.
For the misfortune that is to come, men cannot ward off even with a hundred counterstrokes, save by the strength of their understanding.
For those struck down by the turns of fate there is found no deliverer; but this is the suffering, O Śakra—that one thinks, 'I am the doer.'
If the doer were truly the doer, he would never himself be acted upon; but since the doer too is acted upon, therefore even the doer is not sovereign.
By Time I once conquered you, and by Time I have been conquered by you; Time is the mover of all that moves, Time impels all creatures onward.
O Indra, prattling with your common understanding, you do not comprehend; some hold you in high esteem, deeming you to have won supremacy by your own deed.
How should one such as I, who knows the workings of the world, grieve when struck down by Time, or be bewildered amid the upheaval of his fortunes?
For one ever encompassed by Time—be it I or one of my kind—the intellect, having met with calamity, sinks like a foundering ship.
I and you, and whatever others shall become lords of the gods—all of them, O Śakra, shall travel the road already trodden by a hundred Indras.
Even you, so unassailable, blazing with supreme splendor—when the appointed time has ripened, Time shall drive you on as it has driven me.
Many thousands of Indras of the Daiteyas have passed away through Time, age after age; for Time is hard to transcend.
Yet having gained this station, you hold yourself in high regard, as though you were the eternal god Brahmā, the source of all beings.
But this station is neither unshakable nor endless for anyone; you, with a childish mind, think, 'This is mine.'
You trust in what is not to be trusted, and you deem the impermanent permanent; out of delusion you covet this royal fortune, thinking, 'This is mine.'
She is held to abide steadfast neither with you, nor with us, nor with others; having passed by many another, she rests for now with you.
Having lingered with you for a little while, O Vāsava, this fickle one will forsake you and pass on to another, as a cow forsakes a drinking-trough.
For the worlds of kings that have passed away are more than I can dare to number, and others, far more numerous than you, shall yet come to be, O Puraṃdara.
This earth, with her trees and herbs and jewels, her rivers, mountains, and mines—I no longer see those who once enjoyed her of old.
Pṛthu, Aila, Maya, Bhauma, Naraka, and Śambara likewise, Aśvagrīva and Pulomā, Svarbhānu of boundless banner,
Prahrāda, Namuci, Dakṣa, Vipracitti, Virocana, Hrīniṣedha and Suhotra, Bhūrihan, Puṣpavān, Vṛṣa,
Satyeṣu, Ṛṣabha, Rāhu, Kapilāśva, Virūpaka, Bāṇa, Kārtasvara, Vahni, Viśvadaṃṣṭra, and then Nairṛta,
Riṭṭha and Huṭṭha, Vīra and Tāmra, Varāhāśva, the mighty Ruci, Viśvajit and Pratiśauri, Vṛṣāṇḍa, Viṣkara, Madhu,
Hiraṇyakaśipu as well, and the Dānava Kaiṭabha, and the Daityas and the Kālakhañjas—all of them, together with the Nairṛtas.
These, and many others, those of former times and of times yet earlier, lords of the Daityas and lords of the Dānavas, and still others of whom we have heard in tradition—
many former lords of the Daityas have abandoned the earth and departed, all of them struck down by Time; for Time is the stronger.
By all of them were hundreds of sacrifices offered—you are not the only one of a hundred rites; all of them were devoted to dharma, all unceasing in their sessions of sacrifice.
All ranged through the sky, all fought facing the foe, all were endowed with firm-knit frames, all had arms like iron bludgeons.
All wielded a hundred wiles, all of them roamed at will; of none of them, having joined battle, is it heard that he was vanquished.
All were intent on the vow of truth, all moved at their pleasure, all were devoted to the vows of the Veda, and all were deeply learned.
All those mighty ones attained sovereignty entire and unbroken, yet in those great-souled ones there was never of old any intoxication with their power.
All gave according to desert, all were free of envy, all conducted themselves rightly toward all beings.
All were sons of Dakṣa's daughters, of the lineage of Prajāpati, of mighty strength, blazing and scorching with heat—and all were gathered up by Time.
And you too, when you have enjoyed this earth and must let her go again, you will not then be able, O Śakra, to master the grief within yourself.
Let go your longing for sensual delights, let go this intoxication born of fortune; only thus, when your own sovereignty is lost, will you endure the grief.
In a time of sorrow do not grieve, and in a time of joy do not exult; abandoning the past and the future, live in the present moment.
If Time has now come upon me—ever vigilant, never slack—be patient, O Indra; before long it will come to you as well.
As if to terrify me, O lord of the gods, you cut me to pieces here with words; with me thus bound, you surely think much of yourself.
Time first came upon me, and afterward it runs in pursuit of you; that is why you roar, O lord of the gods, now that I have already been struck down by Time.
For who in the world is able to stand against me, wrathful, in battle? But mighty Time has come; therefore, O Vāsava, you stand unscathed.
That term, ending in a thousand years, must surely have run full—seeing how all my limbs are out of sorts, my vigor undone.
I have fallen from the station of Indra; you are made Indra in heaven, to be honored in this bright and varied world of the living—all through the turning of Time.
For by doing what are you Indra today, and by doing what have we fallen? Time is the maker and the unmaker; everything else is no cause at all.
Meeting with loss and ruin, with sovereignty, with pleasure and pain, with being and non-being, the wise man should neither rejoice nor be distressed beyond measure.
For you, O Indra, know us, and I know you, O Vāsava; why do you boast over me, bound as I am by Time, O shameless one?
For you yourself know of old what manhood was mine in those days, and what prowess in battles—that is proof enough.
The Ādityas and the Rudras and the Sādhyas, together with the Vasus, were all vanquished by me, and the Maruts too, O lord of Śacī.
You yourself know, O Śakra, that in the clash of gods and Asuras the assembled gods were shattered by me in battle through my onset.
And mountains, with their forests and their forest-dwellers, with crags and peaks, terrible to behold, were more than once hurled by me upon your head in battle.
But what can I do, since Time is not to be transcended? It is not that I lack the will to slay you, thunderbolt and all, with a single fist.
But this is no time for valor; a time for forbearance has come. Therefore I bear with you, O Śakra—I who am harder to bear with than you.
When the time has ripened, you boast over me, O Śakra—me encompassed by the fire of Time, fettered fast in the noose of Time.
This is that dark Person, whom the world cannot transcend; terrible, he stands having bound me, as one binds a beast with a tether.
Gain and loss, pleasure and pain, desire and wrath, being and non-being, slaying, bondage, and release—all is obtained through Time.
I am not the doer, nor are you the doer; the doer is he who is forever the Lord. This Time it is that ripens me, like a fruit come to ripeness on a tree.
The very deeds that a man, in doing, is joined by Time to pleasures—doing those same deeds again, he is joined by Time to pains.
One who knows Time, when touched by Time, ought not to grieve. Therefore, O Śakra, I do not grieve; there is no help to be had in grief.
Since for those who grieve the grief does not draw away the calamity, and the grieving man has no power to mend it—therefore I do not grieve today.
Thus addressed, the thousand-eyed lord, the chastiser of Pāka, drawing back his fury, the god of a hundred sacrifices spoke thus:
At the sight of my arm upraised with the thunderbolt and of Varuṇa's nooses, whose mind here would not waver—even Death's, when he sought to kill?
Yet that mind of yours does not waver—unshaken, beholding the truth; you, O you of true prowess, do not falter even as you speak your word.
For what embodied being in the world could dare to place his trust in possessions or in the body, having seen the world set forth upon its passing?
I too know this world to be just so, impermanent—cast into the terrible fire of Time, hidden, ever-moving, imperishable.
And in this there is no escape for any creature touched by Time, as the beings, both small and great, are ripened away.
From Time—subject to no lord, never heedless, ever ripening beings, never turning back—he who has met his ruin is not set free.
Heedful among the heedless, Time keeps watch over embodied beings; never has it been seen by anyone to be overcome, however great the effort.
Ancient, eternal, the law impartial toward all that bears life—Time is not to be evaded, nor is there any transgressing it.
Days and nights and months, instants, kāṣṭhās, kalās, and moments—Time gathers them up against us, as a usurer heaps up his interest.
The man who says, 'This I shall do today, that I shall do tomorrow'—Time, when it has come, sweeps him away as a river's current carries off a raft.
'Just now indeed I saw him—how is it he is dead?'—such is heard the lament of men as they are borne away by Time.

Possessions perish, and so do enjoyments, station, and sovereignty as well; all is fleeting and unstable, and resolve is hard to keep. Risings end in downfalls, and being abides only in the condition of non-being.
That mind of yours does not waver—unshaken, beholding the truth; you do not even in thought take note: 'I once was, before.'
In this world overpowered by mightier Time and ripened thereby, though you are cast about with neither eldest nor youngest spared, you take no heed.
In envy, pride, and greed, in desire, wrath, and fear, in craving, delusion, and conceit, the world clings and is bewildered.
But you, knowing the truth of existence, learned, endowed with knowledge and austerity, behold Time as plainly as a myrobalan fruit upon your palm.
Knowing the truth of Time's course, skilled in all the sacred sciences, you are, O son of Virocana, perfected in soul, to be envied by those who understand.
This whole world, I think, has been encompassed by your intellect; ranging at large, released on every side, you cling to nothing anywhere.
For passion and darkness do not touch you, master of your senses; free of elation, your torment destroyed, you wait upon your own self.
Beholding you—a friend to all beings, free of enmity, serene of mind—there has arisen in me a heart of compassion toward you.
One so enlightened I do not wish to slay in his bondage; non-cruelty is the highest law, and so too is compassion toward you.
These nooses of Varuṇa shall be loosed from you in the turning of Time, through the misconduct of mankind; may it be well with you, O great Asura.
When the daughter-in-law shall set the aged mother-in-law to menial service, and the son out of folly shall send his father to do his tasks;
when the base-born shall make Brāhmaṇas wash their feet, and Śūdras shall take Brāhmaṇa women to wife without fear;
when men shall spill their seed into wombs not their own, bringing about confusion of castes, and shall offer oblation in bronze vessels and in unworthy vessels;
when the whole order of the four castes shall pass beyond its bounds—then, one by one, these nooses of yours shall be loosed in due succession.
From us you have nothing to fear; await the appointed time. Be happy, untroubled, sound of mind, and free of ill.

Having spoken thus to him, the lord of a hundred sacrifices set forth again, borne by the king of elephants; and the lord of the gods, having conquered all the Asuras, rejoiced in gladness and became sole sovereign.

And the great sages straightway praised him, Vṛṣākapi, the lord of all that moves and moves not; the dispeller of cold bore up the oblation in haste, and so was the nectar of immortality offered up to the Lord.

Praised by the foremost of the twice-born who were gathered from everywhere, his splendor blazing forth, his wrath now gone, the lord with a tranquil heart and gladdened, having reached his own abode, the heaven of the gods—Vāsava rejoiced.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O king, tell me, grandsire, of the foretokens of a man who is about to rise and of one who is about to fall.
Bhīṣma said: It is the mind itself, blessings upon you, that proclaims a man's foretokens—both of the one who will prosper and of the one who will not.
On this they recount an ancient tale, the colloquy of Śrī with Śakra. Mark it well, Yudhiṣṭhira.
By the fruit of great austerity he beheld both worlds, the higher and the lower, having attained fellowship with the seers who dwell in Brahmā's realm—
that very Brahman-like Nārada, of boundless blazing might, his sins stilled, great in austerity, roamed at will through the three worlds.
Once, rising at dawn and wishing to touch the pure water, he went to the Gaṅgā that issues from the Gate of Dhruva, and stepped down into her.
And the thousand-eyed wielder of the thunderbolt, slayer of Śambara and Pāka, came likewise to the bank of that river frequented by the divine seers.
The two, self-controlled, having bathed and finished their prayers, sat down together, reaching a sandbank of the river spread with fine golden sand.
Fond of converse, with minds pure and gladdened, the two recited tales told by holy doers and recounted by the divine seers, intent and discoursing of things long past and gone.
Then, beholding the rising sun heralded by its net of rays, its orb made full, the two rose and stood in worship before it.
And close beside that rising sun, like a second sun, there appeared in the sky a radiance whose splendor matched flames leaping upward.
It was seen drawing near to the two, O Bhārata: it had reached the Vaiṣṇava station traversed by Garuḍa and the sun, and shone with peerless rays, illumining the three worlds.
Attended by celestial nymphs of surpassing form and grace, she was vast and sunlike in brilliance, like the flame of the mighty-rayed luminary—
her ornaments arranged like constellations, her garland patterned like the spangling of stars—Śrī, the lotus goddess, they beheld in person, standing upon a lotus-pedestal.
That peerless among women descended from the front of her aerial car and approached Śakra, lord of the three worlds, and the seer Nārada.
Maghavān, with Nārada following him, came up to her in person and, with palms joined in salute, presented himself before the goddess.
And that all-knowing king of the gods rendered her unmatched homage, O king, and to Śrī he spoke these words.
Who are you, O sweetly-smiling one, and on what errand have you come? Whence do you arrive, fair-browed one, and whither must you go, O auspicious lady?
Śrī said: Throughout the three holy worlds all beings, moving and unmoving, desiring to make me their own, strive with their utmost selves.
I am she who was born in the lotus awakened by the sun's rays—Padmā, Śrī, garlanded with lotuses, born for the prosperity of all beings.
I am Lakṣmī, I am Prosperity, and I am Śrī, O slayer of Bala; I am Faith and Wisdom, Modesty, Conquest, and Constancy.
I am Fortitude, I am Success, I am Radiance and Affluence too; I am Svāhā and Svadhā, Praise, Necessity, and Action.
In the vanguards and the banners of kings who go forth to victory, in the dwellings of those of righteous conduct, in their realms and their cities—
in the lord of men who bears the splendor of conquest, who is valiant and never turns back in battles—there do I forever dwell, O slayer of Bala.
In him who is ever devoted to dharma, of great understanding, friendly to brahmins, truthful in speech, humble, and inclined to giving—there do I always dwell.
Once I dwelt among the Asuras, bound to them by their truth and righteousness; but when I knew them turned to their opposites, I resolved to dwell with you.
Śakra said: When the Daityas behaved in what manner did you dwell among them, O fair-faced one? And seeing what here did you come, forsaking the sons of Diti and the Dānavas?
Śrī said: I take my delight in beings who keep to their own duty, who do not waver from steadfastness, who find their joy in the path to heaven.
Among them there ever prevailed giving, study, sacrifice and worship, reverence for elders and gods, and honor shown to brahmins and to guests.
Their houses were well-swept, their womenfolk well-governed, their fires duly offered; they were attentive to their teachers, self-restrained, devoted to brahmins, and truthful.
Faithful, masters of their anger, generous, free from spite, they maintained their sons, their counselors, and their wives, and harbored no envy.
Free from rancor, they never coveted one another's goods, and being steadfast, they were never once tormented by the prosperity of others.
Givers and gatherers alike, noble, knowing compassion, of great graciousness, upright, firm in devotion, their senses subdued—
their servants and ministers content, themselves grateful and sweet of speech, bestowing honor and wealth according to merit, restrained by modesty, firm in their vows.
On the holy days they bathed well, anointed and adorned themselves; given to fasting and austerity, of good repute, expounders of the sacred word.
The sun never rose upon them still asleep, nor were they wakeful through the night; and at night they ever shunned curds and parched-grain meal.
At dawn the pure and continent ones would look upon clarified butter; they gazed too upon auspicious things and gave honor to the brahmins.
Theirs ever was the dharma of those who give and never accept, who sleep for half the night and stay awake by day.
They took constant pleasure in giving and sharing with the wretched, the helpless, the aged, the weak, the sick, and women.
The dejected, the frightened, the agitated, the terror-stricken, the disease-afflicted, the man robbed of his wealth, the calamity-stricken—these they ever consoled.
They followed only dharma and did each other no harm; obliging in their dealings, they waited upon their elders and teachers.
They duly honored the ancestors, the gods, and their guests, and ate only what was left over, ever devoted to truth and austerity.
None ate alone of a well-furnished meal, nor went to another's wife; toward all beings they bore the same compassion as toward themselves.
Never in the open air, nor with beasts, nor in what is no fit womb, nor on the holy days, did they ever consent to the release of their seed.
Ever present in them were giving and skill, uprightness always, energy and freedom from egotism, the highest friendliness, and forbearance.
Truth, giving, austerity, purity, compassion, gentle speech, and no treachery toward friends—all this dwelt in them, O lord.
Drowsiness, sloth, ill-will, unguarded envy, discontent, despondency, and craving never entered them.
It was among the Dānavas, while they bore such virtues, that I once dwelt of old, from the time of creation, through more than one turning of the ages.
Then, in the turning of time, as their virtues were turned about, I saw dharma departed from them, who had become slaves to desire and wrath.
When the elders among the assembly told their true tales, those of lesser worth laughed at them and reviled all their elders.
When the worthy aged came and sat among the young, the young no longer honored them, as once they had, by rising and saluting.
Even while the father still lived and held sway over himself, the sons took over the running of affairs, reducing him to the state of an enemy's servant and proclaiming it shamelessly.
And for those who, by deeds blameworthy and gone from dharma, won great wealth—for such men did their craving grow.
They spoke loudly even by night, while there the fire burned low; sons spoke back to their fathers, and wives answered back their husbands.
Mother, aged father, preceptor, guest, and elder—they no longer welcomed as elders deserve, nor did they look after their children.
Without giving alms or offering oblation, they ate the food themselves, without first making the sacrifice or sharing with ancestors, gods, guests, and elders.
Their cooks no longer observed cleanliness, in thought, deed, or word; the food was left uncovered.
The grains lay scattered, food for crows and mice; the milk stood uncovered, and persons defiled by their leavings touched the clarified butter.
The hoe, the basket, the bronze vessel lay strewn about; the mistress of the house no longer kept watch over the goods and the implements at all.
They did not repair the breaches in their walls and houses, nor did they trouble, having tethered their cattle, to tend them with fodder and water.
Before the very eyes of their watching children they ate the dainties themselves, and so the Dānavas devoured all that belonged to their dependents.
Milk-rice, the dish of rice and sesame, meat, cakes, and wafers they cooked for their own sake, and ate meat killed to no sacred purpose.
They lay asleep past sunrise, and all stayed wakeful through the night; quarrels went on there, day and night, in house after house.

The ignoble there no longer waited upon a noble man as he sat; doers of forbidden deeds hated those settled in the proper stages of life, and one another; confusion of castes prevailed, and purity prevailed no more.
Brahmins learned in the Veda and those plainly ignorant of the hymns were treated with no distinction between them, in honor or in contempt.
To observe their coquetry, their ornament and dress, their gait and their bearing, their servant-maids cultivated the ways of wicked folk.
Women in the garb of men, and men wearing the garb of women, found their highest delight in games, dalliance, and revels.
The gifts once bestowed by men of power upon the worthy they no longer honored, out of unbelief, though they had the means to do so.
When a friend besought a friend in some doubtful matter of wealth, the latter, for a self-interest no greater than the tip of a hair's end, would cheat him of that wealth.
Eager to seize the goods of others, dealing in trade and barter, men of the noble orders came to be seen as Śūdras—while Śūdras, on the other hand, were rich in austerity.
Some studied without keeping their vows, others kept their vows to no purpose; a pupil there was who would not serve his teacher, and a teacher who made a comrade of his pupil.
Father and mother both, worn out as though their feast of life were ended, the aged pair, stripped of all authority, begged their food of their own sons.
There the wise, learned in the Veda, ocean-like in their depth, became absorbed in farming and the like, while fools ate the funeral offerings.
Morning after morning the courteous greeting, the dressing of hair, and the errands that pupils once performed—in that age it was the teachers who did them, sent at the pupils' bidding.
In the very presence of her father- and mother-in-law the young wife gave orders to the servants, and summoning her husband, scolded and ordered him about.
With all his effort the father guarded the favor of his son's mind; and they divided the patrimony in fury, and so dwelt in a wretched dwelling.
When they saw a man's wealth consumed by fire, or carried off by thieves or by kings, they laughed out of malice—though they had once been counted his well-wishers.
Ungrateful, unbelieving, wicked, defilers of their teachers' wives, given to eating what should not be eaten, knowing no bounds, their luster slain—
when they practiced such ways and worse in this perversion, I would no longer dwell among the Dānavas, O lord of the gods—such was my resolve.
Welcome me, lord of Śacī, for I have come to you of my own accord; honored by you, O lord of the gods, the deities will set me at their head.
Wherever I am, there too will dwell my beloved companions—those who cleave to me and offer themselves to me: seven goddesses, with myself the eighth, will abide eightfold at my side.
Hope, Faith, Constancy, Beauty, Victory, Humility, Forbearance—and Conduct as the eighth, who walks before them all, O chastiser of Pāka.
They and I, forsaking the Asuras, have come into your domain; among the Thirty Gods we shall dwell, whose inmost selves are fixed in dharma.
Bhīṣma said: When the goddess had spoken these words, the two rejoiced exceedingly—Nārada, the sage of the three worlds, and Vāsava, the slayer of Vṛtra.
Then through the dwellings of the gods blew the Wind, the friend of Fire, fragrant and welcome, soft to the touch, bringing delight to every sense.
In a place pure and adorned the Thirty Gods stood for the most part assembled, eager to behold Maghavat seated together with Lakṣmī.

Then the Thousand-eyed One, reaching heaven endowed with Śrī, with his friend the divine sage beside him, that bull among gods, drove in his chariot yoked with bay steeds, and went, well honored, to the assembly hall of the gods.

Then Nārada, pondering in his mind the bearing of the wielder of the thunderbolt and of the goddess Śrī—he whose manhood the gods had witnessed—announced to Śrī that her coming there, in auspicious fashion, would be one of great prosperity.
Then the radiant sky rained down nectar over the abode of the Self-existent Grandsire; drums sounded untouched by any hand, and the quarters of the world, grown serene, shone bright.

Vāsava rained upon the crops each in its season, and not a soul strayed from the path of dharma; the earth, adorned with mines of many jewels, rang with auspicious sound at the triumph of the world's dwellers.
Men delighting in sacred rites grew glorious, standing firm on the blessed road of the doers of good; humans and gods, Kiṃnaras, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas became prosperous, happy, and renowned.
Never did a blossom—much less a fruit—fall untimely from a tree, even when shaken by the wind; the cows yielded sweet milk and granted every wish, and no harsh word passed from anyone's lips.
Those brāhmaṇas who in their assemblies recite this worship of Śrī, together with the deities led by Śakra who grant all desires, attain Śrī, their every wish fulfilled.
What you, O best of the Kurus, urged me to tell—the supreme illustration here of prosperity and ruin—all that I have now recounted in full; weighing its truth, you ought to grasp it whole.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Of what character, what conduct, what learning, what refuge is the man who attains the abode of Brahman, that which is supreme, beyond Nature, and unchanging?
Bhīṣma said: He who is steadfast in the disciplines of liberation, sparing in food, and master of his senses attains the abode of Brahman, that which is supreme, beyond Nature, and unchanging.
On this point too they relate an ancient tale, O descendant of Bharata: the dialogue of Jaigīṣavya and Asita.
To Jaigīṣavya, the greatly wise, versed in the whole tradition of the dharmas, who neither grew angry nor elated, Asita Devala spoke.
When praised, you take no pleasure; when blamed, you feel no anger. What is this wisdom of yours, whence does it come, and what is its final ground?
Thus questioned by him, that great ascetic spoke to him a lofty utterance, free of doubt, rich in meaning and words, and pure.
That course, that highest consummation, that peace which belongs to the doers of meritorious deeds—of this I shall tell you fully, O brāhmaṇa, since you ask it of me.
Ever even-minded toward those who blame and those who praise, O Devala—and even toward those who break their compact and deny a good deed done—
When spoken against, the wise do not wish to retort upon the speaker bent on their harm, nor do they desire to strike back at one who would strike them.
They do not grieve over what has not come, but do what the present hour demands; they do not mourn things past, nor dwell upon them.
When honored guests arrive, O Devala, in matters of desire and wealth the capable men of fulfilled vows act as circumstance allows.
Ripe in knowledge, greatly wise, having conquered anger and subdued their senses, they offend against no one in thought, deed, or word.
Free from envy, they never do harm to one another, and the steadfast are never tormented by the prosperity of others.
They neither utter excessive blame nor excessive praise of another, nor are they ever moved by blame or by praise.
Wholly tranquil, devoted to the welfare of all beings, they neither rage nor exult nor wrong anyone; having loosed the knots of the heart, they wander at their ease.
They have no kinsmen of their own, nor are they kinsmen to others; they have no enemies, nor are they enemies to anyone.
Those mortals who live thus dwell ever in happiness, and the knowers of dharma follow dharma alone, O best of the twice-born; but those who fall from this path swing between elation and dismay.
Standing upon that path, whom should I grudge, and how? Whether blamed or praised, by what cause should I be moved to elation?
Men take to whatever path they desire; by blame or by praise I shall suffer neither diminishing nor increase.
The knower of truth would take his fill of contempt as though of nectar, and the discerning man would ever shrink from honor as though from poison.
The despised man sleeps in peace, here and hereafter, in both worlds, freed from all his sins; but the one who despises is himself bound.
And whatever wise men seek the supreme goal, those people, taking up this vow, flourish in happiness.
Drawing in from every quarter all his energies, the man who has mastered his senses attains the abode of Brahman, that which is supreme, beyond Nature, and unchanging.
Once he has reached the supreme goal, neither gods nor Gandharvas, neither Piśācas nor Rākṣasas can trace the path he has trodden.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Who indeed is the man on earth dear to the whole world, welcomed by all beings, and endowed with every excellence?
Bhīṣma said: On this, since you ask, O bull of the Bharatas, I shall recount to you the dialogue of Ugrasena and Keśava concerning Nārada.
Ugrasena said: See how the world warms to the praise of Nārada; I deem him rich in virtues. Tell me this, for I ask you.
Vāsudeva said: O lord of the Kukuras, hear from me, as I would tell them, those noble virtues of Nārada that I count, O ruler of men, set forth in brief.
In him there is no pride born of good conduct that would bring the body low; his learning and his conduct stand unbroken—therefore he is honored everywhere.
Nārada is firmly devoted to austerity; in speech he commits no transgression, whether from desire or from greed—therefore he is honored everywhere.
Knowing the truth of the science of the inner Self, forbearing, capable, master of his senses, upright and truthful in speech—therefore he is honored everywhere.
Eminent in splendor, in fame, in intellect, in statecraft and in modesty, in birth and in austerity—therefore he is honored everywhere.
Of pleasant disposition, easy in fellowship, easily fed, gracious in regard, pure, fair of speech and free from envy—therefore he is honored everywhere.
He works good in full measure; no evil is found in him; he takes no delight in others' wealth—therefore he is honored everywhere.
By the Vedas, the sacred texts, and the old narratives he seeks to win out in argument; enduring and never contemptuous—therefore he is honored everywhere.
Through his evenness none is dear to him nor anyone unwelcome in any way, yet he speaks agreeably to the mind—therefore he is honored everywhere.
Deeply learned, a teller of varied tales, wise, never slothful, without guile, never abject, free from anger and from greed—therefore he is honored everywhere.
Never before has he had a quarrel over wealth, dharma, or pleasure, and his faults are utterly rooted out—therefore he is honored everywhere.
Firm in devotion, blameless in self, learned, full of kindness, and freed from the flaw of delusion—therefore he is honored everywhere.
Unattached amid all attachments, he yet appears as one whose heart is engaged; quick to resolve his doubts and eloquent—therefore he is honored everywhere.
His concentration is never set on winning honor, and he never praises himself; free from envy and steadfast in discourse—therefore he is honored everywhere.
Without reviling the world's manifold ways or the natures of men, skilled in the art of company—therefore he is honored everywhere.
He grudges no body of learning, and he does not live off his own austerity; his time is never barren, his self is under control—therefore he is honored everywhere.
He has done his toil and won his wisdom, yet is never sated in his concentration; fixed in the observances and ever vigilant—therefore he is honored everywhere.
Possessed of modesty and self-restraint, easily led by others toward the good, and never a betrayer of others' secrets—therefore he is honored everywhere.
He does not exult in the gaining of wealth, nor is he distressed in its loss; steady of mind and unattached in self—therefore he is honored everywhere.
Endowed with every virtue, capable, pure, undaunted, knowing the right time and the ways of policy—who would not hold him dear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: I wish to hear, O Kaurava, of the beginning and end of all beings—their contemplation, their action, their measure of time, and likewise their span of life from age to age.
And the truth of the worlds in its fullness—the coming and the going of beings, their creation and their dissolution—whence does all this proceed?
