If your mind is set on showing us favor here, O best of the good, I ask you this; may you declare it to me.
For having heard before the supreme teaching once spoken by Bhṛgu to the brāhmaṇa-sage Bharadvāja, my understanding thence grew most excellent—
—it was born wholly devoted to dharma, established upon a heavenly foundation; therefore I ask once more, and you ought to tell it.
Bhīṣma said: On this I shall recount to you an ancient tale, that which the lord Vyāsa sang to his son when he inquired.
Having studied all the Vedas entire, with their limbs and Upaniṣads, and seeking the final, conclusive course of action through his insight into the niceties of dharma—
—Śuka, son of Vyāsa, asked of his father Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa this doubt, whose perplexity over dharma and meaning was thereby resolved:
"The maker of the host of beings, the certainty in the knowledge of time, and what is the proper task of the brāhmaṇa—that you ought to tell me."
To him, his son who asked, the father declared all of this—the learned one who knew the past and the future, the all-knowing, versed in every dharma.
Without beginning or end, unborn, divine, ageless, unchanging, imperishable, beyond reasoning and beyond knowing—Brahman existed in the beginning.
A kāṣṭhā is fifteen blinks of the eye; thirty kāṣṭhās one should reckon a kalā; thirty kalās in turn make a muhūrta—together with that which is a tenth part of a kalā.

Thirty muhūrtas make a day, and a night—such is the reckoning ordained by the sages; thirty days and nights are called a month, and twelve months are declared a year; and those skilled in reckoning say the year has two courses of the sun, the southern and the northern.
The Sun divides day and night in the world of men: night is for the sleep of beings, and day for the exertion of their works.
In the realm of the ancestors a month is a day and a night, and again its division is this: the dark fortnight is the day for the exertion of works, the bright fortnight the night for sleep.
In the realm of the gods a year is a day and a night, and again its division is this: there the northward course of the sun is the day, and the southward course is the night.
Of that day and night of the gods' world which were first recounted, reckoning their sum of years I shall now declare the day and the night of Brahmā.
I shall declare in due order the sums of their years in the Kṛta age, the Tretā age, the Dvāpara, and likewise the Kali.
They say the Kṛta age numbers four thousand years; its twilight is a hundred years, and its twilight-portion is of like measure.
In the other three ages, together with their twilights and twilight-portions, the thousands and the hundreds diminish, each by one unit.
These sustain the everlasting, eternal worlds; this, my son, is the eternal Brahman known to the knowers of Brahman.
In the Kṛta age dharma stands whole on all four feet, and so does truth; no acquisition through unrighteousness ever arises to set against it.
In the other ages, through what is acquired, dharma is lowered foot by foot, and unrighteousness swells through theft, falsehood, and deceit.
In the Kṛta age men are free of disease, accomplished in all their aims, and live four hundred years; in the Tretā and the rest their span shortens foot by foot.
And the teachings of the Veda diminish age by age—so we have heard—and so too do the life-spans, the benedictions, and the very fruit of the Veda.
The duties of the Kṛta age are one thing, those of the Tretā and the Dvāpara another, and those of the Kali age yet another—as though done according to one's capacity.
In the Kṛta age austerity is supreme, in the Tretā knowledge is highest; in the Dvāpara they declare sacrifice foremost, and in the Kali age, giving alone.
The wise know this cycle named the Yuga to span twelve thousand years; a thousand such cycles completed is called one Day of Brahmā.
The Night of Brahmā is of equal length; at its beginning the Lord, at the dissolution, enters into the inner Self, and having slept, awakens at its end.
Those who know the Day of Brahmā to extend through a thousand Yugas, and the Night to end with a thousand Yugas—those people know day and night truly.
Awakened at the passing of the night, Brahman transforms the imperishable and creates the Great Being, and from that the manifest-natured mind.
Brahman is luminous and radiant, of whom this whole world is born; from that single Being arose the twofold being, the moving and the unmoving.
Awakened at the dawn of the Day, it creates the world by its knowledge, and foremost of all the Great Being, swiftly, the manifest-natured mind.
Surpassing all and radiant, it emitted the seven mind-born ones—mind that ranges far, moves in many directions, and is the seat of desire and doubt.
Mind, urged on by the will to create, brings forth creation; from it is born space, whose quality is held to be sound.
From space as it transforms is born the wind, pure and mighty, the bearer of every scent, whose quality is held to be touch.
From the wind, too, as it transforms, is born the element of fire, dispeller of darkness and shining bright; its quality is said to be form.
From fire too, as it transforms, arise the waters, whose essence is taste; from the waters comes earth, whose quality is scent—this is called the prior creation.
The qualities of each preceding element pass on into each succeeding one; whatever the position each holds, that many qualities it is held to possess.
Should some, through want of discernment, claim to perceive scent in the waters, one should know that scent belongs to earth alone, residing also in water and in wind.
But these seven Puruṣas, of diverse powers, each apart, were unable to create the creatures so long as they had not joined together on every side.
Coming together and resorting to one another, those great ones attained their lodging in a body; thence is the term Puruṣa, the embodied one, derived.
From their resorting together arises the body, embodied and made of sixteen constituents; the great elements enter into it together with action.
Taking up all beings, for the practice of austerity, the primal Maker, the Great Being—him they call Prajāpati, the Lord of creatures.
It is he who creates the beings; he alone is the supreme Puruṣa; unborn, as Brahmā he begets gods, sages, fathers, and men.

He creates the worlds, the rivers and the oceans, the quarters, the mountains and the trees, men, kiṃnaras, and rākṣasas, birds, cattle, wild beasts, and serpents—both the imperishable and the perishable, the twofold realm of the unmoving and the moving.
Whatever deeds these beings took up in the prior creation, those very deeds they take up again as they are created over and over.
Whether harmful or harmless, gentle or cruel, righteous or unrighteous, truthful or false—from this it follows that what the Ordainer assigns to each, that is what pleases him.
The diversity among the great elements, in the objects of the senses and in embodied forms, and the appointment of beings to their tasks—it is the Ordainer alone who arranges all this.
Some, the men versed in action, declare human effort to be the cause; others, the brahmins, say it is destiny; and those who ponder the elements say it is inherent nature.
Human exertion, action, and destiny—by the nature of how their fruits unfold, these three are not in truth distinct; yet some make no discernment of them at all.
"It is thus, and yet it is not thus"—so men speak of the Being that creates the world; those wedded to action speak of inequality, while those grounded in goodness see with an equal eye.
Austerity is the highest good of a creature; its root is self-restraint and tranquillity; by it one attains all the desires the mind may wish.
By austerity one attains that Being which creates the world, and becoming one with that Being, he becomes the lord of all beings.
By austerity the seers studied the Vedas day and night; speech, without beginning or end and eternal, was sent forth by the Self-existent.
The names of the seers, and the creations set forth in the Vedas—to those born at the ends of the nights he assigns those very same names and forms.

The distinctions of name, the designations of austerity, action, and sacrifice, are accomplishments of the world; but the realization of the Self is proclaimed in the Vedas through ten successive stages.
What is set forth in the Vedic teachings, profound to those who see by the Vedas, is discerned, as is fitting, in the Vedānta through the practice of successive stages.
This separateness born of action, bound to the pairs of opposites, belongs to one not yet released; but the realization of the Self, once understood, for the most part casts off its hold.
Two Brahmans are to be known: the Brahman that is sound, and that which is supreme; one well-versed in the Brahman that is sound attains the supreme Brahman.
The sacrifice of undertakings belongs to the kṣatriya, the sacrifice of oblations to the vaiśya; service is the sacrifice of the śūdras, and austerity the sacrifice of the twice-born.
The ordinance of these sacrifices belongs to the Tretā age, not to the Kṛta; in the Dvāpara the sacrifices fall into disorder, and so too in the Kali age.
In the Kṛta age mortals were undivided in their duty; only on seeing the desired prosperity of the Ṛk, Sāma, and Yajus verses set apart did they practice austerity upon austerity.
But in the Tretā age all these appeared together, men of great might, restrainers of the unmoving and the moving on every side.
In the Tretā these sacrifices and the social orders alike held together; but through the shortening of the life-span they are dispersed in the Dvāpara age.
In the Kali age the Vedas are seen and yet not wholly seen; together with the sacrifices, the sole dikes of dharma fall away.
The dharma that is seen among the brahmins in the Kṛta age stands firmly established in those who are self-possessed, austere, and learned in sacred lore.
Age by age, in keeping with the prevailing dharma, the teachings of the Veda, though grounded in their own law, are altered according to the age, taking on a contact with unrighteous observance.
Just as all moving beings are brought forth in greater abundance by rain in the season of the rains, so too are the dharmas in each successive age.
As the marks of the seasons, in their many forms, are seen again and again, ever the same in their turning, so too are they seen in the Days and Nights of Brahmā.
The diversity of time, without beginning or end, is ordained; that which was proclaimed to you before brings forth the creatures and devours them again.
Restraint, the curber, sets in place the station for the arising of beings; and abundantly the things bound to the pairs of opposites move on by their own inherent nature.
Creation, time, action, the Vedas, the doer, the deed to be done, action and its fruit—all this, my son, has been told to you, all that you have inquired of me.
Now I shall speak of the withdrawal, when the Day is gone and the Night begins, how the Lord draws this universe into the most subtle inner Self.
Then seven suns in the sky, flaming-crested, burn with their rays; and this whole world, filled with their flames, blazes forth ablaze.
Vyāsa said: Whatever beings there are upon the earth, moving and fixed, those first dissolve away and pass into the state of earth.
Then, when all has dissolved away, the unmoving and the moving alike, the earth, bare of wood and bare of grass, appears like the back of a tortoise.
When the waters take up scent, the very quality of earth, then the earth, its scent taken from it, is made ready for dissolution.
Then the waters stand established, billowing in waves and loud-roaring; filling all this, they stand and they flow.
When fire takes up the qualities of the waters too, my son, then the waters, their qualities taken away, come to rest within fire.
When the flaming rays conceal the sun set in the midst of heaven, then this whole sky, filled with flames, blazes forth ablaze.
When the wind takes up form, the quality of fire too, then the fire is quenched, and the mighty wind blows tossing on every side.
Then, reaching the root, the source of its own being, the wind shakes violently below and above and sideways, through the ten directions.
When space swallows touch, the quality of wind too, then the wind is stilled, and space alone remains, resounding.
The manifest-natured mind takes up sound, the quality of space; from mind the manifest passes into the unmanifest—this is the reabsorption into Brahman.
Entering that quality of the Self, the moon swallows the mind; and when the mind is stilled, the inner Self comes to rest within the moon.
After a great span of time, resolve brings that under its sway; resolve swallows the thinking faculty, and that supreme knowledge as well.
Time devours discernment—"Time is power," so runs the sacred teaching; Time swallows power, but the wise man brings even Time under his sway.
Then the wise man takes the sound of space into his own Self; that unmanifest is the supreme Brahman, eternal and unsurpassed—thus all beings are but Brahman, the reabsorption.
All this has been duly and rightly proclaimed, beyond doubt; it is to be understood, made of knowledge, beheld by yogins whose souls are set upon the supreme Self.
Thus does the unmanifest Brahman expand and contract again and again, at the onset of the thousand Yugas of the Day and likewise of the Night.
Vyāsa said: That which is appointed for the multitude of beings I have now proclaimed; but the duty proper to a brahmin I shall declare to you, since you ask.
Beginning with the birth-rite, the performance of his sacraments, attended by their fees, should continue until his graduation, under a teacher who has mastered the Veda.
Having studied all the Vedas, devoted to the service of his teacher, and become free of debt to his teachers, the knower of sacrifice should return home as a graduate.
With his teacher's leave, he should observe, according to rule, one of the four stations of life, until the release of the body.
Whether by begetting offspring and taking a wife, or again by chastity, or in the forest in his teacher's presence, or again by the discipline of the ascetic.
Yet the householder is called the root of all the four; for there the self-controlled man, whose impurities are ripened away, succeeds in every station.
Blessed with offspring, learned in scripture, a performer of sacrifice, freed of the three divine debts—he then, purified by his deeds, may afterward pass on to the other stations of life.
Let him dwell in whatever seat of learning is most holy upon the earth, and there strive to attain authority and the highest renown.
By mighty austerity, by mastering the whole range of the sciences, by sacrifice, or by gifts, the renown of the learned brāhmaṇa grows.
For as long as his glory-bringing fame endures in this world, so long does a man enjoy the endless realms won by the doers of holy deeds.
Let him teach and let him study, let him officiate at sacrifices and offer his own; but let him never accept a gift without cause, nor ever give one so.
If great wealth should come to him from one for whom he sacrifices, or from a pupil, or by a bride's dowry, let him sacrifice and give it away; let him never enjoy it alone.
For the householder there is no fit occasion for accepting gifts save this: for the sake of the gods, the seers, the ancestors, and the teacher, and for the aged, the sick, and the hungry.
To those who are ruined and stricken yet wish, as best they can, to lift themselves up, one should give of one's goods even beyond one's power, even past what duty requires.
To the worthy and the fitting there is nothing that may not be given; the good hold that even a steed like Uccaiḥśravas should be bestowed upon them.
So it was that Kāvya, true to his word and bound by mighty vows, won over and saved the lives of brāhmaṇas with his own life, and went to heaven.
And Rantideva, son of Saṃkṛti, having given cool and warm waters to the great-souled Vasiṣṭha, is honored upon the vault of heaven.
The wise king of Atri's line, having given manifold wealth to the worthy Candra and Dama, departed to the endless worlds.
Śibi, son of Uśīnara, having offered up his own limbs and his dear-born son for a brāhmaṇa's sake, passed from here to the vault of heaven.
Pratardana, lord of Kāśi, having given his own eyes to a brāhmaṇa, enjoys matchless fame both in this world and in the next.
Devāvṛdha, having given a divine parasol of gold with polished ribs and of supreme splendor, ascended to heaven together with his realm.
And Sāṃkṛti of Atri's line, mighty in splendor, having taught his pupils the brahman that is beyond all qualities, went to the unsurpassed worlds.
The mighty Ambarīṣa, having given eleven hundred million cows to brāhmaṇas, ascended to heaven together with his realm.
Sāvitrī, giving up her two divine earrings, and Janamejaya, giving up his body, both for a brāhmaṇa's sake, went to the highest world.
Vṛṣādarbha and Yuvanāśva, having given away all their jewels, their beloved women, and their delightful dwelling, attained that other world.
Nimi of Videha gave his kingdom, the son of Jamadagni gave the whole earth, and Gaya too gave the broad earth with its cities, all to brāhmaṇas.
And when the rain-cloud withheld its rain, again and again Vasiṣṭha kept all creatures alive, as Prajāpati keeps his offspring.
And King Marutta, son of Karaṃdhama, having given his daughter to Aṅgiras, swiftly went to heaven.
And Brahmadatta of Pāñcāla, that king foremost among the wise, having given the treasure-conch to the chief of the twice-born, won the higher worlds.
And King Mitrasaha too, having given his beloved Madayantī to the great-souled Vasiṣṭha, went to heaven together with her.
And the royal seer Sahasrajit of great fame, having given up his cherished life for a brāhmaṇa's sake, went to the unsurpassed worlds.
And King Śatadyumna, having given to Mudgala a golden mansion filled with all that heart could wish, went to heaven.
And the mighty king of the Śālvas, Dyutimān by name, having given his kingdom to Ṛcīka, went to the unsurpassed worlds.
And the royal seer Madirāśva, having given his fair-waisted daughter to Hiraṇyahasta, went to the worlds extolled by the gods.
And the royal seer Lomapāda, the lord, having given his daughter Śāntā to Ṛśyaśṛṅga, was joined with all his abundant desires fulfilled.
And King Prasenajit of great splendor, having given a hundred thousand cows together with their calves, went to the unsurpassed worlds.
These and many others, great-souled, refined of spirit and masters of their senses, went to heaven by giving and by austerity.
Their fame stands firm for as long as the earth shall endure; by gifts, by sacrifices, and by the begetting of offspring, these men attained heaven.

Vyāsa said: Let him study the threefold knowledge as set forth in the Vedas, and then through its ancillary sciences — through the words and syllables of the Ṛk and the Sāman, and likewise of the Yajus and the Atharvan.
For those who are skilled in the doctrines of the Veda and skilled in the knowledge of the self, men of purity and great fortune, behold the arising and the passing away of things.
Thus let him conduct himself by dharma and perform his rites as the cultured do; without injury to living beings let the twice-born seek his livelihood.
Having received understanding from the good, cultured and learned in the scriptures, performing his rites in the world by his own dharma, true to his pledged word —
Such a twice-born householder abides in these six observances; and full of faith let him ever worship with the five sacrifices.
Steadfast and vigilant, self-restrained, knowing dharma, master of himself, free of elation, fear, and wrath — such a brāhmaṇa does not sink.
Giving, study, sacrifice, austerity, modesty, uprightness, and self-control — by these he increases his spiritual fire and casts off all evil.
Then, his sins shaken off, wise, of light diet, his senses conquered, having brought desire and wrath under his sway, let him strive toward the abode of brahman.
Let him honor the sacred fires and the brāhmaṇas and bow before the gods; let him shun harsh speech and all violence bound up with unrighteousness.
This is ordained as the more ancient way of life for the brāhmaṇa; performing his works with the acquisition of knowledge, he attains perfection in his works.
The wise man crosses that dreadful river, hard to ford and unassailable, whose waters are the five senses, whose banks are greed, and whose mire is wrath.

This world, ever risen up by desire and wrath, ever utterly deluded, is borne along without ceasing upon the current of its own nature, by a mighty force seen in the ordinance of things, a force that none can resist.
With the great waters that are time, in the unbroken whirl of the year's rains, with the months for waves and the seasons for current, with the fortnights for the grass that floats upon it —
with the closing and opening of an eye for its foam, with the rush of day and night for its swiftness, with the dread crocodile that is desire, and with the raft that is the Veda and sacrifice —
with dharma for the island of living beings, with the roar of wealth and desire, with the shore whose stairway is righteousness, bearing along the trees that are acts of violence —

and through whose midst flows the flood of the ages' deep pools, with brahman for its origin and its end — into this river the Ordainer has cast all creatures, and they are dragged down to the dwelling of Yama.
This the steadfast and the wise cross over by rafts fashioned of insight; but the unthinking, who have no raft, what shall they do?
For it is fitting that the wise man should cross over, and not the common run of folk; for the wise man, in all things, sees merit and fault from afar.
The man whose soul is full of doubt and desire, of wavering mind and feeble understanding, the unwise — he cannot cross over at all; for he who sits idle does not move forward.
For the man without a raft, swept along, meets with great disaster; and for one seized by the crocodile of desire, even his knowledge is no raft.
Therefore let the discerning man strive for the sake of rising up out of the flood; and this is his rising up — that he becomes a true brāhmaṇa.
Born in a family pure through three generations, of threefold lineage, doer of the three rites — let him therefore stand ready to rise up, that he may cross over by his insight.
For the man who is refined, self-restrained, disciplined, perfected in soul, and wise, perfection comes without delay, both in this world and the next.
The householder abides in these observances, free of anger and free of envy; let him ever worship with the five sacrifices and eat what remains after the offering.
Let him conduct himself by the practice of the good and perform his rites as the cultured do; without violating dharma, let him seek a blameless livelihood.
Knowing the truth through scripture and discernment, of cultured conduct, discerning, active in his own dharma — by his works he too remains undefiled.
Active in rites, full of faith, generous, wise, free of envy, knowing well the difference between right and wrong — he crosses over all that is hard to cross.
Steadfast and vigilant, self-restrained, knowing dharma, master of himself, free of elation, fear, and wrath — such a brāhmaṇa does not sink.
This is ordained as the more ancient way of life for the brāhmaṇa; performing his works through the possession of knowledge, he attains perfection everywhere.
For here the undiscerning man, though he desires dharma, does unrighteousness; and dharma that looks like unrighteousness he performs as if in sorrow.

Thinking 'I do dharma,' he does unrighteousness; and desiring unrighteousness, he sometimes does dharma. The fool, not understanding either of these two deeds — that embodied one is born and dies again and again.
Vyāsa said: But if a man should set his heart upon this, and bend his mind toward it with resolve, then, now rising and now sinking, the man of knowledge becomes one possessed of a raft.
By rafts fashioned of insight the steadfast carry the ignorant across; but the ignorant can in no way carry others across, nor even themselves.
With his faults cut away, the sage, intent and disciplined, should practice the twelvefold yoga, free of fear in approaching or withdrawing, his ends the joys that flow from the ten observances.

He who would attain the highest knowledge, wise and skilled in conduct, should restrain his sight by the mind and by insight, and restrain speech and mind by the intellect; and he who would attain the soul's peace should restrain the self by knowledge.
If a man becomes a constant beholder of these, though he be most fierce of nature, or though he know all the Vedas, or though he know neither hymn nor muttered prayer —
whether he be righteous and a sacrificer, or the greatest of evildoers, whether he be a tiger among men, or one beset by weakness —

he crosses indeed that great stronghold, the ocean of old age and death; for one who is yoked by this discipline, even practicing but one of these in the end, even merely seeking to know, passes beyond the brahman that is sound.

Its seat is dharma, its guard-rail modesty, its pole the approaching and the withdrawing; the down-breath is its axle, the breaths its yoke, insight its span of life, and the living being its tether —
made fair by consciousness and lovely, its felly the holding fast to right conduct, drawn forward by sight and touch, borne along by smell and hearing —
its nave wisdom, its goad the mastery of all the doctrines, knowledge its charioteer, ridden over by the Knower of the Field, steadfast, with faith and self-restraint going on before it —
following the road of renunciation, bringing security, moving in purity, ranging in the field of meditation: this divine chariot, yoked with the living self, shines forth in the world of brahman.
Now to one who, hastening, would yoke this chariot, whose mind is set on reaching the Imperishable, I shall declare the swift-bearing rule.
He who, restrained in speech, masters in full the seven fixations of the mind, and likewise the others, behind and to the side, however many those further holdings are —
in due order the lordship over earth, over the windy element, over space and over water, and that which belongs to light, the lordship over the I-principle that springs from the intellect —
and so too the lordship over the Unmanifest he attains in due order; and he in whom these powers are present yokes himself thus by yoga.
Then, when he is yoked in yoga and beholds the perfection within himself, the self, being churned forth, by reason of its subtlety reveals these forms.
As the fine smoke of winter clings to the sky, so does the first appearance arise for one who is freed from the body.
Then, when the smoke has ceased, comes the second vision of form: he beholds, there in his very self, something like the form of water in the sky.
And when the waters are overpassed, the form of fire shines forth; and when that too has subsided, its form is said to be like a yellow garment, and a hue resembling the color of wool shines forth.
Then, having attained the white course, the unborn one becomes airy and subtle—not even white—the subtlety of consciousness, the unmanifest of this Brahman.
And when these too are born, hear from me the fruits that arise: for one born into earthly lordship, creation is ordained as his portion.
Unshakable like Prajāpati, he sends forth creatures from his body—by the measure of a finger or thumb, or likewise by hand or foot.
One quality, that of wind, is remembered as making the earth tremble; and having become ether, it vanishes in the ether through sameness of nature.
It is grasped by its color, and at will it drinks up the receptacles; yet its form is not seen by its own radiance, and likewise it grows still.
By the conquest of the I-maker, these five become obedient to one's will; and when the sixth—the intellect within the self—is conquered, one prevails.
A flawless and complete illumination then attends upon him; and even so the manifest self attains to the unmanifest.
That from which the world issues forth is called the manifest; there hear from me at length the exposition concerning the unmanifest, and first learn from me the reckoning of the manifest as well.
The twenty-five principles are alike and equal on both sides, in Yoga and likewise in Sāṃkhya; hear from me now the distinctions therein.
That is declared to be the manifest which is born, grows, decays, and dies—endowed with these four marks.
But that which is the contrary of this is declared to be the unmanifest; and two selves are spoken of in the Vedas and likewise in the established doctrines.

They declare another fourfold group born of the four marks: the manifest, and that born of the unmanifest, and likewise the intelligent and the other—called sattva and the knower of the field; this pair too has been shown.
There are two selves in the Vedas, and both delight in the sense-objects; withdrawal from the object is the mark of perfection for the followers of Sāṃkhya.
Free of 'mine,' free of the I-maker, beyond the pairs of opposites, his doubts cut away, he neither grows angry nor hates, nor does he utter false words.
Reviled and even struck, he meditates in friendship and harbors no ill thought; he is one who turns away from all three—word, the rod, and the deeds of the mind.
Equal toward all beings, he draws near to Brahman; he neither desires nor is without desire, established in no more than the sustenance of life's journey.
Free of greed, untroubled, self-controlled, neither a doer nor undone, his senses not scattered, his desires not flung far, harming none among all beings—such a follower of Sāṃkhya is liberated.
Now learn from me by what causes men are liberated through Yoga: he who has transcended the lordly powers of Yoga, and goes beyond them, is set free.
Thus has the wisdom born of true being been told to you, beyond all doubt; in this way one becomes free of the pairs of opposites and attains to Brahman.
Vyāsa said: Then the steadfast one, taking hold of the boat of knowledge and abiding in peace, whether rising up or sinking down, should take refuge in knowledge alone.
Śuka said: What is that knowledge, or that wisdom, by which one crosses beyond the pair—the dharma marked by engagement and the dharma marked by withdrawal?
Vyāsa said: But he who, insentient, would see existence apart from inherent nature, and again nourishes all things—he, freed of causes through wisdom, thrives.
And those who hold, with single-minded conviction, that inherent nature alone is the cause—having winnowed grass and chaff, they gain nothing at all.
And those small-minded men who, taking shelter in this view, conduct themselves having deemed inherent nature the cause—they do not attain the highest good.
For inherent nature leads to destruction, arising from delusion, action, and mind; this is the explanation of these two—inherent nature and the supreme being.
For works such as plowing and the gathering of crops, and vehicles and seats and houses, have all been devised by men of wisdom.
Of pleasure-gardens and houses, of diseases and of their cure, the wise are the expounders, and these things are carried out by those who possess knowledge.
Wisdom joins one to worthy ends; wisdom attains the highest good; kings enjoy their kingdoms, alike in the marks that wisdom confers.
But the nearer and farther shore of beings is grasped by knowledge alone; for those brought into being, my son, wisdom is the supreme goal.
The birth of all the manifold beings is of four kinds; one should mark it as womb-born, egg-born, then sprouting, and also sweat-born.
One should mark the moving creatures as superior to the stationary; for of two things to be distinguished, that which is endowed with motion is the more distinguished.
They say the moving creatures are of two kinds, the two-footed and the many-footed; and though many, the two-footed are superior to the many-footed.
They say the two-footed are of two kinds, the earthly and the others; the earthly are superior, for they consume food.
They say the earthly are of two kinds, the middling and the highest; the middling are superior, by the holding fast of the duties of their kind.
They say the middling are of two kinds, the knowers of dharma and the others; the knowers of dharma are superior, by the holding fast of what is to be done and not done.
They say the knowers of dharma are of two kinds, the knowers of the Veda and the others; the knowers of the Veda are superior, for in them the Veda is established.
They say the knowers of the Veda are of two kinds, the expounders and the others; the expounders are superior, by the holding fast of all the dharmas.
For by them the Vedas are understood, with all the fruits of the rites of dharma; the Vedas, with their sacrifices and their supplements, have issued forth from the expounders.
They say the expounders are of two kinds, the knowers of the self and the others; the knowers of the self are superior, by the holding fast of birth and the cessation of birth.
For he who knows the twofold dharma is wholly a knower of all dharma; he is the renouncer, true of resolve; he is the patient one, he is the lord.
For the gods know him to be the brāhmaṇa established in the knowledge of dharma, accomplished in the Brahman-of-the-word and resolved upon the Supreme.
Those who know the Supreme, within and without, as the principle over sacrifice and over the gods—to them we bow; they, my son, are the gods, they are the twice-born.
In them this whole world of beings, and the universe with all that is foremost in it, is set down; nothing is equal to the greatness of their being.
Having wholly transcended beginning and end and action, they are lords of all the fourfold creation of beings—self-existent.
Vyāsa said: This earlier mode of life is ordained for the brāhmaṇa; the man of knowledge alone, while performing works, attains perfection in all things.
And if here it should not be so, a doubt arises in the determination of action: Is this action inherent nature, or is knowledge itself action?
And if here there should be a wish to know whether knowledge pertains to the spirit, I shall expound it by reasoning and by perception; hear that.
Some men declare human effort to be the cause in works; some praise fate, and yet other people, inherent nature.
Human effort, action, and fate, by the inherent nature of how fruits operate—this triad some hold to be separate, but some, undiscriminating, hold otherwise.
'It is thus,' 'it is not thus,' 'it is both,' and 'it is not both'—those caught in action speak unevenly, while those grounded in goodness see with an equal eye.
In the Tretā and the Dvāpara, and those born in the Kali age, are beset with doubt; but ascetics, tranquil and grounded in goodness, belong to the Kṛta age.
In the Ṛc, the Sāman, and the Yajus hymns, all are seers of no division; having seen desire and hatred as distinct, they perform austerity and serve.
Joined to the dharma of austerity, ever devoted to austerity, well disciplined, by it he attains all the desires that he wishes in his mind.
By austerity he attains that, having become which one sends forth the world; and having become that, he then becomes the lord of all beings.
That has been declared, deep and hidden, in the discourses of the Veda by the seers of the Veda; and again in the Vedānta it is made manifest, discerned by the method of gradual progression.

The sacrifices of the kṣatriya are those of undertaking; the vaiśyas are remembered as those whose sacrifices are oblations; the śūdras have the sacrifice of service, and the twice-born the sacrifice of muttered prayer.
For having fully accomplished his task through self-study, one becomes a brāhmaṇa; whether he does other works or does not, the friendly one is called a brāhmaṇa.
At the beginning of the Tretā the Vedas were entire, and so the sacrifices and the orders of caste and stage of life; but through the shortening of lifespan, these are sundered in the Dvāpara age.
In the Dvāpara the Vedas fall into disorder, and so in the Kali age; they are seen and yet not seen, again and again, at the close of the Kali.
And one's own duties decline, oppressed there by unrighteousness, along with the saps of cattle and earth and waters and the healing herbs.
The Vedas, concealed by unrighteousness, and the Veda's dharmas and the orders of life—and creatures stationary and moving, established in their own dharma—undergo corruption.
As the rain rains down upon all earthly beings and sends forth limbs on every side, so do the Vedas, age after age.
The diversity of time spreads forth, and that which is without beginning or end has been proclaimed by me before—that whence beings come together and to which they go.
The Ordainer is this place of origin of beings, the restraint and the restrainer; created in pairs of opposites, beings come forth abundantly by inherent nature.
Creation, time, sustenance, the Vedas, the doer, the deed, the act, and the fruit—this, my son, has been told to you, that which you asked of me.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, and praising this teaching of the supreme sage, joined to the meaning of the dharma of liberation, he set about to ask this.
Śuka said: How does one who has offspring, who is learned in the Veda, a sacrificer, aged, wise, and free of envy, attain that Brahman which has not yet come and is not a matter of tradition?
By austerity, by chastity, by total renunciation, by insight, by Sāṃkhya or by Yoga—being asked this, declare it to me.
And by what means single-pointedness of the mind and of the senses is attained by men—that too you ought to expound.
Vyāsa said: Not otherwise than by knowledge and austerity, not otherwise than by restraint of the senses, not otherwise than by total renunciation does anyone find perfection.
All the great elements are the earlier creation of the Self-existent; they are for the most part settled within embodied beings, in the multitude of the breathing creatures.
From earth comes the body, from water the essence; the two eyes are remembered as from light; wind is the support of the in-breath and out-breath, and ether dwells in the cavities of embodied beings.
In the stride is Viṣṇu, in strength Śakra; the fire in the belly seeks the food consumed; the intermediate quarters are in the ears for hearing, and on the tongue is the speech that is Sarasvatī.
The two ears, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth—these perceivings are declared the senses, the doorways for the attainment of sustenance.
Sound, touch, and likewise form, taste, and smell as the fifth—the senses, each apart, present these objects to the mind.
The mind yokes the senses as a driver yokes obedient horses; and the elemental self, dwelling in the heart, ever yokes the mind as well.
And likewise the mind is the lord of all these senses, in restraint and in release; and so is the elemental self the lord of the mind.
The senses and the objects of the senses, inherent nature, consciousness, mind, the in-breath and out-breath, and the living self—these are ever in the bodies of the embodied.
There is no abode for sattva; the word 'guṇa' is not consciousness; for sattva sends forth radiance, but never indeed the guṇas.
Thus, enwrapped within the body by the sixteen constituents as a seventeenth, the discerning brāhmaṇa, through the mind, beholds the Self within the self.
For this great Self is not to be seen by the eye, nor by all the senses together; only by a mind kindled bright does it shine forth.
That imperishable One, without sound, touch, or form, without taste or smell, bodiless and senseless, one should behold within one's own body.
He who perceives the Unmanifest abiding within manifest bodies, the Deathless seated amid mortals, becomes fit, after death, for union with Brahman.
In a brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and high birth, in a cow, in an elephant, in a dog, and in a dog-eating outcaste alike, the wise look with an equal eye.
For in all beings, the moving and the unmoving, dwells that one great Self, by whom all this universe is pervaded.
When the embodied soul beholds the Self in all beings and all beings within the Self, then it attains to Brahman.
As far as one knows the Self within oneself, so far is the Self present in the Supreme Self; whoever knows this without ceasing becomes fit for immortality.
As for him who has become the Self of all beings and who seeks the welfare of all, even the gods grow bewildered upon his path, searching for the footprint of one who leaves no trace.
As the path of birds through the sky, or of a creature moving through the water, cannot be seen, even so is the course of one of lofty soul.
Time ripens all beings within itself by itself; but the One in whom Time itself is ripened—him no one here can know.
That is not above, not across, not below, not aside, not in the middle; no one anywhere can lay hold of it from any direction.
All these worlds abide within it; outside them there is nothing whatever. Though an arrow sped from the bowstring should fly a thousand leagues,
it could never reach the end of that Cause, even were it swift as thought. Finer than that subtle One there is nothing finer, nor anything grosser than it.
With hands and feet on every side, with eyes, heads, and faces on every side, with ears on every side, it stands in the world, enveloping all.
That very One is smaller than the small, greater than the great; abiding firm within all beings, it remains unseen.
The imperishable and the perishable—this is the twofold being of the Self: perishable in all creatures, but divine, deathless, and imperishable in its higher nature.
Having entered the city of nine gates, the Swan dwells there, self-controlled and master of itself—the Lord of every being, unmoving and moving alike.
Because it takes shelter in successive bodies—new ones subject to loss, decay, and change—those who see to the far shore speak of the unborn One's nature as that of the Swan.
That which is called the Swan, the Imperishable, the Immutable that stands fixed at the summit—the wise man who knows it, attaining that Imperishable, casts off both breath and birth.
Vyāsa said: To you who ask, O worthy son, I have here duly proclaimed, in its very truth, that which is bound up with the method of Sāṃkhya.
Now I shall expound to you the whole practice of Yoga—hear it. The complete oneness of intellect, mind, and the senses for one who meditates upon the Self—this, my son, is the unsurpassed knowledge.
This is to be understood by one who is tranquil, self-restrained, devoted to the inner Self, taking delight in the Self, awakened, and pure in his deeds.
Having wholly cut away the five faults of Yoga which the sages know—desire, anger, and greed, fear, and sleep as the fifth—
one conquers anger by calm and desire by renouncing intention; and by cultivating purity of being the steadfast man is able to root out sleep.
With firmness one should guard the loins and the belly; with the eye, the hands and feet; with the mind, the eye and the ears; and with right action, the mind and speech.
By vigilance one should cast off fear, and greed by attending upon the wise; thus, ever unwearied, one should conquer these faults of Yoga.
He should honor the sacred fires and the brāhmaṇas, and bow before the gods; he should shun angry speech bound up with harm and prompted by an ill mind.
Brahman is radiant, luminous seed, of which all this is the essence; from that one Being arose the twofold creation, the unmoving and the moving.
Meditation, study, charity, truth, modesty, uprightness, forbearance, purity, purity of diet, and the restraint of the senses—
by these one's inner radiance increases and one's evil is drawn away; all his aims are accomplished, and true discernment unfolds.

Even-minded toward all beings, faring on with whatever is gained or not gained, with his evil shaken off, radiant, of light diet, his senses mastered—having brought desire and anger under his sway, he should strive to attain the state of Brahman.
Having made the mind and the senses one-pointed, collected within himself, in the first watch of the night and in the last he should hold the mind steady by the self.
In a creature endowed with the five senses, through whichever single sense is left as an opening, his wisdom leaks away, as water from the foot of a waterskin.
The knower of Yoga should first draw in the mind, as a fisherman draws in the fish; then the ear, then the eye, the tongue, and the nose.
Then, having reined these in, the ascetic should fix them in the mind; and likewise, having banished all intentions, he should hold the mind steady in the Self.

Having gathered the five by knowledge, the ascetic should fix them in the mind; and when these, together with the mind as the sixth, come to rest within the Self and, abiding there, grow serene, then Brahman shines forth.
Like a smokeless flame burning bright, radiant as the sun, like lightning-fire in the sky, he beholds the Self by the self; and there, everywhere, by reason of its all-pervadingness, the All is seen.
Him the great-souled brāhmaṇas behold, those who are discerning, steadfast of resolve, of mighty wisdom, devoted to the welfare of all beings.
Thus passing the appointed time in observance, firm in his vows, seated alone in a solitary place, he may attain union with the Imperishable.
Bewilderment, giddiness, whirling; strange things in smell, hearing, and sight; marvels in taste and touch; sensations of cold and heat, and forms wrought of wind—
such visions and afflictions too may arise through the practice of Yoga; but the knower of truth, disregarding them, should turn them back by his own self.
Self-controlled, the sage should make his practice of Yoga familiar at the three times of day; and he should yoke himself upon a mountain peak, in a sacred shrine, or amid the tops of trees.
Having reined in the host of the senses, like a herdsman attentive to his vessels in the cow-pen, one-pointed he should meditate ever, and not let the mind grow restless from his Yoga.
By whatever means the restless mind can be reined in, by that the yoked one should pursue it, and not stray from it thereafter.
Empty mountain caves, the abodes of the gods, and deserted houses—these the one-pointed seeker should resort to for his dwelling.
He should not cling to another by speech, by deed, or even by thought; indifferent, of measured diet, he should be even-minded toward gain and loss.
Whether one praises him or one reviles him, he should be the same toward both, and should not dwell in thought upon the fair or the foul.
He should not exult in gains nor grieve in losses; even-minded toward all beings, he should share the nature of the wind.
Thus for the holy one, wholly devoted, seeing all things with an equal eye, ever yoked for six months, the Brahman-as-Word is transcended.
Beholding mankind tormented with pain, holding a clod, a stone, and gold as equal, devoted to this path, he should not turn back, nor be deluded.
Even those of the lower two classes, untilled by learning, or a woman longing for dharma—even these may by this path attain the supreme goal.

The unborn, ancient, ageless, everlasting One, which the unwavering man apprehends through the senses—smaller than the small, greater than the great—that the yoked man, possessed of the Self, beholds by the self.
This word of the great-souled mighty sage, duly spoken, having beheld and pondered it in the mind, one should go on to attain union with the Supreme—that goal of beings to which the wise repair.
Śuka said: As for this saying of the Veda—'Perform action' and 'Renounce it'—to what region do men go by knowledge, and to what do they go by action?
This I wish to hear; may you declare it to me, for these two stand opposed to each other, each contrary to the other.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, the son of Parāśara replied to his son: 'I shall expound to you these two—the perishable and the imperishable—wrought of action and of knowledge.'
To what region men go by knowledge, and to what they go by action—hear with single-minded attention, my son, for this distinction is a deep and hidden thing.
'Dharma exists,' it is declared; and should one say in this same matter 'It exists not'—what I have to say here may seem to match that side as well.
There are these two paths, on which the Vedas are established: the dharma marked by engagement in action, and that well-praised dharma which lies in withdrawal from it.
By action the creature is bound, but by knowledge it is set free; therefore the ascetics who see to the far shore perform no action.
By action one is born again after death, an embodied being made of the sixteen parts; by knowledge one is born eternal, imperishable, of imperishable nature.
Yet some praise action—men of the meaner understanding; thereby they take delight in the webs of bodies and cleave to them.
But those who have attained the higher understanding, who see the subtlety of dharma, do not praise action—as one would not praise a well while drinking at a river.
From action one reaps fruit—pleasure and pain, birth and rebirth; but by knowledge one attains that whence, having gone, one grieves no more.
That, having reached which one dies not; having reached which one is not born; having reached which one decays not; having reached which one grows no more—
that supreme Brahman, unmanifest, ageless, abiding, unobstructed, effortless, deathless, and free from all separation;
where men are not afflicted by the pairs of opposites, nor by deed of the mind—even-minded toward all, friendly, devoted to the welfare of all beings.
One Person, my son, is made of knowledge, and another of action; know it like the moon on the new-moon day, abiding in a single subtle digit.
This was declared by the seer, and it is inferred at large by beholding the newborn moon, a curved thread in the sky.
Composed of the eleven modifications, built up by the gathering of digits—know that one to be embodied, my son, made of the qualities born of action.
The divine One that dwells therein, like a drop of water upon a lotus leaf—know that to be the Knower of the Field, eternal, its nature won through renunciation.
Darkness, passion, and purity—know these to be the qualities of the living soul; know the living soul to be a quality of the Self, and the Self a quality of the Supreme Self.
They call the living soul, endowed with consciousness, a quality; it stirs and sets all things in motion. Beyond it the knowers of the Field declare that One who set the seven worlds in motion.
Śuka said: The creation that proceeds from the perishable, the senses together with the qualities, and the auspicious meditation of the Self that serves the unfolding of intellect and lordly power—
yet further, here in this world, the right conduct grounded in livelihood, by which the good go forward—that too I wish to have described.
In the Veda the word is spoken, 'Perform action' and 'Renounce it'; how am I to understand this? That too you ought to expound.
Knowing the truth of the world's affairs, made pure by my teacher's instruction, having fixed my resolve, my self detached, I shall lay down this self untroubled.
Vyāsa said: This mode of life which was ordained of old by Brahman himself was practiced by the good men of former times, the supreme seers.
By the discipline of chastity the supreme seers conquer the worlds; therefore seek the good for your own self within the heart, in the self by the mind.
In the forest, living on roots and fruits, mortifying himself with austerity most vast, ranging among holy sanctuaries and doing no harm to any living being—
When the smoke has cleared and the pestle is laid to rest, dwelling in the hermitage of the forest-recluse, going forth to beg at the appointed hour—such a man grows fit for union with Brahman.
Free of praise, free of obeisance, having cast off the good and the ill alike, let him wander alone in the wilderness, sustained by whatever may come.
Śuka said: When this pronouncement of the Veda stands at odds with the speech of the world, and authority and non-authority are thus in conflict, where then is the standing of scripture?
This I wish to hear; let the venerable one expound it to me: how does this proceed without contradicting the path of works?
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, the son of Gandhavatī answered his son, the sage honoring the question of that boy of measureless splendor.
The householder, the student, the forest-recluse, and the mendicant—all of them, if they do as is enjoined, reach the supreme goal.
He who alone observes these stages of life one by one, each according to its rule, joined neither to desire nor to hatred, is exalted in the world beyond.
For this is a four-runged ladder, set firm upon Brahman; resting upon this ladder, a man is exalted in the world of Brahman.
A quarter of his life let the student dwell, free of envy and skilled in dharma and its purpose, with his teacher or with his teacher's son.
He who would prosper must study, going beyond mere duty for his teacher's sake; let him be deft and never given to reproach, and attend his teacher when summoned.
In the teacher's house let him be the last to lie down and the first to rise; and whatever ought to be done by a pupil, or again by a servant—
all of that, regarding it as simply his to do, let him perform, and then stand ready at his teacher's side—a willing servant, doing all things, skilled in every task.
Pure, capable, endowed with virtue, let him speak straight as an arrow yet unhurried; with his senses mastered and his mind composed, let him look upon his teacher with steady gaze.
While the teacher has not eaten, let him not eat; while the teacher has not drunk, let him not drink; while the teacher stands, let him not sit; while the teacher is awake, let him not sleep.
With both hands upturned let him gently touch his teacher's feet—the right foot with the right hand, the left foot pressing with the left.
Having saluted the teacher, let him say, "Teach, O venerable one"; "This I shall do, O venerable one"; and "This, too, has been done by me."
Thus seeking leave for everything and laying his earnings before the teacher, let him act; and having acted, let him report all of it to the teacher again.
Whatever scents or savors the student forgoes, these he may enjoy once he has returned from his studies—such is the settled rule in matters of dharma.
Whatever restraints have been laid down at length for the student, let him take them all upon himself, and let him not stray from his teacher.
Thus offering his teacher devotion to the best of his power, the pupil should so conduct himself by his works in stage after stage of life.
When through study of the Veda, his vows, and his fasting the first quarter of life has passed, let him give the teacher his fee and return home as the rule prescribes.
United with a wife won by righteous means and kindling the sacred fires according to dharma, let him for the second quarter of life take up the vow of the householder.
Vyāsa said: For the second quarter of life let the householder dwell at home, united with a wife won by righteous means and, true to his vows, having kindled the sacred fires.
Four modes of livelihood for the householder are recorded by the wise: the first is he who stores grain in a granary, then he who stores it in a jar,
then he who keeps no store for the morrow, and then he who gathers his living dove-like, grain by fallen grain; of these, each later one is the higher, and by dharma the best winner of worlds.

One lives by the six occupations, another conducts himself by three, one by two, while the fourth is established in the sacrificial session of Brahman; mighty, they declare, are the householder's vows herein.
He should not cook food for himself alone, nor needlessly slay beasts; whatever, living or lifeless, is fit to be consecrated with the sacrificial formula—that he should so hallow.
Let him never sleep by day, nor in the first or last watches of the night; let him not eat between the proper times, nor approach his wife out of season.
Let no brāhmaṇa dwell unfed and unhonored in his house; and his guests, the bearers of offerings to gods and ancestors, are ever to be revered.

Those bathed in the lore and vows of the Veda, learned in sacred recitation and versed to the end of the Veda, who live by their own dharma, self-controlled, active in rite and rich in austerity—to them the offerings for gods and ancestors are ordained as their due honor.
But not so for the man gone wandering with asses, ignorant of his own dharma, one who has cast aside the fire-offering, or who deals falsely with his teacher.
Herein a fair share is enjoined for all living beings, and likewise the householder should give to those who do not cook for themselves.

Let him ever eat the leavings of others and ever feed on what is like nectar; the remnant of the sacrifice is that nectar, food as sacred as the oblation, and he who eats what is left after his dependents have eaten is called the eater of leavings.

Devoted to his own wife, self-restrained, free of malice, his senses mastered—with the officiating priests, the family priest, and the teachers, with maternal uncles and the guests who shelter with him,
with the aged, the young, the sick, with physicians, kinsmen, relations by marriage, and friends, with mother and father, with sisters, with brother, son, and wife,
with daughter and with the band of servants—let him engage in no quarrel; renouncing such disputes, he is freed from all sins.
By overcoming these contentions he wins, beyond doubt, all the worlds; the teacher is lord of Brahman's world, the father master of the realm of Prajāpati,
the guest is lord of Indra's world, the officiating priests of the world of the gods; sisters belong in the world of the apsarases, and kinsmen in the realm of the Viśvedevas.
Relations by marriage and friends rule in the quarters of space, mother and maternal uncle upon the earth; the aged, the young, the sick, and the frail hold sway in the sky.
An elder brother is the equal of a father; wife and son are one's own body; the band of servants is one's own shadow; and a daughter is the highest object of one's tenderness.
Therefore, though provoked by these, let the wise man ever endure it without fever of resentment—devoted to the householder's dharma, constant in righteousness, master of his weariness.
Nor, bound to wealth, should he perform any rite or any act of dharma for gain; of the three modes of the householder's life, the highest is the one that leads to release.
They say, too, that these stand in mutual relation: this very fourfold order of life's stages. Whatever restraints have been laid down for them, all must be fulfilled by him who would prosper.
That kingdom flourishes wherein dwell such worthy men—those who store grain in a jar, those who live by gleaning fallen ears, and those who hold to the dove-like way.
He purifies ten forebears and ten descendants who, free of distress, lives by these modes of the householder's life.
He attains a goal like that of the dwellers in the wheeling spheres; this destiny is ordained for those whose senses are restrained.
For householders of generous mind the world of heaven is appointed—heaven furnished with celestial cars, beheld in the Veda, in full and lovely flower.

In the world of heaven is the standing-place of householders who are masters of themselves; this rung was ordained by Brahman, and from it one is set free—having reached in due order the second stage, one is exalted in the world of heaven.

Beyond this they declare a noble stage supreme—the third—for those who would forsake the body: matchless for the forest-dwellers who were once householders. Hear now of these who put their bodies to hardship.
Bhīṣma said: The householder's mode of life, as ordained for the wise, has been declared to you; mark now, Yudhiṣṭhira, what is taught as following thereupon.
Shaking off this stage in due order, hear of the third and higher mode of life—of those wearied by the vows of householding, who dwell in the hermitage of the forest-recluse,
Listen, Pārtha—blessings upon you—of those whose souls are a refuge to all the worlds, who set forth with foresight and dwell in holy regions.
Vyāsa said: When the householder sees his own wrinkles and gray hair, and the offspring of his offspring, then let him betake himself to the forest.
For the third quarter of life let him dwell in the order of the forest-recluse, tending those same sacred fires and offering sacrifice to the dwellers in heaven.
Disciplined, of measured food, eating but at every sixth mealtime, and ever vigilant—his is that fire-offering, his those cattle, and his all the appurtenances of sacrifice.
Rice and barley untilled, wild grain, and gleaned leavings—these he should offer as oblations in the five great sacrifices observed here.
In the order of the forest-recluse, too, four modes are recorded: some wash and consume their food the same day, some store enough for a month,
some lay up a year's store, and some a store of twelve years, doing so to honor guests and to accomplish the rites of sacrifice.
In the rains they take the open sky for shelter, in winter they resort to the waters, in summer they sit amid the five fires, and always they eat but sparingly.
They roll upon the bare ground, or stand upon their toes; they pass their lives standing or seated, and bathe at the times of the three pressings.
Some use their teeth for a mortar, others pound their food with stones; some, in the bright fortnight, drink boiled barley-gruel but once a day.
Some drink it in the dark fortnight and eat in due succession; some, firm in their vows, live on roots, some on fruits, some on flowers.
Holding to the doctrine of the Vaikhānasas, they live as the rule requires; these and many other diverse observances belong to those sages.
And the fourth, the dharma of the Upaniṣads, is held to be common to all; from it, beyond the forest-recluse and the householder alike, yet another way proceeds.
In this very age, my child, by brāhmaṇas who beheld all truths—Agastya, the Seven Seers, Madhucchandas, Aghamarṣaṇa,
Sāṃkṛti, Sudivā, Taṇḍi, Yavānna, and Kṛtaśrama, Ahovīrya, Kāvya, Tāṇḍya, and the sage Medhātithi,
Śala, Vāka and Nirvāka, Śūnyapāla and Kṛtaśrama—these, learned in such observances of dharma, thereupon ascended to heaven.
My child, the bands of wandering seers whose righteousness was made manifest, sages of fierce austerity who beheld the fine subtleties of dharma—
brāhmaṇas beyond naming and beyond number who resorted to the forest, the Vaikhānasas, the Vālakhilyas, the Sikatas, and others still—

taking no delight in worldly works, constant in dharma, their senses subdued, all of them—their righteousness made manifest—betook themselves to the forest, and now, beyond the constellations and unassailable, they are seen as hosts of stars.

Worn down by age and afflicted by disease, in the fourth and last remnant of his life let him forsake the order of the forest-recluse, having performed the same-day rite with all his possessions for its priestly fee.
Sacrificing to the Self, taking joy in the Self, sporting in the Self, resting upon the Self, he draws the sacred fires up into his own Self and casts off all possessions.
Let him offer same-day sacrifices and oblations here always; ever, from the outward rite of those who sacrifice, the worship turns back to the Self alone.

And let him duly offer the three fires within the Self itself, for the sake of the Self's release; with the sacrificial formula he should make five offerings to the breaths, and eat six mouthfuls without disdain.
Having shorn his hair, his bodily hair, and his nails, the forest-recluse, now a silent sage, passes purified by his works at once from one stage of life to the next.
The twice-born who, having granted freedom from fear to all living beings, goes forth to the wandering life—worlds of radiance are his, and after death he attains the endless.

Of fair conduct and character, his stains washed away, he strives to act neither for this world nor the next; free of anger and delusion, beyond alliance and enmity, the man who knows the Self should abide as one wholly indifferent.

Let him not waver in the restraints that belong to the Self, his strength lying in his own scripture, sacred thread, oblation, and mantra; a path at will belongs to him who sacrifices to the Self—no doubt of it, for one devoted to dharma whose senses are mastered.

Beyond this, hear of that which is best, surpassing in noble virtues, established above and beyond the other three—the supreme: the fourth, the highest stage of life now declared, the loftiest refuge being proclaimed to you.
Śuka said: While dwelling within the order of the forest-hermit, how should one who longs, to the utmost of his power, for the supreme station discipline his own self?
Vyāsa said: Having gained, through these two orders of life, his consecration, hear now with single-minded attention what task remains to be done thereafter, for the sake of the supreme end.
Having burned away the dross within the three graded stations, let him go forth into the supreme station, the unsurpassed wandering life of renunciation.
Practising thus, let your honoured self abide therein, and hear how it is done: ever alone, without companion, let him wander for the sake of perfection.
He who wanders alone, keeping watch, neither forsakes nor is forsaken. Let him be without sacred fire and without fixed abode, and resort to a village only to seek his food.
Let the sage make no provision for the morrow, filled with inward feeling; eating sparingly, restrained in his food, partaking of a meal but once.
A begging bowl, the roots of trees for shelter, ragged clothing, solitude, and indifference toward all creatures—this much is the mark of the mendicant.
He into whom words enter as stones dropped into a well, never returning to their speaker, may dwell in the order of absolute aloneness.
Let him neither see nor hear anything unfit to be spoken of anyone whatever, and above all let him never in any way speak ill of the brāhmaṇas.
Whatever is for a brāhmaṇa's welfare, that alone let him constantly speak; when reviled, let him sit silent, thereby making a medicine for his own soul.
He by whom alone the empty sky seems forever full, and by whom a place thronged with people seems void—him the gods know to be a true brāhmaṇa.
Covered with whatever comes to hand, fed by whatever comes to hand, lying down to sleep wherever he may be—him the gods know to be a true brāhmaṇa.
He who shrinks from a crowd as from a serpent, from sated fullness as from hell, and from women as from a corpse—him the gods know to be a true brāhmaṇa.
He who, whether honoured or dishonoured, neither flares in anger nor swells with delight, and who grants safety to all creatures—him the gods know to be a true brāhmaṇa.
Let him not welcome death, nor welcome life; let him only await his time, as a hired servant awaits his orders.
Let his mind be unassailed and his speech likewise unassailing; released from all sins, having no enemy, what fear can be his?
Since from him all creatures have nothing to fear, and he in turn has nothing to fear from any creature, for him who is freed from the body there is no fear from any quarter.
As within the footprint of the elephant the footprints of all other creatures that walk are wholly contained,
so within non-injury the whole of righteousness's purpose is contained; immortal forever dwells the man who takes up the practice of non-injury.
Harmless, even-minded, truthful, steadfast, his senses curbed, a refuge to all creatures, he attains the unsurpassed goal.
For the sage thus contented in wisdom and free of fear, death is not a state beyond his reach; rather, he overtakes death itself.
The sage released from all attachments, standing firm like the open sky, owning nothing, wandering alone, at peace—him the gods know to be a true brāhmaṇa.
He whose life is for the sake of righteousness, whose righteousness is for the sake of detachment, and whose days and nights are for the sake of merit—him the gods know to be a true brāhmaṇa.
Free of craving, undertaking nothing, neither bowed to nor praised, undiminished though his works are spent—him the gods know to be a true brāhmaṇa.
All creatures delight in happiness; all shrink in dread from pain. Grieved at the thought of causing them fear, the man of faith should do no deeds that breed it.

The gift whose offering is freedom from fear to all beings surpasses every other gift here below; and he who first lays aside his fierce, cruel nature wins from all creatures a boundless freedom from fear.

Lying upturned, with mouth he pours the oblation—he, the navel of the world, the world's foundation; his limbs are all things, the done and the undone alike, for the All-Pervading Fire has entered into everything.

Into that which rests within the heart, a mere span in measure, the self-sacrificer pours his life-breaths as oblation; his fire-offering, poured and grounded in the Self, reaches through all the worlds together with their gods.

Those who know the divine, threefold in substance, triply enfolded, fair-winged and foremost, and who know its supreme reality—they, honoured in all the worlds, mighty as gods, pass on to the abode of the well-doer.
He who knows the Vedas, the object of knowledge, the ordinance entire, the etymology, and the supreme reality—who knows all this as seated in the Self within the body—for him the gods forever yearn.

Unattached to the earth, immeasurable in heaven, golden, egg-born within the cosmic egg—he who knows that winged one, the bird soaring in the midspace, knows it as the radiant-rayed enjoyer within the Self that is enjoyed.
Revolving, ageless, ever-turning, with six fellies, twelve spokes, and goodly joints—within whose mouth the whole universe wheels round—that is the wheel of Time, set hidden in the cave of the heart.
He who knows the serene radiance to be the body of the world attains here to all the worlds; what is offered into it gratifies the gods, and they, gratified in turn, gratify his mouth.
Made of splendour, of eternal frame, ancient, he passes to the worlds that are endless and free of fear; he of whom creatures never stand in dread is himself never in dread of creatures.
Himself beyond blame, and blaming no other—that sage may behold the supreme Self; his delusion subdued, his stain washed away, he seeks no gain either here or hereafter.

Free of wrath and delusion, holding a clod and gold as equal, his grief abandoned, beyond alliance and enmity, beyond blame and praise, indifferent to the loved and the unloved—such a mendicant wanders as one wholly detached.
Vyāsa said: The knower of the field is surrounded by the modifications of Nature; yet they do not know him, while he indeed knows them all.
Through them—through the senses, with the mind as the sixth—he accomplishes his work, like a charioteer guiding strong and well-broken steeds of the finest breed.
Higher than the senses are their objects; higher than the objects is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect; and higher than the intellect is the great Self.
Higher than the great is the Unmanifest; higher than the Unmanifest is the Immortal; than the Immortal there is nothing higher—that is the limit, that the supreme goal.
Thus the Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth; yet it is seen by those who perceive the truth, through a keen and subtle intellect.
Dissolving by his wisdom into the inner Self the senses, with the mind as the sixth, together with the objects of sense, and ceasing to brood upon the manifold matters of thought—
having brought meditation to its rest, his mind perfected by knowledge, owning no lord, his self wholly tranquil, he then attains the immortal station.
But the mortal who, while mastering all his senses, is shaken in his recollection, by the surrender of his self comes only to death.
But casting off all his wilful imaginings, let him fix his thought in purity; and having fixed his thought in purity, he becomes thereby a conqueror of time.
By the serenity of his thought the ascetic forsakes both good and evil; serene of self, abiding in the Self, he wins the happiness that is without end.
The mark of that serenity is this: as a contented man sleeps happily, or as a lamp that burns in a windless place does not flicker.
Thus joining the self to the Self in the first and the last watches of the night, his being purified by sattvic food, he beholds the Self within the self.
This teaching, the secret of all the Vedas, resting on no mere tradition and no external scripture but on the soul's own conviction—this is the instruction I give to my son.
Whatever treasure lies in all discourses on righteousness and in all discourses on truth—this nectar has been churned forth and drawn up out of ten thousand ṛc-verses.

As butter is drawn from curd, as fire is drawn from wood, so has the wisdom of the learned been drawn forth for the sake of a son. This teaching, this instruction to a son, is to be spoken to those who have completed their studies.
It is not to be told to one who is unquiet, nor to the unrestrained, nor to one without austerity, nor to one ignorant of the Vedas, nor to one who is not a devoted follower.
Not to the envious, not to the crooked, not to one who acts contrary to instruction, not to one scorched by the science of mere argument, nor likewise to the slanderer.

To one worthy of praise who praises rightly, to the tranquil, to the man of austerity, to a beloved son, to a devoted pupil who follows faithfully—to such a one this secret of righteousness is to be told, but to no other in any wise.
Even should a man offer him this whole earth filled with jewels, the knower of truth would still hold this teaching to be the better thing of the two.

Therefore that knowledge of the supreme Self, more hidden in meaning, more than human, which the great seers have beheld and which is sung in the Vedānta—that I shall now declare to you, even as you question me.
Śuka said: Speak to me yet again, and at length, of the knowledge of the Self—what this knowledge of the Self is, and how it stands, O blessed one, O best of seers.
Vyāsa said: This knowledge of the Self, my son, as it is found in man here below—that I shall declare to you; hear now this its exposition.
Earth, water, fire, wind, and likewise space—these are the great elements of created beings, as the waves are of the sea.
As the tortoise stretches forth its limbs here and again draws them in, so the great elements take on their transformations within the lesser beings.
Thus this whole world of things moving and unmoving is made of those very elements, both in its creation and in its dissolution; and therefore it is so declared.
The Maker of beings, my son, fashioned the five great elements within all creatures, and wrought in them the diversity wherein each perceives its own nature.
Śuka said: That which he wrought within bodies—how is it to be discerned? And which qualities belong to the senses—how are these to be discerned?
Vyāsa said: This I shall set forth to you, the doctrine even as it is; hear with single mind the truth here, as it truly stands and how it is.
Sound, hearing, and the bodily openings—these three arise from space. Breath, movement, and touch—these are the three qualities of wind.
Form, sight, and digestion—threefold is fire ordained. Taste, the tongue, and moisture—these are the three qualities of water.
Smell, the nose, and the body—these are the three qualities of earth. Thus is the whole company of the senses, sprung from the five elements, explained.
Touch belongs to wind, taste to water, form is said to belong to fire; sound has its origin in space, and smell is held to be the quality of earth.
Mind, intellect, and the inner disposition—these three are born of the Self's own source; they do not transcend the qualities, yet are held to be higher than the qualities.
In man there are five senses; the mind is reckoned the sixth; the intellect, they say, is the seventh; and the knower of the field is the eighth.
The eye is for mere seeing, the mind raises doubt, the intellect serves for resolve, and the knower of the field is said to be the witness.
Passion, darkness, and goodness—these three are sprung from their own source, present alike in all beings; one should discern them by their respective signs.
As the tortoise here stretches forth its limbs and draws them in again, so the intellect, having sent forth the company of the senses, draws them back.
That which it sees above the soles of the feet and below the crown of the head—in just this task does the highest intellect engage.
The intellect leads on the qualities; the intellect leads the senses too, all of them with the mind as the sixth; and where the intellect is absent, whence then the qualities?
Therein, whatever one marks within oneself as joined with gladness, serene as it were and wholly pure—that one should understand to be goodness.
But whatever arises in the body or the mind joined with torment—that should be passion, the impeller, forever carrying embodied beings away.
But whatever is joined with bewilderment, whose object is unmanifest, beyond reasoning and not to be known—that should be understood to be darkness.
Exultation, gladness, joy, evenness, a self-possessed and settled mind—arising whether without cause or with cause, such is the sattvic quality at work.
Conceit, falsehood, greed, delusion, and impatience—these are the marks of passion, and they arise whether with cause or without.
Likewise delusion and heedlessness, languor and the drowsiness that follows from sleep — these, however they may come upon a man, are to be recognized as the qualities born of tamas.
Vyāsa said: The mind sends forth feeling, the intellect performs the act of resolve, and the heart knows the pleasant and the unpleasant — such is the threefold impulse to action.
Higher than the senses are their objects, and higher than the objects is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect, and higher than the intellect, it is held, is the Self.
The intellect is the self of a man; the intellect is the very essence of the self. When it transforms itself into feeling, then it becomes the mind.
By the distinct functioning of the senses the subtle intellect is modified: while hearing it becomes the ear, while touching it is called touch.
While seeing it becomes sight, while tasting it becomes the tongue, while smelling it becomes the nose — thus the intellect is variously transformed.
These men call the senses; and unseen the intellect presides over them. Abiding within the person, the intellect moves among the three states of feeling.
Sometimes it attains joy, sometimes it grieves, and sometimes here it is joined neither with pleasure nor with pain.
This intellect, whose very being is feeling, transcends these three states, even as the ocean, lord of the rivers, surmounts its mighty wave-tossed shore.
When it desires anything, then it becomes the mind. With the intellect one should keep distinctly in view these several seats; the senses, fit to be purified, are to be wholly mastered.
All of them in due order, whatever is not yet brought under control; the undivided intellect abides as feeling in the mind. And rajas, once set in motion, draws sattva too along after it.
