And whatever states of being there are, all of them turn upon these three; true to their natures they proceed, as the spokes turn upon the felly of a wheel.
A man should make himself a lamp by means of the senses, those finest instruments of the intellect, letting them go forth as is fitting, unattached, of their own accord.
Knowing that such is by nature this whole order of things, the wise man is not deluded: neither grieving nor exulting, ever free from envy.
For the Self cannot be perceived through the senses, ranging amid their objects of desire — senses set upon misrule, hard to restrain, ungoverned by the unperfected.
But when with the mind a man rightly reins in their reins, then the Self shines forth, like a lamp burning within a jar — even as, when the darkness has passed, all beings stand revealed.

As a water-bird, moving over the water, is not wetted by it, so the man of accomplished wisdom, ranging among objects of sense, is not stained by their faults: attached to nothing, he is in no way defiled.
Having renounced the karma wrought before, he whose delight is ever in the Self, who has become the self of all beings, remains unattached to the pathways of the guṇas.
It is sattva, not the Self, that gives birth to the guṇas; the Self at no time does so. The guṇas do not know the Self, but He knows the guṇas always.
He is the witness of the guṇas, and likewise, in truth, their creator. Understand this to be the difference between sattva and the Knower of the Field, the two subtle ones.
The one creates the guṇas, while the other creates them not; the two are by nature distinct, yet they are forever conjoined.
As a fish, though other than the waters, is joined with them, so are those two conjoined; as the gnat and the fig-tree, too, are joined together.
As the reed-blade within the muñja-grass is both apart and together with it, so these two abide united, each established in the other.
Vyāsa said: It is sattva that creates the guṇas, while the Knower of the Field but looks on. The Lord stands as it were indifferent to all the guṇas as they undergo their changes.
All this is bound up with its own nature, that it brings forth these guṇas — as the spider spins forth its thread, so does it spin out the guṇas like threads.
Once destroyed, they return no more, and no continued activity is found: thus some maintain; while others hold that there is a ceasing.
Weighing both these views, let a man resolve according to his own understanding; for by this very course one may yet become a great one lying again in the womb.
Having reached that which is without beginning or end, eternal, let a man move through the world neither angering nor exulting, ever free from envy.
Thus, having passed beyond the firm knot of the heart, fashioned of the intellect's brooding, let him abide in happiness, grieving not, his doubts cut asunder.
As men, slipping from solid ground into a brimming river, are plunged in and suffer, so know that the ignorant are sunk in this world.
But the wise man does not founder; the knower of truth walks upon firm ground. Such is he who finds the Self — the pure knowledge that is of the Self alone.
Having thus understood the whole coming and going of all beings, and rightly considering it little by little, a man attains the highest peace.
This indeed is the worth of being born, above all for the brāhmaṇa: knowledge of the Self and tranquillity — that is sufficient, that is the supreme refuge.
Having understood this, one becomes awakened — what other mark of the awakened is there? Knowing this, the wise are set free, their task accomplished.
For the wise there is no great fear, though for the unwise that fear may be very great; for no one has a goal higher than that which is the wise man's, the eternal one.
People resent the world's distress, and gazing upon this and that they grieve over it; but behold there the skilled who grieve not, who know both the done and the undone.
What he does without forethought of fruit wipes away what was done before; both the agreeable and the disagreeable that come of it, neither does it engender for him who acts thus in this world.
Śuka said: That dharma than which no higher dharma is found here anywhere, that which is the most excellent of all dharmas — let your honored self declare it to me.
Vyāsa said: I shall declare to you that ancient dharma, praised by the seers, most excellent of all dharmas — hear it here with single mind.
With the intellect, by effort, restrain the unruly senses, ever apt to break loose on every side, as a father restrains his wayward sons.
The one-pointedness of mind and senses is the supreme austerity; it is greater than all dharmas — that is declared the highest dharma.
Having gathered them all, the senses with the mind for sixth, by means of wisdom, let him sit content within the Self, not brooding on the many things that might be brooded upon.
When, withdrawn from their objects, they come to rest within their dwelling, then by the Self you shall behold the supreme, eternal Self.
That all-pervading, great Self, like a fire without smoke — those great-souled brāhmaṇas who are wise behold Him.
As a great tree, many-branched, laden with flower and fruit, knows not of itself, 'Where is my flower, where is my fruit?' —
so the self knows not, 'Whither shall I go, and whence am I?' For there is another, an inner Self within, who beholds all things.
By the kindled lamp of knowledge one beholds the Self through the Self. Having seen the Self by the Self, become free of self, all-knowing.
Freed from all sins, like a serpent loosed from its slough, having attained here the supreme intellect, sinless and rid of fever —
that dread river, flowing on every side, bearing the world along in its current, infested with the crocodiles of the five senses, banked by the mind's imaginings;

choked with the weeds of greed and delusion, swarming with the serpents of desire and wrath, with truth for its ford and falsehood for its turbulence, with wrath for its mire — that foremost of rivers;
rising from the Unmanifest, swift, hard for the unperfected to cross — that river, thronged with the crocodiles of desire, cross over by the intellect.
It runs to the ocean of rebirth, hard to cross with its hells of wombs, springing from one's own birth, my son, with the tongue for its whirlpool, difficult to approach.
That river the wise of accomplished understanding, steadfast in resolve, cross over; having crossed it you shall be released on every side, your self made pure, knower of the Self, cleansed.
Resting upon the highest intellect, you shall attain to oneness with brahman, having crossed over all afflictions, your self serene, free from stain.

As one standing on a mountain looks down upon the creatures below on the ground, so look upon beings — neither angering nor exulting, your mind free of cruelty; then shall you behold the arising and the passing away of all beings.
Thus, O best of the upholders of dharma, the wise — the sages who perceive the truth — have deemed this the most excellent of all dharmas.
Having known the imperishable Self, this teaching meant for a son is to be declared to one who is striving, devoted to his welfare, and obedient.
This knowledge of the Self is a secret, the greatest secret of all secrets, mighty — which I have spoken to you, my son, plainly, with the Self for its witness.
This is neither woman nor man, nor yet is it neuter; brahman, free of pain and free of pleasure, whose essence is the past, the future, and the present.
Having known this, neither man nor woman comes again to rebirth; for the attainment of non-becoming this path is laid down.
As all the doctrines are held to be, and yet are not just so, even thus, my son, have they been told by me — they both are and are not.

Being asked this by a son endowed with affection and with virtue, possessed of the qualities of a true son, lovingly and for his good, a father should speak to his son here what has thus been declared.

Vyāsa said: Let him not pursue scents or savors, nor pleasure, nor seek the adornments of this thing or that; let him desire neither honor nor renown nor fame — such is the way of life of the discerning brāhmaṇa.
He may study all the Vedas, attentive and chaste — the Ṛc verses, the Yajus, the Sāman chants — yet by that alone he is not on that account a brāhmaṇa.
Though he be as a kinsman to all beings, all-knowing, knower of all the Vedas, if he never dies free of desire, by that too he is not a brāhmaṇa.
Having performed the various oblations and the great sacrifices with their fees duly given, he does not thereby attain brāhmaṇahood at all without contemplation.
When this one fears nothing and nothing fears him, when he neither desires nor hates — then he attains to brahman.
When he conceives no evil intent toward any being, by deed, by thought, or by word — then he attains to brahman.
The bondage of desire is the one bondage; there is no other bondage here. Freed from the bondage of desire, one becomes fit for oneness with brahman.
Being released from desire, like the moon from a smoke-gray cloud, free of passion, awaiting his time, the steadfast one abides in his firmness.
As the waters enter the ocean, ever filled yet fixed and unmoving — he who is loved of desires yet desires not desires, that embodied one goes from this world to heaven.
The hidden essence of the Veda is truth; the hidden essence of truth is self-restraint; the hidden essence of self-restraint is giving; the hidden essence of giving is austerity.
The hidden essence of austerity is renunciation; the hidden essence of renunciation is happiness; the hidden essence of happiness is heaven; the hidden essence of heaven is tranquillity.
The melting away of grief and of the troubled mind, the burning torment together with craving — if you desire purity of being, then through contentment comes the supreme mark of peace.
Free of grief, free of the sense of 'mine,' at peace, serene of self, the best of knowers of the Self — endowed with these six marks, made whole, he will return no more.
By means of these six, endowed with the quality of sattva, wise and high in counsel, those who know the Self after death know likewise those who abide here as such.
Unfeigned, not to be carried off, natural, unadorned — the inner Self: the man of well-wrought wisdom enjoys this imperishable happiness.
Having made the mind cease its roaming and established it firm on every side, the contentment that this man attains cannot be had in any other way than this.

That by which one is satisfied though not eating, by which one is content though possessing no wealth, by which without attachment one gains strength — he who knows that is the true knower of the Veda.
For that disciplined brāhmaṇa who, guarding well the gates of his own self and closing them, sits in contemplation — he is called one who finds his delight in the Self.
To the one who is fixed upon the supreme truth, established in it, his desires worn away, happiness comes from every side, as light suffuses the orb of the moon.
For the sage who no longer cleaves to creatures with their distinctions, nor to the qualities, sorrow is driven off by happiness, as darkness is driven off by the sun.
That brāhmaṇa who has passed beyond action, passed beyond the wasting of the qualities, and clings to no object of sense — old age and death do not find him.
When, freed on every side, he abides in perfect equanimity, then, though seated in the body, he transcends the senses and their objects.
Having attained the supreme Cause, having passed beyond all that is effect — for him who has reached the highest beyond the high, there is no returning again.

Vyāsa said: The disciple who would know liberation, who has practiced the pairs of opposites and observed both worldly gain and dharma, must first be made to hear this great teaching from a worthy preceptor.
Ether, wind, fire, water, and earth the fifth — together with being and non-being, and time — these abide within all the five elements.
Ether is innermost in nature, and the ear, the organ of hearing, is made of it; one versed in the science and ordinance of embodied forms should know sound to be its quality.
Motion is of the nature of wind, and the in-breath and out-breath are made of it; one should know that the organ of touch, and touch itself, are likewise made of it.
From fire come digestion and light; the eye too is made of it, and its quality is known to be form — that which dispels the darkness inherent in things.
Moistening, fineness, and fluid coherence are taught to be of water; the tongue is the organ of taste, and taste is held to be the quality of water.
Solid mass is the earthen element: bones, teeth, and nails, beard, body-hair and the hair of the head, veins, sinews, and skin.
The organ that perceives by smelling is named the nose; and its object, odor, is to be known as made of earth.
In the later elements all the qualities of the former are present, and the qualities of the later in all — thus the sages understand the unbroken sequence of the five elemental aggregates.
Among these the mind is the ninth, and the intellect is reckoned the tenth; the inner Self is the eleventh, and is declared to be supreme over all.
The intellect is of the nature of resolve, the mind of the nature of discrimination; from the inference of its action that living self, called the knower of the field, is to be known.
The wise one who, with all these principles — the elements together with time as the eighth — sees everything as pervaded by them, undimmed, does not fall prey to delusion.
Vyāsa said: The embodied self, become subtle and wholly released from the body — those whose minds are steeped in scripture perceive it fully through the disciplines the scriptures enjoin.
As rays of light move together, are seen to go and to stand still, so do beings beyond the human, released from their bodies, roam through the worlds.
As the heat of the sun is seen reflected as an image upon the waters, so does the one endowed with the pure essence behold that essence as a reflected likeness.
Those subtle beings, freed from the body and abiding in pure essence, the knowers of truth, their senses controlled, behold by their own true insight.
Whether men sleep or wake, the Self is what all of them ponder — those joined to the duality of primal Nature, who cast off the passion born of works.
As by day, so by night; as by night, so by day — the essential Self stands ever in the mastery of those who are steadfast in yoga.
In them the elemental self, though ever transient, is yet eternal; endowed always with the seven subtle qualities, it wanders on, unaging and undying.
Surpassing mind and intellect, knowing both its own body and others' bodies, even in dreams it remains the one who experiences pleasure and pain.
There too it meets with sorrow, there too it meets with joy; there too, giving way to anger and greed, it comes to misfortune.
It is gladdened too, on gaining great wealth, and there too it performs meritorious deeds; and it sees, even there, as though awake.
This elemental self, with its portion of surpassing radiance, seated within the heart — those overcome by darkness and passion do not perceive it in embodied forms.
Becoming devoted to scripture and yoga, longing to grasp their own Self — those things that are breathless and formless, yet hard as the thunderbolt —
Among the four separately ordained orders of life and their duties, Śāṇḍilya declared this very yoga, in deep meditation, to be the path of inner peace.
Having known the seven subtle principles and the six-membered Great Lord, established in the right ordering of primal Nature, one attains the supreme Brahman.
Vyāsa said: In the heart stands the wondrous tree of desire, sprung from the accumulation of delusion, its great trunk anger and pride, never letting go its craving to possess.
Its support is ignorance, its watering is heedlessness; its foliage is envy, and its sap is the evil done in former times.
Its boughs are confusion and anxious care, its branches grief; terrible to behold, it is wrapped about with creepers of bewildering thirst.
The greedy, longing for its fruit, wait upon that great tree, bound fast by toilsome snares as they wrap themselves around its fruits.
He who, mastering those snares, tears that tree away, striving against the pair of them, reaches the end of both sorrows.
The man of unripe wisdom makes the tree grow again through his own torment, and so it destroys him, as poison destroys the sick man who has swallowed it.
The root of that tree, whose root is lingering attachment, is torn up by force with the supreme sword of equanimity, wrought of renunciation and vigilance.
He who thus knows how utterly desire may be uprooted, and the slaying of the science of desire, passes beyond all sorrows.
The body, they say, is a city, and the intellect is held to be its mistress; within it, seated in the body, subject to the intellect, is the mind, the contemplator of objects.
The senses are the townsfolk, the citizens; and the higher faculty exists for their sake. There dwell two cruel faults, the one named darkness, the other passion.
That very good by which the citizens, together with the lord of the city, sustain themselves — by an unlawful gate those two faults feed upon it.
There the intellect is hard to assail; the mind is said to be of like nature with it. The citizens too are in awe of the mind, and their footing also is unsteady.
The aim upon which the intellect settles does not perish; but the aim upon which the mind settles apart, by itself, that does perish.
When the mind becomes severed from the intellect and stands alone, then passion takes its stand upon it, finding it exposed and empty.
That mind, having joined with passion, makes friendship with it, and taking the people, the citizens, it delivers them over to passion.
Bhīṣma said: Hear once more, my son, the enumeration of the qualities of the elements, fallen from the mouth of Dvaipāyana with high praise, O sinless one.
Like a blazing fire, the venerable one spoke it to Dhūmravarcas; and so I too, my son, shall set forth this teaching again as an illustration.
Of earth: steadfastness, extension, hardness, the power of bringing forth, odor, heaviness, strength, cohesion, the holding of things in place, and firmness.
Of water: coldness, taste, moisture, fluidity, soft unctuousness, the flowing tongue, and the trickling forth of the watery within the earthen.
Of fire: unassailability, brilliance, heat, the power to cook, illumination, purity, color, lightness, sharpness, and tenth, the tendency to move upward.
Of wind: unrestraint, touch, the seat of speech, independence, strength, swiftness, the power to bewilder, activity, the doing of work, and becoming.
The qualities of ether are sound, pervasiveness, and porousness; it is without support, without resting-place, unmanifest, and free from change.
Together with imperviousness, elemental being, and its modifications — these are declared to be the fifty qualities, brought into being from the nature of the five elements.
Restless arising, manifestation, projection, imagination, forbearance, the real and the unreal, and swiftness — these are the nine qualities of the mind.
The choosing between the welcome and the unwelcome, resolve, concentration, doubt, and ascertainment — these are the five qualities that reside in the intellect.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How does the intellect have five qualities? How are the qualities of the nature of the five senses? Explain all this to me, this subtle knowledge, O grandsire.

Bhīṣma said: They speak of sixty qualities of the elements — distinct from the elements yet ever clinging to them, clinging to the elements yet sprung from the Imperishable; and this, my son, they declare to be not eternal here.

This, my son, framed by reflection, has been told you — what was not yet known to you is now made present here. Having grasped the whole truth of the elements and their meaning, become, through understanding the power of the elements, one of tranquil mind.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: These guardians of the earth who lie upon the earth's surface — these mighty ones, fallen amid their armies, their life-breath gone —
Each one of fearful strength, strong as ten thousand elephants — these were struck down in battle by men of strength and splendor equal to their own.
I do not see who, in the battle long ago, could have been the slayer of these living men, endowed as they were with valor and possessed of splendor and strength.
And yet, O greatly wise one, here they lie with their breath departed, and this word 'dead' is used of them whose life has fled.
These dead kings were for the most part of terrible prowess; and a doubt has arisen in me — whence comes this name, 'the dead'?
Whose is death, whence is death, by what means does death carry off creatures here? O you who are like a god immortal, tell me this, O grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: Long ago, in the Kṛta age, my child, there lived a king named Avikampaka; in battle, his forces wasted away, he fell into the power of his foes.
His son was named Hari, equal in strength to Nārāyaṇa; he was slain in the fray by the enemy, together with his army and his followers.
That king, fallen into the enemy's power and overwhelmed with grief for his son, finding no peace, beheld by chance the sage Nārada upon the earth.
To him the lord of men told all that had befallen — his capture by the enemy in battle, and likewise the death of his son.
Hearing those words of his, Nārada, rich in austerities, then related this tale, which takes away grief for a son.
O king, hear now this story, full and far-ranging, even as it came to pass and as it was heard by me, O lord of the earth.
When in the creation of beings the great and mighty Grandsire had brought forth his creatures, those creatures, grown exceedingly numerous, he could no longer endure.
For there was no space anywhere at all left free of living things, O imperishable one; the three worlds, so crammed, became as if unable to breathe, O king.
Then anxious thought arose in him concerning their destruction, O ruler of the earth; yet pondering, he could not find the cause and means for their destruction.
From his wrath, O great king, a fire arose out of his bodily apertures, and with it the Grandsire set ablaze all the quarters of the sky.
Then heaven, earth, and the firmament, and the whole world with all that moves and stands still, that fire, born of the Lord's anger, consumed, O king.
There were beings burned, both moving and unmoving alike, by that mighty surge of wrath, when the great Grandsire was enraged.
Then Sthāṇu, the tawny-matted one, lord of the Vedas and of sacrifice, the auspicious god Śiva, slayer of enemy heroes, went to Brahmā for refuge.
When Sthāṇu had thus come, out of his desire for the welfare of creatures, the boon-granting god, blazing as it were, spoke then to Śiva:
What wish shall I fulfill for you today? You are deemed by me worthy of a boon. For I shall do whatever pleases you, O Śambhu, whatever lies within your heart.
Sthāṇu said: Know, O lord, that this duty laid upon me concerns the bringing forth of creatures. These beings were created by you, O grandsire; do not be angry with them.
By the fire of your splendour, O god, the creatures are being consumed on every side. Seeing them, compassion stirs in me. Be not wrathful, O lord of the world.
Prajāpati said: I am not angry, nor is it my wish that the creatures should cease to be. It is only to lighten the burden of the earth that I will their destruction.
For this goddess Earth, oppressed by her load, has ever urged me to it, O Mahādeva. Burdened, she sinks down into the waters.
When, pondering long with my mind, I could find no means for the destruction of these multiplied beings, then anger entered into me.
Sthāṇu said: Let go your purpose of destruction and be appeased; be not wrathful, O lord of the thirty gods. Do not annihilate the creatures, neither what stands fixed nor what moves.
All the pools, and all the grasses and reeds, the fixed and the moving alike — the whole fourfold host of living beings —
all this is being reduced to ashes; the entire world is overwhelmed. Be gracious, O blessed and holy one — this is the boon I crave of you.
For these creatures, once destroyed, will by no means come again. Therefore let this splendour be withdrawn by your own splendour.
Look to some other means, out of desire for the creatures' welfare, by which all these living beings may be turned back, O scorcher of foes.
Else the creatures, their power of generation cut off, would pass into non-being. I have been appointed by you, O lord, to preside over the divine ordering of the worlds here.
For this world of the fixed and the moving has its origin in you, O lord of the world. Having appeased you, O Mahādeva, I beg for the creatures that they be reborn again and again.
Nārada said: Hearing the words of Sthāṇu, the god, his speech and mind restrained, drew that splendour of his back once more within his own self.
Then, gathering in that fire, the blessed lord, honoured by the worlds, ordained both the going forth into activity and the turning back from it.
As the great-souled one was drawing back that fire born of his wrath, there appeared from all the openings of his body a woman.
Dark she was, clad in red garments, the corners of her eyes tinged red within, furnished with divine earrings and adorned with celestial ornaments.
Having issued forth from those openings, she betook herself to the southern quarter. Then the two gods, both lords of the universe, beheld that maiden.
Then the god, the first lord of the worlds, calling her, said — O protector of earth — "O Death, slay these creatures."
"For you were conceived by me in my wrath, with my mind set upon destruction. Therefore destroy you all the creatures, the foolish and the wise alike.
Without distinction, O lovely one, do you destroy the creatures. By performing this my charge, you shall attain the highest good."
Thus addressed, the goddess Death, garlanded with lotuses, that young maiden, sank into grieving thought, sorrowful, the tears falling fast from her eyes.
And the lord of beings caught up those tears in his two hands, and, for the good of mortals, entreated her once again.
Nārada said: Putting away her grief, that gentle one of long, far-reaching eyes, with palms joined and bowing low like a creeper bent down, then spoke.
"How, O best of speakers, should a woman such as I, created by you, come to be born to so dread a work, terrible to every living thing?
I am afraid of unrighteousness. Appoint me to a righteous task. Look upon me in my fear, O lord, with a kindly eye.
That I should not carry off the guiltless living — children, the aged, those in the prime of life — O lord of all that breathes, I bow to you: be gracious to me.
Beloved sons, friends, brothers, mothers, and fathers too — that men should brood upon these when dead, O god, of that I am afraid.
The flood of their piteous tears would scald me through endless years. Sorely afraid of them, I have come to you for refuge.
To the house of Yama, O god, the doer of evil deeds goes at the last. I beseech you, O giver of boons: show me your grace, O lord.
This is the boon I desire of you, O grandsire of the worlds; and by your grace I would wish to practise austerities, O lord of the gods."
The grandsire said: O Death, you were fashioned by me for the very purpose of destroying the creatures. Go, destroy you all the creatures, and do not hesitate.
This must inevitably come to pass; it cannot be otherwise. Do as I have said, O faultless-limbed and sinless one — fulfil my word.
Nārada said: Thus addressed, O mighty-armed conqueror of hostile cities, Death made no reply, but stood bowed down, her face turned up toward the lord.
Though addressed again and again, that fair one stood silent, as though her very life had gone from her. Then the god, the supreme lord of the gods,
Brahmā, self-possessed, was of himself appeased; and smiling, the lord of the worlds looked out upon all the worlds.
And when that unconquered and blessed one had laid aside his wrath, the maiden slipped away from his presence — so have we heard.
Having withdrawn without consenting to the destruction of the creatures, Death then, as if in haste, O king of kings, went off to Dhenuka.
There the goddess practised supreme and hard austerity: she stood upon one foot for fifteen padmas of years.
As she was thus performing her exceedingly hard austerity there, the mighty-splendoured Brahmā once again spoke these words:
"Carry out my word, O Death." Disregarding it, she swiftly stood again upon one foot for yet another seven —
she stood for six padmas, and five, and two, O bestower of honour; and then for ten thousand padmas more she ranged about in the company of deer.
Then going off again, O king, she kept the most exalted silence within the waters for eight thousand years, O ruler of earth.
Then that maiden went to the Kauśikī, O bull of the Bharatas; and there, feeding on wind and water, she again practised her vow.
Then the greatly blessed one went on to the Gaṅgā and to lonely Meru, and stood there motionless as a log, out of her desire for the good of living beings.

Then on the summit of Himavat, where the gods had performed their sacrifices, there she stood upon her great toe, O king of kings, for yet another nikharva of years, and with effort she gratified the grandsire.
Then He who is the origin and the dissolution of the worlds said to her there: "What is this you do, my daughter? Let my word be carried out."
Then Death spoke again to the blessed grandsire: "I would not carry off the creatures, O god; once more I beseech your grace."
To her, trembling with the fear of unrighteousness and entreating him yet again, the god of gods then spoke these words, restraining her resolve:
"There is no unrighteousness for you, O Death. Gather in these creatures, O fair one. What I have spoken, O blessed lady, shall not in any way prove false here.
The eternal Law itself shall enter into you here; and I and the gods shall ever be intent upon your welfare.
And this further boon, desired in your heart, I grant you: the creatures, afflicted by disease, shall not come to you charged with any fault of yours.
Among men you shall be a man in form, among women a woman in shape, and among the third sort a being of neither kind."
Thus addressed, O great king, she spoke with joined palms once more to that great-souled and imperishable lord of the gods, saying, "No":
Then the god said to her: "O Death, gather in the race of men. No unrighteousness shall touch you; so will I ordain it, O fair one.
Those drops of tears that I saw fallen, which were caught and held in my two hands before — those, O Death, shall become diseases of dreadful form, and when the time comes they shall torment mankind.
At the last hour of all living beings you shall join desire and anger together upon them. Thus measureless Law shall come to you, and, dealing evenly with all, you shall incur no unrighteousness.

Thus you shall guard the Law as I have declared it, and you shall not plunge yourself into sin. Therefore welcome the office that has come to you, and, joining these together, gather in the living beings here."

Then she, for fear of a curse and under the name and charge of Death, said to him, "So be it." And thereafter, at the last hour of living beings, taking hold of desire and anger, she bereaves them of delusion and slays them.

Those diseases of Death, born of her falling tears, by which the bodies of men are racked — they come at the ending of the breath of all that lives. Therefore grieve not, but understand this with your understanding.

All the gods, at the ending of the breath of living beings, having gone forth, return again even so; and so too all men, at the ending of their breath, having gone, return like gods, O lion among kings.

The Wind, dread and dreadful-voiced, of mighty power, is the very life-breath of all living things; he takes manifold courses when the bodies of the embodied break apart. Therefore the Wind is the god of gods, supreme.

All the gods are marked out by the name of mortal, and all mortals are marked out by the name of god. Therefore mourn not your son, O lion among kings: your son, having attained heaven, rejoices there.
Thus Death, created by the god, gathers in the creatures duly when their time has come; and those diseases of hers, born of her tears, when the time has come, gather in the living beings here.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: All these men are perplexed concerning the Law. What is this Law? Whence is the Law? Tell me that, O grandsire.
Is this Law for the sake of this world, or rather for the sake of the next? Or may the Law serve both ends? Tell me that, O grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: Right conduct, the Smṛti, and the Vedas — these are the threefold mark of the Law; and the wise declare profit, the fourth, to be a mark of the Law as well.

Though the rites be already prescribed, men later and former still resolve upon them. It is for the sustaining of worldly life that the rule of Law has here been laid down — a rule that ripens into happiness in both spheres, here and hereafter.
Failing to grasp the subtle Law, the wicked man cleaves to sin; nor do certain doers of evil escape from sin even in time of distress.
When a man becomes a knower of the Law, he speaks no evil. Good conduct is the very ground of the Law; resting upon that alone, you shall come to understand it.
When, possessed by unrighteousness, the thief seizes wealth, the robber takes delight in carrying off another's riches where there is no king.
But when others carry off that wealth of his, then he longs for a king; and then he envies those who are content with their own riches.
The pure man approaches the king's gate unafraid and without misgiving, for he sees no misdeed of any kind within his own inmost self.
The utterance of truth is good; there is nothing higher than truth. By truth is all upheld; upon truth does all stand established.

Even fierce doers of evil, having pledged the truth among themselves each by each, proceed without treachery and without breach of faith, relying upon it; for were they to act faithlessly toward one another, they would assuredly perish.

"Another's wealth is not to be taken" — this is the eternal Law. Yet the strong hold that it was set going by the weak; but when their own weakness is fixed upon them by fate, then that very Law pleases them.
For those who are endowed with strength are not therefore happy without end. Therefore let your mind in no wise be turned toward crookedness.
He has no fear from the wicked, nor from thieves, nor from the king. Doing wrong to no one in any thing, the pure man dwells without fear.
The thief is suspicious of everything, like a deer that has strayed into a village; the sin he himself has done in many ways he sees only in others.
The pure man goes forward glad, ever fearless on every side, for he sees no misdeed of his own reflected in others.
"One ought to give" — this Law has been declared by those devoted to the good of all beings; but the wealthy hold that it was set going by the destitute.
But when fate's stinginess falls upon them, then this very precept pleases them—for those who are rich are not, after all, forever happy.
Whatever deed a man would not wish others to do to him, that let him not do to others, knowing it would be hateful to himself.
He who is another man's paramour—what right has he to reproach anyone? Were another to do the like to him, he would not endure it: such is my conviction.
He who himself wishes to live—how could he slay another? Whatever a man would desire for himself, that let him intend for his fellow too.
With one's surplus enjoyments one should share with others who have nothing; for this very reason the Ordainer set lending at interest in motion.
As to the compact in which the gods would abide, so let it be; and if even in a time of gain one keeps to dharma, that constancy is fair indeed.
The wise declare that all dharma is grounded in what is dear and welcome; behold this marking-out of the signs of dharma and of its opposite, Yudhiṣṭhira.
Bound up with the holding-together of the world, ordained of old by the Disposer, fixed upon the subtle aim of dharma—such is the supreme conduct of the good.
This mark of dharma has now been told to you, O best of the Kurus; therefore let your mind never in any way incline toward crookedness.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Subtle and well has the mark of dharma been set forth by you; yet a certain notion stirs in me, which I would utter by way of inference.
The many questions that were in my heart you have answered; this further one I shall now put—not, O king, in any spirit of contention.
These [precepts] indeed bring men onward, set them forth, and carry them across; yet dharma cannot be known, O Bhārata, by mere rote recitation.
One dharma belongs to the man in easy circumstances, another to him in dire straits; how then can times of calamity be understood by rote?
Right conduct is held to be dharma, and the good are known by their conduct; but how can the attainable and the unattainable be told apart, when right conduct itself bears no fixed sign?
One sees a common man practicing unrighteousness under the guise of righteousness, and some uncommon man practicing righteousness under the guise of unrighteousness.
Again, its standard has been laid down by those versed in the scriptures; yet we have heard it said that the teachings of the Vedas dwindle age by age.
One set of dharmas held in the Kṛta age, another in the Tretā, and others in the Dvāpara; other dharmas hold in the Kali age, framed as it were to suit men's diminished powers.
"The word of sacred tradition is truth"—this is what holds the world together; yet beyond the traditions the Vedas have streamed forth, facing in every direction.
If they are all authoritative, then there is no [single] authority to be found; and when authority and non-authority stand in mutual contradiction, whence the standing of scripture itself?
When dharma is being carried off by the strong and the wicked, whatever ordinance is thereby corrupted—that ordinance too perishes.
Whether we know it thus or know it not, whether it can be known or cannot—[dharma] is finer than the razor's edge and heavier than a mountain.
At first it appears with the shape of a gandharva's city in the sky; but when the wise look closely upon it, it passes again into invisibility.
Like watering-troughs near a herd of cattle, like a channel in a field, O Bhārata—even the eternal dharma, though remembered, once forsaken is no more seen.
Some from desire, some from ruin, and others yet from sundry causes—many of the wicked, and others besides, take to empty and worthless conduct.
Dharma soon comes to be, yet it lies dissolved [unseen] within the good; others call such good men madmen, and even mock them.
For the multitudes have turned away, taking refuge in the law of kings; and no single mode of conduct is seen that is for the good of all.
By that very [conduct] another arises, and he in turn oppresses yet another; and again he is seen, by mere chance, in the selfsame form.
By the very means whereby one man rises, he oppresses others too; one should mark the want of single-pointedness in all modes of conduct alike.
Long ago attained by the seers, dharma was set forth of old; and by that ancient mode of conduct the ordinance abides eternal.
Bhīṣma said: On this point too they recite this ancient tale—the words of Tulādhāra concerning dharma, in his exchange with Jājali.
A certain forest-dwelling brahmin named Jājali, that great ascetic, having come to a spot beside the ocean, practiced austerities there.
Self-controlled and of measured fare, wearing bark-cloth, hide, and matted locks, smeared with dirt and grime, the wise sage [endured] for many a cycle of years.
Once, O lord of earth, that brahmin-seer of mighty splendor, dwelling in the waters, ranged through the worlds, beholding them, swift as thought.
On a certain occasion the sage, standing amid the waters, took to musing, as he gazed upon the earth bounded by the ocean, with its groves and forests:
"There is none in this world, among things moving or unmoving, who is my equal—who else along with me could pass through the waters and through the air?"
Then, being observed by the rākṣasas as he stood amid the waters, he spoke thus; and the piśācas said to him, "You ought not to speak in this manner.
Tulādhāra, a merchant by calling, of great renown in Vārāṇasī—even he does not deserve to speak as you do, O best of the twice-born."
Thus addressed by those beings, the great ascetic Jājali replied: "Let me behold that wise and illustrious Tulādhāra."
As that seer spoke thus, the rākṣasas lifted him up out of the ocean and said, "Go, taking this road, O best of the twice-born."
Thus addressed by those beings, Jājali then set forth downcast, and approaching Tulādhāra in Vārāṇasī, he spoke these words.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: What meritorious deed had Jājali done of old, dear sir, whereby he attained the highest perfection? That you ought to explain to us.
Bhīṣma said: He had become exceedingly devoted to fearsome austerity, that great ascetic, given to bathing in the river at evening and at dawn,
duly tending the sacred fires, intent above all on the recitation of scripture—that brahmin Jājali, versed in the rule of the forest-hermit, blazing with spiritual splendor.
Steadfast in truth and austerity, yet he did not [truly] perceive dharma; in the rains he lay beneath the open sky, in winter he took to the water,
in summer enduring wind and scorching sun—and still he did not find dharma; he bore beds of pain of many kinds, and rolling upon the bare earth.
Then once, during the rains, that sage took his stand beneath the open sky and received the water from the firmament upon his head, again and again.
Then his matted locks grew sodden and tangled, O lord, and from his constant ranging in the wild ever filthy and caked with dirt.
Then once that great ascetic, taking no food and feeding on air alone, stood still as a log, unmoved, and stirred not at all.
While he stood thus, become like a tree-stump, motionless, O Bhārata—a pair of kuliṅga sparrows, O king, made a nest upon his head.
That compassionate brahmin-seer watched the mated pair as they fashioned their little nest there in his matted locks with strands of grass.
And since that great ascetic, become like a stump, stirred not at all, the two birds, grown wholly trusting, dwelt there in ease.
Then, when the rains had passed and the autumn season had come, the pair, made trusting and overcome by desire, after the manner ordained of Prajāpati,
those two skyfarers, O king, let fall their eggs upon his head; and that splendid brahmin of strict vows became aware of them.
And though aware, that mighty Jājali stirred not at all; his mind ever fixed upon dharma, he would not consent to unrighteousness.
And day after day the two would come and dwell upon his head, reassured and full of joy, O mighty one.
Then from the well-grown eggs the little birds were hatched, and they grew up in that very place; yet Jājali did not waver.
Guarding the eggs of the kuliṅgas, that man of disciplined vows, the righteous one, stood thus motionless and composed.
Then in the fullness of time those fledglings grew into birds, and the sage marked the little ones now grown of wing.
Then once, beholding those birds there, that man of disciplined vows, the best of the wise, became filled with the highest delight.
Seeing them thus full-grown, the pair of parent birds attained their joy and dwelt there fearless, together with their offspring.
And the brahmin watched the fledged birds fly off and return again, evening after evening; yet Jājali did not waver.
Sometimes coming back and going off again, unbroken in their comings—and at last forsaken by their mother and father—yet Jājali did not waver.
Then the little birds, having gone off by day to forage, would return again at evening, O king, to dwell in that selfsame place.
Once the birds flew off for five days, and on the sixth day they came back together; yet Jājali did not waver.
And by degrees, when those birds had come fully into their strength, they no longer returned for many days at a time.
Once the birds flew off and for a whole month did not come back; thereupon, O king, Jājali set forth.
Then, when they had vanished away, Jājali, filled with wonder, formed the thought "I am perfected"; and thereupon pride entered into him.
Seeing the birds thus gone forth, that man of fixed vows, esteeming himself, took it for a high thing and became greatly pleased.
Having bathed in the river and gratified the fire with oblation, that great ascetic then went forth toward the rising sun.
Honoring [the memory of] the sparrows upon his head, Jājali, foremost of those who recite, clapped his arms then toward the sky [crying], "Dharma has been attained by me!"
Then there came a voice from the firmament, and Jājali heard it: "In dharma you are not the equal of Tulādhāra, O Jājali.
In Vārāṇasī dwells Tulādhāra, the man of great wisdom; even he does not deserve to speak as you speak, O brahmin."
Falling under the sway of indignation, in his longing to behold Tulādhāra, he ranged over the earth, O king—that sage who made his home wherever evening found him.
After a long while he came to the city of Vārāṇasī, and there he beheld Tulādhāra selling his wares.
And he too, the one who lived by his goods, no sooner saw that brahmin approaching than he rose up full of joy and honored him with a welcome.
Tulādhāra said: That you were coming was known to me, O brahmin—of that there is no doubt; hear now the word that I shall speak, O best of the twice-born.
Resorting to the marshy shore of the ocean, you performed great austerity; and yet, before, you in no wise knew the very meaning of dharma.
Then, O brahmin, when you had been perfected by your austerity, the little birds were quickly hatched upon your head, and they were cherished by you.

And when, fledged at last, they went off here and there to forage—deeming then, O brahmin, that dharma had sprung from those sparrows—you heard a voice in the sky concerning me, O best of the twice-born;
and then, falling under the sway of indignation, you have come here. What kindness may I do you? Tell me that, O best of the twice-born.
Bhīṣma said: Addressed thus by the wise Tulādhāra, the sagacious Jājali, foremost among those who murmur prayers, then spoke these words.
O trader, you who sell all manner of flavors and all manner of fragrances, and trees and herbs, and their roots and fruits as well—
how have you attained this conclusive wisdom? Whence has it come to you? Tell me all of it, entire and without omission, O greatly intelligent one.

Thus addressed by the illustrious brāhmaṇa, Tulādhāra the vaiśya, knower of the truths of dharma and its purpose, then spoke of the subtleties of dharma to Jājali of severe austerities, himself contented in wisdom, O king.
I know, O Jājali, the eternal dharma with its secret—the ancient dharma of goodwill, conducing to the welfare of all beings, which people have known of old.
That mode of life which works no injury to creatures, or but little injury—that is the highest dharma, and by it I live, O Jājali.
With sticks and grasses already cut by others I have made this dwelling of mine; lac, the lotus-perfume, costly aloe-wood, and fragrances both high and low—
and these and those many flavors, save intoxicants, O sage among brāhmaṇas—having bought them from another's hand, I sell them again without any deceit.
He who is ever a friend to all, and devoted to the welfare of all in deed, in thought, and in word—he knows dharma, O Jājali.
I neither praise nor condemn the deeds of others, beholding the manifold variety of the world as one beholds the sky, O sage among brāhmaṇas.
I neither favor nor oppose; I neither hate nor desire; I am the same toward all beings. Behold my vow, O Jājali.
For one freed from the liked and the disliked, with fondness and passion cast out, my scale stands even toward all beings, O Jājali.
Know me then, O Jājali, to be impartial toward the whole world, O best of the wise—one to whom a clod, a stone, and gold are alike.
As the blind, the deaf, and the maddened, having only their breath, are forever with their doors shut by the gods—such, in my seeing, is the likeness of men.
As the old, the sick, and the wasted are without longing for sense-objects, so too has my own longing for wealth, desire, and enjoyments wholly passed away.
When a man fears not, and when others fear not from him, when he neither desires nor hates—then indeed the twice-born is perfected.
When he harbors no evil intent toward any being, in deed, in thought, or in word—then he attains to Brahman.
There has been, and there will be, no dharma whatever to equal it: he who is a refuge of safety to all beings attains the fearless state.
But he from whom the whole world shrinks as from the very jaws of death—through cruelty of speech and harshness of punishment—he himself comes upon great fear.
We follow the conduct of the high-souled elders who lived rightly, blessed with sons and grandsons, who did no harm to any creature.
The eternal dharma has been lost, obscured by what passes for good custom; by that custom the learned, the ascetic, or the mighty is led astray.
Through right conduct, O Jājali, the wise man would swiftly attain dharma—he who, self-restrained, moves among the good with a heart free of malice.
As a log of wood borne along by chance in a river might, by mere chance, come together with some other log—
and there yet other timbers join from this side and that—grasses, sticks, and dung, drifting at times unregarded—even so has this custom of men arisen, from this source and that.
He from whom no creature ever shrinks at all, in any way, attains forever safety from all beings, O sage.
But he from whom the whole world flees, O learned one, as from a wolf, as all water-creatures flee to the shore when one cries out aloud—

One has helpers, another has wealth, yet another is fortunate—it is of just such men that the poets speak in the treatises, clever men of shallow conscience and ready conclusions, all for the sake of fame.
Whatever fruit the gift of safety to all beings yields, that very fruit one enjoys here through austerities, through sacrifices and gifts, and through words rooted in wisdom.

He who in this world gives to all beings the gift of safety as his sacrificial fee gains the reward of the gift of safety, as one who has offered every sacrifice; there is no dharma greater than non-violence toward living beings.
He from whom no creature ever shrinks at all, in any way, attains complete safety from all beings, O great sage.
But he from whom the world shrinks as from a serpent come into the house attains no dharma, neither in this world nor in the next.
For one who has made himself the self of all beings and beholds all creatures rightly, the gods themselves are bewildered as to his path, for he leaves no track, though they seek his footprint.
The gift of safety to living beings, they say, is the highest of all gifts. I tell you this in truth—believe it, O Jājali.
The very man who was fortunate becomes wretched again; seeing the ruinous undoing of deeds, people ever turn away in revulsion.
For no dharma here is without a reason, however subtle, O Jājali; it is for the sake of present and future beings that the teaching of dharma was set forth.
Because of its subtlety it cannot be fully grasped, having many a hidden turn; yet, perceiving it in part, one comes to understand the other customs as well.
Those who cut off the testicles of beasts, those who pierce their nostrils, who load them with heavy burdens, who bind them and break them to the yoke—
and who kill living creatures and devour them—how is it you do not censure these? Men make use of their fellow men, enjoying them as slaves;
by killing, binding, and coercion they force them to labor day and night. You yourself know what pain there is in being struck and slain.
In beings endowed with the five senses dwells all that is divine—Āditya, the moon, Vāyu, Brahmā, the breath of life, sacrifice, and Yama.
When you traffic in these living things, what scruple is there over the dead? What scruple, O brāhmaṇa, over oil, over clarified butter, over honey, water, or herbs?

Cattle reared in comfort in a land free of gadflies and mosquitoes—knowing them dear to their mothers—men seize and in many ways drive off to regions thick with gadflies and sharp grass and deep mire.
Draught-beasts crushed by their loads sink down, others undone against all rule. I do not think even the slaying of an embryo worse than that act.

Men deem agriculture a virtuous calling, yet that livelihood is most cruel: the iron-mouthed plough wounds the earth and the creatures that lodge within it. And look likewise upon the oxen yoked to it, O Jājali.
'Not to be slain'—such is the very name of cattle; who then has the right to slay them? Pṛṣadhra wrought a great evil, as one who slaughters a cow.

For the seers and the ascetics declared this to Nahuṣa: 'You have slain the cow, who is a mother, and the bull, who is the Lord of Creatures; you have done, Nahuṣa, what ought not be done, and through you we shall meet with terror.'

And those greatly blessed seers brought down a hundred and one diseases upon all creatures, upon all living beings, O Jājali, and they pronounced Nahuṣa a slayer of the unborn, saying: 'We shall offer no oblation for you.'
Having spoken thus, those high-souled ones, all beholders of the true meaning—the seers and the tranquil ascetics—at once made their declaration.
Such inauspicious and dreadful customs as these, O Jājali, you do not, for all your skill, perceive, simply because they are universally practiced.
One should seek dharma upon principle, and not merely follow the way of the world. As for him who would strike me and him who praises me—hear of this too, O Jājali:
those two would be alike to me, for I have neither liked nor disliked. Such a dharma as this the wise extol.
For, furnished with sound reasoning, it is honored by ascetics and by those ever devoted to dharma, and it is marked out by its subtlety.
Jājali said: By the dharma you have set forth, you who hold the scale, the gate of heaven and the very livelihood of creatures will be barred.
For from agriculture food arises, and thereby you yourself live; and by cattle and by herbs do mortals live, O trader.
From these too sacrifice arises—yet you prate of the denier's creed; for this world could never go on if it abandoned husbandry altogether.
Tulādhāra said: I shall expound the right way of life, O Jājali; I am no denier, O brāhmaṇa, nor do I condemn sacrifice—yet one who truly knows sacrifice is very hard to find.
Homage to the brāhmaṇa's sacrifice and to those who know sacrifice; for the brāhmaṇas have forsaken their own sacrifice and taken up here the kṣatriya's sacrifice.

It has been set in motion, O brāhmaṇa, by the greedy, by those bent on wealth, by deniers who, not understanding the words of the Veda, take what is false for what merely wears the semblance of truth.
'This must be given, this must be given'—and he seeks no end to it; hence arise theft and forbidden deeds, O Jājali. That oblation alone is well made by which the gods are gladdened.
By reverence, by oblation, by recitation of the Veda, and by herbs let the worship of the gods be performed, as the scriptures show.
From the rites and works of the wicked is born a crooked offspring; from the greedy is born the greedy, from the impartial the impartial.
As is the sacrificer in himself, so too are his priests, and so his offspring; from sacrifice offspring arises, as pure water from the sky.
The oblation cast into the fire, O brāhmaṇa, attends upon the sun; from the sun is born rain, from rain food, and from food creatures.

Therefore, from sacrifice well performed, the men of old won all their desires; the earth ripened her harvests untilled, and the plants grew at their blessings—yet they looked for no reward in their sacrifices or in themselves at all.
But those who, anxious for reward, would sacrifice in any selfish fashion are born again as wicked men, as cheats, as the greedy whose end is gain.

By his unholy deeds such a one goes to the worlds of the doers of evil. The man who would make right out of wrong and do the unholy is of evil soul, of undeveloped wisdom, ever so here, O best of the twice-born.
The brāhmaṇa who knows both kinds of duty—what is to be done as that which is to be done—dwells as Brahman itself in the world, and falls back no more into the bondage of obligation.
And action shorn of its qualities is the higher, so we have heard; that is, to forbear from harming any being, and to be restrained as to its fruit.
Those whose sacrifice is truth, whose sacrifice is self-restraint, who are free of greed and content within themselves, renouncers of whatever arises—all such folk have set envy at a distance.
Knowing the truth of the field and the knower of the field, perfected in their own sacrifice, studying the holy Veda, they gladden even the immortals.
All divinity entire, all Brahman, rests upon the brāhmaṇa; when he is satisfied the gods are satisfied, and they are content when the contented man is content, O Jājali.
As one sated with every flavor takes joy in nothing more, so for him who is content in wisdom there is a contentment, perpetual, that gives rise to bliss.
Delighting in dharma, finding their joy in dharma, wholly resolved, the seekers after wisdom say: 'There is yet more for us, beyond, in very truth.'
Some, possessed of knowledge and discernment, longing to cross to the farthest shore beyond—that shore is supremely holy ever, joined with a holy lineage.
Going whither men neither grieve nor fall away nor suffer pain—those of pure nature attain here to that abode of Brahman.
They desire not heaven, nor do they sacrifice with wealth got for renown; they follow the path of the good, according to their power, through non-violence.
Trees and herbs and fruit and root—these they know for their offerings; greedy priests, set on gain, do not conduct their sacrifices for them.
Pursuing only their own true purpose, the twice-born, perfected in their works, performed sacrifice once again, out of a wish to bless the people.
That they might lead the people to heaven by the practice of their own dharma—such is the conviction that abides in me, impartial in all things, O Jājali.
By those rites which the wise ever employ in sacrifice, O bull among the twice-born, they journey along that path of the gods, O great sage.
For one kind there is return to rebirth, but for the wise there is no returning; both these, O Jājali, travel by the path of the gods.
For such men the oxen yoke and draw of their own accord, and the cows give milk of themselves, by the mere fulfilment of their mind's resolve.
Of themselves they take up the sacrificial posts and worship with their own well-earned offerings; he whose self is so refined is worthy to lay hold of a cow for sacrifice.
But men not of that stature, O brāhmaṇa, should sacrifice with herbs and plants alone; setting the renunciation born of wisdom foremost, such is the path I declare to you.
Free of craving, undertaking nothing, offering no obeisance and no praise, undiminished yet spent of all works — him the gods know as the true brāhmaṇa.

Neither reciting the scriptures aloud, nor sacrificing, nor giving among brāhmaṇas, yet seeking a worldly livelihood — to what goal does such a man come, O Jājali? Tell me how, making this his deity, he may attain the fruit of sacrifice.
Jājali said: We have not heard the very truth of the sages; I ask you, O merchant — this is a hard matter. Not heeding what went ever before, the seers set down no doctrine higher than this.

In this holy ford of the self the beasts could not find their happiness; then by which deed of his own, O merchant, may a man attain happiness? Tell me this, O greatly wise one — deeply indeed do I trust your word.

Tulādhāra said: Whether they offer sacrifices or none, those rites are nowhere worthy of the true offering. With clarified butter, with milk and curds, above all with the full oblation — yes, by her hair, her horn, her hoof, the cow herself brings the sacrifice to be.
And by this rule a man appoints his wife to her office and so performs it; for the sacrificial cake is declared the pure oblation that stands for all the beasts.
All rivers are as the Sarasvatī, all mountains holy; the self alone, O Jājali, is the sacred ford — do not be a stranger wandering from land to land.
Practising such duties as these in this world, O Jājali, while seeking righteousness through outward means, a man does not attain the blessed realms.
Bhīṣma said: Such duties as these does Tulādhāra extol — duties accomplished by sound reasoning and ever followed by the good.
Tulādhāra said: Whether by the good or by the wicked this path has been resorted to, let it be made plain before your eyes, and then you shall know how the matter truly stands.
These many birds wander all about you — hawks and creatures of other kinds, hatched and reared upon your very head.
Call to them, O great brāhmaṇa, as they settle here and there; behold them clinging to your hands and feet and over all your body.
The birds, cherished by you, honour you as their father; beyond doubt you are their father — call to your children, O Jājali.
Bhīṣma said: Then, summoned by that Jājali, the winged ones uttered divine speech, speaking, so it is said, the word of dharma.
The work founded upon non-injury and the rest bears fruit both here and beyond; but rivalry destroys it, O brāhmaṇa, and that rivalry, once roused, destroys the man himself.
Sacrifice cannot save the speech and mind that grow only through faith; here those versed in old lore recite the verses sung by Brahmā.
The mind of the pure man without faith and of the impure man possessed of faith — the gods deemed these alike in the work of sacrifice.
Of the learned but stingy man and of the generous usurer the gods weighed both, and reckoned their food as of equal worth.

Prajāpati said to them: This judgement is unequal. The generous man's food is hallowed by faith; the other's is spoiled by faithlessness. The generous man's food may be eaten, but not the stingy man's, nor the usurer's.
He alone who lacks faith is unworthy of the gods' oblation; his food, and his alone, is not to be eaten — so know those learned in dharma.
Faithlessness is the highest sin; faith is the deliverer from sin. The man of faith casts off his sin as a serpent its worn-out skin.
Greatest among purifying things is renunciation joined with faith; he who has turned away from the faults of conduct and holds fast to faith is verily pure.
What need has such a one of austerity, of observance, of any further discipline of self? This man is made of faith; whatever his faith is, that very thing is he.
Thus has dharma been declared by the good who perceive its meaning and aim; we, desiring knowledge, have come to you out of our vision of dharma.
Cast off rivalry, O greatly wise one, and then you shall attain the highest. Faithful and full of faith, fixed in his own path of duty, this merchant here is the worthier man, O Jājali.
Thus was the matter of high import set forth by Tulādhāra, and rightly was the eternal dharma grasped and declared.
Having heard the words of that Tulādhāra of renowned power, the twice-born one, O son of Kuntī, won his way to peace.
Then before long that Tulādhāra and he, both greatly wise, having gone to heaven, dwelt there in ease, each attaining his own station won by the fruit of his deeds.
For those who are even-minded, faithful, restrained, and pure of heart, when they perform what is called sacrifice, the sacrifice is never found wanting.
Faith indeed is the goddess of the quality of goodness, daughter of Sūrya, O king — Sāvitrī, the bringer-forth, and the giver of trust to all living things.
Faith preserves what is grown through speech and grown through mind, O Bhārata. This has been taught you by way of parable — what more do you wish to hear?
Bhīṣma said: On this point too they tell this ancient tale, sung by King Vicakhnu out of compassion for living creatures.
Seeing a bull with its post struck down and hearing the loud bellowing of the cattle at the cow-pen of the sacrificial ground, that king looked on.
"May it be well with the cattle in all the worlds!" — thus he made his pronouncement; for once slaughter had begun, this blessing was devised.
It was by men of no fixed bounds, deluded, denying the scriptures, of doubting and unsettled mind, that the killing of beasts came to be praised.
In all works non-injury is the law — so spoke Manu whose very self was righteousness; it is from lust and passion that men slaughter beasts outside the altar.
Therefore the subtle dharma should be discharged by the discerning man according to right measure; for non-injury is held greater than all other duties.

Having fasted and become rigorous in vows, yet abandoning the revealed truths the Veda ordains — calling it 'observance,' these are no observances at all, but the wretched practices of men set on reward.
If men, on the pretext of sacrifices, of sacred trees, and of sacrificial posts, eat flesh in vain, this is no dharma to be commended.
Flesh, honey, liquor, fish, strong drink, and rice cooked with sesame — all this was set going by cheats; it is nowhere ordained in the Vedas.
Out of lust, delusion, and greed was this craving set in motion; in all sacrifices the brāhmaṇas recognize Viṣṇu alone, and his worship is held to be with milk-rice and with flowers.
And the trees fit for sacrifice that are appointed in the Vedas, and whatever else is to be done, when well prepared in purity by the great-souled and pure of heart — all that is worthy of the gods.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: For one who does no injury, the body and its distresses are at strife; how shall the body's sustenance be secured for one who undertakes nothing?
Bhīṣma said: So that the body does not waste away, so that it does not fall under the sway of death, in such measure should one engage in works; the able man should practise dharma so.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How should one examine a deed to be done — swiftly, or with long deliberation? In this stronghold of hard choices you are in every way our highest teacher.
Bhīṣma said: On this point too they tell this ancient tale of what befell long ago to Cirakārin in the line of Aṅgiras.
O Cirakārin, blessings on you, blessings on you, O Cirakārin! For the man who acts deliberately is wise, and offends not in his deeds.
Cirakārin, the greatly wise, was the son of Gautama; for he undertook all his tasks long and with careful regard.
Long pondering his aims, long waking, long sleeping, because he carried out his tasks only after long delay, he was therefore called Cirakārin, 'the Slow-Doer.'
He earned the name of sluggard and was called dull-witted by people of nimble but shallow understanding, who see not far ahead.
Now, upon some transgression, passing over his other sons, he was bidden by his enraged father: "Slay this mother of yours!"
Having slowly answered "So be it," by his very nature the Slow-Doer, reflecting in his deliberate way, fell long to pondering.
How shall I carry out my father's command, and how shall I not slay my mother? How shall I keep from sinking, like a wicked man, into this snare disguised as dharma?
A father's command is the highest dharma; yet a son's own duty is the protection of his mother, and sonship is bound and not its own master — how should this not torment me?
Who, having slain a woman, and his mother at that, could ever know happiness? And who, by slighting his father, could ever win a firm standing?
Not to slight the father is fitting; to uphold and protect the mother is fitting too. Both these claims deserve forbearance — how shall I overstep either of them?
For the father places his own self within the wife, that a child be born, for the sustaining of character, conduct, lineage, and family.
I myself am that very self, brought forth again by my father into the state of a son; how then should I lack understanding? — and so he came to know his own origin.
What the father pronounces at the birth-rite and at the rite of initiation — that firm confirmation suffices to establish the reverence due to the father.
The father is the foremost teacher, the highest dharma, a benefactor through nurture and the gift of learning; whatever the father declares is dharma, and that too is firmly settled in the Vedas.
A son is to his father but a source of joy, whereas the father is everything to the son; all things — body and the rest, the gifts that are to be given — the father alone bestows.
Therefore the father's word must be done, and in no way questioned; even his sins are cleansed away for the man who carries out his father's word.
In enjoyment, in fortune, in childbearing, in the witness of all the world, in union with a husband, and in the parting of the bride's hair —
The father is heaven, the father is dharma, the father is the highest austerity; when the father is brought to delight, all the gods are delighted.
Whatever blessings the father pronounces, those come to that man; the father is the expiation of all sins, in whatever he gives his glad approval.
The blossom is loosed from its stalk, the fruit is loosed from its stem; but the father, though wearied by his love for his sons, never lets his love go.
Thus far has the son's reverence for the father been pondered; but the father is the lesser station — now I shall reflect upon the mother.

This frame of mine, formed of the five elements in mortal life — of it my mother is the cause, as the fire-stick is of the fire; the mother is the kindling-block of men's bodies, the soothing of all who suffer.
He grieves not, nor does old age drag him down, who, even bereft of fortune, comes home and finds one to call 'Mother.'
He who, surrounded by sons and grandsons, still takes refuge with his mother, moves about like a child of two years even at the close of a hundred years.
Able or unable, lean or full of flesh — the mother guards her son all the same; no other is his sustainer by ordained right.
Then a man grows old when he grows sorrowful; then the world becomes empty for him, when he is parted from his mother.
There is no shade like a mother's, no refuge like a mother's, no protection like a mother's, no fountain of comfort like a mother's.
For bearing him in her womb she is the sustainer; for giving him birth she is called the mother; for the nourishing of his limbs she is 'Ambā'; and for bringing forth a hero she is the hero's mother.
For tending the infant she is 'Śuśrū'; the mother is the body's own nearest source. The man of sense would slay her only if his head were no hollow vessel — that is, if he had lost all reason.
What compact was made in the joining of the husband's and wife's life-breath, that the mother knows, or the father; but the truth of the matter rests with the mother.
The mother knows the lineage; the mother knows whose son he is. For her mere act of bearing him there is love, while the father's affection toward his offspring rests on trust alone.
Having of their own will taken her hand in marriage and entered upon a shared duty with her, if men then drive their women away, those women do not deserve to be cast off.
For a man is a woman's bhartṛ because he supports her, and her pati because he protects her; but when these virtues fail in him, he is neither her supporter nor her protector nor her lord.
Thus the woman commits no offense; it is the man alone who offends; and in committing a grave transgression, it is the man alone who is at fault.

For a woman's husband is her highest lord, declared to be her supreme deity; and she has given her very self, a self equal to his own, as the highest gift. Since in all matters the fault falls upon the man, women themselves commit no offense.
And as for any command not spoken yet pressed upon a woman for the sating of lust, in him who would so remind her there is plainly unrighteousness; of this there is no doubt.
That a woman, and above all a mother set in the highest reverence, is not to be slain—this even brute beasts, lacking all discernment, understand.
They know the father to be the gathering of all the gods made one; yet out of the affection that belongs to mortals and to gods alike, one turns toward the mother.
As Cirakārin pondered thus at length, in keeping with his slow-acting nature, a long stretch of time passed by; and then his father came to him.
Medhātithi, the deeply wise Gautama, steadfast in austerity, had in that interval reflected upon the breach of his wife's conduct.
Scorched by grief, shedding tears in plenty, and brought through the calm grace of learning and fortitude to remorse, he spoke.
"Purandara, lord of the three worlds, came to my hermitage; taking up the guise of a guest, he assumed the form of a brāhmaṇa.
He was soothed with fitting and gracious words, honored with a welcome, and by her, in due form, was offered the guest-water and the water for his feet.
Told, 'I am subject to another,' yet he said, 'I shall press my suit by craft.' In the misfortune that arose from this, the woman bears no transgression.
Thus neither the woman, nor I, nor that wandering lord of the gods has sinned against dharma; it is heedlessness alone that has done the wrong.
The seers who have raised their seed on high call jealousy a born vice; and I, hurled down by jealousy, am sunk in the ocean of evil deeds.
Should I slay a virtuous woman, and a wife condemned only out of my own vice, a wife who is mine to cherish and sustain—who then will carry me across?"
"Cirakārin, whom I commanded in a moment's haste, is noble of mind; if today he be true to his slow-acting way, he will save me from this sin.
O Cirakārika, blessings on you—blessings on you, O Cirakārika! If today you are still slow to act, then you are truly Cirakārika.
Save me, and your mother too, and the austerity I have amassed, and your own self from sins—be this day Cirakārika!
Slow-acting is your inborn way, joined to a wisdom that takes its time; let it bear fruit for you today—be this day Cirakārika!
Long were you longed for by your mother, long carried in her womb; make your slow-acting nature bear fruit, O Cirakārika!
Out of anguish he lingers long; restrained, he sleeps long—consider the long anguish of us both, O Cirakārika!"
Thus grieving, O king, the great seer Gautama then beheld his son Cirakārin standing close at hand.
And Cirakārin, seeing his father in deepest grief, cast aside his weapon and, bowing his head, set about winning his father's favor.
And Gautama, seeing his son fallen with his head upon the ground, and his wife unharmed, came to the highest joy.
For that great-souled one had not driven his wife to ruin, dwelling as he did in the solitude of the hermitage; and his son too had been composed.
He might have slain her without reproach, with his son standing weapon in hand; yet, the boy having humbly asked his counsel, he could now resolve upon his own course of action.
And seeing his son bowed at his feet, the thought came to him: 'Out of fear he is concealing the rashness of having taken up the weapon.'
Then the father praised him long, long kissed him upon the head, long held him in both arms, and uttered, 'Live long!'
Thus that deeply wise Gautama, filled with love and gladness, embraced his son and spoke these words.
"O Cirakārika, blessings on you—be ever slow to act, and live long! Yet while you tarried, I was long and grievously stricken with sorrow."
And the learned Gautama, best of sages, also spoke these verses, founded on the recital of the virtues of the steadfast slow-acting ones.
"Slowly should one bind a friend, and slowly cast off a friendship once made; for a friend made slowly deserves to be kept long.
In passion, in arrogance, in pride, in enmity, in sinful deeds, and in any unkind act that must be done, the slow-acting man is praised.
In the unproven offenses of kinsmen, of friends, of servants, and of womenfolk, the slow-acting man is praised."
Thus, O Bhārata, that Gautama was pleased with his son for that deed, O Kaurava—pleased by that very slowness to act.
So a man who reflects in all his undertakings, and after long deliberation comes to a decision, does not grieve for long thereafter.
He holds his anger long in check, long restrains his action, and no deed that breeds remorse befalls him.
Long let him wait upon his elders, long attend and honor them; long let him practice the duties of dharma, and long pursue his inquiry.
Long attending upon the wise, long serving the cultured, and long disciplining himself, a man comes in time to a state beyond contempt.
Even when another utters words bound up with dharma, let him question long and answer long; thus he is never long despised.
Having dwelt for many years in that hermitage, the brāhmaṇa of mighty austerities then went to heaven, together with his son.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How should a king protect his subjects and yet cause no one distress? I ask you, best of the good; tell me that, grandfather.
Bhīṣma said: On this too they recite an ancient tale—the dialogue of Dyumatsena with King Satyavat.
Satyavat spoke what had not been spoken before—so we have heard—when, by his own father's order, certain men were being led away to execution.
"Righteousness passes into unrighteousness, and unrighteousness into righteousness, if killing were to be called a duty—this ought not to be."
Dyumatsena said: If non-killing were the law, then what could ever count as duty at all? If robbers were never slain, O Satyavat, a ruinous confusion would arise.
'This is mine'—such a claim would have no force in the age of Kali, and the very course of worldly life could not go on. If you know otherwise, declare it to us.
Satyavat said: All three of the lower orders should be made to hold fast to the brāhmaṇas; and of those bound by the cords of dharma, only a few will go astray.
Whichever of them should transgress, let the twice-born point him out, saying, 'This man will not heed me'; upon such a one let the king sit in judgment.

What the scripture lays down in accord with the truth of each case—that must be carried out; killing is not to be ordered otherwise, nor deeds done without examining them by the science of statecraft as ordained.

When a king slays robbers, more often than not he destroys the guiltless along with them; for when a man is killed, his wife, mother, father, and son are killed in him. Therefore, where one man has wronged another, let the king judge with care.
An evil man may one day come to good character; and even from the good, born of those who are evil, there may spring an unworthy offspring.
No root-and-branch slaughter should be carried out; that is not the eternal law. Indeed, even without killing, expiation may be prescribed.
By rebuke, by imprisonment, by disfigurement, and by the punishment of death are such men to be afflicted, but not at once with the full measure of harm.
When, seeking refuge, they come round to the royal chaplain, saying, 'Brāhmaṇa, we shall do no sin again,'
then they deserve to be released—such is the king's ordinance. A brāhmaṇa, shaven and bearing the staff and deerskin, is worthy to receive a fresh garment of pardon.
For graver and graver offenses, repeated again and again, men deserve release—but not in the same measure as at the first.
