Then Śakra, mounting in the battle that chariot empowered by the gods, his thunderbolt raised in his hand, fixed his gaze upon that Daitya.
Then that great Asura uttered an unearthly roar and gaped wide, O lord of kings, seized by the fierce fever; and as he gaped, Śakra hurled the thunderbolt upon him.
That thunderbolt of mighty splendour, like unto the fire of universal doom, swiftly struck down the vast-bodied Daitya Vṛtra.
Then once more a great cry arose on every side from the gods, O bull of the Bharatas, when they beheld Vṛtra slain.
Having slain Vṛtra with the thunderbolt charged with Viṣṇu's power, the illustrious lord, foe of the Dānavas, ascended into heaven itself.
Then from Vṛtra's body, O Kaurava, there issued forth Brahmahatyā—the sin of brahmin-slaughter—most terrible, savage, a terror to the worlds.
With jagged teeth, dreadful, deformed, black and tawny, her hair flying loose, her eyes terrible, O Bhārata,
garlanded with skulls and gaunt, O bull of the Bharatas, drenched in blood, O knower of dharma, clad in rags she was.
Coming forth in that fearful shape, O lord of kings, she then set out in search of the wielder of the thunderbolt, O best of the Bharatas.
After a certain time, O delight of the Kurus, the slayer of Vṛtra set forth toward heaven, desiring the welfare of the worlds.
But seeing the mighty Śakra slipping away among the lotus-stalks, she seized the king of the gods by the throat and clung fast to him.
For when that terror wrought by the slaying of a brahmin had arisen, he dwelt within a lotus-pond, hidden in the midst of the stalks, for many years.
But that Brahmahatyā, having tracked him down with effort, seized him then, O Kaurava, and he became motionless and helpless.
Śakra made the utmost effort to be rid of her, yet the king of the gods could not drive off that Brahmahatyā.
Held fast by her, O bull of the Bharatas, the king of the gods approached the Grandsire and did him homage, bowing his head.
Knowing that Śakra was held fast by the sin of slaying a foremost of the twice-born, Brahmā then fell to pondering, O best of the Bharatas.
O mighty-armed one, the Grandsire then addressed that Brahmahatyā in a sweet voice, as if to soothe her, O Bhārata:
"Let this lord of the thirty gods be released; do me this kindness, O passionate one. Tell me, what shall I do for you this day? What desire of yours would you have fulfilled herein?"
Brahmahatyā said: "Since the god worshipped in the three worlds, the maker of the threefold world, is pleased, I deem my purpose here already accomplished—only ordain me a dwelling-place."
"This boundary has been set by you, who seek the protection of the worlds; a most weighty ordinance has been established and set in motion by you, O god."
"Since you are pleased, O knower of dharma, lord of all the worlds, O master, I shall depart from Śakra—only ordain me a dwelling-place."
Bhīṣma said: "So be it," the Grandsire then said to that Brahmahatyā, and by a skilful expedient he drove the brahmin-slaughter away from Śakra.
Then Fire, summoned in thought by the high-souled Self-Existent One, drew near to Brahmā and spoke these words:
"I have come into your presence, O blessed god, O subduer of foes. What is to be done by me, O god, that you should be pleased to declare."
Brahmā said: "I shall divide this Brahmahatyā into many parts. For the release of Śakra this day, accept from me a fourth portion of her."
Agni said: "What is to be the end of my release, O Brahman? Reflect upon it, O master. This I wish to know truly, O you who are worshipped by the worlds."
Brahmā said: "Whatever man, drawing near to you when you blaze, shall fail of his own accord to make offering anywhere with the saps of seeds and herbs, O Fire, being veiled in darkness of mind—
to him she shall swiftly pass, O bearer of oblations, and there shall she abide. Let the fever of your mind depart."
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, the blessed bearer of offerings to gods and ancestors accepted the word of the Grandsire, and so it came to pass, O lord.
Then the Grandsire, summoning trees, herbs, and grasses, began to declare this matter to them, O great king.
Then the trees, herbs, and grasses, being told the matter just as it was, were troubled as Fire had been, O king, and spoke thus to Brahmā:
"What is to be the end for us of this Brahmahatyā, O Grandsire of the worlds? Slain already by our own nature, we ought not to be slain by you again."
"We endure forever fire and cold and rain driven by the wind, O god, and the cutting and splitting too."
"This Brahmahatyā we shall take upon ourselves this day at your command, O lord of the three worlds; but let your honour consider our release."
Brahmā said: "When the sacred season of the moon's change has come, whatever man shall in his folly perform cutting and splitting, her she shall follow."
Bhīṣma said: Then the trees, herbs, and grasses, thus addressed by the high-souled one, paid homage to Brahmā and swiftly departed as they had come.
Then the god, the Grandsire of the worlds, summoning the Apsarases, spoke to them in a sweet voice, as if to soothe them, O Bhārata:
"This Brahmahatyā has passed to me from Indra, O fair-limbed ones. So bidden by me, accept a fourth portion of her."
The Apsarases said: "Since we are resolved to take her on at your command, O lord of the gods, consider, O Grandsire, our release upon condition."
Brahmā said: "Whatever man shall have intercourse with women in their courses, to him she shall swiftly pass. Let the fever of your minds depart."
Bhīṣma said: Saying "So be it" with gladdened hearts, the troops of Apsarases reached their own abodes and made merry, O bull of the Bharatas.
Then the god of mighty austerity, maker of the three worlds, once more called the Waters to mind, and being so summoned they came.
And all of them, gathering before Brahmā of measureless might, bowed down to the Grandsire and spoke this word, O king:
"Here are we come into your presence, O god, O subduer of foes, at your command, O lord of the gods. Lay your charge upon us, O all-pervading one."
Brahmā said: "This Brahmahatyā of great terror has passed from Vṛtra to him of the many invocations. Do you accept a fourth portion of her."
The Waters said: "So be it, O lord of the worlds, as you bid us, O master; but you ought to consider our release upon condition."
"For you, O lord of the gods, are the supreme preceptor of all the world. What other grace could there be that would deliver us from distress?"
Brahmā said: "Whatever man, deeming you of slight account in his deluded mind, shall cast phlegm, urine, and excrement into you—
to him she shall swiftly pass, and there shall she abide. Thus shall your release come to be—this I tell you in truth."
Bhīṣma said: Then Brahmahatyā, releasing the king of the gods, O Yudhiṣṭhira, went to the place assigned her, at the god's command.
Thus, O ruler of men, did Brahmahatyā come upon Śakra; and having taken leave of the Grandsire, he performed the Horse Sacrifice.
For it is heard, O great king, that Brahmahatyā came upon Vāsava, and thereafter he won purification by the Horse Sacrifice.
Having regained his royal fortune and slain his foes by thousands, the god Vāsava attained joy beyond compare, O lord of the earth.
And from Vṛtra's blood, O Pārtha, were born the mushrooms, which are not to be eaten by the twice-born, by the consecrated, or by those rich in austerity.
You too in every circumstance should do what is dear to these twice-born; for they are gods made manifest upon the earth, O delight of the Kurus.
Thus, O Kaurava, by Śakra of measureless splendour, through subtlety of intellect and by skilful means, was the great Asura Vṛtra slain.
Even so, O Kaurava, shall you too be unconquered upon the earth, like the god of the hundred sacrifices, the slayer of foes.
And those who shall recite this divine tale of Śakra, season after season, in the midst of the brahmins, shall incur no sin.
Thus, with Vṛtra for its theme, this most wondrous and mighty deed of Śakra has been told to you, my son. What more do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O Grandsire, greatly wise, versed in all the sciences, from the very slaying of Vṛtra a question arises that I would put to you.
Vṛtra, bewildered by fever, was described by you, O ruler of men, as slain here by Vāsava with the thunderbolt, O sinless one.
How, O greatly wise one, did this fever come to be, and whence? I wish to hear with precision the origin of fever, O master.
Bhīṣma said: Hear, O king, the origin of fever, renowned throughout the world; and I shall tell its full account and of what nature it is, O Bhārata.

Of old, O great king, there was a peak of Meru, famed throughout the three worlds, named Jyotiṣka, belonging to the Sun, adorned with every gem, immeasurable and unassailable in all the worlds, O Bhārata.
There upon the mountain-slope, adorned with veins of gold, the god sat, shining as though upon a couch.
And the daughter of the mountain-king, ever stationed at his side, shone there; and so too the high-souled gods and the mighty Vasus.
And likewise the high-souled Aśvins, best of physicians, and King Vaiśravaṇa, surrounded by the Guhyakas,
the glorious lord of the Yakṣas, whose abode is Kailāsa, the master; and the divine sages headed by Aṅgiras, and others besides,
and the Gandharva Viśvāvasu, and Nārada and Parvata, and hosts upon hosts of Apsarases came together in great numbers.
A gentle, pleasant wind blew, pure and bearing manifold fragrances; and the great trees, in flower, were laden with the blossoms of every season.
And likewise the Vidyādharas, and the Siddhas rich in austerity, waited reverently upon the great god, the Lord of Creatures, O Bhārata.
And the spirits, O great king, wearing manifold shapes, and the most savage Rākṣasas, and the mighty Piśācas,
the god's attendants, wearing many forms, joyful, raising weapons of every kind, stood there like blazing fire.
And the blessed Nandī stood there too, by the god's leave, grasping a blazing trident shining with its own splendour.
And Gaṅgā, best of rivers, arising from the waters of all holy fords, in embodied form waited reverently upon that god, O delight of the Kurus.
Thus that blessed Mahādeva abode there, worshipped by the divine sages and by the most exalted gods.
Then after a certain time the Prajāpati named Dakṣa set about to perform a sacrifice according to the ordinance aforesaid.
Then all the gods, with Śakra at their head, gathering together, set their minds upon going to his sacrifice.
Those great-souled ones, in blazing chariots that shone like fire, departed with the god's leave for the Gate of the Gaṅgā — so the tradition tells.
Seeing the gods set forth, the daughter of the king of mountains, that virtuous lady, then spoke these words to her lord, the god Paśupati.
"Blessed lord, where do these gods go, with Śakra at their head? Tell me truly, O knower of truth, for great is this doubt of mine."
Maheśvara said: "O greatly blessed one, there is a foremost lord of creatures named Dakṣa; he is performing the horse-sacrifice, and it is there the dwellers in heaven are bound."
Umā said: "O greatly blessed one, why do you not go to this sacrifice? By what prohibition is your going barred?"
Maheśvara said: "O greatly blessed one, it is the gods themselves who have arranged all this: in none of the sacrifices has a share been appointed for me."
"By a course sanctioned by ancient usage, O fair-complexioned one, the gods do not, as dharma requires, render unto me a share of the sacrifice."
Umā said: "Blessed lord, among all beings you surpass them in power and in virtues; unconquerable and unassailable you are, in splendor, in fame, in majesty."
"By this exclusion from your share, O greatly blessed and sinless one, an overwhelming grief has arisen in me, and a trembling besides."
Bhīṣma said: Having spoken thus to her lord, the god Paśupati, that goddess fell silent, O king, with a heart consumed by grief.
Then, perceiving the mind of the goddess and what purpose lay hidden in her heart, he gave his command to Nandin: "Stand ready!"
Then, summoning the force of yoga, the lord of all lords of yoga, that god of gods of mighty splendor, the bearer of the Pināka, with his terrible attendants suddenly had that sacrifice struck down.
Some let loose roars, some burst into laughter, and others, O king, drenched the sacrificial fire there with blood.
Some, having uprooted the sacrificial posts, roamed about with distorted faces; others devoured with their mouths the very attendants of the rite.
Then that sacrifice, O lord of men, being assailed on every side, took on the form of a deer and fled up into the sky.
But the lord, perceiving the sacrifice fleeing in that shape, took up his bow and an arrow and gave chase.
Then, from the wrath of that lord of gods of measureless splendor, a dreadful drop of sweat issued forth from his brow.
And the instant that drop of sweat fell upon the earth, there arose a vast fire, like the fire of universal dissolution.
And from it, O bull among men, there was then born a being: short of stature, with eyes exceedingly red, tawny-bearded, and terrifying.
His hair stood erect, his limbs were thick with hair; hawk- and owl-like was he, gaping-jawed and black of hue, and clothed in red.
That mighty being burned up the sacrifice as a fire burns dry brushwood, and all the gods, stricken with fear, fled then to the ten directions.
As that being ranged about, O lord of peoples, the earth itself shook violently, O king, O bull of the Bharatas.
When a clamor of "Alas! Alas!" had broken out, a cry that struck terror into the worlds, the Grandsire, addressing Mahādeva, made plain his thought and replied:
"To you too, lord, all the gods shall now indeed grant a share; let the withdrawal be made by you, O lord of all the gods."
"For all these gods and the sages, O scorcher of foes, by reason of your wrath, O Mahādeva, can find no peace."
"And this being who has been born from your sweat, O best of the wise — Fever is his name, O knower of dharma, and as Fever he shall range through the worlds."
"For while his fiery force remains gathered into one, the whole earth, O lord, cannot bear it; let him therefore be released in many parts."
Thus addressed by Brahmā, and his share now appointed, the god said "So be it" to the blessed Brahmā of measureless might.
And the bearer of the Pināka came to supreme delight, smiling broadly; and Bhava then received his share as Brahmā had declared.
And the knower of all dharmas then released Fever in many parts, for the welfare of all beings — hear of that too, my son.
In elephants it is the burning fever of the head; in mountains, the mineral pitch; in waters one should know it as the green scum, and in serpents as their cast-off slough.
In cattle it is the hoof-rot; on the face of the earth, the barren saline soil; and in beasts too, O knower of dharma, it is the dimming of their sight.
In horses it is the malady of the orifices; in peacocks, the splitting of the crest; in cuckoos it is declared by the great one to be a disease of the eye — such is Fever.
In water-born creatures it is the disorder of the bile of them all — so we have heard; and in all parrots, Fever is said to be the hiccup.

In tigers, O knower of dharma, it is said here to be weariness as their fever; but among men, O knower of dharma, it is renowned by the very name of Fever, and it enters a man at death, at birth, and in the time between.
This is the splendor of Maheśvara, the most dreadful thing named Fever — the lord, to be revered and honored by all living beings.
Possessed by this very Fever, Vṛtra, the best of upholders of dharma, gaped wide; and thereupon Śakra hurled the thunderbolt at him.
Entering into Vṛtra, the thunderbolt rent him asunder, O Bhārata; and that great yogin, the mighty Asura, thus sundered by the thunderbolt, went to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu of measureless splendor.
For of old, through his devotion to Viṣṇu, this world had been pervaded by him; and therefore, slain in battle, he attained the abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus, taking Vṛtra for its occasion, the full account of the great Fever has been told by me, my son. What else shall I declare to you?

The man who, undaunted in mind and well-composed, ever reads this story of the origin of Fever shall be freed from disease; happy and filled with joy, he shall obtain his desires according to his heart's wish.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "From grief, from sorrow, and from death, living beings ever tremble. Tell me, Grandsire, how both of these may be undone for me."
Bhīṣma said: On this very matter they relate an ancient tale, the dialogue of Nārada and Samaṅga, O Bhārata.
Nārada said: "You seem to bow forward with your very chest, and to push your way through with your arms; ever glad of mind, you appear like one wholly free from grief."
"Not the slightest agitation, not even the subtlest, do I discern in you here; ever content and at ease, you behave like a child."
Samaṅga said: "What was, what is, and what shall be — all that lies among creatures, O bestower of honor — I know the truths of these; and therefore am I not despondent."
"I know undertakings, and likewise the arising of their fruits; the fruits in this world are of many kinds, and therefore am I not despondent."
"The fathomless and the unsteady, the moving and the wandering, the blind and the dull-witted — all these live, O Nārada; behold us too, that we are living."
"The dwellers in heaven, sound of limb, live by what is ordained; the strong and the weak alike — so too regard us in like manner."
"Those who possess thousands live, and those who possess hundreds live as well; and others live upon mere herbs — behold us too, that we are living."

"When we do not grieve, what then could there be to grieve for, O Nārada, whether through dharma or through action? — since pleasures, being subject to Destiny, and pains likewise, cannot overwhelm us."

"It is to him men attribute wisdom in whom the serenity of the senses is rooted in wisdom; but when the senses are bewildered and sorrow, there is no winning of wisdom for one whose senses are confounded."

"The pride of the deluded man is but delusion once more; for the deluded there is neither this world nor the world beyond. For pains do not come forever, nor is there a perpetual winning of pleasure."

"Over this world of becoming, ever revolving in its course, one such as I would never let himself feel torment; he would not crave for cherished enjoyments or for pleasure, nor would he brood over the sorrow that has come upon him."

"Composed, he would not covet what belongs to others, nor would he rejoice over a gain not yet come; he would not exult at a vast acquisition of wealth, nor, when wealth is lost, would he sink into despair."

"Not kinsmen, not wealth, not high birth, not learning, not sacred counsels, not valor — all these are eager to rescue one from sorrow, yet without character in the life to come they do not attain peace."
"For the undisciplined there is no understanding, and without discipline no happiness is found; steadfastness and the renouncing of sorrow — both of these are for us the wellspring of joy."
"For what is dear gives rise to elation, elation breeds arrogance, and arrogance leads but to hell; therefore I wholly renounce it."
"These — grief, fear, and arrogance, bewilderers in pleasure and in pain — I behold in the world as a witness might, through the workings of this body."
"Having forsaken wealth and desire, free from grief and rid of fever, having cast off craving and delusion, I wander over this earth."
"Neither from death, nor from unrighteousness, nor from greed, nor from any source whatever — like one who has drunk the nectar of immortality, I have no fear at all, here or hereafter."
"This I have come to know, O brāhmaṇa, by performing great and imperishable austerity; and by that attainment, O Nārada, no grief afflicts me."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "For one who does not know the truths of the scriptures, who is forever of doubting mind, who has reached no firm resolve — tell me, Grandsire, what is the highest good."
Bhīṣma said: "Constant honoring of one's teacher, attendance upon the elders, and the hearing of the branches of knowledge — this is declared to be the unfailing highest good."
"On this too they relate an ancient tale, the dialogue of Gālava and of the divine sage Nārada."
To Nārada — a brāhmaṇa freed from delusion and weariness, sated with knowledge, his senses mastered, desiring the highest good and his self subdued — Gālava spoke:
"Whatever the virtues by which a man is esteemed in the world among men, all those abiding virtues do I discern in you."
"You, being such a one, are fit to cut away our doubt — you who are undeluded, for the sake of us long-deluded, who do not know the truth of the world."
"For thus would there be activity grounded in knowledge for one who discerns what should and should not be done; that which we cannot resolve as our duty, you are fit to declare."
"Blessed lord, all the orders of life teach each its own separate conduct, and each runs off in its own way, crying, 'This is the highest good! This is the highest good!'"
"Seeing them thus set apart by their scriptures, each delighting in his own scripture and content with it, we cannot lay hold of the highest good."
"Were there but a single scripture, then the highest good would be made plain; but by the many scriptures the highest good has only been driven the deeper into mystery."
"For this reason the highest good appears to me a tangled thicket; let the blessed lord declare it to me — I have come to you as a suppliant; teach me, I pray."
Nārada said: "The orders of life, my dear, are four, each ordained apart; behold them all, Gālava, taking your stand within them."
"For of each of those several orders, here and there, behold the aim, manifold in form and in quality, set forth apart; and indeed they lead one rightly, without doubt, to the goal intended."
"Looking straight and rightly upon the supreme goal of the orders of life — that which is truly the highest blessedness is also the very thing free from all doubt."
"The favoring of friends, the restraint of foes, and the holding fast of the threefold aim of life — these the wise call the highest good."
"Turning away from sinful action, a constant habit of virtue, and right conduct in the company of the good — this is the highest good, beyond all doubt."
"Gentleness toward all beings, uprightness in one's dealings, and speech that is sweet — this is declared the highest good, beyond all doubt."
"Sharing one's portion with the gods, with the ancestors, and with guests too, and never abandoning one's dependents — this is the highest good, beyond all doubt."
To speak the truth is good, yet the knowledge of truth is hard to win. That which is of utmost benefit to living beings — that I declare to be the truth.
The abandonment of egoism, the restraint of fond craving, contentment, and a solitary course of life — this is called the unshakable, supreme good.
The study of the Vedas according to dharma, and likewise of the Vedāṅgas, and the eager inquiry into the objects of knowledge — this, beyond doubt, is the good.
Sound, form, taste, and touch, together with smell, in their bare forms — let the seeker of the good not pursue these to excess, O scorcher of foes.
Roaming by night, sleeping by day, sloth, slander, intoxicating pride, overexertion and want of effort alike — let the seeker of the good forsake them all.
Let him not seek the exaltation of his deeds by disparaging others; by his own virtues alone let him seek to rise above the common run of men.
For the most part it is men devoid of merit who think highly of themselves; they assail the virtuous with imagined faults, and so squander what merit they have.
And though no one praises them, they fancy themselves more endowed with virtue than the great, puffed up with their own conceit.
Uttering no censure of anyone, sounding no praise of himself, the wise man rich in virtue attains, even so, a great renown.
Without a word the fragrant, pure scent of blossoms wafts abroad; and just so, uttering nothing, the spotless sun shines in the sky.
These things and others like them, embraced through wisdom, blaze with glory in the world — and yet they make no proclamation of themselves.
A fool does not shine in the world by mere self-praise, while the learned man shines forth even though hidden in a pit.
A worthless utterance, though loudly proclaimed, soon dies away; but a word well spoken, even softly, shines among the worlds.
The much, pithless talk of the deluded and the arrogant lays bare their inner self, as the radiant sun reveals form by day.
For this reason men seek wisdom of every kind; for the winning of wisdom appears to me the highest gain of living beings.
Let him speak to no one unasked, nor to one who questions wrongly; though full of knowledge and keen of mind, let him move through the world as if dull-witted.
Then let him test his dwelling-place, choosing among good men ever devoted to dharma, among the generous, and among those intent upon their own duty.
Where the duties of the four varṇas are confounded and overthrown, there let the seeker of the good never make his dwelling, by any means whatever.
Even one who undertakes no works here, living on whatever comes to hand, gains spotless merit among the meritorious and sin among the sinful.
As one feels the touch of water, of fire, and of the moon, so do we perceive the touch of both alike — of sin and of merit.
Those who eat the leavings of a sacrifice partake of food without regard to its source; but know that the eating of food's objects is itself the field of works and their fruit.
Where, to those who come seeking and inquiring, one would expound the dharma of Brahman with disrespect, that land let the self-possessed man forsake.
Where the bond of pupil and teacher is well-ordered and rightly furnished with the scriptures — what man would abandon such a land?
Where men set on high, hungry for their own honour, would surely fasten fault upon the wise — what learned man would dwell there?
Where the dikes of dharma are for the most part churned up and breached by the greedy — who would not forsake that land, as one flees a blazing mountainside?
Where men, free of misgiving and free of envy, would practise dharma — there let him move and there let him dwell, among the good and righteous of conduct.
But where men would practise dharma only for the sake of gain, let him never dwell among them, for those are people who do evil.
Where men cling to life by deeds of sin, from there let him swiftly run away, as from a shelter that holds a serpent.
That deed which, having mounted his deathbed, would leave a man clinging in remorse — such a deed he must not do at the outset, if he desires the welfare of his soul.
Where the king and the king's men, his close attendants, eat before the householders and seize the first share, that realm let the self-possessed man abandon.
But where it is the Vedic scholars, ever devoted to the eternal dharma and engaged in performing sacrifice and teaching, who eat the first share — in such a realm let him take up his abode.
Where the cries of Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭ are rightly performed and ceaselessly maintained, there let him dwell without hesitation.
Where he sees impure practices and brāhmaṇas wasted for want of livelihood, that realm let him abandon, as one shuns meat already gone foul.
Where men in gladness would give even unasked, there let the self-possessed man dwell with tranquil mind, as one whose every task is fulfilled.
Where punishment falls upon the undisciplined and honour is paid to the self-mastered — there let him move and there let him dwell, among the good of holy conduct.
Upon the corrupt and unrestrained, the ill-conducted and the wicked, the undisciplined and the greedy, the wielding of a very great rod of punishment is fitting.
Where a king ever steadfast in dharma rules the realm with care, and the lord of pleasures has cast his desires aside — there let him dwell without hesitation.
For kings of such character swiftly join all the dwellers of their domain to the good, when the good is set before them.
To you who asked, my child, this account of the good has been declared by me; yet the good of one's own soul cannot be reckoned through any single chief means.
For one who conducts his life thus, with self intent and composed, the good in abundance will plainly come to be, even here, through austerity alone.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How then may a king such as I, set free, wander the earth, and endowed with what virtues is one ever released from the snare of attachment?
Bhīṣma said: On this I shall relate to you an ancient tale, spoken by Ariṣṭanemi to Sagara when he questioned him.
Sagara said: What, O holy one, is the highest good, doing which a man enjoys happiness here? How may one neither grieve nor be shaken? This I wish to know.
Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, Tārkṣya, deeply versed in all the scriptures, perceiving the questioner's surpassing fitness, then spoke this true word.
The happiness of liberation is happiness indeed in this world, yet the world does not comprehend it — clinging to sons and cattle, distracted with wealth and grain.
The man whose mind is bound and whose self is unquiet cannot be healed; deluded, fettered by the noose of fondness, he is not fit for liberation.
The bonds born of affection I shall now declare to you — hear them from me; with a head whose ears are open, the discerning man can cut them through.
When in due time you have raised your sons, established them in youth, and known them fit to make their own way in life — then, set free, wander as you please.
Your wife, grown old, blessed with sons and cherished, fond of her children — knowing her so, forsake her in due season, looking to the higher aim.
With offspring or without, set free, wander as you please, having tasted with your senses the objects of sense in due measure.
Your curiosity for them once satisfied, set free, wander as you please; and toward such gains as come to you by chance, remain even-minded.
Thus far the matter of liberation has been declared to you by me in brief; I shall now expound it once more at length — hear it.
The liberated, free of fear, wander happy in the world; but men of clinging nature perish — of this there is no doubt.
Even insects and ants that hoard their food show this: the unattached are happy in the world, while the attached go to ruin.
Nor should you, your mind set on liberation, brood over your kin, thinking, 'How will these fare once parted from me?'
A creature is born of itself and of itself grows up; pleasure and pain, and death as well, it meets of its own accord.
Their food and clothing, and what is gathered for them by mother and father, men obtain by their own past deeds; nothing in the world comes uncaused by what was done before.
With their sustenance ordained by the Creator, all living beings run to and fro across the earth, guarded by their own deeds.
For one who is himself but a lump of clay, forever dependent and infirm of self, what ground is there to nourish his kin or to protect them?
When death strikes down your kin before your very eyes, despite all your great striving — there a man must awaken to the truth within himself.
And though this kinsman still lives, you yourself, the task of his support and protection left unfinished, abandoning him, will die hereafter all the same.
And when you are dead, you will in no way know your kin, whether they are happy or in sorrow — surely a man should awaken to this within himself.
Whether you be dead or alive, the people will enjoy only the fruit of their own deeds; having understood this, surely a man should do what is for his own true good.
Knowing this, and resolved that in this world none truly belongs to another, fix your mind upon liberation, and consider it yet again.
The embodied one who has here conquered the states of hunger, thirst, and the rest, and anger, greed, and delusion as well — that man of inner strength is liberated indeed.
The man who, in gambling, in drink, in women, and in the chase, never grows heedless through infatuation — he is ever liberated indeed.
He who is wearied by the thought, 'Day after day, night after night, forever and again, one must eat' — that man, they say, is of corrupted understanding.
He who, ever steadfast and rightly discerning, sees the nature of the self in women too as already free, again and again — that man is liberated indeed.
He who knows in their true reality the arising and the passing away of beings, and their strivings as well — that man in this world is liberated indeed.
He who sees that, amid thousands of draught-beasts, but a single measure suffices for sustenance, and amid crores of wealth, but the space of a cot within a palace — that man is set free.
He who sees the world smitten by death, oppressed by diseases, and wasted for want of livelihood — that man is set free.
He who sees thus is happy and content, while he who does not see is undone; and he who is content with little — that man in this world is liberated indeed.
He who beholds that all this is but Agni and Soma, and is not touched by wondrous appearances — that man is liberated indeed.
The embodied one to whom a couch for a bed and the bare ground are the same, and fine rice and coarse fare alike — that man is liberated indeed.
He to whom linen and a garment of kuśa grass, silk and bark-cloth, wool and hide are all the same — that man is liberated indeed.
He who beholds the world as risen from the five elements, and having so seen it conducts himself accordingly — that man in this world is liberated indeed.
He to whom pleasure and pain are the same, gain and loss, victory and defeat, desire and aversion, fear and agitation — that man in every way is liberated indeed.
Seeing this body to be a heap of blood, urine, and dung, a heap of morbid humours rife with corruption — by this very seeing he is set free.
He who beholds the coming of wrinkles and grey hair, the wasting and the fading of colour, and the bending of the body brought on by old age — that man is set free.
He who beholds the failing of his manhood with time, the fading of sight, deafness, and the dulling of the vital breath — that man is set free.
He who beholds how the sages have passed away, and the gods likewise, and the asuras too departed, gone from this world to the world beyond — he is released.
Knowing that kings of the earth by the thousand, endowed with this power and that, have departed, abandoning the earth — by this knowledge he is set free.
He who sees how hard wealth is to win in this world, how easily afflictions come, and the suffering borne for the sake of family — he is released.
Seeing so widely in the world the worthlessness of offspring and the unworthiness of people, who would not hold liberation in highest honour?
The man who, awakened by scripture and by the world, sees the whole of human existence as without substance — he is in every way already free.
Having heard this counsel of mine, let your honour wander as one already liberated, even in the householder's life, if your mind is fixed unwavering upon release.
Having rightly heard that counsel of his, the lord of the earth, endowed with the virtues born of liberation, governed his subjects.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: A certain curiosity ever abides in my heart, dear sire; this I wish to hear from you, O grandsire of the Kurus.
How was it that the divine seer Uśanas, son of Kavi, ever of great wisdom, did good to the asuras and delighted in what was unwelcome to the gods?
For what purpose did he augment the might of those of measureless force, the dānavas, who were ever bound in enmity with the best of the gods?
And how did Uśanas, radiant as the immortals, attain to the state of Śukra, and how did he gain his prosperity? Tell me all of this.
And how is it that the luminous one does not pass through the middle of the sky? This I wish to understand in full, O grandsire.
Bhīṣma said: Listen attentively, O king, to all of this as it truly is, according to my understanding and as I have heard it before, O sinless one.
This sage, heir of Bhṛgu, truthful and firm in his vows, did good to the asuras out of a compassionate cause.
Now Indra, and King Kubera the giver of wealth, lord of the yakṣas and rākṣasas — he too was master of the treasury and lord of the world.
The great sage, perfected in yoga, then entering into himself and confining the god Kubera, lord of wealth, by his yoga carried off his riches.
His wealth thus stolen, Kubera could find no peace; seized with wrath and agitated, he went to the best of the gods.
He then made his plaint to Śiva of measureless splendour, to Rudra, foremost of gods, the gracious one of many forms.
Kubera said: By Uśanas, master of yoga, my wealth has been confined and carried off; the great ascetic, having made his course by yoga, has departed.
Bhīṣma said: Hearing this, the great yogin Maheśvara grew wroth; his eyes flushed red, O king, he took up his trident and stood ready.
"Where is he, where is he?" he cried, grasping his supreme weapon; but Uśanas, knowing his intent, shone forth at a distance from him.
Perceiving the wrath of the great-souled, mighty yogin, the lord then knew his going and his coming, and knew his place.
Having meditated by his fierce austerity upon the great-souled Maheśvara, Uśanas, his self perfected in yoga, appeared upon the point of the trident.
His form thus recognized by the bow-bearer perfected in austerity, the lord of gods, perceiving him, bent down the trident with his hand.
With the trident now bent down by his hand of measureless might, the lord of the terrible weapon named that trident "Pināka."
Seeing the descendant of Bhṛgu come into the midst of his hand, the lord of Umā, the bull-marked one, opened his mouth and slowly cast his hand toward it.
But the lord Uśanas, that great-souled delight of Bhṛgu, having entered into the belly of Maheśvara, wandered about within.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: For what reason, O king, did Uśanas wander in the belly of that wise god of gods, and what did the greatly radiant one do there?
Bhīṣma said: Long ago, O king, that great keeper of vows abode beneath the waters, motionless as a post, for millions and tens of millions of years.
Having performed austerity hard to endure, he rose up from the great lake; then Brahmā, god beyond the gods, drew near to him.
He asked after the growth of his austerity and after his unfailing welfare; and the bull-bannered one said, "Well practised is your austerity."
And by that union Śaṃkara perceived his increase — he of great wisdom, of inconceivable nature, ever devoted to truth and dharma.
Enriched thereby in austerity and in wealth, that great yogin, valorous, shone forth throughout the three worlds, O great king.
Then the Pināka-bearer, his self given to yoga, entered into the yoga of meditation; but Uśanas, alarmed, concealed himself within the belly.
And the great yogin, dwelling there, praised the god; but, seeking a way out, he was thrust back by his splendour.
Then Uśanas, the great sage, dwelling in the belly, spoke: "Show me your grace," again and again, O subduer of foes.
Mahādeva said to him, "Go forth; your release shall be by the member" — for the bull of the gods had stopped up all the other openings.
Finding no door, shut in on every side, the sage wandered to and fro, burning in that splendour.
Coming forth by the member, he attained the state of Śukra; and by that very deed he comes not through the middle of the sky.
Then, seeing him come forth blazing as it were with splendour, Bhava, filled with wrath, stood with his trident raised in his hand.
But the goddess restrained her wrathful lord, the master of beasts; and when Śaṃkara was thus stayed by the goddess, the sage came to the state of her son.
The goddess said: This one is not to be slain by you, for he has come to be my son; and none who has issued from a god's womb meets with destruction.
Bhīṣma said: Then he was pleased with the goddess, and laughing said this: "Let him go as he wills," O king, again and again.
Then, bowing to the boon-granting god and to the goddess Umā, the wise Uśanas, the great sage, attained the course he desired.
This deed of the great-souled descendant of Bhṛgu I have related to you, dear son, O best of the Bharatas, as you have asked of me.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Beyond this, O mighty-armed one, tell me what is best; I am not sated with your words, as if with nectar, O grandsire.
By doing what auspicious deed, O best of men, does a man attain the supreme good both hereafter and here? Tell me that.
Bhīṣma said: On this I shall relate to you how, in former times, King Janaka of great fame questioned the great-souled Parāśara.
What is the highest good of all beings in this world and the next, and what ought to be attained — that may your honour declare to me.
Then that sage, endowed with austerity and knowing the whole ordinance of dharma, his mind set on favouring the king, spoke these words.
Dharma alone, when practised, is the better thing both in this world and the next; for there is nothing higher than it, as the wise have declared.

Embracing dharma, a man is exalted in the world of heaven; the ordinance of action is itself of the nature of dharma for embodied beings, O best of kings, and within it the good who keep the stations of life perform their proper duties here.
For the world's course is ordained of four kinds, dear son, in which mortals abide; and it proceeds from desire.
Having performed deeds well-done and ill-done by manifold gradations, manifold is the course of beings, who are divided according to the five elements.
Just as a vessel of gold or of silver is cast in its mould, so is a creature cast, subject to the power of its former deeds.
Nothing arises from no seed, nor does one prosper in happiness without acting; the doer of good deeds, having attained the dissolution of the body, finds happiness.
Fate I do not perceive, dear son; there is no means of accomplishing fate; for gods, gandharvas, and dānavas are perfected by their own nature.
After death, people do not always remember the deeds done in their birth; yet they reap the fruit of that deed, and the deed too is fourfold.
The word resting on the conduct of the world and resting on the Veda was made for the sake of the mind's peace, dear son; this is not the teaching of the elders.
By eye, by mind, by speech, and by action — fourfold; whatever kind of deed a man does, that very kind does he obtain.
Unceasingly, and in mixed measure, does action bear fruit, O king, whether it be good or evil; but there is no destruction of it.
Sometimes, dear son, a good deed stands as though unmoved at the summit, for one sinking in the round of existence, until he is freed from sorrow.
Then, having worn away his sorrow, he enjoys his good deed; and from the exhaustion of the good deed comes the ill-done one — know this, O lord of men.
Self-restraint, forbearance, firmness, vigour, contentment, truthful speech, modesty, freedom from cruelty and from vice, and skill — these bring happiness.
Whether in ill-doing or in good-doing, let a creature not be unrestrained; the discerning man should ever strive for the composure of the mind.
This man does not partake of another's good deed or ill deed; whatever kind of deed he does, that very kind does he obtain.
Having laid by his pleasure and pain, a man departs alone; and by another path goes every man, even he with whom one has been joined, O king.
What a man would resent in others, that let him not do himself; for he who is envious and so disposed brings mockery upon himself.

A cowardly kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa who eats all things, an idle vaiśya, a man of low birth who is slothful, a learned man of bad character, a man of good lineage destitute of conduct, a brāhmaṇa fallen from truth, and a wicked woman —

a passionate ascetic who has renounced, one who cooks for his own sake, a fool who would teach, and a realm without a king — all these come to a pitiable state, O king, and so too the ruler who is heedless and devoid of affection toward his subjects.
Parāśara said: The man who, having gained the chariot of his desires drawn by the horses of the sense-objects, drives it with the reins born of knowledge — he is wise.
For one bereft of livelihood, a mind given to service is commended; sustenance is praised when it comes from the hand of the twice-born, but not from an equal in mutual exchange.
Having gained a life-span not easily won, a man should not drag himself down, O lord of peoples; rather let him strive for his elevation by meritorious action.
Even one fallen away from the classes deserves honour, but not he who, having attained right conduct, then practises deeds of passion.
A man attains elevation of class by meritorious action; but not having gained that hard-won state, he would destroy it by sinful action.

Sin done out of ignorance one may dispel by austerity alone; for a sinful deed bears sinful fruit, the very sin one has done oneself; therefore let none practise sin, the deed whose fruit is the rising of sorrow.
A deed bound up with sin, though it should be of great fruit, the wise and pure man would not practise — even as he would shun foul water.
What greater misery do I behold than the fruit of a sinful deed? For even of one who has turned back and become good, the self does not yet shine forth.
And for the fool in whom no turning-back arises here, exceedingly great is the anguish that comes upon him as he sets forth on his way.
A garment whose dye has faded can be cleansed, but not one steeped in black, for all one's effort; understand sin thus from me, O lord of men.
But the man who, having himself committed an evil deed, then sets himself to do good as an expiation for it — he reaps the fruit of both, each separately.
Harm done through ignorance is drawn off and cancelled by harmlessness — so say the brāhmaṇas who expound the Veda, citing the direction of the scriptures.

And harm done willfully, out of desire, is likewise drawn off only by the renunciation of harm — so declare the brāhmaṇas learned in the dharma-scriptures, who have crossed to the far shore of the Veda.
For my part, I hold that the deed which yields its fruit is the one performed endowed with virtue, open and shining, and untainted by any evil.
Subtle deeds bear their fruit here in just measure, exactly as they are — those, that is, which are done with discernment and with the mind fully present.
But a deed, O knower of dharma, though pursued unceasingly and on a grand scale, bears scant fruit when done without forethought, by violent means.
Those deeds that were done by gods and by sages — the righteous man should not himself perform them; yet, having heard of them, neither should he revile them.
He who, O king, having pondered in his mind and gauged his own strength, performs a good deed — he indeed comes to see blessings.
As water poured into a fresh, unfired vessel seeps away and is lost, so too does happiness, when set in an unprepared soul, come to nothing.
But as water poured into water that is already there only swells what was full, growing greater in the abundant, so does merit added to merit increase.
Thus, O lord of the earth, the deeds done here with discernment are not matched even by the holiest of deeds done without it.

The king must conquer those who are armed and arrogant, and must rightly protect his subjects; he must tend the sacred fire and worship with many sacrifices; and at the end, or even at the middle of life, he should withdraw to dwell in the forest.

A man possessed of self-restraint and of righteous character should regard all beings as he regards himself; he should honor his betters according to his power, and through truth and good conduct, O lord of men, he attains happiness.
Parāśara said: Who renders service to whom, and who bestows anything upon another? This living being performs every deed by himself and for his own sake.
One who has cast off all respect and is devoid of affection should be shunned — even a brother born of the same womb, how much more some other, a stranger of the common crowd.
For a worthy man, the giving and the receiving from another worthy man are of equal merit; yet of the two, the giving is the holier — that is, the gift of a twice-born man who bestows.
Wealth that has come by lawful means to the social orders, and lawfully increased, must be guarded with effort — this is the settled rule — for the sake of dharma.
One who seeks dharma should not earn wealth by cruel means; he should carry out all his undertakings according to his capacity, and should not hanker after riches.
For the man of self-control who, to the best of his means, gives a guest tormented by hunger so much as cool water, or water warmed by fire, reaps the fruit of it.
By great-souled Rantideva the perfection longed for by all the worlds was attained, for he honored the sages with offerings of fruits, leaves, and roots.
With those very fruits and leaves he gratified Māṭhara; and through that the lord of the earth Śaibya too gained the highest station.
A mortal is born a debtor to the gods, to guests, to dependents, to the ancestors, and likewise to his own self; therefore let him strive to be free of debt.
To the great seers the debt is discharged by recitation of the Veda, to the gods by the rite of sacrifice, to the ancestors by the offering of the śrāddha, and to men by hospitable honoring.

By offering of the remnant of one's words, and by the sustaining of one's own self and of the whole body of dependents in due measure — thus let a man set out to fulfill dharma from the very beginning.
Sages, perfected through effort and bereft even of wealth, attained to perfection by rightly making oblation into the fire that bears the offerings.
The son of Ṛcīka, that highly blessed one, came to the sonship of Viśvāmitra, having praised with hymns of the Ṛgveda the gods who partake of the sacrifice.
Uśanas attained the state of the planet Śukra by propitiating the god of gods; having praised the goddess, he now rejoices in the sky, wreathed in his own splendor.
Asita Devala, and likewise Nārada and Parvata, Kakṣīvat, and Rāma the son of Jamadagni, Tāṇḍya, and Aṃśumat —
Vasiṣṭha and Jamadagni, Viśvāmitra and Atri, Bharadvāja, Hariśmaśru, Kuṇḍadhāra, and Śrutaśravas —
these great seers, with collected minds, having praised Viṣṇu with hymns of the Ṛgveda, won perfection through their austerity, by the grace of that wise lord.
Even the unworthy, by praising that very lord, became worthy; but one should not seek prosperity here by doing a deed that is to be despised.
Those gains that come through dharma are real; those that come through unrighteousness — a curse upon them. One should never abandon the eternal dharma in the world out of craving for wealth.
The righteous man who has established the sacred fires is the foremost of doers of merit; for all the Vedas, O lord among kings, O sovereign, abide within the three fires.

That brāhmaṇa who has established the fires, but whose rites lapse — better for him the state of not having established them at all; for the fire-oblation is no fire-oblation when it goes unperformed.
The sacred fire, one's own self, mother, father the begetter, and the teacher, O tiger among men — these are to be tended with service, each in its due measure.

The man who has cast off pride and serves his elders, who though learned looks upon them with the meekness of one without power, out of pure affection — not lacking in diligence, yoked to dharma and self-restrained — such a noble one is honored in this world by the good.
Parāśara said: The livelihood of the lowliest, drawn from the three higher orders, is honorable; offered with goodwill and prescribed by rule, it ever makes men most righteous.
If a śūdra has no fixed livelihood handed down from father and grandfather, he should not seek a calling from another, but should set himself to the service of others.
Fellowship with the good, who perceive dharma, is becoming at all times and in every condition; never fellowship with the wicked — such is my conviction.
As an object glows by its nearness to the mountain of sunrise, so even a man of low birth shines by nearness to the good.
With whatever hue a white cloth is steeped, just that color it takes on — understand the matter from me to be exactly so.
Therefore take your delight in virtues, never in vices; for the life of mortals here is impermanent, ever shifting and unsteady.
The wise man who, whether placed in happiness or in sorrow, gathers up only good deeds — he comes to behold blessings here.
A deed that has fallen away from dharma, though it might bring great reward, the man of insight should not pursue; it is not called wholesome here.
A king who, failing to protect his people, plunders thousands of cattle only to give them away, reaps as his fruit no more than empty repute — such a king becomes a thief.
The Self-existent first created the Ordainer, honored by the worlds; and the Ordainer created a single son, devoted to the upholding of all creatures.
Having worshiped him, the vaiśya should make his wealth abound exceedingly; it is then to be protected by the men of royal blood and put to use by the twice-born.
By śūdras who are honest, free from guile and from anger, and who furnish the means for offerings to the gods and to the ancestors, the cleansing service should be done — thus dharma does not perish.
When dharma is thus kept from perishing, the people become happy; and by their happiness, O lord of kings, the gods rejoice in heaven.
Therefore the king who protects his people is honored through dharma; so too the brāhmaṇa who studies, the vaiśya who is intent on earning,
and the śūdra who renders service, constantly and with senses controlled. Acting otherwise than this, O lord of men, a man falls away from his own dharma.
Even a few small coins, wrung from one's own life's hardship, earned by lawful means and given away, bear great fruit — how much more so other sums by the thousand.
He who, doing them honor, gives to the twice-born, O lord of men, ever reaps a mighty fruit, each according to the manner of his giving.
What is given gladly, the giver himself approaching the recipient, the wise call the most blessed and most praised; but what is given upon being asked, the learned call middling.
What is given with contempt, and likewise without faith, that the truth-speaking sages call the lowest of gifts.
A man, ever sinking in transgression of many kinds, should so exert himself that he may be delivered from the peril.
The brāhmaṇa shines by self-restraint, the kṣatriya by victory, the vaiśya by wealth, and the śūdra ever shines by diligence.

Parāśara said: Goods that come to the brāhmaṇa through acceptance of gifts, to the kṣatriya as won by the sword, to the vaiśya as earned by lawful means, and to the śūdra as gained by service — even when slight, such goods are praised, and bear great fruit when used for the sake of dharma.

The śūdra is declared the perpetual servant of the three orders. A twice-born man who follows the duty of a kṣatriya or of a vaiśya, when no other livelihood remains, does not fall; but when he takes up the work of a śūdra, then indeed the twice-born man falls.
Trade, the keeping of cattle, and a living gained by craftsmanship are ordained even for the śūdra, when no other livelihood arises for him.
Taking to the stage, a living gained by one's looks, subsisting upon liquor and meat, and the sale of iron and of leather —
a deed the world reviles should not be taken up by one who has not done it before; but for one who has done it before and now forsakes it, there is great dharma — so says the sacred tradition.
Whatever evil a man, however accomplished, commits in the world with a mind flooded by intoxicating pride — that too is declared not to be taken as a precedent.
For in the lore of old we hear of peoples who were governed by the rod of reproach alone — self-restrained, holding dharma foremost, and following the path of justice and right.
It is dharma alone, O king, that is ever praised among men here; for men who have grown great in dharma cultivate the virtues upon the earth.
That dharma, my son, the asuras could not endure, O lord of peoples; growing ever stronger, step by step they entered into those creatures.
Then arrogance, the destroyer of dharma, arose in those creatures; and out of their arrogance, wrath in turn was born within them.
Then, in those overpowered by wrath, all conduct accompanied by decency perished, and modesty itself perished, O king; and from this delusion was born.
Then, beset by delusion, they no longer saw, as before, how they might live with one another at ease, without crushing each the other.
When that rod of mere reproach reached such men, it became of no avail against them; and so they went on to despise both the gods and the brāhmaṇas.
At this very time the gods went for refuge to Śiva, foremost of the gods, the hero of many forms, the lord of the hosts.
By him those sky-dwellers, together with their cities — all three — were cast down to the earth with a single arrow, whose splendor the gods had swelled.
Their overlord was the dreadful Bhīma of dreadful prowess, a terror to the gods; he was slain by the Bearer of the Trident.
When he was slain, men returned to their own true nature, and the Vedas and the scriptures were set going once more, as in the days of old.
Then they consecrated Vāsava to the kingship of the gods in heaven, and the Seven Seers appointed men to the wielding of the rod of chastisement.
After the Seven Seers there was a king named Vipṛthu, and kings and kṣatriyas each ruling separately in their several realms.
In those born of great lineages, and in those who lived in former ages, the asura nature does not slip away from the heart.
Therefore, through that very nature clinging persistently to them, kings of dreadful might took to performing asura-like deeds.
They held firm to those very deeds and continue to establish them; and even to this day those men who are most foolish cling to them.
Therefore I tell you, O king, after pondering it in the light of the scriptures: one should pursue what leads to true perfection, and forsake every deed whose essence is harm.
The discerning man should not gather wealth by confusion of duties; to abandon the right way for the sake of dharma is not called auspicious.
Such a one as you are—self-controlled, a kṣatriya dear to your kinsmen—cherish your subjects, your dependents, and your sons in accordance with your own dharma.
Union with the pleasant and the unpleasant, enmity and likewise friendship—through many thousands of births these revolve again and again.
Therefore take delight in virtues, never in faults; for the man devoid of virtue and of evil mind is called his own enemy.
Among human beings, O great king, dharma and adharma have their course; not so among the other creatures here that are devoid of human nature.
The learned man of righteous disposition, whether active in worldly effort or free from it, should always move through the world as one with all, harming no living being.
When his mind has become free of all inner scruple and falsehood no longer dwells in him, then he attains the auspicious state.
Parāśara said: This rule of dharma for the householder, my son, has now been declared; but I shall expound the rule of austerity—listen to me as I speak it.
For in the householder, O best of men, there generally arises what is called "the sense of mine," born of attachment through states of tamas and rajas.
Resting upon his house, a man comes to possess cattle, fields, and wealth, a wife, sons, and servants in this world.
As he goes on thus, ever fixing his gaze upon these things and never perceiving their impermanence, his attraction and aversion grow and grow.
And upon the man overwhelmed by attraction and aversion, enslaved to his possessions, there comes, O ruler of men, what is called delight, born of delusion.
Deeming himself fulfilled by enjoyment and wholly devoted to pleasure, he sees no gain from delight beyond that of vulgar comforts.
Then, his soul overcome by greed, through attachment he increases his household, and he strives in this world to provide for the nourishment and welfare of that household.
Though he knows it ought not to be done, the man pursues it for the sake of gain; his soul wrapped in fondness for his children, he grieves when that wealth is lost.
Then, filled with pride and guarding himself against defeat, he does whatever he thinks will make him an enjoyer of pleasures—and by this he comes to ruin.
For austerity is the eternal vision of Brahman for those who are joined to wisdom—men who seek the auspicious work and renounce mere pleasure.
Through the loss of the objects of his affection, through the loss of wealth, O prince, and through the torment of mental and bodily afflictions, a man attains to disgust with the world.
From world-weariness comes awakening to the self; from awakening, insight into scripture; and from perceiving the meaning of scripture, O king, he comes to behold austerity itself.
Rare indeed, O lord of men, is the reflective man who, when his cherished happiness has waned, resolves to undertake austerity.
Austerity, my son, is open to all, and is ordained even for the lowly; for one who has conquered his senses and is self-restrained, it points out the path to heaven.
In the beginning the lord Prajāpati created living beings through austerity, intent here and there upon vows, undertaking his observances, O prince.
The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and likewise Agni, the Aśvins, and the Maruts, the Viśvedevas and the Sādhyas, the ancestors, and the host of the Maruts—
the Yakṣas, the Rākṣasas, the Gandharvas, the Siddhas, and the other dwellers in heaven—all were perfected through austerity, my son, as were the others who abide in heaven.
And the brāhmaṇas who were created at the beginning by Brahmā through austerity in days of old—they wander, sustaining the earth and likewise the heavens.
And the kings in the world of mortals, and the other householders who are seen in great families—all that is the fruit of austerity.
Silken garments and lovely ornaments, mounts and seats and conveyances—all that is the fruit of austerity.
Lovely women, pleasing to the heart, by the thousands, and a dwelling upon the heights of a palace—all that is the fruit of austerity.
Choice couches and foods of many kinds—all things desired come to those who have performed the deed of austerity.
There is nothing in these three worlds unattainable by austerity, O scorcher of foes; but the renunciation of all enjoyment is the only fruit of those who have done no such deed.
Whether happy or sorrowful, a man should forsake greed, looking with his mind upon scripture and with his intellect, O best of kings.
Discontent leads only to misery; from greed comes the bewilderment of the senses; and thereby his wisdom perishes, like learning bereft of practice.
When a man's wisdom is destroyed, then he no longer perceives the right; therefore, when the loss of happiness has befallen him, let him practice fierce austerity.
What is desired they call happiness; what is hated is here called sorrow. Behold what kind the fruit is, of austerity done and undone.
Those who have performed stainless austerity ever look upon blessings and enjoy the objects of sense, and they attain to renown.
But the seeker of reward who has forsaken the path of the good wins only what belongs to the senses—unpleasant things and dishonors and sorrow of many forms.
In him there arises doubt concerning dharma, austerity, and almsgiving; and having done only evil deeds, he attains to hell.
But whether dwelling in happiness or in sorrow, O best of men, the man who does not swerve from his own conduct—he is one whose eye is scripture.
In the union with touch, the delight lasts but the moment of an arrow's flight, and likewise in taste, in sight, in smell, and in hearing, O lord of the people.
Thereupon, when that delight has waned, sharp pain is born in him again—for which reason the wise extol liberation as the unsurpassed happiness.
Then he acts for the sake of the fruit, and his virtues grow ever greater; and through righteous conduct he is never deprived of pleasure and prosperity.
The objects of sense, when they come without effort, may be enjoyed by householders; but it is one's own dharma that is to be sought with striving—such is my conviction.
For the proud, the high-born, those whose eye is ever upon the meaning of scripture, who are cut off from the performance of dharma and whose selves are hemmed in by helplessness—
when the human deed they undertake comes to naught, for them there is in this world no recourse but the work of austerity.
With his whole soul let the householder hold firm to his resolve in works; with diligence, for the sake of offerings to gods and ancestors, let him follow his own dharma, O king.
As all rivers and streams come to their rest in the ocean, so all who follow the orders of life come to their rest in the householder.
Janaka said: From what, O great sage, does the class of the mixed classes arise? This I wish to hear; tell it to me, O best of speakers.
The scripture says that whatever offspring is born is the same as that from which it springs; how then has one born of a brāhmaṇa come to take on a distinct class?
Parāśara said: It is even so, O great king: one is the same as that from which he is born; but through the falling away of austerity he has come to assume a separate caste.
From a good field and from good seed a meritorious birth comes to be; but when either of the two is deficient, an inferior offspring is born.
From the mouth, from the two arms, from the thighs, and from the feet they were born, as Prajāpati created the worlds—so the knowers of dharma understand.
Born of the mouth are the brāhmaṇas, my son; born of the arms, the kindred of the kṣatriyas; born of the thighs, the men of wealth, O king; and born of the feet, the servants.
There is a scriptural origin only for the four classes, O bull among men; those others who are over and above these are held to be born of intermixture.
The Kṣatrajātis, the Ambaṣṭhas, the Ugras, and likewise the Vaidehakas, the Śvapākas, the Pulkasas, the Stenas, the Niṣādas, the Sūtas, and the Māgadhas—
the Āyogas, the Karaṇas, the Vrātyas, and the Caṇḍālas, O ruler of men—these are born from the four classes in mutual intermixture.
Janaka said: How can there be diversity of lineage among those born of the one Brahman? For there are indeed many lineages in this world, O best of sages.
How is it that the sages, born here and there—some sprung from a śūdra womb, and others from a womb other than their own—came to attain their own proper origin?
Parāśara said: O king, this is not to be taken as if the origin of the great-souled, whose selves are perfected by austerity, were defiled by a lowly birth.
Having begotten sons here and there, O king, the sages, by their own austerity, conferred upon them once again the state of being seers.
My grandfather of old, and Ṛśyaśṛṅga, and Kaśyapa, Vaṭa, Tāṇḍya, and Kṛpa, Kakṣīvān, Kamaṭha, and the rest—
and Yavakrīta, O king, and Droṇa, best of speakers, Āyu, Mataṅga, Datta, Drupada, and Matsya as well—
these, O Vaideha, attained their own true nature through reliance upon austerity; knowers of the Veda, they stood firm in self-restraint and in austerity.
Four root-lineages came into being, O prince: Aṅgiras and Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha and Bhṛgu.
The other lineages arose from works, O prince—they are but names, and through austerity they too win acceptance among the good.
Janaka said: Declare to me, O blessed one, the particular duties of the classes, and likewise their common duties; for you are skilled in all things.
Parāśara said: Receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, and likewise teaching, O king, are the particular duties of the brāhmaṇas; protection is the glory of the kṣatriya.
Tillage, the herding of cattle, and trade belong to the vaiśyas; and the service of the twice-born is the work of the śūdra, O ruler of men.
The particular duties of the classes have now been proclaimed, O king; now hear from me at length, my son, the duties common to all.
Freedom from cruelty, non-injury, vigilance, the sharing of one's goods, the rites for the ancestors, hospitality, truthfulness, and freedom from anger—
contentment with one's own wife, purity, constant freedom from envy, knowledge of the self, and forbearance—these are the common duties, O king.
Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, and vaiśyas—these three classes are the twice-born; among these their entitlement lies in the sacred duties, O best of two-footed beings.
The three classes, when settled in forbidden works, fall low, O king; but they rise up by resorting, as is fitting, to their own proper works here.

And it is settled that the śūdra does not fall low, nor is he entitled here to the sacraments; he does not attain to the dharma that proceeds from scripture, yet no prohibition of dharma has been laid upon him.
The twice-born who are versed in scripture cite the example of the Vaidehaka śūdra, O great king; for I behold, O lord of men, the god Viṣṇu, the foremost principle of the whole universe.
By following the conduct of the good, the lowly who long to lift themselves up are not defiled when they perform the rites of prosperity, save for the use of the sacred mantras.
In just the measure that other folk take hold of the conduct of the good, in that same measure do they win happiness and repose at ease, both here and after death.
Janaka said: Is it conduct that defiles a man, or birth, O great sage? A doubt has arisen in me; this you should explain to me.
Parāśara said: Without doubt, O great king, both are makers of defilement—both conduct and birth; but mark the distinction.
He who, by birth and by conduct alike, pursues defiled deeds is corrupt; but he who, though base by birth, does no evil—he is the true man.
When a man eminent by birth performs a deed that is to be condemned, that deed defiles him; therefore it is the deed that is not fair.
Janaka said: O best of the twice-born, which deeds are in keeping with dharma, such that, when performed in this world, they never bring harm to living beings at any time?
Parāśara said: Hear from me, O great king, the answer to what you ask of me — those deeds free of harm, which always deliver a man to safety.
Having laid aside the sacred fires and sitting in devotion, freed of feverish care, they behold — step by step ascending the dharma-path that leads to the highest good.
Humble, endowed with discipline, ever devoted to self-restraint and well-tempered, they go forth to the ageless abode, having renounced all works.

All the varṇas, O king, having rightly performed the works of dharma and spoken words of truth, having cast off cruel unrighteousness while in the world of the living, attain to heaven — of this there can be no doubt.
Parāśara said: A father, friends, elders, and wives are never, in this world, devoid of worth, O king — they are single-hearted in devotion, kindly in speech, well-wishing, and obedient alike.

The father is the supreme deity of men; greater even than the mother do they call the father. They declare the gaining of knowledge to be the highest gain, and those who have conquered the objects of the senses attain the supreme.

On the battlefield, where the strewn bed is the fire of arrows, the prince who meets his slaying is consumed there; he passes to worlds scarce won even by the immortals, and enjoys the fruit of heaven at his ease.

The weary man, the frightened, the one whose weapon has fallen, the weeping, the one who has turned his back, the one stripped of attendants, the unresisting, the sick, the suppliant — these one must not strike, O king, nor the child nor the aged.
Only one well-furnished with attendants, ready for combat, and come to an equal footing — such a son of the kṣatriyas may the king assail in battle.
Death at the hands of an equal, or of a superior, is the better lot — such is the settled view; but the slaying of the lowly and the timid is, for kings, a blameworthy deed.
To slay one who is wicked, of wicked conduct, and base, O lord of men, is itself declared a sin that leads to hell — so it is determined.
No one, O king, can save the man who has come under the power of his appointed end; yet one whose span of life still has a remainder, someone may indeed drag back from death.
Deeds being done by those who are dear should here be turned away from harm; one should not, by deeds whose nature is violence, seek long life at the cost of another's life.
But for all householders who long for the dissolution of self, the death is a fair one, dear son, when, performing their rites, they die upon the sandbanks of holy rivers.
When one's span comes to its wasting, he attains dissolution into the five elements; this does not happen without cause — it is brought about by causes.
Thus a body comes to be, brought into being from a former body; this one has gone along the road, and this one has passed from house to house.
There is no second cause to be found in this, none other whatsoever; that body, joined to the embodied, abides among the things subject to release.
A frame of veins, sinews, and bones, crowded with what is loathsome and impure, a meeting-place of the elements, the senses, and the qualities —
this, bounded by the skin, the learned who ponder the inner Self call the body; the body, worn away even of its qualities, has come to its mortal end.
Abandoned by the embodied Self, motionless and devoid of consciousness, with its elements returned to their native source, it then sinks down into the earth.

Shaped by the working of past deeds, it is born here and there; this body, O prince of Videha, dies here and there; another such nature is seen, and likewise the casting-off that is the fruit of action.
Yet for a certain time, O king, this elemental self is not born again; it wanders about, like a great rain-cloud across the sky.
Then he is born again, O king, having gained here an abode; for the Self is higher than the mind, and the mind is higher than the senses.
Of beings, which are of two kinds, the moving are held supreme, O king; among the moving, the two-footed are deemed supreme; and among the two-footed, the twice-born are remembered as supreme.
Among the twice-born too, O lord of kings, the wise are deemed supreme; among the wise, those awakened to the Self; and among the awakened, those free of pride.
Death follows close upon the born — this is the settled truth for men; for deeds have their end, and the creatures pursue them according to their qualities.
When the sun has reached its northern course, he who comes to his death under an auspicious constellation and at an auspicious hour, O king, is a doer of merit.
Without burdening folk with affliction, and having washed away his ill deeds, he dies here by a death that is not common, having performed his works according to his own power.
Poison, hanging, burning, slaying at the hand of robbers, and death by fanged beasts and by cattle — such a death is called a common one.
And the doers of meritorious deeds are not joined to these, nor to such as spring from violent intent, nor to many others of like common sort.
Departing upward, the life-breaths take their station, O king, for the doers of merit; from the middle for those of middling merit; and downward for those whose deeds were ill.
There is but one foe, and no second foe, O king, equal to a man's own ignorance; veiled by it and set upon by it, he performs deeds dreadful and most cruel.

He whose path to awakening lies through the dharma of sacred lore and the service of his elders — that foe, O prince, is to be conquered only by effort, and, churned away by the arrow of wisdom, it departs.

Having studied the Vedas in austerity as a celibate, and having here offered the five sacrifices as he is able, the man who desires dharma should go to the forest — having gathered up the higher good and established his lineage.
Even when forsaken by every enjoyment, one should not let the self sink into despair; for human birth, even in the state of an outcaste, is in every way hard to win, dear son.
For this is the foremost birth, O lord of the earth, on attaining which the self can be saved through deeds marked by auspiciousness.
"How may we not fall away from this birth?" — with this thought, O lord, men practise dharma, guided by their regard for the authority of sacred revelation.
The man who, having won this human state so very hard to attain, becomes a despiser of dharma and a slave to desire — he, surely, is deceived of his gain.
But he who, with an eye that goes before in loving-kindness, beholds living beings as lamps — for just so long as the flame does not die out, dear son —
by gentleness, by giving, and by kindly speech, becoming one to whom the sorrow and joy of others are as his own — he is exalted in the world beyond.

Giving, renunciation, and a fair form arise from the waters; the body, moreover, is to be cleansed by austerity — at the Sarasvatī, at Naimiṣa, at Puṣkara, and at whatever other holy places there are upon the earth.

For those whose life-breaths fall away within their homes, the bearing-out is then commended, and the conveying upon a bier to the cremation ground; and surely the burning, performed with purity and according to rule.

Sacrifice and nurture, offering for oneself and officiating for others, giving, and the practice of meritorious works; whatever rite to the fathers is commended, as one is able — all these a man performs for the sake of his own self.
The treatises on dharma, the Vedas, and the six auxiliary sciences, O lord of men, are ordained for the highest good of the man whose deeds are untainted.
Bhīṣma said: Thus indeed was all this declared of old by that sage of mighty soul to the king of the Videhas, for the sake of the highest good, O lord of men.
Bhīṣma said: And once again Janaka, lord of Mithilā, questioned the great-souled Parāśara, supremely resolved in the knowledge of dharma.
What is the highest good? What is the goal? O brāhmaṇa, what deed, once done, does not perish? Gone where, does one not return? Tell me this, O great sage.
Parāśara said: Non-attachment is the root of the highest good; knowledge is the supreme goal of knowing. Austerity rightly practised does not perish, as water does not perish in a field.
When, having cut the noose made of unrighteousness, one delights in dharma, and bestows the gift of fearlessness, then one would attain perfection.
Though a man give thousands of cattle and hundreds of horses, the gift of fearlessness to all beings surpasses that giving.
The wise man, though he dwell amid the objects of sense, dwells not in them at all; while the dull-witted dwells fast in them, even among objects that are unreal.
Unrighteousness clings not to the wise, as water clings not to the lotus-leaf; but to the unwise sin clings the more, as lac clings to wood.

Unrighteousness, awaiting its occasion, does not release the doer; the doer surely, in due time, meets with all of it. But those of perfected self, who behold the Self by direct conviction, are not broken by it.
He who, heedless of his mind, his deeds, and his senses, does not awaken, and whose self is clinging to things good and evil, attains to a very great fear.
He who is free of passion, has conquered anger, and is ever rightly poised — even while moving among the objects of sense, he is not joined to sin.
