Through self-restraint men seek perfection, and so they yearn for me; and because I encompass heaven, earth, and the region between as with a girdle, therefore am I Dāmodara.
Food is called 'pṛśni,' and so too the Vedas, the waters, and the nectar of immortality; these are forever within my womb — therefore am I Pṛśnigarbha.
Thus the seers called upon me, when Trita had been cast into the well by Ekata and Dvita: 'O Pṛśnigarbha, save Trita who has been hurled down!'
Then that Trita, the firstborn son of Brahmā, the best of seers, climbed up out of the well, by the very proclaiming of Pṛśnigarbha's name.

The rays that shine forth from the sun as it scorches the worlds, and from fire and from the moon, are mine, and are called my locks (keśa); therefore the all-knowing, the most excellent of the twice-born, call me Keśava.
A child had been begotten in his own wife by the great-souled Utathya; and once, when Utathya had vanished from sight through the gods' enchantment, Bṛhaspati found that wife of his, O Bhārata.
Then, O son of Kuntī, the child within the womb, already endowed with the five elements, spoke thus to that best of seers as he came to the act of union:
'I have come here before you, O giver of boons; you ought not to trouble my mother.' Hearing this, Bṛhaspati grew wrathful and pronounced a curse.
'Since you have turned me back as I came to the act of union, therefore you shall be born blind by my curse — herein is no doubt.'
By the curse of that chief of seers he passed into long darkness; and so that seer was of old known by the name Dīrghatamas, 'Long-Darkness.'
Having mastered the four eternal Vedas with their primary and secondary auxiliaries, he then made use of this secret name of mine.
By the prescribed rite, in due order, calling "Keśava" again and again, that Gautama regained his sight and became whole once more.
Thus, O Arjuna, this name "Keśava" of mine is a boon-granting name to all the gods and to all the great-souled sages.
Agni joined with Soma was made a single womb, a single mouth; therefore this whole world, moving and unmoving, has the nature of Agni and Soma.
And so it is said in the Purāṇa: Agni and Soma share one and the same womb, and the gods have Agni for their mouth; and because they share one womb, exalting each other, they uphold the worlds.
Arjuna said: How were Agni and Soma first brought forth from a single womb? This doubt has arisen in me; cut it away, O slayer of Madhu.
The Blessed Lord said: Come then, O son of Pāṇḍu, I shall relate to you an ancient tale, arisen from my own splendour; listen to me, O Pārtha, with single-minded attention.

When the time of the great dissolution had passed, at the end of the fourth thousand of the ages, when all beings, moving and unmoving, had merged into the Unmanifest, when light and earth and wind were no more, in blind darkness, the world a single ocean of water, overwhelmed by darkness alone, without consciousness, without a second, established—neither in night nor in day, neither in being nor in non-being, neither in the manifest nor in the unmanifest abiding—in this state, resting on the qualities of Nārāyaṇa, who is imperishable, ageless, beyond the senses, ungraspable, unborn, true, free from injury, the crest-jewel, the source of the manifold special activities, imperishable, ageless and deathless, formless, all-pervading, doer of all, eternal—from that darkness arose the Puruṣa, Hari the undecaying.

And there is an illustration here: "There was no day, there was no night; there was no being, there was no non-being; darkness alone was there at first, having all forms—it was the mother of the universe." Thus is the meaning of this expounded.

Now of that Puruṣa born from the darkness—at the appearance of Brahmā, the lotus-born—that Puruṣa, desiring to create offspring, brought forth Agni and Soma from his two eyes. Then, when the creation of beings had begun, according to the order of progeny, the priestly and the warrior orders came into being: what is Soma, that is the Brahman; what is Brahman, those are the Brāhmaṇas; what is Agni, that is the Kṣatra. Yet the Brahman is mightier than the Kṣatra. Why? This is a quality plain to the world's sight, namely that no being higher than the Brāhmaṇas has ever arisen before; this I say, since it is into kindled fire that one offers oblation.

There is also the declaration of the mantra: "You, O Agni, are the hotṛ of all sacrifices, set among the race of men by the gods." And there is an illustration of this: "O Agni, you are the hotṛ of all sacrifices, set by the gods for men, for the world." For Agni is indeed the hotṛ, the performer of sacrifices.

For without the mantra there is no offering of oblation, and without a man no austerity comes about; the oblation is the honouring of the mantras of gods and men—by this you are appointed as hotṛ. And those human privileges of the hotṛ-office are ordained for the sacrificing of the Brāhmaṇa, not for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, the twice-born. Therefore the Brāhmaṇas, having become Agni, bear up the sacrifices; the sacrifices satisfy the gods; and the gods foster the earth.

For in the Śatapatha there is a Brāhmaṇa text: "It is into kindled fire that he offers, the learned one who offers the oblation of the gift into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa." Thus too, the learned Brāhmaṇas, having become Agni, foster the fire. Agni is Viṣṇu; entering into all beings, he sustains their vital breaths. And here too there are verses sung by Sanatkumāra:
In the beginning Brahmā created the universe, the source of all, free of impurity; by the chants of the Brahman the immortals, born of the Brahman, abide in heaven.
The thought, the speech, the rites, the faith, and the austerities of the Brāhmaṇas uphold the earth and the sky, as the cool water sustains by its coolness, like nectar.
There is no dharma higher than truth; there is no teacher equal to a mother; there is nothing higher than the Brāhmaṇas for one's welfare, here and in the world to come.

For them no bull thrives, nor any draught-ox; no churn is plied at the sacrificial offering. Cast down, turned to barbarians, do those become in whose kingdom the Brāhmaṇas are bereft of their livelihood.

On the authority of the Vedas, the Purāṇas, and the histories, the Brāhmaṇas—issued from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa, having all for their self, doing all, fostering all—the Brāhmaṇas came forth first, simultaneously with the speech of that boon-granting god; and from the Brāhmaṇas the remaining castes came forth. Thus the Brāhmaṇas, distinguished above gods and demons, when of old by me, having become the Brahman, they were myself produced, then the gods, the demons, and the great sages, those distinct kinds of beings, were established and held in check.

For on account of the violation of Ahalyā, Indra received from Gautama a green-tinged beard; and on the Kauśika's account Indra suffered the loss of his testicles and obtained those of a ram. When Purandara had raised his thunderbolt to forbid the libation to the Aśvins, his arm was made rigid by Cyavana. And by Dakṣa, wrathful at the destruction of his sacrifice, having again joined himself to austerity, another eye in the shape of an eye was produced on the forehead of Rudra.

When Rudra had undertaken the consecration for the slaying of Tripura, Uśanas tore the matted locks from his head and cast them down; from them serpents came forth. Tormented by those serpents, his throat was brought to a dark-blue hue. Or else his blue-throatedness came in the former age of Manu Svāyaṃbhuva, from the grip of Nārāyaṇa's binding hand.

At the churning out of the nectar, when Bṛhaspati of the line of Aṅgiras, undertaking the preliminary rite, touched the waters, they did not, it is said, become clear. Then Bṛhaspati grew angry at the waters: "Since, when I touch you, you grow turbid and do not become clear, therefore from this day onward become turbid, teeming with great fish, makaras, fish, tortoises, and creatures." From that day onward the waters became filled with aquatic beasts.
Viśvarūpa, son of Tvaṣṭṛ, was the chaplain of the gods and the sister's son of the demons. Openly he gave the sacrificial portion to the gods, but secretly to the demons.

Then, putting Hiraṇyakaśipu at their head, the demons begged a boon of their sister, the mother of Viśvarūpa: "O sister, this son of yours, Viśvarūpa the three-headed, son of Tvaṣṭṛ, the chaplain of the gods, openly gives the portion to the gods but secretly to us. Thereby the gods wax strong and we wane. You ought therefore to restrain him, so that he may favour us."

Then, when Viśvarūpa had come to the Nandana grove, his mother said to him: "My son, why do you, a fosterer of the other side, work the ruin of your maternal uncles' party? You ought not to do thus." And Viśvarūpa, deeming his mother's word not to be transgressed, did honour to Hiraṇyakaśipu and went over to him.

And from Vasiṣṭha, born of Hiraṇyagarbha, Hiraṇyakaśipu received a curse: "Since another was chosen by you as hotṛ, therefore, with your sacrifice left unfinished, you shall meet your death from a kind of being never seen before." By the giving of that curse Hiraṇyakaśipu met his death.

Viśvarūpa, fosterer of his mother's side, gave himself exceedingly to austerity. To break his vow Indra dispatched many lovely apsarases; and at the sight of them his mind grew troubled, and before long he became attached to those apsarases. Knowing him attached, the apsarases said: "We are going, back the way we came."

To them the son of Tvaṣṭṛ said: "Where will you go? Stay awhile here with me; it will be for your good." They said to him: "We are women of the gods, apsarases; long ago we chose Indra, the boon-giver, the mighty, as our lord."

Then Viśvarūpa said to them: "This very day the gods, with Indra, shall be no more." Then he muttered his mantras, and by those mantras the three-headed one grew great. With one mouth he drank the soma well offered in the sacrifices of ritual-performing twice-born throughout all the worlds; with another he drank the waters; with another he would swallow the gods together with Indra. Then Indra, seeing him swelling, all his limbs nourished by the drinking of soma, fell into anxious thought.

And those gods, together with Indra, went to Brahmā and said: "By Viśvarūpa the soma well offered in all sacrifices is being drunk; we are left without our portion. The demons' party waxes; we wane. You ought therefore to ordain for us whatever good may follow."
To them Brahmā said: "The sage Dadhīca of Bhṛgu's line is performing austerities. Let him be entreated for a boon, that he may give up his body; from his bones let the thunderbolt be made."

The gods went there, where the blessed sage Dadhīca performed his austerities. The gods, with Indra, approached him and said: "O blessed one, is your austerity faring well and without hindrance?" To them Dadhīca said: "Welcome to you. What shall be done? Whatever you shall say, that I will do." They said to him: "For the good of the worlds the blessed one ought to give up his body." Then Dadhīca, untroubled even at this, even-minded in pleasure and pain, the great yogin, collecting himself, made the abandonment of his body.

When his soul had departed into the Supreme Self, the Ordainer took up those bones and made the thunderbolt. With that thunderbolt, unbreakable and unassailable, born of a Brāhmaṇa's bones and entered by Viṣṇu, Indra slew Viśvarūpa and severed his heads. Thereafter Indra slew the foe Vṛtra, arisen from the churning of Viśvarūpa's body and produced by Tvaṣṭṛ.

When that guilt of Brāhmaṇa-slaughter had become twofold, Indra, out of fear, abandoned the kingship of the gods and took refuge in a cool lotus growing in the waters, in Lake Mānasa; and there, by the power of his lordly might, becoming no larger than an atom, he entered into the fibre of a lotus-stalk.

Then, when the lord of the three worlds, the husband of Śacī, had vanished out of fear of the Brāhmaṇa-slaughter, the world became without a ruler. Passion and darkness entered the gods; the mantras of the great sages no longer availed; the rākṣasas came forth; the Brahman went to ruin; and the worlds, without Indra and powerless, became easy prey.

Then the gods and the sages consecrated to the kingship of the gods the son of Āyus, Nahuṣa by name. Nahuṣa, with five hundred blazing luminaries on his forehead that stole away all splendour, governed the heaven; and the worlds returned to their natural state and grew at ease.

Then Nahuṣa said: "All that was enjoyed by Śakra has come to me, save Śacī alone." Having said this, he went near to Śacī and said to her: "O fair one, I am the Indra of the gods; give yourself to me." Śacī answered him: "By nature you are devoted to dharma and sprung from the lineage of Soma; you ought not to do violence to another's wife."

Then Nahuṣa said to her: "The seat of Indra is occupied by me; I am the bearer-off of Indra's royal treasures; there is no unrighteousness in this—you were Indra's enjoyment." She said to him: "I have a certain vow not yet completed. At its concluding bath I shall come to you, in but a few days." Thus addressed by Śacī, Nahuṣa went away.

Then Śacī, afflicted with grief and sorrow, longing for the sight of her husband, seized with fear of Nahuṣa, went to Bṛhaspati. And he, the moment he saw her come, entered into meditation, and knowing her intent upon her husband's cause, Bṛhaspati said: "Endowed with this very vow and austerity, summon the boon-granting goddess Upaśruti; she will show you Indra."

Then she, undertaking a great observance, summoned by mantras the boon-granting goddess Upaśruti. That Upaśruti came near to Śacī and said to her: "Here I am, summoned by you and present. What dear thing shall I do for you?" Bowing to her with her head, Śacī said: "O blessed lady, you ought to show me my husband; you are held to be true." Then Upaśruti led her to Lake Mānasa and showed her Indra, gone into the fibre of a lotus-stalk.

Indra, seeing his wife wasted and worn, fell to thinking: "Alas, this great grief has now come upon me, that she, afflicted with sorrow, has come seeking me out who was lost." Indra said to her: "How do you fare?" She said to him: "Nahuṣa summons me, and a time has been appointed by me for him."

Indra said to her: "Go, and say this to Nahuṣa: 'Mount and bear me away in a wondrous, unheard-of car yoked with sages; for Indra has great vehicles, the heart's delight, which I have mounted. You ought to come to me by some other means.'" Thus addressed, she went gladly; and Indra entered once more into the fibre of the lotus-stalk.
Then, seeing Indra's consort approach, Nahuṣa said: "That time is fulfilled." Śacī told him what Śakra had said; and mounting a vehicle yoked with great sages, he came near to Śacī.

Then Agastya, son of Mitra and Varuṇa, the pitcher-born, saw those great sages being maltreated by Nahuṣa, and was touched by his feet; whereupon he said to Nahuṣa: "Set upon a deed undone, O sinner, fall to the earth; become a serpent, and so remain for as long as the earth and mountains shall stand." And at the very moment of the great sage's word, he fell down from that car.

Then the three worlds were again without an Indra. Thereupon the gods and the sages went for refuge to the blessed Viṣṇu for Indra's sake and said to him: "O blessed one, you ought to deliver Indra, overwhelmed by the guilt of Brāhmaṇa-slaughter." Then that boon-giver said to them: "Let Śakra offer the horse-sacrifice, the Vaiṣṇava rite; thereby he shall regain his own station."

Then, when the gods and the sages did not see Indra, they said to Śacī: "Go, O fair one, and fetch Indra." She again went to that lake, and Indra, rising up out of that lake, went to Bṛhaspati. And Bṛhaspati performed the horse-sacrifice, the great rite, for Śakra; then, releasing a dappled black horse fit for sacrifice and making that his vehicle, Bṛhaspati restored Indra, the lord of the Maruts, to his own station.

Then that king of the gods, praised by gods and sages, abiding in heaven, became free of stain; he distributed the guilt of Brāhmaṇa-slaughter among four receptacles—women, fire, trees, and cattle. Thus Indra, strengthened by the might and splendour of the Brahman, having slain his foe, was restored to his own station.

And of old the great sage Bharadvāja, having come to the celestial Gaṅgā and touching its water, was approached by Viṣṇu as he strode his three steps; he was struck on the chest by Bharadvāja with a water-filled hand, and so came to bear that mark upon his breast.
Cursed by the great sage Bhṛgu, Agni was reduced to the state of devourer of all things.

Aditi cooked food for the gods, thinking, "Having eaten this, they shall slay the demons." There came Budha at the completion of his observance and said to Aditi: "Give me alms." But "this is to be eaten first by the gods, by no other," thought Aditi, and gave no alms. Then Budha, enraged at the refusal of alms, having become the Brahman, killed the egg of Aditi—the egg-named one at the second birth of Vivasvān; that dead egg became Vivasvān, the Mārtaṇḍa, the god of the funeral offerings.

Dakṣa had sixty daughters; of them he gave thirteen to Kaśyapa, ten to Dharma, ten to Manu, and twenty-seven to the Moon. Though all these were equal and bore the names of the lunar mansions, Soma showed excessive affection to Rohiṇī. Then the rest of his wives, grown jealous, went to their father and told him this matter: "O blessed one, though we are of equal worth, Soma favours Rohiṇī above us." He said: "Consumption shall enter him."

By Dakṣa's curse consumption entered King Soma; and seized by consumption he went to Dakṣa. Dakṣa said to him: "You do not deal evenly." Thereupon the sages said to Soma: "You are wasting away with consumption. In the western quarter, in the ocean, is the holy ford of the Golden Lake; go there and bathe yourself." Then Soma went there, to the holy ford of the Golden Lake.

The great sage Sthūlaśiras performed austerities in the north-eastern region of Meru. As he performed his austerity, a pure breeze, bearing all fragrances and blowing gently, touched his body. With his body heated and wasted by austerity, fanned by the wind, he came to gladness of heart. But there, while he took delight in the wind's fanning, the trees did not at once display the beauty of their blossoms; so he cursed them: "You shall not bear flowers at all seasons."

Of old Nārāyaṇa, for the good of the worlds, became a great sage named Vaḍavāmukha. As he performed his austerities on Meru, the ocean, when summoned, did not come. Enraged thereby, by the heat of his own body he made the ocean's waters still, and brought into being its salt nature, like the trickling of sweat. And he said: "You shall become undrinkable, and this water of yours, when drunk by one bearing the name Vaḍavāmukha, shall become sweet." So even to this day the ocean's water is drunk by him called Vaḍavāmukha, ever continuing.

Rudra loved Umā, daughter of the mountain Himavat. The great sage Bhṛgu too came to Himavat and said: "Give me the maiden Umā." Himavat said to him: "Rudra is the suitor desired." Bhṛgu said to him: "Since I, intent on choosing the maiden, have been refused by you, therefore you shall not be a receptacle of jewels." From that day onward this word of the sage has held firm.

Such is the greatness of the Brāhmaṇas. The Kṣatra too, having wedded the everlasting, imperishable Earth as its wife, enjoyed her. This is the Brahman, born of Agni and Soma; by it the world is upheld.
The Blessed Lord said: The sun and the moon, ever with my rays that are called my hair, awakening and warming the world, rise up severally.
By this awakening and warming the gladdening of the world comes about; by these deeds wrought of Agni and Soma, O son of Pāṇḍu, I am Hṛṣīkeśa, the lord, the boon-giver, the fosterer of the worlds.
Through the summoning of the iḍā-offering I take, O tawny one, my portion in the sacrifices; and my colour is the finest tawny-green; therefore am I remembered as Hari.
My abode is the essence of the worlds, and the cosmic order has been discerned; therefore by the wise I am proclaimed Ṛtadhāman, abode of order, and the True.
And of old I recovered the lost earth that had gone into the cavern; therefore the gods extolled me with their voices as Govinda.
And in the name "Śipiviṣṭa": he who is without hair, and whatever is pervaded by him—that is remembered as śipiviṣṭa.
The sage Yāska, untroubled, sang of me in many sacrifices as Śipiviṣṭa; therefore I bear this hidden name.
Having praised me as Śipiviṣṭa, the sage Yāska of noble mind, by my grace, recovered the lost etymology that had fallen away.
I have not been born, I am not born, nor shall I ever be born; I am the Knower of the Field in all beings; therefore am I remembered as the Unborn.
Never before have I uttered anything mean or unseemly; true is that goddess Sarasvatī, daughter of the Brahman, true and unfailing, who is mine.
Both being and non-being, O son of Kuntī, have been set by me within myself; in the lotus-seat, the abode of the Brahman, the sages know me as the True.
Never before have I fallen from goodness; know that goodness is wrought by me; in this birth the goodness that became mine was of an earlier time, O Dhanaṃjaya.
Conceive of me as the Sātvata, joined to action without desire for reward; seen through the knowledge of the Sātvatas, I am the Sātvata, the lord of the Sātvatas.
I plough the earth, O Pārtha, becoming the great ploughshare of black iron; and since my colour is dark, therefore am I Kṛṣṇa, O Arjuna.
By me the earth has been joined with the waters, and the sky with the wind, and the wind together with fire; thence comes my state of Vaikuṇṭha, the unhindered.
Nirvāṇa is the supreme bliss; that is called the highest dharma; and since I have never before fallen from it, by that deed I am Acyuta, the Unfallen.
The earth and the sky are both renowned, belonging to the whole world; and for the upholding of these two, I am rightly called Adhokṣaja.
Those learned in the Veda and those who ponder the meaning of words sing of me by this etymology in the eastern sacrificial hall: "Adhokṣaja" is the established name.
This word has been uttered with one accord by the supreme sages; for there is in the world no other Adhokṣaja than the lord Nārāyaṇa.
The ghee of my flames in the world is the sustenance of the breath of creatures; I am proclaimed Ghṛtārcis, the ghee-flamed, by the untroubled knowers of the Veda.
Three humours are declared, and they are remembered as born of action: bile, phlegm, and wind; this is called their combination.
By these the creature is sustained, and when these decay it decays; therefore those versed in the science of life declare me to be the threefold humour.
The blessed Dharma is renowned in the worlds as the Bull, O Bhārata; know me as the supreme Bull, declared by the word of the lexicon.
Kapi is the boar, the best, and dharma is called the Bull; therefore Kaśyapa the Prajāpati called me Vṛṣākapi.

Neither my beginning nor my middle, nor yet my end, do gods and demons ever know; for, without beginning, without middle, and likewise without end, I am hymned as the Lord, the all-pervading, the witness of the worlds.
Pure things, worthy to be heard, do I hear here, O Dhanaṃjaya, and I take no heed of sinful things; therefore am I Śuciśravas, of pure renown.
Of old, having become the single-tusked boar of divine aspect, I lifted up this earth; and thus am I called Ekaśṛṅga, the One-Tusked.
Likewise was I Trikakud, having taken on the boar's form; through the measure of that body I became renowned as Trikakud, the Three-Peaked.
He who is named Viriñca by those who ponder the wisdom of Kapila — that very Prajāpati am I, the maker of all the worlds out of consciousness.
Me, attended by knowledge, eternal, abiding in the sun, the teachers of Sāṃkhya, firm in their settled certainties, call Kapila.
That radiant Hiraṇyagarbha who is praised in the sacred metres and is ever worshipped by the masters of yoga — that very one am I, remembered as the all-pervading Lord.

Those who know the Vedas declare me to be the Ṛgveda of twenty-one branches, and the Sāman of a thousand branches; and the brāhmaṇas devoted to me who chant the Āraṇyaka — even these are hard to find.
That Yajurveda in which the branches number fifty-six, and eight, and thirty-seven — that am I, remembered in the office of the Adhvaryu priest.
The brāhmaṇas learned in the Atharvan ordain me likewise as the Atharvaveda of five ritual procedures, swollen full with its rites of sorcery.
Whatever divisions of the branches there are, and whatever chants are sung within those branches, and the utterance of their tones and syllables — know all these to be made by me.
That Horse-Headed form, O Pārtha, which rises up bestowing boons — that am I myself in the northern quarter, knower of the divisions of the syllable-sequence.

By the path taught by Rāma, through my grace, the great-souled Pāñcāla obtained the krama-recitation from that eternal Being; and he of the Bābhravya lineage shone forth as the first who reached the far shore of the krama.
Having received a boon from Nārāyaṇa and attained the supreme yoga, that Gālava set forth the krama-recitation and composed the science of phonetics.
And Kaṇḍarīka, and the mighty King Brahmadatta, recalling again and again the suffering born of birth and death, attained the fullness of the yogas through their eminence across seven births.
Of old, O Pārtha, for a certain cause I was made known as the son of Dharma, O tiger of the Kurus; and thus am I remembered as Dharmaja, Dharma-born.
In ancient days Nara and Nārāyaṇa, mounted upon the vehicle of dharma, performed imperishable austerity upon Mount Gandhamādana.
At that very season came to pass the sacrifice of Dakṣa; and Dakṣa apportioned no share to Rudra, O Bhārata.
Then, at the word of Dadhīci, he carried off Dakṣa's sacrifice; in wrath he hurled his trident, blazing forth again and again.

That trident, having reduced Dakṣa's sacrifice in its full extent to ashes, came rushing all at once toward the hermitage of Badarī, near to us both, falling with great force, O Pārtha, upon the breast of Nārāyaṇa.
Then the hairs of Nārāyaṇa, suffused with his own fiery splendour, took on the colour of muñja-grass; and thus am I called Muñjakeśa, he of the muñja-coloured hair.
And that trident, flung back by the great-souled one with a sound of 'Huṃ' and struck aside by Nārāyaṇa, returned to the hand of Śaṃkara.
Then Rudra rushed upon those two sages endowed with austerity; and Nārāyaṇa, the Soul of all, seized him as he sprang up, by the throat with his hand — and from that came Rudra's dark-throated state.
Then, to ward off Rudra, Nara took up a blade of reed-grass and swiftly charged it with sacred formulas; and it became a mighty axe.
Cast suddenly at Rudra, it then met with breaking; and thus am I remembered as Khaṇḍaparaśu, he of the Broken Axe, from the shattering of that axe.
Arjuna said: But in this battle, O Vārṣṇeya, this churning of the three worlds, who then won the victory there? Declare this to me, Janārdana.
The blessed Lord said: When those two, Rudra and Nārāyaṇa in their persons, were locked in combat, all the worlds entire grew suddenly stricken with dread.
The fire would not accept the bright oblation duly offered in the sacrifices; the Vedas no longer shone forth for the sages of disciplined soul.
Passion and darkness then entered into the gods alike; the earth trembled, and the firmament split asunder.
The luminaries lost their radiance, and Brahmā himself was cast down from his seat; the ocean went dry, and the Himālaya crumbled away.
When such a portent had thus arisen, O son of Pāṇḍu, Brahmā, encircled by the hosts of gods and by the great-souled sages, came swiftly to that place where the battle was being waged.

The Four-Faced one, versed in the etymologies, with joined palms held forth, spoke these words to Rudra: 'Let there be welfare for the worlds; lay down your weapons, O Lord of the Universe, for the desire of the good of all that is.'
'That which is the Imperishable and the Unmanifest, the Lord, the source of the world, fixed upon its summit, the agent free of all duality, whom they also know as the non-agent —'
'— of this Being come into manifest form, this is one auspicious embodiment: Nara and Nārāyaṇa, born to uphold the lineage of Dharma.'

'Joined with mighty austerity, foremost of gods, mighty in their vows — I was born of his grace upon some occasion, and you yourself, my son, the eternal one, were born of his wrath in the former creation.'
'Together with me and with the gods and the great sages, swiftly conciliate the boon-giver, that peace may come to the worlds without delay.'
Thus addressed by Brahmā, Rudra let go the fire of his wrath and then conciliated the divine Lord Nārāyaṇa, and took refuge in Hari, the primal, the most excellent, the giver of boons.
Then the boon-giving god, his anger conquered and his senses mastered, became gladdened there, reconciled together with Rudra.
Well honoured by the sages and by Brahmā and the gods, that Hari, the Lord of the world, spoke to the god Īśāna:
'He who knows you knows me; he who follows you follows me. Between us two there is no difference whatever; let your understanding not be otherwise.'
'From this day forward let this Śrīvatsa mark of mine bear the sign of the trident; and marked by my hand, you shall become Śrīkaṇṭha, the Glorious-Throated.'

Having thus brought into being these mutually given marks, and having made an unmatched friendship with Rudra, the two sages, untroubled, dismissed the dwellers of heaven and performed their austerities.

Thus has the victory of Nārāyaṇa in battle been told to you, O Pārtha, and the secret names with their etymologies, O Bhārata, which were spoken here by the sages and which have been proclaimed to you.
Thus in manifold forms do I range over this earth, and over the realm of Brahmā, O son of Kuntī, and the eternal realm of cows; guarded by me in battle, you have won a mighty victory.
And he who goes before you when the battle is joined — know him to be Rudra, O son of Kuntī, the god of gods, the one with matted locks.
That same one I have named to you as Time, born of wrath; those foes already slain by him, those have you in truth struck down.
That god of gods of immeasurable power, the lord of Umā — bow down, intent and reverent, to the god Hara, the Lord of the Universe, the imperishable.
Janamejaya said: O brāhmaṇa, a most lofty narrative has been recounted by you, on hearing which all the sages have passed into the utmost wonder.
For out of the hundred thousand verses of the vast Bhārata narrative, by the churning-staff of the intellect this incomparable ocean of knowledge has been churned —
— as butter is drawn from curds, as sandal from the Malaya hills, as the Āraṇyaka from the Vedas, as the nectar of immortality from the healing herbs —
— so has this peerless nectar of story been drawn up, O brāhmaṇa; for it has been spoken by you, O treasury of austerity, resting upon the tale of Nārāyaṇa.
For he is the Lord, the blessed god, the inmost soul and source of all beings; ah, hard to behold is the splendour of Nārāyaṇa, O best of the twice-born!

Into whom, at the end of an aeon, all the gods led by Brahmā enter, and the sages with the gandharvas, and whatever moving or unmoving thing there is — than him I deem there is nothing higher or more purifying, in heaven or here on earth.
The visiting of all hermitages, the bathing at all sacred fords — none of these is so fruitful as the tale of Nārāyaṇa.
In every way are we here made pure, having heard from the beginning this story of Hari, the Lord of the Universe — a tale that destroys all sins.
It is no marvel that my noble forebear Dhanaṃjaya wrought such deeds there — he who, with Vāsudeva for his ally, attained the highest victory.
And I deem there was nothing unattainable for him in all the three worlds, he for whom Viṣṇu, the Lord of the three worlds, was the friend who lent his aid.
And blessed, O brāhmaṇa, were all those forebears of mine, for whose good and welfare Janārdana stood.
For the blessed one, worshipped of the worlds, is not to be seen even by austerity — yet they beheld him face to face, adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark.

And more blessed than they is Nārada, the son of the Supreme One; nor do I count the imperishable sage Nārada as one of slender splendour, for, reaching the White Island, by him was Hari himself beheld.
Plainly that vision of his came in the train of the god's grace, in that he then beheld the god abiding in the form of Aniruddha.
But that Nārada hastened again to the hermitage of Badarī to behold Nara and Nārāyaṇa — what, O sage, was the cause of that?
And Nārada, the son of the Supreme One, returning from the White Island, having reached the hermitage of Badarī and met with those two sages —
— for how long did he dwell there, and what discourses did he ask of them, when that most great-souled one had returned from the White Island?
What did those two great-souled sages, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, say? All this you ought to tell me in full accordance with the truth.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Homage to that blessed Vyāsa of measureless splendour, by whose grace I shall recount this tale of Nārāyaṇa.

Having reached the great White Island and beheld the imperishable Hari, Nārada, on his return, O king, came swiftly to Meru, bearing in his heart the burden of what had been spoken by the Supreme Soul.
Afterward, O king, a great trembling came over his spirit, in that, having gone so far a road, he had come back here again safe and sound.
Then he set forth from Meru toward Mount Gandhamādana, and descended swiftly from the sky beside the wide-spreading Badarī.
There he beheld the two ancient gods, foremost of sages, performing mighty austerity, fixed upon the Self, steadfast in great vows —
— surpassing in splendour the Sūrya that illumines all the worlds, bearing the Śrīvatsa mark, worthy of worship, wearing crowns of matted hair —
— their hands and feet webbed, marked with the sign of the wheel upon their soles, broad-chested, long-armed, and bearing the fourfold sign —
— with sixty teeth and eight tusks, their voices like a mass of thunderclouds, fair of face and broad of brow, well-jawed, with handsome brows and noses —
— the heads of those two gods like parasols: endowed with such marks, they were known by the name of the Great Persons.
Beholding the two, Nārada rejoiced, and was honoured by them in return; greeted with words of welcome, he was then asked after his well-being.
Gazing upon those supreme persons, his mind turned inward — recalling those who, present in the assembly there, are saluted by all beings:
'On the White Island I beheld two such foremost sages' — thus reflecting in his mind, and making his reverent circuit about them, he seated himself there upon a fair seat made of kuśa-grass.
Then those two sages, the abode of austerities, of glories, and of splendours, possessed of calm and self-restraint, having performed the rite of the forenoon —

— thereafter, unhurried, having honoured Nārada with water for his feet and the guest-offering, those two seated themselves upon their seats, their rites of hospitality and of the day fulfilled, O king.
When they were seated there, that place shone resplendent, as a sacrificial enclosure shines with the great flames of its fires fed by oblations of clarified butter.
Then Nārāyaṇa there spoke these words to Nārada, who was seated at ease, rested, his hospitality received, and abiding in comfort:
'Has that blessed one, the eternal Supreme Soul, the higher nature of us both, now indeed been beheld by you on the White Island?'

Nārada said: I have beheld the glorious, imperishable Person who bears the form of the universe. All the worlds abide within Him, and the gods together with the seers. Even now I see Him, as I gaze upon you two, O eternal ones.
With the very marks that Hari bears, He who wears an unmanifest form, with those same marks are you two endowed, who wear a manifest form.
There I beheld you two at the side of that God, and now this very day I have come here, sent forth by the Supreme Self.
For who indeed could be His equal in splendor, in glory, in majesty, throughout the three worlds, save you two, the sons of Dharma?
By Him was disclosed to me before His name, which is called the Knower of the Field; and the manifestations were told to me, how and which shall come to be.
There the men who are white, free from the five senses, are all of them awakened and devoted to the Supreme Person.
They forever worship the God, and with them He takes delight; for the Lord, the Supreme Self, loves His devotees and is dear to the twice-born.

He delights when worshiped, ever loving of His votaries—the All-devourer, the all-pervading God, the kinsman, tender to the faithful; He of surpassing might and radiance is the doer, the cause, and the effect alike.
Joining Himself to Him through austerity, He attains that which lies beyond Śvetadvīpa, that which is renowned as the splendor, illumined by its own self-shining radiance.
That is the peace, throughout the three worlds, of the perfected ones whose selves are made pure; with this auspicious understanding He has undertaken the steadfast vow.
There the sun gives no heat, nor does the moon shine forth, nor does the wind blow, while in the Lord of gods austerity hard to perform is practiced.

Mounting upon an altar of eight palms' height set upon the ground, the All-devouring God, standing upon one foot, with arms upraised and face turned northward, reciting the Vedas together with their auxiliary lore, performed austerity most hard to bear.
That which Brahmā and the seers, and the Lord of creatures himself, and all the rest, the foremost of the wise, the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas—

the Nāgas, the Suparṇas, the Gandharvas, the Siddhas, and the royal seers, all of the oblation to the gods and to the fathers that they ceaselessly offer according to rule—the whole of it draws near to the feet of that God.
And those rites that are duly performed by men whose minds are bent on Him alone—all of these the God Himself receives upon His head.
None dearer to Him than the awakened great souls is found throughout the three worlds; therefore have I gone to single-minded devotion, and have come here, sent forth by Him, the Supreme Self.
Thus did the blessed God Hari Himself declare to me; intent on Him, I shall dwell forever together with you two.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa said: Blessed are you, and graced, in that the Lord Himself was beheld by you; for none has ever seen Him, not even the lotus-born one himself.
Of unmanifest origin is the blessed Supreme Person, hard to behold; O Nārada, true indeed is the word you have spoken.
None in the world is found dearer to Him than His devotees; therefore He revealed His own Self to you, O best of the twice-born.
That station of the Supreme Self who is performing austerity, none attains it, save we two alone, O best of the twice-born.
Whatever the radiance of a thousand suns gathered together might be, such is the radiance of that station, shining of its own accord through Him.
From that God, the All-pervading Lord, O brāhmaṇa, arises forbearance—O foremost of the forbearing—wherewith the earth is endowed.
And from that God arises savor, the benefactor of all beings, wherewith the waters are endowed and attain their fluidity.
From Him alone has arisen the brilliance whose essence is the quality of form, wherewith the sun is endowed, and thereby illumines the worlds.
From that God, the Supreme Person, has arisen touch, wherewith the wind is endowed, and thereby blows through the worlds.
And from that Lord, the Master of all worlds, arises sound, wherewith space is endowed, and thereby it stands unbounded.
And from that God arises mind, which pervades all beings, wherewith the moon is joined, the bearer of the quality of light.
That station, named the generator of the six elements, is called the Veda, wherein the blessed Lord abides, companioned by knowledge, the enjoyer of oblations to gods and fathers.

For those in the world who are stainless, free of merit and demerit, as they travel the path of safety, O best of the twice-born, the sun, dispeller of the darkness of all worlds, is said to be the gate.
With all their limbs consumed by the sun, unseen by anyone anywhere, having become atoms, they then enter into that God.
Released even from Him, abiding in the body of Aniruddha, become as mind, they then further enter into Pradyumna.
Released also from Pradyumna, the foremost of brāhmaṇas, the followers of Sāṃkhya together with the votaries of the Lord, enter then into Saṃkarṣaṇa, who is the living soul.

Then, freed of the three qualities, they enter straightway into the Supreme Self, O best of the twice-born, the Knower of the Field, whose nature is without quality; know in truth that Vāsudeva, the dwelling-place of all, is the Knower of the Field.
With minds composed, restrained, their senses curbed, attained to single-minded devotion, they enter into Vāsudeva.
We two also were born in the house of Dharma, O best of the twice-born, and, resorting to the lovely and broad Viśālā, have undertaken fierce austerity.
And those manifestations of that very God, dear to the gods, which shall arise abiding within the three worlds—to them be welfare, O brāhmaṇa.
By us two, joined to our own ordinance as of old, O best of the twice-born, the all-difficult vow has been duly upheld, that highest of vows.
By us two also were you seen in Śvetadvīpa, O treasury of austerity, when, having come together with the Lord, you held converse with Him.
For all is fully known to us two, throughout the three worlds with their moving and unmoving things, whatever good or evil shall come to pass, or has passed, or now passes.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing this speech of theirs, Nārada gave himself to fierce austerity, and, with palms joined, became wholly devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
He muttered duly many sacred formulas turned toward Nārāyaṇa for a celestial thousand years in the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
There dwelt that mighty-splendored, blessed seer Nārada, worshiping that very God, and those two, Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then, after some time, Nārada, born of the Lord Supreme, having performed the rite to the gods according to ordinance, performed thereafter the rite to the fathers.
Then the elder one, the lordly son of Dharma, spoke this word: Who is worshiped, O best of the twice-born, when the rite to the gods and the rite to the fathers are ordained?
O foremost of the wise, declare this to me as it is handed down: why is this rite performed, and what fruit of it is sought?
Nārada said: By you it was told before that the rite to the gods is to be done; and the deity, the highest sacrifice, is the eternal Supreme Self.
Therefore, ever absorbed in Him, I worship the imperishable Vaikuṇṭha; and from Him there issued of old Brahmā, the grandsire of the worlds.
It was indeed my father whom the gracious Supreme One begot; and I am that one's son, born of his will, fashioned first of all.

I worship the fathers, O virtuous one, once the ordinance of Nārāyaṇa is fulfilled; thus that very blessed Lord, father, mother, and grandsire, the Master of the world, is forever worshiped by me in the sacrifices to the fathers.

And there is yet another sacred tradition, O god: the fathers worshiped their sons. The Vedic lore, once lost, was again taught by the sons; therefore those sons who gave the sacred formulas attained the rank of fathers.
Surely this was known of old to you two of purified souls: the sons and the fathers worshiped one another.
"Having first strewn the kuśa grass, then set down three rice-balls upon the earth"—but how did those fathers of old come to bear the name of the rice-ball?
Nara and Nārāyaṇa said: This earth, girdled by the sea, once lost, Govinda swiftly raised up, having assumed the form of a boar.
And having set the earth in its own place, the Supreme Person, His limbs smeared with water and mire, rose up for the sake of the world's work.

And when the time for the daily rite had come, the sun having reached the midpoint of the day, the Lord, swiftly shaking off the clods of earth clinging to His tusk, set them down upon the ground, having spread out kuśa grass, O Nārada.
Designating Himself in them, the Lord performed the rite to the fathers as prescribed, having consecrated three rice-balls by His own ordinance.
With sesame seeds born of the warmth of His own body and laden with their oil, the Lord of gods, facing eastward, Himself sprinkled them and brought the rite to its close.
And to establish the bounds of right usage He then spoke this word: I, the maker of the world, am Myself set upon creating the fathers.

As He pondered at once the supreme ordinance of the rite to the fathers, "These clods of mine, shaken from My tusks, have come to rest upon the earth in the southern quarter; therefore these are indeed the fathers."
"These three, though formless, now bearing the form of the rice-ball, let them become the eternal fathers in the world, created by Me."
"Father, grandfather, and likewise great-grandfather—I alone am to be known here, abiding within the three rice-balls."
"There is none greater than Me; whom then should I Myself worship? Who is My father in the world? I alone am the grandsire."
"And the father of the grandsire—I alone am the cause herein." Having spoken this word, the God of gods, Vṛṣākapi,—
on the Boar Mountain, O brāhmaṇa, having offered the rice-balls in full ceremony, and having worshiped His own Self alone, vanished from sight there itself.
For this reason, O fair-minded one, the fathers, called by the name of the rice-ball, ever receive worship, according to the word of Vṛṣākapi.

Those who worship the fathers, the gods, the teachers, and likewise guests, and the cows, and the foremost of the twice-born, and the earth their mother—by deed, by thought, by word, they worship Viṣṇu alone.

That blessed Lord dwells within, abiding in the bodies of all beings, the same in all creatures, the Master over pleasure and pain, the great, the great-souled, the Self of all, who is heard of as Nārāyaṇa.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Hearing this speech uttered by Nara and Nārāyaṇa, Nārada, supremely devoted to the God, attained to single-minded devotion.
Having dwelt a thousand years in the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, having heard the tale of the Lord and beheld the imperishable Hari, he swiftly went to the Himālaya, where his own hermitage lay.
And those two seers, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, renowned for their austerity, in that same lovely hermitage practiced the highest austerity.
You too, of measureless valor, upholder of the line of the Pāṇḍavas, have this day become purified of soul, having heard this tale from its beginning.
Neither the world beyond nor this world is his, O best of kings, who by deed, by thought, by word, should hate the imperishable Viṣṇu.
The fathers of that man sink in hell for everlasting years, who should hate the foremost of the wise, the God Nārāyaṇa, Hari.
How indeed could the Self of anyone in the world be an object of hatred? For the Self, O tiger among men, is to be known as Viṣṇu—such is the settled truth.
He who is our teacher, the seer, the son of Gandhavatī—by him was this greatness of the Supreme Self told, my child; and so it was heard by me and told to you, O sinless one.
Know Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa to be the Lord Nārāyaṇa; for who else, O tiger among men, could be the maker of the Mahābhārata? And who, save that Lord, could declare the manifold ordinances of dharma?
Let your great sacrifice proceed as you have resolved upon it; you have vowed the horse-sacrifice and have truly learned the law.
And the king, the son of Parikṣit, having heard this great narrative, then set about all the rites for the completion of the sacrifice.
This narrative of Nārāyaṇa I have told you, O king, which was declared of old by Nārada to my teacher, while the seers and the Pāṇḍavas listened, and Kṛṣṇa and Bhīṣma too.

For he is the supreme teacher, the lord of the worlds, the bearer of the earth, the treasury of tranquility and restraint, the treasury of scripture and discipline, the highest benefactor of the twice-born—may Hari, the friend of the gods, be your refuge.

He is the treasury of the greatest austerities, the vessel of mighty glory, the slayer of misfortune, the giver of refuge to the single-minded devotees, the bestower of fearlessness—may he who receives his portion of the sacrifice be the granter of your final goal.

Transcending the three qualities, upholder of the four and the five, the receiver of the fruit-share of works of charity and sacrifice—the unconquered one of surpassing strength ever ordains the goal that leads to himself for the virtuous sages.
To him, the witness of the worlds, the unborn Person, sun-hued, the lord's own goal, bow down again and again, O ascetics of single mind; even the lotus-born Brahmā bowed low before that seer.

For he is the womb of the worlds, the abode of immortality—subtle, ancient, unmoving, supreme; held high by the followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, ever known through intellect by those whose selves are restrained.

Janamejaya said: I have heard the greatness of that blessed Supreme Self—his birth in the house of Dharma in the twofold form of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, and the ancient origin of the earth-mass brought forth by the Great Boar.
How he is ordained in the path of action and in the path of withdrawal—just so have we heard it, O brāhmaṇa, as it was recounted by you, O sinless one.

And that great Horse-Head of Viṣṇu, the devourer of oblations to gods and ancestors, which you described before as being in the great ocean to the north-east—that too was seen by the blessed Brahmā, the supreme lord.
What was that form, unprecedented among beings of great power, brought forth of old by Hari, the upholder of the worlds, O best of the wise?
For when he beheld that holy Horse-Head, the foremost of the gods, unprecedented and of immeasurable might, what did Brahmā do, O sage?
Resolve this doubt of ours, O brāhmaṇa—a doubt born of ancient lore and fashioned by the Great Person—O you of supreme mind; we have been purified by you, O brāhmaṇa, as you recount this holy tale.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: I shall tell you the whole of it—the ancient tale equal in worth to the Veda, which the blessed Vyāsa sang to the king, the son of Dharma.
Having heard of the Horse-Headed form of the god whose intelligence is Hari, the king, in whom a doubt had arisen, pressed him with a question.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: That god bearing the horse's head whom Brahmā revealed—for what purpose did that body, fashioned by the god, come into being?
Vyāsa said: Whatever in this world is bound within a body, O lord of peoples, all of it is pervaded by the five elements, born of the Lord's intelligence.

For the Lord, creator of the world, is the sovereign Nārāyaṇa, the all-pervading; he is the inner Self of beings, the giver of boons, possessed of qualities and yet without qualities. Hear now of the unmanifest dissolution of beings, O best of kings.
When of old the earth had dissolved into the waters, and they into the single ocean; when the water, become fire, had dissolved into light, and the light into wind—
when the wind had dissolved into space, and space had followed into mind; when the manifest had dissolved into mind, and the manifest had passed into the unmanifest—
when the unmanifest had gone into the Person, and the Person too into the all-pervading—then there was only darkness, and nothing whatsoever could be discerned.
From that darkness arose Brahman, rooted in darkness, having truth for its essence; it, ending in the name of universal being, took on a body of the Person.
That is called Aniruddha; that they declare to be the Primordial Nature. It is to be known as the Unmanifest, composed of the three qualities, O best of kings.

The god Viṣvaksena, the lord Hari, accompanied by his power of wisdom, made his couch upon the waters and entered the yoga of sleep, pondering the creation of the world—a wondrous creation arising from manifold qualities.

As he pondered creation, the Great Principle, called the quality of the Self, arose; from it was born self-consciousness, and thence Brahmā of the four auspicious faces, the blessed Hiraṇyagarbha, grandfather of all the worlds.
Sprung then from Aniruddha upon a lotus, lotus-eyed and radiant, the eternal one sat upon the thousand-petalled flower.
In that wondrous expanse the lord beheld the worlds made wholly of water; abiding in goodness, the supreme one then brought forth the hosts of beings.
And even before that, upon the petal of the lotus, bright as the sun's rays, there were two drops of water made by Nārāyaṇa, surpassing in their qualities.
The blessed one, without beginning or end, the unfallen, beheld those two; one drop there was the color of honey, of lovely radiance.
That one, born of darkness, became Madhu by the command of Nārāyaṇa; the other drop, hard, born of passion, became Kaiṭabha.
Those two mighty foremost ones, endowed with the qualities of darkness and passion, maces in hand, rushed forth, making their way along the stalk of the lotus.
They beheld Brahmā of immeasurable splendor, seated upon the lotus, first bringing forth the four Vedas of lovely form.
Then those two foremost of demons, having taken bodily form, seeing the Vedas, suddenly seized them as Brahmā looked on.
Then those two foremost of the Dānavas, having seized the eternal Vedas, swiftly entered the netherworld in the great ocean to the north-east.
Then, when the Vedas had been stolen, Brahmā fell into despair; bereft of the Vedas, he spoke these words to the Lord.
"The Vedas are my supreme eye, the Vedas are my supreme strength; the Vedas are my supreme abode, the Vedas are my highest Brahman."

"All my Vedas have been carried off from here by force by the two Dānavas; bereft of the Vedas, my worlds have become wrapped in darkness. What can I do without the Vedas, intent as I am upon creating the worlds?"
"Alas, a great sorrow born of the loss of the Vedas has come upon me; it torments my heart, rending it open to fierce grief."
"Who shall today lift me, sunk in this ocean of grief, out of it, and bring back those lost Vedas? To whom shall I become dear?"
As Brahmā spoke thus, O best of kings, O foremost of the wise, the thought arose in him to praise Hari; then the lord, with hands joined in reverence, intoned a supreme hymn.
"Homage to you, O heart of Brahman; homage to you, my forefather; O first of the worlds, best of all beings, treasury of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, O all-pervading one."
"O inconceivable maker of the manifest and unmanifest, you who abide upon the path of well-being, devourer of the universe, inner Self of all beings, O you who are born of no womb!"
"I am born of your grace, to you the abode of the worlds, the self-existent. From you came my first birth, born of the mind, honored by the twice-born."
"My second birth of old was from the eye; and by your grace my third great birth was from speech."
"From you, too, came my fourth birth, born of the ear, O all-pervading one; and my birth from the nose is called the fifth, again from you."
"And my birth from the egg, the sixth, was fashioned by you; and this is my seventh birth, born of the lotus, O you of measureless splendor."
"In creation after creation I am your son, free of the three qualities, renowned, O lotus-eyed one, fashioned from the qualities of Primordial Nature."
"You are the very nature of the Lord, the self-existent, the supreme Person; by you was I fashioned, having the Vedas for my eye, surpassing all age."
"Those Vedas, my eye, have been stolen; I have become blind. Awake! Restore to me my two eyes. I am dear to you, and you are dear to me."
Thus praised, the blessed Person, facing in every direction, then forsook his sleep, intent upon the task of the Vedas, and by his sovereign power took on a second body.
With a body finely formed and fair as the moon, the lord then made the white horse's head, the abode of the Vedas.
His head became the heavens with their constellations and stars, and his long hairs became bright as the rays of the sun.
His two ears were the sky and the nether regions, his brow the earth that bears all beings; the holy Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī, the great rivers, were his two eyebrows.
His two eyes were the moon and the sun; his nose was held to be the twilight; the syllable Oṃ was his ritual consecration, and lightning was made his tongue.

His teeth, O king, were the ancestors known as the drinkers of soma; the world of cows and the world of Brahmā were the lips of the great one; and his neck, O king, was the Night of Time, surpassing in its qualities.
Having made this horse's head, wrapped about with manifold forms, the lord of all, the sovereign, vanished and entered the netherworld.
Having entered the netherworld once more and taken up the supreme yoga, he, assuming the disciplined tone of the science of recitation, sent forth the sound Oṃ.
That sound, resonant and far-reaching, all-pervading and tender, became hidden within the earth, arising from the qualities of all beings.
Then those two Asuras, having bound the Vedas by a pact and laid them down in the netherworld, rushed toward the place from which the sound came.
In that interval, O king, the god Hari, bearing the horse's head, seized all the Vedas that had been left in the netherworld and gave them back to Brahmā, then returned to his own nature.
Having set the horse's head in the great ocean to the north-east, the Horse-Headed one thus became the abode of the Vedas.
Then the two Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, seeing nothing, came rushing back to that place; and they beheld that the spot where the Vedas had been laid was empty.
Then, taking on their utmost speed, those two foremost of the strong rose up swiftly again from the abode of the waters and beheld that very Person, the lord, the first maker.
White, gleaming pure as the moon, abiding in the body of Aniruddha, of immeasurable valor, he had once more entered the yoga of sleep.
He lay upon a couch fashioned to his own measure, set above the waters, made rich with the coils of the serpent and wreathed about with garlands of flame.
Endowed with stainless goodness and of lovely radiance—seeing him, those two lords of the Dānavas burst into great laughter.
And those two, possessed by passion and darkness, said: "This is that white Person who lies here sunk in sleep."
"Surely it is by him that the Vedas were carried off from the netherworld. Whose is he? Who indeed is this? And why does he sleep in such luxury?"
Having uttered these words, the two roused Hari; and the supreme Person, awaking, perceived that they sought battle.
And gazing upon those two lords of the Asuras, he set his mind upon battle; then there arose a war between the two of them and Nārāyaṇa.
Those two, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, their bodies possessed by passion and darkness—the slayer of Madhu killed them, doing a service of recompense to Brahmā.
Then, by the slaying of those two and by the recovery of the Vedas, the supreme Person swiftly dispelled the grief of Brahmā.
Then Brahmā, his foes slain and honored by the restoring of the Vedas, attended by his retinue, created all the worlds, both the moving and the unmoving.
Having granted to the Grandfather the foremost wisdom for the bringing-forth of the worlds, the god Hari vanished thereupon into the very place from which he had come.
Having slain those two Dānavas and made the horse-headed body, Hari, for the sake of the dharma of activity, again established that very body.
Thus did this greatly blessed Hari become the Horse-Headed one; this ancient form, boon-granting and sovereign, has now been told.
For that brāhmaṇa who should ever hear this or hold it in memory—his learning would never come to ruin at any time.
Having propitiated by fierce austerity the god who bears the horse's head, the Pāñcāla attained the method, and Rāma along the path that was pointed out.
This tale of the Horse-Head, O king, has been recounted to you—the ancient story equal in worth to the Veda, about which you questioned me.
Whatever body the god might wish to make at any time in the ordering of his work, that body he would make, transforming his very self by himself.
This glorious one is the treasury of the Vedas; this indeed is the treasury of austerity; this is Yoga and Sāṃkhya and the foremost Brahman—Hari, the all-pervading lord.
The Vedas have Nārāyaṇa for their goal; the sacrifices have Nārāyaṇa for their essence; austerity has Nārāyaṇa as its highest aim; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme destination.
Truth has Nārāyaṇa for its highest ground; the cosmic order is of Nārāyaṇa's very essence. Dharma too is grounded in Nārāyaṇa, that dharma by which return to rebirth is hard to come by.
The dharma marked by active engagement in the world is likewise of Nārāyaṇa's essence. Scent itself, the foremost quality residing in earth, is taught to be of Nārāyaṇa's essence.
And the quality of the waters, O king—taste—is of Nārāyaṇa's essence; the quality of the luminous bodies—form—is taught to be of Nārāyaṇa's essence.
Touch as well, the quality of wind, is taught to be of Nārāyaṇa's essence; and sound, which arises from space, is likewise of Nārāyaṇa's essence.
And mind too, which has come to be from that, marked by the quality of the Unmanifest—time has Nārāyaṇa for its highest ground, as does the course of the heavenly lights.
Fame has Nārāyaṇa for its highest ground, and the goddesses Śrī and Lakṣmī. Sāṃkhya has Nārāyaṇa for its highest ground, and Yoga is of Nārāyaṇa's essence.
For those who hold the Puruṣa to be the cause, and likewise the primordial Nature as cause, and inherent disposition, and deeds, and fate as cause—
reckoned by these five causes, Hari is verily the final ground in every case—for those who seek to know the truth through reasonings that face in every direction.
The one Reality is the great yogin, Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Lord—of the worlds together with Brahmā, and of the great-souled seers,
of the followers of Sāṃkhya and the yogins, and of the ascetics who know the Self—the inmost thought of all these Keśava knows, but they do not know his.
Whoever in all the worlds perform rites for the gods and for the ancestors, and bestow gifts, and practice great austerity—
the refuge of them all is Viṣṇu, who abides in lordly ordinance; because he has made his dwelling in all beings, he is called Vāsudeva.

For he is the eternal, supreme Great Seer, of vast might, possessed of qualities yet called free of qualities; he swiftly enters into union with the qualities, as time, in its season, joins itself to the seasons.

None can find the going of this great-souled one, nor does anyone here perceive his coming. Only the great seers, made of knowledge and self-restrained, behold forever the Puruṣa who transcends the qualities.
Janamejaya said: Ah, the Lord Hari gives delight to all the single-minded devotees, and the Lord himself receives the worship offered according to ordinance.
But for those in the world whose fuel of karma is burnt away, who are free of merit and demerit, you have set forth the goal that is reached by the unbroken succession of the tradition.
By the fourth course they go to the Supreme Person; the single-minded ones indeed go to the highest abode.
Surely this dharma of single-minded devotion is the most excellent, dear to Nārāyaṇa, since its followers, without passing through the three other courses, go straight to the imperishable Hari.
Those brahmins who, abiding rightly, recite the Vedas together with the Upaniṣads, holding fast to ordinance, and those too who follow the dharma of ascetics—
I know that the goal of the single-minded men is more distinguished than theirs. By whom was this dharma declared—by a god, or by a seer?
And what is the practice of the single-minded ones, and when was it brought forth, O mighty one? Cut through this doubt of mine, for great is my curiosity.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When the armies of the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas had been drawn up for battle, and Arjuna was dispirited, it was sung by the Lord himself.
The coming and the going I have already related to you. For this dharma is profound, hard to comprehend for those who have not perfected the self.
It is measured by the Sāmaveda, established of old in the first age; it is upheld, O king, by the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself.
On this matter, O great king, the highly blessed Nārada, questioned by Pārtha amid the seers, while Kṛṣṇa and Bhīṣma listened—
and this was related by my teacher to me as well, O best of kings. Hear it now just as it was related there by Nārada.

When there was the mind-born birth of Brahmā, sprung from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa, O protector of the earth, then Nārāyaṇa himself, by that dharma, performed the rites for the gods and for the ancestors, O Bhārata.
The Phenapa seers received that dharma; the Vaikhānasas received this dharma from the Phenapas, and from the Vaikhānasas Soma received it; thereafter that god vanished once more.
When there was the second birth of Brahmā, the eye-born one, O king, then from the grandsire Soma he came to know this dharma, of Nārāyaṇa's essence, O king, and he gave it over to Rudra.
Then Rudra, established in yoga, of old in the Kṛta age, O king, taught this dharma to all the Vālakhilya seers; thereafter it vanished once more by the magic power of that god.
When there was the third, the great speech-born birth of Brahmā, then this dharma came forth from Nārāyaṇa himself, O king.
The seer named Suparṇa obtained it from the Supreme Person, through austerity well practiced, through self-control and discipline.
Suparṇa traversed this supreme dharma three times over; for that reason this observance is here called the Trisauparṇa.
This observance, recited in the recitation of the Ṛgveda, is indeed hard to fulfill; and this eternal dharma was obtained from Suparṇa as well.
By Vāyu, O best of bipeds, it was made known—Vāyu, the life-breath of the world; and from the presence of Vāyu it was obtained by the seers who eat the remnants of offerings.
From them the great Ocean obtained this supreme dharma; thereafter it vanished once more, gathered back into Nārāyaṇa.
When once again there was the ear-born creation of the great-souled Brahmā, O tiger among men, listen as I relate it.
The god Hari Nārāyaṇa himself, intent on creating the world, the Lord, brought to mind a Person who would make the creation of the world.
Then, as he was pondering, a Person issued from his two ears—Brahmā, the maker of creatures' generation; and the Lord of the world addressed him:
"Create all the creatures, my son, from the mouth and likewise from the feet; I shall ordain your welfare, your strength and your splendor, O you of good vows."
"And receive from me the dharma named Sātvata by name; by it, establish the whole Kṛta age according to ordinance."
Then Brahmā made obeisance to the god Harimedhas, and he took up the foremost dharma, together with its mystery and its summary, accompanied by the Āraṇyaka, sprung from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa.
Having then imparted to Brahmā of measureless splendor that dharma proper to the Kṛta age, known as action free of desire, he went beyond the darkness, where the Unmanifest abides.
Then the boon-granting god, the grandsire of the world of Brahmā, created at that time all the worlds entire, the unmoving and the moving.
Then at the beginning the auspicious Kṛta age set in; and thereupon the Sātvata dharma, pervading the worlds, stood established.
By that very first dharma, Brahmā, the maker of the worlds' outpouring, worshipped the Lord of gods, Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Master.
And for the sake of establishing dharma, he then taught it to Manu Svārociṣa, out of his desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Then Svārociṣa, undistracted of old, the lord and master of all worlds, himself taught it to his son Śaṅkhapada, O king.
Then Śaṅkhapada too taught it to his own son, born of his body, Sudharman the guardian of a quarter, O Bhārata; thereafter it vanished once more, when the Tretā age had come again.
At the nostril-born birth of Brahmā of old, O best of kings, the god Hari Nārāyaṇa himself, the lotus-eyed Lord, brought forth this dharma while Brahmā looked on.
Then the blessed Sanatkumāra learned it, O king; and from Sanatkumāra the lord of creatures Vīraṇa, at the dawn of the Kṛta age, O tiger of the Kurus, learned this dharma.
And Vīraṇa, having studied it, gave it to Manu Raucya; Raucya gave it to his son, the pure, devout, and wise Suvrata—
that is, he bestowed it upon the righteous guardian of the quarters named Kukṣi; thereafter it vanished once more, the dharma sprung from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa.
At the egg-born birth, again, of Brahmā whose source is Hari, this dharma arose once more from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa.
It was received by Brahmā, O king, and applied according to ordinance; and the sages named the Barhiṣads were instructed in it, O king.
And from the Barhiṣads, Hari—keeper of the observance of the eldest Sāman—passed it on to the twice-born one who had reached the end of the Sāmaveda, renowned by the name Jyeṣṭha.
And from Jyeṣṭha it passed on to King Avikampana; thereafter, O king, this dharma of the Lord Hari vanished away.
This which is the seventh birth of Brahmā, the lotus-born, O king—there this dharma was declared by Nārāyaṇa himself.
To the pure grandsire, the upholder of the worlds at the age's dawn, and the grandsire gave this dharma of old to Dakṣa.
Then Dakṣa bestowed it upon his eldest grandson, O best of kings; and from him Vivasvat received it, the eldest son of Savitṛ among the Ādityas.
And at the dawn of the Tretā age, again, Vivasvat gave it to Manu; and Manu, for the welfare of the worlds, gave it to his son Ikṣvāku.
And declared by Ikṣvāku, it stood pervading the worlds; and at the end of the cosmic dissolution it shall go back again to Nārāyaṇa, O king.
And the dharma which belongs to those who keep the vows, that, O best of kings, was related to you before in the Songs of Hari, set forth in summary form.
By Nārada this dharma was obtained, with its mystery and its summary, directly from the Lord of the world, from Nārāyaṇa, O king.
Thus this great dharma, primordial and eternal, O king, hard to comprehend and hard to practice, is upheld at all times by the Sātvatas.
By this knowledge of dharma, and by action well applied and joined with the dharma of non-injury, the Lord Hari is well pleased.
In one place his distribution is of a single array; somewhere it is called a twofold array; he is reckoned as a threefold array, and a fourfold array too is seen.
For Hari alone is the Knower of the field, free of self-claiming and without parts, and the living soul in all beings, transcending the qualities of the five elements.
He is the renowned mind too, O king, that sets the five senses in motion; he is the wise treasure-house of the worlds, he is the maker of the worlds' outpouring.
He is both the non-doer and the doer, the effect and the cause as well; just as he wishes, O king, so does the imperishable Person play.

This dharma of single-minded devotion has been recounted to you, O best of kings, by me through the grace of my teacher—hard to comprehend for those who have not perfected the self; for single-minded men, O king, are not to be found in great numbers.

If the world were thronged with the single-minded, O joy of the Kurus—men who do no harm, who know the Self, who delight in the welfare of all beings and have renounced action done with desire—then the Kṛta age would be regained.
Thus did the blessed Vyāsa, my teacher, O lord of peoples, the knower of dharma, the best of the twice-born, relate it to the Dharma King.
In the presence of the seers, O king, while Kṛṣṇa and Bhīṣma listened—and to him too, before, Nārada of mighty austerity had related it—
the supreme god, the highest Brahman, white, with the luster of the moon, the unfallen, to whom the single-minded ones go, wholly devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Janamejaya said: This dharma of many kinds, practiced by the awakened—why do other brahmins, established in their various observances, not follow it?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Three natures, O king, are fashioned within the bonds of the body—the sāttvika, the rājasa, and the tāmasa, O Bhārata.
Among those bound in the body, the best of men, O upholder of the Kuru line, is the sāttvika one, O tiger among men—he it is who would be resolved upon the goal of liberation.
And here too he discerns the Person abiding in Brahman; since liberation has Nārāyaṇa for its highest ground, the sāttvika one is verily so esteemed.
And he attains the object of his heart's desire, meditating on the Supreme Person—single-minded in devotion forever, wholly given over to Nārāyaṇa.
For all those wise ascetics who long for liberation, who have severed every craving, it is Hari who bears their welfare and their gain.
Whatever man, at his very birth, Madhusūdana looks upon, that man is to be known as endowed with sattva and assured of liberation.
This dharma practised with single-minded devotion is equal in worth to Sāṃkhya and Yoga; through it men attain the supreme goal, the liberation whose very self is Nārāyaṇa.
The man whom Nārāyaṇa beholds is awakened to truth; but one awakened by his own will alone, O king, is not so awakened.

The rājasic and tāmasic natures are remembered to be intermingled; and the man whose self is composed of these, O lord of peoples, born marked by the signs of worldly engagement, Hari himself does not regard.
It is Brahmā, the grandsire of the worlds, who looks upon such a man at his birth—the mortal flooded over by rajas and tamas.
True, the gods and the sages abide in sattva, O best of kings; yet, lacking that subtle sattva, they are accordingly remembered as belonging to the modified order.
Janamejaya said: How can a man of the modified order attain the Supreme Person?
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Joined to the most subtle sattva, joined to the three syllables, the man, ceasing from action, attains that Person, the twenty-fifth principle.

Thus Sāṃkhya and Yoga are one, and so too the Veda and the Āraṇyaka; these, together with the Pañcarātra, are declared to be limbs of one another. This is the dharma of the single-minded devotees, whose supreme Self is Nārāyaṇa.
As the floods of water gone forth from the ocean enter again, O king, that very ocean, so the great floods of knowledge enter again into Nārāyaṇa.
This Sātvata dharma has been told to you, O kinsman of the Yadus; observe it as is fitting, if you are able, O descendant of Bharata.
For thus did the greatly blessed Nārada declare to my teacher the imperishable, single-minded goal of the white-robed ascetics.
And Vyāsa, out of affection, recounted it to the wise son of Dharma; that very teaching, descended from my teacher, I have now set forth to you.
Hard to follow, indeed, is this dharma, O best of kings; even as you do, so others do not embrace it, for they are bewildered.
For Kṛṣṇa alone is the creator of the worlds, their bewilderer, and their destroyer too, and their very cause, O lord of peoples.
Janamejaya said: Sāṃkhya, Yoga, the Pañcarātra, and the Veda with its Āraṇyaka—these bodies of knowledge, O brahmin sage, are current among the worlds.
Do these rest upon a single foundation, or upon separate foundations, O sage? Being asked by me, declare it, and their origin in due order.

Vaiśaṃpāyana said: To that great sage, knowing many things, supreme and most noble, the self-possessed son whom Gandhavatī bore to Parāśara on the island—to him, dispeller of the darkness of ignorance, be salutation.

They declare him the sixth, counting from the Grandsire, the great sage endowed with the glory of the seers, born of a portion of Nārāyaṇa, the only son, Dvaipāyana, the great treasure-house of the Veda.

Him, in the primal ages, did Nārāyaṇa of mighty majesty, the great treasure-house of the Brahman, create for the sake of a son—the unborn, the ancient one of lofty splendour, brought forth the great-souled Vyāsa.
Janamejaya said: By you yourself was his lineage told before, O best of the twice-born: Śakti was the son of Vasiṣṭha, and Parāśara the son of Śakti.
The heir of Parāśara was the sage Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana; yet now you speak of this same one as the son of Nārāyaṇa.
What, then, is the earlier birth of Vyāsa of measureless splendour? Tell me, O man of excellent mind, of his birth that sprang from Nārāyaṇa.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: While my teacher, most righteous, a treasury of austerity, fixed upon knowledge, longing to understand the meanings of the Vedas, was dwelling at the foot of the Himālaya—
having composed the tale of the Bhārata, the wise one was wearied with austerity; and we, O king, intent upon it, rendered him our devoted service in those days.
Sumantu, and Jaimini, and Paila of firm vows, I myself the fourth disciple, and Śuka, the son of Vyāsa—
surrounded by these five excellent disciples, Vyāsa shone at the foot of the Himālaya like the Lord of beings amid his attendant spirits.
As he recited the Vedas together with their auxiliaries, and the meanings of the Bhārata in every part, we, attentive, waited upon him, the single-minded, the self-controlled.
Then, in the course of some discourse, that best of the twice-born was asked by us about the meanings of the Vedas, the meanings of the Bhārata, and his birth from Nārāyaṇa.
He, the knower of truth, having first spoken of the meanings of the Vedas and of the Bhārata, then set about to relate this birth of his from Nārāyaṇa.
Hear this excellent tale, supreme, belonging to the seers, arising in primal time, O brahmins, attained by me through austerity.
When the time of the creation of creatures had come, in the seventh, the birth from the lotus, Nārāyaṇa, the great yogin, free of good and evil alike—
created from his navel a son, Brahmā of boundless radiance; thereupon that one came forth, and to him he spoke these words:
"You are born from my navel, the lord and maker of the creation of creatures; create manifold beings, O Brahman, both the dull and the wise."
Thus addressed, he turned away, his mind troubled with anxious thought; and bowing to the boon-granting god, he said to Hari, the Lord:
"What power have I, O Lord of the gods, to create creatures? Homage be to you. I am without the requisite wisdom, O god; ordain what is to follow."
Thus addressed, the Blessed One then vanished from sight, and the Lord of the gods, the foremost of the wise, called to mind Buddhi, the faculty of intellect.
Then Buddhi, having taken visible form, presented herself before the Lord Hari; and he, the unattached, himself joined her by his power of yoga.
To that Buddhi, established in the yoga of sovereign power, mighty and true, the imperishable Lord, the god, spoke these words:
"Enter into Brahmā, for the accomplishing of the world's creation." Then, commanded by the Lord, Buddhi swiftly entered into him.
Then Hari beheld him once more, now joined with Buddhi, and again spoke to him this word: "Create these manifold beings."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished there itself, and in a single moment attained his own abode, named after the gods.
And reaching that very nature, Brahmā came to be one with it; thereupon, it is said, another thought arose within him again.

All these creatures were created by Brahmā the supreme one, thronged with hosts of Daityas, Dānavas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas; and this earth, the bearer of wealth, was born, pressed down by the burden and made to suffer.
